units.la: Duo mihi proposui hoc in opere: unum, ut animum meum exuerem opinionibus philosophicis, quae non possunt non adhaerescere iis, qui vulgarium philosophorum scripta, sepositis Scripturis sacris, euoluunt, eaq; sibi proponunt canonem:alterum, ut Biblia sacra in locos communes ita redigerem, ut inde systema methodicum conficerem, pandectasq; [?] illas sacras iuuentuti eo familiariores redderem. Cùm vero primam [?] hâc in re glaciem fregerim, veniam mihi dari peto. Satis mihi fuerit, si hoc assecutus fuero, ut praeceptores & discipuli tandem aliquando intelligant, à Bibliis sacris esse incipiendum, inque illis desinendum. Ita enim fiet, ut non solùm verâ pietate imbuant animos, sed etiam hanc Encyclopadiam Biblicam reddant multò locupletiorem præceptis, exemplis & commentarijs. Ego satis habui, lineas ducere in opere hoc admirando, cuisemper aliquid potest addi ex fonte Scripturarum inex-hausto.
units.tr: I set myself two aims in this work. The first was to free my mind from philosophical opinions, which cannot fail to cling to those who read through the writings of the common philosophers, setting the holy Scriptures aside and taking those writings as their rule. The second was to reduce the holy Bible to commonplaces, so that I might construct from it a methodical system and make those sacred compendia more familiar to young people. Since I have broken the first ice in this matter, I ask to be pardoned. It will be enough for me if I have achieved this much: that teachers and pupils may at last come to understand that one must begin with the holy Bible and end with it. For in this way they will not only imbue minds with true piety, but will also make this Biblical Encyclopaedia far richer in precepts, examples and commentaries. I have been content to draw the outlines in this admirable work, to which something can always be added from the inexhaustible fountain of the Scriptures.

units.la: EA est sacrarum literarum perfectio, lector benevole, ut, praeterquam quòd nos possunt sapientes reddere ad salutem 2. Tim.3.15. ea quoq; contineant, quae pertinent ad sublimiorem eruditionem philosophicam, medicam, & iuridicam. Intellexerunt hoc superiori aevo viri Christianissimi, Franciscus Valesius Hispanus, Leuinus Lemnius Belga, Lambertus Danæus Gallus, Cunradus Heresbachius Germanus. E quibus Franciscus Valesius, medicus &philosophus, aggressus est scribere de sacra philosophia, ea methodo, ut ex sacris Bibliis excerperet ea loca, quæ reconditam philosophiæ doctrinam continent. Hunc suum laborem tali ornauit programmate: Hactenus scripsi ad opinionem, nunc scribam ad veritatem. Quasi dicat, solam Scripturam sacram esse canonem veritatis in philosophia. Tametsi enim Scripturæ sacrę non sunt à Deo datæ, vt discamus inde philosophari: nihil tamen impedit, quo minus inde excerpamus semina & principia bonarum artium, quæ hinc inde sunt ibi sparsa. Leuinus Lemnius scripsit dilucidam explicationem similitudinum ac parabolarum, quæ in Bibliis ex herbis atque arboribus desumuntur: in quâ [illegible, ~2 letters] ratione singula loca explanat, quibus prophetæ, obseruatâ stirpium naturâ, conciones suas illustrant, diuinaque oracula fulciunt. Lambertus Danæus edidit Physi-
units.tr: This is the perfection of Holy Scripture, kind reader: besides making us wise unto salvation (2 Tim. 3.15), it also contains what pertains to the higher learning of philosophy, medicine and law. Men most Christian in the earlier age recognised this: Francisco Valesio of Spain, Levinus Lemnius of Belgium, Lambert Daneau of France, Cunrad Heresbach of Germany. Of these, Francisco Valesio, a physician and philosopher, set himself to write on sacred philosophy, by a method of gathering from the Holy Bible those passages which contain the hidden doctrine of philosophy. He adorned this work of his with such a motto: Hitherto I have written according to opinion; now I shall write according to truth. As if to say that Holy Scripture alone is the rule of truth in philosophy. For although the Holy Scriptures were not given by God so that we might learn philosophy from them, nothing nevertheless prevents us from gathering from them the seeds and principles of the good arts, which lie scattered here and there within them. Levinus Lemnius wrote a clear explanation of the similitudes and parables which the Bible draws from herbs and trees; in it he explains, by a method [illegible], the individual passages by which the prophets, having observed the nature of plants, illustrate their sermons and support their divine oracles. Lambert Daneau published Physi-

units.la: cam, Ethicam, & Politicam Christianam : vbi sacram Scripturam sibi proposuit Lydium veritatis lapidem. Cunradus Heresbachius publicauit epitomen iurisprudetię Christianæ, in quâ leges Moysis elegantissimo ordine digessit. Tantorum virorum vestigia secuti sunt nostrâ ætate Otho Casmannus in Ethicâ & Oeconomicâ theosophicâ; Iohannes Althusius in ciuili conuersatione; Grosius in compendio medicinę ex S. literis deprompto ; & Conradus Aslacus Danus, qui scripsit Physicam & Ethicam Mosaicam. His verò omnibus longè acutiùs vidit author præfationis, quæ præfixa est Latinæ versioni Bibliorum Tiguri editorum. Ille siquidem prolixè ac erudite demonstrat, in sacrorum Bibliorum codice, tanquam in cornu aliquo copiæ, contineri semina universæ philosophiæ. Quod ipsum & ego planum feci superiori anno 1614. in dedicatione & præfatione methodi meæ theologicæ: vbi inter alia recepi, me, ad vmbilicum perductâ ista methodo, cocinnaturum Encyclopædiam Biblicam seu, quod idem est, Triumphum Bibliorum, adeoque philosophiæ, iurisprudentiæ & medicinæ sacræ, & sacrosanctæ theologiæ.
units.tr: cs, Ethics and Christian Politics, where he set Holy Scripture before himself as the Lydian touchstone of truth. Cunrad Heresbach published an epitome of Christian jurisprudence, in which he arranged the laws of Moses in a most elegant order. Following in the footsteps of such great men in our own age came Otho Casmann in his theosophical Ethics and Economics; Johannes Althusius in civil conversation; Grosius in a compendium of medicine drawn from the Sacred Writings; and Conrad Aslak of Denmark, who wrote on Mosaic Physics and Ethics. Yet the author of the preface prefixed to the Latin version of the Bible published at Zurich saw far more keenly than all these men. For he demonstrates at length and learnedly that in the codex of the Sacred Bibles, as in some horn of plenty, the seeds of all philosophy are contained. I myself made this plain in the year 1614, in the dedication and preface of my Theological Method, where, among other things, I undertook that, once this method had been carried to its completion, I would compose a Biblical Encyclopaedia, or what is the same thing, The Triumph of the Bibles, and so of sacred philosophy, jurisprudence and medicine, and of most holy theology.

units.la: Hoc jam nunc Deo duce præsto, & ita præsto, vt, quidquid est rerum philosophicarum, iuridicarum, medicarum & theologicarum in diuinissimo Scripturæ canone, certâ methodo ad facultatum & disciplinarum capita & systemata, vel systematum partes, vel denique variorum systematum combinationes reuocem. Quod vt intelligi possit facilius, ita statuere oportet, disciplinam siue scientiam, homine dignam, aut esse integrum aliquod systema, aut syftematis partem,aut denique plurium systematum farraginem. Sic verbi gratiaPhysica est systema integrum: Cosmologia est systematis physici pars : Magia naturalis est farrago physices & mathefeos. Unde liquet, omnem , quæ cum rectâ ratione suscipitur, tractationem, esse tripartitam. Quod quidem hoc loco præterire minimè oportuit: ne varietas titulorū inhoc opere hanc forte alicui ingereret opinionem, innumerabiles esse philosophici circuli disciplinas. Oportet hic accurate discernere inter disciplinam, & partem disciplinæ: & rursus inter disciplinam , & plurium disciplinarum combinationem. Sic itaque habeas velim. Quidquid in hoc opere occurrit,aut est disciplina integrè[?] tractata, aut pars disciplinæ, aut denique duarum vel plurium disciplinarum farrago. In quibus tradendis ita sum versatus, ut ex sacris literis desumpserim vel res, vel methodum, vel exempla: & rursum res, vel αὐτολεξεὶ[?], vel per bonam consequentiam. Tuum est, lector Christiane, hunc nostrum laborem benigne interpretari, atque ita apud animum statuere tuum, optimum philosophandi, genus esse, si quis ex Bibliis petat ἱμα ἢ ποδήρη[?], vestem & purpuram, laudatissimi huius studij. Ita enim fit, ut iuventus reddat sibi familiarem hunc sacratissimum codicem, & coniungat pietatem cum eruditione, & ab his certissimis initijs assurgat ad apicem philosophiæ sobriæ & solidæ.
units.tr: This work is now ready, with God as my guide, and it is ready in such a way that whatever is philosophical, juridical, medical and theological in the most divine canon of Scripture I may bring back, by a fixed method, to the heads and systems of the faculties and disciplines, or to the parts of systems, or finally to combinations of various systems. To make this easier to understand, we must lay down that a discipline or science worthy of a human being is either a complete system, or a part of a system, or finally a mixture of several systems. Thus, for example, Physics is a complete system; Cosmology is a part of the physical system; Natural magic is a mixture of physics and mathematics. From this it is clear that every treatment undertaken with right reason is threefold. This ought not to be passed over here, lest the variety of titles in this work give anyone the impression that there are countless disciplines in the philosophical circle. Here one must carefully distinguish between a discipline and a part of a discipline, and again between a discipline and a combination of several disciplines. So I would have you understand it thus. Whatever occurs in this work is either a discipline treated as a whole, or a part of a discipline, or finally a mixture of two or more disciplines. In setting these out I have so dealt with them that I have drawn from the Sacred Writings either the matters, or the method, or the examples; and again the matters either word for word [αὐτολεξεί], or by good inference. It is for you, Christian reader, to interpret this my labour kindly, and so to settle it in your mind that the best kind of philosophising is this, if anyone seeks from the Bible garments and purple [ἱμάτιον ἢ ποδήρη] of this most praiseworthy study. For in this way young people will make this most sacred book familiar to themselves, will join piety with learning, and from these most certain beginnings will rise to the summit of sober and solid philosophy.

units.la: De iurisprudentia & medicina idem est iudicium. Sed quid ego iuuentutem commemoro? Senes philosophi, iurisconsulti & medici portum suae sapientiae constituunt sacram Scripturam. Quin itaque imitamur Alexandrum Magnum, qui tanto erga Homeri Iliada flagrauit amore, ut illam velut ἐφόδιον τῆς ἀρετῆς[?] in castris circumferre, noctuque loco puluinaris capiti suo substernere sit solitus: & Platonem, qui Sophronem suum noctu sub culcitra collocauit, & iam moribundus capiti suo subiectum habuit: deniq; Scipionem Africanum, qui Xenophontem de παιδείας[?] Cyri nunquam e manibus deposuit. Hos, inquam, ethnicos cur non imitamur in sanctiore & utiliore studio, lectione nimirum Scripturae sacrae, quae sola est
units.tr: The same judgement holds for jurisprudence and medicine. But why do I mention young people? Philosophers, lawyers and physicians in their old age set up Holy Scripture as the harbour of their wisdom. Why then do we not imitate Alexander the Great, who burned with such love for Homer's Iliad that he was accustomed to carry it about in his camp as a provision of virtue [ἐφόδιον τῆς ἀρετῆς], and at night to place it under his head in place of a pillow; and Plato, who placed his Sophron under his blanket at night, and when already dying kept it under his head; and finally Scipio Africanus, who never put down Xenophon's Education of Cyrus [παιδείας] from his hands? Why, I say, do we not imitate these heathens in a holier and more useful study, namely the reading of Holy Scripture, which alone is

units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Sed quid ago? Valde metuo, ne hoc seculo arrogante & proteruo idem accidat, quod post Italiæ vastitatem à Gothis Vandalisq; affectam accidisse, in historijs legimus. Religiosi tū fuerunt attentiores in legedis mœdijs, quàm in euangeliis: nobiles matronę cum maiore plausu audiuerunt lyram Flacci, quàm præcepta Salomonis: exercitatiores fuerunt in artibus Nasonis, quàm in lectione Pauli: illud Damaso pontifici conqueritur Hieronymus, hoc abbati Salmoni Victor Massiliensis.
units.tr: But what am I doing? I greatly fear that in this arrogant and insolent age the same thing will happen that we read in histories happened after the devastation of Italy by the Goths and Vandals. Then the pious were more attentive to the comedies of the stage than to the Gospels; noble matrons listened with greater applause to the lyre of Flaccus than to the precepts of Solomon; they were more skilled in the arts of Naso than in the reading of Paul. Jerome complained of this to Pope Damasus; Victor of Marseilles complained of it to the abbot Salmon.

units.la: PRÆCOGNITA.
units.tr: PRÆCOGNITA.

units.la: I. PRÆCOGNITA sunt axiomata, quibus praeparatur animus ad faciliorem rei tractationem. Duo sunt modi docendi, abruptus & praeparans. Modus docendi abruptus est, quando ad ipsam rem venitur absque praevia praeparatione. Ita Moses Gen.1. ex abrupto incipit telam historiae suae. Modus docendi praeparans est, quando aliquid dicitur in antecessum, ut via muniatur sequenti tractationi. Sic Lucas auspicatur suum euangelium Luc.1. & Paulus suam disputationem Act. 17. verf. 22. 23. Ad hunc posteriorem docendi discendique modum pertinent Praecognita, hoc est, eiusmodi theoremata, quae praemittuntur cognitionem alicuius rei, ut illa fiat facilior. Huiusmodi praecognita sunt varia. Et primo quidem sunt praecognita integri alicuius systematis: unde tot sunt praecognita, quot sunt facultates & artes: videlicet praecognita theologica, iuridica, medica, philosophica; & haec rursus metaphysica, physica, logica &c. Deinde sunt praecognita alicuius loci communis. Ita si quis instituat seorsim agere de iustitia, oportet ut tradat praecognita de ethica, de affectibus, de virtute in genere. Similiter si differendum sit de liberatione hominis, praemittenda sunt praecognita de hominis miseria. Postremo sunt praecognita disputationum, quae sumuntur ex parte subiecti & praedicati. e.g. si disputanda sit quaestio, An Petrus fuerit episcopus Romae, ex parte subiecti praecognoscendum est, quod Petrus fuerit apostolus Iudaeorum; ex parte praedicati, quid sit episcopum agere. Nobis hoc loco propositum est agere de Praecognitis facultatum.
units.tr: I. Prolegomena are axioms by which the mind is prepared for an easier treatment of a subject. There are two modes of teaching: the abrupt and the preparatory. The abrupt mode of teaching is when one comes to the subject itself without any previous preparation. So Moses in Gen. 1 begins the web of his history abruptly. The preparatory mode of teaching is when something is said in advance, so that the way is paved for the following treatment. So Luke begins his Gospel in Luke 1, and Paul begins his disputation in Acts 17, verses 22 and 23. To this latter mode of teaching and learning belong the Prolegomena, that is, those theorems which are set out before knowledge of a thing, so that it may be made easier. There are various kinds of prolegomena. First, there are prolegomena of a whole system: hence there are as many prolegomena as there are faculties and arts, namely theological, legal, medical and philosophical prolegomena, and these again metaphysical, physical, logical and so on. Next, there are prolegomena of a common topic. Thus, if someone undertakes to treat justice separately, he must set out prolegomena on ethics, on the affections and on virtue in general. Similarly, if one is to discuss the liberation of man, prolegomena on man's misery must be put first. Lastly, there are prolegomena of disputations, which are drawn from the side of the subject and of the predicate. For example, if the question is to be disputed, Whether Peter was bishop of Rome, then on the side of the subject it must be known beforehand that Peter was apostle of the Jews; on the side of the predicate, what it is to act as bishop. For our present purpose, we propose to treat the prolegomena of the faculties.

units.la: II. Praecognita facultatum & disciplinarum duabus continentur partibus, quarum prima naturam, altera studium facultatis & artis alicuius explicat. Nam hæc duo præsupponuntur & præexiguntur, si quis ad frugalem alicuius facultatis & systematis notitiam pervenire desideret.
units.tr: II. The prolegomena of the faculties and disciplines are contained in two parts, of which the first explains the nature of a faculty or art, and the second the study of a faculty or art. For these two things are presupposed and required beforehand, if anyone wishes to attain a sound knowledge of some faculty and system.

units.la: III. Natura facultatis & artis alicuius est eius propria affectio, consistens in conuenientia & differentia. Discuntur autem ista duo, si attendatur ad facultatis & artis principia, genus habitus, & sedem, quam ista facultas & ars obtinet. De principiis tractat Archelogia, de habitibus Hexilogia, de fede Technologia.
units.tr: III. The nature of a faculty or art is its proper affection, consisting in agreement and difference. These two things are learned if one attends to the principles of the faculty or art, the genus of its habit, and the seat which this faculty or art occupies. The principles are treated by Archelogia, the habits by Hexilogia, the seat by Technologia.

units.la: IV. Studium facultatis & artis est, quo facultas & ars discitur, quantum satis est. Doctrinaenarrans rationem istius studij appellatur Didactica.
units.tr: IV. The study of a faculty or art is that by which the faculty or art is learned, as far as is sufficient. The doctrine which sets out the method of this study is called Didactica.

units.la: Atque hæ sunt quatuor partes præcognitorum, quæ in omnibus facultatibus & artibus obseruari debent. Est enim v.g. Archelogia theologica, philosophica, iuridica &c. Similiter hexilogia, technologia & didactica theologica, philosophica, &c. Nos persequemur illa, quæ omnibus facultatibus & artibus sunt communia.
units.tr: These are the four parts of the prolegomena, which ought to be observed in all faculties and arts. For there is, for example, a theological, philosophical, legal and so on Archelogia. Similarly there are theological, philosophical and other Hexilogia, Technologia and Didactica. We shall pursue those things which are common to all faculties and arts.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: ARCHELOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED ARCHELOGIA

units.la: I. ARchelogia sacra est prima pars præcognitorum, monstrans rationem colligendi principia cuiusque facultatis, idque adminiculo literarum. Huiusmodi archelogiam tradit Moses Exod. 20. vbi promulgat decalogum, qui complectitur principia legum, quæ deinceps recitantur in Exodo.
units.tr: I. Sacred Archelogia is the first part of the prolegomena, showing the method of gathering the principles of each faculty, and this with the help of letters. Moses hands down this kind of archelogy in Exod. 20, where he promulgates the decalogue, which comprises the principles of the laws that are afterwards recited in Exodus.

units.la: II. Principia alicuius facultatis sunt fundamenta, quibus illa nititur.
units.tr: II. The principles of a faculty are the foundations on which it rests.

units.la: III. Principia ista sunt essendi vel cognoscendi. Hæc diuisio sumta est ex ipsa rei natura, & occurrit Exod. 20. vbi verf. 1. & 2. est principium essendi, Deus: verf. 3. & seqq. vsque ad 18. sunt principia cogno-scendi.
units.tr: III. These principles are of being or of knowing. This division is taken from the very nature of the thing, and it occurs in Exod. 20, where in verses 1 and 2 the principle of being is God, and in verse 3 and following, up to 18, are the principles of knowing.

units.la: IV. Principia essendi alicuius facultatis sunt quatuor causæ, quibus facultas suam debet originem. Ex his causis duæ sunt externæ, efficiens & finis; & totidem internæ, materia & forma. Efficiens causa facultatis alicuius est partim prima, partim secunda. Prima est Deus, qui per Spiritum suum bonum dat sermonem sapientiæ, sermonem notitiæ, donum sanationum, operationem virtutum, prophetiam, discretionem spiritum, genera linguarum, interpretationem linguarum. 1.Cor.12. vers.6.7.8.9.10. Efficiens fecunda est triplex. I. Inventrix: homo, heroico intellectus agentis lumine præditus. Gen. 4. vers.2.20.21.22. II. Impulsiva: ut est, in homine quidem cognitio defectuum naturæ humanæ, & naturale sciendi desiderium omnibus insitum, in rebus autem sciendis & agendis eximia pulchritudo, dignitas, certitudo, iucunditas, & utilitas. III. Instrumentalis: ut sunt quatuor illa inveniendarum, constituendarum, & examinandarum facultatum, methodico systematice comprehensarum & naturæ lumine notarum, instrumenta: Sensus, Observatio, Experientia, & Inductio: e quibus Sensus primò facit suum officium, habetque vim scientiæ: Observatio est plurium sensionum collectio: Experientia est plurium observationum comprehensio: Inductio est plurium experientiarum collectio. Quatuor hæc instrumenta quomodo coniunxerit Salomon, vide Ecclesiastis 1. vers. 2.12.13.14.15.16.17. & cap. 2. vers. 2. & seqq. & cap. 3. per totum: vbi Salomon dicit, se vidisse applicasse animum ad disquirendum, cognovisse (scilicet experiundo) & tandem dixisse cum animo suo, ecce ista omnia sunt vanitas. Eundem in modum omnia dogmata & axiomata artium sunt constituta, e.g. homo vidit, magnetem trahere ferrum: & hoc aliquoties observavit: & observando expertus est: & deniq; post multiplice experientia ita collegit inducendo, Magnes trahit ferrum in Germania, India, Persia, &c. Ergo o-mnis magnes trahit ferrum. Ex his efficitur, quatuor ista instrumenta aureis literis præscribenda esse scholiis liberalibus ob eximiam, quam nobis adferunt, utilitatem, etiam in theologicis. Nam & ibi locum habet ista catena, iuxta illud Psaltis, Gustate & videte, quam suauis sit Dominus, Psal. 34: verf. 9. Sequitur finis, qui propositus est facultatibus & artibus ingenuis. Et primo quidem finis generalis, ad quem collineare debent omnes facultates & artes, est triplex: videlicet purgatio, illuminatio, & vnio. Qua de re insignis est locus apud Dionysium Carthusianum de fonte lucis, vbi ait: Triplex est via salubris. Prima est via purgatiua: secunda, illuminatiua: tertia, unitiua seu perfectiua. Purgatio est, qua intellectus, affectus, & lingua liberantur sordibus illis, quibus inquinantur. Illuminatio est, qua lumen infunditur intellectui liberato a ford bus, indeque transfunditur in voluntatem & linguam. Vnio est, qua homo iam purgatus & illuminatus coniungitur cum Deo, Patre illo luminis. Atque haec est scala illa finium, per quam in omnibus artibus debemus ascendere: quatenus nempe hoc debemus agere, vt a sordibus & defectibus nostris liberati purgemur, purgati illuminemur, illuminati vniamur Deo. Hoc sibi vult ista solennis formula qua Deus compellat populum suum: Sancti estote, quia ego sanctus sum. Leuit. 11. verf. 43. 44. Huic fini generali adiungi debet Specialis siue proprius, quem habet aliqua facultas & ars, quaeque proinde cum illa reciprocatur. Sic finis proprius Grammaticae est bene loqui, Arithmeticae bene numerare &c. Materia facultatis alicuius sunt termini, praecepta definitionum & distributionum, regulae, & commentaria, quibus illa absoluitur. Ex his terminis sunt notiones simplices: definitiones & distributiones, notionum simplicium explicatio: regula, definitionum & distributionum consectaria: commentarij, terminorum, praeceptorum, & regularum uberior explicatio, & ad usum ap-plicatio. Forma facultatis alicuius est pulcherrimus ordo, quo singulae partes harmonice inter se cohaerent, sibique invicem respondent.
units.tr: IV. The principles of being of a faculty are the four causes to which the faculty owes its origin. Of these causes two are external, efficient and final; and as many are internal, matter and form. The efficient cause of a faculty is partly first, partly secondary. The first is God, who through his Spirit gives to one "the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, gifts of healing, the working of miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, various kinds of tongues, the interpretation of tongues," 1 Cor. 12, verses 6 to 10. The secondary efficient cause is threefold. (I.) The inventor: man, endowed with the light of the active intellect. Gen. 4, verses 2, 20, 21, 22. (II.) The impelling cause: namely, in man, the knowledge of the defects of human nature and the natural desire to know which is implanted in all; and, in the things to be known and done, their singular beauty, dignity, certainty, pleasantness and usefulness. (III.) The instrumental cause: such are the four instruments of discovering, establishing and examining the faculties, which are comprehended methodically and systematically and known by the light of nature: sense, observation, experience and induction. Of these, sense first performs its office and has the force of knowledge; observation is the collection of several sensations; experience is the comprehension of several observations; induction is the gathering of several experiences. For how Solomon joined these four instruments, see Ecclesiastes 1, verses 2, 12 to 17, and chapter 2, verse 2 and following, and chapter 3 throughout, where Solomon says that he had seen, applied his mind to inquire, come to know (by experimenting, of course), and at last said to his own mind, behold, all these things are vanity. In the same way all the dogmas and axioms of the arts have been established. For example, a man saw that a magnet draws iron; he observed this several times; by observing he made trial; and finally, after many experiences, he so gathered by induction: the magnet draws iron in Germany, India, Persia, and so on. Therefore every magnet draws iron. From this it follows that these four instruments ought to be written in letters of gold in the liberal schools, on account of the singular usefulness they bring us, even in theological matters. For this chain holds there too, according to that saying of the Psalmist, Taste and see how gracious the Lord is, Ps. 34, verse 9. Next comes the end, which is set before the liberal faculties and arts. First, the general end, to which all faculties and arts ought to aim, is threefold: namely purgation, illumination and union. On this matter there is a notable passage in Denys the Carthusian, On the Fountain of Light, where he says: The way of salvation is threefold. The first is the purgative way, the second the illuminative, the third the unitive or perfective. Purgation is that by which the intellect, the affections and the tongue are freed from those filths by which they are defiled. Illumination is that by which light is poured into the intellect, freed from filths, and thence passed over into the will and the tongue. Union is that by which man, now purged and illumined, is joined with God, the Father of light. And this is that ladder of ends by which we ought to ascend in all the arts: namely, that we should so act that, freed from our filths and defects, we may be purged, purged we may be illumined, and illumined we may be united to God. This is what that solemn formula means by which God addresses his people: Be holy, for I am holy, Lev. 11, verses 43 and 44. To this general end must be added the special, or proper, end, which any faculty and art has, and which is therefore reciprocal with it. Thus the proper end of grammar is to speak well, of arithmetic to count well, and so on. The matter of a faculty consists of its terms, the precepts of definitions and divisions, the rules, and the commentaries by which it is completed. Of these, the terms are simple notions; definitions and divisions are the explanation of simple notions; the rule is the corollary of definitions and divisions; the commentaries are a fuller explanation of terms, precepts and rules, and their application to use. The form of a faculty is the most beautiful order by which the individual parts cohere harmoniously with one another and correspond to each other.

units.la: V. Principia cognoscendi alicuius facultatis sunt axiomata, à quibus pendet accurata istius facultatis cognitio. Huiusmodi axiomata apud theologos continentur in quinque capitibus Catecheticis, apud ICtos in regulis iuris, apud medicos in aphorismis Hippocratis, apud Chymicos in tabulâ smaragdinâ Hermetis, apud mathematicos in elementis Euclidis. Horum principiorum necessitas est longè maxima. Sunt enim veluti radices, ex quibus propagines omnium artiū deducuntur: norma, secundum quas discursus dirigitur: elementa, ex quibus omnia primò componuntur, & in quæ ultimò resoluuntur. Unde scitè appellantur prima veritates, dignitates, axiomata confessa &c.
units.tr: V. The principles of knowing a faculty are the axioms on which accurate knowledge of that faculty depends. Among theologians such axioms are contained in the five catechetical heads; among the jurists, in the rules of law; among physicians, in the aphorisms of Hippocrates; among the chemists, in the Emerald Tablet of Hermes; among mathematicians, in the Elements of Euclid. The necessity of these principles is by far the greatest. For they are like roots, from which the shoots of all the arts are derived; the norm according to which reasoning is directed; and the elements out of which everything is first composed and into which it is finally resolved. Hence they are aptly called first truths, dignities, acknowledged axioms, and so on.

units.la: VI. In his principiis considerare oportet fontes, proprietates, & diuisiones.
units.tr: VI. In these principles we must consider their sources, properties, and divisions.

units.la: VII. Fontes principiorum cognoscendi sunt, e quibus illa deriuantur. Suntque duo: putà liber naturæ, & liber Scripturæ. Nam quidquid scimus, aut ex opificio mundi per lumen naturæ nobis insitum, aut ex verbo Dei per lumen gratiæ nobis infusum, deducitur. De priori fonte vide Rom. 1. verf. 19. 20. c. 2. verf. 14. 15. de posteriori, Rom. 1. verf. 16. cap. 15. verf. 4. Cum hac sententia non pugnat, quod vulgo dicunt, tria esse artium & facultatum omnium criteria, Rationem, Experientiam, & Scripturam sacram. Nam experientia pertinet ad librum naturæ.
units.tr: VII. The sources of the principles of knowing are those from which they are derived. There are two: the book of nature and the book of Scripture. For whatever we know is deduced either from the workmanship of the world through the light of nature implanted in us, or from the word of God through the light of grace infused into us. For the former source see Rom. 1. verse 19, 20; ch. 2, verse 14, 15. For the latter, see Rom. 1. verse 16; ch. 15, verse 4. The common saying that there are three criteria of all arts and faculties, Reason, Experience, and Holy Scripture, does not conflict with this view. For experience belongs to the book of nature.

units.la: VIII. Proprietates principiorum cognoscendi sunt veritas, necessitas, simplicitas, & facilitas. Nam principia scientiarum ita se habent, ut sint πρώτως ἀληθῆ[?], primò-vera, adeoque causa veritatis conclusionum: primò-necessaria, adeoque causa omnis necessitatis: simplicissima, ita ut in ipsa resoluantur conclusiones: denique facillima, ita ut statim possint intelligi, si modò constet de vocum sive terminorum significatione. Quatuor has proprietates observare licet in singulis decalogi praeceptis : item in illo, Quod tibi fieri non vis, alteri ne feceris. Confer Matth. 7. verf. 12. Luc. 6. verf. 31.
units.tr: VIII. The properties of the principles of knowing are truth, necessity, simplicity, and ease. For the principles of the sciences are such that they are [πρώτως ἀληθῆ], first-true, and so the cause of the truth of the conclusions; first-necessary, and so the cause of all necessity; most simple, so that the conclusions are resolved into them; and finally most easy, so that they can be understood at once, provided only that the meaning of the words or terms is settled. We can observe these four properties in each of the precepts of the Decalogue, and likewise in the saying "What you do not want done to you, do not do to another." Compare Matt. 7:12; Luke 6:31.

units.la: IX. Diuisiones principiorum cognoscendi sunt variæ : è quibus præcipuæ sunt istæ:
units.tr: IX. The divisions of the principles of knowing are various; the chief of them are these:

units.la: 1. Principia sunt theoretica, vel practica. Illa gubernant cognitionem veri, hæc actionem boni, siue illud sit morale, siue artificiale. Tenentur hic duo axiomata valde illustria ; Optima speculatio non est nisi ratione optimi speculabilis[?], quod est Deus:Beatitudo est optima actio, optima potentia in optimo obiecto.
units.tr: 1. Principles are theoretical or practical. The former govern the knowledge of truth, the latter the performance of good, whether that good is moral or artificial. Here two very famous axioms hold: The best speculation is only by reason of the best object of speculation, which is God. Blessedness is the best action, the best power in the best object.

units.la: 2. Principia sunt communia, vel propria. Illa pluribus artibus inseruiunt, vt sunt principia metaphysica & logica: hæc ad vnam duntaxat artem pertinent, vt sunt principia physica. Sic decalogus complectitur principia, quibus communiter vtuntur ethica, œconomica, politica, iurisprudentia.
units.tr: 2. Principles are common or proper. The former serve several arts, as the metaphysical and logical principles do; the latter pertain to one art only, as the physical principles do. Thus the Decalogue contains principles which ethics, economics, politics, and jurisprudence commonly use.

units.la: 3. Principia sunt immediata, vel mediata. Illa sunt simpliciter prima, ideoque à priori non possunt demonstrari: hæc ab aliis dependent, & proinde admittunt demonstrationem.
units.tr: 3. Principles are immediate or mediate. The former are simply first, and therefore cannot be demonstrated a priori; the latter depend on others, and so admit of demonstration.

units.la: 4. Principia sunt naturalia, vel supernaturalia. Illa vel nascuntur nobiscum, vel acquiruntur studio proprio: hæc reuelantur & infunduntur à Deo. Hinc oriuntur tres gradus principiorum. In supremo gradu sunt principia supernaturalia, quæ Deus reuelat in schola gratiæ, vel gloriæ. Illa videntur lumine fidei, hæc lumine visionis beatificæ.
units.tr: 4. Principles are natural or supernatural. The former either are born with us or are acquired by our own study; the latter are revealed and infused by God. Hence arise three grades of principles. In the highest grade are the supernatural principles which God reveals in the school of grace or of glory. The former are seen by the light of faith, the latter by the light of the beatific vision.

units.la: 1. Cor. 13. verf. 9. 10. 12. In medio gradu sunt principia naturalia innata, quæ bonis authoribus appellantur ἐννοήματα[?], ζωπυρεῖς[?], προλήψεις, κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι, igniculi, scintillæ, semina, anticipationes, notiones communes, notiones per excellentiam, notiones ingeneratæ, intelligentiæ inchoatæ, adumbratæ, complicatæ, & inuoluta, notiones præceptæ seu ante perceptæ, notiones insitæ, decreta passiua, id est, omnibus communia. De his principiis est aurea Epicteti sententia: Caue notiones singulis rebus temere & vane accommodare. Hæc est causa mortalibus omnium malorum, non posse communes notiones aptare singularibus. Sic notio est in animo, Mala sunt vitanda, bona sequenda: sed cum ad facta venitur, alias notiones nobis formamus, hoc & illud malum bonumque esse, quæ reuera non sunt, & sic principio bono in malum finem definimus. Ita si quis tria ista principia iuris, Honestè viuere, Neminem ledere, Suum cuique tribuere, male applicet, conclusiones malæ deducentur ex bonis principiis. Hic itaque tenenda est regula, Communis notio non opinione aut affectu, sed Scriptura, Ratione, & Experientiâ duce accommodari debet ad circumstantias. Cæterum quando dicimus, huiusmodi principia naturaliter nobis esse insita, nobisque concreata, non intelligimus literas & syllabas, sed rem ipsam: neque intelligimus naturas distortas & Cyclopicas, de quibus Psalm. 14. sed re-ste se habentes: denique non intelligimus facultatem intelligendi omnibus insitam, sed species quasdam intellectui agenti impressas, quæ in omnibus hominibus sunt eædem. Rom. 2. vers. 14. 15. Atque hic est secundus gradus principiorum. In tertio, eoque infimo, gradu sunt principia naturalia acquisita per institutionem humanam: cuiusmodi sunt innumera philosophorum principia. Varietas ista graduum certitudinis & dignitatis parit varia principiorum nomina, quibus ipsa appellantur: puta, principia αὐτόπιστα[?] & ἀξιώματα, axiomata primò prima, principia illimitata, principia limitata, postulata, petitiones, pronuntiata honoraria, &c.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 13:9, 10, 12. In the middle grade are the innate natural principles, which good authors call [ἐννοήματα], [ζωπυρεῖς], [προλήψεις], [κοιναὶ ἔννοιαι]: sparks, embers, preconceptions, common notions; also sparklets, seeds, anticipations, common notions, notions by excellence, ingenerate notions, inchoate, shadowed, folded and involved understandings, notions prescribed or previously perceived, implanted notions, passive decrees, that is, those common to all. On these principles is the golden saying of Epictetus: Beware of carelessly and vainly fitting general notions to single things. This is the cause of all evils for mortals, that they cannot apply common notions to particulars. Thus there is in the mind the notion, Evils are to be avoided, goods are to be pursued; but when we come to deeds, we form other notions, that this or that is evil or good, which in truth they are not, and so from a good principle we define an evil end. So if anyone misapplies those three principles of law, To live honourably, to harm no one, to render to each his due, wrong conclusions will be drawn from good principles. Here, therefore, this rule must be held: A common notion must be fitted to circumstances not by opinion or feeling, but with Scripture, Reason, and Experience as guide. Moreover, when we say that such principles are naturally implanted in us and born with us, we do not mean letters and syllables, but the thing itself; nor do we mean distorted and Cyclopean natures, of which Psalm 14. speaks, but rightly disposed ones. Finally, we do not mean a faculty of understanding common to all, but certain species impressed on the agent intellect, which are the same in all men. Rom. 2. verse 14, 15. And this is the second grade of principles. In the third and lowest grade are the natural principles acquired through human instruction, such as the countless principles of the philosophers. This variety of grades of certainty and dignity gives rise to various names by which the principles themselves are called: namely, principles [αὐτόπιστα] and [ἀξιώματα], axioms first of all, unlimited principles, limited principles, postulates, petitions, honorary pronouncements, and so on.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: HEXILOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: Sacred Hexilogy.

units.la: I. HExilogia sacra est secunda pars præcognitorum, ex s.[?] Scriptura monstrans habitum illum, qui nos in facultatibus instar luminis dirigit in cognoscendo & agendo. Habitus est qualitas firma, per quam homo potest agere expeditè.
units.tr: Hexilogy is the second part of the prolegomena. Drawing on Holy Scripture, it shows the habit that guides us, like a light, in our faculties when we know and act. A habit is a firm quality through which a person can act with ease.

units.la: Estque verus vel falsus ; bonus vel malus ; necessarius vel contingens; simplex vel mixtus; extremus vel indifferens; intellectualis vel moralis; totalis vel partialis; ordinarius vel extraordinarius; theoreticus vel practicus; innatus, acquisitus, vel infusus, &c. Ex his habitibus illi sunt hoc loco considerandi, qui facultatibus & artibus sunt loco vel generis, e.g. physicae genus est scientia, ethicae prudentia, &c. vel fundamenti: vt ὁ νοῦς[?] est fundamentum philosophiae theoreticae, ὑπηρέτης[?] practicae.
units.tr: A habit is true or false, good or bad, necessary or contingent, simple or mixed, extreme or indifferent, intellectual or moral, total or partial, ordinary or extraordinary, theoretical or practical, innate, acquired or infused, and so on. Of these habits, those to be considered here are the ones that serve as the genus or foundation of the faculties and arts. For example, the genus of physics is science, and of ethics prudence. Or as foundation: intellect [ὁ νοῦς] is the foundation of theoretical philosophy, and assistant [ὑπηρέτης] of practical philosophy.

units.la: II. Habitus, qui nos in facultatibus dirigit, consideratur in se, vel oppositè: & rursus in se, vel simpliciter, vel composite.
units.tr: II. The habit that guides us in the faculties is considered either in itself or in opposition to something else, and again either in itself, simply, or in combination.

units.la: III. Habitus iste simpliciter spectatur in lumine naturae & gratiae. Quod attinet ad lumen gloriae, illud non est praesentis, sed futurae, vitae.
units.tr: III. This habit is viewed simply in the light of nature and of grace. As for the light of glory, that belongs not to the present life but to the life to come.

units.la: IV. Lumen naturae est habitus innatus, vel acquisitus, quo inclinamur ad assentiendum principijs & conclusionibus naturalibus. Eius radij'sunt[?] sex: intelligentia & synterefis, sapientia & scientia, prudentia & ars. Confer Proverb. 1. ver. 2. 4. 5. c. 2. ver. 2. 6. Rom. 2. verf. 15. Exod. 39. v. 6. 29. Ex his intelligentia est habitus primorum principiorum theoreticorum, quo fit, vt homo intelligat, hoc est, statim sine instructione & demonstratione admittat prima principia theoretica, qualia sunt, Totum est maius sua parte, Bis duo sunt quatuor. Synterefis est habitus primorum principiorum practicorum, quo fit, vt homo sine mora approbet prima principia practica, cuiusmodi sunt in decalogo. Rom. 2. v. 14. 15.
units.tr: IV. The light of nature is an innate or acquired habit by which we are inclined to assent to natural principles and conclusions. It has six rays: understanding and synteresis, wisdom and knowledge, prudence and art. Compare Proverbs 1:2, 4, 5; 2:2; 6; Romans 2:15; Exodus 39:6, 29. Of these, understanding is the habit of first theoretical principles, by which a person understands, that is, immediately and without instruction or demonstration accepts first theoretical principles such as: the whole is greater than its part; twice two is four. Synteresis is the habit of first practical principles, by which a person without delay approves first practical principles, of the kind found in the Decalogue. Romans 2:14, 15.

units.la: Sapientia est habitus conclusionum theoreticarum, quo fit, vt homo assentiatur conclusionibus theoreticis demonstratis per primas & altissimas causas. Scientia est habitus conclusionum theoreticarum, quo fit, vt homo assentiatur conclusionibus theoreticis demonstratis per proxiproximas causas. Prudentia est habitus conclusionum practicarum, quo fit, ut homo assentiatur conclusionibus practicis, quatenus illæ deducuntur ex suis principijs ad omnes circumstantias congruentibus. Ars denique est habitus conclusionum poeticarū siue organicarum (earumq; tum liberalium, tum mechanicarum) quo fit ut homo assentiatur conclusionibus poeticis, quatenus illæ deducuntur ex suis principijs iam ante bono artifici probatis. Hi sunt radii luminis naturæ, quibus illuminantur omnes facultates & disciplinæ, quas homo citra reuelationem diuinam potest docere & discere, cuiusmodi sunt philosophia, iurisprudentia, & medicina. De usu horum radiorum est hic canon: Quidquid est intelligibile, recolibile, & amabile seu volibile, illud est statuendum & approbandum. Sic e.g. magis est intelligibile, recolibile, & amabile, afferere, Deum esse, quam, Deum non esse. Quare si aliquid occurrat naturali lumine diiudicandum, excutiamus opes rationis post lapsum reliquas tanquam naufragi alicuius tabulam, ne simus ut equus & mulus, expertes intelligentiæ
units.tr: Wisdom is the habit of theoretical conclusions, by which a person assents to theoretical conclusions demonstrated through first and highest causes. Knowledge is the habit of theoretical conclusions, by which a person assents to theoretical conclusions demonstrated through proximate causes. Prudence is the habit of practical conclusions, by which a person assents to practical conclusions insofar as they are deduced from principles that fit all the circumstances. Art, finally, is the habit of productive conclusions, whether of the organic arts (both liberal and mechanical), by which a person assents to productive conclusions insofar as they are deduced from principles already proved beforehand by a skilled craftsman. These are the rays of the light of nature, by which are illumined all the faculties and disciplines that a person can teach and learn without divine revelation, such as philosophy, jurisprudence, and medicine. The rule for the use of these rays is this: Whatever is intelligible, memorable, and lovable or desirable, that is to be affirmed and approved. Thus, for example, it is more intelligible, memorable, and lovable to affirm that God exists than that God does not exist. Therefore, if anything arises that must be judged by natural light, let us search the resources of reason that remain after the Fall, like the plank of some shipwrecked man, lest we be like the horse and mule, which lack understanding.

units.la: Psal. 32. vers. 9.
units.tr: Psalm 32:9.

units.la: V. Lumen gratiæ est fides saluifica, qua inclinamur ad assentiendum principijs & conclusionibus supernaturalibus. Fieri siquidem non potest, ut lumen naturæ pertingat ad ea, quæ superant naturam: cum nihil agat supra vires & vltra speciem suam. Necesse est itaque est, ut nobis infundatur lumen supernaturale, quo res supernaturales videamus. Heb. 11. vers. 1.
units.tr: V. The light of grace is saving faith, by which we are inclined to assent to supernatural principles and conclusions. For the light of nature cannot reach those things that surpass nature, since nothing acts beyond its powers and beyond its own kind. It is necessary, therefore, that a supernatural light be infused into us, by which we may see supernatural things. Hebrews 11:1.

units.la: VI. Habitus compositè spectatus admittit variam mixtionem. Et primò quidem lumen naturæ coniungitur cum lumine gratiæ, ut in primo symboliarticulo, & in alijs quibusdam videre est. Deinde intelligentia & synteresis, intelligentia & sapientia, intelligentia & ars, synteresis & prudentia &c. multifariam coniungi possunt, ita nempe, ut unus habitus alteri veluti manum porrigat. Sic quintum decalogi præceptum, Honora patrem & matrem, pertinet ad synteresin, quatenus est principium: ad prudentiam, quatenus incidit specialis casus & circumstantia circa honorem parentum, magistratuum, praeceptorum, &c. Similiter rhetorica est ars, quae multum requirit prudentiae, vt grammatica multum scientiae.
units.tr: VI. Considered in combination, habits admit of various mixtures. First, the light of nature is joined with the light of grace, as can be seen in the first article of the Creed and in some others. Then understanding and synteresis, understanding and wisdom, understanding and art, synteresis and prudence, and so on, can be joined in many ways, so that one habit, as it were, stretches out a hand to another. Thus the fifth commandment of the Decalogue, Honour your father and mother, belongs to synteresis insofar as it is a principle, and to prudence insofar as a particular case and circumstance arise concerning the honour due to parents, magistrates, teachers, and so on. Similarly, rhetoric is an art that requires much prudence, as grammar requires much knowledge.

units.la: VII. Habitus oppositè spectatur in iis, quae pugnant cum lumine naturae, vel gratiae. Eiusmodi autem res sunt variae, quarum aliae habent rationem nebulae, aliae tenebrarum. Ibi sunt opinio, fides humana, dubitatio, & suspicio: hic est error, & incredulitas. Quatuor priora tolerantur in hac humana imbecillitate: duo priora tolerari non debent.
units.tr: VII. Habits are considered in opposition in those things that fight against the light of nature or of grace. Such things are various, some of which have the character of a mist, others of darkness. Of the former kind are opinion, human faith, doubt, and suspicion; of the latter kind are error and unbelief. The first four are tolerated in this human weakness; the first two ought not to be tolerated at all.

units.la: Atque haec est-hexilogia, cuius usus inter alia esse debet, vt in omnibus actionibus nostris dispiciamus, num aliquid consentiat cum lumine naturae vel gratiae, necne. Oportet enim, vt illa sint luce aliquâ praedita, quae sunt vera & bona. Neque verò id est mirum. Nam nihil est verum aut bonum; quod non consentit cum Deo, qui est mera lux. Oremus itaque cum Dauide: In lumine tuo videbimus lumen Psal. 36. vers. 11.
units.tr: This is the hexilogy, whose use, among other things, should be that in all our actions we examine whether something agrees with the light of nature or of grace or not. For those things that are true and good ought to be endowed with some light. Nor is this surprising, for nothing is true or good that does not agree with God, who is pure light. Let us therefore pray with David: In your light we shall see light, Psalm 36:9.

units.la: IV. Technologia[?] sacra
units.tr: IV. Sacred technology

units.la: I. Technologia sacra est tertia pars praecognitorum e Scriptura enarrans varietatem rerum homine dignarum, vel indignarum.
units.tr: I. Sacred technology is the third part of the prolegomena. From Scripture it sets out the variety of things, both worthy and unworthy of man.

units.la: II. Res homine dignae traduntur in quatuor facultatibus, & artibus mechanicis.
units.tr: II. Things worthy of man are handed down in the four faculties and in the mechanical arts.

units.la: III. Quatuor facultates sunt philosophia, theologia, iurisprudentia & medicina. Confer
units.tr: III. The four faculties are philosophy, theology, jurisprudence and medicine. Compare

units.la: 1. Reg. 4. vers. 29. 30. 31. 32. 33. 2. Tim. 3. vers. 16. Exod. 21. Gen. 50. vers. 2. Coloss. 4. vers. 14. Esa. 3. vers. 2. 3. Sirach. 43. vers. 3. 4. 5. 6. Harum comprehensio dicitur Encyclopaedia.
units.tr: 1 Kings 4, verses 29, 30, 31, 32, 33; 2 Timothy 3, verse 16; Exodus 21; Genesis 50, verse 2; Colossians 4, verse 14; Isaiah 3, verses 2, 3; Sirach 43, verses 3, 4, 5, 6. The comprehension of these is called Encyclopaedia.

units.la: IV. In iis spectatur ordo & habitudo.
units.tr: IV. In these the order and the relation between them are considered.

units.la: V. Ordo inter facultates est naturae, dignitatis, vel melioris cognitionis. Ordo naturae progreditur à simplicioribus ad composita, & ita philosophia est omnium simplicissima, dehinc medicina, tum iuris prudentia, postremò theologia. Nam medicina paucioribus philosophiae partibus utitur, quàm iurisprudentia vel theologia. Ordo dignitatis est, quo praemittuntur honorabilia minus honorabilibus. Ita theologia primas tenet: utpote quae docet modum perveniendi ad summum hominis bonum. Eam proximè sequitur iurisprudentia, quatenus propositum sibi habet bonum publicum societatis ciuilis. Hanc sequitur medicina, occupata circa bonum corporis. Ultimum locum obtinet philosophia, tanquam instrumentum tribus superioribus facultatibus inserviens. Atque haec est comparatio[?] sive contentio quatuor facultatum minimè dubia. Ordo[?] melioris cognitionis incipit à philosophiâ, & progreditur ad illam facultatem, cui aliquis se addicere cupit.
units.tr: V. The order among the faculties is either that of nature, that of dignity, or that of better knowledge. The order of nature proceeds from the simpler to the composite. So philosophy is the simplest of all, then medicine, then jurisprudence, and last of all theology. For medicine makes use of fewer parts of philosophy than jurisprudence or theology does. The order of dignity is that by which more honourable things are placed before less honourable ones. Thus theology holds the first place, since it teaches the way of attaining man's highest good. Next after it comes jurisprudence, insofar as it has as its aim the public good of civil society. Then comes medicine, occupied with the good of the body. Philosophy holds the last place, serving as an instrument for the three higher faculties. This comparison, or contest, of the four faculties is quite beyond doubt. The order of better knowledge begins with philosophy and proceeds to whichever faculty someone wishes to devote himself to.

units.la: VI. Philosophia est comprehensio disciplinarum, quae tribus superioribus facultatibus inserviunt. Disciplinae istae sunt pragmaticae, vel philologicae. Disciplinae pragmaticae tradunt ipsas res: unde etiam reales & obiectivae dicuntur. Suntque theoreticae, vel practicae. Theoreticae dicuntur scientiae; quarum tria sunt capita: metaphysica, physica, & mathematica. Inter metaphysicam & physicam interiecta est Pneumatica; quam alij ad metaphysicam, alij ad physicam referunt. Mathematica completitur arithmeticam, geometriam, cosmographiam, uranoscopiam, geographiam, opticam, musicam, & architectonicam. Disciplinae practicae appellantur prudentiae; quarum capita itidem sunt tria: ethica, oeconomica, politica. Politicae subordinatur scholastica. Disciplinae philologicae dicuntur artes, quae tradunt instrumenta liberalia: unde etiam directivae, organicae, & poeticae appellantur. Ipsarum capita itidem sunt tria: grammatica, rhetorica, logica; quae vulgò appellantur trivium. Grammaticam anteit lexica: rhetoricam & logicam sequitur oratoria: ex omnibus istis resultant poetica & mnemonica. Atque hæ sunt disciplinæ philosophicæ, inter quas itidem est triplex ordo, videlicet naturæ, dignitatis, & facilioris cognitionis. Ordo naturæ progreditur à disciplinis theoreticis ad practicas, & ab his ad poeticas, siue à notionibus primis ad secundas. Quem ordinem modò expressimus. Ordo dignitatis est varius. Ita enim politica præcedit reliquas omnes, tanquam συστατικὴ καὶ ἀρχιτεκτονική. Rursus logica præcedit grammaticam, &c. Ordo facilioris cognitionis progreditur ab iis, quæ sunt faciliora respectu nostræ imbecillitatis. Ita notiones secundæ præmittuntur primis, eaque de causâ artes appellantur disciplinæ pueriles, quia in pueritiâ & iuuentute sunt discendæ: scientia, virtutes, quia virilis ætas iis inprimis impenditur: prudentia, [illegible, ~4 letters]ues & libera, quia ingrauescens & affecta ætas circa eas inprimis occupatur. De his philosophiæ partibus (vt & reliquis tribus facultatibus) insignis est locus Sap. 7. versic. 15.16.17.18.19.20.21. [?]Ἐμοὶ δὲ δώη ὁ θεὸς εἰπεῖν κατὰ γνώμην, καὶ ἐνθυμηθῆναι ἀξίως τῶν δοθέντων, ὅτι αὐτὸς ὁδηγὸς σοφίας ἐστὶ καὶ σοφῶν διορθωτής. Ἐν χειρὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἡμεῖς καὶ οἱ λόγοι ἡμῶν, πᾶσά τε φρόνησις καὶ ἐπιστήμη ἔργων τε καὶ τεχνῶν. Αὐτὸς γάρ μοι ἔδωκε τῶν ὄντων γνῶσιν ἀψευδῆ, εἰδέναι σύστασιν κόσμου, καὶ ἐνέργειαν στοιχείων. Ἀρχὴν καὶ πέρας καὶ μεσότητα χρόνων, τροπῶν ἀλλαγὰς καὶ μεταβολὰς καιρῶν. Ἐνιαυτοῦ κύκλος καὶ ἀστέρων θέσεις. Φύσεις ζῴων καὶ θυμοὺς θηρίων, πνεύματα βίας καὶ διαλογισμοὺς ἀνθρώπων, διαφορὰς φυτῶν, καὶ δυνάμεις ῥιζῶν· ὅσα τε ἔστι κρυπτὰ καὶ ἐμφανῆ, ἐγνων· ἡ γὰρ πάντων τεχνῖτις ἐδίδαξέ με σοφία. hoc est, Deus mihi dedit ex sententia dicere, ac pro dignitate eorum quæ dantur, cogitare: quoniam ipse & sapientiæ dux est, & sapientum moderator. Nam in manu ipsius sumus tum nos, tum sermones nostri, omnis etiam prudentia, scientiaque opificiorum. Mihi enim dedit Deus, eorum quæ sunt in natura, veram cognitionem, vt mundi constitutionem, vimq; elementorum intelligam: Initium, exitum, medium q; temporum, solstitiorum vicissitudinem, ac temperatum varietatem, Annorum circuitus, ac situs stellarum: Naturas animalium, irasque bestiarum, ventorum vim, & cogitationes hominum, differentias plantarum, radicumque facultates. Omnia denique, quae sunt recondita & aperta cognoui: Nam omnium artifex sapientia me docuit. Confer cum 1. Reg.verf. 32. 33. vbi de Salomone ita legimus: Locutus quoq; est tria millia parabolarum: & fuerunt cantica eius quinque & mille. Locutus est praeterea de arboribus, a cedro quae est in Libano, ad hyssopum quae egreditur de pariete. Locutus est insuper de animalibus, & de volatilibus, & de reptilibus, & depiscibus.
units.tr: VI. Philosophy is the collection of the disciplines that serve the three higher faculties. These disciplines are either pragmatic or philological. Pragmatic disciplines deliver the things themselves, and so are also called real and objective. They are either theoretical or practical. Theoretical ones are called sciences, and they have three heads: metaphysics, physics and mathematics. Between metaphysics and physics lies pneumatics, which some refer to metaphysics and others to physics. Mathematics is completed by arithmetic, geometry, cosmography, uranoscopy, geography, optics, music and architecture. Practical disciplines are called prudences, and they too have three heads: ethics, economics and politics. Subordinate to politics is scholastic discipline. Philological disciplines are called arts, which deliver the liberal instruments; hence they are also called directive, organic and poetic. Their heads too are three: grammar, rhetoric and logic, which are commonly called the trivium. Before grammar comes lexicography; after rhetoric and logic comes oratory; from all of these result poetics and mnemonics. These are the philosophical disciplines, and among them too there is a threefold order, namely of nature, of dignity, and of easier knowledge. The order of nature proceeds from theoretical disciplines to practical ones, and from these to poetic ones, or from first notions to second ones. This is the order we have just set out. The order of dignity varies. Thus politics precedes all the others, as συστατικὴ καὶ ἀρχιτεκτονική [architectonic and constitutive]. Again, logic precedes grammar, and so on. The order of easier knowledge proceeds from those things that are easier, given our weakness. Thus second notions are placed before first ones, and for this reason the arts are called boyish disciplines, because they are to be learned in boyhood and youth; sciences and virtues are so called because manly age is devoted chiefly to them; prudence [illegible] and free, because an age that grows heavy and enfeebled is chiefly occupied with them. An outstanding passage about these parts of philosophy (as also about the other three faculties) is Wisdom 7:15–21: Ἐμοὶ δὲ δώη ὁ θεὸς εἰπεῖν κατὰ γνώμην, καὶ ἐνθυμηθῆναι ἀξίως τῶν δοθέντων, ὅτι αὐτὸς ὁδηγὸς σοφίας ἐστὶ καὶ σοφῶν διορθωτής. Ἐν χειρὶ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἡμεῖς καὶ οἱ λόγοι ἡμῶν, πᾶσά τε φρόνησις καὶ ἐπιστήμη ἔργων τε καὶ τεχνῶν. Αὐτὸς γάρ μοι ἔδωκε τῶν ὄντων γνῶσιν ἀψευδῆ, εἰδέναι σύστασιν κόσμου, καὶ ἐνέργειαν στοιχείων. Ἀρχὴν καὶ πέρας καὶ μεσότητα χρόνων, τροπῶν ἀλλαγὰς καὶ μεταβολὰς καιρῶν. Ἐνιαυτοῦ κύκλος καὶ ἀστέρων θέσεις. Φύσεις ζῴων καὶ θυμοὺς θηρίων, πνεύματα βίας καὶ διαλογισμοὺς ἀνθρώπων, διαφορὰς φυτῶν, καὶ δυνάμεις ῥιζῶν· ὅσα τε ἔστι κρυπτὰ καὶ ἐμφανῆ, ἔγνων· ἡ γὰρ πάντων τεχνῖτις ἐδίδαξέ με σοφία. That is: God has given me to speak according to my judgement, and to think worthily of what is given, since he himself is the guide of wisdom and the corrector of the wise. For in his hand are both we and our words, and all prudence and knowledge of works and arts. For he himself gave me true knowledge of the things that exist, to know the constitution of the world and the operation of the elements; the beginning, end and middle of times, the changes of the solstices and the alterations of seasons; the cycle of the year and the positions of the stars; the natures of animals and the wrath of beasts, the force of winds and the thoughts of men, the differences of plants and the powers of roots. Whatever is hidden and whatever is manifest, I have known, for wisdom, the artificer of all things, taught me. Compare 1 Kings 4:32–33, where we read of Solomon: He also spoke three thousand proverbs, and his songs were a thousand and five. He spoke also of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that springs out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of fowl, and of creeping things, and of fishes.

units.la: VII. Theologia est facultas ad summum bonum perueniendi. Eius partes sunt multae: puta theologia positiua, theologia naturalis, catechetica, didactica, polemica vel potius irenica, casuum, prophetica, & acroamatica siue moralis.
units.tr: VII. Theology is the faculty of attaining the highest good. Its parts are many: namely positive theology, natural theology, catechetical, didactic, polemical or rather irenic, casuistic, prophetic, and acroamatic or moral.

units.la: VIII. Iurisprudentia est facultas constituendi quod æquum & iustum est. Eius partes sunt ius Mosaicum, ius ciuile Iustiniani, ius canonicum, ius Saxonicum &c.
units.tr: VIII. Jurisprudence is the faculty of determining what is equitable and just. Its parts are Mosaic law, the civil law of Justinian, canon law, Saxon law, and so on.

units.la: IX. Medicina est facultas bene medendi. Eius partes sunt physiologica, diætetica, semeiotica, pharmaceutica, hygieina, prophylactica, therapeutica.
units.tr: IX. Medicine is the faculty of healing well. Its parts are physiology, dietetics, semeiotics, pharmacy, hygiene, prophylactics and therapeutics.

units.la: X. Habitudo quatuor facultatum est ipsarum affectio, iuxta has regulas.
units.tr: X. The relation of the four faculties is their mutual disposition, according to these rules.

units.la: 1. Omnis facultas habet suas metas, quas non licet transilire. Quia utagrorum, ita quoque facultatum & artium terminos manere distinctos interest omnium.
units.tr: 1. Every faculty has its boundaries, which it is not lawful to cross. For just as the limits of fields, so too the boundaries of faculties and arts should remain distinct, and this is in everyone's interest.

units.la: 2. Omnis facultas habet finem proprium, possibilem, & praestatem, traditq; media ad illum consequendu sufficientia & facilia.
units.tr: 2. Every faculty has its own end, which is possible and attainable, and it hands down means sufficient and easy for attaining it.

units.la: 3. Omnis facultas habet subiectum proprium: in quo scilicet explicando est occupata.
units.tr: 3. Every faculty has its proper subject, namely that with which it is occupied in its exposition.

units.la: 4. Omnis facultas habet praecepta vera, perspicua, facilia, vtilia, necessaria, homogenea, & sufficientia.
units.tr: 4. Every faculty has precepts that are true, clear, easy, useful, necessary, homogeneous and sufficient.

units.la: 5. Omnis facultas potest comprehendi certa methodo.
units.tr: 5. Every faculty can be comprehended by a certain method.

units.la: 6. Facultates in vsu sunt coniuncta.
units.tr: 6. In use the faculties are joined together.

units.la: 7. Omnis facultas habet theoriā & praxin.Sic theologia est theoretica & practica. Quod vetustissimi Patres putant expressum fuisse in nominibus Iohannis & Petri, ita vt Iohannes fuerit symbolum contemplationis, Petrus actionis. Hoc enim sensu Theophylactus in cap. 25. Lucæ, Petrum & Iohannem vocat προσξιν τῆς θεωρίας, actionem & contemplationem. Et Origenes ait: Petrus in forma actionis accipitur. Iohannes autem contemplationis atque scientiæ typum imitatur. Hinc Iohannes dictus est filius tonitrui, & Chrysostomo dicitur βροντῆν θεολογίαν, scientiam de Christi deitate in star tonitru tradere: Petrus autem à petra nomen accepit, quæ significat vitam variis periculis & casibus obnoxiam. Porrò quod dixi de theologia, idem de reliquis tribus facultatibus, & de omnibus in vniuersum disciplinis est iudicium. Sic v.g. logica habet suam theoriam & praxin: similiter physica, geometria, &c. Hoc autem sensu late accipiuntur vocabula theoria & praxis. Alias stricte loquendo quædam disciplinæ sunt tantum theoreticæ, & quædam tantum practicæ.
units.tr: 7. Every faculty has theory and practice. So theology is both theoretical and practical. The most ancient Fathers thought this was expressed in the names of John and Peter, so that John was the symbol of contemplation and Peter of action. For in this sense Theophylact, on Luke 25, calls Peter and John προσξιν τῆς θεωρίας [the persons of contemplation], that is, action and contemplation. And Origen says: Peter is taken in the form of action, while John imitates the type of contemplation and knowledge. Hence John was called the son of thunder, and Chrysostom calls him βροντῆν θεολογίαν [the thundering theologian], meaning that he delivered the science of Christ's deity in the manner of thunder. Peter, however, took his name from the rock, which signifies a life exposed to various dangers and chances. Moreover, what I have said of theology, the same judgement holds for the other three faculties and for all disciplines in general. Thus, for example, logic has its theory and practice; likewise physics, geometry, and so on. In this sense the words theory and practice are understood broadly. Otherwise, strictly speaking, some disciplines are only theoretical, and some only practical.

units.la: 8. Facultatibus accidit multiplex abusus. Hic vero nihil pertinet ad essentiam, ideoque non tollit visum. De abusu philosophiæ vide 1. Cor. 1. & 2. & Coloss. 2. verf. 8.
units.tr: 8. Multiple abuse befalls the faculties. Yet this does not pertain to their essence, and therefore does not take away their standing. On the abuse of philosophy see 1 Cor. 1 and 2, and Col. 2, verse 8.

units.la: 9. Facultatibus & artibus accidit multiplex mixtio. Sic v. g. magia, Cabbala, Critica, Paradoxologia, &c. sunt plurium facultatum & artium farrago. Eodem pacto historia & chronologia le habent.
units.tr: 9. Multiple mixture also befalls the faculties and arts. Thus, for example, magic, Cabbala, criticism, paradoxology and the like are a hodgepodge of several faculties and arts. History and chronology are in the same case.

units.la: 10. Singulæ facultates & disciplinæ habent peculiares partes, quæ videri possint integræ artes. Sic ars precandi & bene moriendi est pars theologiæ, dæmonologia est pars Pneumaticæ.
units.tr: 10. Each of the faculties and disciplines has particular parts which may be regarded as arts in their own right. Thus the art of praying and of dying well is a part of theology, and demonology is a part of pneumatics.

units.la: XI. Artes mechanicæ sunt propago quædam & praxis artium mathematicarum, itemq; phi- losophiæ practicæ. Harum numerus est longe maxi- mus. Præcipuæ numerantur septem hoc versu:
units.tr: XI. The mechanical arts are a kind of offshoot and practice of the mathematical arts, and likewise of practical philosophy. Their number is by far the greatest. The chief ones are counted as seven in this verse:

units.la: Rus, Nemus, Arma, Faber, Vulnera, Lana, Rates. Id est, Agricultura, Venatoria, Militaris, Fabrilis, Chirurgia, Textoria, Nautica. Hæ artes vulgo dicuntur illiberales, in sensu comparato. Neq; enim per se sunt indignæ liberali ingenio: cum Christus fuerit faber lignarius, & quidam ex apostolis piscatores, & Paulus artis textoriæ peritus. Marc. 6. Matt. 4. Act. 18. De Bezaleele vide Exod. 31. versic. 2.
units.tr: Field, Grove, Arms, Smith, Wounds, Wool, Ships. That is, agriculture, hunting, the military art, smithing, surgery, weaving, and seamanship. These arts are commonly called illiberal, in a comparative sense. For they are not in themselves unworthy of a liberal mind, since Christ was a carpenter, some of the apostles were fishermen, and Paul was skilled in the art of weaving. Mark 6. Matt. 4. Acts 18. On Bezaleel see Exod. 31. verse 2.

units.la: XII. Res homine indignæ sunt curiositatis vel impietatis nomine infames. Eiusmodi sunt magia necromantica seu cacomagia, hydromantia, geomantia, &c. de quibus Peucerus libro de divinationum generibus. Insignis hac de re est locus Act. 19. versic. 19. Multi vero ex iis, qui curiosa ista exercuerant, comportatos libros exusserunt in omnium conspectu: quorum supputatis pretijs, repererunt denariorum quinquaginta millia. Quæ summa excrevit ad 32000. thalerorum Philippicorum. Huc etiam refer falsò nominatam scientiam, de quâ apostolus, 1. Tim. 6. versic. 20.
units.tr: XII. Things unworthy of a man are infamous on account of curiosity or impiety. Such are necromantic magic, or cacomagic, hydromancy, geomancy, and so on, concerning which see Peucer's book on the kinds of divination. A notable passage on this matter is Acts 19. verse 19: Many of those who had practised these curious arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all; and when the price of them was reckoned up, they found fifty thousand denarii. That sum amounted to 32,000 Philippine thalers. Refer here also to the falsely so-called science of which the apostle speaks, 1 Tim. 6. verse 20.

units.la: V. DIDACTICA SACRA.
units.tr: V. Sacred Didactics.

units.la: I. Didactica sacra est quarta pars præcognitorum explicans methodum docendi & discendi ex præscripto S. literarum. Ex Tertulliano lib. de animâ licet appellare Discentiam. Eius finis est, ut in hominis intellectu efficiatur facilior apprehensio, & firmior impressio.
units.tr: I. Sacred didactics is the fourth part of the preliminaries, explaining the method of teaching and learning according to the prescription of the Holy Scriptures. It may be called Discentia, after Tertullian's book On the Soul. Its end is that a easier apprehension and a firmer impression be produced in the human intellect.

units.la: II. Didacticæ partes duæ sunt: una de devotione, altera de intentione docentis & discentis.
units.tr: II. There are two parts of sacred didactics: one concerning devotion, the other concerning the intention of the teacher and the learner.

units.la: III. Devotio est animi & corporis ad Deum elevatio, consistens in precatione & sanctimonia. Speculum huius devotionis lucidissimum est Salomon 1. Reg. 3. à versic. 4. ad 16. & Sap. 9. Precatio debet esse partim solennis & stata, partim varians. Precatio solennis ordinarie concipi debet horis vere canonicis, mane, me-ridie ridie & vesperi, exemplo Dauidis & Danielis. Psalm. 55. verf. 16.17. Dan. 6. verf. 10. Huiusmodi preces fiunt ardentiores, si accedat γονυκλισία, genuflexio. Precatio varians est iaculum siue gemitus cordis ad Deum, quo fit, vt ante tractationem, in tractatione, & post tractationem studiorum nostrorum demus Deo gloriam, humiliter ab ipso petentes gratiam Spiritus sancti, & ardenter gratias ipsi agentes pro lumine intelligentiae nobis concesso. Iacob. 1. verf. 5. Ad hanc precationem pertinet cantio sacra Coloss. 3. verf. 16.17. Sanctimonia consistit in quotidiana praxi & inftauratione poenitentiae, qua fit, vt peccatum habeamus pro turpitudine omnium turpissima 1. Ioh. 3. verf. 8. & Iesum Christum pro pulchritudine omnium pulcherrima Pfalm. 45. verf. 3.8.9. cui nostras actiones & cupimus & conamur conformare Pfal. 45. verf. 10.12.14. lanctofque angelos hoc pacto nobis conciliamus doctores, ductores, & amicos Matth. 18. verf. 10. Luc. 15. verf. 10.
units.tr: III. Devotion is the lifting up of mind and body to God, consisting in prayer and holiness. The clearest mirror of this devotion is Solomon, 1 Kings 3:4–16 and Wisdom 9. Prayer ought to be partly solemn and fixed, partly varied. Solemn prayer should ordinarily be offered at the canonical hours, morning, midday and evening, after the example of David and Daniel. Ps. 55:16–17; Dan. 6:10. Such prayers become more fervent if genuflection [γονυκλισία], genuflexio, is added. Varied prayer is a dart or sigh of the heart toward God, by which, before the handling of our studies, during it, and after it, we give glory to God, humbly asking from him the grace of the Holy Spirit and ardently giving thanks to him for the light of understanding granted to us. James 1:5. To this prayer belongs sacred singing: Col. 3:16–17. Holiness consists in the daily practice and renewal of repentance, by which we come to hold sin to be the most shameful of all shameful things, 1 John 3:8, and Jesus Christ to be the most beautiful of all beautiful things, Ps. 45:3, 8–9, whose actions we both desire and strive to conform our own to, Ps. 45:10, 12, 14. In this way we also win the holy angels as our teachers, guides and friends: Matt. 18:10; Luke 15:10.

units.la: IV. Intentio docentis & discentis est accurata diligentia, quae respicit personas, res, & actiones didacticas.
units.tr: IV. The intention of the teacher and the learner is careful diligence, which regards the persons, the things and the actions of teaching.

units.la: V. Personae didacticae sunt praeceptor & discipulus. Praeceptor quaerendus est talis, qui possit & velit docere, quique adeo nobis fit charus instar parentis. Manet enim illud πολυμαθήτην[?]: Non habueris praeceptorem, nisi eundem & amicum. Talis fuit Elias praeceptor Elisaei 2.Reg.2. verf. 12. Talis quoque fuit Christus, qui toto ministerij sui tempore, doctoris munus egregie sustinuit. Vnde passim in euangeliis vocatur ῥαββί, ῥαββοῦνι, διδάσκαλος, & καθηγητής, magister & praeceptor, frequentius multo quam κύριος, dominus. Et qui Christum sequebantur, μαθηταί, discipuli, in euangeliis vocantur: eamque appellationem fideles, etiam post Christi assumtionem, initio nascentis ecclesiae, retinuerunt, dicebanturque & viri discipuli, & foeminae μαθήτριαι, discipulae. Act. 9. verf. 36. Porro apostolus Paulus in hunc bonorum praeceptorum numerum est etiam referendus 1. Tim. 1. verf. 2. Discipulus requiritur talis, qui & possit, & velit discere. Quam ad rem tria ista requiruntur: ingenium aptum, amor, & admiratio. Ingenium aptum est vel moderatum, vel heroicum. Ingenium moderatum est, quod non est nimis mobile, vel nimis stabile: heroicum, quod peculiari numinis afflatu & priuilegio extra ordinem gubernatur, vt in Salomone 1. Reg. 3. & 4. item in Bezaleele & Ahaliabo videre est Exod. 35. verf. 30. & seqq. & c. 36. verf. 1. Hinc colligere est, quaenam ingenia sint inepta, videl. nimis mobilia, vel nimis stabilia. Atq; haec sunt capita ad quae quidquid est ingeniorum referri potest: puta ingenia magna, parua & mediocria; felicia & infelicia; apta & inepta; viuida, & torpida; acuta & obtusa; ignea, terrea, & temperata; ordinaria, & extraordinaria; praecocia, serotina, & matura. Quae diuersitas non tam a qualitatibus corporum, quam a prouidentia Dei dependet, itemque a cultura sedula. Ita enim est, vt Hippocrates dixit: Quae feminis ad tellurem est proportio, eadem est scientiae ad humanum ingenium: quae neque vniuersa eadem est, ac quamuis aliqua sit pinguis & foecunda, excolenda tamen est, ac dispiciendum, cuinam femini sit aptior. At ne hoc quidem satis. Tempus enim sationi idoneum expectandum est: mox enatum semen expurgandum, multumque in id impendendum laboris & temporis, vt maturescat. Hinc Clemens Alexandrinus in paedagogo cum animos nostros vocallet agros animatos, eisdem diuersitatibus, quibus sunt agri, subiectos esse homines ostendit. Oportet itaque in examine & cultura ingeniorum accurate perpendere in-clinationem naturae, quo nempe quisque feratur: & prudenter atque humiliter dona sua cognoscere: deniq; nulli inuidere dotes ingenii, quas a Deo accepit, sed illas potius exosculari & imitari. Cum enim Deus libere dispenset cuique suum talentum Matth. 25. v. 14. & seqq. si omnibus non det omnia, non est dicendum, Cur me fecisti sic: sed cuique proprius est colendus ager, ex quo non plus quàm deceat, tributi est exigendū. Cæterum sub ingenio complectimur εὐμάθειαν, docilitatem; & ἀγχίνοιαν, subtilitatem. Secundum requisitum discipuli est amor, quo ille complecti debet præceptorem, totoque impetu, & velut contactu magnetico ferri in rem discendam. Amorem excipere debet admiratio, qua discipulus præceptorem & rem discendam sic æstimat, ut supra vulgus & illum & istam ponat. Ex his efficitur, in discipulo qualificato requiri, ut primo eligat præceptorem doctum & fidelem: deinde illum charitate complectatur: tertio, assiduò audiat: quartò, sæpius interroget: quintò, fidem eius dictis adhibeat: & denique in his, quæ laudabilia sunt, imitetur. Neque vero est, quod nobis obijcias ingenia αὐτοδιδάκτα: cum illa sint rara. Cæteroqui sub ingenio, amore, & admiratione complectimur omnia requisita discipuli frugi, qualia sunt propensio in rem discendam, docilitas, subtilitas, ignorantia conscientia, φιλοπονία, abstinentia à voluptatibus, perturbationum carentia, curarum & solicitudinum vacuitas, &c. de quibus accurate Bonnæus tractatu de ratione discendi.
units.tr: V. The persons of didactics are the teacher and the pupil. A teacher should be sought who can and wishes to teach, and who is thus dear to us as a parent. For that saying remains true: [πολυμαθήτην?] You should not have a teacher unless he is also your friend. Elijah was such a teacher to Elisha, 2 Kings 2:12. Christ too was such, who throughout the whole time of his ministry admirably discharged the office of teacher. Hence in the Gospels he is called everywhere rabbi [ῥαββί], rabbouni [ῥαββοῦνι], didaskalos [διδάσκαλος], and kathēgētēs [καθηγητής], master and teacher, far more often than kyrios [κύριος], lord. And those who followed Christ are called in the Gospels mathētai [μαθηταί], disciples. Even after Christ's ascension, at the beginning of the nascent Church, the faithful kept that name: men were called disciples, and women mathētriai [μαθήτριαι], female disciples. Acts 9:36. Moreover the apostle Paul is also to be counted among this number of good teachers, 1 Tim. 1:2. A pupil is required who can and wishes to learn. For this three things are required: an apt wit, love, and admiration. An apt wit is either moderate or heroic. A moderate wit is one that is neither too mobile nor too stable; a heroic one is governed outside the ordinary order by a special inspiration and privilege of the divine power, as can be seen in Solomon, 1 Kings 3 and 4, and likewise in Bezalel and Aholiab, Exod. 35:30ff. and 36:1. From this one may gather which wits are unfit, namely those that are too mobile or too stable. These are the heads to which whatever kinds of wits there are can be referred: great, small and middling; fortunate and unfortunate; apt and inept; lively and sluggish; sharp and blunt; fiery, earthy and temperate; ordinary and extraordinary; precocious, late and mature. This diversity depends not so much on the qualities of bodies as on the providence of God, and likewise on diligent cultivation. For it is as Hippocrates said: the relation that seed bears to the soil is the same relation that knowledge bears to the human mind. Nor is that soil everywhere the same; although some is rich and fertile, it must still be cultivated, and one must consider for which seed it is more suitable. But even this is not enough. A suitable time for sowing must be awaited; soon after the seed has sprouted it must be weeded, and much labour and time must be spent on it so that it may ripen. Hence Clement of Alexandria in the Paedagogue, calling our minds animated fields, showed that men are subject to the same diversities to which fields are subject.
