It is therefore necessary, in the examination and cultivation of wits, to weigh carefully the inclination of nature toward which each is borne, and prudently and humbly to know one's own gifts. Finally, one should envy no one the gifts of mind received from God, but rather embrace and imitate them. For since God freely distributes to each his talent, Matt. 25:14ff., if he does not give all things to all, one must not say, "Why did you make me thus?" Rather each must cultivate his own field, from which no more is to be exacted in tribute than is fitting. Moreover under wit we include docility [εὐμάθειαν] and acuteness [ἀγχίνοιαν]. The second requirement of a pupil is love, by which he ought to embrace the teacher and be borne with his whole impulse, as if by magnetic contact, toward the thing to be learned. Love should be followed by admiration, by which the pupil esteems both the teacher and the subject to be learned so highly that he places both above the common crowd. From this it follows that in a qualified pupil one requires that he first choose a teacher who is learned and faithful; second, embrace him with affection; third, listen to him constantly; fourth, question him often; fifth, give credence to his words; and finally imitate him in those things that are praiseworthy. Nor have you grounds to object to us the self-taught wits, since such are rare. Otherwise, under wit, love and admiration we embrace all the requisites of a sober pupil, such as a propensity for the thing to be learned, docility, acuteness, awareness of one's ignorance, love of labour [φιλοπονία], abstinence from pleasures, freedom from disturbing passions, and absence of cares and anxieties, and so on, about which Bonnaeus, in his treatise On the Method of Learning, treats carefully.

units.la: VI. Res didacticæ sunt primariæ, vel secun- dariæ.
units.tr: VI. The objects of teaching are either primary or secondary.

units.la: Res primariæ sunt illa ipsa, quæ doceri & discì debent: ubi tenentur istæ regulæ:
units.tr: The primary objects are those very things which ought to be taught and learned, and for them these rules hold:

units.la: 1. Non nisi unum uno tempore. Proinde nonnisi una materia uno die, & nonnisi unus author in unâ re.
units.tr: 1. Only one thing at a time. Therefore only one subject on one day, and only one author on one topic.

units.la: 2. Omnia discuntor per notiora siue priora.
units.tr: 2. Everything is learned through what is better known or prior.

units.la: 3. Omnis superfluitas vitanda. Itaque Nihil dediscendum discitor: & Nihil, quod caret usu, discitor.
units.tr: 3. Every superfluity is to be avoided. Therefore nothing is to be unlearned, and nothing that lacks use is to be learned.

units.la: 4. Biblia sacra sunto centrum omnis doctrinæ. Itaque Nihil admittitor, quod cum hoc canone pugnat.
units.tr: 4. Holy Scripture is to be the centre of all teaching. Therefore nothing is to be admitted that conflicts with this canon.

units.la: 5. Omnia docentor harmonicè.
units.tr: 5. Everything is to be taught harmoniously.

units.la: 6. Universalia docentor prius quam singularia.
units.tr: 6. Universals are to be taught before particulars.

units.la: 7. Universalia docentor in singularibus, adeoque totum in partibus. 8. Notitia confusa præcedat distinctam.
units.tr: 7. Universals are to be taught in particulars, and so the whole in the parts. 8. Confused knowledge should precede distinct knowledge.

units.la: 9. Magis necessaria, & faciliora prius docentor.
units.tr: 9. What is more necessary and easier is to be taught first.

units.la: Res subsidiaria sunt variæ circumstantiæ, quæ seruiunt rebus palmariis. Huc pertinent museum, bibliotheca, diæta, libri, & similia, de quibus sunt hæc axiomata:
units.tr: The secondary objects are various circumstances that serve the principal objects. To these belong the museum, the library, diet, books and the like, concerning which these axioms hold:

units.la: 1. Museum amœnum & mundum esto.
units.tr: 1. The museum should be pleasant and clean.

units.la: 2. Bibliotheca complectatur libros rares & selectos.
units.tr: 2. The library should contain rare and select books.

units.la: 3. In libris comparetur memoria localis.
units.tr: 3. A memory of place should be formed from the books.

units.la: 4. Charta sit munda, & typus elegans in libris excusis, itemq; in manuscriptis.
units.tr: 4. The paper should be clean, and the type elegant, in printed books and likewise in manuscripts.

units.la: 5. Situs rei discenda ornatè in libro dispositus esto.
units.tr: 5. The matter to be learned should be arranged elegantly in the book.

units.la: 6. Aer corrigatur per suffitum, flores, & ambram griseam balsamus mnemonicus naribus applicetur: aloë & cubebæ in vsu sint frequenti.
units.tr: 6. The air should be corrected by fumigation, flowers, and grey ambergris; mnemonic balm should be applied to the nostrils; aloes and cubebs should be in frequent use.

units.la: VII. Actiones didacticæ sunt commoratio & peregrinatio literata.
units.tr: VII. The actions of teaching are the literary sojourn and the literary journey.

units.la: Commorationis literatæ axiomata hæc sunt:
units.tr: The axioms of the literary sojourn are these:

units.la: 1. Omne tædium in docendo & discendo quam diligentissimè vitator. Itaque Quotidie nonnisi octo horæ studiis impenduntur; & hæ illæ quidem vel integræ, vel continuæ, sed certis recreationibus distinctæ, ita ut ultra quadrantem horæ nō detineas mentem in lectione, scriptione, aut meditatione, sed interponas aliquod veluti sabbatum, & postea redeas ad studium. Quòd si etiam accidat, ut hâc horâ sentias te non satis dispositum, differ negotium in aliud tempus. Nam ut dies, sic etiam hora, quandoque parens, quandoque nouerca est.
units.tr: 1. Every weariness in teaching and learning is to be avoided with the greatest diligence. Therefore only eight hours a day are devoted to study; these hours are indeed either whole or continuous, but divided by certain recreations, so that you do not hold the mind to reading, writing or meditation for more than a quarter of an hour, but interpose some sort of sabbath and afterwards return to study. But if it happens that at this hour you feel you are not sufficiently disposed, postpone the business to another time. For as the day, so also the hour is sometimes a parent, sometimes a stepmother.

units.la: 2. In discipulo nullum sit præiudicium.
units.tr: 2. In the learner there is to be no prejudice.

units.la: 3. Experientia nulla authoritas præiudicet, neque consuetudo aut præconcepta opinio præualeat.
units.tr: 3. No authority of experience is to prejudge, nor is custom or a preconceived opinion to prevail.

units.la: 4. Omnia fiant absq; violentia.
units.tr: 4. Everything is to be done without violence.

units.la: 5. Non omnia, quæ discenda sunt, simul obiciantur intellectui.
units.tr: 5. Not all the things that are to be learned should be presented to the intellect at once.

units.la: 6. Prima repræsentatio, quæ fit intellectui, sit accurata.
units.tr: 6. The first representation that is made to the intellect should be accurate.

units.la: 7. Repetitio sit crebra & continua: ita nempe, ut fiat cū eleuatione mentis ad Deum, cum imaginatione obiećti, cum ordine inuariabili, cum instantiâ laboris, ita vt singulis prope horis repetamus ea quæ didicimus. Porrò repetitio ista erit socia vel solitaria; summaria vel plena; cursoria vel fixa; horaria, diurna, hebdomadaria, menstrua, semestris; explicatiua vel applicatiua; nuda vel extensa, & hæc analytica, epistolica, dialogistica,&c.
units.tr: 7. Repetition should be frequent and continual: namely, so that it is done with a lifting up of the mind to God, with imagination of the object, with an unvarying order, with urgency of labour, so that we repeat what we have learned almost every hour. Moreover, this repetition will be either shared or solitary; summary or full; cursory or fixed; hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, half-yearly; explanatory or applicative; bare or extended, and this in analytic, epistolary, dialogic forms, and so on.

units.la: 8. Discendum est visu & auditu simul.
units.tr: 8. One must learn by sight and hearing together.

units.la: 9. Nihil est dimittendum prius, quàm solidè sit perceptum.
units.tr: 9. Nothing is to be abandoned before it has been solidly perceived.

units.la: 10. Studium cuiusque artis in certa interualla siue partes distribuitor.
units.tr: 10. The study of each art is to be distributed into set intervals or parts.

units.la: 11. Id, quod præ manibus habes, ita vt velis firmiter tibi imprimere, id, inquam,
units.tr: 11. Whatever you have at hand, so that you wish to imprint it firmly upon yourself, that, I say,

units.la: Primò describe eleganter:
units.tr: First, describe it elegantly;

units.la: Deinde, ita descriptum clarâ voce lege:
units.tr: Then, having so written it down, read it aloud;

units.la: Tertiò, aliquoties relege:
units.tr: Third, read it over several times;

units.la: Quarto, per partes edìsce:
units.tr: Fourth, build it up part by part;

units.la: Quinto, memoriter recita:
units.tr: Fifth, recite it from memory;

units.la: Sextò, epistolam, dialogum, disputationem, declamationem, aut simile quippiam de illâ materia compone:
units.tr: Sixth, compose a letter, dialogue, disputation, declamation, or something similar on that matter;

units.la: Septimò, quotidiè repete.
units.tr: Seventh, repeat it daily.

units.la: Hi sunt septem gradus scalæ didacticæ, per quos oportet quotidie ascendere & descendere quàm solicitissimè.
units.tr: These are the seven steps of the didactic ladder, by which it is necessary to ascend and descend every day with the greatest care.

units.la: 12. Auditio sit attenta, benevola & repetita : illamque excipiat analysis, crisis, & eclogæ.
units.tr: 12. Hearing should be attentive, benevolent and repeated; and it should be followed by analysis, criticism and selection.

units.la: 13. Lectio sit certa, ordinata, attenta, repetita, sonora, & moderata: illamque excipiat analysis, crisis, & eclogæ. Cæterum tria sint interualla lectionis. Primum esto lectionis incipientis à compendio: secundum, progredientis ad locos communes: tertium, variæ, peruoluentis multos authores.
units.tr: 13. Reading should be certain, orderly, attentive, repeated, audible and moderate; and it should be followed by analysis, criticism and selection. Moreover, there should be three stages of reading. The first is that of the beginner, starting from a compendium; the second is that of one making progress, toward commonplaces; the third is that of the varied reader who peruses many authors.

units.la: 14. Collatio sit publica, priuata, epistolaris, symposiaca, &c. & instituatur cum præceptore, æqualibus, & peritioribus.
units.tr: 14. Conference should be public, private, by letter, at symposia, and so on, and should be held with a tutor, with peers, and with those more skilled.

units.la: 15. Meditatio sit logica.
units.tr: 15. Meditation should be logical.

units.la: 16. Scriptio fiat vel ediscendi gratiâ, vel styli causâ, vel conseruationis ergò, quò pertinent loci communes, de quibus hac tenenda est regula: Loci communes parentur in ea disciplina, in qua cupimus excellere: & ita parentur, vt sequamur ductum alicuius systematis methodici: denique non semel & simul impleantur, sed per interualla, adnotatis solùm iis, quæ sunt rariora.
units.tr: 16. Writing is done either for the sake of learning by heart, or for the sake of style, or for the sake of preservation; to the last belong commonplaces, concerning which this rule is to be kept: commonplaces should be prepared in that discipline in which we wish to excel, and they should be prepared so that we follow the guidance of some methodical system; finally, they should not be filled in once and all at the same time, but at intervals, noting only those things that are rarer.

units.la: Peregrinationis literatæ axiomata hæc sunt:
units.tr: The axioms of the literary journey are these:

units.la: 1. De fine peregrinationis diu multumq; cogitato, & prudentium quoque amicorum consilio hac in parte utere.
units.tr: 1. Think long and hard about the aim of the journey, and in this matter make use also of the counsel of prudent friends.

units.la: 2. Inperegrinando diligens & intelligens esto.
units.tr: 2. In travelling, be diligent and intelligent.

units.la: 3. Tum demum ad peregrinandum appelle animum, quando iecisti fundamenta solida doctrina; & tam diu emaneto, donec fructum & scopum peregrinationis tuæ sis assecutus[?].
units.tr: 3. Then at last turn your mind to travelling, when you have laid the solid foundations of learning; and let it remain so long until you have attained the fruit and aim of your journey[?].

units.la: 4. In diario notato quæ inter peregrinandum occurrunt insigniora.
units.tr: 4. In a diary, note the more remarkable things that occur while travelling.

units.la: 5. Doctum & pium peregrinationis socium delige.
units.tr: 5. Choose a learned and pious companion for the journey.

units.la: 6. Accurate dispice, quanam tibi adeunda sint loca: & partim ex doctis viris atq; amicis, partim ex libris geographicis cognosce, quid in hoc vel illo loco sit imprimis obseruandum.
units.tr: 6. Examine carefully which places you must visit, and learn from learned men and friends in part, and from geographical books in part, what is especially to be observed in this or that place.

units.la: 7. Illorum amicitiam & beneuolentiam tibi concilia, qui à ra-rà eruditione commendantur[?].
units.tr: 7. Win for yourself the friendship and goodwill of those who are recommended for their rare learning[?].

units.la: 8. Peregrinatio literata, sit vel grammatica, sive philologica, h.e. linguarum exoticarum causâ suscipiatur: vel topica, h.e. cognoscendorum locorum causâ instituatur: vel ethica, i.e. morum causâ perficiatur: vel pragmatica, h.e. suscipiatur rerum ipsarum causâ, quæ in singulis locis raræ visu auditue reperiuntur. Peregrinatio valetudinaria, militaris, & religiosa non conuenit literarum studiolo, quâ tali.
units.tr: 8. The literary journey is to be undertaken either grammatical or philological, that is, for the sake of foreign languages; or topical, that is, carried out for the sake of knowing places; or ethical, that is, accomplished for the sake of manners; or pragmatic, that is, undertaken for the sake of the things themselves which are rarely found in each place, by sight or by hearing. A journey for health, a military journey, and a religious journey do not suit the study of letters as such.

units.la: Et hactenus quidem vidimus ea, quæ quatuor facultatibus sunt communia: deinceps singulas persequemur, quatenus quidem in Iacris[?] literis ipsarum vestigia occurrunt.
units.tr: And so far indeed we have seen those things which are common to the four faculties; henceforth we shall pursue each one, insofar as traces of them occur in the sacred letters.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: PHILOSOPHIA IN GENERE
units.tr: Philosophy in general

units.la: I. PHilosophia est vera, vel falsa. Hæc distinctio fundata est Rom. 1. v. 19. 20. 21. & c. 2. v. 14. 15.
units.tr: I. Philosophy is either true or false. This distinction is grounded in Rom. 1. v. 19. 20. 21. &c., and c. 2. v. 14. 15.

units.la: II. Philosophia vera est theoretica, vel practica. Hæc diuisio lucem accipit ex celebri isto Vrim & Thummim Exod. 28. vers. 30. Nam Vrim, id est, lucus, significat lumen intellectus: Thummim, id est, perfectiones siue integritates, significat rectitudinem voluntatis. Verus itaq; philosophus est, qui coniungit Vrim & Thummim. Idē iudicium est de theologo, medico & iurisconsulto: qui omnes ita debent instituere actiones suas, ut congruant ad Vrim & Thummim.
units.tr: II. True philosophy is either theoretical or practical. This division takes its light from the famous Urim and Thummim, Exod. 28. vers. 30. For Urim, that is, lights, signifies the light of the intellect; Thummim, that is, perfections or integrities, signifies the uprightness of the will. The true philosopher, therefore, is the one who joins Urim and Thummim. The same judgment holds for the theologian, the physician and the jurist: all of them ought to order their actions so that they agree with Urim and Thummim.

units.la: III. Philosophia theoretica docet rectam contemplationem operum, siue magnaliū, Dei, ita nimirum, vt ex operibus istis colligat, Deum esse, & esse potentem, æternum &c. Rom. 1. vers. 19. 20. Hoc est, quod Plato docuit, gratissimam de Deo famam in artibus esse sparsam.
units.tr: III. Theoretical philosophy teaches the right contemplation of the works of God, or of his great works, so that from these works one may infer that God exists, and that he is powerful, eternal, and so on. Rom. 1. vers. 19. 20. This is what Plato taught, that a most gracious report of God had been scattered abroad in the arts.

units.la: IV. Philosophia practica docet rectum vsum legis naturæ, Rom. 2. vers. 14. 15. Ita nimirum, vt hominem contineat in officio iustitiæ vniuersalis, cuius dictamen impressum est cordibus nostris.
units.tr: IV. Practical philosophy teaches the right use of the law of nature. Rom. 2. vers. 14. 15. It does so in such a way as to keep a man within the duty of universal justice, whose dictate has been impressed on our hearts.

units.la: V. Philosophia falsa est, quæ vel obscurat legem siue lumen naturæ, vel se opponit lumini gratiæ siue euangelio. De priori abusu vide Rom. 1. v. 21. & seqq. de posteriori 1. Cor. 1. vers. 20. 26. & c. 2. v. 1. 4.6.13. Act. 17. vers. 18. Vbi fit mentio philosophorum Epicureorum & Stoicorum, qui Paulo bellum indixerunt. Confer Coloss. 2, v. 8. vbi apostolus ait: Videte, ne quis vos decipiat per philosophiam & inanem fallaciam, secundum traditionem hominum, secundum elementa mundi, & non secundum Christum. Hunc apostoli locum explanans Tertullianus lib. de præscriptionibus aduersus hæreticos cap. 7. dicit, apostolum fuisse Athenis, & istam sapientiam humanam, affectatricem, & interpolatricem veritatis, de congressibus nouisse, ipsam quoque in suas hæreses multipartitam varietate sectarum inuicem repugnantium. Idem de anima cap. 3. ait: Athenis expertus linguarum civitatem, cum omnes illic sapientiae atque facundiae caupones degustas-set, inde concepit præmonitorium illud edictum. His verbis damnat Tertullianus artem illam ταρικχὴν[?] (quam alibi vocat struendi & destruendi versipellem artificem) quæ probabilia tantum consectans nusquam pedem figit. Hanc philosophiam lib. de anima appellat concussionem veritatis: & lib. aduersus Hermogenem cap. 8. huius philosophiæ professores philosophos appellat Patriarchas hæreticorum. At doctrinam rectè differendi ipsemet Tertullianus accuratè est persecutus. Ita Moses universam sapientiam Ægyptiorum didicit & excoluit. Act. 7. 22. Et apostolus Paulus educatus ad pedes Gamalielis sapientiæ & eloquentiæ studia coniunxit. Act. 22. vers. 3. cap. 17. vers. 22. ad vers. 30. Verè itaque dictum est à Nazianzeno orat. ad 150. episcopos, veritatem logicis disputationibus tritam in lucè proferri: & à Basilio in 5. cap. Esaiæ, dialecticæ virtutem esse, naturas rerum distinctè diuidere, quæ sunt affinia dignoscere, & discernere contraria. Cum his consentit illud Augustini lib. 3. contra Academicos: Si dialectica est scientia veritatis, sic illam nouit sapiens, ut sophistarum calunias contemnendo enecet. Placet hoc loco insignem locum adscribere ex Nicephoro, lib. 8. hist. eccles. cap. 39. Veluti arcana, & diuina quaedam res cœlitus ad homines delapsa est Christiana philosophia: quippe quæ & disciplinarum artes, & disputationum nugas, ut quæ superuacaneæ sint, otium, quod in studiis melioribus poni queat, sibi vendicent, impedimentoque adeo ad puritatem vitæ sint, prorsus negligat: solaque naturâ vtens virtute, ea, quæ ad illam perficiendam, & ad vitia tollenda faciunt, doceat & excolat: quæ vero inter hæc habentur media, eorum nullam ducat rationem: prorsus autem circa res versetur honestas: atque eos, qui à vitiis longè absint, virtutem autem minus consectentur, prauos atque improbos censeat. Non enim ostentationem, sed actionem virtutis admittit: nihilque prorsus eam, quæ ab hominibus prouenit, gloriam faciens. Et cum generosè fortiterque animæ perturbationes expugnat, tum necessarias naturæ res non supra modū curat, vilipendens etiam quascunque corporis imbecillitates. Viribus autem à divinâ mente acceptis, ad immortalem illam mentem sublimis tollitur, nocte dieque illam cogitans atque intuens: mirificis etiam modis colens, continuisque precibus concilians. Puritate vero animi, bonorumque operum factis, ad sinceritatem religionis grassans, externas expiationes, & quascunque eius generis sunt lustrationes despuit, & unum piaculum esse peccatum ipsum putat. Atque ita rebus externis superior facta, imperiumque, ut ita dicam, in eas obtinens, neque ab inordinata vita, neque ab ulla necessitate, ab honesto debitoque proposito suo transuersa agitur, neque contumeliis affecta perturbatur. Sed neq; indignum quidquam patiens, vindictam meditatur. Tantum etiam abest, ut vel morbus, vel rerum necessariarum inopia eam adurgens, de statu suo deturbet, ut talibus quoque aerumnis magis laetetur, generositatem & mansuetudinem suam declarans. Per vitam itidem omnem illud studet, ut quam minimo indigeat, atque quantum natura humana captus permittit, proxime ad Deum accedere nititur. Transfitum[?] autem siue diuerticulum praesentem exi∫timans esse vitam, neque occupationibus negotiorum irretitur, neque prouidentia rerum praesentium tenetur. Et habitum hominis succinctum expeditumque, qui nullis sit superfluis rebus oneratus, laudans, ad futuram respicit beatitudinem, felicemque illam quietem expectat: omni quoque erga Deum pietate, in animo suo, veluti in domicilio, exceptâ, verborum fœditatem, ut rem ingratam, repudiat. Quas enim illa actiones a moribus suis longe proscripsit, earum neq; mentionem verbis facere sustinet. Natura vero necessitates paulatim constringens, ut carnem moderatione domans, lasciuiam castitate comprimit, iniustitiam aequitatis amusi propellit, mendacium exigit veritate, composito viuendi more omnem accidit inaequalitatem. Familiarius etiam pro societate humanâ se hominum moribus accommodando, & proximorum animis conformando, bene viuendi institutum confirmat: extraneorum simul & amicorum, ut eis prouideat, curam habet: egentium res suas & opes ducit esse comunes, &, cuicunque debentur, tribuit. Gaudet illa cum gaudentibus, mœrentibus nihil non adhibet consolationis. In summâ, ad id, quod reuerâ summum bonum est, studium omne conuertens, sermonibus castis, & cogitationibus spiritualibus, seipsam erudit, cultum formæ superfluum prorsus negligit, maledicta magnopere auersatur: colloquia cum veneratione & honoris præfatione ingreditur, auditorem prius veluti medicamento curans. Longe ab eâ abest iracundia, conuicium, iurgium. Quòd enim vera ratione prædita est, irrationalem omnem declinat motum: &, vt semel dicam, perturbationum, quæ vel in anima, vel in corpore sunt, omnium domina existit. Hæc Nicephor. de sanâ & Christianâ philosophiâ. De profanæ & vanæ philosophiæ cum sanâ collatione accipe illud Iohannis Mosci in prato spirituali cap. 156.
units.tr: V. False philosophy is that which either obscures the law, or the light of nature, or sets itself against the light of grace, that is, the gospel. On the former abuse see Rom. 1. v. 21. and following; on the latter, 1. Cor. 1. vers. 20. 26. and c. 2. v. 1. 4. 6. 13. Act. 17. vers. 18. where mention is made of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers, who declared war on Paul. Compare Col. 2. v. 8. where the apostle says: See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ. Explaining this passage of the apostle, Tertullian, in his book On Prescription against Heretics, chapter 7, says that the apostle had been at Athens and had learned from encounters there that this human wisdom, a seeker after and corrupter of truth, has itself been divided into many parts by the variety of sects that contradict one another. In his book On the Soul, chapter 3, he says: having experienced at Athens the city of tongues, when he had tasted all the tavern-keepers of wisdom and eloquence there, he took from that the warning edict. With these words Tertullian condemns that art, called in Greek [ταραχήν] (which elsewhere he calls the shifty craftsman of building up and tearing down), which pursues only probabilities and never plants its foot anywhere. In the book On the Soul he calls this philosophy a shaking of truth; and in the book Against Hermogenes, chapter 8, he calls the professors of this philosophy the patriarchs of the heretics. But Tertullian himself carefully pursued the doctrine of disputing rightly. So Moses learned and cultivated all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Acts 7. 22. And the apostle Paul, educated at the feet of Gamaliel, joined the study of wisdom with that of eloquence. Acts 22. vers. 3; c. 17. vers. 22 to vers. 30. Rightly, therefore, did Nazianzen say, in his oration to the 150 bishops, that truth is brought into the light by logical disputations that have been well trodden; and Basil, on the fifth chapter of Isaiah, that the virtue of dialectic is to divide the natures of things distinctly, to recognise what is related, and to discern what is opposed. With these agrees that saying of Augustine, in book 3 against the Academics: If dialectic is the science of truth, then the wise man knows it in such a way that by despising the sophists' calumnies he puts them to death. It is fitting here to add a notable passage from Nicephorus, Ecclesiastical History, book 8, chapter 39. "Like some hidden and divine thing come down from heaven to men is Christian philosophy: for it claims for itself neither the arts of the disciplines nor the trifles of disputations, as being superfluous, nor the leisure which could be spent on better studies, and it altogether neglects them as hindrances to purity of life; using only natural virtue, it teaches and cultivates those things which tend to perfect that virtue and to remove vices. As for the things that are held to be intermediate, it takes no account of them; it is altogether occupied with honourable matters, and it judges those who keep far from vices but pursue virtue less eagerly to be depraved and wicked. For it admits not the display but the practice of virtue, and it makes nothing of the glory that comes from men. And when it bravely and nobly overcomes the disturbances of the soul, it also does not care excessively for the necessary things of nature, despising also all the weaknesses of the body. But with the powers received from the divine mind it is lifted up to that immortal mind, thinking upon it and gazing on it night and day, honouring it also in marvellous ways and winning it by continual prayers. By the purity of the soul and the doing of good works, pressing on to the sincerity of religion, it spurns external expiations and all lustrations of that kind, and holds that sin itself is the only pollution. And so, having become superior to external things and obtaining, as it were, dominion over them, it is driven from its honourable and due purpose neither by disordered living nor by any necessity, and when afflicted with insults it is not disturbed. Yet suffering nothing unworthy, it does not plan revenge. So far is it from being cast down from its condition by sickness or by lack of necessary things pressing upon it, that it rejoices all the more in such afflictions, declaring its nobility and gentleness. Throughout its whole life it also strives to need as little as possible, and, as far as the capacity of human nature allows, it endeavours to draw as near to God as it can. Judging life to be a passing or a resting-place, it is entangled neither in the business of affairs nor held by the care of present things. Praising the habit of a man girded and ready, burdened with no superfluous things, it looks to future blessedness and awaits that happy rest; with all piety towards God it keeps him, as in a dwelling, in its own mind, and as for the foulness of words, it rejects them as an unpleasant thing. For those actions which it has long banished from its manners, it does not suffer itself even to mention in words. Gradually restraining the necessities of nature, mastering the flesh by moderation, it checks lasciviousness by chastity, drives out injustice by the rule of equity, exacts truthfulness from lying, and by a composed manner of living it removes all inequality. Accommodating itself more familiarly to human fellowship, adapting itself to the minds of its neighbours, it strengthens the purpose of living well; it takes care to provide for strangers and friends alike; it counts the goods of the needy as common property and gives to whomever is owed. It rejoices with those who rejoice, and for those who mourn it applies every kind of consolation. In sum, turning all its zeal to that which is truly the highest good, it instructs itself by chaste words and spiritual thoughts, altogether neglects superfluous care of appearance, shrinks greatly from curses; it enters conversations with reverence and a preface of honour, first healing the hearer as with a medicine. Anger, reproach and quarrelling are far from it. For since it is endowed with true reason, it avoids every irrational motion; and, to say it once, it is mistress of all the disturbances that are either in the soul or in the body." These are Nicephorus's words on sound and Christian philosophy. For a comparison of profane and vain philosophy with the sound kind, take that passage of John Moschus in the Spiritual Meadow, chapter 156.

units.la: Duo, inquit, philosophi accedentes ad senem quendam, cum orabant, vt eis verbum ædificationis diceret. Senex verò silebat. Tum philosophi, Nihil respondes nobis, pater? At senex, Quod sitis, inquit, eloquentiæ studiosi, non ignoro, quod autem non veri sitis philosophi affirmo. Quamdiu enim loqui didicitis, quasi loqui nesciatis? Sit ergo philosophia vestra opus, semper meditari mortem: silentioque & quieti vos assuefacite.
units.tr: Two philosophers, he says, came to an old man and asked him to speak a word of edification to them. But the old man kept silent. Then the philosophers said, "Will you not answer us, father?" And the old man said, "I am not unaware that you are lovers of eloquence, but I affirm that you are not true philosophers. For how long have you learned to speak, as if you did not know how to speak? Let your philosophy therefore be the work of meditating on death always, and accustom yourselves to silence and quiet."

units.la: VI. Philosophia vera duos habet gradus. Aut enim ex veris gentilium dogmatis colligitur, aut ex sacris literis extruitur. Illa vulgaris, hæc adepta dicitur. De vulgari pronuntiat Clemens Alexandrinus, illam esse βαθμὸν ἡ ὑποβαθρὸν τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ φιλοσοφίας[?], gradum & scalam Christianæ philosophiæ: recte & vere, si appellatione philosophiæ illud intelligit, quod Paulus nominat τὸ γνωστὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ Rom. 1. verf. 19. opera nempe Dei, quæ mortales ad creatoris aliquam notitiam possunt perducere, & amplioris cognitionis desiderium, si mens ipsis non læva, in eorum animis ingenerare. Verum Clemens philosophiæ nomine eiusmodi notitiam intelligit, per quam ad iustificationem & vitam æternam posset peruenire. Affirmat hoc differte lib.1. Στρωματέων, h.e. Centonum seu Stragulorum: καθ' ἑαυτὴν ἐδικαίου ποτὲ ἡ φιλοσοφία τὰς Ἑλληνικὰς[?], philosophia quondam per se Græcos iustificabat. At qui operum Dei notitia sine cognitione Christi non est satis ad salutem. Act. 4. verf. 12. Nimium itaque Clemens tribuit philosophiæ gentilium, puræ scil. & incontaminatæ. Nihil enim deferendum est philosophiæ ipsorum impuræ & contaminatæ, siue falsæ, quæ est κακοδαιμονικὴ[?] ψευδοσοφία[?]. Videamus nunc philosophiam adeptam. Ea sic dicitur, quia adipiscitur centrum veritatis ductu sacrarum literarum, in quibus nerui sapientiæ, prudentiæ, & eloquentiæ hincinde sese offerunt. Appellatur etiam philosophia sacra & Christiana. Quanquam hoc nomine interdum etiam venit ipsa theologia.
units.tr: VI. True philosophy has two grades. It is either gathered from the true doctrines of the Gentiles or built up from the holy letters. The former is called common, the latter acquired. Concerning the common kind, Clement of Alexandria pronounces that it is a step and ladder [βαθμὸν ἢ ὑποβάθρον τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ φιλοσοφίας] to the Christian philosophy, and he is right and true if by the name of philosophy he understands what Paul calls "that which is known of God" (Rom. 1. v. 19), namely the works of God, which can lead mortals to some knowledge of the Creator and kindle in their minds, if the mind is not perverse, a desire for fuller knowledge. But Clement understands by the name of philosophy a knowledge of this kind through which one could attain justification and eternal life. He asserts this in the first book of the Stromata, that is, Patchworks or Coverlets: "Philosophy once justified the Greeks by itself" [φιλοσοφία ποτὲ τοὺς Ἕλληνας καθ' ἑαυτὴν ἐδικαίου]. Yet knowledge of God's works without knowledge of Christ is not enough for salvation (Acts 4. v. 12). Clement therefore ascribes too much to the philosophy of the Gentiles, namely the pure and undefiled kind. For nothing should be conceded to their impure and defiled philosophy, or rather their false wisdom, which is demonic [κακοδαιμονικὴ ψευδοσοφία]. Let us now look at the acquired philosophy. It is so called because it attains the centre of truth by the guidance of the holy letters, in which the sinews of wisdom, prudence and eloquence present themselves on every side. It is also called holy and Christian philosophy, although under this name theology itself sometimes comes.

units.la: VII. Vera philosophia est facultas, ambitu suo complexa eas disciplinas, quarum vsus est in tribus superioribus facultatibus. Facultas est vis agendi expedita: vt est facultas intelligendi & volendi. Hinc artes & scientiæ appellantur facultates: quia reddunt hominem expeditum ad agendum ea, quæ homine ingenuo sunt digna. Nominatim philosophia & theologia, iurisprudentia & medicina, hoc nomine insigniuntur per excellentiam. Et philosophia quidem est veluti metropolis, ex quâ deducuntur coloniæ & propagines principiorum & conclusionum, quibus vtuntur tres superiores facultates. Certè prophetæ & apostoli interdum ex intimâ philosophiâ petunt documenta insignia, vt ex sequentibus patebit. Vnum hoc loco adduxisse sufficiat. Christus Iohan. 12. verf. 24. egregium adhibet φιλοσοφικὸν ἀκρόαμα seu philosophicum acroama: Amen, Amen dico vobis, nisi granum frumenti ceciderit in terram, & mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet: si vero mortuum fuerit, multum fructum adfert. Hinc patet, veram philosophiam non pugnare cum theologia, sed ipsi ancillari. Vnde Patres theologiam comparârunt Sarae, veiam philosophiam Hagari obsequiosae, falsam Hagari elatae & refractariæ. Vera philosophia est dogmatica, h. est, dogmata & decreta scientifica ponit: falsa, est vel apatetica, quæ seducit; vel academica, quæ pleraque, vel sceptica, quæ omnia facit incerta,
units.tr: VII. True philosophy is the faculty which, within its compass, embraces those disciplines whose use lies in the three higher faculties. A faculty is a ready power of acting, as the faculty of understanding and of willing is. Hence the arts and sciences are called faculties, because they make a man ready to do those things that are worthy of a free-born person. By name, philosophy and theology, jurisprudence and medicine are distinguished by this title above all others. Philosophy is, as it were, the metropolis from which the colonies and offshoots of the principles and conclusions used by the three higher faculties are led out. Certainly the prophets and apostles sometimes draw remarkable teachings from inner philosophy, as will be clear from what follows; it is enough to adduce one example here. Christ, in John 12. v. 24, uses a fine philosophical discourse [φιλοσοφικὸν ἀκρόαμα], or philosophical saying: "Verily, verily I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." From this it is plain that true philosophy does not fight with theology but serves it as a handmaid. Hence the Fathers likened theology to Sarah, true philosophy to the obedient Hagar, and false philosophy to the proud and rebellious Hagar. True philosophy is dogmatic, that is, it lays down doctrines and scientific decrees; false philosophy is either apathetic, which deceives, or academic, which doubts most things, or sceptical, which makes everything uncertain,

units.la: VII. PRIMA PHILOSOPHIA SEV ME- taphysica Sacra.
units.tr: VII. FIRST PHILOSOPHY, OR SACRED METAPHYSICS

units.la: I. PHilosophiam vidimus in genere: philosophia in specie est prima, vel orta.
units.tr: I. We have considered philosophy in general. Philosophy in particular is either first philosophy or derived philosophy.

units.la: II. Prima philosophia vulgo appellatur metaphysica, quae est scientia entis qua ens, hoc est, entis universè, sive notionum primarum generalissimarum: id est, istorum terminorum, qui de omnibus in universum rebus enuntiantur, quibusque vtuntur omnes facultates & scientiae, ut sunt ens, unum, verum, bonum, actus, potentia, &c. Per res intellige entia positiva, non verò defectus rerum. Trademus autem metaphysicam sacram, quae est scientia entis universè, sumta ex s.[?] literis.
units.tr: II. First philosophy is commonly called metaphysics. It is the science of being as being, that is, of being in general, or of the most general first notions: namely, those terms which are predicated of all things in general and which all faculties and sciences use, such as being, one, true, good, act, potency, etc. By things I understand positive beings, not the lacks of things. We shall set out sacred metaphysics, which is the science of being in general, drawn from the sacred letters.

units.la: III. Notiones primae generalissimae sunt fi-gna convenientiae & differentiae omnium rerum.
units.tr: III. The first and most general notions are signs of the agreement and difference of all things.

units.la: IV. Suntque vel transcendentia, vel praedicamenta. Unde prima philosophia distribuitur in partem communem de transcendentibus, & propriam de praedicamentis.
units.tr: IV. They are either transcendentals or predicaments. Hence first philosophy is divided into a common part, concerning the transcendentals, and a proper part, concerning the predicaments.

units.la: V. Transcendentia sunt notiones sive vocabula omnibus praedicamentis communia. Hinc ita dicuntur, quòd transcendant seriem praedicamentalem. Sic Gen. 1. v. vlt. dicitur, omnia Dei opera fuisse valde bona: quod de substantiis & accidentibus verum est.
units.tr: V. Transcendentals are notions or terms common to all predicaments. They are so called because they transcend the series of predicaments. Thus Gen. 1. v. vlt. says that all God's works were very good, which is true of substances and accidents alike.

units.la: VI. Transcendentia sunt numero tria: ens, & entis momenta atque modi.
units.tr: VI. There are three transcendentals: being, and the moments and modes of being.

units.la: VII. Ens est, quod non est nihil. Vulgo definitur ens, quod habet essentiam. Sed accurate loquendo Deus non habet essentiam, sed est ipsa sua essentia. Proinde generaliter definiendum, vel potius vtcunque describendum, fuit ens, quod non est nihil: & quidem ita, ut vel sit ipsa sua essentia, vel differat à sua essentiâ. Priori modo solus Deus est ens: posteriori modo ens est, quidquid praeter Deum est. Ita homo est ens, in quo ens & essentia differunt ut concretum & abstractum, siue ut formatum & forma. Porrò entis vocabulum tam est nobile, ut Deus nomen suum proprium, & quidem proprium in quarto modo, inde formauerit. Nam יהוה Iehouah ducitur ab היה quod est esse. Similiter אהיה Eheieh Exod. 3. v. 14. Quod attinet ad nomen Iehouah, illud à LXX. vertitur ὁ ὢν: à Iohanne Apoc. 1. verse. 4. ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος & cap. 16. verf. 5. ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐσόμενος: aliis, ὁ ὢν καὶ ἅγιος, i.e. ens & essentiam dans, ita ut Iehoua sit nomen actus eius, quo Deus summe est, siue, ut Gregorius scitè loquitur, perest, & esse dat aliis suo modo. Unde clare perspicitur excellentia nominis ens: cui opponitur non-ens, τὸ μὴ ὄν, siue nihil. Solum ens est scientificum. Hinc omnes artes & scientiae occupantur circa ens. Quo pertinent istae locutiones, ens physicum, ens grammaticum, ens logicum, ens arithmeticum, &c. Rectè itaque dicitur, Non-entis non est scientia. Item, Non-entis nulla est causa, nullum effectum, subiectum, adiunctum, definitio, distributio.
units.tr: VII. Being is that which is not nothing. Commonly being is defined as that which has an essence. But, speaking strictly, God does not have an essence; he is his own essence. Therefore being must be defined generally, or rather described in some way, as that which is not nothing; and indeed in such a way that it either is its own essence or differs from its essence. In the first way only God is being; in the second way, being is whatever exists besides God. Thus a man is a being, in whom being and essence differ as the concrete and the abstract, or as the formed and the form. Moreover, the term being is so noble that God formed from it his own proper name, and indeed a proper name in the fourth mode. For Iehouah [יהוה] is derived from hayah [היה], which means to be. Similarly Eheieh [אהיה] at Exod. 3. v. 14. As for the name Iehouah, the Seventy translate it ho on [ὁ ὢν]; John at Apoc. 1. verse 4 has ho on, kai ho ēn, kai ho erchomenos [ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος], and at chapter 16, verse 5, ho on, kai ho ēn, kai ho esomenos [ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν, καὶ ὁ ἐσόμενος]. Others have ho on kai hagios [ὁ ὢν καὶ ἅγιος], that is, the one who is and gives being and essence; so that Iehovah is the name of that act by which God supremely is, or, as Gregory aptly puts it, is of himself, and gives being to others in their own way. From this the excellence of the name being is clearly seen; its opposite is non-being [τὸ μὴ ὄν], or nothing. Only being is the object of science. Hence all the arts and sciences are concerned with being. To this belong such expressions as physical being, grammatical being, logical being, arithmetical being, etc. It is rightly said, There is no science of non-being. Likewise, non-being has no cause, no effect, no subject, no attribute, no definition, no division.

units.la: VIII. Momenta entis sunt, per quae illud est momento sum: hoc est, certis proprietatibus & viribus agendi praeditum. Omne siquidem ens ita est momentosum, siue alicuius momenti & pretij.
units.tr: VIII. The moments of being are those by which a thing is of moment, that is, endowed with certain properties and powers of acting. For every being is thus momentous, that is, of some weight and worth.

units.la: IX. Momenta entis duo sunt, essentia & existentia.
units.tr: IX. There are two moments of being, essence and existence.

units.la: X. Essentia est natura communis, seu primum entis momentum, quod efficit conuenientiam rei cum re. Haec itaque est fundamentum & radix eorum, quae se habent vt genus & species. Sic in Deo essentia est communis tribus personis: unde etiam proprietates & actiones essentiales sunt communes Patri, Filio, & Spiritui sancto. Similiter in Platone essentia est per quam Plato est homo. Essentia proprium est, non variare, sed semper & vbique sui esse similem. Vnde præceptaartium scribuntur de essentia siue de idea rerum v.g. rosæ, equi. Porro essentia est archetypa vel ectypa. Essentia archetypa rursus est absoluta, vt est essentia Dei: vel relatiua, vt est essentia ideæ diuinæ, quam Deus ab æterno concepit intra se, vt esset exemplar rerum extra Deum in tempore producendarum: quo sensu Eph. 1. ver. 4. apostolus dicit, Deum nos elegisse in Christo ante iactum mundi fundamentum. Essentia ectypa est, quæ respondet suæ ideæ: quomodo Deus Eph. 1. verf. 5. dicitur nos adoptasse in filios per Iesum Christum in sese pro beneuolo affectu voluntatis suæ. Confer Psal. 115. ver. 3. Act. 2. verf. 23. Eph. 1. verf. 11. cap. 3. verf. 11. Inter homines quoque visu venit, vt essentia sit archetypa vel ectypa: vt quando Moses iussus fuit facere tabernaculum iuxta exemplar ipsi ostensum in monte Exod. 25. verf. 9. 40. Heb. 8. verf. 5.
units.tr: X. Essence is the common nature, or the first moment of being, which makes a thing agree with other things. It is therefore the foundation and root of those things which stand as genus and species. So in God the essence is common to the three persons; hence the essential properties and actions are also common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Similarly in Plato the essence is that by which Plato is a man. A proper feature of essence is not to vary but always and everywhere to remain like itself. Hence the precepts of the arts are written concerning the essence, or idea, of things, for example of a rose or a horse. Further, essence is either archetypal or ectypal. An archetypal essence is again either absolute, as is the essence of God, or relative, as is the essence of the divine idea, which God conceived from eternity within himself, to be the pattern of things to be produced outside God in time. In this sense the apostle says at Eph. 1. verse 4 that God chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world. An ectypal essence is that which corresponds to its idea; thus God is said at Eph. 1. verse 5 to have adopted us as sons through Jesus Christ, in himself, according to the good pleasure of his will. Compare Ps. 115. verse 3; Acts 2. verse 23; Eph. 1. verse 11; Eph. 3. verse 11. Among men too it is seen that an essence may be archetypal or ectypal, as when Moses was commanded to make the tabernacle according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain, Exod. 25. verses 9, 40; Heb. 8. verse 5.

units.la: XI. Existentia est natura singularis, seu secundum entis momentum, quod efficit vltimam rei differentiam. Hæc itaque est fundamentum & radix eorum, quæ se habent vt individuum. Sic in Deo existentia est personalitas, a quâ proficiscuntur proprietates & actiones singulares, hoc est, singulis personis competentes: in Platone existentia est id, per quod Plato est talis homo, prædituspeculiari ingenio, temperamento, statura &c. Hinc existentia proprium est, admittere varietatem. Porro existentia in substantijs dicitur subsistentia: in accidentibus, inexistentia: in substantiis intelligentibus, personalitas. Subsistentia est inseparabilis a substantia: quia vt accidentis esse est inesse, id est, inhærere: sic substantiæ esse est per se subsistere. Alia est ratio personalitatis. Hæc siquidem potest separari a re, vt docet mysterium incarnationis Christi: vbi humana Christi natura est quidem substantia, sed non est persona. Porro existentiam immediatè sequitur duratio, quæ est perseueratio existentiæ, & in Deo est æternitas, in spiritibus æuum, in corporibus tempus.
units.tr: XI. Existence is the singular nature, or the second moment of being, which makes the last difference of a thing. It is therefore the foundation and root of those things which stand as individuals. So in God existence is personality, from which the singular properties and actions proceed, that is, those belonging to each single person. In Plato existence is that by which Plato is such a man, endowed with his own particular talent, temperament, stature, etc. Hence a proper feature of existence is to admit variety. Further, existence is called subsistence in substances, inexistence in accidents, and personality in intelligent substances. Subsistence is inseparable from substance, because just as the being of an accident is to inhere, that is, to be in something, so the being of a substance is to subsist through itself. The nature of personality is different. For this can be separated from the thing, as the mystery of Christ's incarnation teaches: where the human nature of Christ is indeed a substance but is not a person. Further, duration immediately follows existence; it is the perseverance of existence, and in God it is eternity, in spirits it is aeon, in bodies it is time.

units.la: XII. Modi entis sunt attributa gradum rei designantia. Si malis, ita defini: Modi sunt determinationes rei, tum quatenus est, vel fit, tum quatenus cognoscitur, vel cognoscenda datur. Hinc modi rerum neque sunt res ipsæ, neque componunt aut destruunt res, sed sunt affectiones rerum, quibus illæ ornantur, distinguuntur, & illustrantur. Sunt autem varij modi, hoc modo. 1. Modi essendi sunt, qui sequuntur essentiam, id est, naturam communem: vt sunt unitas, veritas, necessitas, contingentia. 2. Modi existendi sunt, qui sequuntur naturam singularem: vt sunt circumstantiæ cuiuslibet rei. 3. Modi subsistendi, in naturis intelligentibus sunt characteres personales, quibus persona distinguitur à persona vt Plato à Socrate: in naturis non intelligentibus sunt characteres indiuiduales, vt in Bucephalo. 4. Modi inessendi sunt, quibus vnum est in altero, vt causa in effecto, effectum in causa, adiunctum in subiecto, genus in specie, pars in toto, &c. Sic omnes creaturæ sunt in Deo, tanquam in causa omnipotente Act. 17. verf. 28. Rom. 11. verf. vlt. 5. Modi possendi sunt, quibus aliquid potest esse, agere, vel pati. 6. Modi agendi, seu operandi, sunt, quibus aliquid exerit vires suas. 7. Modi patiendi sunt, quibus aliquid recipit vires ab alio. 8. Modi habendi sunt, quibus aliquid habet substantiam, quantitatem, qualitatem, &c. Ita quoque causa habet effectum, effectum causam, subiectum adiunctum, adiunctum subiectum, genus speciem, &c. 9. Modi se habendi sunt, quibus aliquid se habet vel aliter, vel ad aliud. Ita homo se habet aliter in creatione, aliter in regeneratione: sed Deus creans & redimens non habet se aliter ac aliter, sed ita se habet ad aliud, vt non fiat alius. 10. Modi recipiendi sunt, quibus aliquid recipit rem sibi similem vel dissimilem: vt cùm terra recipit influxum cœli. 11. Modi considerandi sunt, quibus aliquid in hac vel illa disciplina expenditur: vt cum homo alio modo consideratur in medicina, alio in theologia.12. Modi intelligendi, seu apprehendendi, sunt, quibus aliquis aliquid intelligit pro naturæ suæ conditione: vt cùm homo pro modulo suo intelligit Dei essentiam, & attributa. 13. Modi significandi, seu accipiendi, sunt quibus aliquid accipitur in hac vel illa significatione. 14. Modi loquendi sunt, quibus aliquis peculiariter vtitur. Suntque populares, vel exquisiti. 15. Modi prædicandi, seu enuntiandi, sunt, qui certo artificio exprimunt modum essendi: vt, cùm Christus in eucharistiæ institutione de pane dicit, Hoc est corpus meum, est prædicatio sacramentalis. Ex his quindecim generibus modorum, decem priora pertinent ad primam philosophiam: vndecimum, duodecimum & decimumquartum, ad singulas facultates & disciplinas: decimum tertium, ad lexicam, grammaticam & rhetoricam: decimum quintum, ad logicam & reliquas facultates atque disciplinas.
units.tr: XII. The modes of being are attributes designating the degree of a thing. If you prefer, define it thus: modes are determinations of a thing, both insofar as it is or becomes, and insofar as it is or can be known. Hence the modes of things are neither the things themselves, nor do they compose or destroy things; rather they are affections of things, by which they are adorned, distinguished and illustrated. There are, however, various modes, as follows. (1) Modes of being are those that follow the essence, that is, the common nature, such as unity, truth, necessity, contingency. (2) Modes of existing are those that follow the singular nature, such as the circumstances of any given thing. (3) Modes of subsisting are, in intelligent natures, the personal characters by which one person is distinguished from another, as Plato from Socrates; in non-intelligent natures they are individual characters, as in Bucephalus. (4) Modes of inbeing are those by which one thing is in another, as a cause in its effect, an effect in its cause, an attribute in its subject, a genus in its species, a part in its whole, etc. Thus all creatures are in God, as in an omnipotent cause (Acts 17. verse 28; Rom. 11. last verse). (5) Modes of being able are those by which something can be, act, or suffer. (6) Modes of acting, or operating, are those by which something exerts its powers. (7) Modes of suffering are those by which something receives powers from another. (8) Modes of having are those by which something has substance, quantity, quality, etc. So too a cause has an effect, an effect a cause, a subject an attribute, an attribute a subject, a genus a species, etc. (9) Modes of relating are those by which something stands otherwise or in relation to something else. Thus man stands one way in creation and another way in regeneration; but God, creating and redeeming, does not stand otherwise and otherwise, but so stands towards another that he does not become other. (10) Modes of receiving are those by which something receives a thing like or unlike itself, as when the earth receives the influence of heaven. (11) Modes of considering are those by which something is examined in this or that discipline, as when man is considered one way in medicine and another way in theology. (12) Modes of understanding, or apprehending, are those by which someone understands something according to the condition of his nature, as when a man, according to his measure, understands the essence and attributes of God. (13) Modes of signifying, or of taking, are those by which something is taken in this or that meaning. (14) Modes of speaking are those which someone uses in a special way. These are either common or refined. (15) Modes of predicating, or of stating, are those which express by a certain art the mode of being; as when Christ, in instituting the Eucharist, says of the bread, This is my body, this is a sacramental predication. Of these fifteen kinds of modes, the first ten pertain to first philosophy; the eleventh, twelfth and fourteenth to the individual faculties and disciplines; the thirteenth to lexicography, grammar and rhetoric; and the fifteenth to logic and the remaining faculties and disciplines.

units.la: XIII. Modi entis sunt uniti, vel diuisi. Illi di-cuntur attributa entis simplicia & communissima, hi, primæ entis differentiæ, & attributa composita.
units.tr: XIII. The modes of being are either united or divided. The former are called the simple and most common attributes of being; the latter are the first differences of being, and composite attributes.

units.la: XIV. Attributa entis communissima sunt, quæ conuertuntur cum ente: suntque numero septem, hoc ordine: unitas, veritas, bonitas, numerus, ordo, perfectio, & pulchritudo. Ista enim septem prædicantur de ente sine distinctione per oppositionem, ita vt rectè dicamus, omne ens esse unum, verum, bonum, numerabile, &c. Hinc attributa entis simplicia dicuntur nullum habere contrarium in ente: quia nullum est ens, quod non sit unum, verum, &c. quâ ens, in suo genere. Proprium horum modorum est, conuerti inter se. Nam omne unum est verum, bonum, numerabile, ordinatum, perfectum & pulchrum: rursus omne verum est unum, bonum, &c. & omne bonum est unum, verum, &c. Quæ quidem obseruatio est momenti longè maximi. Quia sic oportet de rebus differere, vt nihil statuatur his communissimis principiis contrarium. Oportet itaque in omni re attendere, quomodo sit vna, & quomodo illa vnitas sit vera, & veritas bona, &c. Sic e.g. Deus est prima, siue suprema, vnitas, veritas, bonitas, perfectio, pulchritudo: & nostri officii est, in omnibus actionibus ita nos gerere, vt vnitatem, veritatem, bonitatem, & reliqua exprimamus, possideamus, respiciamus. Quâ de re pie & erudite disputat Iohannes Picus Mirandula lib. de ente & vno cap. 10.
units.tr: XIV. The most common attributes of being are those that are convertible with being. There are seven of them, in this order: unity, truth, goodness, number, order, perfection, and beauty. These seven are predicated of being without any distinction by opposition, so that we may rightly say that every being is one, true, good, countable, and so on. Hence the simple attributes of being are said to have no contrary within being, because there is no being that is not one, true, and so on, insofar as it is a being in its own kind. The property of these modes is that they are convertible with one another. For everything that is one is true, good, countable, ordered, perfect, and beautiful; and again, everything that is true is one, good, and so on, and everything that is good is one, true, and so on. This observation is of the greatest importance, because we must discuss things in such a way that nothing is set up as contrary to these most common principles. So in every thing we must attend to how it is one, how that unity is true, how truth is good, and so on. Thus, e.g., God is the first, or highest, unity, truth, goodness, perfection, and beauty; and it is our duty to conduct ourselves in all our actions so that we express, possess, and regard unity, truth, goodness, and the rest. On this matter Giovanni Pico della Mirandola discusses piously and learnedly in his book On Being and the One, chapter 10.

units.la: XV. Vnitas est, per quam ens habet essentiam in se indiuisam, & ab alio quocunque diuisam. Vnum itaque est, quod in seipso est indiuisum, & ab alio quocunque diuisum, hoc est, ita comparatum, vt habeat essentiam certae speciei, à seipsâ non discrepantem. Sic Deus est vnus Deut. 6. verf. 4. hoc est, indiuisus in se, & diuisus siue distinctus ab aliis naturis. Proprium vnitatis est conseruare rem, & ipsius perfectionem augere. Quamdiu enim res est vna, integra est, sana, & valida. Ita quò quid magis est vnum in physicis, politicis, ecclesiasticis & similibus, eò magis est perfectum, & aptum conseruari. Psal. 133. Luc. 11. verf. 17. 18. Dixi, quò quid magis est vnum. Dantur enim gradus vnitatis. Nam aliquid ita est vnū, vt sit indiuisum & indiuisibile, vt Deus: velita, vt sit quidem indiuisum, sed diuisibile, vt est creatura quælibet. Rursus aliquid ita est vnū, vt sit vel vnicum & solū, vt Deus, sol, luna: vel non-vnicum, vt homo. Denique aliquid est vnum absolutè vel comparatè, puta numero, genere, specie, analogia, causâ, effecto, subiecto, adiuncto, definitione, &c. Quò pertinet, quòd aliquid est vnum essentiâ, personâ, voluntate, vel actu: item vnum substantiâ, quātitate, qualitate, actione, &c. Vnitati transcendentali opponitur multitudo, vel potiùs multiplicitas, quæ reciprocatur cum non-ente. Nam non-ens est multiplex ac inexplicabile: vt purgatorium, Chimæra.
units.tr: XV. Unity is that by which a being has its essence undivided in itself and divided from anything else whatever. Thus one is that which is undivided in itself and divided from anything else whatever; that is, it is so constituted that it has the essence of a certain species, not differing from itself. Thus God is one Deut. 6:4, that is, undivided in himself and divided or distinct from other natures. The property of unity is to preserve a thing and to increase its perfection. For as long as a thing is one, it is whole, sound, and strong. So the more a thing is one in physical, political, ecclesiastical, and similar matters, the more perfect it is and the better fitted to be preserved. Ps. 133; Luke 11:17–18. I have said, the more a thing is one, for there are degrees of unity. For something is one in such a way that it is undivided and indivisible, as God is; or again, in such a way that it is indeed undivided but divisible, as is any creature. Again, something is one in such a way that it is either unique and alone, as God, the sun, or the moon; or not unique, as a man is. Finally, something is one absolutely or comparatively, for instance in number, genus, species, analogy, cause, effect, subject, accident, definition, and so on. To this belongs the fact that something is one in essence, person, will, or act; likewise one in substance, quantity, quality, action, and so on. Opposed to transcendental unity is multitude, or rather multiplicity, which is reciprocal with non-being. For non-being is manifold and inexplicable, as purgatory or the Chimaera.

units.la: XVI. Veritas est conformitas siue congruentia entis cum suo archetypo. Nihil enim est verum, nisi consentiat cum exemplari isto, cui essentia ipsius debet esse conformis. Ita Deus sibi ipsi est conformis: res naturales, morales, & supernaturales sunt conformes intellectui Dei: res artificiales sunt conformes intellectui artificis. Intellectus itaque Dei & creaturæ est archetypū siue exemplar, cui congruere debent res. Proprium veritatis est, magnetico contactu ad se rapere intellectum, & harmonico concentu consentire secum ipsâ & cum aliâ veritate. Proinde veritas natura suâ est facilis, seu facile intelligibilis: & quod in unâ arte est verum, non potest in altera esse falsum. Pertinent huc ista usitata axiomata: Verum vero consonat: Verum vero non opponitur, sed subordinatur. Porrò inter proprietates veritatis etiam commemoratur, quòd sit antiqua & inuicta. Et primò quidem veritas est antiqua iuxta illud Tertulliani, Verissimum antiquissimū. Intellige eam veritatem, quam Deus in naturâ & scripturâ expressit. Alia enim est ratio veritatis in rebus artificialibus, ubi multa de novo inveniuntur. Deinde veritas est inuicta: quia etsi interdum latitat, & minùs aliquando in oculos aliud agentium mortalium incurrit, semper tamen victrix ad hæc sæcula durauit, duratura sine dubio ad sæculorum usque finem, & de omnibus suis inimicis plenissimum tandem & gloriosissimum triumphum reportatura. Unde veritas dicitur πανδαμάτωρ [?], omnia domans, quę, φίλος ὡς ἀβάσανιστος [?], ut suber immersabilis undis, omnes aduersarum tempestatum fluctus decumanos eluctetur. Inprimis hæc duo attributa veritatis conspicua sunt in eâ veritate, quam Deus in verbo suo patefecit. Huic enim veritati nemo præscribere potest, non spatium temporum, non patrocinia personarum, non priuilegia regionum, ut sunt verba Tertulliani de velandis virginibus. Et ut idem ait de præscriptionibus: Principalitas (ea est vera antiquitas) veritati, potestas mendacitati deputanda. Ideo apostolus 1. Cor. 11. v. 23. ait, Ego à Domino accepi, quod & tradidi vobis. Ideo Iudas v. 3. hortatur pios ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι[?] τὴν ἅπαξ παραδοθεῖσαν[?] τοῖς ἁγίοις, ut fortiter decertent pro fide quæ semel tradita fuit sanctis. Ideo denique Christus Matth. 19. vers. 8. ait, A principio non fuit ita. Itaque si volumus scire, quæ sit vera fides, retemus tres illos gladios, Pauli, Iudæ & Christi, atque ita statuamus, illam demum esse veram fidei regulam, quæ semel fuit tradita: quæque, ut ait Tertullianus, una omnino est, sola immobilis & irreformabilis. Quare vero hoc? Quia unde res habet ut sit, inde quoq; habet ut vera sit. Iam vero fides catholica a solo Deo suam habet essentiam. Ergo etiā ab illo solo habet veritatem. Itaq; nihil hodie post semel a Christo traditam fidei regulam licet alicui παρεισφέρειν[?], de novo inducere, ut Chrysostomus eleganter loquitur. Idcirco & Gregorius Nazianzenus orthodoxam fidem εὐσεβὲς[?] δόγμα, pietatem scripturis comprehensam, hæresin vero Arianam, ἀσεβὲς[?] καινοτομίαν, novitatem extra scripturas inductam, nominat.
units.tr: XVI. Truth is the conformity or agreement of a being with its archetype. For nothing is true unless it agrees with that exemplar, to which its essence ought to be conformed. Thus God is conformed to himself; natural, moral, and supernatural things are conformed to the intellect of God; artificial things are conformed to the intellect of the maker. Therefore the intellect of God and that of the creature is the archetype or exemplar with which things ought to agree. The property of truth is to draw the intellect to itself with a magnetic contact, and to agree with itself and with other truth in a harmonious concord. Accordingly truth is by its nature easy, or easily understood; and what is true in one art cannot be false in another. To this belong the common axioms: Truth agrees with truth; truth is not opposed to truth, but subordinated to it. Further, among the properties of truth it is also reckoned that it is ancient and unconquered. And first, truth is ancient, according to that saying of Tertullian, The truest is the most ancient. Understand by this the truth which God has expressed in nature and in Scripture. For the nature of truth is different in artificial things, where many things are discovered anew. Next, truth is unconquered: for although at times it lies hidden, and sometimes falls less under the eyes of mortals busy with other things, yet it has always endured victorious through the ages, and will without doubt endure to the end of the ages, and will at last win a most full and most glorious triumph over all its enemies. Hence truth is called πανδαμάτωρ [pandamator], all-subduing, which, [φίλος ὡς ἀβάσανιστος], like cork that cannot be sunk by the waves, struggles through all the great waves of adverse storms. Above all, these two attributes of truth are conspicuous in that truth which God has revealed in his Word. For no one can prescribe to this truth: not the lapse of time, not the patronage of persons, not the privileges of regions, as Tertullian says in his work on veiling virgins. And as he says elsewhere about prescriptions: Priority (which is true antiquity) belongs to truth; power belongs to falsehood. Therefore the apostle says, 1 Cor. 11:23, I received from the Lord that which I also delivered to you. Therefore Jude, v. 3, exhorts the godly to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints [ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι τὴν ἅπαξ παραδοθεῖσαν τοῖς ἁγίοις]. Therefore, finally, Christ says, Matt. 19:8, From the beginning it was not so. Thus, if we wish to know what the true faith is, let us hold fast those three swords, of Paul, Jude, and Christ, and so establish that the true rule of faith is the one which was delivered once for all, which, as Tertullian says, is altogether one, alone unchanging and not to be reformed. But why is this so? Because whence a thing has its being, thence it also has its truth. Now the catholic faith has its essence from God alone; therefore it also has its truth from him alone. Hence it is not lawful for anyone today, once the rule of faith has been delivered by Christ, to introduce anything further, to bring in something new, as Chrysostom elegantly puts it. For this reason Gregory Nazianzen also calls the orthodox faith a pious doctrine [εὐσεβὲς δόγμα], comprehended in the Scriptures, and the Arian heresy an impious innovation [ἀσεβὲς καινοτομίαν], introduced outside the Scriptures.

units.la: XVII. Bonitas est congruentia rei cum app- etitu.
units.tr: XVII. Goodness is the agreement of a thing with appetite.

units.la: Sicut veritas facit ut ens sit intelligibile, ita bonitas facit ut idem sit volibile, appetibile, amabile. Hinc bonum & appetibile inter se conuertuntur: & bonum definitur, quod omnia appetunt. Proprietas boni est, esse communicatiuum siue diffusiuum sui, & diffipatiuum mali: sicut mali ea est indoles, ut sit destructiuum tum sui tum boni sibi oppositi. Matth. 5. v. 45. Psal. 5. v. 5. 6. 7. Cæterum quod dictum est de appetitu, accipi debet de ordinato appetitu, à quo res habet esse approbationis: non vero de inordinato, quo fit, ut bonum apparens habeatur pro vero bono. Vnde non obscure licet colligere, fines bonorum & malorum arcessendos esse à voluntate Dei & diaboli, ita nempe ut illud censeatur bonum, quod conforme est voluntati Dei, & malum, quod conforme est voluntati diaboli. Nam voluntas Dei est appetitus ordinatissimus, sicut e contrario voluntas diaboli est appetitus inordinatissimus. Vnde porrò illud consequitur, Deum esse summum bonum: vtpote qui est maxime volibilis, appetibilis, amabilis, & prima regula omnis boni. Non itaque sine causa Christus pronunciat, neminem esse bonum nisi unum Deum Marc. 10. vers. 18. Intellige summum bonum, siue bonum à se. Alias etiam opera Dei sunt bona. Gen. 1. bonitate scil. participatâ, quatenus sunt à Deo, & ad ipsum ordinantur atq; referuntur. Hinc tres gradus bonorum statuuntur: videl. bonum summum extra hominem, quod est Deus: bonum summum in homine, q; est fruitio Dei, seu unio & communio cum Deo: & bonum sub summo, quod subseruit summo bono, & ad illud perducit atque conducit. Nihil itaque censeri debet bonum, quod à summo bono abducit. Ex his facile est iudicium ferre de comparatione bonorum. Nam quo quid est propius summo bono, & quo magis conducit ad summum bonum, eo debet censeri melius. Sic bonum honestum praeferendum est utili, permanens caduco, spirituale corporali. Breuiter: Bonum, quod est supra hominem, est praestantissimum: huic proximum, quod est iuxta hominem: vltimas tenet, quod est infra hominem.
units.tr: Just as truth makes a being intelligible, so goodness makes the same thing desirable, appetible and lovable. Hence the good and the appetible are convertible with each other, and the good is defined as that which all things seek. The property of the good is to communicate and diffuse itself, and to scatter evil, just as the nature of evil is to destroy both itself and the good opposed to it. Matt. 5. v. 45. Ps. 5. v. 5, 6, 7. Moreover, what has been said about appetite must be understood of ordered appetite, from which a thing has the character of being approved, and not of disordered appetite, by which an apparent good comes to be held as a true good. Hence it may readily be gathered that the ends of good and evil are to be sought from the will of God and the will of the devil: that is judged good which conforms to the will of God, and evil that which conforms to the will of the devil. For the will of God is the most ordered appetite, while on the contrary the will of the devil is the most disordered appetite. From this it further follows that God is the supreme good, as he who is most desirable, appetible and lovable, and the first rule of all good. Not without reason, therefore, Christ declares that no one is good but God alone, Mark 10. v. 18. Understand the supreme good, or good in itself. Otherwise the works of God are also good, Gen. 1., by participated goodness, insofar as they are from God and are ordered and referred to him. Hence three grades of good are established: the supreme good outside man, which is God; the supreme good in man, which is the enjoyment of God, or union and communion with God; and the good under the supreme, which serves the supreme good and leads and brings us to it. Nothing, therefore, ought to be judged good which draws us away from the supreme good. From this it is easy to pass judgment on the comparison of goods: the nearer a thing is to the supreme good, and the more it leads to it, the better it ought to be judged. Thus the honourable good is to be preferred to the useful, the lasting to the perishable, the spiritual to the bodily. In brief: the good which is above man is most excellent; next to it is that which is beside man; the last place is held by that which is below man.

units.la: XVIII. Numerus est, per quem res est expers turpis infinitudinis. Turpem dico infinitudine, de qua loquitur vsitatum dictum, Natura abhorret ab infinito, item, à progressu in infinitum. Videmus enim omnes res certo numero contineri, de quo poëta ex Sap. 11. v. 21. Pondere, mensurâ, numero Deus omnia fecit. Etsi enim multae res nobis sunt innumerabiles, qualia sunt beneficia Dei, itemque stellae: reuerâ tamen, in seipsis constant numero, quem Deus nouit. Psal. 147. vers. 4. Hic est ille numerus, qui harmoniam efficit in omni ente: vnde aliquis non male definiuerit hunc numerum, affectionem entis, quâ fit vt essentia sit harmonica.
units.tr: XVIII. Number is that by which a thing is free from base infinitude. By base infinitude I mean what the common saying refers to, "nature abhors the infinite," and likewise "progress to infinity." For we see that all things are contained within a fixed number, of which the poet in Wisd. 11. v. 21 says: God made all things by weight, measure and number. For although many things are innumerable to us, such as the benefits of God, and likewise the stars, in truth they stand in themselves by a number which God knows. Ps. 147. v. 4. This is that number which produces harmony in every being; whence someone has not badly defined this number as the affection of being, by which essence is made harmonious.

units.la: XIX. Ordo est affectio, per quam res habet essentiam confusionis expertem. Eius tanta est vis, vt nihil sine ipso possit consistere. Tametsi enim multa sunt confusa in comparatione aliorum, & respectu intellectus nostri, qui 'pro imb'cillitate sua non femperaffequi potest ordinem in rebus: nihil tamen in natura absolute in fe, vel etiam in ordine ad Deum est confusum. Hinc ordo est in Deo & operibus Dei: in homine, & rectis operibus hominis: in universitate rerum, & disciplinis: in intellectu bene se habente, & in re intelligibili. Quod attinet ad ἀταξίαν peccati, illa non sequitur essentiam rei, sed carentiam essentiae bonae. De ordine, illiusque dignitate vide Psal. 148.verf. 6.Ier. 31. ver. 36. 1. Cor.14. verf.33.40. Coloss. 2. verf.5. Exempla vide Gen. 1. Num. 1.2.3. & alibi.
units.tr: XIX. Order is an affection through which a thing has an essence free from confusion. Its power is so great that nothing can subsist without it. For although many things are confused in comparison with others, and with respect to our intellect, which on account of its weakness cannot always grasp the order in things, nothing in nature is confused absolutely in itself, or even in relation to God. Hence order is in God and in the works of God; in man and in the right works of man; in the universe of things and in the disciplines; in a well-disposed intellect and in the intelligible thing. As for the disorder [ἀταξία] of sin, it does not follow the essence of a thing but the lack of good essence. On order and its dignity see Ps. 148. v. 6; Jer. 31. v. 36; 1 Cor. 14. v. 33, 40; Col. 2. v. 5. For examples see Gen. 1; Num. 1, 2, 3, and elsewhere.

units.la: XX. Perfectio est, per quam res habet essentiam defectus expertem in suo genere: ita nempe, ut habeat essentiam, existentiam, operationem, & finem suum; quae quatuor cohaerent in omni ente. Hinc persectum scite definitur, cui nihil deest, in suo scil. genere: ite, extra quod non est ullam partem accipere. Vsitate appellatur perfectio essentiae: cui opponitur perfectio gradus, quae non competit omni enti. Vtraque est in Deo. Matt.5. verf.48. perfectio essentiae est in regenitis Gen. 6. verf.9. c.17.v.3.Matt.5.v.48. perfectio gradus secundum plus & minus est in operibus Dei. Gen.2.v.1.Deut.32. verf.4.
units.tr: XX. Perfection is that through which a thing has an essence free from defect in its own kind: namely, so that it has its essence, existence, operation and end, which four cohere in every being. Hence a perfect thing is neatly defined as that to which nothing is lacking in its own kind, outside which there is no part to be taken. Commonly it is called perfection of essence, to which is opposed perfection of degree, which does not belong to every being. Both are in God. Matt. 5. v. 48. Perfection of essence is in the regenerate: Gen. 6. v. 9; c. 17. v. 3; Matt. 5. v. 48. Perfection of degree, according to more and less, is in the works of God: Gen. 2. v. 1; Deut. 32. v. 4.

units.la: XXI. Pulchritudo est affectio, per quam res habet essentiam deformitatis expertem. Ita nempe ut eleganti proportione constet, atque etiam delectare possit. Psal. 92. verf.5. & 111. verf.3. Intellige proportionem, non mathematicam illam, sed entitatiuam, quae cō- sistit in correspondu essentiae, existentiae, & modorum, puta unitatis, veritatis, bonitatis, &c. Nam pulchritudo est affectio entis colophonia, resultans ex praecedentibus affectionibus, unitate videl. veritate, bonitate, numero, ordine, & perfectione. Ideo enim aliquid est pulchrum, quia habet proportionem unitatis, veritatis, bonitatis, &c. Sic Christus θεάνθρωπος, μεσίτης [?] ἀνθρώπων[?], est pulchritudo pulcherrima, ut constat ex Canticorum: quia est unus ille, & verus,& bonus,& persectus mediator inter Deum & homines. E contrario peccatum est turpitudo omnium turpissima: quia habet disproportionem meram multiplicitatis, falsitatis, malitiæ, confusionis, & imperfectionis. De pulchritudine Christi & Ecclesiæ vide Psal. 45. quem confer cum Cantico Canticorum. Intellige hic pulchritudinem partim increatam, partim creatam, & hanc spiritualem, non corporalem.
units.tr: XXI. Beauty is an affection through which a thing has an essence free from deformity: namely, so that it consists in elegant proportion and can also delight. Ps. 92. v. 5, and 111. v. 3. Understand proportion not in the mathematical sense but the entitative, which consists in the correspondence of essence, existence and modes, such as unity, truth, goodness, etc. For beauty is the crowning affection of being, resulting from the preceding affections, namely unity, truth, goodness, number, order and perfection. Something is beautiful because it has the proportion of unity, truth, goodness, etc. Thus Christ, the God-man [θεάνθρωπος], the mediator of men [μεσίτης ἀνθρώπων], is the most beautiful beauty, as is clear from the Song of Songs: because he is the one, true, good and perfect mediator between God and men. On the contrary, sin is the most base of all ugliness, because it has the sheer disproportion of multiplicity, falsity, malice, confusion and imperfection. On the beauty of Christ and the Church see Ps. 45, which compare with the Song of Songs. Understand here beauty partly uncreated and partly created, and this spiritual, not corporeal.

units.la: XXII. Primæ entis differentiæ sunt modi, per quos ens primo diuiditur. Hinc appellantur generalissimæ diuisiones, item distinctiones, quæ dicuntur de omnibus rebus. Nam quidquid in mundo est, i.e. est per se vel per accidens, simpliciter vel secundum quid, a se vel ab alio, independens vel dependens, &c. hoc modo.
units.tr: XXII. The first differences of being are the modes through which being is first divided. Hence they are called the most general divisions, and also distinctions, which are said of all things. For whatever is in the world is either per se or per accidens, simply or in a certain respect, from itself or from another, independent or dependent, etc., in this way.

units.la: XXIII. Omne ens est per se, vel per accidens. Ens per se est, quod suâ naturâ est tale: & quia per se est, etiam per se agit, & per se prædicatur. Nam modus agendi & prædicandi sequitur modum essendi. Sic vinum per se est bonum; & per se agit bene, id est, exhilarat; & hoc de ipso prædicatur per se, denominatione interna & essentiali. Ens per accidens est, quod aliunde habet, ut sit tale: & quia per accidens est tale, etiam per accidens agit & prædicatur: ut, vinum est malum, quatenus immoderatè sumitur; & male afficit hominem, hoc est, ipsum inebriat; & hoc de ipso prædicatur per accidens, denominatione externa. Ita Christus per se & suâ naturâ est lapis angularis, & lapis defensionis, & petra salutis. Psal. 118. ver. 22. Matt. 16. v. 18. per accidens, & nostro vitio est signum cui contradicitur, positum εἰς πτῶσιν, in ruinam, & lapis offensionis, & petra scandali. Luc. 2. verf. 34. Rom. 9. verf. 32.33. 1. Cor. 1. verf. 23.24. Similiter euangelium per se est odor vitæ ad vitam, per accidens odor mortis ad mortem. 2. Cor. 2, verf. 14.15.16.
units.tr: XXIII. Every being is either per se or per accidens.
