A being per se is what is such by its own nature; and because it is per se, it also acts per se and is predicated per se, for the mode of acting and of predicating follows the mode of being. Thus wine is good per se, and acts well per se, that is, it cheers; and this is predicated of it per se, by internal and essential denomination. A being per accidens is what has from elsewhere that it is such; and because it is such per accidens, it also acts and is predicated per accidens: as, wine is bad insofar as it is taken immoderately, and it affects a man badly, that is, it inebriates him; and this is predicated of it per accidens, by external denomination. Thus Christ, per se and by his nature, is the cornerstone, the stone of defence and the rock of salvation. Ps. 118. v. 22. Matt. 16. v. 18. Per accidens, and through our fault, he is a sign that is contradicted, set "for a fall" [εἰς πτῶσιν], to ruin, and a stone of offence, and a rock of scandal. Luke 2. v. 34. Rom. 9. v. 32, 33. 1 Cor. 1. v. 23, 24. Similarly the gospel is per se an odour of life unto life, and per accidens an odour of death unto death. 2 Cor. 2. v. 14, 15, 16.

units.la: XXIV. Omne ens est tale simpliciter, vel secundum quid. Ens tale simpliciter est, quod nullam admittit limitationem: vt, Deus est immutabilis. Ens tale secundum quid est, quod admittit limitationem: vt, Christus θεανθρωπῳ[?] est subiectum limitandum, quatenus de illo praedicantur attributa & apotelesmata vel diuina, vel humana, vel θεανθρωπικά[?]. Confer Iohan.3.v.13. Act.20.v.28.
units.tr: XXIV. Every being is either such absolutely or such in a certain respect. A being such absolutely is one that admits no limitation, for example, God is immutable. A being such in a certain respect is one that admits limitation, for example, Christ, the God-man [θεανθρωπῳ?], is a subject capable of being limited, insofar as the divine, human, or theanthropic [θεανθρωπικά?] attributes and apotelesmata are predicated of him. Compare John 3:13; Acts 20:28.

units.la: XXV. Ens aut est a se, aut ab alio. Ens a se est, quod suae est originis. Ens ab alio est, quod alteri suam debet originem. Intellige originem essentiae, subsistentiae, vel potentiae. Sic Filius Dei non habet originem essentiae aut potentiae, sed subsistentiae. Hebr. 1. v. 3. at res creatae sunt a Deo quantum ad essentiam & potentiam Iohan.1.v.3. Rom.11.v. vlt. Anima rationalis originem essentiae habet a Deo Heb.12. v.9. originem subsistentiae habet a parentibus. Gen.5.v.3.
units.tr: XXV. A being is either from itself (a se) or from another (ab alio). A being from itself is one whose origin lies in itself. A being from another is one that owes its origin to another. Understand this as origin of essence, of subsistence, or of power. Thus the Son of God has no origin of essence or power, but only of subsistence, Heb. 1:3. Created things, however, are from God as to essence and power, John 1:3; Rom. 11:36. The rational soul has its origin of essence from God, Heb. 12:9, but its origin of subsistence from its parents, Gen. 5:3.

units.la: XXVI. Ens est independens, vel dependens. Independens est, quod a se habet aliquid: eftq; tale vel simpliciter, vt solus Deus, qui est Alpha & Omega Apoc.1.v.8. vel secundum quid, vt magistratus Psal.82. Rom.13.v.1. Dependens est, quod ab alio habet essentiam, subsistentiam, potentiam & notitiam sui: vt effectum dependet a causa, adiunctum a subiecto, & correlatum a relato. Act.17.v.28.29.
units.tr: XXVI. A being is either independent or dependent. Independent is that which has something from itself. This is so either absolutely, as God alone, who is Alpha and Omega, Rev. 1:8, or in a certain respect, as the magistrate, Ps. 82; Rom. 13:1. Dependent is that which has from another its essence, subsistence, power, and knowledge of itself: as an effect depends on its cause, an adjunct on its subject, and a correlative on its correlate. Acts 17:28, 29.

units.la: XXVII. Ens est permanens, vel successiuum. Ens permanens est, quod esse suum habet simul: vt est aeternitas, quae dicitur esse Nunc semper stans, siue status immobilis. Vide Psal.102.v.27.28. Ens successiuum est, quod partes sui esse habet in fluxu quodam: vt motus & tempus. In motu siquidem & tempore est prius & posterius; praeteritum, praesens, & futurum, fuisse, esse, & fore. Successioni isti obnoxia sunt omnia corpora, etiam coelestia. Quod attinet ad actiones Dei, quae fiunt in tempore, illae quoq; admittunt successionem, non ex parte Dei agentis, sed ex parte creaturarum.
units.tr: XXVII. A being is either permanent or successive. A permanent being is one that has its being all at once. Such is eternity, which is called an ever-standing Now, or an immovable state. See Ps. 102:27, 28. A successive being is one whose parts have their being in a certain flow, as motion and time do. In motion and time there is a before and an after, a past, a present, and a future, a was, an is, and a will be. All bodies, even the heavenly ones, are subject to this succession. As for the actions of God that take place in time, these too admit succession, not on the part of God who acts, but on the part of the creatures.

units.la: XXVIII. Ens est simplex, vel compositum. Simplex est, quod partium est expers: idque vel simpliciter & absolute, vel modo quodam. Priori modo solus Deus est simplex; quia in eo omnes perfectiones redigunturad simplicissimam unitate: posteriori modo quaedam creaturae sunt simplices, tametsi nulla creatura tam fit simplex, quin simul fit composita. Simplicitas Dei inde apparet, ꝙ fit spiritus, habitans lucè inaccessam, quem nemo hominum vidit, neq; videre potest, & cuius nomè est Eheich & Jehovah. Ioh.4. v.24.1. Tim.6.v.16. Exod.3.v.14. Simplicitas creaturarum certos admittit gradus. In primo gradu sunt angeli & anima hominis Pf.104.v.4. Heb.1.v.14. Gen.2.v.7. In secundo gradu est lux Gen.1.v.3. In tertio gradu sunt coelum & stellae, in quarto elementa lucida. Compositum est, in quo est interna partium diuersitas, seu, in quo est natura alterius. Compositio ista est generalis, vel specialis. Compositio generalis est, quae in omnib. in vniuersum rebus creatis reperitur. Eius quinq; sunt genera. 1. ex esse & effentia, h. e. ex concreto & abstracto, seu formato & forma. 2. ex effentia & existentia, (seu, ex natura & supposito, i.e. ex natura communi & singulari. 3. ex potentia (passiua) & actu. 4. ex genere & differentia. 5. ex subiecto & accidente. Compositio specialis est, quae in corporibus reperitur: estque 1. ex materia (sensili) & forma. 2. ex partibus quantis.
units.tr: XXVIII. A being is either simple or composite. Simple is that which is free of parts, and this either simply and absolutely, or in a certain manner. In the first way only God is simple, since in him all perfections are reduced to the most simple unity. In the second way some creatures are simple, although no creature is so simple that it is not at the same time composite. The simplicity of God appears from the fact that he is spirit, dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen or can see, and whose name is Eheieh and Jehovah. John 4:24; 1 Tim. 6:16; Exod. 3:14. The simplicity of creatures admits of certain degrees. In the first degree are the angels and the soul of man, Ps. 104:4; Heb. 1:14; Gen. 2:7. In the second degree is light, Gen. 1:3. In the third degree are the heavens and the stars; in the fourth, the bright elements. Composite is that in which there is internal diversity of parts, or in which there is the nature of something else. This composition is either general or special. General composition is that found in all created things without exception. It has five kinds: (1) of existence and essence, that is, of the concrete and the abstract, or of the formed and the form; (2) of essence and existence (or of nature and supposit, that is, of common nature and singular nature); (3) of (passive) potency and act; (4) of genus and differentia; (5) of subject and accident. Special composition is that found in bodies, and it consists of (1) (sensible) matter and form, and (2) quantitative parts.

units.la: XXIX. Omne ens est infinitum, vel finitum. Infinitum est, ꝙ habet essentiam interminata: estq; vel interminatae perfectionis, essentiae, virtutis, & durationis, ut Deus Esa.66.v.1. Pf.48.v.15. vel interminatae imperfectionis, quo sensu numerus, magnitudo, materia prima, & similia dicuntur infinita. Quò pertinet illud Platonicorum, asserentium, omnia componi ex infinito & termino, h.e. ex potentia & actu. Nam potentia passiva in rebus creatis est indeterminata atq; indefinita. Caue tamè hic intelligas istâ infinitatem, quae reciprocatur cum non-ente, de qua supra theoremate 18. Finitum est, ꝑ certis terminis circumscribitur, ut mundus & res in eo contentae. Esa.40.v.12. Dan.4.v.35.
units.tr: XXIX. Every being is either infinite or finite. Infinite is that which has an unbounded essence. This is either of unbounded perfection, essence, power, and duration, as God is, Isa. 66:1; Ps. 48:15; or of unbounded imperfection, in which sense number, magnitude, prime matter, and similar things are called infinite. To this belongs the saying of the Platonists, who assert that all things are composed of the infinite and the limit, that is, of potency and act. For passive potency in created things is indeterminate and indefinite. Take care, however, not to understand here that infinity which is interchangeable with non-being, of which above in theorem 18. Finite is that which is circumscribed by certain limits, as the world and the things contained in it. Isa. 40:12; Dan. 4:35.

units.la: XXX. Omne ens est actu vel potentia. Ens actu est vel actus, vel compositum ex actu & potentia. Actus est perfectio potentiae: estq; purus, vel impurus. Actus purus habet rationem efficientis immobilis: quo pacto solus Deus est actus. Psal. 121. verf. 4. Nostrum itaque est vnice in id incumbere, vt Deo assimilemur per actus bonos: quia hac in re vertitur omnis nostra perfectio in hac & futura vita.
units.tr: XXX. Every being is either in act or in potency. A being in act is either act itself, or something composed of act and potency. Act is the perfection of potency, and it is either pure or impure. Pure act has the character of an immovable efficient; in this way God alone is act. Ps. 121:4. It is therefore our task to strive solely toward this, that we be made like God through good acts, because in this matter our whole perfection turns, in this life and in the life to come.

units.la: Actus impurus habet rationem efficientis mobilis, formæ, proprietatis, vel operationis. Primo modo angelus & anima dicitur actus: secundo & tertio forma & proprietas dicitur actus primus siue signatus: quarto denique modo actio quælibet dicitur actus secundus siue exercitus. Actus primus est inseparabilis a re, secundus potest inhiberi vel separari. Sic ab aqua maris rubri, cum transierunt Israelitæ, non separata est mobilitas siue fluiditas, sed motus siue fluxus inhibitus. Idem iudicium est de sole, qui stetit cursum suum tempore Iosuæ: de ferro, quod natauit tempore Elisæi: de igni, qui non læsit socios Danielis in fornace Babylonica. Exod. 14. Iof. 10. 2. Reg. 6. Dan. 3. Ens compositum ex actu & potentia est, quod ita est, vt vel non esse, vel aliter esse aliudue fieri possit: vti omnes creaturæ se habent. Solus quippe Deus est immobilis seu immutabilis. Psal. 102. verf. 26. Heb. 1. verf. 10. 11.12. Potentia est dispositio rei ad actum: seu, est vis & facultas eius, quod potens, ad id, quod possibile; sicut actus est id, quo aliquid agit. Potentia est actiua, passiua, vel obiectiua. Potentia actiua est, qua res potest agere bonum. Ea in Deo est omnipotentia, Gen. 17. verf. 1. Ier. 32. v. 17. 18. 19. Luc. 1. verf. 37. in creaturis vis & facultas agendi id, quod debet ex lege creationis vel redemtionis. Gen. 1. verf. 11. 20. 24. 27. Matth. 5. verf. 16. Potentia passiua est, qua res potest pati bonum & malum, vel agere malum. Nam agere malum arguit passionem & imperfectionem. Potentia ista passiua non cadit in Deum. Iacob. 1. v. 17. Potentia obiectiua est, qua res obiicitur suo agenti tanquam possibilis: quo sensi nos fuimus electi in Christo ante iacta mundi fundamenta. Eph. 1. v. 4. Deinde potentia est præceptiua, vel obedientialis. Illa est, qua Deus præcipit, vt hoc vel illud fiat. Gen. 1. vbi per verbum FIAT vel EST o natura rerum est produɂta: hæc est, quâ creatura obedit Deo præcipienti: Quam in sententiam apud Iobum dicitur Deus præcipere soli & pluuiis. Iob. 9. vers. 7. cap. 37. vers. 15. Nam Deus est velut imperator, quo dicente, est quidquid est, & quo præcipiente existit. Psal. 33. vers. 9. & 148. vers. 5. Hinc appellatur Ichoua Zebaoth, i. e. Deus exercituum. Huic obedientiali potentiæ opponitur naturalis, quâ fit, vt aliquid fiat vi principij interni, quod appellamus naturam. Sic ex vite potest nasci vinum potentiâ naturali; ex aquâ potest fieri vinum potentiâ obedientali, virtute Dei Iohan. 2. Porrò potentia Dei est absoluta, vel ordinata siue actualis. Illa fit supra leges à diuinâ voluntate positas, vt cùm Deus inhibuit motum solis & lunæ: hæc sequitur istas leges, vt cùm Deus sinit solem suum oriri super bonos & malos. Matth. 5. vers. 45. Priori illâ potentiâ Deus plura potest quàm vult. Matth. 3. vers. 9. cap. 26. v. 53.
units.tr: Impure act has the character of a movable efficient, of form, of property, or of operation. In the first sense the angel and the soul are called act; in the second and third senses, form and property are called first act, or determinate act; in the fourth sense, any action is called second act, or exercised act. First act is inseparable from the thing, whereas second act can be inhibited or separated. Thus the mobility or fluidity of the water of the Red Sea was not taken away when the Israelites crossed it, but its motion or flow was restrained. The same judgment applies to the sun, which stood still in its course in the time of Joshua; to the iron, which floated in the time of Elisha; and to the fire, which did not harm Daniel's companions in the Babylonian furnace. Exod. 14; Josh. 10; 2 Kings 6; Dan. 3. A being composed of act and potency is one that is such that it can either not be, or be otherwise, or become something else, as all creatures are. For God alone is immobile or immutable. Ps. 102:26; Heb. 1:10–12. Potency is the disposition of a thing toward act; or it is the power and capacity of that which is able, toward that which is possible, just as act is that by which something acts. Potency is active, passive, or objective. Active potency is that by which a thing can do good. In God this is omnipotence, Gen. 17:1; Jer. 32:17–19; Luke 1:37; in creatures it is the power to do what they ought, by the law of creation or of redemption, Gen. 1:11, 20, 24, 27; Matt. 5:16. Passive potency is that by which a thing can suffer good or evil, or do evil. For doing evil argues passion and imperfection. This passive potency does not fall upon God. James 1:17. Objective potency is that by which a thing is presented to its agent as possible; in this sense we were chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world. Eph. 1:4. Further, potency is preceptive or obediential. This is the potency by which God commands that this or that be done, Gen. 1, where by the word LET THERE BE or IT IS the nature of things was produced; it is the potency by which a creature obeys God when he commands. In this sense God is said in Job to command the sun and the rains, Job 9:7; 37:15. For God is like a commander: at his word whatever is, is, and at his command it exists, Ps. 33:9; 148:5. Hence he is called Jehovah Zebaoth, that is, God of hosts. Opposed to this obediential potency is natural potency, by which something comes about through an internal principle, which we call nature. Thus wine can be born from the vine by natural potency; wine can be made from water by obediential potency, by the power of God, John 2. Moreover, the power of God is absolute, or ordained, or actual. The former operates above the laws established by the divine will, as when God halted the motion of the sun and moon; the latter follows those laws, as when God allows his sun to rise on the good and the evil, Matt. 5:45. By the former power God can do more than he wills, Matt. 3:9; 26:53.

units.la: XXXI. Ens est vniuersale, vel singulare.
units.tr: XXXI. Being is either universal or singular.

units.la: Vniuersale est, quod communiter & varie ad multa pertinet. Estque tale in essendo, vt sunt genera & species, id est, naturæ communes, quæ in inferioribus rebus existunt & multiplicantur: vel in causando, vt Deus, qui est causa causarum in bonis Esa. 50. v. 2. Ier. 32. v. 17. 18. 19. vel in significando & repræsentando, vt voces quibus indicantur multa in singularibus multiplicata: vel denique in prædicando, vt sunt ea, quæ de multis enuntiantur. e. g. de omnibus credentibus asseuerat Christus, illos consecuturos præmiū vitæ æternæ Iohan. 3. Singulare est individuum suâ proprietate determinatum: vt est Deus Deut. 4. v. 35. Esa. 44. v. 1. Singulare est primo variabile, vt hic homo; vel inuariabile, vt sol. Illius scientia non datur: huius, datur. Deinde est primum, vel vltimum. Singulare primum, siue antecedens, est, quod respicit primum entis momentum. Sic essentia Dei est res singularis. Singulare vltimum, siue consequens est, quod respicit secundum entis momentum. Sic tres personæ in essentiâ Dei sunt singulares. Vnde patet essentiam Dei ita esse singularem, vt nihilominus sit communis tribus personis, non tamen vt genus vel species, sed vt induiduum .1.Ioh.5.v.7. Etsi enim effentia Dei ad multas, id est, tres, personas pertinet: non tamen pertinet ad illas varie, sed per modum τωτότητος, ideoque non debet appellari vniuersale.
units.tr: A universal is that which pertains commonly and in various ways to many things. It is such in being, as genera and species are, that is, common natures which exist and are multiplied in lower things; or in causing, as God is the cause of causes in good things, Isa. 50. v. 2. Jer. 32. v. 17, 18, 19; or in signifying and representing, as words which indicate many things multiplied in singulars; or finally in predicating, as those things which are asserted of many. For example, Christ affirms of all believers that they will obtain the reward of eternal life, Iohan. 3. A singular is an individual determined by its own property, as God is, Deut. 4. v. 35. Isa. 44. v. 1. A singular is first either variable, like this man, or invariable, like the sun. Knowledge of the former is not given; knowledge of the latter is. Next, it is either first or last. A first singular, or antecedent, is that which regards the first moment of being. Thus the essence of God is a singular thing. A last singular, or consequent, is that which regards the second moment of being. Thus the three persons in the essence of God are singulars. Hence it is clear that the essence of God is so singular that nevertheless it is common to the three persons, yet not as a genus or species but as an individual, 1 John 5. v. 7. For although the essence of God pertains to many, that is, three, persons, it does not pertain to them in various ways but by way of sameness [ταυτότητος], and therefore it ought not to be called universal.

units.la: XXXII. Ens est increatum, vel creatum. In-
units.tr: XXXII. Being is either uncreated or created.

units.la: creatum est, quod ab aeuo est in aeuum: vt solus Deus. Esa. 45.v.21.22. Creatum est, quod ab increato productum est, idque vel ex nihilo Gen.1.verf.1.2.Cor.4.verf.6. vel ex aliqua materia creata Gen.2.v.7.19.
units.tr: Uncreated is that which is from eternity to eternity, as God alone is, Isa. 45. v. 21, 22. Created is that which has been produced by the uncreated, and this either out of nothing, Gen. 1. vers. 1, 2; 2 Cor. 4. vers. 6, or out of some created matter, Gen. 2. vers. 7, 19.

units.la: XXXIII. Ens est àfe, vel ab alio. Ens à fe est, quod à fe habet aliquid. Ens ab alio est, quod alij fert aliquid acceptum: idque vel ratione essentiae & potentiae, vti creaturae sunt à Deo Rom.11.v.vlt. vel ratione personae seu modi subsistendi, vt Filius Dei est à Patre Heb.1.v.3. XXXIV. Ens est absolutum, vel respectiuum. Absolutum est, cuius natura est non referriad aliud: vt effentia Dei est res absoluta. Refpectiuum est, cuius natura est referri ad aliud: vt persona in effentia Dei est res refpectiua. Nam Pater ad Filium, & vterque ad Spiritum sanctum refertur. Pfal.2.v.7.1.Ioh.2,v.23.Ioh.15.verf.26. Refertur autem vna res ad aliam relatione tranfcendentali vel praedicamentali, generali vel speciali. Relatio transcendentalis est, quae immediate fundatur in substantia, fine interuentu accidentis. Ita fe habent relationes, quae Deo tribuuntur. Relatio praedicamentalis est, quae fundatur in re, mediante quantitate vel qualitate aliqua. Sic Adam dicitur pater Caini, quia illi genuit vi naturali, quae in ipso fuit qualitas.Gen.4.v.1.Relatio generalis est, quae extra essentiam rei est posita, & competit omnibus rebus absolutis fecundum varia loca inuentionis logicae. Sic coelum refertur ad terram, solem, hominem, Deum. Relatio specialis est illarum rerum, quarum esse positum est in respectu. Dicitur eleganter relatio interna, sicut generalis, externa. Relationis internae exempla sunt pater & filius, dare & accipere',& similia, quæ non possunt exuere naturam relationis.
units.tr: XXXIII. Being is either from itself or from another. A being from itself is that which has something from itself. A being from another is that which bears something received from another; and this either by reason of essence and power, as creatures are from God, Rom. 11. last verse, or by reason of person or mode of subsisting, as the Son of God is from the Father, Heb. 1. v. 3. XXXIV. Being is either absolute or respective. An absolute is that whose nature is not to be referred to another, as the essence of God is an absolute thing. A respective is that whose nature is to be referred to another, as the person within the essence of God is a respective thing; for the Father is referred to the Son, and both to the Holy Spirit, Ps. 2. v. 7; John 2. v. 23; John 15. verse 26. Now one thing is referred to another by a relation that is either transcendental or predicamental, general or special. A transcendental relation is that which is founded immediately in substance, without the intervention of an accident. Such are the relations which are attributed to God. A predicamental relation is that which is founded in a thing by means of some quantity or quality. Thus Adam is called the father of Cain, because he begot him by the natural power which was a quality in him, Gen. 4. v. 1. A general relation is that which is posited outside the essence of a thing and belongs to all absolute things according to the various places of logical invention. Thus heaven is referred to earth, the sun, man, and God. A special relation is that of those things whose being is posited in the relation. It is aptly called an internal relation, just as the general one is called external. Examples of internal relation are father and son, to give and to receive, and similar things, which cannot put off the nature of relation.

units.la: XXXV. Ens est incorruptibile, vel corruptibile. Incorruptibile est, cuius essentia semper manet sibi similis. Estque tale simpliciter, vel ex hypothesi. Incorruptibile simpliciter est, quod naturæ necessitate, seu immutabilitate, est tale: ut est solus Deus, qui ut non transiit a non esse ad esse, ita quoque transire non potest ab esse ad non esse. Psal. 102. ver. 27. 28. Rom. 1. v. 23. Incorruptibile ex hypothesi est, quod tale est ex voluntate Dei. Nam Deus vult aliquid esse incorruptibile, vel ut creator, vel ut redemptor, vel ut iudex seuerus. Primi modi exemplum sunt angeli & anima rationalis; secundi, corpora electorum in cœlis; tertii, corpora damnatorum in gehennâ. Corruptibile est, cuius essentia tendit ad non esse. 2. Pet. 3. ver. 12. 13. Est autem corruptio totalis, vel partialis, bona, vel mala; naturalis, vel violenta: vbi diligenter tenenda est regula, Corruptio naturalis est mater generationis, violenta, destructionis. Iohan. 12. v. 24. 1. Cor. 15. v. 42, 43.
units.tr: XXXV. Being is either incorruptible or corruptible. Incorruptible is that whose essence always remains like itself. It is such either simply or by hypothesis. Simply incorruptible is that which is such by necessity of nature, or by immutability, as God alone is; for just as he has not passed from non-being to being, so he cannot pass from being to non-being, Ps. 102. vers. 27, 28; Rom. 1. v. 23. Incorruptible by hypothesis is that which is such by the will of God. For God wills something to be incorruptible, either as creator, or as redeemer, or as severe judge. Examples of the first kind are angels and the rational soul; of the second, the bodies of the elect in heaven; of the third, the bodies of the damned in hell. Corruptible is that whose essence tends toward non-being, 2 Pet. 3. vers. 12, 13. Corruption, moreover, is total or partial, good or bad, natural or violent; and here the rule must be carefully observed: natural corruption is the mother of generation, violent corruption of destruction, John 12. v. 24; 1 Cor. 15. v. 42, 43.

units.la: XXXVI. Ens est naturale, vel non-naturale. Naturale est, quod habet principium actionis & passionis sibi insitum lege ordinaria creationis. Gen. 1. ver. ii.[?] Non - naturale est, quod mouetur a principio externo; estque vel supra, vel præter, vel contra naturam. Supra naturam est, quod naturam euehit ex regno potentiæ in regnum gratiæ vel gloriæ, non tollendo naturam, sed defectum naturæ. Sic regeneratio non tollit, sed extollit naturam hominis Iohan. 3. Præter naturam est, quod fit vi artis, & ideo dicitur artificiale. Contra naturam est, quod destruit naturam: scil. particularem, seu huius & illius individui. Fieri enim non potest, ut natura vniuersalis destruatur quamdiu hic mundus durat. Gen. 8. v. vlt.
units.tr: XXXVI. Being is either natural or non-natural. Natural is that which has a principle of action and passion implanted in it by the ordinary law of creation, Gen. 1. vers. 11. Non-natural is that which is moved by an external principle; and it is either above, or beyond, or against nature. Above nature is that which raises nature from the realm of power into the realm of grace or glory, not by abolishing nature but by removing its defect. Thus regeneration does not destroy but raises up the nature of man, John 3. Beyond nature is that which is done by the force of art, and is therefore called artificial. Against nature is that which destroys nature, namely particular nature, that is, the nature of this or that individual. For universal nature cannot be destroyed as long as this world endures, Gen. 8. last verse.

units.la: XXXVII. Ens est completum, vel incompletum. Completum est, quod per se subsistit: ut homo, arbor, & omnia illa, quæ Deus creauit Gen. 1. Incompletum est, quod est pars alterius: vt est manus hominis.
units.tr: XXXVII. Being is either complete or incomplete. Complete is that which subsists of itself, as man, a tree, and all those things which God created, Gen. 1. Incomplete is that which is a part of another, as the hand is a part of a man.

units.la: XXXVIII. Ens est totum vel pars. Totum est, quod non est mutilum. Estque indiuisibile, vel diuisibile. Totum indiuisibile est, quod nullas habet partes: vt Deus, qui est ὅλως ὅλον, totaliter totum, i.e. habens totam persectionem in fe toto. Eph. 4. verf. 6. Totum diuisibile est, quod partes habet: vt est caula, effectum, subiectum, adiunctum, genus, species, indiuiduum compositum. Pars est, quae continetur à toto[?]. Estque essentialis, vel integralis: & haec est principalis, vel minus principalis. Illa æque poteft atque pars essentialis. v.g. cor in animali est pars integralis principalis, quae æque facit ad esse animalis atque pars essentialis.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Being is either a whole or a part. A whole is that which is not mutilated. It is either indivisible or divisible. An indivisible whole is that which has no parts, as God is, who is wholly whole [ὅλως ὅλον], that is, having the whole perfection in his whole self, Eph. 4. vers. 6. A divisible whole is that which has parts, as a cause, an effect, a subject, an adjunct, a genus, a species, and a compound individual are. A part is that which is contained within a whole. It is either essential or integral, and the integral is either principal or less principal. The former can be just as much a part as an essential part is. For example, the heart in an animal is a principal integral part, which contributes just as much to the being of the animal as an essential part does.

units.la: XXXIX. Ens est prius, connexum, vel posterius. Prius est, cp antecedit: connexum, cp est simul: posterius, quod sequitur. Sunt autem varii modi prioris, conexi, & posterioris; qui omnes reuocantur ad quatuor capita, videl. ad naturam siue essentiam, personam siue modum subsistendi, circumstantiam, & cognitionem. Nam aliquid est prius, simul, vel posterius natura; modo subsistendi; circumstantia loci, temporis, dignitatis, virtutis, obiecti; vel denique cognitione. Sic Christus vt Deus est prior natura siue origine essentiae omnibus creaturis Prouerb. 8. Pater est prior Christo Filio, non origine essentiae, sed personae Iohan. 1. coelum est prius terra loco, dignitate, virtute.
units.tr: XXXIX. Being is either prior, connected, or posterior. Prior is that which goes before; connected is that which is simultaneous; posterior is that which follows. There are, however, various modes of the prior, the connected, and the posterior, all of which are referred to four heads, namely to nature or essence, to person or mode of subsisting, to circumstance, and to knowledge. For something is prior, simultaneous, or posterior by nature; by mode of subsisting; by circumstance of place, time, dignity, virtue, or object; or finally by knowledge. Thus Christ as God is prior to all creatures by nature or by origin of essence, Prov. 8. The Father is prior to the Son Christ, not by origin of essence but of person, John 1. Heaven is prior to earth in place, dignity, and virtue.

units.la: XL. Omne ens est idem, vel diuersum. Idem est, quod non distinguitur, quâ tale. Estque tale genere, specie, numero, causâ, effecto, subiecto, adiuncto, definitione, & analogia seu similitudine: ad quos modos reliqui referri possunt, puta idem natura siue essentia, voluntate, consensu, instituto &c. Sic idem numero Christus resurrexit ex morte Psal. 16. v. 10. Luc. 24. verf. 42.46. eadem numero caro resurget in vltimo die Iob. 19. ver. 27.
units.tr: XL. Every being is either the same or different. The same is that which is not distinguished, as such. It is the same in genus, species, number, cause, effect, subject, adjunct, definition, and analogy or likeness; to these modes the rest can be referred, such as the same in nature or essence, in will, in consent, in institution, and so on. Thus Christ rose from death as the same in number, Ps. 16. v. 10; Luke 24. vers. 42, 46; the same flesh in number will rise on the last day, Job 19. vers. 27.

units.la: 1. Cor. 15. verf. 42.43. trespersonæ ss.[?] trinitatis sunt idem essentia 1. Ioh. 5. v. 7. maritus & vxor sunt idem, seu vna caro, partim Φύσει[?] creationis, partim θέσει[?] relationis, quatenus vxor est pars viri, & Dei institutio in matrimonium ipsi tradita. Gen. 2. verf. 24. Diversum est, quod ab alio distinguitur. Distinguitur autem distinctione rei, vel rationis. Distinctio rei est, qua res à re distinguitur citra operationem mentis nostræ. Estque essentialis, inter rem & rem essentiâ peculiari prœditam: vel personalis, inter rem & rem essentiâ eandem, sed charactere essentiæ diversam: vel modalis, inter diversos unius rei modos atq; gradus.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 15:42-43. The three persons of the holy Trinity are 1 John 5:7 the same essence. A husband and wife are the same, or one flesh, partly by nature [φύσει] of creation and partly by placement [θέσει] of relation, inasmuch as the wife is part of the husband and was given to him in marriage by God's institution. Gen. 2:24. That which is different is that which is distinguished from another. It is distinguished either by a distinction of thing or of reason. A distinction of thing is that by which one thing is distinguished from another apart from any operation of our mind. It is essential, between things endowed with distinct essences; or personal, between things having the same essence but a different character of essence; or modal, between different modes and degrees of one thing.

units.la: 10 Primo modo distinguuntur illa, quæ habent separatas essentias, ut homo & arbor, Plato & Socrates: secundo, personæ sacrosanctæ Trinitatis, quæ sunt homousiæ 1. Ioh. 5. v. 7. tertio, lux matutina à meridianâ, vetus testamentum à novo, ut constat ex epistolâ ad Hebræos. Distinctio rationis est, quæ pendet à collatione, quam mens nostra instituit inter rem & rem: ut, cùm dextrum & sinistrum in columnâ distinguit pro diverso corporis positu; & cùm proprietates Dei distinguit pro varietate obiectorum & effectorum, proque modulo captus humani, ad 20 quem Deus se accommodauit in scripturis συγκαταβάσεως[?] plane paterna Exod. 34. verf. 6. 7.
units.tr: 10 In the first way are distinguished those things which have separate essences, such as man and tree, Plato and Socrates. In the second way, the persons of the most holy Trinity, which are of one essence 1 John 5:7. In the third way, morning light and midday light, the Old Testament and the New, as appears from the Epistle to the Hebrews. A distinction of reason depends on the comparison which our mind makes between one thing and another: as when it distinguishes right and left in a column according to the different position of the body, and when it distinguishes the properties of God according to the variety of objects and effects, and according to the measure of human understanding, to which God accommodated himself in the Scriptures by a condescension [συγκαταβάσεως] that is plainly fatherly Exod. 34:6-7.

units.la: XLI. Omne ens est illocale, vel locale.
units.tr: XLI. Every being is either unlocated or located.

units.la: Illocale est, quod supra & extra omnem locum existit: ut solus Deus. Hic enim ut est supra tempus suâ æternitate, ita quoque est supra locum suâ immensitate 1. Reg. 8. v. 27. Esa. 66. 1. Quòd autem vulgo dicitur Deus esse in loco repletivè, id accipiendum est de ipsius omnipræsentiâ, quâ est in omni loco Act. 17. v. 27. 28. Quò pertinet istud elegans:
units.tr: An unlocated being is that which exists above and outside every place, as God alone does. For as he is above time by his eternity, so he is also above place by his immensity 1 Kings 8:27; Isa. 66:1. But when it is commonly said that God is in a place by filling it, this must be understood of his omnipresence, by which he is in every place Acts 17:27-28. To this belongs that elegant line:

units.la: Enter, præsenter, Deus hic & ubique potenter. Nonitaque Deus est in loco ut locatum, sed ut causa omnis loci: unde Cabbalistis Deus appellatur מקום[?] i. e. locus. Locale est, quod locatur in suo loco: ut est omne ens præter Deum.
units.tr: Within, present, God is here and everywhere in power. Therefore God is not in a place as something located, but as the cause of every place; hence by the Cabbalists God is called place [makom, מקום], that is, locus. A located being is that which is placed in its own place, as is every being except God.

units.la: 35 Nam & spiritus creati sunt in loco, & corpora. Illi definitivè, hæc circumscriptivè: illi designando sibi locum, sed non occupando siue implendo; hæc occupando seu implendo. Marc.5.v.9: Luc.8.v.30.
units.tr: 35 For created spirits too are in a place, and so are bodies. The former are in place definitively, the latter circumscriptively; the former by designating a place for themselves but not occupying or filling it, the latter by occupying or filling it. Mark 5:9; Luke 8:30.

units.la: XLII. Omne ens est mensura, vel mensuratum. Mensura est, per quam deducimur in alicuius rei cognitionem: siue, est norma metiendi, qua cognoscimus, quantum sit aliquid. Estque mensurans, vel mensurata. Mensura mensurans est, quæ in aliquo genere prima est: vt est canon frumentarius & nummarius, vel exemplar authenticum. Sic Deus est mensura prima in latitudine seu vniuersitate entium: quia ex eo, per eum, & ad eum sunt omnia. Rom.11.v.vlt. Mensura mensurata est, quæ aliquo respectu est norma metiendi: vt effectum est mensura causæ ratione melioris cognitionis, quatenus ἔργων ἐλέγχος[?]. Sic ex operibus Dei cognoscitur ipsius æterna deitas & potentia. Rom.1.v.20. Mensuratum est, quod à mensura sua pendet: vt ecclesia mensuratur per scripturam sacram tanquam canonem fidei, vitæ, & vocationis nostræ. Eph.2.v.20.
units.tr: XLII. Every being is either a measure or something measured. A measure is that through which we are led to the knowledge of a thing; or it is the rule of measuring by which we know how great something is. A measure is either measuring or measured. A measuring measure is that which is first in its kind, as the standard grain measure or coin, or an authentic exemplar. So God is the first measure in the breadth or universality of beings, because from him, through him, and to him are all things. Rom. 11:36. A measured measure is that which, in some respect, is the rule of measuring, as an effect is a measure of its cause by way of better knowledge, as a proof from works [ἔργων ἐλέγχος]. Thus from the works of God his eternal deity and power are known. Rom. 1:20. A measured thing is that which depends on its measure, as the Church is measured by Holy Scripture as the rule of our faith, life, and calling. Eph. 2:20.

units.la: XLIII. Omne ens est possibile, vel impossibile. Possibile est, quod esse vel fieri potest: quod nempe ita est comparatum, vt eo non enervatur natura eius, quod possibile dicitur: vt possibile fuit, Nebucadnezarem degenerare in sortem brutorum. Dan.4. Impossibile est, quod esse vel fieri non potest: estque tale vel natura, vel naturæ. Impossibile natura est, quod propter sui imperfectionem, & agentis perfectionem fieri non potest: vt Deus non potest mentiri Heb.6.v.18. Impossibile natura est, quod propter imperfectionem agentis fieri non potest: vt impossibile fuit Abrahamo subducere numerum stellarum. Gen.16. v.5. Sic multa nobis sunt impossibilia, quæ Deo sunt possibilia. Matth.16.v.26. Marc.10.v.27. Luc.18.v.27. Insignis est locus apud Ambrosium lib.4.de fide, hanc in sententiam: Multa sunt impossibilitatum differentia. Est aliquid natura impossibile. Et est aliquid, quod est possibile per naturam, impossibile per infirmitatem. Est etiam tertium, quod sit possibile per corporis & animi animi firmitatem, impossibile per imperitiam aut impotentiam. Est etiam, quod per definitionem immutabilis propositi & constantiae perseverantiam voluntatis atque amicitiae fidem fit impossibile mutari. Sic non erat possibile, ut à Christo abiret poculum crucis Matth. 26. v. 39.
units.tr: XLIII. Every being is either possible or impossible. Possible is that which can be or come to be, that is, that which is so constituted that its nature, which is called possible, is not weakened by it; as it was possible for Nebuchadnezzar to degenerate into the lot of the beasts. Dan. 4. Impossible is that which cannot be or come to be, and this is so either by nature or by the nature of something. That is impossible by nature which, on account of its own imperfection and the perfection of the agent, cannot come to be, as God cannot lie Heb. 6:18. That is impossible by the nature of something which, on account of the imperfection of the agent, cannot come to be, as it was impossible for Abraham to count the number of the stars. Gen. 15:5 (cf. Gen. 16:5 as printed). So many things are impossible for us which are possible for God. Matt. 19:26; Mark 10:27; Luke 18:27. There is a notable passage in Ambrose, Book 4 On the Faith, to this effect: There are many differences of impossibility. Some things are impossible by nature. And some things are possible by nature but impossible through weakness. There is also a third kind, which is possible through firmness of body and mind, but impossible through inexperience or lack of power. There is also that which, by the definition of an unchangeable purpose, and by the perseverance of constancy, the will's steadfastness and the faithfulness of friendship, is made impossible to change. So it was not possible that the cup of the cross should pass from Christ Matt. 26:39.

units.la: XLIV. Ens est archetypum, vel ectypum. Archetypum est primigenium exemplar, ex quo aliquid exprimitur: alias prototypum. Ectypum est, quod ex archetypo exprimitur. Sic essentia Dei est idea seu archetypum omnis boni in natura & supra naturam. Hinc veritas, bonitas, iustitia, lex, & res similes diuiduntur in archetypas & ectypas. Similiter in rebus artificialibus datur archetypum & ectypum: quomodo apostolus Hebr. 8. v. 5. pronuntiat, Mosen iussum esse omnia facere ad exemplar ipsi ostensum in monte. Teneatur hic regula: Non debet esse plus in ectypo, quàm in archetypo.
units.tr: XLIV. A being is either archetypal or ectypal. An archetype is the original exemplar from which something is expressed; otherwise called a prototype. An ectype is that which is expressed from an archetype. Thus the essence of God is the idea or archetype of all goodness, both in nature and above nature. Hence truth, goodness, justice, law, and similar things are divided into archetypal and ectypal. Similarly, in artificial things there is an archetype and an ectype, as the apostle declares, Heb. 8:5, that Moses was commanded to make all things according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain. Let this rule be held here: There ought not to be more in the ectype than in the archetype.

units.la: XLV. Ens est reale, vel intentionale. Ens reale est, quod in rerum natura existit: ut sol. Ens intentionale est, quod obiicitur menti; seu, quod habet esse intentionale. Estque rationis, ut notiones secundae: vel fidei, ut caro Christi Abrahamo fuit praesens obiectiue, seu intentionaliter, quatenus Abraham vera fide praeditus vidit diem Domini. Iohan. 8. v. 56.
units.tr: XLV. A being is either real or intentional. A real being is that which exists in the nature of things, as the sun. An intentional being is that which is presented to the mind, or which has intentional existence. It is either of reason, as second notions; or of faith, as the flesh of Christ was present to Abraham objectively, or intentionally, inasmuch as Abraham, endowed with true faith, saw the day of the Lord. John 8:56.

units.la: XLVI. Omne ens est abstractum, vel concretum. Abstractum est, quod ab alio secretam habet naturam. Eius autem modi sunt quatuor. Primus est essentiae spiritualis in Deo, angelis, & anima rationali: secundus est duarum naturarum in Christo: tertius est formarum, ut sapientiae, iustitiae, aureitatis: quartus est conceptuum, ubi mens nostra dicitur abstrahere unum ab alio, quando considerat unum non considerato alio, cuiusmodi abstractio datur in metaphysicis, logicis, physicis, & mathematicis. Concretum est, quod habet naturam cum alio unitam sive coniunctam: ut aurum, homo, & omne compositum ex materia & forma. Sic persona Christi est aliquid concretum, iuxta illud theologorum: Communicatio idiomatum valet in concreto, e.g. Filius hominis descendit e coelo Iohan.3.verf.13. Dominum gloriae crucifixerunt 1.Cor.2. verf.8.
units.tr: XLVI. Every being is either abstract or concrete. An abstract being is that which has a nature set apart from another. There are four kinds of this. The first is of spiritual essence, in God, angels, and the rational soul; the second is of the two natures in Christ; the third is of forms, as of wisdom, justice, gold-ness; the fourth is of concepts, where our mind is said to abstract one thing from another when it considers one thing without considering the other. This kind of abstraction occurs in metaphysics, logic, physics, and mathematics. A concrete being is that which has a nature united or joined with another, as gold, man, and everything compounded of matter and form. So the person of Christ is something concrete, according to the theologians' saying: The communication of properties holds in the concrete, e.g. The Son of man came down from heaven John 3:13. They crucified the Lord of glory 1 Cor. 2:8.

units.la: XLVII. Ens est principium, vel principiatum. Principium est, quod in suo genere primum est: in genere, inquam, causae, loci, temporis, motus, essentiae, personae, notitiae seu cognitionis. Usitate ita diuiditur principium, ut statuatur aliud esse essentiae seu essendi, aliud cognitionis seu cognoscendi. Utrumque est incomplexum, vel complexum. Illud est res, ut Deus, natura, Scriptura sacra: hoc est sententia, ut, Deus est, Natura est ordo Dei creatoris, Scriptura sacra est verbum Dei. Principiatum est, quod a principio pendet. Sic Christus est principium, a quo pendent omnes creaturae Coloss.1.v.18. & inprimis electi, quorum ipse est caput & ἀρχῆς[?]. De principio primo temporis vide Gen.1.v.1.
units.tr: XLVII. A being is either a principle or something derived from a principle. A principle is that which is first in its kind: in the kind, I mean, of cause, place, time, motion, essence, person, or knowledge or cognition. It is customary to divide a principle in such a way that one kind is affirmed to be of essence or being, and another of knowledge or knowing. Each of these is either incomplex or complex. The former is a thing, as God, nature, Holy Scripture; the latter is a proposition, as God is, Nature is the order of God the Creator, Holy Scripture is the word of God. A derived thing is that which depends on a principle. Thus Christ is the principle on whom all creatures depend Col. 1:18, and above all the elect, of whom he is the head and beginning [ἀρχῆς]. Concerning the first principle of time, see Gen. 1:1.

units.la: XLVIII. Ens est causa, vel causatum. Causa est, quae aliquid influit in causatum: idque ratione essentiae, permissionis, vel directionis seu regiminis. Sic Deus essentiam & regimen influit rebus bonis Gen.1.v.31. Psal.104. Act.17.v.25.26. malis culpae influit permissionem & directionem, sed non essentiam. Psal.5.v.5.6. 1.Reg.22.v.21.22. Caeterum causa consideratur in genere, vel in specie. Causa in genere est per se, vel per accidens; prima, vel secunda; potentia, vel actu; sufficiens, vel insufficiens; totalis, vel partialis; uniuoca, vel aequiuoca, universalis, vel particularis; remota, vel propinqua. Quae divisiones omnibus & singulis causis applicari debent. Causa in specie est efficiens, finis, materia, & forma: qui ordo est secundum naturam, ut constat ex historia creationis Gen.1. ubi Deus tanquam prima causa efficiens & finalis antecessit omne materiam & formam. Causalitas efficientis est, producere effectum procreando, conseruando, corrumpendo, permittendo, vel dirigendo. Causalitas finis est, perficere suum finitum.Causalitas materia est,concurrere cum forma,vt existat materiatum. Causalitas denique forma est, concurrere cum materiâ, vt existat formatum. Causatum est, quod à cau·â accipit influxum. Speculum quatuor causarum longè pulcherrimum vide Gen.1.&2.
units.tr: XLVIII. A being is either a cause or something caused. A cause is that which flows some influence into the thing caused, and this by reason of essence, permission, or direction or governance. Thus God gives essence and governance to good things Gen. 1:31; Ps. 104; Acts 17:25-26; to evil things, through fault, he gives permission and direction, but not essence Ps. 5:5-6; 1 Kings 22:21-22. Moreover a cause is considered either in its kind or in its species. A cause in kind is either per se or per accidens; first or second; in power or in act; sufficient or insufficient; total or partial; univocal or equivocal; universal or particular; remote or proximate. These divisions ought to be applied to all and each of the causes. A cause in species is efficient, final, material, and formal; and this order is according to nature, as appears from the history of creation Gen. 1, where God, as first efficient and final cause, preceded all matter and form. The causality of the efficient cause is to produce an effect by begetting, preserving, corrupting, permitting, or directing it. The causality of the final cause is to complete its end. The causality of matter is to concur with form so that the thing material exists. Finally, the causality of form is to concur with matter so that the thing formed exists. A caused thing is that which receives influence from a cause. For a most excellent survey of the four causes, see Gen. 1 and 2.

units.la: XLIX. Omne ens est necessarium, vel contingens. Necessarium est, quod aliter esse non potest. Est autem necessitas incomplexa, vel complexa. Illa dicitur necessitas rei, secundùm varia loca inuentionis logicæ: hæc est, vel consequentis, in axiomate, vel consequentiæ, in syllogismo. Necessitas rei est independens, vel dependens. Necessitas independens & illimitata est vehementia essendi illius, quod per se & primò necesse est esse: quo sensu solus Deus est ens necessarium, vtpote cui soli repugnat non-esse. Hincipsi [?] soli competit nomen Iehouah. Apoc.16.v.5. Necessitas dependens & limitata est, quâ aliquid est necessarium ex hypothesi alicuius causæ, purâ efficientis, finis, materiæ, vel formæ. Huc pertinent isti modi: necessitas naturalis siue naturæ; necessitas fatalis seu infallibilitatis & præscientiæ diuinæ, necessitas violentiæ & coactionis, necessitas prædictionis, determinationis, expedientiæ, indigentiæ, præcepti, iuris, obedientiæ, medij, meriti, &c. Sic v.g. necesse fuit Christum pati & resurgere Luc.24.v.26. quia Deus ita decreuerat, & per prophetas prædixerat, & salus nostra ita exigebat. Mutato sacerdotio leuitico, necessariò facta est legis mutatio Heb.7.v.12. quia Deus ita ordinauerat, vt sacerdotium Leuiticum cum nouo sacerdotio Christi commutaretur. Necessitas coactionis opponitur libertati 1.Cor.7.v.37. Philem.v.14.& 1.Petr.5.v.2. Sed reliqui modi necessitatis eleganter consentiunt cum libertate: vt, Adam peccauit necessariò, respectu decreti Dei, liberè, respectu voluntatis suæ: Deus necessariò odit peccatum, necessitate naturæ, & liberè, quia non coacte. Ex his patet, libertatem subordinari necessitati, neque rectè referri ad contingentiam. Vide infra in Ethicis. Necessitas consequentis est, cum immutabiliter duo vel plura cohærent in oratione: unde dicitur necessitas immutabilitatis, quâ aliquid alicui attribuitur, conuenienter immutabili naturæ, vt vel necessario antecedens, vel comitans, vel consequens. Appellatur etiam necessitas propositionis, axiomatis, & sententiæ. Sic necessarium est, Deum esse bonum, hominem esse animal. Necessitas consequentiæ est, cum vna propositio ex alia sic deducitur, vt inter se immutabiliter cohæreant: vt Heb. 8. v. 3. Omnis Pontifex ad offerenda dona & victimas constituitur: unde necesse fuit hunc quoque (Christum) habere quod offerret. Appellare possis necessitatem syllogisticæ illationis. Contingens est, quod aliter esse potest: idque ratione rei, prædicationis, vel illationis. εὐδηλον[?] ex modo dictis.
units.tr: XLIX. Every being is either necessary or contingent. That is necessary which cannot be otherwise. Necessity is either unconnected or connected. The former is called the necessity of a thing, according to the various places of logical invention; the latter is either the necessity of the consequent, in an axiom, or the necessity of the consequence, in a syllogism. The necessity of a thing is either independent or dependent. Independent and unlimited necessity is the strength of that being which is necessary of itself and in the first place; in this sense God alone is a necessary being, since to him alone non-existence is impossible. Hence the name Jehovah belongs to him alone. Rev. 16:5. Dependent and limited necessity is that by which something is necessary on the supposition of some cause, whether efficient, final, material or formal. To this belong the following kinds: natural necessity or the necessity of nature; fatal necessity, or the necessity of infallibility and divine foreknowledge; the necessity of force and compulsion; the necessity of prediction, determination, expediency, need, precept, right, obedience, means, merit, and so on. Thus, for example, it was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise again, Luke 24:26, because God had so decreed, had foretold it through the prophets, and because our salvation required it so. With the Levitical priesthood changed, a change of the law was necessarily made, Heb. 7:12, because God had so ordained that the Levitical priesthood should be exchanged for the new priesthood of Christ. The necessity of compulsion is opposed to liberty, 1 Cor. 7:37; Philem. 14; 1 Pet. 5:2. But the other kinds of necessity agree well with liberty: for example, Adam sinned necessarily with respect to God's decree, and freely with respect to his own will; God necessarily hates sin by the necessity of his nature, and yet freely, because not under compulsion. From this it is plain that liberty is subordinate to necessity, and is not rightly referred to contingency. See below in the Ethics. The necessity of the consequent is when two or more things cohere unchangeably in a statement; hence it is called the necessity of immutability, by which something is attributed to something, agreeably to an unchangeable nature, as either antecedent, accompanying or consequent. It is also called the necessity of a proposition, an axiom and a sentence. Thus it is necessary that God be good, and that man be an animal. The necessity of the consequence is when one proposition is so deduced from another that they cohere unchangeably with each other: as in Heb. 8:3, "Every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; hence it was necessary that this one also (Christ) should have something to offer." You may call this the necessity of syllogistic inference. Contingent is that which can be otherwise, whether by reason of the thing, of the predication, or of the inference. This is clear from what has been said.

units.la: L. Omne ens est subiectum, vel adiunctum. Subiectum est, quod alicui subiicitur: seu, cui aliquid adiungitur. Sic materia est subiectum formæ, substantia accidentis, obiectum, adiuncti occupati, & pars antecedens in axiomate est subiectum partis consequentis. Adiunctum est, quod alicui adiungitur: seu, cui aliquid subiicitur: vt forma est adiunctum materiæ, accidens substantiæ, &c. Adiunctum est essentiale, vel accidentale; proprium, vel commune; separabile, vel inseparabile. Sic devotio est adiunctum precationis essentiale siue internum, locus & tempus sunt adiuncta circumstantialia seu externa. Matt. 6. Luc. 18.
units.tr: L. Every being is either a subject or an adjunct. A subject is that which is placed under something, or to which something is joined. Thus matter is the subject of form, substance the subject of an accident, the object is the subject of the thing occupied by it, and the antecedent part in an axiom is the subject of the consequent part. An adjunct is that which is joined to something, or to which something is placed under it: thus form is an adjunct of matter, an accident of substance, and so on. An adjunct is either essential or accidental, proper or common, separable or inseparable. Thus devotion is an essential or internal adjunct of prayer, while place and time are circumstantial or external adjuncts. Matt. 6; Luke 18.

units.la: LI. Omne ens est signum, vel signatum. Signum est, quod alicui aliquid signat. Unde perspicitur, omne signum duas relationes includere. e.g. unam ad id, quod significatur, alteram ad id, cui significatur. Quod dixi de significatione, idem de obsignatione, & reliquis modis signandi est iudicium. Est autem signum aliud speculatiuum, aliud practicum. Illud in nuda significatione consistit: hoc significationi addit obsignationem & applicationem. Ideo in definitione signi non diximus, significat, sed signat: quia signare est significare, declarare, exprimere evidenter, obsignare conferendo, claudere signo apposito. Caeterum signum est vel γνώρισμα[?], indicium, ein Kenn vnd Merckzeichen / vel μνημόσυνον, memoriale, ein Denckzeichen; vel σφραγίς, Sigillum. Rursus signum est vel ἐνδεικτικὸν[?], rei praesentis; vel μνημόσυνον, rei praeteritae; vel προγνωστικὸν[?], rei futurae. Exempla plurima occurrunt in sacris. Iris est signum gratiae Dei Gen.9.Circumcisio est signum & sigillum foederis gratiae Gen.17. verf.11. Rom.4. verf.11. Pascha est memoriale (seu monumentum transitus Exod.12. v.13. Praecepta Dei alligata manibus Israelitarum erant signum & typus accuratae & perpetuae observationis. Deut.6. v.8. Ionas in ventre ceti fuit signum filij hominis commoraturi in ventre terrae. Matth.16. v.4. rubedo caeli est prognosticum tempestatis. ibid. v.2. ceremoniae V.T. erant typi Christi. epist. ad Hebr. passim. sacramenta sunt signa donantia, sive pingentia & significantia; obsignantia, sive certificantia; denique applicantia, sive praebentia & exhibentia ipsum signatum in legitimo usu. 1. Cor.11. verf.24.25. Signatum est, quod a signo repraesentatur, nempe significando, obsignando, vel exhi-bendo.
units.tr: LI. Every being is either a sign or a thing signified. A sign is that which signifies something to someone. Hence it is clear that every sign includes two relations: one to that which is signified, the other to that to which it is signified. What I have said of signification applies equally to sealing and the other modes of signifying. A sign is either speculative or practical. The former consists in bare signification; the latter adds to signification sealing and application. Therefore in the definition of a sign I have not said significat but signat, because signare means to signify, to declare, to express clearly, to seal by conferring, to close with an applied seal. Moreover a sign is either a gnōrisma [γνώρισμα], an indication, a sign and mark; or a mnēmosynon [μνημόσυνον], a memorial, a reminder; or a sphragis [σφραγίς], a seal. Again, a sign is either endeiktikon [ἐνδεικτικὸν], of a present thing; or mnēmosynon, of a past thing; or prognōstikon [προγνωστικὸν], of a future thing. Very many examples occur in the sacred writings. The rainbow is a sign of God's grace, Gen. 9. Circumcision is a sign and seal of the covenant of grace, Gen. 17:11; Rom. 4:11. The Passover is a memorial (or monument) of the passing over, Exod. 12:13. The commandments of God bound on the hands of the Israelites were a sign and type of accurate and perpetual observance, Deut. 6:8. Jonah in the belly of the whale was a sign of the Son of Man who would remain in the belly of the earth, Matt. 16:4. The redness of the sky is a forecast of tempest, ibid. 2. The ceremonies of the Old Testament were types of Christ, throughout the Epistle to the Hebrews. Sacraments are signs that give, or depict and signify; sealing, or certifying signs; and finally applying signs, that is, those which present and exhibit the thing signified itself in lawful use, 1 Cor. 11:24, 25. The thing signified is that which is represented by a sign, namely by signifying, sealing or exhibiting.

units.la: LII Explicatis transcendentibus restant praedicamenta, quae sunt summa entis genera, numero decem. Quintilianus scite ait: Aristoteles decem elementa constituit, circa quae versari videatur omnis quaestio. Et Melanchthon praedicamenta eleganter vocat classes seu series rerum omnium. Est enim praedicamentum locus, quo omneens, sive omnis conceptus simplex realis, refertur ad potest, hoc ordine: substantia, quantitas, qualitas, actio, passio, relatio, quando, ubi, situs, habitus.
units.tr: LII. Having explained the transcendentals, there remain the categories, which are the highest genera of being, ten in number. Quintilian rightly says: Aristotle set up ten elements, about which every question seems to turn. And Melanchthon elegantly calls the categories classes or series of all things. For a category is the place to which every being, or every simple real concept, is referred, in this order: substance, quantity, quality, action, passion, relation, when, where, position, state.

units.la: LIII. Praedicamentum aliud est substantiae, aliud accidentis. Nam species entis sunt duae, substantia & accidens. Substantia est ens per se subsistens, hoc est, non indigens subiecto inhaesionis, seu, non inhaerens alij: ut Deus, Spiritus creatus, & corpus. Gen. 1. & 2. Heb. 1. v.14. Accidens est ens substantiæ inhærens. Eius genera sunt nouem, hoc ordine. 1. Quantitas est accidens, quod habet partem extra partem. 2. Qualitas est accidens, quod creaturam reddit aptam ad agendum & patiendum. 3. Actio est accidens, quo ag ens occupatur circa patiens. 4. Passio est accidens, quo patiens recipit vim agentis. 5. Relatio est accidens, quo relatum r[?]respicit[?] correlatum propter quantitatem vel qualitatem aliquam. 6. Quando est accidens, quo res est in tempore. 7. Vbi est accidens, quo res est in loco. 8. Situs: est accidens, quo res certo modo ponitur in loco. 9. Habitus: est accidens, quo rei adiacet ornatus: puta vestitus, vel quasi-vestitus. Nouem ista accidentia cùm in toto mundo Gen. 1. tum in singulis creaturis corporeis sunt manifesta, ideoque in illarum examine non oscitanter debent obseruari, atque adeò transcendentibus adiungi. e g. si differtatio fit instituenda de solo, Platone, Bucephalo, rosa, &c. ex transcendentium & prædicamentorum doctrinâ peti possunt innumera, quæ suppeditant materiam uberrimi & felicissimi discursus. De hac materiâ vide infrà Prædicamenta sacra.
units.tr: LIII. One category belongs to substance, another to accident. For there are two kinds of being, substance and accident. Substance is a being that subsists through itself, that is, one that does not need a subject of inherence, or that does not inhere in another, as God, created spirit and body. Gen. 1 and 2; Heb. 1:14. Accident is a being that inheres in substance. Its genera are nine, in this order. (1) Quantity is an accident that has part outside part. (2) Quality is an accident that makes a creature fit for acting and suffering. (3) Action is an accident by which an agent is occupied about a patient. (4) Passion is an accident by which a patient receives the force of an agent. (5) Relation is an accident by which the relative regards its correlate on account of some quantity or quality. (6) When is an accident by which a thing is in time. (7) Where is an accident by which a thing is in place. (8) Position is an accident by which a thing is placed in a place in a certain manner. (9) State is an accident by which an adornment lies upon a thing, such as clothing or quasi-clothing. These nine accidents are evident both in the whole world, Gen. 1, and in each corporeal creature, and so they must not be observed carelessly in their examination, and must be joined to the transcendentals. For example, if a dissertation is to be undertaken on the soil, on Plato, Bucephalus, a rose, and so on, innumerable things can be drawn from the doctrine of the transcendentals and categories, which supply material for a most rich and happy discourse. On this matter see below, Sacred Categories.

units.la: VIII. PNEVMATICA SACRA.
units.tr: VIII. Sacred Pneumatics.

units.la: I. PHilosophiam primam vidimus: sequitur jam philosophia orta, in quâ primò se offert Pneumatica, & ea quidem sacra, quæ est scientia Spiritus, quatenus est spiritus, sumta ex literis. Postea enim de ente, qua ens est, i.e. de ente universè, tractauimus, ordo postulat, ut consideremus tale ens, ubi primò se nobis offert ens spirituale.
units.tr: I. We have seen first philosophy. Next comes the philosophy that arises from it, in which Pneumatics comes first, and specifically sacred Pneumatics, which is the science of the Spirit, insofar as he is spirit, drawn from the Scriptures. For after we have treated of being, insofar as it is being, that is, of being in general, order requires that we consider such being where spiritual being first presents itself to us.

units.la: II. Spiritus est substantia corporis expers. Vulgò dicimus, Melius potest dici, quid non sit spiritus, quàm quid sit. Etideò Spiritus definitur substantia incorporea, seu corporaturæ expers. Quam definitionem Christus expressit Luc. 24. v. 39.
units.tr: II. A spirit is a substance free of body. We commonly say, It is easier to say what a spirit is not than what it is. And therefore a spirit is defined as an incorporeal substance, or one without bodily substance. Christ expressed this definition in Luke 24:39.

units.la: III. Spiritus consideratur in genere, & in specie. Hinc Pneumatica dividitur in generalem, & spe-cialem.
units.tr: III. Spirit is considered in general and in particular. Hence Pneumatics is divided into general and special.

units.la: IV. Spiritus in genere consideratur quantum ad proprietates suas, siue communes assectiones, hoc ordine. 1. Spiritus est liber ab omni, tum crassa, tum subtili corporatura. Hinc Spiritus opponitur corpori. Quæ etiam causa est, quòd pars regenita in electis appellatur spiritus, pars non-regenita, caro. Rom. 8. verf. 6. 9. 10. Gal. 5. v. 17. Facit huc usitatus canon: Contradistinctum includit contradistincti negationem. 2. Spiritus est magnitudinis proprie dictæ expers, hoc est, non habet partem extra partem. Hæc proprietas est consectarium primæ. 3. Spiritus per se est insensilis: quia τὸ αἰσθητὸν[?] est affectio corporis. Dico per se: quia per accidens, ratione nempe variorum effectuum, spiritus afficit sensum: ut quando Deus locutus est, quando tonat, & alia opera sensum afficientia edit. Sic angeli locuti sunt hominibus, & iis apparuerunt in assumtis corporibus. Anima quoque rationalis se prodit per varias actiones sensibiles. 4. Spiritus ubi ubi est, ibi totus est. Nam quia non habet partes, non potest alicubi esse divisibiliter. Hinc eleganter dicunt, Spiritum se habere in-star puncti, quod est ἄτομον[?] seu ἀμερὲς[?]. De hoc modo ineffendi vide Psal. 139. & Marc. 5. v. 9. Rectè itaque pronuntiatur à cordatis philosophis, animam rationalem efse totam in toto corpore, & totam in singulis partibus.
units.tr: IV. Spirit in general is considered with respect to its properties, or common affections, in this order. 1. A spirit is free of every body, whether gross or subtle. Hence spirit is opposed to body. This is also the reason why the regenerate part of the elect is called spirit, and the unregenerate part flesh (Rom. 8:6, 9, 10; Gal. 5:17). The familiar rule applies here: a contrasted term includes the negation of the other contrasted term. 2. Spirit is without magnitude in the proper sense, that is, it does not have one part outside another. This property follows from the first. 3. Spirit is in itself insensible, since what is perceptible [to aisthēton] is an affection of body. I say in itself, because spirit does affect the senses by accident, namely by reason of its various effects: as when God speaks, when he thunders, and when he performs other works that strike the senses. So angels spoke to men and appeared to them in assumed bodies. The rational soul also reveals itself through various sensible actions. 4. Spirit is wholly wherever it is. For since it has no parts, it cannot be somewhere divisibly. Hence they aptly say that spirit is like a point, which is indivisible [atomon] or without parts [amerés]. On this mode of being present see Psalm 139 and Mark 5:9. Thus it is rightly pronounced by sound philosophers that the rational soul is whole in the whole body and whole in each of its parts.

units.la: 5. Spiritus est immortalis. Mors siquidem est separatio animæ a corpore, & proinde non habet locum in iis, quæ habent naturam merè spiritualem. 6. Spiritus præditus est intellectu & voluntate. Nam vita spiritualis est posita in intelligendo & volendo. 7. Spiritus est præditus potentiâ agendi promtâ. Nam si corpora, quò subtiliora, eò sunt virtutis penetrantioris, quid amabo de spiritibus erit statuendum, qui subtilitatem corporum longo interuallo anteeunt ? Efficaciæ istius exemplum insigne suppeditat historia Senhacheribi 2.Reg.19. Pertinet huc regula: Quod potest virtus inferior, potest & superior, modo sit excellentiore.
units.tr: 5. Spirit is immortal. For death is the separation of the soul from the body, and so it has no place in things that have a purely spiritual nature. 6. Spirit is endowed with intellect and will. For spiritual life consists in understanding and willing. 7. Spirit is endowed with a ready power of acting. For if bodies, the more subtle they are, the more penetrating their power is, what, pray, must we hold concerning spirits, which far surpass the subtlety of bodies? A notable example of this efficacy is supplied by the history of Sennacherib (2 Kings 19). To this belongs the rule: What a lower power can do, a higher power can also do, provided it is of greater excellence.

units.la: V. Spiritus in specie est infinitus, vel fini-tus.
units.tr: V. Spirit in particular is either infinite or finite.

units.la: VI. Spiritus infinitus est Deus. Deum esse spiritum docet Christus Iohan. 4.v.24. Eum est spiritum infinitum docet apostolus Eph. 4 v. 6. his verbis: Vnus Deus & pater omnium, qui est super omnes, & per omnes, & in omnibus vobis. Confer cum 1.Reg. 8.v.27. An reuera habitaret Deus in terrâ? Ecce cœli ipsi, & cœli cœlorum non capiunt te: quanto minus domus hæc, quam ædificaui?
units.tr: VI. The infinite spirit is God. Christ teaches that God is spirit (John 4:24). The apostle teaches that he is an infinite spirit, in these words (Eph. 4:6): One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all. Compare 1 Kings 8:27: But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you; how much less this house which I have built?

units.la: VII. Deus est spiritus essentia vnus, personis & operibus trinus. Hoc theorema est fundamentum omnis solidæ sapientiæ: quia omnis sapientia extra & citra hoc dogma est pura puta stultitia. Quod quàm sit verum, non norunt nisi illi, qui vestigium vnitatis & trinitatis in totâ naturâ oculis mentis se ingerere animaduerterunt. Percurre omnes & singulas creaturas, videbis vnitatem non esse sine trinitate, neque trinitatem sine vnitate. Placet intueri corporeas naturas? Vides ibi corpus, spiritum & animam. In homine id est euidens. 1.Thes.5.v.23. In reliquis creaturis corporeis id euincit ratio, quam comitatur experientia. Nihil iam dico de tribus principiis, quæ distinctè constituunt vnum corpus. Assurgamus ad animam rationalem & angelos, & dispiciamus, quomodo ibi sit vnum & trinum. Tria ibi sunt intimè vnita, videl. intellectus, voluntas, & potentia agendi spiritualis. Præterea alia, quæ multa sunt. Neque vero est, quòd aliquis criminetur hanc similitudinem, quòd maxima ibi sit dissimilitudo. Nam paulò ante dixi, vestigium duntaxat huius arcani cerni in naturâ, non expressam similitudinem. Sed euoluamus theorema nostrum. Principio vnitas essentia in Deo adeo est magna , vt omnes ipsius proprietates sint vnum in essentia : puta simplicitas, immutabilitas, immensitas, æ-ternitas, sapientia , veracitas, bonitas, iustitia, potentia & beatitudo. Nam Deus ita est simplex, vt simplicitas eius sit essentia eius, & immutabilitas eius , & immensitas eius &c. Hinc Deus est simplex, bonus, verus, sapiens, potens &c. non per qualitatem, sed per essentiam. Atque hæc est causa, quòd Deus dicit, nomen suum esse Eheieh afcher Eheieh , ero qui ero, seu , sum qui sum.
units.tr: VII. God is spirit, one in essence and threefold in persons and works. This theorem is the foundation of all solid wisdom, because all wisdom outside and apart from this doctrine is pure foolishness. How true this is, only those know who have noticed that the vestige of unity and trinity forces itself upon the eyes of the mind throughout all of nature. Run through all creatures, one by one, and you will see that there is no unity without trinity, nor trinity without unity. Do you wish to look at corporeal natures? There you see body, spirit and soul. In man this is evident (1 Thess. 5:23). In the other corporeal creatures, reason proves it, and experience accompanies reason. I say nothing now of the three principles which distinctly constitute one body. Let us rise to the rational soul and the angels, and let us see how there is one and three there. There are three things there intimately united, namely intellect, will, and spiritual power of acting, and besides these many others. Nor should anyone accuse this comparison because there is a very great dissimilarity. For I said a little earlier that only a vestige of this mystery is discerned in nature, not an express likeness. But let us unfold our theorem. First, the unity of essence in God is so great that all his properties are one in essence: namely simplicity, immutability, immensity, eternity, wisdom, truthfulness, goodness, justice, power and blessedness. For God is so simple that his simplicity is his essence, and his immutability is his essence, and his immensity is his essence, and so on. Hence God is simple, good, true, wise, powerful, etc., not by quality but by essence. And this is the reason why God says that his name is Eheieh asher Eheieh, that is, I am who I am (Exod. 3:14-15).

units.la: Exod. 3. verf. 14. 15. Deinde trinitas personarum ita se habet in Deo, vt Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus sint vnum essentia, & omnibus proprietatibus essentiæ, solis proprietatibus personalibus distincti. 1.Ioh.5. verf. 7. Matt.28. verf. 19. Hinc licet Pater sit omnipotens, & Filius omnipotens, & Spiritus sanctus omnipotens, non tamen sunt tres omnipotentes , sed hi tres sunt vnus omnipotens Deus, seu vna essentia omnipotens. De reliquis proprietatibus essentialibus idem est iudicium. Alia est ratio proprietatum personalium, siue hypostaticarum, quas Græci eleganter vocant characteres essentiæ. Hæ liquidem realiter, id est , reuerà , citra mentis nostræ operationem, sunt distinctæ. Nam Pater est prima persona deitatis, quæ non subsistit aliunde, & genuit Filium ( vnde Pater dici ur) & producit Spiritum sanctum: Filius est secunda persona deitatis, quæ genita est à Patre, vnde Filius dicitur; & cum Patre producit Spiritum sanctum: Spiritus sanctus est tertia persona deitatis, quæ à Patre & Filio, vt vnà spirantibus, procedit: vnde Spiritus sanctus appellatur. Iohan. 1. Matth. 3. Iohan. 15. verf. 26. Denique opera Dei, quæ ab ipsius essentia feruntur extra ipsum, sunt creatio in regno potentiæ, redemtio in regno gratiæ , & glorificatio in regno gloriæ. Creatio est , quâ Deus ex nihilo produxit cœlum & terram , & omnia quæ in iis sunt. Cum hac cohæret gubernatio. Gen. 1. & 2. Hebr. 11. v. 3. Redemtio est, quâ Deus per Filium suum Iesum Christum liberauit electos ex potestate diaboli. Gal. 3. v. 13 Cum hâc immediatè cohæret sanctificatio, quâ Deus nos regenerat Spiritu suo sanctoad[?] nouam vitam Rom. 8. v. 1. & seqq. Hic non est prætereundum silentio, quomodo tria ista opera certo quodam respectu tribuantur, singula singulis, personis sacrosanctæ Trinitatis. Pater nempe est principium Trinitatis. Huic itaque peculiari quodam respectu tribuitur creatio, per quam creaturæ incipiunt esse. Filius est media persona inter Patrem & Filium. Huic itaque peculiari quodam respectu tribuitur redemtio, per quam homines vniuntur Deo. Spiritus sanctus est tertia persona deitatis, quæ spiratur à Patre & Filio. Huic itaque peculiari quodam respectu tribuitur sanctificatio, per quam magis magisque spirituales efficimur. Glorificatio est, quâ Deus electos suos in cœlo perfundit gaudio, & coronat gloriâ, ineffabilibus. Rom. 8. v. 29. Atque hæc summatim tenenda sunt de Deo, de quo dixerimus multa, nec tamen assecuti erimus: caterùm summa dictorum est, ipsum esse omnia. Ad laudandum eum quæ nostra est facultas? ipse enim maior est omnibus suis operibus. Terribilis est Dominus, & perquam magnus: potentiaque eius mirabilis. Quantum potestis, extollite Dominum laudando: adhuc enim omni laude maior erit. Sirach. 43. v. 29. 30. 31. 32.
units.tr: Next, the trinity of persons is such in God that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are one in essence and in all the properties of the essence, distinguished only by the personal properties (1 John 5:7; Matt. 28:19). Hence, although the Father is almighty, and the Son almighty, and the Holy Spirit almighty, they are nevertheless not three almighties, but these three are one almighty God, or one almighty essence. The same judgment holds for the other essential properties. The personal, or hypostatic, properties are of another kind, which the Greeks elegantly call characters of the essence. These are truly distinct in reality, that is, in fact, apart from any operation of our mind. For the Father is the first person of the Godhead, who does not subsist from another, and who begets the Son (whence he is called Father) and produces the Holy Spirit. The Son is the second person of the Godhead, who is begotten of the Father, whence he is called Son, and who with the Father produces the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Godhead, who proceeds from the Father and the Son as breathing together, whence he is called Holy Spirit (John 1; Matt. 3; John 15:26). Finally, the works of God, which proceed from his essence outside himself, are creation in the kingdom of power, redemption in the kingdom of grace, and glorification in the kingdom of glory. Creation is that by which God produced out of nothing heaven and earth and all that is in them. To this is joined governance (Gen. 1 and 2; Heb. 11:3). Redemption is that by which God, through his Son Jesus Christ, freed the elect from the power of the devil (Gal. 3:13). Immediately joined to this is sanctification, by which God regenerates us by his Holy Spirit to a new life (Rom. 8:1ff.). Here it must not be passed over in silence how these three works are attributed, each to each, with a certain respect, to the persons of the most holy Trinity. The Father, namely, is the principle of the Trinity. To him, therefore, in a certain peculiar respect, is attributed creation, through which creatures begin to be. The Son is the middle person between the Father and the Spirit. To him, therefore, in a certain peculiar respect, is attributed redemption, through which men are united to God. The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Godhead, who is breathed forth by the Father and the Son. To him, therefore, in a certain peculiar respect, is attributed sanctification, through which we are made more and more spiritual. Glorification is that by which God fills his elect in heaven with joy and crowns them with unspeakable glory (Rom. 8:29). And these things are to be held in summary concerning God, of whom we have said many things, and yet we have not attained to him; but the sum of what has been said is that he is all things. For what is our ability to praise him? For he is greater than all his works. The Lord is terrible and exceedingly great, and his power is wonderful. As much as you can, extol the Lord by praising him, for he will still be greater than all praise (Sirach 43:29-32).

units.la: VIII. Spiritus finitus est angelus, & anima rationalis. Ibi est angelographia, hic psychologia. Communiter angelo & animæ rationali convenit, esse ex nihilo, suâ naturâ ordinari ad Deum, posse redigi in nihilum à Deo, proprietatibus & viribus esse supra corpora, sed infra Deum.
units.tr: VIII. A finite spirit is either an angel or a rational soul. The first belongs to angelography, the second to psychology.
