Angels and rational souls share these features: they are created out of nothing, by their nature they are ordered towards God, they can be reduced to nothing by God, and in their properties and powers they are above bodies but below God.

units.la: IX. Angelus est spiritus finitus, à contubernio corporis seiunctus. Differentia specifica inter angelum & animam rationalem est, quòd ille sit spiritus liber & separatus à communione & commercio corporis, hæc spiritus natura suâ coniunctus corpori, eiusque commercio & vnione gaudens. Coloss. 1. verf. 16. Gen. 2. v. 7.
units.tr: IX. An angel is a finite spirit, separated from the company of a body. The specific difference between an angel and a rational soul is that the angel is a free spirit, separate from fellowship and dealings with a body, whereas the soul, by its nature a spirit, is joined to a body and delights in its association and union with it. Col. 1, v. 16; Gen. 2, v. 7.

units.la: X. Angelus consideratur in genere, & in specie.
units.tr: X. An angel is considered in general and in particular.

units.la: XI. Angelus in genere consideratur quantum ad principium & attributa. Principium angeli est, quo ille a Deo productus est primo creationis die. Iob. 38. verf. 4. 5. 6. 7. Nam si angeli hymnos cecinerunt Deo, cum ille terram crearet, vt testatur locus ex Iobo allegatus, & vero terra creata est primo die, vt constat ex Gen. 1. ver. 1. angeli utique producti sunt antequam terra fuit fundata. Attributa angelorum sunt ista. 1. Integritas intellectus & voluntatis ex creatione longe maxima: sed vtraq; mutabilis.Nam si omnia Dei opera fuerunt valde bona, oportet vt angeli, creaturae nobilissimae, primum bonitatis gradum inter opera Dei sint sortiti. Quantumuis autem magna fuit ista bonitas, fuit tamen mutabilis: quia πᾶν [illegible, ~8 letters], omne creatum mutabile. Psal. 102. verf. 27. 28.
units.tr: XI. An angel in general is considered with respect to its origin and its attributes. The origin of an angel is the moment at which it was produced by God, on the first day of creation. Job 38, vv. 4, 5, 6, 7. For if the angels sang hymns to God when he was creating the earth, as the passage cited from Job attests, and the earth was created on the first day, as is clear from Gen. 1, v. 1, then the angels were certainly produced before the earth was founded. The attributes of angels are these. 1. Integrity of intellect and will, by creation very great, but yet both mutable. For if all God's works were very good, the angels, the most noble creatures, must have received the first rank of goodness among God's works. But however great that goodness was, it was mutable, because [πᾶν ...], everything created is mutable. Ps. 102, vv. 27, 28.

units.la: 2. Numerus longe maximus, sed tamen finitus. Ratio prioris est; quia Scriptura commemorat myriades & legiones angelorum Dan. 7. Matth 26. & Marc. 5. Ratio posterioris est; quia numerus ille nobis infinitus, & in se, & ratione Dei, est finitus. 3. Ordo ex creatione longe pulcherrimus. Si enim omne ens est ordinatum, nec ullum ens quo est pulchrius, eo quoque esse ordinatius. Hic ordo remansit inter angelos bonos, mutatus est inter malos. Confer Col.1. v. 16. cum Eph. 6. v. 12. 4. Nullam facere in loco distantiam. Angelus enim ita est in loco, vt non repleat illum. Vnde fit, vt plures angeli possint esse vno in loco: Marc. 5. v. 9. 5. Moueri e loco in locum quasi in instanti. Angelos mutare locum docet Scriptura, quando ipsos e coelo descendere & mitti, ad nos venire & redire in coelum, diabolu circuire hinc inde in mundo. Gen. 19. Matt. 2. Luc. 1. Hebr. 1. Iob. 1. 1. Petr. 5. Est autem ille motus pnicissimus: quia si fulgur celerrime e coelo in terram illabitur, quid putas de motu angeli est dicendum? Non tamen est simpliciter instantaneus ille motus: quia in eo est prius & posterius. v.g. cum angelus e coelo in terram descendit. Hinc diximus esse quasi instantaneum. 6. Cognoscere res modo essentia ipsorum conuenien te. Itaque angeli non cognoscunt res cognitione sensitiuâ; nó cognitione infinitâ; nó deniq; cognitione intimâ.Ratio primi est;quia nó habent organa sensuum:vnde eleganter appellantur intelligentiæ.Ratio secundi est; quia infinitas essentiæ,& scientię,& potentiæ, soli Deo cōpetit. Ratio tertij est; quia solus Deus intimè,hoc est,immediatè penetrando, cognoscit essentiam cuiusq; rei. Hebr.4.v.13. Quæ cùm ita sint, angeli non intelligunt omnia per suam essentiam, sed pleraque per imagines sibi concreatas, vel à Deo reuelatas, vel per experientiam à rebus acceptas: item non intelligunt cogitationes cordis humani: neque omnia norunt sine discursu. 7.Habere affectus immediatè fundatos in voluntate: ita nempe, vt non sint in quodam θυμικῷ vel ἐπιθυμητικῷ[?],sed in mere λογικῷ. Hinc affectus gaudij, tristitiæ, & similes, non sunt sensitiui in angelis,sed intellectiui, seu mere spirituales, 8.Apparere posse in forma visibili: quâ scil. homines exhilarentur, vel perturbentur. Exempla passim sunt obuia in sacris, nominatim Gen. 19. Num. 22. 9. Efficere posse mira, sed non miracula. Ratio prioris est; quia si homines possunt efficere multa mirabilia, vtiq; angeli possunt efficere multò mirabiliora. Ratio posterioris est; quia requiritur virtus infinita & omnipotens ad edendum miracula.
units.tr: 2. Number by far the greatest, yet finite. The reason for the first is that Scripture mentions myriads and legions of angels (Dan. 7; Matt. 26; Mark 5). The reason for the second is that this number, infinite to us, is finite both in itself and in relation to God. 3. Order by creation by far the most beautiful. For if every being is ordered, and no being is more beautiful than another for being more orderly, then this order remained among the good angels and was changed among the evil. Compare Col. 1, v. 16 with Eph. 6, v. 12. 4. Occupying no distance in place. For an angel is in a place in such a way that it does not fill it. Hence several angels can be in one place: Mark 5, v. 9. 5. Moving from place to place as if in an instant. Scripture teaches that angels change place, when they descend from heaven and are sent, come to us and return to heaven, and go about the world hither and thither like the devil. Gen. 19; Matt. 2; Luke 1; Heb. 1; Job 1; 1 Pet. 5. Now that motion is most swift: for if lightning falls from heaven to earth most quickly, what do you suppose should be said of an angel's motion? Yet that motion is not strictly instantaneous, for in it there is a before and an after, for example when an angel descends from heaven to earth. Hence we have said it is as it were instantaneous. 6. Knowing things only in a way that agrees with their essence. Thus angels do not know things by sensitive cognition, nor by infinite cognition, nor finally by intimate cognition. The reason for the first is that they have no organs of sense, whence they are elegantly called intelligences. The reason for the second is that infinity of essence, knowledge and power belongs to God alone. The reason for the third is that God alone knows the essence of each thing intimately, that is, by penetrating it immediately. Heb. 4, v. 13. Since these things are so, angels do not understand all things through their own essence, but many things through images created together with them, or revealed by God, or received from things by experience. Likewise they do not understand the thoughts of the human heart, nor do they know all things without discursive reasoning. 7. To have affections immediately grounded in the will: that is, not located in some thymic [θυμικῷ] or appetitive [ἐπιθυμητικῷ] part, but in the purely rational [λογικῷ] part. Hence the affections of joy, sorrow and the like are not sensitive in angels but intellective, or purely spiritual. 8. Being able to appear in visible form, by which, of course, men are gladdened or disturbed. Examples are found everywhere in the sacred books, notably Gen. 19; Num. 22. 9. Being able to effect marvels, but not miracles. The reason for the first is that if men can effect many wonderful things, angels can surely effect much more wonderful ones. The reason for the second is that infinite and omnipotent power is required to work miracles.

units.la: XII. Angelus in specie est bonus, vel malus. Ille Eudæmon, hic Cacodæmon dicitur.
units.tr: XII. An angel in particular is either good or evil. The former is called Eudaemon, the latter Cacodaemon.

units.la: XIII. Angelus bonus est,qui in primæva suâ integritate, singulari gratiâ creatoris perstitit.
units.tr: XIII. A good angel is one who, in its original integrity, persisted by the singular grace of the Creator.

units.la: In eo perpendenda sunt tria: videl. causa efficiens bonitatis,propria attributa &effecta,& deniq; ordo.Causa efficiens bonitatis primaria,est gratuita Dei benevolentia:secundaria,voluntas & allensus[?] permanendi in sanctitate.Eph.i. v.11.Matth.18.v.10. Propria attributa boni angeli sunt in intellectu claritas notitiæ, quanta in nudam creaturam cadere potest, summa; in voluntate puritas affectuum spiritualium; in potentia agendi alacritas & vis promtisma; denique in tota substantia ipsorum, acquiescentia perfecta in Deo, eaque in coelo tertio ordinarie. Matt. 18. v. 10. c. 6. v. 10. 2. Reg. 19. Matt. 22. v. 30. Propria effecta boni angeli sunt, respectu Dei, angelorum bonorum & malorum, totius mundi, & hominum electorum ac reproborum, hoc ordine. Angeli boni perpetuo celebrant Deum, eiusque iussa capessunt: bonos angelos amant & iuvant: malis angelis resistunt: mundum & res in eo fovent & tuentur contra Satanam eiusque molitiones: piorum hominum intellectum illustrant, voluntatem & affectus regunt, valetudinem tuentur, bona ipsorum sarta tecta praestant, &, si Deus iubeat, ipsos castigant: denique impios puniunt iuxta sententiam divinitus adversus ipsos latam Gen. 19. Psal. 91. & 103. Matth. 4. 10. 25. Act. 12. Hebr. 1. Apoc. 6. 7. 8. 11. 12. 15. 16. 17. 20. 21. 22. Ordo inter bonos angelos est, quod alij sunt superiores, alij inferiores. Col. 1. v. 16. & rursus, quod praesunt regnis, ecclesiis, familijs, vel uni homini. Dan. 9. v. 21. c. 10. Matth. 4. v. 6. Apoc. 11.
units.tr: In this case three things are to be considered: namely, the efficient cause of its goodness, its proper attributes and effects, and finally its order. The primary efficient cause of goodness is the free benevolence of God; the secondary is the will and assent of remaining in holiness. Eph. 1, v. 11; Matt. 18, v. 10. The proper attributes of a good angel are: in the intellect, clarity of knowledge, as great as can fall upon a bare creature, that is, the highest; in the will, purity of spiritual affections; in the power of acting, eagerness and ready strength; and finally, in its whole substance, perfect acquiescence in God, which ordinarily exists in the third heaven. Matt. 18, v. 10; Matt. 6, v. 10; 2 Kings 19; Matt. 22, v. 30. The proper effects of good angels, with respect to God, to good and evil angels, to the whole world, and to elect and reprobate men, are these, in order. Good angels perpetually celebrate God and carry out his commands; they love and help good angels; they resist evil angels; they foster and guard the world and the things in it against Satan and his schemes; they illuminate the understanding of pious men, rule their will and affections, watch over their health, preserve their goods safe and sound, and, if God commands, chastise them; finally they punish the wicked according to the sentence pronounced against them by God. Gen. 19; Ps. 91 and 103; Matt. 4, 10, 25; Acts 12; Heb. 1; Rev. 6, 7, 8, 11, 12, 15, 16, 17, 20, 21, 22. The order among good angels is that some are superior and others inferior, Col. 1, v. 16, and again, that some preside over kingdoms, churches, families or a single man. Dan. 9, v. 21; ch. 10; Matt. 4, v. 6; Rev. 11.

units.la: XIV. Angelus malus est, qui à Deo defecit, & fecit deficere hominem. In eo, itidem ut in bono, videnda sunt tria: videl. causa efficiens malitiae, propria attributa & effecta, denique ordo. Causa efficiens malitiae est abusus liberi arbitrij, quo factum est, ut diabolus non perstiterit in veritate, factusque sit homicida. Iohan. 8. v. 44. Propria adiuncta sunt, perplexitas in intellectu inextricabilis; in voluntate odium erga omne bonum, & amor erga omne malum; in potentia agendi, resistentia erga Deum, bonos angelos, & homines pios, in tota denique substantia, incredibilis dolor & ignominia. Iohan. 8. v. 44. 2. Eph. 6. v. 12. Petr. 2. v. 4. Iud. v. 6. Propria effecta sunt respectu Dei, angelorum bonorum & malorum, totius mundi, & hominum tum in genere, tum in specie electorum & reproborum, hoc ordine. Angeli mali calumniantur Deum, eiusque nomen perpetuo detestantur: oderunt bonos angelos, & adversus ipsos pugnant: flagrant odio adversus seipsos, & interim tamen communi opera regnum suum amplificant: confundunt & laedunt res in mundo, quantum possunt per Dei providentiam: hominum corpora & mentes obsident, ipsorumque bona lædunt, & oculos sæpe fascinant: hominespios tentant & castigant; denique homines impios seducunt & puniunt. Iob. 1. 1. Petr.5 v 8. Gen.3. v.4.5.15. 2.Cor.12.v.7. Apoc.12. Luc.8.v.27.30.32. Exod. 8. v. 7. Matth. 12. v. 25. 26. Ordo inter malos angelos est, quòd diabolus tanquam princeps præest reliquis. Matt. 25. v. 41. 2. Cor. 12. v. 7.
units.tr: XIV. An evil angel is one who fell from God and caused man to fall. In this case, just as with the good, three things are to be considered: namely, the efficient cause of its wickedness, its proper attributes and effects, and finally its order. The efficient cause of wickedness is the abuse of free will, by which it came about that the devil did not persist in the truth and became a murderer. John 8, v. 44. The proper accompaniments are: in the intellect, an inextricable perplexity; in the will, hatred towards every good and love towards every evil; in the power of acting, resistance towards God, good angels and pious men; and finally, in its whole substance, incredible pain and shame. John 8, v. 44; 2 Cor. 12? Eph. 6, v. 12; 2 Pet. 2, v. 4; Jude v. 6. The proper effects are, with respect to God, good and evil angels, the whole world, and men both in general and in particular, elect and reprobate, in this order. Evil angels slander God and perpetually detest his name; they hate good angels and fight against them; they burn with hatred against themselves, and yet meanwhile by common effort they enlarge their kingdom; they confound and harm things in the world as far as they can, under God's providence; they beset the bodies and minds of men, harm their goods, and often bewitch their eyes; they tempt and chastise pious men; finally they seduce and punish wicked men. Job 1, v. 1; 1 Pet. 5, v. 8; Gen. 3, vv. 4, 5, 15; 2 Cor. 12, v. 7; Rev. 12; Luke 8, vv. 27, 30, 32; Exod. 8, v. 7; Matt. 12, vv. 25, 26. The order among evil angels is that the devil, as prince, presides over the rest. Matt. 25, v. 41; 2 Cor. 12, v. 7.

units.la: XV. Anima rationalis est spiritus, ordinatus ad vnionem & communionem corporis.
units.tr: XV. The rational soul is a spirit, ordained for the union and communion of the body.

units.la: XVI. Eius consideratio est generalis, & specialis. In genere consideretur anima rationalis quantum ad principium & propria adiuncta atque effecta. Principium animæ est solus Deus, qui ex nihilo creat animam hominis, non autem illam producit ex traduce. Gen. 2. v. 7. Zach. 12. v. 1. Hebr. 12. v. 9. Propria eius adiuncta sunt, immortalitas in corpore mortali, & extra illud Matth. 10. v. 28. Apoc. 6. v. 10. 11. intellectus, qui potest aliquid cognoscere immediatè, sine ope phantasmatum, vel mediatè per phantasmata, in corpore vel extra corpus Luc. 16. Apoc. 6. v. 9. 10. voluntas, quæ fertur in obiectum suum, vel immediatè, absque appetitu sensitivo & affectibus corporeis, vel mediatè per appetitum sensitivum, in corpore, vel extra corpus. Matth. 22. v. 30. Marc. 12. v. 25. Luc. 20. v. 36. denique potentia agendi, quâ illa in corpore quidem movet corpus, & agit per corpus, separata autem à corpore agit immediatè. Gen. 2. v. 7. Luc. 16. Propria effecta animæ rationalis sunt proportionata adiunctis modo recitatis: videl. intelligere, meminisse, velle, movere, agere, in corpore vel extra corpus, hoc est, in statu vnionis vel separationis.
units.tr: XVI. Its consideration is general and special. In general the rational soul is considered with regard to its principle, its proper attributes and its effects. The principle of the soul is God alone, who creates the soul of man out of nothing, and does not produce it from traduction. Gen. 2. v. 7. Zech. 12. v. 1. Heb. 12. v. 9. Its proper attributes are: immortality, both in the mortal body and outside it, Matth. 10. v. 28. Rev. 6. v. 10. 11; the intellect, which can know something immediately, without the aid of phantasms, or mediately through phantasms, in the body or outside the body, Luke 16; Rev. 6. v. 9. 10; the will, which is directed to its object either immediately, without sensitive appetite and bodily affections, or mediately through the sensitive appetite, in the body or outside the body, Matth. 22. v. 30; Mark 12. v. 25; Luke 20. v. 36; and lastly the power of acting, by which the soul, while in the body, moves the body and acts through the body, but when separated from the body acts immediately. Gen. 2. v. 7; Luke 16. The proper effects of the rational soul are suited to the attributes just recited, namely: to understand, to remember, to will, to move, to act, in the body or outside the body, that is, in the state of union or of separation.

units.la: In specie anima rationalis consideratur in statu felicitatis & miseriæ. Status felicitatis est, quo anima vnionem & communionem habet cum Deo, in quo vno acquiescit & triumphat. Et hæc dicitur monarchia animæ, quâ fit vt ipsa incipiat à Deo, inque ipso desinat, tanquam primo intelligibili, & amabili, adeoque longo interuallo superet statum rerum caducarum, tum in hac tum in futura vita. Haec monarchia animae ita est comparata, ut homo electus imperet affectibus suis, & despiciat ex alto res caducas, tanquam infra se positas, & tandem regnet cum Christo. Rom. 7. v. 17. Apoc. 5. v. 10. c. 20. v. 4. 6. c. 22. ver. 5. Status miseria est, quo anima a fruitione Dei est exclusissima, & experitur triste iugum polyarchiae, ita nempe ut seruiat & multis & malis, puta variis affectibus, opinionibus, hominibus nequam, & malis angelis, idque in hac & futura vita. Rom. 6. v. 6. 13. 14. c. 7. v. 1. 2. Matth. 25. v. 41. Uterque ille status diuiditur in primum, intermedium, & extremum. Primus animae status est in hac vita: intermedius, cum a corpore separatur: extremus, cum corpori reunitur. Atque haec est Pneumatica, cuius finis est, assimilari Deo & bonis angelis, quantum fieri potest, & sugere malos angelos, illosque fugare per imitationem sanctorum spirituum.
units.tr: In particular the rational soul is considered in the state of happiness and of misery. The state of happiness is that in which the soul has union and communion with God, in whom alone it rests and triumphs. This is called the monarchy of the soul, by which it comes about that the soul begins from God and ends in him, as in the first intelligible and lovable object, and thus far surpasses the state of perishable things, both in this life and in the life to come. This monarchy of the soul is so ordered that the elect man rules over his affections and looks down from on high on perishable things, as placed beneath himself, and at last reigns with Christ. Rom. 7. v. 17; Rev. 5. v. 10; c. 20. v. 4. 6; c. 22. v. 5. The state of misery is that in which the soul is utterly shut out from the enjoyment of God, and experiences the harsh yoke of polyarchy, so that it serves many masters and evil ones, namely various affections, opinions, wicked men and evil angels, and this both in this life and in the life to come. Rom. 6. v. 6. 13. 14; c. 7. v. 1. 2; Matth. 25. v. 41. Each of these states is divided into the first, the intermediate and the last. The first state of the soul is in this life; the intermediate, when it is separated from the body; the last, when it is reunited to the body. And this is Pneumatics, whose end is to become like God and the good angels, as far as it can be, and to flee the evil angels, and to put them to flight by imitating the holy spirits.

units.la: IX. PHYSICA SACRA.
units.tr: IX. SACRED PHYSICS.

units.la: I. Physica sacra est corporis naturalis scientia ex s. literis sumta. Hoc est, considerat naturam corporis, prout illa est a Deo condita & cuilibet rei implantata, & simul in verbo ipsius ob oculos nobis posita. Cum itaque sacrae literae non uno in loco mentionem faciant rerum naturalium, recte fecerunt, qui Physicam sacram & Christianam conscripserunt. Id quoque nos cum Deo praestare conabimur.
units.tr: I. Sacred physics is the science of natural body drawn from the sacred writings. That is, it considers the nature of body as God created it and implanted it in each thing, and at the same time sets it before our eyes in his Word. Since the Holy Scriptures mention natural things in more than one place, those who wrote a Sacred and Christian Physics did well. With God's help we shall attempt the same.

units.la: II. Physicae sacrae occurrit fundamentum, & explicatio methodica.
units.tr: II. The foundation and methodical explanation of sacred physics lie before us.

units.la: III. Fundamentum Physicae sacrae est primum caput Genesis: vbi describitur πρωτοπλαστικα [illegible, ~12 letters] siue ϰεῶ͂μο ϖοιέω, hoc modo. Narratur hoc capite, quomodo Deus sex dierum spatio mundum & omnia illo comprehensa creauerit. Distingui potest in sex partes, secundum sex dies, quibus absolutum est opus creationis, quod inde vsitatè appellatur Hexaëmeron.
units.tr: III. The foundation of sacred physics is the first chapter of Genesis, where protoplastics [πρωτοπλαστικά] (the first formation, or cosmopoeia [κοσμοποιέω]) is described in this way. This chapter narrates how God created the world and all things contained in it in the space of six days. It can be divided into six parts, according to the six days on which the work of creation was completed, which is commonly called the Hexaemeron.

units.la: Opera primi diei.
units.tr: Works of the first day.

units.la: Die primo creauit Deus cœlum, terram, aquam, & lucem, hoc modo.
units.tr: On the first day God created heaven, earth, water, and light, as follows.

units.la: Vers. 1. In principio (temporis) creauit (ex nihilo fecit) Deus (Pater, Filius, & Spiritus sanctus) cœlum (primum, secundum & tertium) & terram.
units.tr: Verse 1. In the beginning (of time) God (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) created (made out of nothing) the heaven (first, second and third) and the earth.

units.la: 1. Terra autem erat res informis & inanis, & tenebræ erant in superficie abyssi (aquarum terram circumdantium) & spiritus Dei incubabat superficiei aquarum.
units.tr: 2. And the earth was without form and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep (of the waters surrounding the earth), and the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.

units.la: 3. Tum dixit Deus, Esto lux: & exitit lux: (corpus globosum lucis, seu globus lucidus.)
units.tr: 3. Then God said, Let there be light: and there was light. (A globular body of light, or a luminous globe.)

units.la: 4. Viditque Deus lucem illam esse bonam: & distinctionem fecit Deus inter illam lucem & tenebras.
units.tr: 4. And God saw that the light was good, and God divided the light from the darkness.

units.la: 5. Lucemque illam Deus vocauit diem (naturalem) tenebras vero vocauit noctem: atque ita facta fuit vespera (à quâ dies ciuilis incipit) & factum fuit mane, dies primus: (ciuilis.)
units.tr: 5. And God called the light day (natural), and the darkness he called night: and so there was evening (from which the civil day begins), and there was morning, the first day. (Civil.)

units.la: Opera secundi diei.
units.tr: Works of the second day.

units.la: Secundo die Deus creauit aërem & nubes.
units.tr: On the second day God created air and clouds.

units.la: 6. Deinde dixit Deus, Esto expansum (aer) inter aquas: vt sit distinguens inter aquas vnas & alteras (superiores & inferiores.)
units.tr: 6. Then God said, Let there be an expanse (air) between the waters, so that it may divide between the waters, one from the other (upper and lower).

units.la: 7. Fecit ergo Deus expansum, quod distingueret inter aquas, quæ sunt sub expanso, & aquas, quæ sunt super expanso: & factum est ita.
units.tr: 7. So God made the expanse, which divided between the waters that are under the expanse and the waters that are above the expanse: and it was so.

units.la: 8. Expansum autem illud Deus vocauit cœlum: (infimum) atque ita facta fuit vespera, & factum fuit mane, dies secundus.
units.tr: 8. And God called that expanse heaven (the lowest): and so there was evening, and there was morning, the second day.

units.la: Opera tertij diei.
units.tr: Works of the third day.

units.la: Tertio die Deus segregauit aquam à terra, & aquas collegit in certos alueos, atque ita fecit maria, fluuios, & fontes: terramque vestiuit plantis, herbis scil. & arboribus, itemque impleuit illam metallis, & aliis mineralibus.
units.tr: On the third day God separated the water from the land, gathered the waters into fixed channels, and so made the seas, rivers, and springs; he clothed the earth with plants, namely herbs and trees, and likewise filled it with metals and other minerals.

units.la: 9. Postea dixit Deus, Confluant aquæ ista, quæ sub cœlo sunt, in vnum locum, & conspicua sit arida: & factum fuit ita.
units.tr: 9. Afterwards God said, Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear: and it was so.

units.la: 10. Aridam autem vocauit Deus terram; singula verò aquarum conceptacula vocauit maria: & vidit Deus id esse bonum.
units.tr: 10. And God called the dry land Earth, and the gatherings of the waters he called Seas: and God saw that it was good.

units.la: 11. Iterum dixit Deus, Germinet terra teneram herbam, item herbas proferentes semen, arbores fructiferas proferentes fructum, secundum speciem suam, in quibus suum sit semen super terram: & factum fuit ita.
units.tr: 11. Again God said, Let the earth bring forth tender grass, herbs yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, in which there is seed upon the earth: and it was so.

units.la: 12. Nam produxit terra teneram herbam, item herbas proferentes semen secundum speciem suam, & arbores ferentes fructum, in quibus semen ipsarum secundum speciem suam: & vidit Deus id esse bonum.
units.tr: 12. For the earth brought forth tender grass, and herbs yielding seed after their kind, and trees bearing fruit, in which is their seed after their kind: and God saw that it was good.

units.la: 13. Atque ita facta fuit vespera, & factum fuit mane, dies tertius.
units.tr: 13. And so there was evening, and there was morning, the third day.

units.la: Opera quarti diei.
units.tr: Works of the fourth day.

units.la: Die quarto Deus lucem illam primigeniam dispertiuit in solem, lunam, cæterasque stellas: easque collocauit in cœlo mediano.
units.tr: On the fourth day God divided that primal light into the sun, the moon, and the other stars, and placed them in the middle heaven.

units.la: 14. Post dixit Deus, Fiant luminaria in expanso cœli (mediani siue secundi) ad distinctionem faciendum inter diem (naturalem) & noctem, & sint in signa, & stata tempora, & dies, & annos.
units.tr: 14. Afterwards God said, Let there be lights in the expanse of heaven (the middle or second heaven) to make a distinction between day (natural) and night, and let them be for signs, and for set times, and for days and years.

units.la: 15. Sintque in luminaria in expanso cœli, ad afferendum lucem super terram: & factum fuit ita.
units.tr: 15. And let them be lights in the expanse of heaven, to give light upon the earth: and it was so.

units.la: 16. Fecit enim Deus duo illa luminaria magna: luminare ma-ius ad præfecturam diei, & luminare minus ad præfecturam no-ctis, atque stellas.
units.tr: 16. For God made the two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars.

units.la: 17. Et collocauit ea Deus in expanso cœli, ad afferendum lu-cem super terram.
units.tr: 17. And God set them in the expanse of heaven, to give light upon the earth.

units.la: 18. Et ad præsidendum diei ac noctì, & ad distinctionem faciendum inter lucem & tenebras: viditq; Deus id esse bonum.
units.tr: 18. And to rule over the day and the night, and to make a distinction between the light and the darkness: and God saw that it was good.

units.la: 19. Atque ita facta fuit vespera, & factum fuit mane, dies quartus.
units.tr: 19. And so there was evening, and there was morning, the fourth day.

units.la: Opera quinti diei.
units.tr: Works of the fifth day.

units.la: Die quinto Deus creavit pisces, seu animalia aquatilia, & aves seu volatilia.
units.tr: On the fifth day God created fishes, or water animals, and birds, or flying creatures.

units.la: 20. Postea dixit Deus, Abundè progignunto aquæ reptilia animantia: & volucres volanto super terram, in superficie expansi cœlorum.
units.tr: 20. Afterwards God said, Let the waters bring forth abundantly the moving creatures that have life, and let birds fly above the earth, across the face of the expanse of heaven.

units.la: 21. Et creavit Deus cetos magnos: & animantia omnia repentia, qua[?] abundè progenuerunt aqua secundum species ipsorum, omnesque volucres alatos secundum species ipsarum: viditque Deus id esse bonum.
units.tr: 21. And God created the great sea monsters, and every living creature that moves, which the waters brought forth abundantly after their kinds, and every winged bird after its kind: and God saw that it was good.

units.la: 22. Et benedixit eis Deus, dicendo: Fœtificate, ac multiplicamini, implete aquas in mari, & volucres multiplicantur in terrâ.
units.tr: 22. And God blessed them, saying: Be fruitful and multiply, fill the waters in the seas, and let the birds multiply on the earth.

units.la: 23. Atque ita facta fuit vespera, & factum fuit mane, dies quintus.
units.tr: 23. And so there was evening, and there was morning, the fifth day.

units.la: Opera sexti diei.
units.tr: The works of the sixth day.

units.la: Die sexto creavit Deus animalia terrestria, & hominem: & tum huic, tum illis suum designavit cibum.
units.tr: On the sixth day God created the land animals and man, and he assigned food to both, to the one and to the others.

units.la: 24. Deinde dixit Deus, Producat terra animantia secundum species ipsorum, pecudes & reptilia, bestiasque terrestres, secundum species ipsarum: & fuit ita.
units.tr: 24. Then God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds, livestock and creeping things and beasts of the earth, according to their kinds." And it was so.

units.la: 25. Fecit enim Deus bestias terrestres secundum species ipsarum, & pecudes secundum species ipsarum, omniaque reptilia terræ secundum species ipsorum: & vidit Deus id esse bonum.
units.tr: 25. For God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, and the livestock according to their kinds, and all the creeping things of the earth according to their kinds. And God saw that it was good.

units.la: 26. Postea dixit Deus, (Patet ad Filium & Spiritum sanctum.) Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostram, secundum similitudinem nostram: qui dominentur in pisces maris, & in volucres cœli, & in pecudes, & in universam terram, atque in omnia reptilia reptantia super terrâ.
units.tr: 26. Afterwards God said (this applies to the Son and the Holy Spirit), "Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness, to rule over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heavens, and over the livestock, and over the whole earth, and over all the creeping things that creep upon the earth."

units.la: 27. Itaque creavit Deus hominem ad imaginem suam, ad imaginem Dei creavit eum: marem & fœminam creavit eos.
units.tr: 27. So God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.

units.la: 28. Deinde benedixit eis Deus; & dixit eis, Fœtificate, & multiplicamini, & implete terram, eamque subjicite vobis: & dominamini in pisces maris, & in volucres cœli, & in omnes bestias reptantes super terrâ.
units.tr: 28. Then God blessed them, and said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it; and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heavens, and over every living thing that creeps upon the earth."

units.la: 29. Præterea dixit Deus, Ecce dedi vobis omnes herbas proserentes semen, quæ sunt in superficie totius terræ, omnesque arbores, in quibus est fructus arboreus; proferentes semen: vestra ad comedendum erunt.
units.tr: 29. Moreover God said, "Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is on the surface of the whole earth, and every tree in which is fruit bearing seed; they shall be yours for food."

units.la: 30. Omnibus autem bestiis terræ, & omnibus volucribus cœli, omnibusque reptantibus super terrâ, in quibus est anima viuens, dedi omnes herbas virides ad comedendum: & factum fuit ita.
units.tr: 30. But to every beast of the earth, and to every bird of the heavens, and to everything that creeps upon the earth, in which there is a living soul, I have given every green herb for food." And it was so.

units.la: 31. Tum inspexit Deus, quidquid fecerat, ecce autem bonum erat valde. Atque ita facta fuit vespera, & factum fuit mane, dies sextus.
units.tr: 31. Then God looked at everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And so evening came and morning came, the sixth day.

units.la: Addamus ex capite secundo, quæ faciunt ad pleniorem descriptionem creationis primæ.
units.tr: Let us add from the second chapter what contributes to a fuller description of the first creation.

units.la: 1: Atque ita perfecta sunt cælum & terra, omnisque exercitus illorum,
units.tr: 1: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all their host.

units.la: 4. Ista igitur sunt generationes cœli & terra, quando creata sunt: quo die Jehoua Deus fecit cœlum & terram.
units.tr: 4. These are therefore the generations of the heavens and the earth, when they were created, on the day that Jehovah God made the earth and the heavens.

units.la: 5. Et omnem fruticem agri, qui nondum fuerat in terrâ, omnemq; herbam agri, quæ nondum orta fuerat. Sed Jehoua Deus nondum demiserat pluuiam super terram, & nullus homo fuerat, qui coleret terram.
units.tr: 5. And every shrub of the field, which had not yet been in the earth, and every herb of the field, which had not yet sprung up. But Jehovah God had not yet sent rain upon the earth, and there was no man to till the ground.

units.la: 6. Sed vapor ascenderat è terra: qui irrigabat universam superficiem terræ.
units.tr: 6. But a mist went up from the earth, which watered the whole surface of the ground.

units.la: 7. Finxit vero Jehoua Deus hominem ex pulvere terræ, sufflauitque in nares ipsius halitum vitæ: sic factus est homo anima viuens.
units.tr: 7. Then Jehovah God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

units.la: 8. Plantauerat autem Jehoua Deus hortum in Edene ab Oriente: vbi collocauit hominem, quem finxerat:
units.tr: 8. And Jehovah God had planted a garden in Eden, toward the east, where he placed the man whom he had formed.

units.la: 9. Feceratque Jehoua Deus, vt germinaret ex humo illâ quæ-uis[?] arbor desiderabilis ad aspectum, & bona ad cibum.
units.tr: 9. And Jehovah God caused to grow out of that ground every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food.

units.la: 18. Dixerat autem Jehoua Deus, Non est bonum esse hominem solum: faciam ei auxilium, quod sit coram ipso.
units.tr: 18. And Jehovah God had said, "It is not good for the man to be alone; I will make him a helper who is suitable for him."

units.la: 19. Nam cum formauisset Jehoua Deus è terrâ omnes bestias agri, omnesque volucres cœli, & adduxisset ad Adamum, vt videret quomodo vocaret singulas (etenim quocunque nomine vocauit illas Adam, animantem quamque, id nomen eius est.)
units.tr: 19. For when Jehovah God had formed out of the ground all the beasts of the field and all the birds of the heavens, he brought them to Adam, to see what he would call each one (for whatever Adam called each living creature, that is its name).

units.la: 20. Vocauissetque Adam nominibus pecudem quamlibet, & volucrem cœli, omnemque bestiam agri: non aderat Adamo auxilium, quod esset coram ipso.
units.tr: 20. And Adam gave names to every livestock, and to the birds of the heavens, and to every beast of the field; but for Adam there was not found a helper who was suitable for him.

units.la: 21. Quapropter iniecit Iehoua Deus soporem altum in Adamum, quo obdormiuit: & desumta vna ex costis eius, inclusit carnem pro illâ.
units.tr: 21. Therefore Jehovah God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept; and he took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place.

units.la: 22. Et ædificauit Iehoua Deus ex costâ illâ, quam sumserat de Adamo, mulierem: eamque adduxit ad Adamum.
units.tr: 22. And Jehovah God built up the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam.

units.la: 23. Tum dixit Adam: Hac demum vice adestos ex ossibus meis, & caro ex carne mea: hæc vocabitur vira, eò quòd hæc ex viro desumta est.
units.tr: 23. Then Adam said, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called woman, because she was taken out of man."

units.la: 24. Idcirco relicturus est vir patrem suum & matrem suam, & adhærebit vxori suæ, eruntque in carnem vnam.
units.tr: 24. Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.

units.la: 25. Erant autem illi ambo nudi, Adam & vxor eius: & non erubescebant.
units.tr: 25. And the two of them, Adam and his wife, were naked, and were not ashamed.

units.la: IV. Explicatio Physices methodica sequitur
units.tr: IV. The methodical explanation of Physics follows.

units.la: in ipsius partibus, quas hoc modo recensemus ex Gen. 1. & 2. Corpus naturale (de angelis vide Pneumaticam) consideratur seorsim, vel collectiue. Seorsim confideratur, vt est pars mundi, ipsum integrans. Ita Deus produxit cœlum, terram, lucem, stellas, animalia &c. ex quibus mundus constat. Gen. 1. & c. 2. v. 1. vbi hæ partes eleganter appellantur exercitus cœli & terræ. Nam creaturis, quæ sunt in cœlo & in terra, cohonestatur Deus, sicut imperator suis numeris & exercitibus. Pars mundi aut est principium, aut principiatum. Principium mundi est cœlum & terra. Gen. 1. v. 1. Principiatum est inanimatum, vel animatum. Inanimatum est naturæ constantis, vel inconstantis. Corpus naturæ constantis est naturæ cœlestis, vel terrestris. Ibi est lux & stella. ibid. v. 3. 14. hic est planta. v. 11. sub quâ comprehenduntur fossilia seu mineralia. Corpus naturæ inconstantis est meteorum. Gen. 2. v. 6. Animatum est bestia, vel homo. Bestia est aquatilis, volatilis, vel terrestris. vers. 20. 24. Homo constat ex animâ rationali & corpore. ibid. v. 26. & c. 2. v. 7. Corpus naturale consideratum collectiue appellatur mundus, qui est systema constans è cœlo & terrâ, omnique exercitu illorum. Gen. 2. vers. 1. Hæc methodus est desumta ex Gen. 1. & 2. Merito itaque illam sequimur in physicâ sacrâ, cuius sectiones sunt numero decem, hoc ordine. 1. Physica generalis, de principiis mundi. 2. Physica specialis de luce & stellis. 3. Botanica, de plantis. 4. Oryctologia, de fossilibus seu mineralibus. 5. Meteorologia, de corporibus imperfectè mixtis. 6. Ichthyologia, de piscibus. 7. Ornithologia, de avibus. 8. Theriologia, de bestiis terrestribus. 9. Anthropologia, de natura hominis. 10. Cosmologia, de mundo. Persequamur itaque has decem partes, duce Scriptura sacra, in quâ liber naturæ satis accurate est propositus & expositus.
units.tr: in its parts, which we enumerate in this way from Gen. 1 and 2. The natural body (on angels see Pneumatics) is considered either separately or collectively. It is considered separately as a part of the world, integrating it. Thus God produced the heaven, the earth, the light, the stars, the animals etc., of which the world consists. Gen. 1 and c. 2 v. 1, where these parts are elegantly called the host of heaven and earth; for God is adorned by the creatures which are in heaven and on earth, as a commander is by his numbers and armies. A part of the world is either a principle or a principiate. The principle of the world is heaven and earth (Gen. 1 v. 1). A principiate is inanimate or animate. The inanimate is of constant nature or of inconstant nature. A body of constant nature is either heavenly or earthly. In the heavenly there are light and stars (ibid. v. 3, 14); here on earth is the plant (v. 11), under which are comprehended fossils or minerals. A body of inconstant nature is the meteors (Gen. 2 v. 6). The animate is the beast or man. A beast is aquatic, flying, or terrestrial (vers. 20, 24). Man consists of a rational soul and a body (ibid. v. 26 and c. 2 v. 7). The natural body considered collectively is called the world, which is a system consisting of heaven and earth and all their host (Gen. 2 vers. 1). This method is taken from Gen. 1 and 2. Rightly, therefore, we follow it in sacred physics, whose sections are ten in number, in this order: (1) General physics, on the principles of the world; (2) Special physics, on light and the stars; (3) Botany, on plants; (4) Oryctology, on fossils or minerals; (5) Meteorology, on imperfectly mixed bodies; (6) Ichthyology, on fish; (7) Ornithology, on birds; (8) Theriology, on terrestrial beasts; (9) Anthropology, on the nature of man; (10) Cosmology, on the world. Let us therefore pursue these ten parts, with Holy Scripture as our guide, in which the book of nature is set out and expounded with sufficient accuracy.

units.la: PHYSICA GENERALIS SACRA De Principiis mundi.
units.tr: GENERAL SACRED PHYSICS: On the Principles of the World.

units.la: I. PRincipium mundi est, ex quo principiata naturalia, h e. mundus & corpora in mundo sunt composita. Intelligitur enim hic principium naturale & materiale, non supernaturale & efficiens, quod est Deus..
units.tr: I. The principle of the world is that from which natural things arise, that is, the world and the bodies composed within it. Here what is meant is a natural and material principle, not a supernatural and efficient one, which is God.

units.la: II. Estque partim cœlum, partim terra. Sic enim docet nos Moses, Oceanus ille sapientiæ. Gen. 1. v. 1.
units.tr: II. It is partly heaven and partly earth. For so Moses, that ocean of wisdom, teaches us. Gen. 1. v. 1.

units.la: 2. Hinc Lambertus Danæus lib. 1. Phys. Christ. cap. 12. rectè fecit, q hæc duo, cœlum & terram, statuit omnium rerum naturalium principia, his verbis: Vt omnium rerum summa sunt duo genera, vnum cœleste, alterum terrenum: sic duplex materia à Deo constituta primum omnium fuit; à Deo, inquam, qui cuius & quotuplicis naturæ futura erant sua opera, non ignorabat: sed iam tum præparabat. Cœlestium enim mundi partium cœlestis materies parata est, & perfecta quidem, cœlum: terrenarum autem terra, & ea etiam madida, humida, & vliginosa. Eodem modo verba Mosis explicat Hieronymus Zanchius lib. 1. de operib. creationis cap. 2. Ego, inquit, omissis aliorum opinionibus, meam dicam sententiam. Censeo nomine הַשָּׁמַיִם[?] intelligendum esse quidquid postea tum in hoc capite, tum in aliis Scripturae locis nomine coeli appellatur. Voce autem coeli venit primo aer, secundo orbes, tertio sedes beatorum. Terra vero nomine interpretor terram cum oceano & omnibus aquis. His ita praemissis tradamus quasdam regulas de principiis rerum naturalium.
units.tr: 2. Hence Lambert Daneau lib. 1. Phys. Christ. cap. 12. rightly made these two, heaven and earth, the principles of all natural things, in these words: As the sum of all things is of two kinds, one heavenly and the other earthly, so the twofold matter constituted by God was first of all. By God, I say, who did not ignorant of what nature and how many kinds his works were to be, but was already then preparing them. For the heavenly matter of the heavenly parts of the world is ready, and indeed perfected: heaven; and of the earthly parts, earth, and that moist, wet and watery. In the same way Jerome Zanchius explains the words of Moses lib. 1. de operib. creationis cap. 2. He says: Setting aside the opinions of others, I will give my own view. I judge that by the word [הַשָּׁמַיִם] must be understood whatever is afterwards called by the name of heaven, both in this chapter and in other places of Scripture. By the word heaven, air comes first, second the spheres, third the seat of the blessed. By earth, however, I mean the earth together with the ocean and all waters. With these things thus set forth, let us lay down certain rules concerning the principles of natural things.

units.la: 1. Principia rerum naturalium catholica debent esse prima simpliciter. Principia rerum naturalium sunt universalia, vel particularia. Principia universalia sunt, ex quibus omnia principiata constant: particularia, ex quibus haec vel illa. Sic v.g. granum tritici est principium particulare. Similiter lux est principium particulare stellarum. Quo pertinent illud Peucerii in elementis Sphaericis: Condidit mitio Deus solo verbo ἐκ τῶν μὴ ὄντων, id est, ex nihilo, tria haec, διαφανὲς ἐνέργειᾳ, id est, perspicuum actu seu lucidum; διαφανὲς δυνάμει, id est, perspicuum potentia, lucis per se & sua natura expers, sed tale, quod communicatione lucis splendescit; & opacum: hoc est, ut sacra literaloquuntur, lucem, coelum, & terram, tanquam sutura principia reliquorum corporum. Reliqua vero ex his formavit, ut historia creationis testatur. In quibus verbis tria principia recensentur, lux, coelum, & terra: ita nempe, ut lux fit principium particulare, coelum & terra, principia universalia, hoc est, simpliciter prima, (seu primo prima: ita nempe, ut ex iis componantur reliqua corpora omnia, ipsa vero ex nullo sint compositae. Quam conditionem Ariftoteles requirit in principiis rerum naturalium. 2. Prima rerum principia sunt hypostatica, h.e. ita comparata, ut per se subsistant. Facessat itaque schola vulgarium physicorum, qui nescio quam materiam primam nobis obtrudunt.
units.tr: 1. The catholic principles of natural things must be first simply. Principles of natural things are either universal or particular. Universal principles are those from which all the things that arise from them consist; particular ones are those from which this or that thing consists. Thus, for example, a grain of wheat is a particular principle. Similarly, light is the particular principle of the stars. To this belongs that saying of Peucer in his Elements of the Sphere: "God, by the word alone, out of [ἐκ τῶν μὴ ὄντων, ek tōn mē ontōn] things that are not, that is, out of nothing, created these three: [διαφανὲς ἐνέργειᾳ, diaphanes energeia] transparent in act, that is, transparent or luminous in act; [διαφανὲς δυνάμει, diaphanes dynamei] transparent in potency, that is, transparent in potential, lacking light in itself and by its own nature, but such that it shines by the communication of light; and the opaque: that is, as the sacred writings speak, light, heaven and earth, as the future principles of the other bodies." The rest he formed from these, as the history of creation testifies. In these words three principles are listed: light, heaven and earth. So light becomes a particular principle, while heaven and earth are universal principles, that is, first simply (or first in the primary sense): in such a way that all the other bodies are composed of them, but they themselves are composed of nothing. Aristotle requires this condition in the principles of natural things. 2. The first principles of things are hypostatic, that is, so constituted that they subsist through themselves. Let the school of the common physicists, who foist upon us I know not what prime matter, therefore go away.

units.la: 3. Prima rerum principia sunt domicilia & principia simul. Sunt domicilia & matrices, quatenus continent res corporeas. Videmus enim coelum esse domicilium rerum superiorum & coelestium, terram, inferiorum & terrestrium. Atque haec est causa, quod in scripturis passim haec duo, coelum & terra, coniunguntur. Gen.1.v.1.cap.2.v.1.24.c.14. v.19.22.c.24.v.3.7. Exod.20.v.11.c.31.v.17.Deut.3.v.24.c.4.
units.tr: 3. The first principles of things are at once dwelling-places and principles. They are dwelling-places and wombs, insofar as they contain corporeal things. For we see heaven to be the dwelling-place of higher and heavenly things, and earth of lower and earthly things. And this is the reason why in the Scriptures these two, heaven and earth, are everywhere joined together. Gen. 1. v. 1; c. 2. v. 1, 24; c. 14. v. 19, 22; c. 24. v. 3, 7. Exod. 20. v. 11; c. 31. v. 17. Deut. 3. v. 24; c. 4.

units.la: Rursus hæc eadem sunt principia, quatenus in se continent rerum omnium semina. Neque enim cœlum & terra constituunt res naturales, quatenus ipsorum substantia externa consideratur, sed quatenus vis interior in ipsis abscondita spectatur. Quò facit illud Trismegisti, principia rerum omnium esse lucem & umbram, hoc est, abdita rerum semina, quæ in cœlo & terra latent. Nam in cœlo lux, in terra umbra cospicitur. Idem Trismegistus author est, omnia constare ex sole & lunâ: ubi per solem intelligit cœlum, per lunam, aquam, de quâ Moses testatur, illam circumdedisse terram. 4. Prima corporum naturalium principia sunt constantia, vel inconstantia. Constans est, quod vicissitudini non est obnoxium, ut cœlum: unde illud est quintæ cuiusdam essentiæ. Inconstans est, quod vicissitudini est obnoxium, ut terra, quæ complectitur aquam & ignem. Et hæc tria elementa semper sunt simul. Quod attinet ad aerem, ille ambit hæc tria elementa, utpote qui est cœlum infimum, terræque adeò proximum. 5. Cœlum solum & per se potest constituere corpus naturale: terra nonnisi cum cœlo. Sic videmus lucem solam esse materiam stellarum: sed terra sine cœlo est fœmina sine viro. Hinc cœlum recte appellatur pater, & terra mater omnium rerum nascentium.
units.tr: Again, these same are principles insofar as they contain within themselves the seeds of all things. For heaven and earth do not constitute natural things insofar as their external substance is considered, but insofar as the inner power hidden within them is regarded. To this pertains that saying of Trismegistus, that the principles of all things are light and shadow, that is, the hidden seeds of things which lie concealed in heaven and earth. For light is seen in heaven, shadow in earth. The same Trismegistus is the author that all things consist of sun and moon, where by sun he understands heaven and by moon water, of which Moses testifies that it surrounded the earth. 4. The first principles of natural bodies are constant or inconstant. That is constant which is not subject to change, as heaven; whence it is of a certain fifth essence. That is inconstant which is subject to change, as earth, which embraces water and fire. These three elements are always together. As for air, it surrounds these three elements, being the lowest heaven and so closest to the earth. 5. Heaven alone and by itself can constitute a natural body; earth only with heaven. Thus we see that light alone is the matter of the stars; but earth without heaven is a woman without a man. Hence heaven is rightly called the father, and earth the mother of all things that are born.

units.la: III. Cœlum est corpus spirituale, subtilissimè supra terram expansum, omniaque permeans, replens, & suo complexu continens & fovens. Evoluamus singula. Primò cœlum est corpus: quia habet partem extra partem, estque molis vastissimæ, & proinde trina dimensione constat vel maximè. Deinde cœlum est corpus spirituale, hoc est, simplicissimæ naturæ. Quæ causa est, quòd aër in scripturis non semel appella-turtur spiritus Iohan. 3. v. 8. Act. 2. v. 2. & alibi. Eodem sensu subtilis illa natura in corpore nostro, quæ vitalis & animalis functionis ministra est, spiritus appellatur, vt vt corporeum quiddam sit. Recte itaque philosophi Ægyptij docuerunt, cœlum esse spirituale quoddam corpus. Recte quoque Aristoteles cœlum existimat esse quintam quandā essentiam, siue quintum elementum. Et Plinius lib. 2. cœlum appellat omne id, quod inani simile vitalem hunc spiritum fundit. Iohannes Pena in Opticam Euclidis, cœlum ait esse animabilem quendam spiritum per omnia dissusum. Zanchius quoque lib. 1. de operibus Dei ait, cœlum propter summam subtilitatem corpus esse tale, quod spirituale merito appellari potest. Iamblichus denique cœleste corpus incorporeis ait esse cognatissimum. Non igitur abs re cœlum appellauimus corpus spirituale, id est, spiritum corporeum omnia permeantem & fouentem, qui cum spiritu nostro naturali, vitali, & animali magnam habet affinitatem & familiaritatem. Est autem hic cœli spiritus purior, vel impurior. Purior est in cœlo supremo & mediano: impurior in aëerio. Nam quoniam aër pabulum corporibus viuentibus suppeditare debet, merito ipsius spiritus est crassiusculus. Tertio cœlum est subtilissimè expansum supra terram. Hinc appellatur [illegible, ~3 letters]. Subtilitas illa est tanta, vt omnia corpora inoffenso cursu motuque per hoc cœli corpus ire & redire, ascendere & descendere possint. Quarto expansum hoc omnia permeat, replet, continet atque fouet. Nam subtilitas ipsius est fluida: quo fit, vt omnia cœlesti hoc corpore compleantur, vacuumque prohibeatur, atque ita superiora inferioribus vniantur, & hæc ab illis foueantur.
units.tr: III. Heaven is a spiritual body, spread out most subtly above the earth, permeating all things, filling them, and containing and cherishing them in its embrace. Let us unfold the individual points. First, heaven is a body, because it has part outside part, and is of the vastest mass, and therefore consists most fully of three dimensions. Next, heaven is a spiritual body, that is, of the most simple nature. This is why air is more than once called spirit in Scripture (John 3:8; Acts 2:2, and elsewhere). In the same sense, that subtle nature in our body which serves the vital and animal functions is called spirit, although it is something corporeal. Rightly, therefore, the Egyptian philosophers taught that heaven is a certain spiritual body. Rightly also Aristotle thinks heaven is a fifth essence, or fifth element. And Pliny in book 2 calls heaven all that which, resembling the void, pours forth this vital spirit. John Pena, in his commentary on Euclid's Optics, says heaven is an animating spirit diffused through all things. Zanchius too, in book 1 of de operibus Dei, says heaven, on account of its supreme subtlety, is a body of such a kind that it can rightly be called spiritual. Finally, Iamblichus says the heavenly body is most akin to incorporeal beings. Not without reason, therefore, have we called heaven a spiritual body, that is, a corporeal spirit permeating and cherishing all things, which has great affinity and familiarity with our natural, vital and animal spirit. This spirit of heaven is, however, purer or less pure: purer in the highest and middle heaven, less pure in the aerial heaven. For since air must supply nourishment to living bodies, its spirit is rightly somewhat grosser. Third, heaven is spread out most subtly above the earth. Hence it is called [illegible]. Its subtlety is so great that all bodies can go and return, ascend and descend, through this body of heaven with unhindered course and motion. Fourth, this expanse permeates, fills, contains and cherishes all things. For its subtlety is fluid; hence it comes about that all things are filled with this heavenly body and a vacuum is prevented, and so higher things are joined to lower, and these are cherished by those.

units.la: IV. Cœlum est supremum, medianum, vel infimum.
units.tr: IV. Heaven is either supreme, middle, or lowest.

units.la: V. Cœlum supremum est extima expansi pars, habitatio Dei, & sedes beatorum. In Scripturis appellatur cœlum cœlorum, id est, excelsissimum & excellentissimum cœlum. Deut.10. ver.14.1.Reg 8. v.27. 2.Chron.2.v.6.c.6.v.18. item cœlum tertium. 2.Cor.12.v.2. item simpliciter cœlum, vt in oratione Dominicâ Matt.6. v.9.10. Hoc cœlum est longè nobilioris naturæ quàm cœlum medianum & infimum. Videmus enim ita esse co-paratum, vt quò quid est superiori loco in hoc mundo positum, eò fit excellentius.
units.tr: V. The supreme heaven is the outermost part of the expanse, the habitation of God and the seat of the blessed. In Scripture it is called the heaven of heavens, that is, the most high and most excellent heaven. Deut. 10. v. 14; 1 Kings 8. v. 27; 2 Chron. 2. v. 6; c. 6. v. 18. Likewise it is called the third heaven, 2 Cor. 12. v. 2, and simply heaven, as in the Lord's Prayer, Matt. 6. v. 9, 10. This heaven is of far nobler nature than the middle and lowest heaven. For we see that it is so constituted that the higher a thing is placed in this world, the more excellent it becomes.

units.la: VI. Cœlum medianum est media expansi pars inter cœlum supremum & infimum, in quo stellæ sunt à Deo collocatæ. De hoc cœlo vide Gen.1. v.14.17.c.15.v.5.Deut.1.v.10.Ios.10.v.13.2.Reg.17.v.16.c.21. v.3.5.c.23.v.4.5.Psal.19.v.1. Hoc cœlum vt supremo est proximum loco, sic & dignitate.
units.tr: VI. The middle heaven is the middle part of the expanse between the highest and lowest heaven, in which God placed the stars. On this heaven see Gen. 1.14, 17; 15.5; Deut. 1.10; Josh. 10.13; 2 Kings 17.16; 21.3, 5; 23.4, 5; Ps. 19.1. As this heaven is nearest the highest in place, so it is also nearest in dignity.

units.la: VII. Cœlum infimum est inferior expansi pars, quæ terram attingit, & vsitatè appellatur aër. De hoc cœlo vide Gen. 1.verf. 26.30.c.7.v.11.c.9.v.14. Psal.8. v. 8. Matth.6.v.26. Ioban.6.v.31. Hoc cœlum vt vltimum locum, ita quoque postremum dignitatis gradum[?] obtinet. Etsi enim est simplicis qualitatis vt cœ'um[?] summum & medium: varias tamen qualitates admittere potest. Nam non solùm variis coloribus depingi atque illustrari, sed etiam calorem & frigus, siccitatem & humiditatem, aliasque qualitates elementares recipere potest. Hoc autem omne fit per accidens, quatenus videl. cœlum hoc infimum est destinatum generationi meteororum. Vtut enim varie impressiones aërem imbuant variis qualitatibus: ipse tamen retinet subtilem & fluidam suam substantiam, eâque fouet ac recreat corpora omnia terrena. Est enim tam gratum rerum omnium alimentum & fomentum, vt sine eius præsidio corpora viuentia subito emori & extingui sit necesse. Aër quoque per varios terræ, arborum, frugum, & aliarum rerum poros atque meatus se insinuans vigorem rebus omnibus impertit. Denique est vehiculum, quo lux, radij, & vires stellarum occultæ in hanc inferiorem naturam dimanant. Ex his colligere est, quanta sit cœli utilitas. Nimirum omnis spiritus vitalis inde ducit suam originem. Quod quàm probè sit obseruandum naturæ scrutatoribus, nonnisi experti norunt.
units.tr: VII. The lowest heaven is the lower part of the expanse, which touches the earth and is commonly called the air. On this heaven see Gen. 1.26, 30; 7.11; 9.14; Ps. 8.8; Matt. 6.26; John 6.31. As this heaven holds the last place, so it also holds the lowest rank of dignity. For although it has a simple quality, as the highest and middle heavens do, it can admit various qualities. It can not only be painted and illuminated with various colours, but can also take on heat and cold, dryness and moisture, and other elemental qualities. All this happens accidentally, namely insofar as this lowest heaven is destined for the generation of meteors. For however variously the impressions imbue the air with various qualities, it still keeps its subtle and fluid substance, and with it cherishes and refreshes all earthly bodies. It is so pleasant a nourishment and support of all things that without its protection living bodies must suddenly die and be extinguished. The air also, insinuating itself through the various pores and passages of the earth, of trees, of crops and of other things, imparts vigour to all things. Finally, it is the vehicle by which the light, rays and hidden powers of the stars flow down into this lower nature. From these things one may gather how great the usefulness of the heaven is. Indeed every vital spirit takes its origin from it. How carefully this must be observed by investigators of nature, only those who have experienced it know.

units.la: VIII. Terra est corpus opacum, igni & aquâ permixtum, sinu suo fovens semina omnium rerum sublunarium. Cœlum est principium actiuum, terra passiuum. Sicut enim cœlum est corpus spirituale, quod omnia permeat & circumplectitur: sic terra est corpus opacum, quod sinu suo fouet res omnes sublunares. Est autem hoc corpus ita comparatum, ut semper in se habeat ignem & aquam, ut è seqq. patebit.
units.tr: VIII. The earth is an opaque body, mixed of fire and water, cherishing in its bosom the seeds of all sublunary things. Heaven is the active principle, earth the passive. For as heaven is a spiritual body which permeates and embraces all things, so earth is an opaque body which cherishes all sublunary things in its bosom. This body is so constituted that it always has fire and water within itself, as will be clear from what follows.

units.la: IX. Terra est informis, vel formata. Hæc diuisio sumta est ex Gen.1.v.2.9.10.11.
units.tr: IX. The earth is either formless or formed. This division is taken from Gen. 1.2, 9, 10, 11.

units.la: X. Terra informis est moles ex aquâ & terrâ inter se permixtis constans. Hoc est illud Tohu & Bohu, quod describitur Gen. 1. v. 2. Quæ duæ voces notant vastitatem & vacuitatem, ita ut sensus sit, terram ab initio fuisse aquis undique coopertam, omnique cultu & ornatu destitutam, ut patet ex collatione huius loci cum Esa. 34. v. 11. & Ier. 4. v. 23. Atque hæc fuit interna conditio istius molis indigestæ. Sequuntur duæ aliæ conditiones externæ. Dicit enim Moses: Et tenebræ erant in superficie abyssi, & Spiritus Dei incubabat superficiei aquarum. Sed videamus paulò prolixius tres hasce conditiones. Nam clauis Physicæ practicæ in his rebus est quærenda. Et primò quidem aquarum vorago siue abyssus fuit commista cum terrâ, ita ut constituerint unum corpus. Necessaria enim erat huiusmodi permixtio, ut terra esset rerum omnium sublunarium materia unâ cum aquâ. Nimirum semen & materiam rerum omnium formabilem esse oportuit, id est, ductilem & tractabilem: id quod sine humore esse non poterat in terrâ. Itaque terra admistum humorem habuit, ut inde omnia educi possent. Quæ omnia in primâ materiam fuisse necessaria, ipsi etiam profani philosophi agnouerunt. Huc pertinent ipsorum dissertationes de chao, quæ procul dubio suam originem ex hac historia sum serunt.Et sane terra illa informis hactenus fuit chaos, quatenus destituta fuit εὐταξίᾳ [?] & κατασκευῇ [?]. Quam ob cau5 sam terra cum aquâ confusa appellatur à Mose abyssus.Deinde tota illa terræ & aquæ moles siue abyssus densis ,fuit inuoluta tenebris. Aberat enim lux, quæ in cœlo summo & mediano duntaxat fulgebat, vnde postea fuit sparsa in superficiem abyssi. Tertiò Spiritus Domini hanc rudem 10 massam, siue molem aquarum & terræ, fouebat & sustentabat, eique vim igneam communicabat, per quam ad parturiendum & velut concipiendum incalesceret, vt infinita animalium, mineralium, herbarum, & plantarum genera ex se in hanc mundanam scenam producere 15 posset. Hæc, hæc est vera philosophia de primâ materiâ, quam philosophi maximam partem solent considerare tanquam tenuem & fugientem quandam vmbram, prorsus destitutam omni formâ, paruâque magnitudine præditam : cum ex toto contextu Mosis pateat, primam o20 mnium rerum sublunarium materiam esse ingentem illâ molem & globum, qui postea in suas partes seorsum deductus & dissectus, terram hanc, quam calcamus, & mare immensum, quod nauigamus, continebat. Confer 2.Petr.3.v.5. qui locus est quasi clauis secretioris physicæ.
units.tr: X. Formless earth is a mass consisting of earth and water mixed together. This is that Tohu and Bohu described in Gen. 1.2. These two words denote emptiness and void, so that the sense is that the earth was at the beginning covered on all sides by waters and destitute of all cultivation and adornment, as is clear from comparing this passage with Isa. 34.11 and Jer. 4.23. This was the internal condition of that undigested mass. Two other, external conditions follow. For Moses says: And darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. But let us look a little more fully at these three conditions, for the key of practical physics in these matters is to be sought there. And first, the gulf or abyss of water was mixed with earth, so that they formed one body. Such a mixture was necessary, so that earth together with water might be the matter of all sublunary things. For the seed and matter of all things had to be capable of being formed, that is, pliable and workable, which could not be in earth without moisture. Therefore the earth had moisture mixed into it, so that all things could be drawn out of it. That all these things were necessary in first matter, even the profane philosophers themselves recognised. To this belong their discourses on chaos, which without doubt draw their origin from this history. And indeed that formless earth was chaos so far as it was destitute of good order and arrangement [εὐταξίᾳ and κατασκευῇ]. For this reason Moses calls the earth confused with water an abyss. Secondly, that whole mass of earth and water, or abyss, was wrapped in thick darkness. For light was absent; it shone only in the highest and middle heaven, whence it was afterwards scattered over the surface of the abyss. Thirdly, the Spirit of the Lord cherished and sustained this crude mass, or mass of waters and earth, and communicated to it a fiery power, by which it might grow warm for bearing young, as it were conceiving, so that it could bring forth from itself the infinite kinds of animals, minerals, herbs and plants onto this worldly stage. This, this is the true philosophy of first matter, which philosophers for the most part are accustomed to consider as a thin and fleeting shadow, utterly destitute of form and endowed with small magnitude. Yet from the whole context of Moses it is plain that the first matter of all sublunary things is that huge mass and globe which afterwards, drawn apart and divided into its parts, contained this earth we tread on and the immense sea we sail. Compare 2 Pet. 3.5, which passage is as it were the key to the more secret physics.

units.la: 25 XI. Terra formata est corpus bonâ sui parte ab aquis liberatum, siccatum, & vi fructificante præditum. Et primò quidem terra fuit ab aquis liberata duobus modis. Deus secundo die disparauit aquas in superiores & inferiores, atque ita terram leuauit magnâ 30 mole aquarum, quæ supra expansum, hoc est, inferiorem aëris regionem, fuerunt euectæ [?]. Sed quia ingens adhuc aquæ portio sub cœlo vndique terram tegebat, quibus ipsa quoque liberanda erat, quò conspicua & habitabilis 35 fieret, Deus tertio die aquas in certos alueos collegit. Hinc aquæ aliæ sunt superiores & cœlestes, aliæ inferiores &c subcœlestes. Deinde Deus terram vliginosam & humidam exsiccauit, vt fieret habitabilis, & tractabilis. Quoniam vero terra omni humore carere non poterat, idcirco aquas in certa receptacula collegit, vt inde per poros & meatus ad ipsam interius irrigandam deriuari possent. Tertiò Deus terrae indidit δύναμιν πλαστικήν[?], qua germinauit herbas, frutices & arbores. Hic rursus diligenter aduertant animum physici practici,& dilcant,qua namratione tractanda fit prima materia philosophis adeptis. Diximus terram aqua temperatam esse materiam mundi magni & parui. De mundo magno vide Gen.i.v.ii. 20.24.c.2.v.9. de paruo Gen.2.v.7.c.3.v.19. Terra ista fuit liberata aquis, verùm ita, vt supra illam & infra atque intra illam fuerint aquæ collectæ. Et quidem supra, vt subinde desdenderent,terramque fœcundarent: infra verò & intra, vt illam irrigarent. Vnde Isaac Gen.27.v.30. precatur filio suo Esau, vt Deus ipsi det de rore cœli & pinguedine terræ q.d. terram vberrimo suo prouentu tum demum beare homines, si fœcundetur aquis superioribus & inferioribus. Confer Gen.2.v.6.10. Psal.65.v.12. Quòd si hæc diligenter perpendamus,videbimus in praxi physices requiri primò separationem terræ & aquæ,& postea crebram imbibitionem terræ, siue aquæ istius affufionem. Hocipsum in omni generatione & nutritione obseruare licet. Sed quid ago? Non-intelligentium plena sunt omnia.
units.tr: XI. Formed earth is a body freed in a good part of itself from the waters, dried, and endowed with a fructifying power. And first, indeed, the earth was freed from the waters in two ways. On the second day God separated the waters into upper and lower, and so lightened the earth of the great mass of waters, which were carried above the expanse, that is, the lower region of the air. But since still a great portion of water covered the earth on all sides under heaven, and it too had to be freed, so that it might become conspicuous and habitable, God on the third day gathered the waters into certain channels. Hence some waters are upper and heavenly, others lower and sub-heavenly. Then God dried up the marshy and damp earth, so that it might become habitable and workable. But since the earth could not be without all moisture, he therefore gathered the waters into certain receptacles, so that from there they could be channelled through pores and passages to water it within. Thirdly, God imparted to the earth a plastic power [δύναμιν πλαστικήν], by which it sprouted herbs, shrubs and trees. Here again let practical physicists attend diligently and learn in what manner the first matter is to be handled by philosophers who have attained it. We said that earth tempered with water is the matter of the great and the small world. On the great world see Gen. 1.11, 20, 24; 2.9; on the small, Gen. 2.7; 3.19. This earth was freed from the waters, but in such a way that waters were gathered above it, below it and within it. Above, so that they might from time to time descend and make the earth fruitful; below and within, so that they might water it. Whence Isaac in Gen. 27.30 prays that God give his son Esau of the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, as if to say: the earth then blesses men with its most abundant yield when it is made fruitful by the upper and lower waters. Compare Gen. 2.6, 10; Ps. 65.12. But if we weigh these things carefully, we shall see that in the practice of physics there is required first a separation of earth and water, and afterwards a frequent soaking of the earth, or pouring of that water upon it. This can be observed in every generation and nourishment. But what am I doing? All things are full of the unintelligent.

units.la: PHYSICA SPECIALIS SACRA De Luce & Stellis.
units.tr: Special Sacred Physics On Light and the Stars

units.la: I. PRincipiatum est corpus naturale ex cœlo & terrâ, primis illis principiis, constans.
units.tr: I. A natural body is produced, consisting of heaven and earth as its first principles.

units.la: II. Estque inanimatum, vel animatum. Etsi enim totus mundus ex cœlo & terrâ constans habet suam animam & vitam, id est, spiritum efficaciæ plenum: non tamen vulgo dicitur animatus, vel viuens, etsi commodè possit: sed tantùm vehiculum animæ & vitæ, quæ in alijs est obscurior, unde illa dicuntur inanima, in alijs evidentior, unde illa nominantur animata. Vide infrà Cosmologiam.
units.tr: II. It is either inanimate or animate. For although the whole world, composed of heaven and earth, has its own soul and life, that is, a spirit full of efficacy, it is not commonly called animate or living, though it could properly be so. Rather it is only the vehicle of soul and life, which in some things is more obscure, whence those things are called inanimate, and in others more evident, whence they are named animate. See below under Cosmology.

units.la: III. Corpus inanimatum est, cuius vita in occulto est.
units.tr: III. An inanimate body is one whose life is hidden.

units.la: IV. Estque naturæ constantis, vel inconstantis.
units.tr: IV. A body is either of constant or of inconstant nature.

units.la: V. Corpus naturæ constantis est, quod in suo statu naturali diutiùs perdurat: estque naturæ cœlestis, vel terrestris.
units.tr: V. A body of constant nature is one that endures for a long time in its natural state; and it is of heavenly or of earthly nature.

units.la: VI. Corpus naturæ cœlestis est partim lux, partim stella.
units.tr: VI. A body of heavenly nature is partly light, partly star.

units.la: VII. Lux est corpus cœlestę primo die à Deo conditum, ut diem efficeret, stellarumque materia foret. Principio lux hæc dicitur corpus, hoc est, moles quædam lucida in cœlo aerio posita. Neque enim hæc lux fuit producta in cœlo tertio vel secundo: quia hæc duo corpora per se suâque naturâ sunt lucida. Sed alia est ratio aëris. Videmus enim illum suâ naturâ est-se tenebrosum, & opus habere illuminatione à sole vel lunâ. Sic itaque statuendum est, Deum ex cœlo mediano suâ naturâ lucido eduxisse molem quandam lucidam, quæ aërem & abyssum illuminaret, atque ita diem efficeret. Deinde hæc eadem lux fuit materia stellarum. Nam lux il-la primigenia primo, secundo, & tertio die idem præstitit quod sol, quantum attinet ad præfecturam diei. Fuit itaque solis vicaria, in quâ latuit ipsius semen. Sicut enim eadem fuit operatio, ita quoque natura eadem lucisistius [?] primigeniæ & solis. Huc accedit, quòd reliqua corpora omnia, quæ post primum diem producta fuerunt, ex præiacente aliquâ materiâ, prin.o [?] die à Deo conditâ, prodierunt. Itaque de stellis hoc idem est statuendum. Quare ut in mole tenebricosa elementa & rerum omnium sublunarium femina delituerunt, sic in luce primi diei stellae fuerunt ἑωσφόρα[?]. Addamus & istud. Si die quarto creationis stellae subrogatae sunt in locum primae illius lucis, oportet illam vel in nihilum esse redactam, vel in stellas collectam. At statim eam in nihilum esse redactam, absurdum est. Erat enim valde bona, & efficiebat diem aeque atque sol. Relinquitur itaque illam in solem, lunam, & reliquas stellas fuisse congregatam, ita ut stellae a Basilio recte appellentur ὀχήματα[?], & a Damasceno δοχεῖα τοῦ φωτὸς, i.e. vehicula & receptacula lucis.
units.tr: VII. Light is the heavenly body which God created on the first day, in order to make the day and to be the matter of the stars. At first this light is called a body, that is, a certain luminous mass set in the aerial heaven. For this light was not produced in the heaven on the third or second day, because those two bodies are by their own nature luminous. But the case of the air is different. For we see that by its nature it is dark and needs to be illuminated by the sun or the moon. So it must be held that God drew out of the middle heaven, which is luminous by nature, a certain luminous mass, which would illuminate the air and the abyss and so make the day. Then this same light was the matter of the stars. For that primeval light performed on the first, second and third days what the sun does, as far as the governance of the day is concerned. It was therefore the sun's vicar, in which its seed lay hidden. For just as the operation was the same, so too the nature of that primeval light and of the sun is the same. Moreover, all the other bodies which were produced after the first day came forth from some pre-existing matter created by God on the first day. Therefore the same must be held concerning the stars. Wherefore, as the elements and the seeds of all sublunary things lay hidden in the dark mass, so in the light of the first day the stars were dawn-bringers [ἑωσφόρα]. Let us add this too. If on the fourth day of creation the stars were substituted in the place of that first light, that light must either have been reduced to nothing or gathered into the stars. But that it was at once reduced to nothing is absurd, for it was very good and made the day just as the sun did. It remains, then, that it was gathered into the sun, the moon and the remaining stars. Hence the stars are rightly called by Basil vehicles [ὀχήματα], and by Damascene receptacles of light [δοχεῖα τοῦ φωτὸς], that is, vehicles and receptacles of light.

units.la: VIII. Stella est corpus caeleste in expanso caeli mediani collocatum, ad afferendum lucem super terram. Haec definitio desumta est ex Gen. 1. verf.15.17.
units.tr: VIII. A star is a heavenly body placed in the expanse of the middle heaven, to shed light upon the earth. This definition is taken from Gen. 1, verses 15 and 17.

units.la: IX. In stellis videnda est divisio & usus ipsarum.
units.tr: IX. In the stars we must consider their division and their use.

units.la: X. Divisio stellarum est, quod aliae sunt luminaria, aliae stellae prestius ita dictae. Vide Gen.1.v.16. &c.37.v.9. Psal.8.v.4. & 136.v.9. Eccles.12.v.4. Luminaria stricte dicta sunt duo, sol & luna. Sol est luminare maius, conditum ad praefecturam diei. Gen.1.v.16. Psal.104.v.22. Luna est luminare minus, conditum ad praefecturam noctis. Gen.1.v.16. Haec duo luminaria dicuntur magna respectu quantitatis apparentis, & qualitatis praedominantis. Rursus luna dicitur luminare paruum ratione solis. Est enim sole inferior & mole corporis, & lumine, & viribus. Stellae prestius ita dictae sunt corpora caelestia de natura solis & lunae participantia. Possunt etiam appellari luminaria ex Gen.1.v.14.15. Vide infra Sphaericam. Stellae stricte ita dictae ex Iob.9. & 38. dividuntur in evidenter conspicuas, & a nobis remotiores, h.e. in septentrionales & meridionales: item in extremas & intermedias, & extremæ in septentrionales& meridionales.Confer cum Sphæricis.
units.tr: X. The division of the stars is that some are luminaries, others are called stars in the narrower sense. See Gen. 1, verse 16, etc., 37, verse 9; Psal. 8, verse 4, and 136, verse 9; Eccles. 12, verse 4. Strictly speaking, there are two luminaries, the sun and the moon. The sun is the greater luminary, made to govern the day (Gen. 1, verse 16; Psal. 104, verse 22). The moon is the lesser luminary, made to govern the night (Gen. 1, verse 16). These two luminaries are called great with respect to apparent quantity and predominant quality. Again, the moon is called the lesser luminary in comparison with the sun, for it is inferior to the sun in bulk of body, in light and in powers. Stars in the narrower sense are heavenly bodies partaking of the nature of the sun and the moon. They may also be called luminaries, from Gen. 1, verses 14 and 15. See below under Spherics. Stars in the strict sense, from Job 9 and 38, are divided into those that are plainly visible and those more remote from us, that is, into northern and southern; again, into extreme and intermediate, and the extreme into northern and southern. Compare with the Spherics.

units.la: XI. Usus stellarum est partim significatio, partim influentia. Intellige usum physicum sive naturalem. Usus ipsarum hyperphysicus sive supernaturalis est partim gloria Dei Psal.8.& 19. partim excitatio nostri ad solis,& lunæ, reliquarumque stellarum cursum indefatigatâ diligentiâ in officijs pietatis & charitatis imitandum.
units.tr: XI. The use of the stars is partly signification, partly influence. Understand the physical or natural use.
