Their hyperphysical or supernatural use is partly the glory of God (Psal. 8 and 19), partly the stirring up of ourselves to imitate the course of the sun, the moon and the other stars in tireless diligence in the duties of piety and charity.

units.la: XII. Significatio stellarum est duplex. Nam primò stellæ designant ac describunt tempora, id est; annos & dies: inprimis sol & luna. Deinde sunt indicia pluuiæ, serenitatis, tempestatis, tranquillitatis,frigoris, æ-statis, & similium qualitatum, quibus aër afficitur. De priori usu est manifestus textus Gen. 1. v.14. De posteriori vide Iob.9.&38. Quanquam sunt qui vocem temporaGen.1. v.14. malunt vertere tempestates.
units.tr: XII. The signification of the stars is twofold. For, first, the stars mark and describe times, that is, years and days, especially the sun and the moon. Then they are signs of rain, of fair weather, of storm, of calm, of cold, of heat, and of similar qualities by which the air is affected. The text of Gen. 1, verse 14, is plain evidence for the former use; for the latter see Job 9 and 38. Yet there are some who prefer to render the word times in Gen. 1, verse 14, as storms.

units.la: XIII. Influentia stellarum est, quâ illæ variis modis agunt in hæc inferiora. Voluit nempe Deus vt hæc inferiora penderent à superioribus,& inter omnia ipsius opera mutuus quidam esset consensus. Qui tam evidens est inter corpora cœlestia & subcœlestia,vt illum negare sit hominis omnium ineptissimi. Videmus enim quotidie corpora illa superiora vi quâdam sibi à Deo infusâ in res hasce inferiores eiaculari temperamenta & varias qualitates,eaque mouere ac excitare, adeò quidem, vt nihil in hoc mundo inferiori possit produci & conservari sine benigno stellarum influxu. Hinc cœlum est velutithesaurus Dei, per quem terra fit fertilis. Et si cœlum maledictione Dei fiat ferreum, hoc est, immite, terra fit infœcunda. Deut. 26.v.12. 23. Quò etiam pertinet insignis illa rerum naturalium catena Hos. 2. verf. 21. Et erit in die illa, exaudiam, dicit Iehoua, exaudiam cœlos, & ipsi exaudient terram: terra verò exaudiet triticum, & vinum, & oleum. His testimoniis adde quotidianam experientiam, quæ in epilepticis, valetudinariis, cancris, arboribus, herbis, fruti, & aliis innumeris fatis superque docet, hæc inferiora non vno modo affici à superioribus. Neque tamen hoc ita est accipiendum, quasi corpora cœlestia vim habeant in omnia inferiora, vel quod sine discrimine & æqualiter agant in hunc mundum sublunarem. Non ita est. Nam primò stellæ in ea tantum agunt & agere possunt, quæ ἀπροαιρέτως[?] naturæ modo ac lege fiunt atque gubernantur: cuiusmodi sunt aër, mineralia, plantæ, & animalia quatenus animalia. Est enim earum rerum gubernatio omnis merè παθητικῶς[?], & naturæ ordinario vinculo & legi adstricta. Quæ verò pendent à merâ hominis προαιρέσει[?], vel à supernaturali gratiâ Dei, illa non subijciuntur astris. Deinde corpora cœlestia in res naturales non agùt eodem modo. Nam in quibusdam excitant duntaxat iacentes in ipsis vires, & semina actionum latentia corroborant, in quibusdam qualitates inditas conturbant, in quibusdam novas vires gignunt & multiplicem temperiem vel intemperiem iis imprimunt.
units.tr: XIII. The influence of the stars is that by which they act in various ways upon these lower things. God willed, namely, that these lower things should depend upon the higher, and that among all his works there should be a certain mutual harmony. This is so evident between the heavenly and the sublunary bodies that to deny it would befit only the most foolish of men. For we see every day that those higher bodies, by a certain power infused into them by God, dart down upon these lower things temperaments and various qualities, and move and stir them, to such an extent that nothing in this lower world can be produced and preserved without the kindly influence of the stars. Hence heaven is as it were the treasury of God, through which the earth becomes fertile; and if heaven becomes iron through the curse of God, that is, harsh, the earth becomes unfruitful (Deut. 26, verse 12; 28, verse 23). To this also belongs that notable chain of natural things in Hos. 2, verse 21: "And it shall come to pass in that day, I will hear, saith Jehovah; I will hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth, and the earth shall hear the corn, and the wine, and the oil." To these testimonies add daily experience, which teaches abundantly, in epileptics, invalids, cancers, trees, herbs, fruits and countless other things, that these lower things are not affected in one way only by the higher. Yet this is not to be understood as if the heavenly bodies had power over all lower things, or as if they acted without distinction and equally upon this sublunary world. That is not so. For, first, the stars act, and can act, only on those things which come about and are governed by the manner and law of nature without choice: such are the air, minerals, plants, and animals as animals. For the whole governance of those things is purely passive, and bound by the ordinary bond and law of nature. But those things which depend on the mere choice of man, or on the supernatural grace of God, are not subject to the stars. Then, heavenly bodies do not act in the same way upon natural things. For in some they merely stir up the powers lying in them and strengthen the hidden seeds of action; in some they disturb the qualities implanted in them; in some they generate new powers and impress upon them a manifold temperament or intemperament.

units.la: BOTANICA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED BOTANY.

units.la: I. BOtanica sacra est physica specialis de plantis, sumta ex sacris literis.
units.tr: I. Sacred botany is the special physics of plants, drawn from the sacred letters.

units.la: II. Planta est corpus animâ vegetante præditum: estque herba, vel arbor. Hæc distributio occurrit Gen. 1. v. 11. vbi herbæ diuiduntur in herbulas & herbas femen proferentes, h.e. in voluntarias seu insatiuas, quæ sponte suâ proueniunt, & satiuas, quæ culturam hominis requirunt. Sub arboribus continentur frutices siue arbusta, & suffrutices. Videamus quoque definitionem traditam. Illa etiam totidem fermè verbis apud Mosen occurrit. Deus siquidem dicitur herbis & arboribus indidisse duplicem potentiam, internam & externam[?]. Interna potentia est, quòd semen fœcundum intra se conceperunt, ita vt simile ex se indiuiduum ad perpetuam eiusdem speciei conseruatione producere possent. Externa facultas est, quòd omnis generis fructus ad alias naturas conseruandas essent producturæ, qui fructus viles essent vel ad alimentum, vel ad medicamentum, vel ad honestam oblectationem, vel ad institutionem, vel ad hæc omnia.
units.tr: II. A plant is a body endowed with a growing soul, and it is either an herb or a tree. This division occurs in Gen. 1 v. 11, where herbs are divided into those that bear seed and those that do not, that is, into wild or unsown herbs, which come up of their own accord, and cultivated herbs, which need human tending. Under trees are included shrubs, or bushes, and undershrubs. Let us also look at the definition given. It occurs in almost the same words in Moses. For God is said to have put into herbs and trees a twofold power, internal and external. The internal power is that they conceived fruitful seed within themselves, so that they could produce from themselves a like individual for the perpetual preservation of the same species. The external faculty is that they were to produce fruits of every kind for the preservation of other natures, and these fruits would be useful either for food, or for medicine, or for honest delight, or for instruction, or for all of these.

units.la: III. Herba est planta humilis, tenui caule, sed neque lignoso, neque per omnia perennis. Estque alimentaria, medicamentosa, vel coronaria. Herba alimentaria destinatur ad cibum: estque olus, fruges, vel gramen: medicamentosa habet vsum in medicina: coronaria facit ad ornatum.
units.tr: III. An herb is a low plant with a slender stalk, but neither woody nor perennial in every respect. It is alimentary, medicinal, or coronary. An alimentary herb is destined for food: it is a vegetable, a grain, or a grass. A medicinal herb has use in medicine. A coronary herb serves for ornament.

units.la: IV. Arbor est planta lignea, crassa & procera, cum trunco simplici & perenni. Sub hac in Scripturis continetur frutex & suffrutex. Frutex est planta multiplici caudice & perenni, vt sambucus, balsamus. Suffrutex est simplici caudice & perenni, minimæ inter stirpes lignosas altitudinis, vt ruta, lavendula.
units.tr: IV. A tree is a woody plant, thick and tall, with a single, perennial trunk. Under this heading the Scriptures include the shrub and the undershrub. A shrub is a plant with many stems and perennial, such as the elder or the balsam. An undershrub has a single stem and is perennial, of the least height among woody stocks, such as rue and lavender.

units.la: V. In sacris literis multæ occurrunt herbæ & arbores, quarum natura vtcunq; exinde cognosci potest. Si nempe omnes circumstantiæ accuratè expendantur. Videris elegantem libellum Leuini Lemnij hac inscriptione: Similitudinum ac parabolarum, quæ in Bibliis ex herbis atq; arboribus desumuntur, dilucida explicatio. units.la: ORYCTOLOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: Sacred Oryctology.

units.la: I. ORyctologia sacra est physica speciali de fossilibus siue mineralibus, ex S. literis petita.
units.tr: I. Sacred oryctology is a special branch of natural philosophy concerning fossils, or minerals, drawn from the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: II. Fossilia sunt corpora, quæ in terræ visce- rib̄s generantur à sulphure aquæ infito.
units.tr: II. Fossils are bodies generated in the bowels of the earth from the sulphur infused in water.

units.la: Suntque impositionis primæ, secundæ, vel tertiæ. In primo ordine sunt metalla; in secundo media mineralia, cuiusmodi sunt succi & terræ metallares; in tertio, lapides. Quærat hoc loco aliquis, Cur fossilium nulla fit facta mentio in historiâ πρωτοπλάστως? Resp. Quoniam de iis tantum operum Dei generibus Moses tractare instituit, quæ à nobis passim cernuntur. Deinde mineralia sub vegetabilibus videntur esse comprehensa, quandoquidem ipsorum generatio & natura proximior est vegetabilibus quàm animalibus.
units.tr: They are of a first, second, or third kind of formation. In the first order are the metals; in the second, the intermediate minerals, such as juices and metallic earths; in the third, stones. Someone may ask here why no mention of fossils is made in the history of the first creation. The answer: Moses intended to treat only those kinds of God's works that are everywhere visible to us. Further, minerals seem to be included under plants, since their generation and nature are more closely related to plants than to animals.

units.la: III. Scriptura sæpe meminit metallorum.
units.tr: III. Scripture often mentions metals.

units.la: Sunt qui quatuor duntaxat species metallorum constituunt, videl. aurum, argentum, ferrum & plumbum. Sed fi ea, quæ sunt Ezech. 22. v. 18. & 27. v. 12. cum Num. 31. v. 22. & Dan. 2. v. 31. conferantur, plura quàm quatuor metallorum genera esse facile perspici poterit. Inter illa autem facile primas tenet aurum, & inter gradus auri primum obtinet locum, quod appellatur in Scripturis aurum Ophir.
units.tr: Some recognise only four kinds of metal, namely gold, silver, iron and lead. But if the passages in Ezekiel 22:18 and 27:12 are compared with Numbers 31:22 and Daniel 2:31, it can easily be seen that there are more than four kinds of metal. Among them, gold easily holds the first place, and among the grades of gold the first rank belongs to what is called in Scripture "the gold of Ophir".

units.la: Dicamus itaque primo de auro. Eius natura est, non posse destrui, nisi peculiari & raro quodam artificio, cuius non fuit ignarus Moses. Num. 32. v. 20. Ignis certè tantum abest, ut aurum destruat, ut illud magis magisque perficiat & purget, multò magis quàm argentum, quod septima flamma recoxit, ut poëta ex Psal. 12. v. 7. loquitur. Hebræi constituunt septem genera siue gradus auri ex Iob. 28. v. 1. 2. & seqq. Thren. 4. v. 2. nempe Sagur, Ophir, Dahab, Barsir, Zahab, Paz, Cetem, Charab. Ex his gradibus in Scriptura illud dicitur aurum Ophir, quod est commendatissimum. Nam in Ophir provenit aurum optimum. Vide infra in Geographicis. Quæritur hic quale sit aurum, quod Apoc. 21. v. 21. dicitur esse purum tanquam vitrum pellucidum? Resp. Est aurum defæcatissimum. Adauri naturam quàm proximè accedit argentum, quod ideo ideò à quibusdam appellatur aurum album. Sæpe fit metio huius metalli in sacris, quemadmodū & auri, quo supra modum abundauit Salomo. Pondus quippe auri, quod ipsi quotannis obueniebat, erat 666. talentorum, id est, tricies centies mille, nongenties nonagies sexies[?] mille aureorum. Porrò Scriptura etiam meminit Chalcolibani Apoc. 1. v. 15. & 2. v. 18. quo dalij putant esse orichalcum: alij è Libano monte effossum aliquem nouum lapidem; alij incognitum nostris temporibus metallum: alij æs candidissimum ac lucidissimum, quale est Dan. 10. v. 6. Quid verò est orichalcum, cuius modò facta est mentio?
units.tr: Let us therefore speak first of gold. Its nature is that it cannot be destroyed, except by some peculiar and rare art, of which Moses was not ignorant (Numbers 31:22). Fire is so far from destroying gold that it rather perfects and purifies it more and more, much more than silver, which the poet says was refined in the seventh furnace (Psalm 12:6). The Hebrews set out seven kinds or grades of gold from Job 28:1–2 and following, and Lamentations 4:2, namely Sagur, Ophir, Dahab, Barsir, Zahab, Paz, Cetem and Charab. Of these grades, the one called in Scripture "the gold of Ophir" is the most highly prized, for the best gold comes from Ophir. See below, under the Geographical matters. Here it is asked what kind of gold is meant by the gold that in Revelation 21:21 is said to be pure as transparent glass. The answer: it is gold most thoroughly refined. Closest in nature to gold is silver, which for this reason is called by some "white gold". Mention is often made of this metal in the sacred books, as also of gold, of which Solomon had an extraordinary abundance. For the weight of gold that came to him each year was 666 talents, that is, three hundred thousand times... nine hundred and ninety-six thousand golden pieces. Furthermore, Scripture also mentions chalcolibanus (Revelation 1:15 and 2:18), which some think is orichalcum; others a certain new stone dug out of Mount Lebanon; others a metal unknown in our times; others a most white and bright bronze, such as is found in Daniel 10:6. But what exactly is orichalcum, of which mention has just been made?

units.la: Resp. Quidam putant esse illud æs, quod in montibus effoditur, vnde Græco vocabulo putant ὀρείχαλκον appellatum. Alij dictum voluntab[?] auro, quod olim orum pronuntiabatur, quòd sit metalli quædam species ex ære & auro vi naturæ ferruminata & concreta: quod genus metalli appellant electrum.
units.tr: The answer: some think it is that bronze which is dug out of the mountains, whence they think it was called by the Greek word oreichalkon [ὀρείχαλκον]. Others say it was named from gold, which was once pronounced aurum, because it is a certain kind of metal fused and joined together by the force of nature from bronze and gold; this kind of metal they call electrum.

units.la: Et hæc sententia plerisque probatur. Hinc orichalcum ipso cupro longè præstantius & pretiosius æstimatur: quia nempe conflatum est ex ære & auro, naturali quadam concretione, cui etiam aliquid argenti admixtum est.
units.tr: This opinion is approved by most people. Hence orichalcum is valued far more highly and preciously than copper itself, because it is evidently compounded of bronze and gold by a natural kind of union, to which some silver is also added.

units.la: IV. Mediorum mineralium multa sunt gene- ra, e quibus Scriptura tria quatuorue attingit.
units.tr: IV. There are many kinds of intermediate minerals, of which Scripture touches on three or four.

units.la: Meminit enim fauonis & nitri Ier. 2. v. 22. sulphuris Gen. 19. Deut. 29. & salis sæpissime. Vbi non est silentio prætereundum, sal esse principium omnium corporum sublunariū. Sal enim nihil est aliud, quàm aqua sicca, h. e. aqua terrea, & terra aquea. Quod vtinam sophistæ animaduerterent! Maneat itaque immotum, quod adeptus quidam philosophus scribit: Centrum vniuersi est terra, centrum terræ est sal. Possem hic digredi in plenâ dissertatione de sale, & scribere sacram aliquam haligraphiam. Sed contentus ero tribus verbis indicasse ipsius methodum. Haligraphia est institutio de natura & usu salis. Natura salis, est omnes res sublunares constituere radicaliter, & illas conseruare à putredine. Vsus ipsius est naturalis, & supernaturalis. Naturalis est partim in culinâ, partim in medicinâ: supernaturalis, in significando mysteria, vt quod nullum sacrificium debuit offerri sine sale Leuit. 2. v. 13. Marc. 9. v. 49. quod apostoli appellantur sal terrae. Matth. 5. verf. 13. quod sermo nostrer debet esse conditus sale Coloss. 4. v. 6. quod denique debemus in nobis ipsis habere salem, ita vt igne saliamur. Marc. 9. v. 49. 50.
units.tr: For it mentions natron and nitre (Jeremiah 2:22), sulphur (Genesis 19; Deuteronomy 29), and salt very often. Here it must not be passed over in silence that salt is the principle of all sublunary bodies. For salt is nothing other than dry water, that is, earthly water and watery earth. Would that the sophists would take note of this! Let it therefore stand firm, what a certain philosopher who had attained understanding wrote: the centre of the universe is the earth, and the centre of the earth is salt. I could here digress into a full dissertation on salt and write a kind of sacred haligraphy. But I shall be content to indicate its method in three words. Haligraphy is the teaching concerning the nature and use of salt. The nature of salt is to constitute all sublunary things radically and to preserve them from putrefaction. Its use is both natural and supernatural. The natural use is partly in the kitchen, partly in medicine; the supernatural use is in signifying mysteries, as when no sacrifice was to be offered without salt (Leviticus 2:13; Mark 9:49); when the apostles are called the salt of the earth (Matthew 5:13); when our speech ought to be seasoned with salt (Colossians 4:6); and finally when we ought to have salt in ourselves, so that we are salted with fire (Mark 9:49–50).

units.la: V. Lapidum vulgarium & pretiosorum mentio fit in sacris. Ex lapidibus vulgaribus frequenter fit mentio lapidum, quorum vsus est in aedificiis: item petrae, silicis, marmoris & arenae. Ex lapidibus pretiosis celebrantur margaritae, & XII. gemmae Exod. 28. de quibus infra in Lithologia. Quia vero interpretes variant in reddendis nominibus Hebraicis istarum gemmarum, aliquot sententias breviter commemorabo. Vatablus. | Iunius. | Brugthonus. | Danæus. units.tr: V. Mention is made in the sacred books of common and precious stones. Among common stones, frequent mention is made of stones used in buildings, likewise of rock, flint, marble and sand. Among precious stones, pearls and the twelve gems of Exodus 28 are celebrated, of which more below under Lithology. But since the interpreters differ in rendering the Hebrew names of these gems, I shall briefly recall several opinions. units.la: Hic solent quaerere, quid sit bdellium Gen. 2. verf. 12. Resp. Alij volunt esse iaspidem: alij carbunculum: alij album quendam lapidem: alij arborem, quae Arabibus dicatur etiamnum hodie Bdolchon: alij denique margaritam praestantissimam. Cui postremae sententiae vt astipuler facit collatio huius loci Gen. 2. cum Exod. 16. v. 14. 15. & Num. 11. v. 7, vbi color mannae dicitur fuisse sicut color bdellij & pruinæ: qualis nempe est color margaritarum. Neque valet, quod afferunt patroni eius sententiæ, quâ bdellium Gen. 2. dicitur esse arbor, apud Mosen Num. 11. intelligi colorem gummi arboris bdellij. Hæc siquidem expositio est coacta. Nam Scriptura dicit: Et color eius sicut color bdellij.
units.tr: Here people usually ask what bdellium is (Genesis 2:12). The answer: some hold that it is jasper, others carbuncle, others a certain white stone, others a tree which is still today called bdolach by the Arabs, and others finally the most excellent pearl. To this last opinion the comparison of this passage, Genesis 2, with Exodus 16:14–15 and Numbers 11:7 lends support, where the colour of the manna is said to have been like the colour of bdellium and frost, which is precisely the colour of pearls. Nor is there force in the objection of its defenders, by which bdellium in Genesis 2 is said to be a tree, while in Moses (Numbers 11) it is understood to be the colour of the gum of the bdellium tree. For that explanation is forced. Scripture says: "and its colour was as the colour of bdellium."

units.la: METEOROLOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED METEOROLOGY.

units.la: I. Meteorologia sacra est physica specialis de natura meteororum, petita ex sacris literis.
units.tr: I. Sacred meteorology is the special physics of the nature of meteors, drawn from the sacred writings.

units.la: II. Meteora sunt corpora inconstantis naturæ. Nam quia elementa in iis non sunt redacta ad medium, hoc est, iustam atque exactam proportionem & temperiem, natura ipsorum facile mutatur, ut in nive, grandine, rore, & similibus meteoris videre est.
units.tr: II. Meteors are bodies of an inconstant nature. For because the elements in them are not brought to a mean, that is, to a just and exact proportion and temperament, their nature is easily changed, as can be seen in snow, hail, dew and similar meteors.

units.la: III. Meteora diuiduntur bifariam. Et primò quidem ex loco alia sunt ascendentia, ut nebula, nubes: alia descendentia, ut pluuia, nix: alia hærentia vel in aere, ut fulmen, cometa; vel in terra, ut terræmotus. Deinde meteora sunt hypostatica, vel emphatica. Meteora hypostatica sunt naturæ valde realis, & crassiorem habent materiam: suntque vel ignea, ut fax, ignis perpendicularis, bolis, capra saltans, scintillæ volantes, stella cadens, lancea ardens, draco volans, ignis lambens, ignis fatuus, sidus Helenæ, Castor & Pollux, Cometa, fulmen: vel aerea, ut ventus & terræmotus: vel aquea, ut nubes, pluuia, nix, ros, pruina, grando, nebula: vel terrea, ut lapides e nubibus decidentes. Meteora emphatica sunt naturæ coloris intentionalis: suntque numero septem, puta varii colores, chasma, halo, parelius, parasclene, virgæ & iris.
units.tr: III. Meteors are divided in two ways. First, by place: some are ascending, such as mist and cloud; others descending, such as rain and snow; others remain either in the air, such as lightning and comets, or on the earth, such as earthquakes. Then meteors are either hypostatic or emphatic. Hypostatic meteors are of a very real nature and have a grosser matter. They are either fiery, such as the torch, the perpendicular fire, the bolis, the leaping goat, flying sparks, the falling star, the burning lance, the flying dragon, the licking flame, the will-o'-the-wisp, Helen's star, Castor and Pollux, the comet and lightning; or airy, such as wind and earthquake; or watery, such as cloud, rain, snow, dew, hoarfrost, hail and mist; or earthy, such as stones falling from the clouds. Emphatic meteors are of an intentional nature of colour. They are seven in number, namely the various colours, chasma, halo, parhelion, parascene, rods and the rainbow.

units.la: IV. Scriptura meminit sequentium meteororum. Nubium duo sunt perpetui fontes, videlicet mare & terra, e quibus in cœlum hoc nostrum vapores ascédunt[?] Ier. 4. v. 13. 1. Reg. 18. v. 44. tum aquæ superiores sunt cœlestes, quæ nunquam non manent inaëre. Nubium aliæ sunt steriles, quæ pluuia carent, aliæ vberes & fœcundæ, quæ pluuiam effundunt. Iob. 36. v. 29. Iudæ v 12. Prou. 25. v. 14. Proprius enim nubium fœtus, & velut fructus, sunt pluuiæ, ad quas vel gestandas & coriinendas, vel effundendas sunt à Deo conditæ & constitutæ, tanquam cœ-leftes quidam vtres. Iob. 38. v. 27. Sed & eæ ipsæ sursum expanduntur à Deo, vt nos omniaq; hæc inferiora à nimio solis æstu & ardore defendant, atque tanquam pulcherrimum & latissimum πέτασμα & velum tegant. Iob. 36. v. 30. 32. Porro nubes à vento & sole excitantur, & discutiuntur Iob. 37. v. 11. Nubes est mater, vas, & veluti pluuiæ, vt modo diximus. De pluuia igitur secundo loco tractabimus. Est autem pluuia nubis dissolutio in guttas aquæ. Nam eliquatur nubes in guttas calore solis moderato (nam summo exsiccatur 1. Sam. 12. v. 16.) & spargitur hinc inde viuenti, tanquam si quispiam inflatis buccis multam aquam contineat, & eam vi eiiciat. Multis autem de causis pluuia immittitur à Deo. Iob. 37. verf. 13. Et plurimum quidem ad hominum vsus & vtilitates maximas, veluti vt terram inebriet, atque emolliat, & fœcundam reddat, vt germina & arbores crescant, & vt nimij solis ardores temperentur. Psal. 65. verf. 11. Sæpe etiam Deus demittit pluuias ad nos flagellandos. Nam interdum per eas omnia terræ fata, & ipsum victus atque messis corrumpit. Iob. 36. verf. 31. & 37. v. 8. Genera pluuiæ in Scripturis traduntur duo: unum naturale & ordinarium, alterum miraculosum & extraordinarium. Pluuia naturalis aut confertim cadit, estque copiosior & vehementior, & appellatur nimbus Ezech. 13. v. 11. aut est leuior & moderatior, quæ vocatur imber Iob. 37. v. 6. Rursus pluuia naturalis est tem-peftiua vel serotina. Pluuia tempestiua est, quæ sequitur culturam: serotina, quæ antecedit collectionem fructuum. Deut. 11.v.14. Ier. 5. v. 24. Sunt qui interpretantur pluuiam matutinam & serotinam. Sed inepta est ista sententia. Nam Deus pluuiam tempestiuam vocat eam, quæ decidit semente iam factâ germinationis causâ. Et hæc dicitur Hebraeis יורה [?] à docendo & erudiendo, quòd quasi doceat & erudiat terram, vt proferat fructus. Huiusmodi est pluuia, quæ decidit in autumno & vere, postquam agri culti sunt, & semen terræ mandatum. Serotina itaq; pluuia fuerit, quæ sub tempus messis antecedit collectionem frugum, vt spicas impleat & contineat.
units.tr: IV. Scripture mentions the following meteors. There are two perpetual sources of clouds, namely the sea and the earth, from which vapours rise into this our heaven Jer. 4. v. 13; 1 Kings 18. v. 44. Then the upper waters are heavenly, and never cease to remain in the air. Some clouds are barren and lack rain; others are fertile and fruitful and pour forth rain Job 36. v. 29; Jude v. 12; Prov. 25. v. 14. For the proper offspring of clouds, and as it were their fruit, is rain; for carrying and holding it, or pouring it out, they have been created and established by God, like heavenly skins Job 38. v. 27. But they are also spread out on high by God, so that they may defend us and all these lower things from the excessive heat and glare of the sun, and cover them like a most beautiful and very wide awning and veil Job 36. v. 30, 32. Moreover, clouds are stirred up and dispersed by wind and sun Job 37. v. 11. The cloud is the mother, the vessel and, as it were, the source of rain, as we have just said. We shall therefore treat of rain in the second place. Rain is the dissolution of a cloud into drops of water. For the cloud melts into drops by the moderate heat of the sun (for by excessive heat it is dried up 1 Sam. 12. v. 16), and is scattered hither and thither over the living, as if someone with puffed-out cheeks held a great deal of water and drove it out by force. Rain is sent by God for many reasons Job 37. v. 13. And chiefly for the use and very great benefit of men: to drench and soften the earth and make it fruitful, so that the shoots and trees grow, and so that the excessive heat of the sun is tempered Ps. 65. v. 11. God often also sends down rains to scourge us; for sometimes through them he destroys all the produce of the earth, and food and harvest itself Job 36. v. 31; 37. v. 8. Two kinds of rain are handed down in the Scriptures: one natural and ordinary, the other miraculous and extraordinary. Natural rain either falls in a heavy downpour, and is more copious and violent, and is called nimbus Ezek. 13. v. 11; or it is lighter and gentler, and is called imber Job 37. v. 6. Again, natural rain is either timely or late. Timely rain is that which follows the tilling; late rain is that which precedes the gathering of the fruits Deut. 11. v. 14; Jer. 5. v. 24. Some interpret this as morning and evening rain, but that view is unsuitable. For God calls timely rain that which falls after the seed has been sown, to cause it to germinate. And by the Hebrews this is called יורה [yoreh], from teaching and instructing, because it as it were teaches and instructs the earth to bring forth fruit. Such is the rain that falls in autumn and spring, after the fields have been tilled and the seed committed to the earth. Late rain, then, will be that which falls near the time of harvest, before the gathering of the crops, to fill and hold the ears of grain.

units.la: Vnde Hebraeis dicitur מלקוש [?] ex מלא [?] impleuit, & שִׁבֳּלֶת [?] spica, quòd descendat super spicas & culmos, ne nimis siccitate grana dispergantur, & culmi exarescant. Alij tamen hanc vocé deriuant à יורה [?] tardauit: quòd hæc sit vltima pluuia, quam recipit seges ante messem. Pluuia miraculosa & prodigiosa fit certissimo Dei iudicio, ita vt decidant lapides, sulphur, ignis, & similia. Gen. 19. Iof. 10. v. 11. Quod diximus de vtilitate pluuiæ, illam facere ad foecunditatem terræ: item aliam esse tempestiuam, aliam serotinam: hoc, inquam, in praxi physices oportet imitari. Si quis enim ibi velit facere pretium suæ operæ, oportet vt terram suâ irriget pluuiâ, eâque tum tempestiuâ, tum serotinâ. Sed videamus de niue. Nix est nubis dissolutio in floccos. Vtilitas eius est longè maxima. Terram enim foecundat, cui optimi sterquilinij, simi & pinguedinis loco datur à Deo, penes quem sunt thesauri niuium. Iob. 38. v. 22. 23. Ps. 148. v. 8. Prou. 26. v. 1. Grando est nubis dissolutio in globulos, quibus Deus scitur tanquam sclopis tormentarijs ad nos castigan. Ios. Psal. 148. v. 8. & 105. v. 32. Iob. 38. v. 27. Eccl. 43. v. 16. Est autem alia grando naturalis, vt illa, de quâ modò diximus: alia miraculosa, de quâ Exod. 9. v. 24. Apoc. 16. v. 21. Pruina quoque fit mentio in Scriptura: vt Iob. 38. v. 29. Psal. 147. v. 16. Ros est vapor subtilior & tenuior, qui leui & mitì frigore compingitur, vt terram eiusque fructus foueat, & aërem, in quo versamur, refrigeret. Iob. 38. v. 28. Gen. 27. v. 30. Rori affine est manna: quod est naturale, vel miraculosum. Manna naturale est tenue & globosum corpus, quod ex rore cœlesti & sudore liue cremore earum rerum, quibus insidet, à Deo compactum, magnâ aëris temperie, decidit in terram, herbas, & arbores. Ideo nōn generatur in quâuis terræ regione, sed eâtantum, in quâ temperatio est aër propter æstus & frigoris successionem, vt in monte Libano, Calabria, & alibi. Optimum perhibetur manna, quod in Arabia crescit, & ab Arabibus vocatur Tereniabin. Manna miraculosum erat, quod per 40. annos pluebat diuinâ virtute, & populum Dei alebat instar panis. Exod. 16. Num. 11. Tonitru est sonus ille, qui fit propter nubem effractam per antiperistasin caloris & frigoris. Fit autem sonus ille, vti si pannum abrumpas violentius, aut si aër aliquis in folle conclusus vi erumpat. Id quod observari potest in castaneis ad ignem positis. Nam fit sonus, cùm earum cortex frangitur. Sic dum vi dissilit ignis ex ruptâ & discissâ nube, fit fragor ingens & sonitus, idquod tonitru appellatur, ab Hebraeis autem vox Dei ex Psal. 29. & vox superbiæ: quia Dominus per eam vocem homines, bestias, terram, & cœlum ipsum terrefacit, atque superbiam hominum domat. Iob. 26. v. 11. Terræmotus id est in terrâ, quod tonitru in nube. Est enim flatus intra cauernas terræ coarctatus, quidum sibi viam hinc inde parat, terram concutit. Eius exemplum est Amos. 1. v. 1. Matth. 27. v. 54. cap. 28. v. 2. Act. 16. ver. 26. Sequitur ventus, qui est fluor aëris, vt ait Arnobius. Quam in sententiam Augustinus dicit, ventum esse aërem fluctuante.Sed si velimus rem penitius inspicere, ventus est motus & dispersio exhalationis in sublime eductæ, & fit in aëre immobili. Natura siquidem expansa à Deo creati est non agitari vel dissipari, sed manere in statu quodam immobili. Ventus est alius vehementior, qui dicitur turbo: alius leuior, qui appellatur ventus nomine generis. Turbine Deus vtitur extraordinariè ad homines puniendos. Est enim tanquam manus quædam robustissima, quæ quidquid apprehendit, arctè constringit & eleuat;& instar teli atque pili, quod omnia penetrat atque diruit. Vento ordinario Deus utitur, ut aërem purget atque refrigeret, herbas item, arbores, bestias & homines excitet, fœcundet, foveat, ventilet; aquam denique & naues impellat. Iob. 38. v. 24. 1. Reg. 19. v. 11. 12. Iob. 37. v. 9. §[?] 22. Prou. 25. v. 23. Eccles. 43. v. 18. 19. 22. & seqq. Act. 27.
units.tr: Hence the Hebrews call it מלקוש [malqosh], from מלא [male], "he filled", and שִׁבֳּלֶת [shibbolet], "ear of grain", because it falls upon the ears and stalks, lest the grains be scattered through excessive dryness and the stalks wither. Others, however, derive this word from יורה [yoreh], "he delayed", because this is the last rain that the crop receives before the harvest. Miraculous rain comes by the most certain judgment of God, so that stones, sulphur, fire and similar things fall Gen. 19; Josh. 10. v. 11. What we have said about the usefulness of rain, that it makes the earth fruitful, and that one rain is timely and another late, ought, I say, to be imitated in the practice of physics. For if anyone wishes to make a return for his labour there, he must water the earth with his rain, and that both timely and late. But let us turn to snow. Snow is the dissolution of a cloud into flakes. Its usefulness is by far the greatest, for it fertilises the earth, to which God, in whose hands are the treasuries of snows, gives the place of the best dung, muck and fat Job 38. v. 22, 23; Ps. 148. v. 8; Prov. 26. v. 1. Hail is the dissolution of a cloud into globules, with which God chastises us as with artillery guns Ios.; Ps. 148. v. 8 and 105. v. 32; Job 38. v. 27; Eccl. 43. v. 16. There is natural hail, such as that of which we have just spoken, and there is miraculous hail, of which Exod. 9. v. 24; Rev. 16. v. 21. Hoarfrost too is mentioned in Scripture Job 38. v. 29; Ps. 147. v. 16. Dew is a subtler and finer vapour, which is condensed by a light and gentle cold, to cherish the earth and its fruits and to cool the air in which we live Job 38. v. 28; Gen. 27. v. 30. Akin to dew is manna, which is either natural or miraculous. Natural manna is a fine and globular body, which, formed by God from heavenly dew and the sweat or cream of the things on which it settles, falls upon the earth, the herbs and the trees in a great mildness of the air. It is therefore not produced in every region of the earth, but only in those where the air is temperate because of the alternation of heat and cold, as on Mount Lebanon, in Calabria and elsewhere. The best manna is said to be that which grows in Arabia and is called by the Arabs Tereniabin. Miraculous manna was that which rained down for forty years by divine power and nourished the people of God like bread Exod. 16; Num. 11. Thunder is the sound that is made when a cloud is broken by the opposition of heat and cold. The sound is made as when you tear cloth more violently, or when some air shut up in a bellows bursts out by force; which can be observed in chestnuts placed in the fire, for a sound is made when their shell is broken. So when fire leaps out forcibly from a cloud burst and split open, there is a great crash and noise, and this is called thunder; by the Hebrews, however, it is the voice of God Ps. 29, and the voice of pride, because the Lord by that voice terrifies men, beasts, earth and heaven itself, and tames the pride of men Job 26. v. 11. Earthquake is, in the earth, what thunder is in the cloud. For a wind confined within the caverns of the earth makes its way hither and thither and shakes the earth. An example is Amos 1. v. 1; Matt. 27. v. 54; 28. v. 2; Acts 16. v. 26. Next comes wind, which is a flow of air, as Arnobius says. To this effect Augustine says that wind is air in motion. But if we wish to look into the matter more deeply, wind is the motion and dispersal of an exhalation drawn up on high, and it occurs in air that is otherwise motionless. For the nature of the expanse created by God is not to be agitated or scattered, but to remain in a certain motionless state. There is one wind that is more violent, which is called a whirlwind (turbo), and another that is gentler, which is called wind in the general sense. God uses the whirlwind extraordinarily to punish men; for it is as it were a most powerful hand, which seizes whatever it grasps, binds it tightly and lifts it up, and like a dart or a javelin it pierces and breaks down everything. God uses the ordinary wind to purify and cool the air, and likewise to stir up, make fruitful, cherish and fan herbs, trees, beasts and men, and finally to drive the waters and ships Job 38. v. 24; 1 Kings 19. v. 11, 12; Job 37. v. 9, 22; Prov. 25. v. 23; Eccl. 43. v. 18, 19, 22 and following; Acts 27.

units.la: ICHTHYOLOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: Sacred Ichthyology.

units.la: Ichthyologia sacra est physica specialis de natura piscium, sumta ex codice scripturæ sacræ.
units.tr: Sacred ichthyology is a special branch of physics concerning the nature of fishes, drawn from the code of Holy Scripture.

units.la: II. Pisces sunt animalia ex aquis producta, & in aquis natantia. Ex aquis productos esse pisces docet Moses Gen.1.v.20. Nimirum aqua iussu Dei sic est constricta, coagulata, & incrassata, ut inde corpus solidum & tenax prodierit, quod æque est caro, atque caro quadrupedum. 1. Cor.15.v.39. etsi temperamento & gradu differt.
units.tr: II. Fishes are animals produced from waters and swimming in waters. Moses teaches that fishes were produced from waters, Gen.1.v.20. By God's command, the water was so constricted, coagulated and thickened that a solid and tenacious body came forth from it, which is truly flesh, just as the flesh of quadrupeds is flesh, although it differs in temperament and degree. 1. Cor.15.v.39.

units.la: III. Piscium varia sunt genera. Sunt enim 1. Pisces proprie dicti, iisque tum maiores, ut salmo: tum mediocres, ut halec: tum minores, ut fundulus. 2. Pisces improprie dicti, ut belluæ marinæ, puta balæna, delphinus. 3. Zoophyta sive plantanimantia aquatilia: ut spongia marina. 4. serpentes aquatiles, ut hydrus. 5. insecta aquatilia, ut hirudo, pulex marinus. Ex his piscibus alij sunt mundi, alij immundi de lege Mosis. Leuit. 11. Frequenter fit mentio piscium, quos ceperunt apostoli, & quos Christus miraculose benedixit. Matt. 14. & 15. Marc. 6. Luc. 5. 9. 24. Iohan. 6. & 21. sed de vno solum pisce Scriptura diserte agit, eumq; nobis tanquam operum Dei aquatilium miraculum proponit Iob. 40. & 41. quem Leviathan appellat. Vbi tenenda est regula, In omni rerum corporearum genere esse quiddam minimum & maximum. Sic pumiliones & pygmei in vniuerso hominum genere sunt res minima, gigantes, res maxima: in terrestribus animalibus elephas est maximus, minimus autem musaut gurgulio:in auibus est maxima struthiocamelus, minima, regulus. Sic in uniuerso piscium genere maximus est Leuiathan, minimus, apua, quam alij appellant millecantonem. Est autem Leuiathan balaena, cuius moles & robur sunt plane stupenda: unde figurate intelligitur hac voce sublimitas omnis spiritualis uel corporalis, quae ui uel fraude se aduersus Deum effert. Esa. 27. v. 1.
units.tr: III. Fishes are of various kinds. For there are: 1. fishes properly so called, and of these some are larger, like the salmon; some middling, like the herring; and some smaller, like the fundulus. 2. Fishes improperly so called, such as sea monsters, for example the whale and the dolphin. 3. Zoophytes, or aquatic plant-animals, such as the sea sponge. 4. Aquatic serpents, such as the hydrus. 5. Aquatic insects, such as the leech and the sea flea. Of these fishes, some are clean and some unclean under the law of Moses. Lev. 11. Mention is frequently made of the fishes which the apostles caught and which Christ miraculously blessed: Matt. 14 and 15; Mark 6; Luke 5, 9, 24; John 6 and 21. But Scripture speaks expressly of only one fish, and sets it before us as a marvel among the aquatic works of God: Job 40 and 41, which it calls Leviathan. Here the rule must be held: In every kind of corporeal things there is something smallest and largest. Thus pygmies and dwarfs are the smallest thing in the whole human race, giants the largest; among land animals the elephant is the largest, and the smallest is the mouse or the weevil; among birds the largest is the ostrich-camel, and the smallest the regulus. So in the whole genus of fishes the largest is Leviathan, and the smallest is the apua, which others call the millecanton. Leviathan is the whale, whose bulk and strength are truly astonishing; whence by this word is figuratively understood every loftiness, spiritual or bodily, which lifts itself up against God by force or by fraud. Esa. 27. v. 1.

units.la: ORNITHOLOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED ORNITHOLOGY.

units.la: I. ORnithologia sacra est physica specialis de natura auium, petita ex sacris literis.
units.tr: I. Sacred ornithology is the special physics of the nature of birds, drawn from the sacred letters.

units.la: II. Aues sunt animalia ex aquis producta, & in aere volantia. Aues ex aquis productas esse docet Moses Gen. 1. verf. 20. Hinc ut recte scripsit Ambrosius, aquam & pisces eiusdem inter sese generis esse & materiae: ita Fulgentius & alij recte docent, aues & pisces eiusdem esse materiae. Sed, inquis, supra cœlum & terra statuebantur omnium corporum principia? Resp. Intelligite terram aquâ coniunctam, ita ut vel terra praedominetur, vel aqua. In piscibus & auibus dominium habet aqua, in quadrupedibus & omnino bestiis terrestribus ipsoque etiam homine quantum ad corpus praedominium habet terra.
units.tr: II. Birds are animals produced from the waters and flying in the air. Moses teaches that birds were produced from the waters, Gen. 1, verse 20. Hence, as Ambrose rightly wrote, water and fish are of the same kind and matter among themselves; so Fulgentius and others rightly teach that birds and fish are of the same matter. But, you will say, were the principles of all bodies set down as above heaven and earth? Answer: understand earth joined with water, so that either earth or water predominates. In fish and birds water holds dominion; in quadrupeds and in all terrestrial beasts, and even in man himself as regards the body, earth holds predominance.

units.la: III. Auium varia sunt genera. Et primò quidem sunt aues proprie dicta: eaeque tum maiores, ut aquila, ciconia: tum mediocres, ut columba, gallina: tum minores, ut luscinia, hirundo. Deinde sunt insecta alata: ut apes, muscae. Tertiò sunt serpentes alati: ut draco, basiliscus.
units.tr: III. The kinds of birds are various. First, there are birds properly so called, and these are either larger, such as the eagle and stork; or medium, such as the dove and hen; or smaller, such as the nightingale and swallow. Then there are winged insects, such as bees and flies. Third, there are winged serpents, such as the dragon and basilisk.

units.la: De his tribus generibus varia occurrunt in Scripturis: quę nos breuiter persequemur. Principio Exod. 14. & Leuit. 11. recensentur aues mundæ & immundæ, ubi variant interpretes hoc modo. Vatablus. Aquila. Gryphus. Haliaetus. Vultur. Miluus. Coruus. Struthio. Noctua. Larus. Accipiter. Nycticorax. Mergulus. Ibis. Porphyrio. Pelecanus. Cygnus. Ciconia. Charadrius. Upupa. Vespertilio. Locusta. Attacus. Ophiomachus. Bruchus. Iunius. Aquila. Ossifraga. Haliaetus. Miluus. Pica. Coruus. Ulula. Hirundo. Aesalo. Accipiter. Bubo. Mergus. Noctua. Monedula. Platea. Merops. Ciconia. Ardea. Attagen. Vespertilio. Locusta. Bombyx. Cantharus. Cicada. Vulgata versio. Aquila. Gryphus. Haliaetus. Miluus. Vultur. Struthio. Noctua. Larus. Accipiter. Bubo. Mergulus. Ibis. Cygnus. Onocrotalus. Porphyrio. Herodio. Charadrius. Upupa. Vespertilio. Bruchus. Attacus. Ophiomachus. Locusta. Hutterus. Aquila. Gryphus. Haliaetus. Vultur. Miluus. Coruus. Struthio. Noctua. Larus. Cuculus. Nisus. Accipiter. Nycticorax. Mergulus. Bubo. Ibis. Porphyrio. Pelicanus. Onocrotalus. Cygnus. Ardea. Ciconia. Choradrius. Icterus. Galgulus. Upupa. Vespertilio.
units.tr: Various things occur in the Scriptures about these three kinds, which we will briefly pursue. First, in Exod. 14 and Lev. 11 the clean and unclean birds are listed, and the interpreters vary as follows. Vatablus: Eagle. Griffon. Sea-eagle. Vulture. Kite. Raven. Ostrich. Owl. Gull. Hawk. Night heron. Diver. Ibis. Purple gallinule. Pelican. Swan. Stork. Plover. Hoopoe. Bat. Locust. Attacus. Snake-killer. Bruchus. Junius: Eagle. Bone-breaker. Sea-eagle. Kite. Magpie. Raven. Screech-owl. Swallow. Hobby. Hawk. Owl. Merganser. Owl. Jackdaw. Spoonbill. Bee-eater. Stork. Heron. Attagen. Bat. Locust. Silkworm. Beetle. Cicada. The Vulgate version: Eagle. Griffon. Sea-eagle. Kite. Vulture. Ostrich. Owl. Gull. Hawk. Owl. Diver. Ibis. Swan. Pelican. Purple gallinule. Heron. Plover. Hoopoe. Bat. Bruchus. Attacus. Snake-killer. Locust. Hutterus: Eagle. Griffon. Sea-eagle. Vulture. Kite. Raven. Ostrich. Owl. Gull. Cuckoo. Sparrow-hawk. Hawk. Night heron. Diver. Owl. Ibis. Purple gallinule. Pelican. Pelican. Swan. Heron. Stork. Plover. Icterus. Galgulus. Hoopoe. Bat.

units.la: Ex his auibus aquila dicitur magna auis Ezech. 17. verf.3: Quem enim inter quadrupedes gradum obtinet leo, eūdem inter aues aquila. Ea nidulatur altissimo loco Iob. 39. v.30.31. nempe in saxis & petris Obad. v. 4. videt acutissimè & longissimè Iob. 39. verf.32.33. est auis perniciosissima. Thren. 4. v.19. volat altissimè. Esa. 40. v.30. in senectute renouatur Psal. 103.v.5. quoniam non deficit senio aut ægritudine, vt aliæ aues, sed semper, etiam in extremâ se-nectâ, nectâ, vegeta est. Tamen cùm superius rostrum itaaccrescat, vt aduncitas aperiri non possit, fame tandem perit, quia etsi ad tempus solo potu viuit, tandem tamen ne bibere quidem potest. Porrò aquila delectatur cadaueribus Matth. 24. v. 28. Eundem in modum veri Christiani delectantur morte Christi. Accipiter plumas nouas sumturus it versus Austrum propter æstum, vt est Iob. 39. v. 29. Bubo est auis nocturna, inauspicata, & solitaria. Psal. 102. v. 7. Esa. 13. & 34. Ciconia & Grus nôrunt sua tempora Ier. 8. v. 7. Columba est auis simplex, gemens perpetuò, gemitu placidissimo, non autem obmurmurante: est timida, petit alta tecta, tutò deponit ova, & parit latens, est candida. Matth. 10. v. 16. Esa. 38. v. 14. Psal. 55. v. 7. Cant. 2. v. 14. Ier. 48. v. 28. Corvus est ferum animal, & crudele in natos.
units.tr: Among these birds, the eagle is called a great bird, Ezek. 17, verse 3: for the rank the lion holds among quadrupeds, the eagle holds among birds. It nests in the highest place, Job 39, verses 30, 31, namely in rocks and crags, Obad. verse 4. It sees most sharply and from the greatest distance, Job 39, verses 32, 33; it is a most destructive bird. Lam. 4, verse 19; it flies very high, Isa. 40, verse 30. It is renewed in old age, Ps. 103, verse 5, because it does not fail with age or sickness as other birds do, but is always vigorous, even in extreme old age. Yet when its upper beak grows so curved that it cannot be opened, it at last perishes of hunger, since although for a time it lives on drink alone, in the end it cannot even drink. Moreover the eagle delights in carcasses, Matt. 24, verse 28. In the same way true Christians delight in the death of Christ. The hawk, about to take new feathers, goes towards the south because of the heat, as in Job 39, verse 29. The owl is a nocturnal bird, unlucky and solitary: Ps. 102, verse 7; Isa. 13 and 34. The stork and the crane know their seasons, Jer. 8, verse 7. The dove is a simple bird, moaning continually with a very placid moan, not with grumbling. It is timid, seeks high roofs, lays its eggs safely, and bears its young hidden away; it is white. Matt. 10, verse 16; Isa. 38, verse 14; Ps. 55, verse 7; Cant. 2, verse 14; Jer. 48, verse 28. The raven is a savage animal, and cruel towards its young.

units.la: Psal. 147. v. 9. Iob. 39. v. 3. Draco est fera auis, ex serpentū genere. Ier. 14. v. 6. Pauo alis exultat, & illâ coloris atque plumarum varietate, quæ in caudâ tanquam oculi quidâ fictitij elucet, Iob. 39. v. 16. Pelecanus, vel vt vulgo scribunt, pelicanus, est auis in defertis viuens. Psal. 102. v. 7. Dicitur sanguine suo effuso mederi pullorum cœcitati, atque ita est insignis Christi pro nobis morientis, & morte suâ nos redimentis, typus. Struthio pennas & plumas habet plurimas, & tamen omnibus hisce adiumentis propter molem corporis vix se potest è terrâ subleuare. Habitat in defertis. Est crudelis in fœtum. Nam cùm multa oua pariat, eorum partem in terrâ deserit, & reliquis incubat, quæ sentit fœcunda: ex infœcundis autem pastum præbet pullis suis. Vide de hâc aue Iob. 39. v. 16. Esa. 43. v. 20. Thren. 4. v. 3. Turtur est columbinæ h.e. puræ & simplicis naturæ, vnde in sacrificijs habuit visum, & est symbolum ecclesiæ. Leuit. 1. & 5. Cant. 1. v. 12. Vultur mortem & cadauera hominum sequitur, & eò congregatur, vbi acies sunt conflicturæ. Esa. 34. v. 15. Vlula, scopes, & similes aues, sunt deformes motu satyrico, tristes ob solitudinem loci, & horrificæ ob tempus nocturnum quo delectantur.
units.tr: Ps. 147, verse 9; Job 39, verse 3. The dragon is a wild bird, of the kind of serpents: Jer. 14, verse 6. The peacock exults in its wings and in that variety of colour and plumage which shines in its tail like certain artificial eyes: Job 39, verse 16. The pelican, or as it is commonly written, pelicanus, is a bird living in the deserts: Ps. 102, verse 7. It is said to heal the blindness of its young with its own shed blood, and so it is a notable type of Christ dying for us and redeeming us by his death. The ostrich has very many feathers and plumes, yet with all these aids it can scarcely raise itself from the ground because of the bulk of its body. It lives in the deserts. It is cruel to its offspring. For although it lays many eggs, it abandons part of them on the ground and sits on the rest, which it perceives to be fertile; but from the infertile ones it provides food for its chicks. See about this bird Job 39, verse 16; Isa. 43, verse 20; Lam. 4, verse 3. The turtle-dove is of dove-like, that is, pure and simple, nature, whence it had a place in the sacrifices, and it is a symbol of the Church: Lev. 1 and 5; Cant. 1, verse 12. The vulture follows death and human carcasses, and gathers where armies are about to clash: Isa. 34, verse 15. The screech-owl, the scops owl, and similar birds are deformed in their movement, satyr-like, sad from the solitude of their place and dreadful from the night-time in which they delight.
Isa. 13, verses 21, 22; ch. 14, verse 23; ch. 34, verses 11, 12, 13, 14; Jer. 50, verse 39.

units.la: Apes putantur nasci sine coitu. Ex cadauere leonis ortum est examen illud, de quo Iud. 14. v. 8.15. Examen apum est hieroglyphicum hostium ecclesiae. Psal. 118. v. 12. Cicadae & locustae quibusdam in locis sunt edules. Leuit. 11. verf. 22. Matth. 3. v. 4. vbi frustra sunt, qui ἀκρίδες & ἀκρόδρυα [?] confundunt, & existimant ἀκρίδες esse ἄκρα δένδρων [?], summitates ramorum in arboribus. Vide Casaubonum exercit. 13. sect. 7. 8. Per muscas, locustas, & similia animalcula Deus grauissima sua iudicia in homines, ac totas gentes, etiam potentissimas, saepenumero exercet. Exod. 8. & 10. Psal. 105. v.30. Ioel. 1. v. 4.
units.tr: Bees are thought to be born without coition. From the carcass of a lion arose that swarm of which Judg. 14, verses 8, 15 speaks. A swarm of bees is a hieroglyph of the enemies of the Church: Ps. 118, verse 12. Cicadas and locusts are edible in certain places: Lev. 11, verse 22. Matt. 3, verse 4, where those are wrong who confuse ἀκρίδες [akrides] and ἀκρόδρυα [akrodrya], and think that ἀκρίδες are ἄκρα δένδρων [akra dendron], the summits of branches on trees. See Casaubon, Exercitation 13, sections 7 and 8. Through flies, locusts and similar little creatures God often executes his most grievous judgements on men and on whole nations, even the most powerful: Exod. 8 and 10; Ps. 105, verse 30; Joel 1, verse 4.

units.la: I. Theriologia sacra est physica specialis de natura bestiarum terrestrium, ex Scripturis sumta.
units.tr: I. Sacred theriology is the special physics of the nature of terrestrial beasts, drawn from the Scriptures.

units.la: II. Bestiae terrestres sunt animalia ex terra condita, & in terra degentia. Ex terra, inquam, quae in iis praedominatur reliquis elementis. Genef. i. verf. 24.25.
units.tr: II. Terrestrial beasts are animals made from earth and living on earth. From earth, I say, which predominates in them over the other elements. Gen. 1, verses 24, 25.

units.la: III. Varia sunt genera bestiarum terrestrium. Ac primùm quidem Moses partitur eas in iumenta, reptilia, & bestias agri: Iumenta sunt, quae homini commoditatem adferunt. Itaque ab eo tractari possunt: velut boues, equi, oues, canes. Bestiae agri sunt ferae, quae procul ab hominum consortio fugiunt, vt leones, tigres, vrsi. Reptilia sunt serpentes terreni. Deinde bestiae terrestres sunt ruminantes, vel non: item vnguifidae, vel non Leuit. ii. Deut. 14. Cum hac partitione coincidit illa Aristotelis lib. 2. de hist. animal. cap. 1. Animantium aliae sunt πολυσχιδεῖς[?], pedibus multùm fissis, vt canis: aliae δισχιδεῖς[?], pedibus bifidatis, vt bos: aliae ἀσχιδεῖς[?], quas solipedes Plinius appellat, vt est equus. Quorum pedes sunt πολυσχιδεῖς[?], aut sunt imperfectissimae conditionis, aut rapacissimae: quorum pedes sunt solidi, ea perfectiorem habent naturam: quorum vero bifidati, ea quodam modo absunt à naturæ perfectione. Tertiò animalia terrestria sunt ζωοτόκα, viuipara, vt vacca: vel ὠοτόκα, ouipara, vt serpens. Quartò septem sunt classes siue ordines brutorum terrestrium. In prima classe sunt pecudes, quæ sub imperio hominis pabulum capiunt: vt bos, asinus, ouis, capra, sus domestica. In secunda classe sunt bellua, quæ sunt naturæ feræ, & sine hominis imperio in siluis & campis vagantur: vt leo, tigris. In tertia classe sunt bestiæ similes pecudibus, vt canis, felis. In quarta classe sunt bestiæ similes belluis, vt lepus, vulpes, cuniculus. In quinta classe sunt serpentes terrestres, vt aspis, vipera. In sexta classe sunt infecta terrestria, vt araneus, vermis. In septima classe sunt Zoophyta terrestria, vt arbor pudica, asthynomene herba.
units.tr: III. There are various kinds of terrestrial beasts. First, Moses divides them into cattle, reptiles and beasts of the field. Cattle are those that bring convenience to man, and so can be handled by him, such as oxen, horses, sheep and dogs. Beasts of the field are wild animals that flee far from human company, such as lions, tigers and bears. Reptiles are earthly serpents. Then terrestrial beasts are either ruminant or not, and likewise either cloven-hoofed or not: Lev. 11; Deut. 14. With this division coincides that of Aristotle, book 2 of the History of Animals, chapter 1: of animals, some are πολυσχιδεῖς [polyschides], with many-cleft feet, as the dog; others are δισχιδεῖς [dischides], with two-cleft feet, as the ox; others are ἀσχιδεῖς [aschides], which Pliny calls solipeds, as the horse. Those whose feet are polyschides are either of the most imperfect condition or the most rapacious; those whose feet are solid have a more perfect nature; but those whose feet are bifid are in some way removed from natural perfection. Third, terrestrial animals are either ζωοτόκα [zootoka], bearing live young, like the cow, or ὠοτόκα [oötoka], laying eggs, like the serpent. Fourth, there are seven classes or orders of terrestrial brutes. In the first class are the cattle, which take their fodder under man's rule, such as the ox, ass, sheep, goat and domestic pig. In the second class are the beasts of prey, which are wild by nature and wander in woods and fields without man's rule, such as the lion and tiger. In the third class are beasts similar to cattle, such as the dog and cat. In the fourth class are beasts similar to wild beasts, such as the hare, fox and rabbit. In the fifth class are terrestrial serpents, such as the asp and viper. In the sixth class are terrestrial insects, such as the spider and worm. In the seventh class are terrestrial zoophytes, such as the sensitive plant and the asthynomene herb.

units.la: Nunc perseguamur bestias terrestres, quarum Scriptura meminit. Elephas inter quadrupeda animalia est maximum. Itaque cum sit instar multorum animalium, Behemoth ab Hebræis appellatur terminatione plurali. Iob. 40. v. 10. Sunt qui crocodilum ibi putant intelligi.
units.tr: Now let us pursue the land animals that Scripture mentions. The elephant is the largest of the four-footed animals. Since it is like many animals together, Behemoth is called by the Hebrews by a plural ending. Job 40:10. Some think the crocodile is meant here.

units.la: Equus est animal robustum, impauidum, militare, velox, docile, placidum, ac hominis, inprimis autem domini sui, manu & consuetudine gaudens, eiusque affectus pene intelligens. Eius natura pulcherrimè descripta est Iob. 39. v. 19. & seqq. Leo est animal superbum, ferox, clemens in supplices, generosum, forte. Iob. 39. v. 1. Psal. 104. v. 21. Est veluti rex terrestrium animalium.
units.tr: The horse is a robust, fearless, warlike, swift, teachable, gentle animal, which delights in the hand and companionship of man, and especially of its master, and almost understands his feelings. Its nature is most beautifully described in Job 39:19 and following. The lion is a proud, fierce, yet merciful toward suppliants, noble and strong animal. Job 39:1; Psalm 104:21. It is, as it were, the king of the land animals.

units.la: Lupus est animal vorax, maximè autem lupus vespertinus. Hab. 1. verf. 8. Ier. 5. v. 6. Onager in desertis habitat, & ferus admodum est. Iob. 24. v. 5. c. 39. v. 8. Ier. 2. v. 24. Dan. 5. v. 21. Hos. 8. v. 9. Mulorum & mularum visus in Iudæa fuit frequentissimus, vti & hodie est in Syria. Hoc vecturæ & equitationis genere etiam reges ipsi vtebantur 2. Reg. 8. Mulas alibi gentium quàm in Iudæa steriles esse scribunt: sed in Iudæa admodum fœcundas.
units.tr: The wolf is a voracious animal, especially the evening wolf. Habakkuk 1:8; Jeremiah 5:6. The wild ass lives in the deserts and is very untamed. Job 24:5; 39:8; Jeremiah 2:24; Daniel 5:21; Hosea 8:9. Mules and she-mules were very common in Judea, as they are still today in Syria. Kings themselves used this kind of conveyance and riding. 2 Kings 8. Writers say that mules elsewhere in the world are barren, but in Judea they are very fruitful.

units.la: Vulpes vineas maximè laedit. Cant. 2. v. 15. est animal valde astutum & dolosum. Luc. 13. v. 32. Aper depopulatur vites Psal. 80. v. 14. Canis est animal fidele, industrium, & homini familiare: sed propter libidinem in Scripturis est animal turpe, fœdum & minimi pretij. Deut. 23.v.18. Psal.22.v.17. 21. Matth.7.v.6. 2. Petr.2.v. 21. Phil.3.v.2. Apoc.22.vers.15. Ceruus est animal timidissimum, quod sitibundum aquas etiam cum clamore & barritu inuestigat diligentissimè & pertinacissime. Psal.29.v.9. & 42.v.1. Cerua parit fœtus suos difficillimè ac ægerrimè. Iob.39.vers.5.6. Sus est animal fœdum. Leuit.11. Matth.7.vers.6. 2. Petr.2.vers.21. Apoc.22.v.15. Camelus & Lepus Leuit.11. numerantur in animalibus immundis. Serpens est animal à Deo maledictum, & pœnæ fugæque perpetuò addictum, ac etiam vniuerso hominum generi infestissimum & inimicissimum redditum. Gen.3.vers.14. Psal.91.vers.14. Esa.19.vers.5. Itaque perpetuò quærit latebras, fugitque ab homine. Est tamen hoc ipsum animal astutissimum, & sibi prospicientissimum. Ideo Christus iubet nos imitari prospicientiam & prudentiam serpentum Matth.10.
units.tr: The fox does the greatest harm to vineyards. Song of Solomon 2:15. It is a very crafty and deceitful animal. Luke 13:32. The wild boar lays waste the vines. Psalm 80:14. The dog is a faithful, diligent animal, familiar with man; but because of its lust it is, in the Scriptures, a shameful, foul animal of little worth. Deuteronomy 23:18; Psalm 22:17, 21; Matthew 7:6; 2 Peter 2:21; Philippians 3:2; Revelation 22:15. The stag is a very timid animal, which, thirsting, seeks out water even with a cry and bellowing, most diligently and most persistently. Psalm 29:9; 42:1. The hind bears her young with the greatest difficulty and pain. Job 39:5, 6. The pig is a foul animal. Leviticus 11; Matthew 7:6; 2 Peter 2:21; Revelation 22:15. The camel and the hare Leviticus 11 are counted among the unclean animals. The serpent is an animal cursed by God, condemned forever to punishment and flight, and made most hostile and most inimical to the whole human race. Genesis 3:14; Psalm 91:14; Isaiah 19:5. Therefore it always seeks hiding places and flees from man. Yet this very animal is most crafty and most provident for itself. Therefore Christ bids us imitate the foresight and prudence of serpents. Matthew 10.

units.la: I. ANthropologia sacra est physica specialis de natura hominis, ex S. literis collecta. Hæc ultimum obtinet locum inter partes physicæ nō dignitate, sed ordine naturæ. Sicut enim homo creatus est postremo loco, tanquam finis & compendium omnium creaturarum: ita tractatio physica de homine merito colophonem addit reliquis physicæ partibus.
units.tr: I. Sacred anthropology is the special physics of the nature of man, gathered from the Holy Scriptures. It holds the last place among the parts of physics, not by dignity but by the order of nature. For just as man was created last, as the end and summary of all creatures, so the physical treatment of man rightly adds the crowning touch to the other parts of physics.

units.la: II. Homo est animal creatum ad imaginem Dei. Hæc est prærogativa hominis præ reliquis creaturis visibilibus. Gen. 1. v. 27.
units.tr: II. Man is an animal created in the image of God. This is the prerogative of man above the other visible creatures. Genesis 1:27.

units.la: III. In homine considerantur partes & sexus.
units.tr: III. In man, the parts and the sexes are considered.

units.la: IV. Partes hominis sunt duæ: corpus organicum, & anima intelligens. Utraq; fuit condita ad imaginem Dei. Nam in animæ substantiā[?] fuit spiritualis simsimplicitas & immortalitas; in intellectu fuit eximia sapientia;in voluntate sanctitas,& libertas a coactione,seruitute, & miseria; in corpore pulcherrima temperies & relatio siue κρᾶσις[?] ad animam; in toto deniq; compositô, maiestas imperatoria. Sed videamus distincte vtramque hominis partem. Anima hominis fuit a Deo inspirata Gen. 2. v. 7. Et haec proprie est ψυχὴ[?]. Corpus hominis primi fuit formatum ex rubra terra. ibid. secundi, ex costa ibid. v.21. Et haec proprie est πλάσις[?], id est, figuratio siue figularis factura: qua ratione commendatur opificij diuini in creando homine admirabilitas. Animae itaque origo est coelestis, corporis, terrestris. Sed, inquis, cur Moses non fecit mentionem spiritus: cum homo constet ex corpore, animâ & spiritu 1. Thess. 5. v. 22? Resp. Spiritus continetur sub nomine animae, cuius natura est spiritualis iure creationis & redemtionis, vitio autem nostro fit corporalis & bestialis,quando seruimus peccato,& fimus canes atq; porci. Quomodo corpora nostra formentur ex sanguine, docet Iob. c. 10. v. 10. 11. Caeterum anima est vna τῇ οὐσίᾳ, sed multiplex τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ[?]: quod quidem est signum perfectionis. Nam quò quid magis est vnum, eò est perfectius in agendo, & quidem ita,vt plurima possit agere. Sic anima nostra intelligit, vult, regit corpus & singula ipsius membra, meminit, numerat, inuenit, disponit, apprehendit, componit, diuidit, discurrit, mensurat, & alia innumera praestat. Corporis ratio est alia. Illud siquidem instructum est multis & diuersis organis, quae ad certas operationes sunt destinata. Sic oculus ad videndum, aurisad audiendum &c. propendet suâ natura,vt merito dixerit Aristoteles, Oculus est quifacit operationes oculi. No possum quin hoc loco inseram elegantissimâ illam allegoriam,quaSalomon depingit membra corporis humani & quaedam hominis accidentia. Eccl. 12. v. 5.6.7.8. Brachia vocat custodes domus,i.e. corporis,in quo anima tanquin domo habitat. Hanc domum custodiunt brachia. Crura nominat viros robustos: quia corpus gestant, robore suo sustinent. Dentes appellat molitrices, quia cibum quasi molunt, id est, mandunt. Oculos vocat eos qui spectant per fenestras, id est, per foramina, quibus inclusi sunt. Abstinentiam a cibo duriore vocat occlusionem valuarum in plateam vergentium, id est, labiorum. Nam sunt etiam valuae, quae in corpore hominis latent, ut est operculum gulae & vesiculae fellis. Exilis sonus mala est impotentia madendi. Canitiem vocat florentem amygdalum. Curvitatem dorsi vocat onerationem loquutae: quia dorsum refert speciem loquutae. Medullam vocat funem argenteum: quia medulla in spina dorsi habet speciem funis, & alba est ut argentum. Meningem, id est, membranulam seu peliculam in qua situm est cerebrum, vocat lenticulam vel phialam auream. Venas mesaraicas iuxta hepar sitas vocat hydriam ad scatebram, quia ex hepate tanquam e scatebra hauriunt succum sanguineum, eumque in sanguinem perfectum commutant. Pulmones vocat rotam ad cisternam; quia sicut rota ad cisternam vel puteum nunc demittit, nunc attrahit hydriam, ita pulmo continuo motu halitum nunc attrahit, nunc repellit. Corpus hominis appellat puluerem, quia ex puluere initio est formatum. Spiritus rediens ad Deum, qui dedit illum, est anima, quam Deus ad se recipit, cum homo moritur. Sic autem Deus recipit animam hominis, ut receptam tradat vel angelis sanctis, ut eam portent in cœlum, si homo fuerit pius: aut malis spiritibus, ut eam portent in gehennam, si homo fuerit impius.
units.tr: IV. The parts of man are two: the organic body and the intelligent soul. Both were fashioned in the image of God. For in the substance of the soul there was spiritual simplicity and immortality; in the intellect there was outstanding wisdom; in the will there was holiness, and freedom from compulsion, servitude and misery; in the body there was the most beautiful temperament and proportion [κρᾶσις] to the soul; and finally, in the whole composite there was imperial majesty. But let us look at each part of man separately. The soul of man was breathed into him by God. Genesis 2:7. And this is properly the soul [ψυχή]. The body of the first man was formed from red earth, and that of the second from a rib. Ibid. Genesis 2:21. And this is properly the moulding [πλάσις], that is, shaping or potter's work; by which the wonderful skill of the divine workmanship in creating man is commended. The origin of the soul, then, is heavenly; of the body, earthly. But, you will say, why did Moses make no mention of the spirit, since man consists of body, soul and spirit, 1 Thessalonians 5:22? I reply: the spirit is contained under the name of soul, whose nature is spiritual by right of creation and redemption, but by our fault it becomes corporeal and bestial when we serve sin and become dogs and swine. How our bodies are formed from blood, Job 10:10, 11 teaches. Moreover, the soul is one in its essence [οὐσία], but many in its activity [ἐνέργεια]; which indeed is a sign of perfection. For the more a thing is one, the more perfect it is in acting, and indeed it can perform very many actions. So our soul understands, wills, rules the body and each of its members, remembers, counts, discovers, arranges, grasps, composes, divides, runs through, measures, and performs countless other tasks. The nature of the body is different. For it is equipped with many and diverse organs, which are destined for certain operations. So the eye, by its nature, is inclined to seeing, the ear to hearing, and so on; so that Aristotle rightly said: The eye is that which performs the operations of the eye. I cannot help inserting here that most elegant allegory in which Solomon depicts the members of the human body and certain accidents of man. Ecclesiastes 12:5, 6, 7, 8. He calls the arms the keepers of the house, that is, of the body, in which the soul dwells as in a house. The arms guard this house. He names the legs strong men, because they carry the body and sustain it by their strength. He calls the teeth grinders, because they grind the food, that is, chew it. He calls the eyes those that look out through the windows, that is, through the openings in which they are enclosed. He calls abstinence from harder food the closing of the doors that face the street, that is, of the lips. For there are also doors that lie hidden in the human body, such as the lid of the gullet and of the gall bladder. The faint sound he calls the inability to grind. He calls grey hair the blossoming almond. He calls the bending of the back the burden of the almond tree, because the back resembles the shape of an almond tree. He calls the marrow the silver cord, because the marrow in the spine has the appearance of a cord and is white like silver. The membrane, that is, the little skin or film in which the brain is situated, he calls the golden bowl or phial. The mesenteric veins, situated near the liver, he calls the pitcher at the spring, because from the liver, as from a spring, they draw the juice of blood and change it into perfect blood. He calls the lungs the wheel at the cistern; because just as a wheel at a cistern or well now lowers and now draws up the pitcher, so the lung with continual motion now draws in breath and now expels it. He calls the body of man dust, because at the beginning it was formed from dust. The spirit returning to God who gave it is the soul, which God takes back to himself when man dies. God receives the soul of man in such a way that, once received, he entrusts it either to holy angels, to carry it to heaven if the man was pious, or to evil spirits, to carry it to hell if the man was impious.

units.la: V. Sexus hominis est masculinus, vel fœmininus. Uterque est factus ad imaginem Dei Gen. 1. v. 27. sed ille est potior, hic sequior. 1. Cor. 11. v. 7. & hic est ex illo, & propter illum. Ubi diligenter obseruandum est physicis practicis, quomodo in ipsorum opere ex mare sumatur fœmina. Sicut enim in prima creatione hominis Deus Euam formauit ex Adamo, atque ita ex uno sanguine omne hominum genus produxit Act. 17. v. 26. ita necesse est, vt physicus practicus ex subiecto suo catholico faciat haec duo, marem & foeminam, per debitam separationem.
units.tr: V. The sex of man is either masculine or feminine. Both were made in the image of God, Genesis 1:27, but the one is the more excellent, the other the inferior. 1 Corinthians 11:7; and the one is from the other, and for the sake of the other. Here practical physicians must carefully observe how, in their own work, the woman is taken out of the man. For just as in the first creation of man God formed Eve from Adam, and thus produced the whole human race from one blood, Acts 17:26, so it is necessary that the practical physician, from his universal subject, make these two, male and female, by due separation.

units.la: COSMOLOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: COSMOLOGIA SACRA.

units.la: I. Cosmologia sacra est pars physicae de natura mundi, petita ex sacris literis.
units.tr: I. Sacred cosmology is the part of physics concerning the nature of the world, drawn from the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: II. Mundus est systema ex coelo & terra, & quae his continentur, pulcherrime constans. Haec definitio sumta est ex Gen. 1. v. 1. Et ita quidem vox mundi sumitur generaliter pro tota rerum creatarum vniuersitate: quo pertinet illa appellatio mundi apud Aristotelem, τὸ πᾶν [?] τὸ ὅλον. Specialiter etiam accipitur nunc pro terra 2. Pet. 3. v. 6. Ioh. 1. v. 9. nunc pro [illegible, ~6 letters] & depravatione, quae per peccatum introducta est in hunc mundum inferiorem 1. Ioh. 2. v. 16. nunc pro ipsis hominibus, iisque vel omnibus Rom. 5. v. 12. vel fidelibus Ioh. 3. v. 16. c. 17. v. 23. 24. vel infidelibus Ioh. 1. v. 10. 1. Ioh. 5. v. 19. Prima, eaque generalissima significatio, huius est loci.
units.tr: II. The world is a system, most beautifully constituted, of heaven and earth and the things contained in them. This definition is taken from Gen. 1. v. 1. The word "world" is used generally for the whole universe of created things, to which belongs Aristotle's expression for the world, "the all, the whole" [τὸ πᾶν, τὸ ὅλον]. It is also taken in a narrower sense: sometimes for the earth (2 Pet. 3. v. 6; John 1. v. 9); sometimes for [illegible] and the corruption introduced into this lower world by sin (1 John 2. v. 16); sometimes for the people themselves, either all of them (Rom. 5. v. 12), or the faithful (John 3. v. 16; 17. v. 23, 24), or the unbelieving (John 1. v. 10; 1 John 5. v. 19). The first and most general meaning is the one of this place.

units.la: III. In mundo spectantur principia & affec- tiones.
units.tr: III. In the world we observe principles and affections.

units.la: IV. Principia mundi sunt externa, vel interna. Principia externa sunt efficiens & finis, interna, materia & forma. Efficiens mundi est solus Deus, Pater, Filius & Spiritus sanctus. Gen. 1. v. 1. Pfal. 33. v. 6. & 104. v. 30. Iob. 9. v. 8. Ioh. 1. v. 3. 1. Cor. 8. v. 6. Hebr. 1. v. 2. Est, inquam, efficiens tum procreans, tum conseruans. Procreans; quia omnia produxit, & quidem partim per κτίσιν [?], i. e. creationem ex nihilo; partim per ποίησιν [?], id est, facturam; partim per πλάσιν [?], id est, figurationem. Primo modo creauit angelos, coelum, terram & animam hominis: secundo, herbas, stellas, aues, pisces & bestias terrestres: tertio, corpus Adami & Euae. Gen. 1. & 2. Deinde Deus est causa mundi efficiens conseruans; quia omnia à se condita sustinet ac veluti portat, virésque ipsis inditas stabilitatque fouet. Psal. 104. Act. 17. Heb. 1. Huc pertinet generatio rerum sublunarium, cuius fundamentum est vox illa Dei imperatoria Gen. 1. Proferat terra herbas: Aquæ progignunt reptilia: Fœtificate, ac augescite, & implete aquas per maria, & volucres augescunt in terra: Producat terra animantia: Fœtificate, ac augescite, & implete terram, eamque subiicite. Atque hæc est Natura omnibus rebus creatis implantata, ita ut illa nihil sit aliud, quàm vis ordinaria, quâ Deus instruxit singulas res à se conditas. 1. Cor. 11 v. 14. Rom. 2. v. 14. Finis mundi est principalis vel minùs principalis. Finis principalis & præcipuus est Deus ipse, hoc est, gloria, ipsius. Prov. 16. v. 4. Rom. 1. v. 20. Iob. 36. v. 24. Conditus ig. est hic mundus, ut sit typus visibilis Dei invisibilis, speculum nempe sapientiæ, bonitatis & potentiæ ipsius, in quo maiestatem eius contemplemur, admiremur, & deprædicemus. Finis minùs principalis & non-præcipuus est homo, & is quidem vel quilibet, vel fidelis tantùm. Unde hic finis est generalis vel specialis. Finis itaque generalis est, quiad omnes in universum homines pertinet: estque vsus omnium hominum, & is quidem partim immediatus, partim mediatus. Nam mundus & res in eo comprehensæ sunt homini vtiles vel immediate, vel mediate. Immediate res omnes homini sunt vtiles, quantum ad corpus & animum. Quantum ad corpus, res naturales conducunt homini ad nutritionem, vel medicinam, vel defensionem, eaque vel singula, vel universa. Et quamuis plurima sint, quorum vsus nos latet, siue id fiat originali, siue affectata ignorantia: tamen ex hac nostra inscitia nō tollitur rerum vtilitas, quam illæ habent vi creationis. Quantum ad animum attinet, mūdus est schola illustris, quæ 1. nos instituit de æternitate, sapientiâ, potentiâ, & bonitate opificis. Psal. 8. & 19. Rom. 1. 2. facit ad excitandum in nobis fiduciam in Deum, item amorem, & timorem eius Psal. 146. v. 5. 6. 3. facit ad oblectationem animi. 4. affert varias consolationes. Nam Deus, qui creauit hunc mundum, potest nobis opem ferre in omnibus noftris calamitatibus, publicis & priuatis, magnis & paruis* Ier. 10. v. 10. 11.c. 45. v. 2. 3. 4. 5. Atque hæc pædagogia naturalis nobis non est contemnenda, ne primum symboli articulum videamur velle ignorare. Mediatè res creatæ homini inseruiunt, quatenus vel sunt pœnæ, quibus corrigimur, castigamur & emendamur: vel rectè præparantur, vt nobis præstent vsum salutarem, quomodo videmus venena, & alia, quæ vulgo inutilia putantur, adhibitis præparationibus conuenientibus singularem adferre vtilitatem. Specialis finis mundi est peculiaris & proprius ecclesiæ seu cœtui fidelium. Est enim creatus mundus, vt fit domicilium & hospitium ecclesiæ, quæ in hac domo ad tempus commoretur, eâque iure quodam proprio vtatur. Materia mundi est cœlum & terra, in quibus innumeræ creaturæ continentur, ex quibus mundus constat tanquam ex partibus integralibus: quomodo videmus corpus humanum constare ex variis membris. Quemadmodum autem ex membris corporis nostri deciditur femen: ita ex cœlo & terrâ oriuntur omnia omnium rerum naturalium femina, quæ per debitam putrefactionem eo rediguntur, vt ex iis nascantur corpora glorificata: vnde putrefactio non fine causâ appellatur clauis naturæ & artis. Vide Iohan. 12. v. 24. & 1. Cor. 15. v. 36. 37. 38. 42. 43. 46. Quibus verbis continetur legitima præparatio materiæ physicæ. Forma mundi est inimitabilis illa dispositio partium, quæ Græcis dicitur διακοσμησις [?]. Hæc est catena Homeri aurea, per quam fit, vt omnes res totius mundi fœdere quodam inter fe fe deuinciantur, & reciprocâ actione & passione nihil non efficiant, quod ad mundi decus pertinet. Hæc forma Gen. 1. comprehenditur sub nomine bonitatis, quâ omnia à Deo creata dicuntur suisfe prædita. Bonitas siquidem illa fuit in substantiâ, facultatibus & actionibus rerum creatarum, adeoque in ipsa-rum rum forma, vtpote sine qua neque οὐσία[?], neque δύναμις[?], neque ἐνέργεια vlla esse potest in rebus creatis.
units.tr: IV. The principles of the world are either external or internal. The external principles are the efficient and the final cause; the internal are the matter and the form. The efficient cause of the world is God alone: Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Gen. 1. v. 1; Ps. 33. v. 6; 104. v. 30; Job 9. v. 8; John 1. v. 3; 1 Cor. 8. v. 6; Heb. 1. v. 2). He is, I say, the efficient cause both creating and preserving. He is creating because he has produced all things, and indeed partly by creation [κτίσιν], that is, creation out of nothing; partly by making [ποίησιν], that is, fashioning; partly by forming [πλάσιν], that is, shaping. By the first mode he created the angels, the heavens, the earth and the soul of man; by the second, the herbs, stars, birds, fishes and land animals; by the third, the body of Adam and of Eve (Gen. 1 and 2). Then God is the efficient cause of the world by preserving, because he sustains and, as it were, carries all the things made by him, and cherishes the powers implanted in them and keeps them steady (Ps. 104; Acts 17; Heb. 1). To this belongs the generation of things below the moon, whose foundation is that imperative word of God in Gen. 1: Let the earth bring forth grass; let the waters bring forth creeping things; be fruitful and multiply, and fill the waters in the seas, and let the birds multiply on the earth; let the earth bring forth living creatures; be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth and subdue it. And this is Nature, implanted in all created things, so that nature is nothing other than the ordinary power by which God has equipped each thing he has made (1 Cor. 11. v. 14; Rom. 2. v. 14).
