The end of the world is either principal or less principal. The principal and chief end is God himself, that is, his glory (Prov. 16. v. 4; Rom. 1. v. 20; Job 36. v. 24). Therefore this world was made so that it should be a visible type of the invisible God, a mirror, namely, of his wisdom, goodness and power, in which we may contemplate, admire and proclaim his majesty. The less principal and non-chief end is man, and that either every man or the faithful only. Hence this end is either general or special. The general end concerns all men in general, and is the use of all men, and this use is partly immediate, partly mediate. For the world and the things comprised in it are useful to man, either immediately or mediately. Immediately, all things are useful to man as regards body and mind. As regards the body, natural things serve man for nourishment, or medicine, or defence, and these either singly or collectively. And although there are very many whose use escapes us, whether this comes from original ignorance or from affected ignorance, yet this our unskilfulness does not take away the usefulness which those things have by virtue of creation. As regards the mind, the world is an illustrious school which (1) teaches us about the eternity, wisdom, power and goodness of the Maker (Ps. 8 and 19; Rom. 1 and 2); (2) serves to arouse in us trust in God, and likewise love and fear of him (Ps. 146. v. 5, 6); (3) serves to delight the mind; (4) brings various consolations. For God, who created this world, can bring us help in all our calamities, public and private, great and small (Jer. 10. v. 10, 11; 45. v. 2, 3, 4, 5). And this natural pedagogy is not to be despised by us, lest we seem to wish to ignore the first article of the creed. Mediately, created things serve man insofar as they are either punishments by which we are corrected, chastised and amended, or are rightly prepared so as to afford us a salutary use, as we see poisons and other things commonly thought useless, when suitable preparations are applied, bring a singular usefulness. The special end of the world is peculiar and proper to the Church, or the assembly of the faithful. For the world has been created to be the dwelling and lodging of the Church, which for a time sojourns in this house and enjoys it by a certain proper right. The matter of the world is heaven and earth, in which innumerable creatures are contained, and out of which the world consists as out of integral parts, just as we see the human body consists of various members. And just as seed is shed from the members of our body, so out of heaven and earth arise all the seeds of all natural things, which through due putrefaction are brought to the point that bodies glorified come forth from them; whence putrefaction is not without cause called the key of nature and of art (see John 12. v. 24; 1 Cor. 15. v. 36, 37, 38, 42, 43, 46). In these words is contained the lawful preparation of physical matter. The form of the world is that inimitable arrangement of parts which the Greeks call the ordering [διακόσμησις]. This is Homer's golden chain, by which it comes about that all the things of the whole world are bound together by a certain covenant, and by reciprocal action and passion effect nothing that does not pertain to the beauty of the world. This form is comprehended in Gen. 1 under the name of goodness, by which all things created by God are said to have been endowed. For that goodness was in the substance, faculties and actions of created things, and so in their very form, since without it no essence [οὐσία], no power [δύναμις] and no activity [ἐνέργεια] can exist in created things.

units.la: V. Affectiones mundi referuntur ad quantitatem, vel qua itatem ipsius.
units.tr: V. The affections of the world are referred either to its quantity or to its quality.

units.la: VI. Affectiones mundi ratione quantitatis referuntur ad quantitatem discretam, vel continuam. Ibi est unitas: hic finitas.
units.tr: VI. The affections of the world, with respect to quantity, are referred either to discrete or to continuous quantity. To the former belongs unity; to the latter, finitude.

units.la: VII. Unitas mundi est, qua non sunt plures mundi, sed unicus tantum. Ille nempe, cuius Scriptura passim meminit. Ioh. 1. & 3. Iob. 28. verf. 24. Act. 17. verf. 24. Valeant itaque somnia illorum, qui mundos infinitos fabricarunt.
units.tr: VII. The unity of the world is that by which there are not several worlds but only one. This is the one of which Scripture makes mention everywhere (John 1 and 3; Job 28. v. 24; Acts 17. v. 24). Let, therefore, the dreams of those who have fabricated infinite worlds be of no account.

units.la: VIII. Finitas mundi est, qua ille finitur & circumscribitur terminis essentiae suae, ita ut sit in loco & tempore. Mundum esse finitum sic patet. Solus creator est infinitus, & omnis creatura est finita. Deinde plura infinita esse non possunt. Denique mundus constat ex partibus [?]finitis. Ex quibus efficitur mundum revera & in se esse finitum, ut nobis videatur infinitus. Quod si stupenda haec moles cum Deo conferatur, vix aliquam notabilem habebit magnitudinē. Sic enim terra cum coelo collata instar puncti est, sane mundus cum Deo comparatus erit aliquid puncto minus. Vide Esa. 40. v. 12.
units.tr: VIII. The finitude of the world is that by which it is bounded and circumscribed by the limits of its being, so that it exists in place and time. That the world is finite is shown thus. Only the Creator is infinite, and every creature is finite. Further, several infinites cannot exist. Finally, the world consists of finite parts. From which it follows that the world is in truth and in itself finite, though it may seem infinite to us. But if this stupendous mass is compared with God, it will have scarcely any notable magnitude. For earth compared with heaven is like a point; surely the world compared with God will be something less than a point. See Isa. 40. v. 12.

units.la: Porro finitas mundi cernitur in loco & tempore. Locus est, ubi aliquid consistit, sive in quo est locatum: estque universalis, vel particularis. Locus universalis est, in quo hic mundus est a Deo collocatus, cum ante in eo nihil esset. Locus particularis est, in quo collocatae sunt res in mundo comprehensae. Sic stellae, herbae, homines, & res similes habent locum suum particularem. Proprietates loci sunt, rem locatam conseruare, illamque magnetica vi ad se trahere, & in sinu suo suaviter continere, ut ibi quiescat. Hinc est, quod terra in suo loco manet, quod stellae in coelo mouentur, quod pisces extra aquam degere non possunt. Porrò locus rei est vel apparens, vel verus. De loco terræ apparente, accipiendus est locus Psal. 104. v.5. Fundauit terram super bases eius, ne dimoueatur in seculum & perpetuum.. Quænam amabo sunt istæ bases? Respondet Psalmus 24. v. 2. Namq; ipse super maria fundauit eam, & super flumina stabiliuit illam, hoc est, Deus ita statuit terram, vt depulsis in suos alueos maribus & fluentis, supra extet, ita vt aquæ sint veluti statumina, quibus latera eius circumquaque fulciuntur. Et Exod. 20. verf.4. disertè dicuntur aquæ esse sub terrâ. Aquæ itaque sunt locus terræ apparens. Locus verus est spatium illud, in quo terra cum aquis est à Deo collocata; quod quidem spatium philosophi appellant imaginarium, non quòd non sit ens reale, sed quòd imaginatione tantùm à nobis comprehendatur. Tempus est duratio, notabili momentorum successione constans: vnde Scaligero eleganter dicitur nunc fluens, sicut locus eidem dicitur vbi continuatum. De successione temporis & immobili statu æternitatis loquitur Psalmus 102. v.27.28.
units.tr: Moreover, the finitude of the world is seen in place and time. Place is where something exists, or the space in which a thing is located. It is either universal or particular. The universal place is that in which this world was set by God, since before that there was nothing in it. The particular place is that in which the things contained in the world are located. Thus the stars, plants, men and similar things each have their own particular place. The properties of place are to keep the located thing, to draw it to itself by a magnetic force, and to hold it gently in its bosom so that it rests there. Hence the earth stays in its place, the stars move in the heavens, and fish cannot live out of water. Further, the place of a thing is either apparent or true. The apparent place of the earth is what is meant by Psal. 104. v.5. He laid the earth upon its foundations, that it should not be removed for ever and ever. What, I ask, are these foundations? Psalm 24. v. 2 answers: For he has founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the rivers. That is, God so set the earth that, with the seas and streams driven into their channels, it stands up above them, so that the waters are like props by which its sides are supported on every side. And Exod. 20. v.4 plainly says that waters lie under the earth. The waters, therefore, are the apparent place of the earth. The true place is that space in which God set the earth together with the waters; philosophers call this space imaginary, not because it is not a real being, but because we grasp it only by the imagination. Time is duration consisting of a noticeable succession of moments; hence Scaliger neatly calls it a flowing now, just as place is called by him a continuous where. Psalm 102. v.27, 28 speaks of the succession of time and of the unchanging state of eternity.

units.la: IX. Affectiones mundi [illegible, ~4 letters]ione qualitatis concernunt qualitatem internam, vel externam. Ibi sunt vita & plenitudo mundi. hic figura & duratio eiusdem.
units.tr: IX. The affections of the world ... concern its internal or external quality. Here belong its life and fullness; there its figure and duration.

units.la: X. Vita mundi est virtus toti mundo rebusque omnibus à Deo in primâ creatione indita. Philosophis secretioribus dicitur anima & spiritus mundi. De hac vitâ loquitur Scriptura Gen. 1. verf. 11. Herbascat terra herbulas sementantes semen, arbores fructiferas edentes fructum in species suas. Confer cum verf. 12. 20. 22. 23. & 28. eiusdem capitis. Insignis hanc in sententiam est locus Nehem. 9. v.6. quem Vatablus rectè ita vertit. Tues â Iehoua solus, tu fecisti cœlum, cœlum cœlorum, & omnem exercitum eorum: terram & omnia quæ sunt in eâ: maria, & vniuersa quæ sunt in eis: viuificas quoque omnia hæc, [?]מחיה את כלםq. d. tu vitalem quandam facultatem omnibus à re creatis communicas, largiendo videl. spiritum, qui omnia reddit vegeta. Et sane nisi vita siue virtute illa vitali essent praeditae creaturae, de illis non potuisset dici, quod fuerint valde bonae. Gen. 1. Neque enim bonum fuerit, quod omni vitali energia est destitutum. Recte itaque Trismegistus pronuntiat in Poemandro: Spiritu agitatur & gubernatur omnia in mundo species[?]. Spiritus implet omnia. Et ibidem: Spiritu ministrantur omnia & vegetantur in mundo. Huc respexit Plato, quando dixit totum mundum esse animatum. Et Aristoteles 2. de generat. c. 3. recte obseruat, spiritum quendam in semine omnium esse, qui proportionem habet cum elemento stellarum. Clarius hoc ipsum indicat Theophrastus 2. de causis plant. vbi omnia illa corpora, in quibus facultates sunt, ἔμψυχα[?], h.e. vitalia appellat. Et Galenus de methodo medendi asserit vitam (late acceptam) nihil aliud esse quam vires ipsas, aut virium actiones. Quare cum mundus totus sit virtute praeditus eximia, non video quo iure vita ipsi denegari possit. Haec vita est quinta illa essentia, siue balsamus & mumia naturae, in qua praecipua cuiusque rei vis continetur, quaeque ex omnibus rebus corporeis certo quodam artificio elici potest. Ea vero neque est animae vegetatiuae, neque sensitiuae portio, sed superioris cuiusdam virtutis ζωτικῆς καὶ ἐνεργητικῆς[?], quae est spiritus & anima mundi communis, de quibus poeta Aeneid. 6. ita canit:
units.tr: X. The life of the world is the power that God impressed on the whole world and on all things at the first creation. To the more secret philosophers it is called the soul and spirit of the world. Scripture speaks of this life in Gen. 1. v. 11. Let the earth bring forth grass, herbs yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind. Compare vv. 12, 20, 22, 23 and 28 of the same chapter. A notable passage to this effect is Neh. 9. v.6, which Vatablus rightly renders thus: Thou, O Lord, alone; thou hast made heaven, the heaven of heavens, and all their host; the earth and all that is in it; the seas and all that is in them; and thou givest life to all these [מחיה את כלם], that is, you impart to all created things a certain vital faculty, namely by bestowing the spirit that makes all things living. And indeed, unless the creatures were endowed with life or a vital power, it could not have been said of them that they were very good (Gen. 1). For that which is destitute of all vital energy would not be good. Rightly, therefore, Trismegistus says in the Poimandres: All the forms in the world are moved and governed by spirit. Spirit fills all things. And in the same place: All things in the world are ministered and quickened by spirit. Plato had this in view when he said that the whole world is animated. And Aristotle, On Generation 2, ch. 3, rightly observes that there is a certain spirit in the seed of all things, which has a proportion to the element of the stars. Theophrastus indicates the same more clearly in On the Causes of Plants 2, where he calls all those bodies in which there are powers animated [ἔμψυχα], that is, living. And Galen, On the Method of Healing, asserts that life (taken broadly) is nothing other than the powers themselves, or the actions of the powers. Therefore, since the whole world is endowed with outstanding power, I do not see by what right life can be denied to it. This life is that fifth essence, or the balsam and mummy of nature, in which the principal power of each thing is contained, and which can be drawn out of all corporeal things by a certain art. It is neither a part of the vegetative nor of the sensitive soul, but of a higher power, vital and active [ζωτικῆς καὶ ἐνεργητικῆς], which is the common spirit and soul of the world. The poet in the Aeneid 6 sings of these things thus:

units.la: Principio cœlum ac terras, camposque liquentes, Lucentemque globum lunæ, Titaniaque astra Spiritus intus alit: totamque infusa per artus Mens agitat molem, & magno se corpore miscet. Inde hominum pecudumque genus vitaeque volantum, Et quæ marmoreo fert monstra sub æquore pontus. Igneus est ollis vigor, & cœlestis origo.
units.tr: First, heaven and earth, and the flowing plains, and the shining globe of the moon, and the Titanian stars, a spirit within nourishes; and mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass and mingles itself with the great body. Hence come the race of men and of beasts, and the life of flying things, and the monsters that the sea bears under its marble surface. Fiery is their vigour, and their origin is heavenly.

units.la: Et idem Georg. 4.
units.tr: And the same in the Georgics 4:

units.la: Esse apibus partem diuinæ mentis, & haustus Ætherios dixere. Deum namque ire per omnes Terrasque tractusque maris, cœlumque profundum.
units.tr: They have said that bees have a part of the divine mind and draughts of ethereal air. For God pervades all lands and stretches of the sea and the deep sky.

units.la: Hinc pecudes armenta, viros, genus omne ferarum, Quemque sibi tenuesnascentem arcceffere vitas. Scilicet huc reddi deinde, ac resoluta referri Omnia, nec morti esse locum, sed viva volare Sideris in numerum, atque alto succedere caelo.
units.tr: From this, flocks and herds, men, every kind of wild beast, and each new-born life, as it is made tender, is called to itself. Certainly all things are then restored and carried back when dissolved, and there is no place for death, but they fly living into the number of the stars, and go up into the lofty heaven.

units.la: Quae quidem sententia Virgilij, paucis castigatis, est praeficiis physicis omnino admittenda. Sed videamus, quomodo se habeat vita, sine anima mundi tum in genere, tum in specie. Ac in genere quidem vita mundi tamdiu manet in re, quamdiu vis aliqua remanet. Sic plantae a radice sua auulsae, amittunt vitam vegetantem: at nihilominus viuunt, quantum attinet ad vitam ἐνεργητικήν[?], qua fit vt in medicina vel culina suum habeant vsum. De mortuorum animalium membris idem est iudicium. Nam sales, olea, quintae essentiae &c. cranij humani, vngulae alcis, cornu cerui &c. amissa vita sensitiua retinent vitalem quandam facultatem aduersus epilepsiam, & similes morbos. In specie vita mundi cernitur in coelo, elementis, & mixtis. Vita in coelo est spiritus ille, quem stellae in se habent, quemq; his rebus inferioribus impartiuntur. Vita in elementis est spiritus partim insitus, partim a coelo influens. Ita spiritus ignis calefacit & purgat, aeris refocillat, terrae & aquae nutrit. Huius spiritus effecta sunt calor, frigus, humiditas, siccitas, gravitas, levitas, densitas, odor, sapor, sonus: sicut lux, color, sympathia & antipathia sunt effecta spiritus aetherij. Vita in mixtis est obscurior, vel evidentior. Vita obscurior est in mineralibus. Quo pertinent stupendae virtutes terrarum sigillatarum, boli, nitri, aluminis, succini, spiritus vitrioli, auri in formam pulueris nitrarij re-dacti, &c. Vita evidentior est in plantis, bestiis & homine. In plantis est vita vegetatiua, quae posita est in generatione, nutritione, auctione, attractione, retentione, concoctione, & expulsione. In bestiis est vita sensitiva, quae consistit in sanguine, vt Scriptura testatur; cernitur in sensu & motu. Sensus est partim externus, vt visus, auditus, olfactus, gustus & tactus: partim internus, vt sensus communis, phantasia, & memoria. Motus est respiratio, pulsus, appetitus sensitiuus (isque partim cupiditas, partim affectus) locomotiua, vigilia, & somnus. In homine est vita intellectiua, eaque tum intellectus agentis & patientis, tum voluntatis, idque vel in hac vita, vel post hanc vitam. Atque hic est locus communis physicus de vita, amplissimus quidem ille & vtilissimus. Huc refer quae passim in Scripturis occurrunt de coloribus, odoribus, calore, frigore, saporibus, fame, siti, visu, auditu, gustu &c.
units.tr: This opinion of Virgil, with a few corrections, is wholly to be admitted by physicists. But let us see how life stands, without the soul of the world, both in general and in particular. In general, the life of the world remains in a thing for as long as some power remains in it. Thus plants torn from their root lose their growing life; yet they nevertheless live as far as their active life [ἐνεργητικήν] is concerned, so that they have their use in medicine or the kitchen. The same judgment holds for the limbs of dead animals. For salts, oils, quintessences, etc., of a human skull, of elk's hoof, of a stag's horn, etc., having lost sensitive life, retain a certain vital faculty against epilepsy and similar diseases. In particular, the life of the world is seen in the heavens, the elements and mixed bodies. Life in the heavens is that spirit which the stars have in themselves and impart to these lower things. Life in the elements is a spirit partly innate, partly flowing in from the heavens. Thus the spirit of fire heats and purifies, that of air refreshes, and that of earth and water nourishes. The effects of this spirit are heat, cold, moisture, dryness, weight, lightness, density, smell, taste and sound; just as light, colour, sympathy and antipathy are effects of the ethereal spirit. Life in mixed bodies is either more obscure or more evident. More obscure life is found in minerals. To this belong the marvellous virtues of sealed earths, bole, nitre, alum, amber, spirit of vitriol, gold reduced to the form of powder of nitre, etc. More evident life is found in plants, beasts and man. In plants there is vegetative life, which consists in generation, nutrition, growth, attraction, retention, concoction and expulsion. In beasts there is sensitive life, which resides in the blood, as Scripture testifies; it is seen in sensation and motion. Sensation is partly external, as sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch; partly internal, as common sense, imagination and memory. Motion is breathing, pulse, sensitive appetite (which is partly desire, partly emotion), locomotion, waking and sleep. In man there is intellective life, and this both of the agent and the patient intellect, and of the will, whether in this life or after this life. And this is the general natural topic concerning life, very wide and very useful. To it refer the things that occur everywhere in the Scriptures concerning colours, odours, heat, cold, tastes, hunger, thirst, sight, hearing, taste, etc.

units.la: XI. Plenitudo mundi est, qua nullum in mundo est vacuum. Mundus enim est corpus continuum & contiguum, spiritu aereo & caelesti, omnia replente & fouente, plenum. Hinc pendet connexio omnium corporum adeo firma & indissolubilis, vt vacuum a nullo mortalium vel angelorum in hanc mundanam scenam introduci possit. Confer Hof. 2. v. 21. 22.
units.tr: XI. The fullness of the world is the condition in which there is no void anywhere in the world. For the world is a continuous and contiguous body, full, filling and cherishing all things with an airy and heavenly spirit. From this comes such a firm and indissoluble connection of all bodies that no void can be introduced into this worldly stage by any mortal or angel. Compare Hos. 2. v. 21. 22.

units.la: XII. Figura mundi est circularis. Haec siquidem figura est pulcherrima & perfectissima, in praecipuis mundi corporibus a Deo expressa. Quod autem ex Apoc. 21. adfertur de quadratura caelestis Hierosolymae, id est mysticum.
units.tr: XII. The figure of the world is circular. For this figure is the most beautiful and most perfect, and God has impressed it on the chief bodies of the world. What is brought from Rev. 21 about the square shape of the heavenly Jerusalem is mystical.

units.la: XIII. Duratio mundi est spatium illud temporis inde a primo mundi exordio vsque ad ipsius exitum ac finem. Hoc ex traditione Eliae definitur (ex[?] millibus annorum. Sed nos infra in Chronologia demonstrauimus ex Dan. 12. & Apoc. 20. longius esse extendendum hoc spatium, vt fiat annorum 6642. Quaeris quomodo fit periturus mundus? Resp. ex 2. Petr. 2. v. 12. 13. coeli conflagrantes soluentur, & elementa aestuantia liquescent, igne scil. calcinationis miraculosae, quae longo interuallo superabit calcinationem corporum artificialem, qua illa rediguntur in cinerem, & ex cinere fit corpus gloriosum[?].
units.tr: XIII. The duration of the world is that span of time from the very beginning of the world until its departure and end. This is defined from the tradition of Elijah (six thousand years. But we have demonstrated below in the Chronology, from Dan. 12 and Rev. 20, that this span must be extended further, so that it comes to 6642 years. You ask how the world will perish? Answer: from 2 Pet. 2. v. 12. 13, the burning heavens will be dissolved and the glowing elements will melt, namely by the fire of a miraculous calcination, which will far exceed the artificial calcination of bodies, by which they are reduced to ash, and from the ash a glorious body is made.

units.la: X. ARITHMETICA SACRA.
units.tr: X. Sacred Arithmetic

units.la: I. Arithmetica sacra est scientia bene numerandi ex S. literis sumta. De hac Augustinus recte pronuntiat: Ratio numeri contemnenda non est, quæ in multis sanctarum Scripturarum locis quàm magni æstimada sit, elucet diligenter intuentibus. Nec frustra in laudibus Dei dictum est, Omnia in mensura, numero, & pondere disposuisti. Item: Nemo aspirare debet ad cognitionem divinarum artium ac disciplinarum sine illa quasi duplici scientia, bonæ disputationis, potentiaque numerorum. Et Hieronymus ait, magnam vim innumeris inesse, ad plurima mysteria in S. Scripturis intelligenda. Huc accedit, quòd intellectus ordinis & numerorum perspicuè testatur de providentiâ Dei.
units.tr: I. Sacred arithmetic is the science of numbering well, drawn from the Holy Scriptures. Augustine rightly pronounces concerning it: The reckoning of number is not to be despised, whose great worth in many places of the holy Scriptures shines out to those who look at them carefully. Nor was it said in vain in the praises of God, You have arranged all things in measure, number, and weight. Likewise: No one ought to aspire to the knowledge of divine arts and disciplines without that double science, of good reasoning and of the power of numbers. And Jerome says that there is great force in numbers for understanding very many mysteries in the holy Scriptures. Besides this, the understanding of order and of numbers clearly bears witness to the providence of God.

units.la: II. Partes eius duæ sunt: prima, de numeris abstractis, altera de concretis.
units.tr: II. It has two parts: the first concerns abstract numbers, the second concrete numbers.

units.la: III. Numeri abstracti sunt, qui in genere considerantur. Consideratio ista generalis est numeri simplicis, vel comparati. Illa absoluitur notatione, & numeratione: ista progressione, proportione, & radicum extractione. Notatio docet numerum recte cognoscere & exprimere. Numeratio docet e duobus datis numeris tertiū legitimè invenire: estque integrorum, vel partium. Numeratio integrorum est simplex, in additione & subductione: vel multiplex, in multiplicatione, & divisione. Numeratio partium cernitur in his quatuor: videl. in prolatione fractionum, valore & reductione illarum, denique in quatuor speciebus, puta fractionum additione, subductione, multiplicatione, & divisione. Exempla notationis & utriusque numerationis peti possunt ex chronologiâ sacrâ. e.g. ex Gen. 5. & 11. Exod. 12. verf. 40. item ex Num. 1. 1. Reg. 4. 5. 6. 7. Apoc. 7. &c. Progressio est arithmetica, vel geometrica. Proportio cernitur in regulâ aurea directâ & obliquâ. Extractio radicis est quadrata, vel cubica. Harum operationum exempla non sunt obuia in sacris.
units.tr: III. Abstract numbers are those considered in general. This general consideration concerns a simple or a compared number. The former is completed by notation and numeration; the latter by progression, proportion, and extraction of roots. Notation teaches us to know and express a number correctly. Numeration teaches us to find lawfully a third number from two given numbers; it is of whole numbers or of parts. Numeration of whole numbers is simple, in addition and subtraction, or manifold, in multiplication and division. Numeration of parts is seen in these four: namely, in the expression of fractions, their value and reduction, and finally in the four operations, that is, the addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of fractions. Examples of notation and of both kinds of numeration may be sought from sacred chronology, for instance from Gen. 5 and 11, Exod. 12 verse 40; likewise from Num. 1, 1 Kings 4, 5, 6, 7, Apoc. 7, etc. Progression is arithmetical or geometrical. Proportion is seen in the direct and inverse rule of three. Extraction of a root is square or cube. Examples of these operations are not obvious in the sacred books.

units.la: IV. Numeri concreti sunt, qui rebus certis applicantur. Applicantur, inquam, rebus diuinis, physicis, mathematicis, ethicis, politicis, œconomicis. Nos monstrabimus, quomodo in Scriptura sacra applicentur rebus sacris, itemque nummis, quorum fit mentio in V. & N.T.
units.tr: IV. Concrete numbers are those applied to certain things. They are applied, I say, to divine, physical, mathematical, ethical, political, and economic things. We shall show how they are applied in holy Scripture to sacred things, and likewise to coins, which are mentioned in the Old and New Testaments.

units.la: V. Numeri sic applicantur rebus sacris. Principio vnitas est symbolum diuinæ perfectionis. Vnus enim est Deus & Pater omnium, quiest super omnes, & per omnes, & in omnibus vobis, vt ait apostolus Eph.4. verf.6. Hinc pie dicunt, nihil vno esse prius, & ipsum esse rerum omnium principium: item, vsque ad vnum omnia, & vltra vnum nihil: item, Quemadmodum vnitas omnem numerum simplicissimè penetrat, & semper est eadem, principium & finis numerorum, supra numerum & infra ipsum, intra numerum & extra ipsum: ita Deus om-nia penetrat, est omnium principium & finis, supra & infra, extra & intra omnia subsistens, à quo, ex quo, per quem, in quo, ad quem, & propter quem sunt omnia. Est etiam vna fides, vnum baptisma, & vnus mediator Iesus Christus, vt ait apostolus d.l. Deinde binarius figurat coniugium, duas tabulas legis, duos cherubim, duas naturas in Christo, duo testamenta & sacramenta &c. Ternarius in memoriam nobis renocat tres personas sacrosanctæ Trinitatis: quaternarius, quatuor animalia Ezechielis, Danielis, & Iohannis in apocalypsi, quatuor monarchias Danielis, quatuor euangelistas &c. quinarius, quinque panes, quibus Christus pauit aliquot millia hominum &c. senarius, sex dies creationis, quibus operari debemus &c. septenarius, septimum diem, qui est sabbati, septimum annum sabbatarium, septem spiritus, ecclesias, stellas, candelabra, sigilla, phialas, tubas, & similia in apocalypsi: octonarius, octauum diem circumcisionis, octo beatitudines, octo animas seruatas in arca &c. nouenarius, nouem ingratos à Christo mundatos &c. denarius, decem præcepta legis &c. vndenarius, vndecim saga cilicina in tabernaculo, vndecim apostolos perseuerantes &c. duodenarius, duodecim tribus Israëlis, duodecim gemmas in Exodo & Apocalypsi, duodecim apostolos, duodecim portas nouæ Hierosolymæ &c. atque ita pergendo ad alios numeros, qui occurrunt in Scripturis, & colligi possunt partim ex Patribus, partim ex Concordantijs Bibliorum. Sed, inquis, hæc sunt affinia superstitioni. Ita sane videtur ignaris & ignauis ingeniis, quæ non mittunt mentem ad profundiora meditationum mysteria, quibus nihil plane commercij est cum superstitione. Sed vno al-tero exemplo planam faciamus praxin huius arithmologiæ. Vnitas est radix omnis numeri, quæ in se ducta nihil producit aliud quàm seipsam, quæque omnem numerum metitur, & certam habet proportionem ad omnes numeros &c. Quæ omnia si quis perpendat, deprehendet res illas, quæ maximam cum unitate conuenientiam habent, esse perfectiores, diuturniores, digniores. Duo, quatenus duo, nihil efficiunt in arithmetica. Oportet vt rite coniungantur. Ita in regno naturæ & gratiæ nisi duo conueniant in vno tertio, inter se non conueniunt, neque aliquid efficere possunt. At verò si recte coniungantur, plurimùm possunt & prosunt. Ternarius in figuris & harmonijs est princeps & systaticus: quaternarius est primus numerus quadratus &c. Hinc patet numerum quemque habere aliquid peculiare in se. Non itaque casu fortuito factum esse arbitrari debemus, quòd Deus hos vel illos numeros his vel illis rebus attribuerit: vt quòd voluit septem dies metiri sæculum, quòd quatuor creauit elementa &c. Huc refer, quòd arbores in quincuncem positæ feliciùs crescunt. Atque hæc est prima vtilitas huius nostræ arithmologiæ. Deinde collatio inter numeros similes instituta præclaras suggerit meditationes. e.g. duoduodecim gemmæ collatæ cum duodecim tribubus & apostolis, anni 365. vitæ Enochi cum 365. diebus annissolaris[?], decem præcepta decalogi cum decem digitis manuum &c. Tertiò arithmologia ista iuvat memoriam: ut si dicas ex Proverbiis Salomonis, sex esse, quæ odio prosequitur Dominus, septimum autem abominari; quatuor esse minima in terra, à quibus tamen omnes sapientes sapientiâ superentur: si ex Siracho, tria speciosa videri in oculis Dei & hominum, tria esse omnibus odiosa & molesta, &c.
units.tr: V. Numbers are applied to sacred things in this way. First, unity is the symbol of divine perfection. For there is one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all, as the apostle says in Eph. 4 verse 6. Hence the pious say that nothing is prior to the One, and that it is the principle of all things; also that all things go up to the One and nothing beyond the One; also that, just as unity most simply penetrates every number and is always the same, the beginning and end of numbers, above number and below it, within number and outside it, so God penetrates all things, is the beginning and end of all, subsisting above and below, outside and within all things, from whom, through whom, in whom, to whom, and for whom all things are. There is also one faith, one baptism, and one mediator, Jesus Christ, as the apostle says in the passage cited. Then the binary figures marriage, the two tables of the law, the two cherubim, the two natures in Christ, the two testaments and sacraments, and so on. The ternary calls to our memory the three persons of the most holy Trinity; the quaternary, the four living creatures of Ezekiel, Daniel, and John in the Apocalypse, the four monarchies of Daniel, the four evangelists, and so on. The quinary, the five loaves with which Christ fed several thousand men, and so on. The senary, the six days of creation, in which we ought to work, and so on. The septenary, the seventh day, which is the Sabbath, the seventh sabbatical year, the seven spirits, churches, stars, candlesticks, seals, bowls, trumpets, and similar things in the Apocalypse. The octonary, the eighth day of circumcision, the eight beatitudes, the eight souls saved in the ark, and so on. The nonary, the nine ungrateful men cleansed by Christ, and so on. The denary, the ten precepts of the law, and so on. The undenary, the eleven goat-hair curtains in the tabernacle, the eleven apostles who persevered, and so on. The duodenary, the twelve tribes of Israel, the twelve gems in Exodus and the Apocalypse, the twelve apostles, the twelve gates of the new Jerusalem, and so on. And so on through the other numbers which occur in the Scriptures, and which can be gathered partly from the Fathers, partly from the concordances of the Bible. But, you will say, these things are close to superstition. Indeed they seem so to ignorant and lazy minds, which do not direct their thought to the deeper mysteries of meditation, and which have absolutely nothing to do with superstition. But let us make the practice of this arithmology plain by one or two examples. Unity is the root of every number, which, multiplied by itself, produces nothing but itself, which measures every number, and which has a fixed proportion to all numbers, and so on. If anyone weighs all these things, he will find that those things which have the greatest agreement with unity are more perfect, more lasting, and more worthy. Two, as two, accomplish nothing in arithmetic; they must be rightly joined. So too in the kingdom of nature and of grace, unless two agree in a third, they do not agree with each other, and cannot accomplish anything. But if they are rightly joined, they can do and profit very much. The ternary is the chief and constitutive principle in figures and harmonies; the quaternary is the first square number, and so on. From this it is plain that each number has something peculiar in itself. We ought not, therefore, to suppose that it happened by chance that God assigned these or those numbers to these or those things: as that he willed seven days to measure the age, that he created four elements, and so on. To this belongs the fact that trees planted in a quincunx grow more happily. And this is the first use of our arithmology. Next, a comparison instituted between similar numbers suggests excellent meditations; for example, the twelve gems compared with the twelve tribes and apostles; the 365 years of Enoch's life with the 365 days of the solar year; the ten precepts of the decalogue with the ten fingers of the hands, and so on. Thirdly, this arithmology helps the memory: so that if you say, from the Proverbs of Solomon, that there are six things which the Lord hates, and a seventh which he abominates; that there are four smallest things on earth, yet all wise men are surpassed by them in wisdom; or, from Sirach, that three things seem beautiful in the eyes of God and of men, and three are hateful and troublesome to all, and so on.

units.la: VI. Nummi,quorum mentio fit in sacris,ita se habent.
units.tr: VI. The coins mentioned in Scripture are as follows.

units.la: 1. Λεπτὸν[?], dimidius obolus Germanorum. Marc.12.v.42.2. Κοδράντης[?], obolus Germanorum. Matt.5. v.26.3. Ἀσσάριον[?], duo oboli Germanorum. Matt.10.v.29. 4. Gerah, albus Germanorum, octo obolorum. Exod.30. v.13. Leuit. 27.v.25.5. Agorah, eiusdem cum præcedente valoris. 1. Sam. 2.v.36.6. Keschitah, eiusdem cum duobus præcedentibus valoris. Gen.33.v.19.7. Zur, siue Zuz[?] est denarius. Denarius autem est octaua pars thaleri imperialis, pendens tantum argenti, quantum pendit ducatus Vngaricus, ein Quintlein / quæ est quarta pars lothonis, vti vocant. Moneta nostrate sunt quinque albi, seu 10. crucigeri. De Zur vide Tob. 5.v.21. de denario Iohan.6. v.7.8. Adarcon, siue darcemon erat eiusdem cum præcedenti valoris in argento: in auro erat ducatus. Est drachma Græcorum. Vide 1.Paral.29.v.7.Neh.7.v.70.9.Siclus erat integer,& diuisus in partes. Siclus integer erat Hebraicus, vel gentilis. Siclus Hebraicus fuit argenteus, isque tum sacer, æstimatus semisse thaleri imperialis: tum vulgaris, quartâ parte thaleri æstimatus. Leuit.27.v.3.4.5.6.7. Gen.20.v.16. Siclus gentilis erat Ægyptius, 16. obolorum Atticorum, & Persicus, dimidio minor Ægyptio. Partes sicli erant semisses, triens, & quadrans: quæ variant in siclo sacro & vulgari. 10. Maneh, siue minah, sanctuarij, in argento æstimabatur 25. thaleris imperialibus, in auro 100. ducatis. 1. Reg. 10.v.17. vulgaris seu regia, thaler. 1½. 11. Kikar, scil. nummamarium, erat maxima mensura in nummis, & respondebat talento. Kikar sanctuarij æstimabatur in auro 12000. ducatis, in argento 1500. thaleris Exod. 39. v.24. Esdr. 8. v.26. commune, in auro 6000. ducatis, in argento 750. thalimp.
units.tr: (1) Lepton [Λεπτὸν], half a German obol. Mark 12:42. (2) Kodrantes [Κοδράντης], a German obol. Matt. 5:26. (3) Assarion [Ἀσσάριον], two German obols. Matt. 10:29. (4) Gerah, a German albus, eight obols. Exod. 30:13; Lev. 27:25. (5) Agorah, of the same value as the preceding. 1 Sam. 2:36. (6) Keschitah, of the same value as the two preceding. Gen. 33:19. (7) Zur, or Zuz, is the denarius. The denarius is the eighth part of an imperial thaler, containing as much silver as a Hungarian ducat, <bl>ein Quintlein</bl>, which is the fourth part of a lothonis, as they call it. Our current coinage gives five albi, or 10 crucigeri. On the Zur see Tob. 5:21; on the denarius, John 6:7, 8. (8) Adarcon, or darcemon, was of the same value as the preceding in silver; in gold it was a ducat. It is the Greek drachma. See 1 Chron. 29:7; Neh. 7:70. (9) The shekel was whole and also divided into parts. The whole shekel was either Hebrew or gentile. The Hebrew shekel was of silver, and was either sacred, valued at half an imperial thaler, or common, valued at a quarter of a thaler. Lev. 27:3–7; Gen. 20:16. The gentile shekel was Egyptian, equal to 16 Attic obols, or Persian, half the weight of the Egyptian. The parts of the shekel were halves, thirds and quarters, and these vary between the sacred and the common shekel. (10) The maneh, or minah, of the sanctuary was valued in silver at 25 imperial thalers, and in gold at 100 ducats. 1 Kings 10:17. The common or royal maneh was a thaler and a half. (11) The kikar, that is, the money-talent, was the largest measure of money and corresponded to a talent. The kikar of the sanctuary was valued in gold at 12,000 ducats, and in silver at 1,500 thalers. Exod. 39:24; Ezra 8:26. The common kikar was valued in gold at 6,000 ducats, and in silver at 750 thalers.
1 Kings 16:26. 2 Chron. 3:8.

units.la: XI. GEOMETRIA SACRA.
units.tr: XI. SACRED GEOMETRY

units.la: I. GEometria sacra est scientia bene metiendi ex S. literis sumta. Proprie Geometria est terræ dimensio. Sed per synecdochen est dimensio cuiusque corporis.
units.tr: I. Sacred geometry is the science of measuring well, drawn from the Holy Scriptures. Properly, geometry is the measuring of the earth, but by synecdoche it is the measuring of any body whatever.

units.la: II. Geometriæ partes duæ sunt. prima de magnitudine, secunda de mensurâ magnitudinis.
units.tr: II. Geometry has two parts: the first concerns magnitude, the second the measure of magnitude.

units.la: III. Magnitudo est longitudo, latitudo vel altitudo. Vulgo appellatur trina dimensio: à quâ multæ metaphoræ geometricæ in sacris literis sumuntur: ita ut hic locum habeat illud Platonis, θεὸν ἀεὶ γεωμετρεῖν. Hoc, inquam, verum est in schola naturæ & gratiæ. Et primò quidem in schola naturæ, hoc est, in opificio huius mundi, Deus omnia ordinavit in mensurâ, numero, & pondere Sap. 11. v.21. Verba Græca eleganter sonant: πάντα μέτρῳ [?] ἀριθμῷ [?] σταθμῷ διέταξας. Deus sane omnis generis figuras, pondera & proportiones in totâ naturâ nobis expressit, ut nihil sit in geometricis, quod non possit mostrari in naturâ. Illeque quoq; mensus est pugillo suo aquas, & cœlos spithamâ expandit, & complexus est trientali pulverem terræ, & ponderavit statera montes, & colles lancibus. Esa. 40. v.12. Deinde in schola gratiæ, siue in ecclesiâ, profundæ admodum sunt diuitiæ tum sapientiæ, tum cognitionis Dei. Rom. 11.v.33. & Deus distribuit cuilibet suam mensuram. 2. Cor. 10. verf. 13. videlicet pro mensurâ Christi Eph.4.v.7. Nostri quoque officij est,huic sacræ geometriæ operam dare , vt valeamus assequi cum omnibus sanctis, quæ sit illa latitudo, & longitudo,& profunditas,& sublimitas. Eph.3.v.18. vbi apostolus profunditati addit altitudinem,quia distinguuntur [illegible, ~4 letters] siue § ratione. Porrò trinæ istius dimensionis exempla passim obuia sunt in Scripturis , vt in arcâ Noe , tabernaculo Mosis, templo Salomonis& Ezechielis, cœlesti Hierosolymâ Iohannis &c. de quibus vide infra in Architectonicâ.
units.tr: III. Magnitude is length, breadth or height. It is commonly called three-fold dimension, and many geometrical metaphors are taken from it in the sacred books. Hence Plato's saying applies here: God always geometrizes [θεὸν ἀεὶ γεωμετρεῖν]. This is true, I say, in the school of nature and in the school of grace. First, in the school of nature, that is, in the workmanship of this world, God has ordered all things in measure, number and weight (Wisd. 11:21). The Greek words sound elegantly: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure, number and weight" [πάντα μέτρῳ ... ἀριθμῷ ... σταθμῷ διέταξας]. Certainly God has set before us figures of every kind, weights and proportions throughout all of nature, so that there is nothing in geometry that cannot be shown in nature. He "has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and marked out the heavens with a span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance" (Isa. 40:12). Then, in the school of grace, or in the Church, the riches both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God are very deep (Rom. 11:33), and God "has distributed to each a measure" (2 Cor. 10:13), namely according to the measure of Christ (Eph. 4:7). It is also our duty to devote ourselves to this sacred geometry, that we may be able to comprehend with all the saints "what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height" (Eph. 3:18), where the apostle adds height to depth, because they are distinguished [illegible, about four letters] or by reason. Moreover, examples of this threefold dimension are everywhere to be found in the Scriptures: in Noah's ark, the tabernacle of Moses, the temple of Solomon and that of Ezekiel, the heavenly Jerusalem of John, and so on, concerning which see below under Architectonics.

units.la: IV. Longitudo est magnitudo vnius inter- ualli.
units.tr: IV. Length is the magnitude of a single interval.

units.la: Vsitatè dicitur linea, quæ est magnitudo omnium prima,& fimpliciffima. Latitudo est magnitudo composita : profunditas fiue altitudo, decomposita. Exempla longitudinis vi.le Gen. 6. verf.15.cap.13. v.17.Exod.25.26. 27.28.30.36.37.38. Deut.2. verf. 21. c.3. verf.11.1.Reg.6.2. Chron.3.Ezech. 40.41.42.43.45.48. Zach. 2.v.2.c.5.v.2. Apoc.21. Cæterum linea consideratur absolutè, vel comparatè. Linea absolutè est recta, vel obliqua,& hæc est peripheria, vel helix: compa ate, est parallela, vel perpendicularis, vel neutra, id est, neque parallela neque perpendicularis. Huiusmodi lineas videre est in manibus & herbis.
units.tr: It is commonly called a line, which is the first and simplest of all magnitudes. Breadth is a composite magnitude; depth or height is a magnitude resolved into its parts. Examples of length are found in Gen. 6:15, 13:17; Exod. 25:26, 27, 28, 30, 36, 37, 38; Deut. 2:21, 3:11; 1 Kings 6:2; 1 Chron. 3; Ezek. 40, 41, 42, 43, 45, 48; Zech. 2:2, 5:2; Rev. 21. Moreover, a line is considered either absolutely or comparatively. A line absolutely considered is straight or curved, and the curved line is either a circumference or a helix. Comparatively considered, a line is either parallel, or perpendicular, or neither, that is, neither parallel nor perpendicular. Lines of this kind may be seen in hands and in plants.

units.la: V. Latitudo est magnitudo duorum interuallorum. Componitur itaque ex lineis. Latitudo est angulus, vel superficies. Angulus, inquam, planus. Nam datur etiam angulus solidus in corporibus. Exempla vide Exod.25.26.27.36.37.38.1.Reg.6.&7.Nehem.3.Ezech.41. 43.45.46. Vide etiam de lapide angulari Christo Pfal.118. v.22.Matth.21.v.42. Marc.12.v.10.Luc.20.verf.17.Act.4. v.11.1.Petr.2.v.7. Angulus est rectus, acutus, vel obtusus. Ille facit ad stabilitatem,iste ad motum penetrantem, hic participat de recto & acuto. Typos angulorum varios videre licet in auibus volantibus, in animalium corporibus, & nominatim in hominis brachiis eleuatis & contractis, item in pedibus divaricatis[?]: denique in literis Hebraicis. Superficies est area lineis circumcirca comprehensa. Exempla huius latitudinis vide locis paulo ante citatis ad longitudinem. Porro superficies est plana, vel gibba: & plana est rectilinea, vel curuilinea. Illa est triangulum, vel triangulatum. Triangulum est superficies a tribus lineis comprehensa. Huius praerogatiua est longe maxima: quia omnes aliae figurae in hanc resolui possunt. Typos varios huius figurae videre est in manibus & foliis herbarum atque arborum. Triangulatum est, quod e triangulis componitur. Estque quadrangulum, vel multangulum. Quadrangulum est quadratum, oblongum seu ἑτερόμηκες, rhombus, rhomboides, & trapezium. Multangulum est pentagonum, hexagonum, heptagonum &c. Ex his quadratum inprimis celebratur ob firmitatem & æqualitatem. Tale est sanctum sanctorum 1. Reg. 6. v. 20. item cœlestis Hierosolyma Apoc. 21. Quadrato proximum est oblongum: quâ figurâ fuit prædictum tabernaculum, itemque templum. Confer cum Architectonicâ. Talem quoque figuram exprimit Marcus cap. 6. vers. 40. vbi ait ἀνέπεσαν συμπόσια συμπόσια ἀνὰ ἑκατὸν καὶ ἀνὰ πεντήκοντα[?], Discubuerunt ergo per areolas distributi in centenos & quinquagenos, tali fermè proportione.
units.tr: V. Breadth is the magnitude of two intervals. It is therefore composed of lines. Breadth is an angle or a surface. I mean a plane angle, for there is also a solid angle in bodies. Examples are in Exod. 25:26, 27, 36, 37, 38; 1 Kings 6 and 7; Neh. 3; Ezek. 41, 43, 45, 46. See also concerning Christ as the corner stone, Ps. 118:22; Matt. 21:42; Mark 12:10; Luke 20:17; Acts 4:11; 1 Pet. 2:7. An angle is right, acute or obtuse. The first serves for stability, the second for penetrating motion, and the third partakes of both the right and the acute. Various types of angles may be seen in flying birds, in the bodies of animals, and especially in the human arms raised and bent, and likewise in legs spread apart, and finally in Hebrew letters. A surface is an area enclosed on all sides by lines. Examples of this breadth may be found in the places cited a little above for length. Further, a surface is either plane or curved, and a plane surface is either rectilinear or curvilinear. The rectilinear surface is a triangle or a polygon. A triangle is a surface enclosed by three lines. Its pre-eminence is by far the greatest, because all other figures can be resolved into it. Various types of this figure may be seen in the hands and leaves of plants and trees. A polygon is that which is made up of triangles, and it is either a quadrilateral or a many-sided figure. A quadrilateral is a square, an oblong or heteromecic, a rhombus, a rhomboid, and a trapezium. A many-sided figure is a pentagon, hexagon, heptagon, and so on. Of these, the square is especially celebrated for its firmness and equality. Such is the holy of holies (1 Kings 6:20), and likewise the heavenly Jerusalem (Rev. 21). Next to the square is the oblong, the figure of the aforesaid tabernacle and likewise of the temple. Compare Architectonics. This figure is also expressed in Mark 6:40, where it says: "They reclined in companies, company by company, by hundreds and by fifties" [ἀνέπεσαν συμπόσια συμπόσια ἀνὰ ἑκατὸν καὶ ἀνὰ πεντήκοντα], discubuerunt ergo per areolas distributi in centenos et quinquagenos, in roughly this proportion.

units.la: Hîc decem puncta dispolita sunt in longitudinem, quinque verò in latitudinem. Eadem autem est proportio centum ad quinquaginta, quæ est decem ad quinque: videlicet dupla, vt sunt verba Iohan. Piscatoris super Iohan. 6. ver. 10. Superficies curuilinea est circulus, vel circuliformis, vt oualis, conchalis &c. Superficies gibba cernitur in sphæ-râ, corâ, cono, & cylindro. Harum figurarum typos vide passim apud interpretes sacrarum literarum in schematibus tabernaculi, templi, & rerum in utroque contentarum.
units.tr: Here ten points are set out in length, but five in breadth. The proportion of a hundred to fifty is the same as that of ten to five, namely double, as John Piscator says on John 6:10. A curvilinear surface is a circle or circle-shaped figure, such as an oval, a shell-shape and so on. A curved surface is seen in a sphere, a cube, a cone and a cylinder. For types of these figures see everywhere among the interpreters of Holy Scripture in the diagrams of the tabernacle, the temple, and the things contained in both.

units.la: VI. Altitudo est magnitudo trium interuallorum. Componitur itaque ex lineis & superficiebus.
units.tr: VI. Height is the magnitude of three intervals. It is therefore composed of lines and surfaces.

units.la: Estque angulus, vel corpus. Angulus, inquam, solidus, qui dicitur hedra. Huiusmodi anguli conspicui erant in exedris atriorum templi. 1. Paralip. 8. Corpus est planum, vel gibbum. Planum est pyramis, vel pyramidatum: & hoc est pentaedrum, hexaedrum, vel polyedrum. Inter hexaedra excellit cubus. Gibbum est sphaera, conus, vel cylindrus. Exempla harum figurarum vide Gen.6.v.15.Exod.25. 27.30.37.38.1.Reg.6.2.Chron.3.Ezech.40.& 41.Apoc.21.v.16. item in sole, luna, corde & reliquis membris animalium, denique in fossilibus, quae varias referunt figuras, ita ut de illis iure merito usurpetur versus
units.tr: It is either an angle or a body. An angle, I mean a solid angle, which is called a hedra. Angles of this kind were conspicuous in the exedrae of the courts of the temple (1 Chron. 8). A body is either plane or curved. A plane body is a pyramid or a pyramidal figure, and this is a pentahedron, hexahedron or polyhedron. Among hexahedra the cube excels. A curved body is a sphere, a cone or a cylinder. See examples of these figures in Gen. 6:15; Exod. 25, 27, 30, 37, 38; 1 Kings 6:2; 2 Chron. 3; Ezek. 40 and 41; Rev. 21:16; likewise in the sun, the moon, the heart and the other members of animals, and finally in minerals, which display various shapes, so that the line may rightly be applied to them:

units.la: Ludit in humanis divina potentia rebus.
units.tr: Divine power plays in human affairs.

units.la: VII. Mensurae, quibus exploratur magnitudo, sunt longitudinis, latitudinis, vel profunditatis.
units.tr: VII. The measures by which magnitude is tested are those of length, breadth or depth.

units.la: VIII. Mensurae longitudinis sunt, quibus exploratur lineae magnitudo. Dicuntur aliâs mensurae continuorum. Tales in sacris literis sunt, 1.Palmus, mensura quatuor digitorum. Exod. 28. v. 24. & 37. v. 13. 2. Spithama, mensura trium palmorum, seu duodecim digitorum. Exod. 28. v. 16. 1. Sam. 17. v. 4. Ezech. 43. v. 13. 3. Cubitus; isque vulgaris, geometricus, & sacer. Cubitus vulgaris, seu communis, item paruus, est sesquipedalis, seu 24. digitorum, itaut huius cubiti mensura sit manus virilis, illa quae ab extremo flexi brachij angulo ad medij digiti summitatem protenditur, non quidem in brachio pueri, sed hominis perfectae aetatis, puta triginta circiter annorum: non etiam gigantis, sed staturae quadratae, hoc est, per omnia proportionatae, cuiusmodi putatur fuisse Adam, quando a Deo est creatus, & Iesus Christus, quando est crucifixus. Hic cubitus complectitur quartam circiter partem viri illius, cuius est. Dicitur etiam cubitus ciuilis, & architectorum. Cubitus geometricus complectitur sex cubitos vulgares. Cubitus sacer, siue legalis & ecclesiasticus, item sanctuarii, veritatis, & aedificij, i.e. templi: hic, inquam, cubitus erat duplo maior quam vulgaris. Quidam tamen existimant, cubitum vulgare fuisse 5. palmorum, sacrum 6. De cubito vulgari vide Gen. 7. verf. 20. Num. 11. v. 31. 1. Reg. 7. de sacro Exod. 25. 26. 27. 30. 1. Reg. 6. & 7. & 2. Chron. 3. v. 3. vbi appellatur mensura princeps. 4. Arundo, siue pertica & virga mensoria, longa sex cubitos sacros. Ezech. 40. v. 3. Apoc. 11. v. 21. & 21. v. 15. 5. Funiculus, arbitrarie longitudinis, & apud varios varie. Iof. 17.
units.tr: VIII. Measures of length are those by which the magnitude of a line is tested. They are otherwise called measures of continuous quantities. Such measures in the sacred books are: 1. The palm, a measure of four fingers (Exod. 28:24; 37:13). 2. The span, a measure of three palms, or twelve fingers (Exod. 28:16; 1 Sam. 17:4; Ezek. 43:13). 3. The cubit, which is common, geometrical and sacred. The common cubit, or ordinary one, also the small one, is a cubit and a half, or twenty-four fingers, so that the measure of this cubit is a man's hand, that which extends from the outer angle of the bent arm to the tip of the middle finger; not indeed in the arm of a boy, but in that of a man of full age, say about thirty years old; not of a giant either, but of a well-proportioned stature, that is, proportioned in all parts, such as Adam is thought to have been when he was created by God, and Jesus Christ when he was crucified. This cubit makes up about a quarter of the man whose it is. It is also called the civil and architects' cubit. The geometrical cubit makes up six common cubits. The sacred cubit, or legal and ecclesiastical one, likewise that of the sanctuary, of truth and of the building, that is, the temple: this cubit, I say, was twice as large as the common one. Some nevertheless think that the common cubit was five palms and the sacred one six. For the common cubit see Gen. 7:20; Num. 11:31; 1 Kings 7; for the sacred one Exod. 25, 26, 27, 30; 1 Kings 6 and 7; and 2 Chron. 3:3, where it is called the principal measure. 4. The reed, or rod and measuring staff, six sacred cubits long (Ezek. 40:3; Rev. 11:1; 21:15). 5. The cord, of arbitrary length, and varying with different people (Josh. 17).

units.la: 2. Sam. 8. Amos 7. v. 17. 6. Stadium, passuum 125. siue pedum 625. ita vt octo stadia complectantur vnum milliare Italicum. Luc. 24. verf. 13. Apoc. 14. & 21. 7. Milliare, mille passuum populi cuiusuis. Hebraicum ig. milliare Hebraicos, Chaldaicum Chaldaicos continebat passus. Matth. 5. verf. 41. 7. Iter sabbati, σαββατον, milliari maiori Hebraeorum. Act. 1. verf. 12. 8. Iugerum, dimidia pars milliaris 1. Sam. 14. v. 15.
units.tr: 2 Sam. 8; Amos 7:17. 6. Stadium: 125 paces, or 625 feet, so that eight stadia make one Italian mile. Luke 24:13; Rev. 14 and 21. 7. Mile: a thousand paces of any people. The Hebrew mile contained 2,000 Hebrew paces, the Chaldean mile Chaldean paces. Matt. 5:41. 7. Sabbath day's journey [σαββατον], the greater mile of the Hebrews. Acts 1:12. 8. Iugerum, half a mile. 1 Sam. 14:15.

units.la: IX. Mensurae latitudinis sunt, quibus explo- ratur magnitudo superficiei, siue area figurae.
units.tr: IX. Measures of breadth are those by which the magnitude of a surface, or the area of a figure, is explored.

units.la: Hic adhibentur mensurae longitudinis, ita vt vnaquaeq; bis sumatur, semel in longitudinem, & semel in latitudinem. Ezech. 48. v. 13. & seqq.
units.tr: Here measures of length are used, each of them taken twice: once for the length and once for the breadth. Ezek. 48:13 and following.

units.la: X. Mensurae profunditatis sunt, quibus explo-ratur capacitas rei: vnde mensurae istae di-cuntur capaces. Suntque aridorum, vel liquidorum. Mensura aridorum in sacris sunt, 1. Kabus, mensura minima, 24. ouorum gallinaceorum. 2. Reg. 6. v. 25.
units.tr: X. Measures of depth are those by which the capacity of a thing is explored; hence these measures are called capacious. They are of dry or of liquid things. The measures for dry things in Scripture are: (1) the cab, the smallest measure, equal to 24 hen's eggs. 2 Kings 6:25.

units.la: 2. Gomer, siue Homer, decima pars Ephae; siue Ouorum 43. & quintae partis oui. Exod. 16. v. 37. 3. Seah, siue Satum, tertia pars Ephae, siue ouorum 144. Gen. 18. v. 6. Matth. 13. v. 33. 4. Epha, seu Ephi, trium satorum, seu 18. caborum. H Iudic. 6. Iudic. 6.v. 19. Ruth. 2.17. Hæc fuit communissima & notissima Hebræorum mensura, & quasi reliquarum mensurarum mensura, quæ tantum capiebat in aridis, quantum in liquidis bathus. 5. Letech, siue Semicorus, 5.epharum. Hos.3.v.2. 6. Corus, siue Chomer, amplissima aridorum mensura, 10.epharum. 1.Reg. 4.verf. 22.cap. 5.ver. 11. 2.Chron. 27.v.5.Luc. 16.v.7. Sequuntur mensura liquidorum in sacris, hoc ordine. 1.Logus, mensura minima, erat vigesima quarta pars sati, seu duodecima hinis. Leuit.14. 2. Hin, sexta pars bathi, capiens 12.logos. Exod.29. v. 40.c. 30.v. 24.Leuit. 19.v.36. 3. Bathus, mensura amplissima, eiusdem capacitatis in liquidis, cuius erat epha in aridis. Fuit 72.logorum, (u limidiæ[?] ohmæ nostratis. 1.Reg. 7.v.26. 2.Paral. 4.v.5. Bathus præcisè capiebat amphoram, siue metretam, seu cadum. Hinc colligere est, quantum ceperint (ex hydriæ seu aquales Iohan.2.v.6. nimirum singulæ binas aut ternas amphoras id est bathos totidem, qui efficiunt ohmas nostrates sex. Cæterum pondera etiam seruiunt explorandæ magnitudini corporum siue solidorum. In sacris celebrantur ista. 1. Siclus; qui erat sacer, regius & communis. Sacer in auro ponderabat aureos Vngaricos quatuor. Num. 7.v.50. communis, duos Gen.24.v.22. sacer in argento ponderabat dimidium Imperialem thalerum, Num. 7.v.13. communis quadrantem. 2.Sam.14.verf. 27. sacer in ære & ferro semunciam, communis didrachmum. 1.Sam. 17.v.57. 2.Sam. 21.v.16. Ad siclum regium quod attinet, ille ponderabat tres drachmas, drei Quintlein[?]. 2.Maneh vulgaris, ponderabat 15. thaleros imperiales; regia totidem; sanctuarij, 30. imperiales. 1.Reg. 10.v.17. 2.Paral. 9.v.16. Neh. 7.v.71. 72. Ezech. 45.v.12. 3. Kikar vulgare minus, ponderabat 750. Imperiales: maius, 1250. regium, 1125. sanctuarij, 1500. Imperiales. 1.Reg. 16.verf. 26. Exod. 38.v.25. 1.Reg. 9.v.14. Exod. 39.verf. 24. Intellige hic Kikar ponderale, non nummarium.
units.tr: (2) The gomer, or omer, a tenth part of the ephah, or 43 and a fifth eggs. Exod. 16:37. (3) The seah, a third part of the ephah, or 144 eggs. Gen. 18:6; Matt. 13:33. (4) The ephah, or ephi, of three seahs, or 18 cabs. Judg. 6:19; Ruth 2:17. This was the most common and best-known Hebrew measure, and as it were the measure of the other measures: for dry goods it held as much as the bath held of liquids. (5) The letech, or semicorus, of five ephahs. Hos. 3:2. (6) The corus, or chomer, the largest dry measure, of ten ephahs. 1 Reg. 4:22; 5:11; 2 Chron. 27:5; Luke 16:7. Next follow the measures for liquids in Scripture, in this order: (1) the log, the smallest measure, was the twenty-fourth part of a seah, or the twelfth of a hin. Lev. 14. (2) The hin, a sixth part of the bath, holding 12 logs. Exod. 29:40; 30:24; Lev. 19:36. (3) The bath, the largest measure, of the same liquid capacity that the ephah had for dry goods. It was of 72 logs (about half of our own ohm). 1 Reg. 7:26; 2 Chron. 4:5. The bath held precisely one amphora, or metretes, or cadus. From this one may gather how much the water-jars held: John 2:6, namely each holding two or three amphorae, that is, as many baths, which make six of our ohms. Moreover, weights also serve to explore the magnitude of bodies or solids. In Scripture these are the following. (1) The shekel, which was sacred, royal and common. The sacred shekel in gold weighed four Hungarian ducats. Num. 7:50. The common shekel in gold weighed two. Gen. 24:22. The sacred shekel in silver weighed half an imperial thaler. Num. 7:13. The common shekel in silver weighed a quarter. 2 Sam. 14:27. The sacred shekel in bronze and iron weighed half an ounce; the common weighed a didrachm. 1 Sam. 17:57; 2 Sam. 21:16. As for the royal shekel, it weighed three drachms, "drei Quintlein". (2) The maneh: the common maneh weighed 15 imperial thalers; the royal one the same; the sanctuary maneh 30 imperial thalers. 1 Kings 10:17; 2 Chron. 9:16; Neh. 7:71-72; Ezek. 45:12. (3) The kikar: the lesser common kikar weighed 750 imperial thalers; the greater 1,250; the royal 1,125; the sanctuary kikar 1,500 imperial thalers. 1 Kings 16:26; Exod. 38:25; 1 Kings 9:14; Exod. 39:24. Understand here the kikar as a unit of weight, not as a coin.

units.la: Intellige hic Kikar ponderale, non nummarium.
units.tr: Understand here the kikar as a unit of weight, not as a coin.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: COSMOGRAPHIA.
units.tr: COSMOGRAPHY.

units.la: I. COsmographia sacra est sphaerae mundi scientia ex S. literis illustrata.
units.tr: I. Sacred cosmography is the knowledge of the sphere of the world, illustrated from the Sacred Writings.

units.la: II. Sphaera mundi est systema constans ex cœlo & terrâ. Hic itaque traduntur ea, quæ communiter conveniunt globo cœlesti & terrestri.
units.tr: II. The sphere of the world is a system made up of heaven and earth. Here, therefore, are set out those things which apply in common to the celestial and terrestrial globe.

units.la: III. In Sphærâ mundi considerantur cardines & circuli. De cardinibus aliquid invenitur in Scriptura sacra: circuli sunt hypotheses artificum.
units.tr: III. In the sphere of the world, the poles and circles are considered. Something about the poles is found in Holy Scripture; the circles are hypotheses of the craftsmen.

units.la: IV. Cardines mundi sunt quatuor: videlicet oriens & occidens, septentrio & meridies. Gen. 13. verf. 14. Psal. 107. verf. 3. Oriens est veluti porta, per quam stellæ ingrediuntur in horizontem: occidens, per quem discedunt ex horizonte: Septentrio est cardo, in quo locu habet polus superior: meridies, in quo inferior. In Scriptura vocatur quatuor anguli terræ. Apoc. 7. v. 1. c. 20. v. 8. Crebro fit illorum mentio: ut orientis sive ortus Gen. 11. v. 2. c. 12. v. 8. Exod. 27. v. 13. Ios. 16. 17. 18. Ezech. 40. 41. 42. 43. 44. 45. 46. 47. Matth. 2. v. 1. 2. 9. Luc. 13. v. 29. Apoc. 21. v. 13. occidentis sive occasus Gen. 12. v. 8. c. 13. v. 14. Exod. 27. v. 12. Ios. 11. v. 3. Ezech. 46. & 48. Zach. 14. verf. 4. Matth. 24. v. 27. Luc. 13. v. 29. septentrionis Gen. 28. v. 14. Iudic. 21. verf. 19. Ezech. 47. & 48. meridiei Gen. 12. verf. 9. Exod. 27. v. 9. Deut. 1. v. 7. Ezech. 47. & 48. In quibusdam locis iam citatis coniunguntur duo vel plures cardines. Cæterum iuxta hos cardines numeratur longitudo & latitudo mundi: quæ duo coniunguntur Gen. 13. v. 17. Longitudo mundi numeratur ab oriente versus occidentem, vel contra: latitudo, à septentrione versus meridiem, vel vicißim.
units.tr: IV. There are four poles of the world: namely east and west, north and south. Gen. 13. verse 14. Psal. 107. verse 3. The east is as it were a gate through which the stars enter the horizon; the west, through which they depart from the horizon; the north is the pole in which the upper pole lies; the south, that in which the lower one lies. In Scripture they are called the four corners of the earth. Rev. 7. v. 1. c. 20. v. 8. Mention of them is frequent: of the east or rising Gen. 11. v. 2. c. 12. v. 8. Exod. 27. v. 13. Josh. 16. 17. 18. Ezek. 40. 41. 42. 43. 44. 45. 46. 47. Matt. 2. v. 1. 2. 9. Luke 13. v. 29. Rev. 21. v. 13. of the west or setting Gen. 12. v. 8. c. 13. v. 14. Exod. 27. v. 12. Josh. 11. v. 3. Ezek. 46. & 48. Zech. 14. verse 4. Matt. 24. v. 27. Luke 13. v. 29. of the north Gen. 28. v. 14. Judg. 21. verse 19. Ezek. 47. & 48. of the south Gen. 12. verse 9. Exod. 27. v. 9. Deut. 1. v. 7. Ezek. 47. & 48. In some of the places already cited two or more poles are joined together. Moreover, according to these poles the length and breadth of the world are reckoned: these two are joined together Gen. 13. v. 17. Longitude of the world is reckoned from east towards west, or the reverse; latitude from north towards south, or vice versa.

units.la: V. Circuli, quos oportet in Sphæra mundi, hoc est, tum in cœlo, tum in terra imaginari, sunt numero octo. Ex his sunt quatuor maiores, qui mundum diuidunt in duas partes æquales; vt horizon, meridianus, æquator, & Zodiacus: & totidem minores, qui mundum diuidunt in duas partes inæquales; vt tropicus cancri & capricorni, polaris arcticus & antarcticus. Quod attinet ad duos coluros, vnum solstitiorum, alterum æqui noctiorum, illi locum duntaxat habent in cœlo. Ex his circulis horiζon visibilem cœli & terræ partem ab inuisibili dirimit: meridianus inter ortum & occasum est medius, ita vt respondeat puncto verticali: æquator inter duos mundi polos, siue inter septentrionem & meridiem, est medius: Zodiacus obliquè secat æquatorem, duosque tropicos attingit: tropicus cancri in superiori, capricorni, in inferiori parte Zodiacum contingit: polaris arcticus circuit polum superiorem, antarcticus, inferiorem.
units.tr: V. The circles which must be imagined in the sphere of the world, that is, both in heaven and on earth, are eight in number. Of these, four are greater, which divide the world into two equal parts: namely the horizon, the meridian, the equator, and the zodiac; and as many smaller, which divide the world into two unequal parts: namely the tropic of Cancer and of Capricorn, and the arctic and antarctic polar circles. As for the two colures, one of the solstices and the other of the equinoxes, these have a place in heaven only. Of these circles, the horizon separates the visible part of heaven and earth from the invisible; the meridian is midway between rising and setting, so that it passes through the vertical point; the equator is midway between the two poles of the world, or between north and south; the zodiac cuts the equator obliquely and touches the two tropics; the tropic of Cancer touches the zodiac in its upper part, and that of Capricorn in its lower part; the arctic polar circle encircles the upper pole, the antarctic the lower.

units.la: Hos circulos oportet partim mente concipere, partim delineare. Mente concipiendi sunt partim in cœlo & in terra, partim in museo, partim in compasso, partim denique in solario. Delineandi sunt in globo cœlesti & terrestri, in Sphæra pertusa siue armillari, in mappis siue tabulis geographicis tum vniuersalibus, tum particularibus; denique in compasso & solario maioribus.
units.tr: These circles must be partly grasped in the mind and partly drawn. Some are to be conceived in the mind in heaven and on earth, some in the museum, some in the compass, and some finally in the sundial. They are to be drawn on the celestial and terrestrial globe, on the perforated or armillary sphere, on maps or geographical charts, both universal and particular; and finally on the larger compass and sundial.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: I. Vranoscopia sacra complectitur duas solum partes: videlicet Sphæricam, & Cōputum. Nihil enim ex sacris potest colligi, quod illustret Theoriam planetarum, & Astrologiam, quæ sunt duæ reliquæ partes Vranoscopiæ.
units.tr: I. Sacred uranoscopy embraces only two parts, namely the spherical and the computation. For nothing can be gathered from the sacred writings that illustrates the theory of the planets and astrology, which are the two remaining parts of uranoscopy.

units.la: II. Sphærica sacra explicat dimensionem cœli & stellarum fermè ex S. literis. Duæ itaque sunt illius partes. Appellatur etiam hæc Astronomiæ pars Sphæra cœlestis.
units.tr: II. Sacred spherics explains the dimension of heaven and the stars, almost entirely from the Sacred Writings. Its parts are therefore two. This part of astronomy is also called the celestial sphere.

units.la: III. Dimensio cœli est exploratio longitudinis, latitudinis, & altitudinis. Omne siquidem corpus habet tres istas dimensiones. Intelligitur autem hoc loco cœlum stelliferum. Memineris hic per longitudinem intelligi peripheriam, per latitudinem, superficiem. Alias longitudo est linea ab ortu versus occasum ducta, vel contra: & latitudo, linea ducta a septentrione versus meridiem, vel contrà.
units.tr: III. The dimension of heaven is the investigation of its length, breadth, and height. For every body has these three dimensions. In this place, however, the starry heaven is meant. You should remember that here by length is understood the periphery, and by breadth the surface. Otherwise, length is a line drawn from east towards west, or the reverse; and breadth a line drawn from north towards south, or the reverse.

units.la: IV. Longitudo cœli stelliferi, sive firmamenti est semidiametrorum terræ 88000. id est, milliarium Germ. 7568000. Quilibet circulus apud mathematicos est graduum 360. Prout autem circulus est maior vel minor, ita etiam gradus sunt maiores & minores. Uni gradui cœlesti respondent 15. milliaria Germ. in globo terrestri. At in cœlo unus gradus habet longe plura milliaria, prout circulus in corpore cœlesti attollitur, vel deprimitur. Sic in firmamento circulus magnus extenditur semidiametris terræ 88000. seu milliarib. 7568000. ut iam diximus. At circulus diurnus solis est milliarium Germanicorum 6540914. Nimirum quia sol est inferiori loco quam firmamentum, circulus eius etiam sit[?] minor. Franciscus Maurolicus existimat, quantitatem cœli æquare milliaria Germanica vicies quinquagies quater millena, nouies mille centum & sexaginta. Cæterum longitudinem cœli metimur per æquatorem, Zodiacum, meridianum, coluros, horizontem, tropicos & polares: quorum circulorum situs & officia in globo cœlesti sunt manifesta. Quod si longitudo & latitudo sumantur more vulgari, ex circulis hisce meridianus & coluri serviunt latitudini, reliqui, longitudini.
units.tr: IV. The length of the starry heaven, or firmament, is 88,000 semidiameters of the earth, that is, 7,568,000 German miles. Every circle, among mathematicians, has 360 degrees. However, as a circle is greater or smaller, so too its degrees are greater or smaller. One celestial degree corresponds to 15 German miles on the terrestrial globe. But in heaven one degree has far more miles, according as the circle is raised or lowered in the heavenly body. Thus in the firmament the great circle extends to 88,000 semidiameters of the earth, or 7,568,000 miles, as we have already said. But the daily circle of the sun is 6,540,914 German miles. Clearly, because the sun is in a lower place than the firmament, its circle is also smaller. Francis Maurolico thinks that the quantity of heaven equals twenty times fifty-four thousand, plus nine thousand one hundred and sixty German miles. Moreover, we measure the length of heaven by the equator, the zodiac, the meridian, the colures, the horizon, the tropics and the polar circles, whose position and functions are evident on the celestial globe. But if length and breadth are taken in the common manner, of these circles the meridian and the colures serve for latitude, the rest for longitude.

units.la: V. Latitudo cœli est area ipsius. Hæc est, superficies: eaque tum plana, tum conuexa. Superficies plana est area perimetro inclusa, milliarium Germanic. 388285700000000000. Superficies conuexa est milliarium 155314280000000000. Illa resultat ex multiplicatione semissis circuli maximi in semissem diametri eiusdem circuli: haec ex multiplicatione superficiei planae per 4.
units.tr: V. The breadth of heaven is its area. This is its surface, and that both flat and convex. A flat surface is an area enclosed by a perimeter, 388,285,700,000,000,000 German miles. A convex surface is 155,314,280,000,000,000 miles. The former results from multiplying half of the greatest circle by half of the diameter of the same circle; the latter from multiplying the flat surface by 4.

units.la: VI. Altitudo caeli est primo ipsius distantia a terra, deinde eiusdem capacitas.
units.tr: VI. The height of the heaven is, first, its distance from the earth, and then its capacity.

units.la: Altitudo iuxta Tychonem est milliarium Germ. 12040000. siue semidiametrorum terrę 14000. Eant nunc Epicurei, & negent esse Deum. Capacitas caeli inde a terra est mill. Germ. 3109391885600000000.
units.tr: According to Tycho, the height is 12,040,000 German miles, or 14,000 semidiameters of the earth. Let the Epicureans now go and deny that there is a God. The capacity of the heaven from the earth is 3,109,391,885,600,000,000 German miles.

units.la: VII. Dimensio stellarum potissimum specta- tur in altitudine & motu ipsarum. Sunt autem stellae ordinariae, vel extraordinariae. VIII. Stellae ordinariae sunt luminaria quar- to creationis die a Deo collocata in expanso, ad distinctionem faciendum inter diem & noctem, ut sint in signa cum tempestatibus, tum diebus, & annis, & adferant lucem super terram. Haec definitio totidem verbis desumta est ex Gen. 1. v. 14. 15. IX. Luminaria ista sunt magna, vel parua. Haec distributio sumta est ex Gen. 1. v. 16.
units.tr: VII. The magnitude of the stars is chiefly considered in their height and motion. Stars are either ordinary or extraordinary. VIII. The ordinary stars are the lights that God placed in the firmament on the fourth day of creation, to divide day from night, so that they serve as signs for seasons, for days and for years, and give light upon the earth. This definition is taken word for word from Genesis 1:14–15. IX. These lights are either great or small. This division is taken from Genesis 1:16.

units.la: X. Luminaria magna sunt duo, sol & luna. Sol est luminare maius, conditum ad praefecturam diei: luna est luminare minus, conditum ad praefecturam noctis. Gen. 1. v. 16. Vtrumque quidem est magnum respectu reliquarum stellarum: sed luna comparata cum sole est luminare minus. At ais, multae stellae sunt multo maiores sole & luna. Curitaque Scriptura solem & lunam appellat luminaria magna. Resp. Intellige hic magnitudinem, non molis, sed virtutis, siue luminis. Caeterum sol est maior terra centies sexagies sexies, vel septies: quando est altissimus, distat a terra iuxta Tychonem milliaribus Germanic. 1016520. iuxta alios, decies centies mille octingenti sexaginta octo: movetur singulis horis, milliaribus 172538[?]. ortu & occasu suo efficit diem & noctem: obliquo incessu efficit vicissitudinem sementis & messis, frigoris & aestus, aestatis & hyemis. Vide Psal.19.v.6.7. Eccles. 1.v.5.6. Gen.8.v.vlt. Luna est minor terrâ tricies novies: distat a terra 44916. seu numero rotundo 50000. quinquaginta millibus milliarium Germanicorum: obliquo suo incessu efficit mensem lunarem. Psal.104.v.19. Solis & lunae accidit eclipsis: eaque tum naturalis, tum supernaturalis. Eclipsis solis naturalis fit in coniunctione luminarium; lunae, in oppositione diametrali eorundem. Supernaturalis fit extra duos istos casus: qualis fuit eclipsis solis tempore passionis Christi. Luc. 23. v. 45.
units.tr: X. There are two great lights, the sun and the moon. The sun is the greater light, made to rule the day; the moon is the lesser light, made to rule the night (Gen. 1:16). Both are indeed great in comparison with the other stars, but the moon compared with the sun is the lesser light. But you say: many stars are much greater than the sun and the moon, so why does Scripture call the sun and the moon great lights? I answer: understand greatness here not of bulk but of power, that is, of light. Moreover, the sun is about 166 times larger than the earth, or seven times as large; when it is at its highest it is distant from the earth, according to Tycho, 1,016,520 German miles, and according to others 10,000,000 ... 868 (sic: decies centies mille octingenti sexaginta octo). It moves at 172,538 miles each hour. By its rising and setting it makes day and night; by its oblique course it brings about the alternation of sowing and harvest, of cold and heat, of summer and winter. See Psalm 19:6–7; Ecclesiastes 1:5–6; Genesis 8:22. The moon is thirty-nine times smaller than the earth; it is distant from the earth 44,916, or in round numbers 50,000 German miles; by its oblique course it makes the lunar month. Psalm 104:19. An eclipse of the sun and moon occurs, and it is both natural and supernatural. A natural eclipse of the sun happens at the conjunction of the lights, and of the moon at their diametrical opposition. A supernatural eclipse happens outside these two cases, such as the eclipse of the sun at the time of Christ's passion (Luke 23:45).

units.la: XI. Luminaria parua sunt omnes stellae ordinarie lucentes praeter solem & lunam. Hæpersynecdochen appellantur stellae Gen. 1.v.16. ubi Deus dicitur fecisse solem, lunam, & stellas. Sic quoque alibi, ut Gen.37.v.9. Psal.8.v.4. & 136.v.9. & 148.v.3. Eccles.12. v.2. De stellis istis Job ita philosophatur cap.9. verf.9. Qui facit Arcturum, Orionem, ac Pleiadas, ac penetralia Austri. Et Deus eandem istarum stellarum tetrachotomiam tradit licet alio ordine Job.38.v.31.32. his verbis: An constringes delicias pleiadum? aut lora Orionis dissolues? Educes ne remotiora signa, quodque tempore suo? aut Arcturum cum filiis suis duces? Horum verborum sensus genuinus hic est. Pleiades, siue Vergiliae, una cum vere oriuntur, adeoque suas delicias tum proferunt; & durant usque ad autumnum. Orion totis noctibus mense Decembri conspicitur, & deinceps usq; ad ortum Vergiliarum in nostro hemisphærio versatur, & suo ortu tanq̃ loro constringit aerem frigore. Remotiora signa, siue, penetralia Austri, sunt sidera meridionalia, a nostro aspectu remota. Hæc designant nobis æstatem, duce Canicula. Arcturus cum suis filiis, id est, stellis, oritur initio septembris, vndecim ante aequinoctium diebus. Ex his sequentia obseruamus ἀκροάματα[?]. 1. In verbis Iob indicatur initium anni ciuilis, eiusque decursus. Ille siquidem ab autumno incipit. At in verbis Dei indicatur initium anni sacri siue ecclesiastici: vtpote qui a vere incipit.
units.tr: XI. The lesser lights are all the ordinary shining stars apart from the sun and the moon. By synecdoche these are called stars in Genesis 1:16, where God is said to have made the sun, the moon and the stars. So also elsewhere, as in Genesis 37:9, Psalm 8:4, 136:9, 148:3, Ecclesiastes 12:2. Concerning these stars Job philosophises thus in chapter 9, verse 9: who makes Arcturus, Orion and the Pleiades, and the chambers of the south. And God gives the same fourfold division of these stars, though in a different order, in Job 38:31–32, in these words: Can you bind the sweet influences of the Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?
