Can you bring forth the constellations in their season? Or can you guide Arcturus with his sons? The true sense of these words is this. The Pleiades, or Vergiliae, rise together with spring, and so then they bring forth their sweet influences; and they last until autumn. Orion is seen all night in the month of December, and then remains in our hemisphere until the rising of the Pleiades, and by its rising, as with a band, it binds the air with cold. The remoter constellations, or the chambers of the south, are the southern stars, remote from our view. These mark for us the summer, led by the Dog Star. Arcturus with his sons, that is, with his stars, rises at the beginning of September, eleven days before the equinox. From these things we observe the following points [ἀκροάματα]. 1. In the words of Job the beginning of the civil year and its course are indicated. For that begins in autumn. But in the words of God the beginning of the sacred or ecclesiastical year is indicated, since that begins in spring.

units.la: 2. Effecta stellarum sunt praebere delicias, vel aduehere frigus, tempestates & imbres: item discernere quatuor partes anni, ver, aestatem, autumnum, & hyemem. 3. Stellae vel sunt nobis euidenter conspicuae, vel a nobis remotiores. Illae sunt septentrionales, hae meridionales, quae eleganter dicuntur cameris siue penetralibus Austri includi, nostri scil. respectu. 4. Omnes stellae ad quatuor haec capita, tanquam familias, reuocari possunt: videl. ad naturam Arcturi, Pleiadum, Orionis, & Caniculae. 5. Arcturus designat stellas cis Zodiacum; Pleiades, in Zodiaco; Orion & Canicula, vltra Zodiacum.
units.tr: 2. The effects of the stars are to give delights, or to bring cold, storms and rain, and also to distinguish the four seasons of the year: spring, summer, autumn and winter. 3. Some stars are plainly visible to us, others are more remote from us. The former are northern, the latter southern, which are elegantly said to be enclosed in the chambers or recesses of the south, with respect to us. 4. All stars can be referred to these four heads, as to families: namely, to the nature of Arcturus, of the Pleiades, of Orion, and of the Dog Star. 5. Arcturus denotes the stars on this side of the Zodiac; the Pleiades, those in the Zodiac; Orion and the Dog Star, those beyond the Zodiac.

units.la: XII. Stellae extraordinariae sunt, quae singu- lari Dei providentia ad tempus lucent.
units.tr: XII. Extraordinary stars are those which shine for a time by the singular providence of God.

units.la: Talis fuit stella ista Matth. 2. v. 2. ubi magi dicunt, Vidimus enim eius stellam in oriente: ubi noua illa stella dicitur stella Christi, hoc est, signum natiuitatis Christi, veri illius Phosphori animarum nostrarum. In harum stellarum numerum etiam referri debent nouae illae stellae an. 1572. 1576.85.96. 1602.607. Constat enim faces istas non fuisse cometas, sed astra.
units.tr: Such was that star in Matthew 2:2, where the magi say, For we have seen his star in the east: which new star is called the star of Christ, that is, the sign of the nativity of Christ, that true Phosphorus of our souls. To the number of these stars should also be referred those new stars of the years 1572, 1576, 1585, 1596, 1602 and 1607. For it is certain that those torches were not comets but stars.

units.la: COMPUTUS SACER.
units.tr: THE SACRED COMPUTATION.

units.la: I. COmputus sacer explicat dimensionem temporis e Scriptura. Naturam caeli, stellarum, & temporis explicat Physica: dimensionem caeli & stellarum, Sphaerica, temporis, Computus.
units.tr: I. Sacred computation explains the measurement of time from Scripture. Physics explains the nature of the heavens, the stars and time; spherics explains the measurement of the heavens and the stars; computation explains time.

units.la: II. Tempus, cuius meminerunt sacrae literae, est minus, vel maius. Minus est dies: maius est septimana, mensis, & annus.
units.tr: II. The time mentioned in the sacred letters is either smaller or larger. The smaller is the day; the larger are the week, the month and the year.

units.la: III. Dies proprie est illud tempus, quo sol nobis lucet. Sic enim legimus Gen. 1. v. 5. Lucemque Deus vocauit diem, tenebras vero noctem. Et hic est dies naturalis, cui opponitur nox. Hinc Isidorus lib. 3. c. 50. eleganter ait: Sol oriens diem facit, occidens noctem inducit. Nam dies est sol supra terras, nox est sol sub terra. Et lib. 5. c. 30. Dies est praesentia solis. Sic & Gyraldus lib. de annis & mensibus: Naturalis dies est tempus, ab exoriente sole ad solis occasum. Diei naturali opponitur dies ciuilis: de quo idem Gyraldus d.l. Ciuilis dies (quem legitimum Isidorus vocat) tempus id est, quod vno fit coeli circumactu, quo dies verus, & nox continentur: vt cum dicimus, aliquem dies tantum 30. vixisse. Tunc enim etiam noctes intelligimus. De hoc die accipiendum est comma illud Gen. 1. v. 5. Sic fuit vespera, & fuit mane dies primi: & sic deinceps verf. 8. 13. 19. 23.
units.tr: III. Properly speaking, a day is that time in which the sun shines on us. For so we read in Gen. 1. v. 5. And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night. This is the natural day, which is opposed to night. Hence Isidore, book 3, chapter 50, neatly says: The rising sun makes the day, the setting sun brings on the night. For day is the sun above the earth, night is the sun below the earth. And book 5, chapter 30: Day is the presence of the sun. So also Gyraldus, in his work on years and months: The natural day is the time from sunrise to sunset. Opposed to the natural day is the civil day, of which the same Gyraldus, in the place cited, says: The civil day (which Isidore calls the lawful day) is the time that is completed by one turn of the heavens, in which the true day and the night are contained, as when we say that someone lived only thirty days. For then we also understand the nights. It is of this day that the passage Gen. 1. v. 5, And there was evening and there was morning, one day must be understood, and so on in verses 8, 13, 19, 23.

units.la: 31. Priori itaque modo nox opponitur diei, posteriori, est pars diei: unde dies ciuilis eleganter appellatur Hebraeis tempus matutinum & vespertinum, Dan. 8. v 14. 26. & Graecis νυχθήμερον, & ἡμερονύχιος, & definitur spatium viginti quatuor horarum. Hoc autem spatium appellatur dies ciuilis, quia illo vtimur in communi & ciuili vita. Appellatur etiam dies artificialis eodem sensu: quia artifices, hoc est, astronomi, & alij in computis & Kalendariis hoc die vtuntur. Interim videas passim confundi has appellationes, vt Cuiacius recte obseruat lib. 15. obseru. c. 32. ita nempe vt dies naturalis vocetur spatium 24. horarum, ciuilis seu artificialis, tempus lucis. Porro dies naturalis, itemque nox, diuiditur in quaternas partes, quae respondent veri, aestati, autumno & hyemi: & dies ciuilis, id est, νυχθήμερον, ab Hebraeis in quatuor partes fuit diuisus, quas vigilias vocabant. Prima vigilia erat a vespere, secunda a media nocte, tertia a mane, quarta a meridie. Exod. 14. v. 24. Iudic. 7. v. 11. 19. Matth. 14. v. 25. Marc. 6. v. 48. Luc. 2. v. 8. c. 12. v. 38. Quidam tamen putant noctem fuisse diuisam in quatuor vigilias, quibus excubiae fiebant. Caeterum Graeci in 24. horas partiti sunt diem ciuilem: quae partitio tandem ad Romanos, & ab illis ad Iudaeos sub ipsorum imperio translata est. Primam diei horam, cum primum diescieret, vocabant: duodecimam, extremum diei tempus. Par horarum noctis ratio. Quo numero cum dies & nox circumscriberetur, pro quoque anni tempore, ac dierum noctiumque productione atque contractione, longiores quoque ac breviores horas, diversis quidem temporibus, fuisse necesse est. Atque hae dicuntur horae inaequales, de quibus accipiendum est illud Christi Iohan. II. Nonne duodecim horae sunt diei? Huiusmodi horas putantur antiqui habuisse usque ad annum Christi 300. quo dicunt coepisse horas aequales, quae semper sunt eiusdem quantitatis, ut sunt horae nostrates. Unde fit ut dies & nox nunc habeant plures, nunc pauciores horas, prout sunt longiores vel breviores. Horae illae nostrae tempore aequinoctiali ita conveniunt cum horis Iudaeorum. Prima Iudaeorum est nobis sexta matutina, tertia est nona, sexta est duodecima seu meridies, duodecima est sexta vespertina. Itaque locus Matth. 27. A sexta hora tenebrae factae sunt super universam terram, usque ad horam nonam, sic exponi debet, a nostra duodecima ad tertiam. Christus itaque crucifixus est circa horam sextam. Cur vero Marcus scribit c. 15. v. 25. id factum esse hora tertia? Resp. Ibi intelligitur vel tertia pars diei, quae horam 9. 10. 11. 12. complectitur: vel ultimus quadrans, qui appellabatur hora tertia. Solebant enim veteres partiri diem in tres partes, ita ut quilibet complecteretur quatuor horas: vel in quatuor quadrantes ternarum horarum, eosque ab ultima cuiusque quadrantis hora denominabant. Prioris modi typus est: I. 1.2.3.4. II. 5.6.7.8. III. 9.10.11.12.
units.tr: 31. In the former sense, then, night is opposed to day; in the latter sense, night is a part of the day. Hence the civil day is elegantly called by the Hebrews the morning and evening time, Dan. 8. v. 14, 26., and by the Greeks [nychthemeron] and [hemeronychios], and it is defined as a space of twenty-four hours. This space is called the civil day because we use it in common and civil life. It is also called the artificial day in the same sense, because artificers, that is, astronomers, and others use this day in their calculations and calendars. Meanwhile you may see these designations commonly confused, as Cuiacius rightly observes, book 15 of Observations, chapter 32, so that the natural day is called the space of twenty-four hours, and the civil or artificial day the time of light. Further, the natural day, and likewise the night, is divided into four parts, which correspond to spring, summer, autumn and winter. The civil day, that is, the [nychthemeron], was divided by the Hebrews into four parts, which they called watches. The first watch was from evening, the second from midnight, the third from morning, the fourth from noon. Exod. 14. v. 24. Judg. 7. v. 11, 19. Matt. 14. v. 25. Mark 6. v. 48. Luke 2. v. 8. ch. 12. v. 38. Some, however, think that the night was divided into four watches, during which the night guards kept vigil. Moreover, the Greeks divided the civil day into twenty-four hours; this division was at last transferred to the Romans, and from them to the Jews under their rule. The first hour of the day they called the hour when day began to dawn; the twelfth, the last part of the day. The night's hours are reckoned in the same way. Since day and night were bounded by this number, it was necessary that, according to the time of year and the lengthening and shortening of days and nights, the hours should be longer or shorter at different times. These are called unequal hours, and it is of them that the saying of Christ must be understood: John 11, Are there not twelve hours in the day? The ancients are thought to have used such hours until the year of Christ 300, from which time they say equal hours began, which are always of the same length, as our hours are. Hence it comes about that day and night now have more hours, now fewer, according as they are longer or shorter. At the equinox our hours agree with the hours of the Jews in this way: the first hour of the Jews is for us the sixth in the morning, the third is the ninth, the sixth is the twelfth or noon, the twelfth is the sixth in the evening. Thus the passage Matt. 27, From the sixth hour there was darkness over the whole earth, until the ninth hour must be explained as running from our twelfth to our third hour. Christ was therefore crucified about the sixth hour. But why does Mark write, ch. 15. v. 25, that this happened at the third hour? Answer: here is meant either the third part of the day, which takes in the hours 9, 10, 11, 12; or the last quarter, which was called the third hour. For the ancients were accustomed to divide the day into three parts, each containing four hours; or into four quarters of three hours each, and they named each quarter from its last hour. The pattern of the former way is: I. 1, 2, 3, 4. II. 5, 6, 7, 8. III. 9, 10, 11, 12.

units.la: Posterioris modi typus est iste: I. 1. 2. 3. II. 4. 5. 6. III. 7. 8. 9. IV. 10. 11. 12. Iuxta priorem typum dicendum est, crucifixionem Christi fuisse absolutam hora tertia maiore, iuxta posteriorem, coepisse hora tertia maiore, post sextam videl. horam minorem. Per maiores horas intellige tres illas 5 partes & quatuor quadrantes diei, per minores, proprie dictas. Haec ratio non satisfacit Casaubono, qui exercit.16. pag.479. inclinat in sententiam eorum, qui putant esse mendam librarij in litera numerali. Porro datur in Scripturis dies propheticus, qui est annus solaris vel lunaris. Vide 10 Dan.12.v.11.12. Apoc.11.v.3.
units.tr: The pattern of the latter way is this: I. 1, 2, 3. II. 4, 5, 6. III. 7, 8, 9. IV. 10, 11, 12. According to the former pattern, it must be said that the crucifixion of Christ was completed in the third of the greater hours; according to the latter, that it began in the third greater hour, after the sixth, namely the lesser hour. By greater hours understand those three parts and four quarters of the day; by lesser, those properly so called. This explanation does not satisfy Casaubon, who, Exercitation 16, p. 479, inclines to the opinion of those who think there is an error of a scribe in the numeral letter. Further, in the Scriptures there is a prophetic day, which is a solar or lunar year. See Dan. 12. v. 11, 12; Rev. 11. v. 3.

units.la: IV. Septimana est septem dierum interual- lum.
units.tr: IV. A week is an interval of seven days.

units.la: De hac Isidorus eleganter lib.5.c.32. Hebdomada, inquit, dicta a numero septem dierum, quorum repetitione & menses, & anni, & seculaparaguntur. Et paulo post: Octauus autem dies, id est primus, est, ad quem redditur, & a quo rursus hebdomadis feries orditur. Hoc dierum systema fuit sancitum a Deo Gen.2.v.2.3. Datur etiam in Scriptura septimana annorum, quae est systema annorum septem, in orbem recurrens: estque Mosaica, vel prophetica. Septimana annorum 15 Mosaica dicitur hebdomas annalis remissionis, & septimus ipsius annus appellatur Semittah, licet & ipsa hebdomas appelletur hoc nomine. Vox ista ad verbum est ἄνεσις[?], leuatio oneris, sive excussio debitorum: quia debita remittebantur in fine hebdomadis. Propterea & hebdomas remissionis 20 vocatur. Ac licet ultimus annus proprie remissio vocatur: tamen Iudaei & Samaritae dicunt annum primum, secundum &c. Semittah, totam hebdomadem Semittah vocantes. Sic cum septimus dies Sabbath vocatur: tamen & hoc nomine tota hebdomoda vocatur ab 25 Hebraeis. Leuit.23.v.15. Amos.8. Luc.18.v.12. De Semittah vide Deut.15. Septimana prophetica est spatium septem annorum prophetis visitatum. Tales sunt hebdomades sive septimanae Danielis. cap.9.
units.tr: Isidore discusses this elegantly in Isidorus lib.5.c.32. Hebdomada, inquit, ... Let me restate the quotation precisely: Isidore, in lib.5.c.32. says: "A week is so called from the number of seven days, by whose repetition months, years and ages are completed." And a little later: "The eighth day, that is, the first, is that to which the week returns and from which the cycle of days begins again." This system of days was ordained by God in Gen.2.v.2.3. Scripture also knows a septimana annorum, a system of seven years recurring in a cycle, and this is either Mosaic or prophetic. The Mosaic Septimana annorum is the annual week of release, and its seventh year is called Semittah, although the week itself is also called by this name. The word means literally "release" [ἄνεσις], the lifting of a burden, or the shaking off of debts, because debts were remitted at the end of the week. For this reason it is also called the "week of remission." Although the last year is properly called the remission, the Jews and Samaritans call the first year, the second year, and so on, Semittah, calling the whole week Semittah. So too the seventh day is called the Sabbath, yet the Hebrews also call the whole week by this name. Lev. 23:15. Amos 8. Luke 18:12. On the Semittah see Deut. 15. A prophetic week is a span of seven years visited by the prophets. Such are the weeks or sevens of Daniel, ch. 9.

units.la: V. Mensis late sumto vocabulo, est duodecima anni pars: proprie est tempus, lunae cursu definitum. finitum. Ita nempe, vt numeretur à lunæ coniunctione cum sole, vel à prima lunæ apparitione. Posteriori modo Iudæi suos menses numerabant: vtpote qui obseruabant nouâ lunæ faciem. Vulgo hic mensis appellatur lunaris, ad discrimen mensis solaris, qui est transitus solis à signo ad signum. Itaque hoc sensu mensis erit pars anni 12. vt paulo ante diximus. Datur etiam mensis propheticus, qui est annorum 30. Sed nos hoc loco tractamus de mense proprie in Scripturis accipitur, vbi mensis cum luna incipit & terminatur. Etsi enim ante exitu ex Ægypto menses solares vsitati fuerunt in populo Dei: tamen in cōputo sacro non curatur nisi menses lunares, vt patebit ex sequentibus. Principio autem tenendum est, mensem plenum esse dierum 30. cauù, 29. Iudæi tamen definiunt mensem dierum 29. hor. 12. Deinde nomina ista Nisan, Iiar, Siuan, &c. iunt[?] Chaldaica, quæ Iudæi post captiuitatem reuersi retinuerunt. Ante exilium Babylonicum alia fuerunt nomina: vt, primus mensis appellatus fuit Abib, secundus Sif, quæ nomina solum extant in canone: vbi præter hæc duo non inueni nisi has appellationes, mensis primus, secundus, tertius &c. Tertio mensium ordo est duplex, ecclesiasticus siue ciuilis. Ibi primus est Nisan, hic Tisri. Sed iam videamus singulos menses ordine, & dies festos, qui in iis occurrunt, explicemus, deniq; ad nostrates menses applicemus. Primus Iudæorum mensis in anno sacro fuit Nisan siue Abib, Exod. 12. v. 2. Dicitur Abib voce Hebraica q.d. mensem spicæ siue spicarum, q; isto mense spicæ exeant è calamis. Hoc in terra sancta fiebat exeunte Martio nostro, & incipiente Aprili. Nam æquinoctiū vernū erat initium anni ecclesiastici, sicut autumnale, politici. Æquinoctium autem vernū olim sex tantum diebus abfuit à fine Martij. Atq; hinc est, q; plurimi scriptores ecclesiastici mensem Nisan ad Aprilem potius q; ad Martium referunt, Iijar ad Maium, & sic deinceps. Accuratior tamen est illorum connexio, quiNisan ita connectunt cum nostris mensibus, vt pars ipsius aliqua respondeat Martio, maxima Aprili. Defequentium mensium Iudaicorum cum noftratibus cōnexione idem est iudicium. Porrò primus dies huius méfis, vt & sequentium, celebris erat apud Hebraeos, non quòd in eo perinde, ac in die festo ab operibus necessariò cessaretur, sed quòd Deus certis sacrificiis solenni ritu coleretur. Hebraei vocant hunc diem ראש[?] caput, i.e. initium mensis: LXX. Interpretes semper neomeniam: Latinus interpres, nunc neomenias, nunc calendas appellat. Dicitur autem neomenia quasi nouus mensis. Mensis enim cum luna incipiebat, & cum eadem desinebat. Proinde dies primus mensis idem erat, qui primus dies lunae.
units.tr: V. Month, taking the word broadly, is the twelfth part of a year; properly it is a period defined by the course of the moon. That is, it is counted either from the conjunction of the moon with the sun or from the moon's first appearance. The Jews counted their months in the latter way, since they observed the new face of the moon. Commonly this month is called lunar, to distinguish it from the solar month, which is the passage of the sun from one sign to another. So in this sense a month will be the twelfth part of a year, as we said a little earlier. There is also the prophetic month, which is of thirty years. But in this place we are treating of the month as it is properly taken in Scripture, where the month begins and ends with the moon. For although before the exodus from Egypt solar months were in use among the people of God, yet in the sacred calendar only lunar months are reckoned, as will become clear from what follows. First, it must be held that a full month has thirty days and a hollow one twenty-nine; yet the Jews define the month as twenty-nine days and twelve hours. Second, the names Nisan, Iyar, Sivan, etc. are Chaldean, which the Jews retained after they returned from captivity. Before the Babylonian exile there were other names: thus the first month was called Abib, the second Ziv, and these names survive only in the canon; apart from these two, I have found in it only the designations "first month," "second month," "third month," and so on. Third, the order of the months is twofold, ecclesiastical or civil. In the former the first is Nisan, in the latter Tishri. But now let us look at the individual months in order, explain the festivals that occur in them, and finally apply them to our own months. The first month of the Jews in the sacred year was Nisan or Abib, Exod. 12:2. It is called Abib from a Hebrew word, as if to say the month of the ear or of ears, because in this month the ears come forth from the stalks. In the Holy Land this happened at the end of our March and the beginning of April. For the vernal equinox was the beginning of the ecclesiastical year, as the autumnal equinox was of the civil year. The vernal equinox, however, in former times was only six days away from the end of March. Hence it is that most ecclesiastical writers refer the month Nisan to April rather than to March, Iyar to May, and so on. Yet the connection of those who link Nisan with our months so that a small part of it corresponds to March and most of it to April is more exact. The same judgement holds for the connection of the following Jewish months with ours. Furthermore, the first day of this month, as of the following ones, was celebrated among the Hebrews, not because work had to be stopped on it as on a festival day, but because God was worshipped on it with set sacrifices in solemn rite. The Hebrews call this day head [ראש], that is, the beginning of the month. The Septuagint translators always render it new moon, while the Vulgate translator sometimes says neomenias and sometimes calends. It is called neomenia as if to say "new month," for the month began with the moon and ended with it. Accordingly the first day of the month was the same as the first day of the moon.

units.la: Et quemadmodum septimo quoq; die hebdomadæ sabbatum colebatur, vt in memoriam reuocaretur beneficium acceptum à Deo, quo vniuersa sunt ex nihilo facta: sic primo quoque die mensis Deo sacrificia offerebantur, vt memores essent beneficij, quo Deus omnia gubernat. Quemadmodum etiam Deus sibi offerri voluit primos fructus rerum è terra nascentium, itemque primogenita: sic & primos dies mensium sibi reseruauit. Denique, vt Deum precibus & sacrificiis, sibi placatum redderent Hebraei ad ipsos menses feliciter inchoandos. Vide Num. 10. & 28. In decimum quartum diem huius mensis incidebat Pascha ex praescripto Dei Exod. 12. Leuit. 23. Haec celebritas instituta fuit, vt Hebraei in memoriam reuocarent illud insigne beneficium, quo Dominus primogenitos Ægyptiorum occidendo, domos Hebræorum non tetigit, quorum postes & superliminaria sanguine mactati agni tincta fuerant. Et quoniam id accidit decimâ quartâ lunâ primi mensis, ideo praecepit Deus, vt singulis annis, eodem die, Iudaei immolarent agnum, & cöederent, & quidem inter duas vesperas. Quod vt recte intelligatur, tenendum est, vesperam esse duplicé, priorem & posteriorem. Prior est inclinantis solis, quae post meridiem incipit: posterior est occidentis solis & horizontem subeuntis. Illam Graeci appellarunt δείλην πρω-[?]ΐαν, hanc ὀψίαν δείλην[?]. Illa incipiebat à nonâ horâ, hoc est, à tertiâ exactâ post meridiem, quod erat tempus oblationis vefpertinæ:altera paulò ante occafum folis,quod principium erat Iudæis diei fequentis. Alij primam vefperam interpretantur occafum radiorum folis, alteram, occafum corporis folis. Hic quæritur, An Chriftus anticipauerit pafcha Luc. 22? Plerique exiftimant, Chriftum legitimo tempore celebraffe pafcha, videl. decimaquarta lunâ ineunte, fub vefperam, & ipfum, tanquam verum agnum, qui tollit peccata mundi, oblatum effe eâdem decimaquartâ lunâ exeunte, tempore oblationis vefpertinæ: Iudæos autem tranftulifle pafcha ifto anno in lunam decimam quintam: ita vt decimaquarta Nifan nô fuerit ἀ πρὸ τῆς ἡμέρας ἀλλ᾽ ἐξηγήσατο[?], vt in eâdem verus agnus mactaretur, in quâ agnus myfticus immolari folitus, & eâdem horâ, quâ verus agnus de cruce deponebatur, Iudæi fuum agnum mactarent. Vnde Marcus tempus proximum poft mortem Chrifti appellat parafceuen, & vefperam, nempe priorem: & Iohannes cap. 19. ver. 31. fabbatum, quod fecutum eft crucifixionem Chrifti, appellat μεγάλην ἡμέραν, diem magnum: quia in eum fuerat Pafcha translatum. Quare aliud fuit pafcha commune Iudæorum, aliud Chrifti proprium. Vide Cafaubonum exerc. 16. fect. 16.17. & 18. Porrò feptem dies, inde à 14. Nifan vfque ad 21. fuerunt appellati dies azymorum, & ex iis primus & vltimus, dies magnus. Vide Exod. 12. Leuit. 23. Num. 19. & 28. & primus erat verus & folus dies Pafchalis, h.e. talis, quo immolabatur & manducabatur pafcha. Decima fexta Nifan appellatur fabbatum δευτερόπρωτον, fecundò-primum, quia proximè poft folenne pafchatis fequebatur. Nam ἀπὸ δευτέρας τῶν πάσχα lex iubet feptem hebdomadas putare. Itaque hebdomades omnes & fabbata iumunt appellationem fuam ἀπὸ δευτέρας τῶν πάσχα: vt δευτεροπρώτου[?] ἐβδομάς[?] ἐστι πρώτη, fic δευτεροδευτέρω, δευτεροτέτω &c. Confer Leuit. 23. v. 15. cum Luc. 6. v. 1. Sequitur iam menfis fecundus, nomine Chald. Iiar, Hebraico Ziu, vel vt alij legunt & fcribunt Sif, quæ pofterior vox à fplendore dućta eft. Chaldæus paraparaphraftes appellat mensem apertionis florum. Vtraq; appellatio conuenit cum re, itemque cum nomine Aprilis. Sicut enim Aprilis ab aperiendo dicitur, quòd tunc natura aperiat suas dotes: ita s a splendore siue decore florum dicitur, quòd in eo primum appareant flores. Neque tamen soli Aprili respondet hic mensis, sed etiam Maio, vt ex superioribus intelligi potest. Tertius mensis appellatur Siuan, respondens Maio & Iunio. Celebris est hic mensis festo Pentecostes, de quo Leuit. 23. Pentecoste significat quinquagesimum diem, scil. inde à die Paschæ. In veneratione erat hic dies quinquagesimus, in recordationem legis diuinitus datæ quinquagesimo die ab egressu ex Ægypto. Exod. 19. Quo fit, vt hæc celebritas quoque dicta sit hebdomadarum: quia ab altero die post primum festum diem azymorum computabantur septem hebdomadæ plenæ, quæ quadraginta nouem dies conficiunt, & die statim proximè sequenti celebritas Pentecostes agebatur. Erat autem hæc celebritas vna de tribus, in quibus omnes viri singulis annis venire Hierosolymam cogebatur, vt patet ex Deut. 16. Quartus mensis fuit Tamuz, respondens Iunio & Iulio: quintus, Ab, respondens Iulio & Augusto: sextus, Elul, respondens Augusto & Septembri. Septimus mensis ecclesiasticus, idemque primus politicus seu ciuilis, fuit Tisri, qui etiam appellatur Ethanim, à fortitudine, quòd tum temporis colligantur fructus maturi, & veluti fortes, atque fortificantes i. e. confirmantes cor hominum: vel quòd hic mensis sit nobilis quatuor festis, videl. festo tubarum, expiationis, & scenopegiæ seu tabernaculorum, & cœtus seu collectæ. Quemadmodum ig. septimus quisque hebdomadæ dies sanctus erat: sic mensis quoque septimus erat magnâ veneratione celebris. De festo tubarum opinantur Hebræi, illud coli in memoriam illius beneficij, quo Deus Isaacum de gladio patris eripuit, & arietem loco eius immolandum substituit Gen. 22. & ideo eum diem celebrari cornibus arietinis. Sed hæc sententia caret fundamento. Vulgo putatur, eum diem festum esse institutum, ut tubarum clangore, ad celebritates venturas, scil. Expiationis & Tabernaculorum, quæ illo mense celebrabantur, cum iucunditate populus præpararetur. Duplex autem erat huius festi solennitas: una ipsi propria, altera communis cum cæteris neomeniis, quia celebrabatur primo die mensis Tisri. Leuit. 23. Num. 29. De festo expiationis legere est Leuit. 25. Putatur institutum, quia eo die diuinitus dimissum sit peccatum, quod populus Hebraicus in colendo vitulo aureo perpetrauit Exod. 32. Quidquid huius sit, hic dies Deo dicatus fuit, & sacer ad peccata per pœnitentiam expianda. Ideo præceptum est, ut animas suas in eo affligerent, videl. ieiunando. Celebritas tabernaculorum erat magna, & una ex illis tribus, in quibus omnes masculi ter venire Hierosolymam singulis annis debebant. Deut. 16. Leuit. 23. Num. 29. Nomen habet à faciendis tabernaculis: quia hæ feriæ agebantur ad recolendum beneficium, quo Hebræi, ex Ægyptiaca seruitute liberati, & per solitudinem deducti, quadraginta annis in tentoriis habitauerant. Colebantur per septem dies: quibus exactis celebrabatur festum cœtus siue collecta, 22. die huius mensis. Leuit. 23. Videtur hoc festum celebratum, ut recordarentur beneficij, quo absolutâ & confectâ peregrinatione, simul omnes terram summis votis expetitam & precibus efflagitatam tandem obtinuerunt:quemadmodum feriæ tabernaculorum Iudeis in memoriam reuocabant annos peregrinationis. Dicitur itaque collecta, quia relictis tabernaculis, in vnum populus colligebatur ad gratias Deo agendas precibus & sacrificiis in commune oblatis, eo quod post longam quadraginta annorum peregrinatione tandem in terram patrib. promissam omnes salui & incolumes peruenissent. Non tamen omnes octo illi dies erant festi, quanquam omnes erant celebres oblatione aliquâ. Octauus mensis fuit Marchesuan, siue Bul, qui respodet Octobri & Nouembri :nonus Cisleu, qui Nouembri & Decembri, Vigesimoquinto die huius mensis Iudæi colccolebant festum Encæniorum, præter dies festos à Mose præscriptos. Vide 2. Maccab. 1. & Iohan. 10. Sunt autem Encænia dies dedicationis templi: Græci namque ἐγκαινίζειν[?] dicunt, quod Latini renouare, vel dedicare. Templum Iudæorum ter est dedicatum: primò, cùm est extructum à Salomone 1. Reg. 8. secundò, cùm est iterum ædificatum post reditum è captiuitate Babylonica. Esdr. 6. tertiò, cùm ex parte dirutum & pollutum à gentibus sub Antiochò Epiphane, mundatum & dedicatum est tempore Iudæ Maccabæi. 1. Maccab. 4. In huius postremi beneficij memoriam colebantur singulis annis Encænia, & quidem diebus octo: quia Iudæi dies octo in illa dedicatione templi lætissimè consumserunt, memores celebritatis tabernaculorum, quam Iudæi per octo dies magna cum lætitia ex præscripto Dei colebant. 2. Maccab. 10. Quare verisimile est, primum & octauum diem Encæniorum fuisse festos & solennes, cæteros non item, sed celebros tantum ob sacrificia, quæ in illis offerri solebant. Fit quoque metio diei ignis cælitus dati 2. Maccab. 1. qui non tam festus, quàm celebris videtur fuisse. Decimus mensis est Tebeth, respondens Decembri & Ianuario: vndecimus, Schebeth, respondens Ianuario & Februario: duodecimus, Adar, respondens Februario & Martio. Duodecim his mensibus in anno bisexto accedit decimus tertius Veadar. q. d. secundus Adar:
units.tr: Just as the seventh day of every week was kept as the Sabbath, to recall the benefit received from God by which all things were made out of nothing, so on the first day of every month sacrifices were offered to God, that they might remember the benefit by which God governs all things. Just as God wished the first fruits of what grows from the earth to be offered to him, and likewise the firstborn, so he also reserved the first days of the months for himself. Finally, the Hebrews began the months with prayers and sacrifices, so that they might render God favourable to them and bring the months to a happy start. See Num. 10. and 28. On the fourteenth day of this month, by God's appointment, fell the Passover, Exod. 12., Leuit. 23. This observance was instituted so that the Hebrews might recall that remarkable benefit by which the Lord, in killing the firstborn of the Egyptians, passed over the houses of the Hebrews, whose doorposts and lintels had been stained with the blood of the slaughtered lamb. And since this happened on the fourteenth day of the first month, God commanded that every year, on that same day, the Jews should sacrifice a lamb and eat it, and indeed between the two evenings. To understand this rightly, we must keep in mind that there are two evenings, the earlier and the later. The earlier is that of the declining sun, which begins after midday; the later is that of the setting sun, when it sinks toward the horizon. The Greeks called the first [δείλην πρωΐαν, early afternoon] and the second [ὀψίαν δείλην, late afternoon]. The first began at the ninth hour, that is, at the exact third hour after noon, which was the time of the evening offering; the second was shortly before sunset, which was the beginning of the following day for the Jews. Others interpret the first evening as the fading of the sun's rays, and the second as the setting of the sun's body. Here the question is raised: Did Christ anticipate the Passover, Luke 22? Most think that Christ celebrated the Passover at its lawful time, namely at the beginning of the fourteenth day of the moon, toward evening; and that he himself, as the true Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, was offered on the same fourteenth day of the moon, at the end of it, at the time of the evening offering. They hold that the Jews that year moved the Passover to the fifteenth day of the moon, so that the fourteenth of Nisan was not [ἀ πρὸ τῆς ἡμέρας ἀλλ᾽ ἐξηγήσατο, not before the day but on it], so that on the same day on which the true Lamb was slain, the mystical lamb, which was customarily sacrificed, was also slain, and at the same hour at which the true Lamb was taken down from the cross, the Jews slew their own lamb. Hence Mark calls the day immediately after the death of Christ the preparation [parasceuen], and the evening, namely the earlier one; and John 19:31 calls the Sabbath that followed the crucifixion of Christ [μεγάλην ἡμέραν, a great day], a great day, because the Passover had been transferred to it. Therefore the common Passover of the Jews was one thing, and the proper Passover of Christ another. See Casaubon, Exercitation 16, sections 16, 17 and 18. Furthermore, the seven days from the fourteenth of Nisan to the twenty-first were called the days of unleavened bread, and of these the first and the last were called a great day. See Exod. 12, Leuit. 23, Num. 19 and 28. The first was the true and only Passover day, that is, the day on which the Passover was slain and eaten. The sixteenth of Nisan is called the Sabbath [δευτερόπρωτον, second-first], because it immediately followed the solemn Passover feast. For the law orders that seven weeks be counted [from the second of the Passover, ἀπὸ δευτέρας τῶν πάσχα]. Thus all the weeks and Sabbaths take their name from the second of the Passover: as the first week of the second-first is first, so the second-second and the second-third, and so on. Compare Leuit. 23 v. 15 with Luke 6 v. 1. Next follows the second month, called in Chaldee Iiar, in Hebrew Ziu, or as others read and write it Sif, the latter word being derived from brightness. The Chaldee paraphrast calls it the month of the opening of flowers. Both names agree with the thing and likewise with the name April. For just as April is said to be named from opening, because then nature opens its gifts, so this month is named from the brightness or beauty of flowers, because in it the flowers first appear. Yet this month does not correspond only to April, but also to May, as can be understood from what was said above. The third month is called Siuan, corresponding to May and June. This month is famous for the feast of Pentecost, of which Leuit. 23. Pentecost means the fiftieth day, namely counted from the day of the Passover. This fiftieth day was held in reverence, in remembrance of the law given by God on the fiftieth day after the departure from Egypt, Exod. 19. Hence this feast was also called the feast of weeks, because seven full weeks were counted from the day after the first day of unleavened bread, which make forty-nine days, and on the very next day the celebration of Pentecost was held. This celebration was one of the three at which all men were required to come up to Jerusalem each year, as is clear from Deut. 16. The fourth month was Tamuz, corresponding to June and July; the fifth, Ab, corresponding to July and August; the sixth, Elul, corresponding to August and September. The seventh month, the ecclesiastical month and at the same time the first civil or political month, was Tisri, which is also called Ethanim, from strength, because at that time the ripe fruits are gathered, and as it were strong and strengthening, that is, confirming the heart of man; or because this month is noble for four feasts, namely the feast of trumpets, of atonement, of tabernacles or booths, and of assembly or gathering. Just as every seventh day of the week was holy, so the seventh month too was celebrated with great reverence. Concerning the feast of trumpets, the Hebrews hold that it is kept in memory of that benefit by which God snatched Isaac from his father's sword and substituted a ram to be sacrificed in his place, Gen. 22., and that therefore this day is celebrated with ram's horns. But this opinion lacks foundation. It is commonly thought that this day was instituted so that the people might be prepared with joy, by the sound of trumpets, for the coming celebrations, namely the Atonement and the Tabernacles, which were celebrated in that month. The solemnity of this feast was double: one proper to itself, the other shared with the other new moons, because it was celebrated on the first day of the month Tisri. Leuit. 23. Num. 29. Concerning the feast of atonement one may read Leuit. 25. It is thought to have been instituted because on that day sin was forgiven by God, the sin which the Hebrew people committed in worshipping the golden calf, Exod. 32. Whatever the reason, this day was dedicated to God and holy for the expiation of sins through repentance. Therefore it was commanded that they should afflict their souls on it, namely by fasting. The feast of tabernacles was great, and one of those three feasts at which all males were bound to come to Jerusalem three times a year. Deut. 16. Leuit. 23. Num. 29. It takes its name from making booths, because these holidays were kept to recall the benefit by which the Hebrews, freed from Egyptian slavery and led through the wilderness, had dwelt in tents for forty years. They were observed for seven days, and when these were over, the feast of assembly or gathering was celebrated on the twenty-second day of this month. Leuit. 23. This feast seems to have been celebrated so that they might remember the benefit by which, when the journey was finished and completed, all together at last obtained the land desired with highest vows and begged for with prayers, just as the days of the tabernacles reminded the Jews of the years of wandering. It is therefore called the gathering, because, leaving their tabernacles, the people assembled as one to give thanks to God with prayers and with sacrifices offered in common, because after the long journey of forty years they had at last all arrived safe and sound in the land promised to the fathers. Not all eight of those days were festal, although all were observed with some offering. The eighth month was Marchesuan, or Bul, which corresponds to October and November; the ninth was Cisleu, which corresponds to November and December. On the twenty-fifth day of this month the Jews kept the feast of Encaenia, in addition to the festal days prescribed by Moses. See 2 Maccab. 1 and John 10. Encaenia are the days of the dedication of the temple: for the Greeks say ἐγκαινίζειν [to dedicate], which the Latins call renew or dedicate. The temple of the Jews was dedicated three times: first, when it was built by Solomon, 1 Kings 8; second, when it was built again after the return from the Babylonian captivity, Ezra 6; third, when, partly thrown down and defiled by the Gentiles under Antiochus Epiphanes, it was cleansed and dedicated in the time of Judas Maccabeus, 1 Maccab. 4. In memory of this last benefit the Encaenia were celebrated every year, and indeed for eight days, because the Jews in that dedication of the temple spent eight days in the greatest joy, mindful of the feast of tabernacles, which the Jews kept with great gladness for eight days by God's command, 2 Maccab. 10. Hence it is likely that the first and the eighth days of the Encaenia were festal and solemn, but the others not in the same way, only celebrated because of the sacrifices which were customarily offered on them. There is also mention of the day of the fire given from heaven, 2 Maccab. 1, which seems to have been not so much a festival as a notable day. The tenth month is Tebeth, corresponding to December and January; the eleventh, Schebeth, corresponding to January and February; the twelfth, Adar, corresponding to February and March. In a leap year a thirteenth month, Veadar, is added to these twelve months, that is to say, the second Adar.

units.la: VI. Annus est tempus perfecto mensium numero completum. Estque solaris, vel lunaris. Annus solaris accommodatur ad motum solis, mensesque folares. Putatur fuisse visitatus in populo Dei ante exitum ex Ægypto. Annus lunaris accommodatur ad lunam, mensesque lunares. Is in populo Dei fuit sacer & ciuilis. Annus lunaris sacer, siue ecclesiasticus, incipiebat mense Nisan. Exod. 12. Annus lunaris ciuilis, siue politicus, incipiebat mense Tisri. Exod. 23. v. 16. Hinc sumebant initium emtiones, tiones, seruitutes, remissio terræ, annus sabbatarius & Iubilæus. Annus sabbatarius, siue annus Seminta[?], erat septi-mus mus annus hebdomadis annalis. Iubilæus erat systema annorum lunarium 49. fiue, systema septem hebdomadum annalium. Leuit. 25. Cur vero, inquies, iubilæus dicitur annus quinquagesimus Leuit. 25. v. 10. fi compleatur folum annos 49? Refp. Est annus quinquagesimus a iubilæo antecedente inclusive, ut Iudæi supputare solent. Schindlerus, & alii quidam aliter sentiunt: quasi scilicet duo anni sacri concurrerint, quadragesimus nonus, qui fuerit [illegible, ~5 letters], & quinquagesimus, qui fuerit [?]. Hic non est prætereundum, quòd annus diuidatur in quatuor quadrantes, quos Scriptura reuocat ad duos semisses, æstatem & hyemem: & quòd mensis quilibet respondeat quatuor istis quadrantibus, ita vt prima septimana fit veluti ver, fecunda æstas, tertia autumnus, & quarta hyems, fcil. ratione motus lunæ.
units.tr: VI. A year is a period completed by a fixed number of months. It is either solar or lunar. A solar year is adjusted to the motion of the sun, and its months are solar months. It is thought to have been in use among the people of God before the exodus from Egypt. A lunar year is adjusted to the moon, and its months are lunar months. Among the people of God this was both sacred and civil. The sacred lunar year, or ecclesiastical year, began in the month Nisan. Exod. 12. The civil lunar year, or political year, began in the month Tishri. Exod. 23. v. 16. From these beginnings were reckoned purchases, sales, servitudes, the remission of land, the sabbatical year and the Jubilee. The sabbatical year, or Schemitta, was the seventh year of the annual week. The Jubilee was a system of 49 lunar years, or a system of seven annual weeks. Leuit. 25. But why, you will ask, is the fiftieth year called the Jubilee, Leuit. 25. v. 10, if it is completed in only 49 years? Answer: the fiftieth year is counted inclusively from the preceding Jubilee, as the Jews usually reckon it. Schindler and certain others think otherwise: as if two sacred years coincided, the forty-ninth, which was [illegible, ~5 letters], and the fiftieth, which was [?]. Here it must not be passed over that the year is divided into four quarters, which Scripture reduces to two halves, summer and winter, and that each month corresponds to these four quarters, so that the first week is as it were spring, the second summer, the third autumn, and the fourth winter, namely by reason of the motion of the moon.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: GEOGRAPHIA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED GEOGRAPHY.

units.la: I. GEographia sacra explicat dimensionem terræ fermè ex S. literis.
units.tr: I. Sacred geography explains the dimensions of the earth, almost entirely from the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: II. Dimensio terræ spectatur in globo terrestri communiter, vel in terra & aquâ singulariter. Hinc tres constituuntur partes geographiæ: prima est de aquæ & terræ dimensione, quatenus ista duo conftituunt vnum globum, fiue vnam sphæram: fecunda est de dimensione terræ, feorfim spectatæ: tertia est de dimenfione aquæ, feorfim spectatæ: quæ vltima pars vocatur Hydrographia.
units.tr: II. The dimension of the earth is considered either in the terrestrial globe as a whole, or in land and water separately. Hence three parts of geography are constituted. The first concerns the dimension of water and land insofar as these two together make up one globe, or one sphere. The second concerns the dimension of the land considered by itself. The third concerns the dimension of the water considered by itself; this last part is called Hydrography.

units.la: III. In globo terrestri communiter confideramus longitudinem, latitudinem, & profunditatem.
units.tr: III. In the terrestrial globe as a whole we consider length, breadth and depth.

units.la: IV. Longitudo globi ex aquâ & terrâ composita est linea circularis ipsum ambiens. Dicitur aliàs ipsius perimeter, & circumferentia : estque milliarium Germanic. 5400. cuius diameter est milliar. Germanic. 1718 1/11[?], siue numero rotundo 1720. semidiameter, milliar. Germ. 859. siue numero rotundo 860. Alio etiam sensu longitudo sumitur ab occidente versus occidentem. Atque hoc sensu æquator & meridianus seruiunt longitudini.
units.tr: IV. The length of the globe, composed of water and land, is the circular line that encircles it. It is also called its perimeter and circumference. It measures 5,400 German miles. Its diameter is 1718 1/11 German miles, or in round numbers 1720; its semidiameter is 859 German miles, or in round numbers 860. In another sense, length is taken from east to west, and in this sense the equator and the meridian serve to measure length.

units.la: V. Latitudo globi exaquâ & terrâ compacti est area ipsius siue superficies: eaque tum plana, tum gibba. Superficies plana est area perimetro inclusa, milliarium Germ. 231945, vel iuxta alios 232000. Superficies conuexa est milliar. Germ. 927700. vel iuxta alios 928000. Alio etiam sensu latitudo est linea ducta à septentrione versus meridiem. Atque hoc sensu æquator, tropici, & polares seruiunt latitudini indagandæ, & distinguunt globum terrenum in zonas & climata.
units.tr: V. The breadth of the globe, compounded of water and land, is its area or surface, and this is both flat and curved. The flat surface is the area enclosed by the perimeter, 231,945 German miles, or according to others 232,000. The curved surface is 927,700 German miles, or according to others 928,000. In another sense, breadth is a line drawn from north to south. In this sense the equator, the tropics and the polar circles serve to determine breadth, and they divide the terrestrial globe into zones and climates.

units.la: VI. Profunditas globi ex aquâ & terrâ constantis est vel linea crassitiei, vel soliditas. Linea crassitiei est ipsa diameter paulò ante indicata. Soliditas est tota ipsius moles, trinâ dimensione constans: estque milliarium Germanic. 2656933936. vel iuxta alios 2662560000.
units.tr: VI. The depth of the globe, consisting of water and land, is either a line of thickness or solidity. The line of thickness is the diameter just indicated. Solidity is its whole mass, consisting of three dimensions; it is 2,656,933,936 German miles, or according to others 2,662,560,000.

units.la: VII. Dimensio terræ singulariter spectatur in terra partim iam satis cognitâ, partim aliquo modo cognita. Ibi sunt terra subborealis & subaustralis, itemque America; hic Europa, Africa, & Asia. Vbi admiratione non caret, quòd ex vno sanguine tot terræ fuerint repletæ hominibus. Act. 17. vers. 26. Hic quæritur, quomodo tres filij Noë, illorumq; posteri, cupauerint has sedes? Resp. Iapheto & ipsius posteris fermè cessit Europa ; Semo & ipsius filiis atque nepotibus Asia ; Chamo & eius posteritati Africa. Americam videntur occupasse Asiaticorum coloniæ traductæ per fretum Anian, terram subborealem Europæi, subaustralem Africani. Cæterum nos persequemur eas terræ partes, quarum mentio est in Scripturis.
units.tr: VII. The dimension of the earth is considered separately in the land partly already well known and partly known in some measure. Of the first kind are the sub-Boreal and sub-Austral lands, and also America; of the second kind are Europe, Africa and Asia. It is a matter for wonder that from one blood so many lands were filled with men (Acts 17:26). Here it is asked how the three sons of Noah and their descendants obtained these seats. Answer: Europe fell largely to Japheth and his posterity; Asia to Shem and his sons and grandsons; Africa to Ham and his posterity. America seems to have been occupied by colonies of Asians who crossed by the Strait of Anian; the sub-Boreal land by Europeans, the sub-Austral by Africans. Otherwise we shall pursue those parts of the earth that are mentioned in the Scriptures.

units.la: VIII. Palæstina est particularis provincia Asiæ, valde insignis cum locorum, tum vero rerum gestarum, quas Scripturæ sacræ commemorant, celebritate. Sub hac comprehenduntur Idumæa, Iudæa, Samaria, & Galilæa. Dicta fuit antiquitus terra Canaan, à filio Cham: deinde terra Israël & Palæstina, ab Israelitis & Palæstinis, quos Scriptura appellat Philistim: denique terra promissionis & terra sancta. Iacet inter mare mediterraneum, & Arabiam, quâ ex parte montibus fere continuis natura vltra Iordanem fluuium vallatur, atque ab extremâ Ægyptiorâ incipiens vsque ad Phœniciam porrigitur. Vnde his continetur finibus: à septentrione, Phœniciæ parte; ab ortu æstiuo, Libano monte; à meridie, & partim ab oriente, Arabia; ab occasu, maris mediterranei parte, quo in loco mare Syriū & Phœnicium appellatur. Extenditur à meridie in septentrionem gradu 31. vsque ad 33. & paulò plus, hoc est, inter medium tertij, ac medium quarti climatis, occupans 9. & 10. parallelos. Vnde ifthic maior dies æstatis accidit hor. 14. & versus borealem limitem horarum 14. cum quadrante. Atque hæc est latitudo eius. Longitudinem verò occupat à meridiano grad. 63. cum dimidio vsque ad meridianum gr. 67. Hinc longitudo eius est leucarum 64. vt Brocardus definit, ab vrbe scil. Dan, quæ olim Lachis & Cæsarea Philippi dicebatur, vsque ad Berfabee, quæ nunc Giblim appellatur. Latitudo eidem Brocardo, ab occidente in meridiem est leucarum 16. à Iordane scil. fluuio vsque ad mare magnum, seu mediterraneum. Verùm tamen vltra Iordanem regio etiam hæc extenditur, quæ quidem portio Transjordanis nuncupatur, & Peræa Plinio. Cùm ab Israelitis occuparetur, in duodecim partes, quas tribus vocarunt, fuit diuisa. Vide librum Iosuæ, & typos interpretum, nominatim Iof. c. 14.15.16.17.18.19.20.21. vbi est geodæsia primò generalis, tum specialis. Sub Roboam vero, Salomonis filio, cum haec provincia per seditionem in duas partes discerneretur, duae ex his tribus in unam ceciderunt, nempe Iuda & Beniamin, quae tamen sub regni Iuda nomine comprehendebantur: reliquae de-cem tribus obtinuerunt nomen Israel. Post captiuitatem Babylonicam in duas iterum regiones est distincta, videl. in Samariam & Galilaeam, & haec distincta fuit in superiorem & inferiorem. Post haec tempora, vsque ad Christi aduentum, atque etiam deinceps, haec ipsa terra in tres partes cis Iordanem fuit diuisa, nempe in Galilaeam, quae fuit superior pars versus Sidonem & Tyrum, vrbes Phoeniciae; in Samariam, quae media est; & in Iudaeam, quae inferior est pars ad Austrum, & Arabiam Petraeam: quibus aliqui adiiciunt quartam partem, Idumaeam, quae vsque ad Sirbonis lacum producitur prope confinia Aegypti. Quatuor quoque partes sunt trans Iordanem: videl. Ituraea, Trachonitis, Peraea & Abilene. Luc.3.v.1. Ex his partibus (vt ordine retrogrado agamus) Peraea est asperis dispersa montibus, Trachonitis est sita e regione Peraeae, neque ipsa fatis culta, vt nec Ituraea, quae finitima est Galilaeae Gentium: Abilene, prope Chalcidem, est fertilissima. Galilaea regio, Libani & Antilibani, altissimorum montium, iugis, a septentrione clauditur: ab occidente Phoeniciam vicinam habet: ab ortu Coelesyriae coniungitur: meridionalem eius partem Samaria & Arabia deserta concludunt. Diuiditur in superiorem & inferiorem. Galilaea superior, quae etiam gentium dicitur, contermina est Tyro, vrbi Phoeniciae, vbi Salomon 25. urbes Chiramo regi Tyri dono concessit. Galilaea inferior (quae etiam Tiberiadis dicitur, vel ab vrbe, vel a lacu id nominis) iacet ad meridiem, atque etiam trans Iordanem extenditur. In ea situs fuit pagus Nazareth, vbi Christus conceptus fuit & educatus: item mons Thabor, mira rotunditate sublimis. Galilaeae gentium proxima fuit Decapolis, regiuncula. Marc.7.v.31. Samaria iacet inter Iudaeam & Galilaeam: & habet ab occasu aestiuo mare mediterraneum: à septentrione, & partim ab oriente confinis est Galilææ, proximè locum Tiberiadis, atque Iordanem egressa vsque ad Arabiæ deserta extenditur. Memorabiles ipsius vrbes fuerunt; Samaria, quæ postea Sebaste, regia & metropolis: Cæsarea Palæstinæ, vel Stratonis, hodie Azon: Neapolis, quæ in historia sacra dicitur Sichar & Sichem, nunc Napolosa, vbi fuit puteus ille Iohan. 4. Iudæa, cæteris Palæstinæ partibus celebrior, iacet inter mare mediterraneum, & lacum Asphaltitem, atq; etiam inter Samariam & Idumæam. Vrbes & oppida in eâ fuerunt complura, quorum omnium clarissima fuit Hierusalem, sita edito in loco, hoc est, in montanis, ita vt vndequaque fuerit ad eam ascendendum. Hieronymus author est, eam non solùm medii Iudææ occupare, sed etiam esse vmbilicu vniuersi. Namque orientalis est illi Asia, occidentalis Europa, à meridie siue ab Austro Libya, à Septentrione Scythæ, Armeni, Persæ, & reliquæ Ponti nationes, vt ait Maginus. Vide Casaubonum in exercitationibus ad annales Baronij: vbi exerc. 1. sect. 3. ait, vrbem sanctam in medio vndecim toparchiarum, in quas Iudæa fuit diuisa, eminuisse, vt in clypeo vmbilicum: & exerc. 16. f. 34. dicit. Hierosolymam aliquando in Scripturis dici medium & vmbilicum terræ, vt Psal. 73. v. 13. Ezech. 38. v. 12. nimirum ratione latitudinis septem climatum, quæ veteribus erant cognita. Vide paulò post de Euphrate. Præter Hierosolymam etiam celebria fuerunt hæc loca, Bethlehem, pagus exiguus, in quo Christus est natus: Rama, & Gaza, quam postremam alij sub Idumæa reponunt: Bethania, Emmaus, Bethphage: Iudæa, in sacris Edom, versus mare & Iudæam eximiè est fertilis, sed in Arabiæ confinibus sterilescit & montibus exasperatur. Hanc Strabo facit Iudææ parte. Et sanè Idumæi vrbem sanctam vocabant [?]κοινὴν πόλιν, sibi & Iudæis, fratribus suis, communem vrbem. Plura vide in exercit. Casauboni pag. 23. 24. edit. Francof.
units.tr: VIII. Palestine is a particular province of Asia, very notable both for the places and for the fame of the deeds that the Holy Scriptures record. Under this name are included Idumaea, Judea, Samaria and Galilee. In antiquity it was called the land of Canaan, from the son of Ham; then the land of Israel and Palestine, from the Israelites and the Palestines, whom Scripture calls Philistines; and finally the land of promise and the holy land. It lies between the Mediterranean Sea and Arabia, and on that side it is walled in by an almost continuous range of mountains beyond the river Jordan; it stretches from the far end of Egypt as far as Phoenicia. It is bounded thus: on the north by the part of Phoenicia; on the east in summer by Mount Lebanon; on the south, and partly on the east, by Arabia; on the west by the part of the Mediterranean Sea which here is called the Syrian and Phoenician Sea. It extends from south to north from the 31st degree to the 33rd and a little more, that is, between the middle of the third climate and the middle of the fourth, occupying the 9th and 10th parallels. Hence the longest summer day there is 14 hours, and toward the northern border 14 and a quarter hours. This is its latitude. Its longitude extends from the meridian of 63½ degrees to the meridian of 67 degrees. Hence its length is 64 leagues, as Brocardus determines it, namely from the city Dan, which was formerly called Laish and Caesarea Philippi, as far as Beersheba, which is now called Giblim. According to the same Brocardus, its breadth from west to south is 16 leagues, namely from the river Jordan to the Great or Mediterranean Sea. Yet this region also extends beyond the Jordan, and that portion is called Transjordan, and by Pliny Peraea. When it was occupied by the Israelites, it was divided into twelve parts, which they called tribes. See the book of Joshua and the interpreters' figures, especially Joshua chapters 14 to 21, where there is first a general and then a particular geodesy. Under Rehoboam, son of Solomon, when this province was divided into two parts by sedition, two of these tribes fell into one, namely Judah and Benjamin, which were nonetheless comprised under the name of the kingdom of Judah; the remaining ten tribes obtained the name Israel. After the Babylonian captivity it was again divided into two regions, namely Samaria and Galilee, and these were divided into upper and lower. After these times, until the coming of Christ, and also afterwards, this same land was divided on this side of the Jordan into three parts: namely Galilee, which was the upper part toward Sidon and Tyre, cities of Phoenicia; Samaria, which is the middle part; and Judea, which is the lower part toward the south and Arabia Petraea. To these some add a fourth part, Idumaea, which extends as far as the lake Sirbonis near the borders of Egypt. There are also four parts beyond the Jordan, namely Ituraea, Trachonitis, Peraea and Abilene. Luke 3:1. Of these parts (to proceed in reverse order), Peraea is scattered with rough mountains; Trachonitis lies opposite Peraea and is not very well cultivated, nor is Ituraea, which borders on Galilee of the Gentiles; Abilene, near Chalcis, is very fertile. The region of Galilee, bounded on the north by the ridges of Lebanon and Antilebanon, the highest mountains, has Phoenicia as its neighbour on the west; on the east it is joined to Coele-Syria; its southern part is bordered by Samaria and the Arabian desert. It is divided into upper and lower. Upper Galilee, which is also called Galilee of the Gentiles, borders on Tyre, a city of Phoenicia, where Solomon gave 20 cities as a gift to Hiram, king of Tyre. Lower Galilee (which is also called Tiberias, either from the city or from the lake of that name) lies to the south and extends also beyond the Jordan. In it was situated the village of Nazareth, where Christ was conceived and brought up; likewise Mount Tabor, lofty with wonderful roundness. Next to Galilee of the Gentiles lay Decapolis, a small region. Mark 7:31. Samaria lies between Judea and Galilee, and has the Mediterranean Sea on its west toward the summer sunset; on the north, and partly on the east, it borders Galilee, near the place Tiberias, and, going out past the Jordan, extends as far as the Arabian desert. Its notable cities were: Samaria, afterwards Sebaste, the royal seat and metropolis; Caesarea of Palestine, or Stratonis, today Azor; Neapolis, which in sacred history is called Sychar and Sichem, now Nablus, where was that well of John 4. Judea, more celebrated than the other parts of Palestine, lies between the Mediterranean Sea and the Dead Sea (the Lake Asphaltites), and also between Samaria and Idumaea. It contained many cities and towns, of which the most famous was Jerusalem, set on a high place, that is, among the mountains, so that one had to go up to it from every side. Jerome is the authority that it occupies not only the middle of Judea but is also the navel of the whole world. For to its east lies Asia, to its west Europe, to its south Libya, to its north the Scythians, Armenians, Persians and the other nations of Pontus, as Maginus says. See Casaubon in his exercitations on Baronius's annals, where in exercitation 1, section 3, he says the holy city rose up in the middle of the eleven toparchies into which Judea was divided, like a navel on a shield; and in exercitation 16, p. 34, he says that Jerusalem is sometimes called in Scripture the middle and navel of the earth, as in Ps. 73:13; Ezek. 38:12, namely by reason of the breadth of the seven climates, which were known to the ancients. See a little later on the Euphrates. Besides Jerusalem, these places also were famous: Bethlehem, a small village in which Christ was born; Rama, and Gaza, which some place last under Idumaea; Bethany, Emmaus, Bethphage. Judea, in the sacred books Edom, toward the sea, is exceedingly fertile, but toward the borders of Arabia it becomes barren and is roughened by mountains. Strabo counts this as a part of Judea. And indeed the Idumaeans called the holy city [κοινὴν πόλιν], a city common to themselves and to the Jews, their brothers. See more in Casaubon's exercitation, pp. 23–24, Frankfurt edition.

units.la: IX. Phœnicia est Galilææ contigua. Vrbes ipsius celebriores sunt Sidon & Tyrus, nobilissima emporia, quorum etiam Scriptura meminit. Inter Tyrum & Sidonem sita fuit Sarepta.
units.tr: IX. Phoenicia adjoins Galilee. Its more famous cities are Sidon and Tyre, most noble trading centres, which Scripture also mentions. Between Tyre and Sidon lay Sarepta.

units.la: X. Arabia ab occidente habet Ægyptum, à septentrione Palæstinam, & Mesopotamiam, ab oriente Assyriam; & diuiditur in tres partes, desertam, petræam, & felicem. In Arabiâ Petræâ est mons Sinai, nobilissimus ob datam Mosi legem, qui numeratur inter altissimos totius orbis montes. Est portio montis Horeb; etsi hic propeculiari etiam monte habetur, estq; non ita sterilis, altus, & horridus, vt mons Sinai, altera ipsius pars. Epiphanius Magodiam facit Arabiæ regionem, unde venerunt Magi Matth. 2. & addit, à nomine Magodia dictos esse Magos. Sed neque huiusmodi regio est in Arabiâ, neq; magi inde venerunt (nam historiæ non alios narrant magos nisi Persarum) & analogia non patitur, vt à nomine Magodia formetur nomen gentile Magus.
units.tr: X. Arabia has Egypt to the west, Palestine to the north, and Mesopotamia and Assyria to the east. It is divided into three parts: desert, stony (Petraea), and fortunate (Felix). In Arabia Petraea is Sinai, most noted for the giving of the law to Moses, and it is counted among the highest mountains in the whole world. It is a portion of Horeb, although here it is also regarded as a separate mountain of its own. It is not as barren, high and rugged as Sinai, the other part of the same range. Epiphanius makes Magodia a region of Arabia from which the Magi came (Matth. 2.), and he adds that the Magi were named after the name Magodia. But there is no such region in Arabia, and the Magi did not come from there, for the histories speak of no magi other than Persian ones. Nor does analogy allow the gentile noun Magus to be formed from the name Magodia.

units.la: XI. Persiæ & Mediæ fines hi sunt. Persia claditur à meridie sinu Persico: à septentrione, Media ab occasu Babylonia: ab ortu solis Carmania. Media terminatur à septentrione, parte Hircanimaris: ab occasu, Assyriâ: à meridie, Persidæ: ab oriente, Hyrcaniâ & Parthia. Ex Persiâ venerunt magi illi Matt. 2. qui procul dubio fuerunt reguli & toparchę ditionis alicuius Persicę, quę illâ ætate plures habuit toparchas & dynastas, vt etiâ in Media, Parthiâ, & Assyriâ erat more receptum. Hoc itaq; sensu tres isti magi possunt appellari reges, quo Iosephus lib. 6. excidij cap. 16. Abennerigum vocat regem castri Spasini.
units.tr: XI. These are the borders of Persia and Media. Persia is enclosed on the south by the Persian Gulf, on the north by Media, on the west by Babylonia, and on the east by Carmania. Media is bounded on the north by part of the Hyrcanian Sea, on the west by Assyria, on the south by Persis, and on the east by Hyrcania and Parthia. From Persia came those Magi (Matt. 2.), who were without doubt petty kings and toparchs of some Persian district, which at that time had many toparchs and dynasts, as was the accepted custom also in Media, Parthia and Assyria. In this sense those three Magi can be called kings, in the way that Josephus, Book 6 of the War, chapter 16, calls Abennerigus the king of the camp of Spasinus.

units.la: XII. Ægyptus, Mesopotamia, Syria, Assyria & Chaldæa hoc modo cum Palæstinâ, & inter sese conferuntur. Ægyptu ita positam esse in Africa, vt aliqua eius pars ad Asiam pertineat, nonnulli asserunt. Sed rectius sub Africa locatur. Contermina est terræ Canaan ad ortum & meridiem, sita inter mare mediterraneum & rubrum. Ægyptum cotingit Arabia versus ortum & meridiem. Mesopotamia sic dicta est, quod inter duos fluuios, Tigrim & Euphratem fit media: in sacris literis Aram vocatur: ab Hebraeis Aram Nchaaroth, id est, Syria fluuiorum; ab occidente habet Palaestinam, a septentrione Syriam, aborien te Assyriam, a meridie Chaldaeam. Syria Hebraeis dicitur Aram, & ab Antilibano recta ad Euphratem tendit, & eo trajecto Tigrim legit, & per Mesopotamiam subDamascifines confidens, ad ipsam Arabiam Petraeam terminatur. Complectitur sex regiones. Harum prima, maxima, & antiquissima est Mesopotamia, quae ideo {ideo} κατ' ἐξο-χὴν appellatur Aram: aliquando Aram Paddan, h. e. iugum Syriae, q. d. Syriam iugatam seu missam sub iugum duorum fluuiorum: unde & Aram Naharaim, vt modo diximus, appellatur, Latinis interamnis. Secunda est Aram Zobah, 2. Chron. 8. verf. 3. tertia, Aram Beth Rechob, Gen. 36. verf. 37. quarta, Aram Maachah, 2. Sam. 8. & 10. quinta, Aram Damascus, quae est Κοίλη Συρία, q. d. caua Syria; quae id nomen inde habet, quod duorum montium, Libani & Antilibani, vallibus terminetur. Atque hae quinque regiones in S. literis diuerte appellantur Aram. Sexta est Syria Comagena, seu Antiochena, cuius incolas a veteribus Arimos appellatos esse author est Strabo: quae appellatio ex Hebraeo manauit. Assyria (quae hodie Syriae nomine comprehenditur) terminatur ab occasu Mesopotamia, ab ortu Media, a septentrione mari Hircano, a meridie Chaldaea & Persia. Chaldaea (alias Babylonia) diuiditur in tres partes, summam, medianam, & infimam. Summa est contermina Mesopotamiae, ad Euphratem fluuium, & appellatur Auranitis; mediana vocatur Chaldaea ad Arabiam desertam: infima, vocatur Amordacia, ad finum Persicum. In Chaldaea (summa) fuit Eden fiue paradisus, cuius topographia est Gen. 2. Vide hac de re paulo post in hydrographia. Caeterum totum systema Chaldaeae hos habuit fines: ab ortu, Mediam & Persiam: a meridie, Sufianam & Arabiam: ab occidente, Aegyptum & Palaestinam: a septentrione, Syriam, Mesopotamiam, & Assyriam.
units.tr: XII. Egypt, Mesopotamia, Syria, Assyria and Chaldaea are situated thus, both with respect to Palestine and to one another. Some assert that Egypt is placed in Africa in such a way that some part of it belongs to Asia, but it is more rightly located under Africa. It borders the land of Canaan to the east and south, lying between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea. Arabia touches Egypt toward the east and south. Mesopotamia is so called because it lies in the middle of two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. In Holy Letters it is called Aram; by the Hebrews it is called Aram Naharaim, that is, Syria of the rivers. On the west it has Palestine, on the north Syria, on the east Assyria, and on the south Chaldaea. Syria is called Aram by the Hebrews. It runs straight from Antilebanon to the Euphrates, crosses it, and takes in the Tigris, and through Mesopotamia, bordering on Damascus, it ends at Arabia Petraea itself. It comprises six regions. The first, largest and most ancient is Mesopotamia, which for this reason is called Aram par excellence [κατ' ἐξοχήν]. Sometimes it is called Aram Paddan, that is, the yoke of Syria, as if to say Syria yoked, or sent under the yoke of two rivers; hence it is also called Aram Naharaim, as we have just said, by the Latins interamnis. The second is Aram Zobah (2 Chron. 8, v. 3). The third is Aram Beth Rechob (Gen. 36, v. 37). The fourth is Aram Maachah (2 Sam. 8 and 10). The fifth is Aram Damascus, which is hollow Syria [Κοίλη Συρία], as if to say "hollow Syria", and has that name because it is bounded by the valleys of two mountains, Lebanon and Antilebanon. These five regions are variously called Aram in Holy Scripture. The sixth is Syria Comagena, or Antiochene, whose inhabitants, according to Strabo, were called Arimi by the ancients; that name flowed from the Hebrew. Assyria (which today is comprehended under the name of Syria) is bounded on the west by Mesopotamia, on the east by Media, on the north by the Hyrcanian Sea, and on the south by Chaldaea and Persia. Chaldaea (otherwise Babylonia) is divided into three parts: upper, middle and lower. The upper borders Mesopotamia, at the river Euphrates, and is called Auranitis. The middle is called Chaldaea toward the Arabian desert. The lower is called Amordacia, at the Persian Gulf. In upper Chaldaea was Eden or paradise, whose topography is given in Gen. 2. See on this matter a little later, under hydrography. Moreover, the whole system of Chaldaea had these borders: on the east, Media and Persia; on the south, Susiana and Arabia; on the west, Egypt and Palestine; on the north, Syria, Mesopotamia and Assyria.

units.la: XIII. Multæ partes Asiæ minoris comme- morantur in Scripturis.
units.tr: XIII. Many parts of Asia Minor are mentioned in the Scriptures.

units.la: Asiam vulgo diuiduntur in maiorem & minorem. Quæ partes terræ in superioribus commemoratæ sunt, ad Asiam maiorem seu vniuersale pertinent. Præter illas Scriptura etiam meminit aliarum, quæ spectant ad Asiam minorem & propriam, quæ est prouincia seu pars quædam Asiæ maioris. Est autem Asia minor tota illa Cherfonesus, seu peninsula inter mare Euxinū, Ciliciū & Pamphylium, versus mare Ægæū protensa, quæ hodie Natolia, & Turcia maior dicitur. Complectitur has regiones, Pontum, Bithyniam, Asiam propriā, Lyciam, Galatiam, Pamphyliam, Cappadociam, Ciliciā, & Armeniam minorem. In Ponto & Bithynia celebrantur hæ vrbes; Chalcedon, Nicomedia, Apamia, Prusa, Nicæa, & Heraclea Ponti. Asia propria complectitur has regiones: Phrygiam, Cariam, Mysiam, Æolidem, Ioniam, Doridé, Lydiam. Phrygia est maior, & minor, quæ dicitur Troas, in quâ fuit vrbs Pergamus. Caria metropolis fuit Miletus. Mysia est maior, & minor, quæ etiam interdum dicitur Aeolia. Aeolis est regio in litore maris Ægæi. Ionia habet insulam Chios, & vrbem Ephesum, quæ olim Asiæ lumen fuit appellata. Doris in cherfonesi formam in mare porrigitur. Lydia dicitur etiam Mæonia. Lycia vergit ad mare, ab ipsâ Lycium appellatum. Galatia, seu Gallogræcia, & Græcogallia, comprehendit Paphlagoniam regionem. Pamphylia complectitur Pergam, Sidam, & Attaliam, vrbes. Cappadocia, regio ampla, habet has vrbes celebres, Trapezuntem, Amasiam, Iconium, & Mazam siue Cæsaream. Cilicia vrbes insigniores sunt Hama, olim Tarsus, patria S. Pauli; & Heraclea. Minor Armenia a meridie habet Ciliciam, a septentrione Ponticas gentes. Porrò insulæ ad minorem Asiam pertinentes sunt Tenedos ad Hellespontum; Lesbos in mari Ægæo; Chios, Samos, & Icaria in Icario mari; Pa-hmos, Leria, Clarós, Cous, in mari Myrtoo: Casos & Carpathos in mari Carpathio; Rhodos, in Rhodiensi pelago. Multa ex his locis celebrantur in Actis apostolorum, epistolis Pauli & Apocalypsi Iohannis.
units.tr: Asia is commonly divided into Greater and Lesser. The regions mentioned above in the earlier passages belong to Greater Asia, or Asia in general. Besides these, Scripture also mentions other places that belong to Lesser Asia proper, which is a province or part of Greater Asia. Asia minor is that whole peninsula between the Euxine, Cilician and Pamphylian seas, stretching towards the Aegean Sea, which today is called Natolia and Turcia maior. It embraces these regions: Pontus, Bithynia, Asia propria, Lycia, Galatia, Pamphylia, Cappadocia, Cilicia and Minor Armenia. In Pontus and Bithynia these cities are famous: Chalcedon, Nicomedia, Apamea, Prusa, Nicaea and Heraclea Pontica. Asia propria comprises these regions: Phrygia, Caria, Mysia, Aeolis, Ionia, Doris and Lydia. Phrygia is divided into Greater and Lesser; the Lesser is called Troas, and in it was the city of Pergamum. The metropolis of Caria was Miletus. Mysia is Greater and Lesser; the Lesser is sometimes also called Aeolia. Aeolis is a region on the coast of the Aegean Sea. Ionia has the island of Chios and the city of Ephesus, which was once called the light of Asia. Doris stretches out into the sea in the shape of a peninsula. Lydia is also called Maeonia. Lycia borders on the sea and takes its name from Lycus. Galatia, or Gallograecia and Graecogallia, includes the region of Paphlagonia. Pamphylia comprises the cities of Perga, Side and Attalia. Cappadocia, a wide region, has these famous cities: Trapezus, Amasia, Iconium and Mazaca, or Caesarea. The notable cities of Cilicia are Hama, formerly Tarsus, the homeland of St Paul, and Heraclea. Minor Armenia has Cilicia to the south and the Pontic peoples to the north. Furthermore, the islands belonging to Lesser Asia are: Tenedos, near the Hellespont; Lesbos, in the Aegean Sea; Chios, Samos and Icaria, in the Icarian Sea; Patmos, Leros, Claros and Cos, in the Myrtoan Sea; Casos and Carpathos, in the Carpathian Sea; and Rhodes, in the Rhodian waters. Many of these places are mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, the Epistles of Paul and the Revelation of John.

units.la: XIV. Æthiopia est pars Africæ, subiecta zonæ torridæ sub Ægypto. In sacris dicitur Chus, siue Cusch. Gen. 11. verf. 6. 2. Reg. 19. v. 9. Ier. 13. verf. 23. Cusch ille fuit filius Cham, qui Arabibus & Æthiopibus nomen dedit. Æthiopum reginæ communi nomine appellabantur Candacæ. Act. 8. v. 27. Hic memineris, duas solum Africæ regiones, puta Ægyptum & Africam, in historiâ factâ celebrari.
units.tr: XIV. Ethiopia is a part of Africa, lying under the torrid zone beyond Egypt. In the sacred books it is called Chus, or Cush. Gen. 11. verf. 6. 2. Reg. 19. v. 9. Ier. 13. verf. 23. That Cush was a son of Ham, who gave his name to the Arabs and Ethiopians. The queens of the Ethiopians were commonly called Candaces. Act. 8. v. 27. Here you should remember that only two regions of Africa, namely Egypt and Africa proper, are mentioned in the historical narrative.

units.la: XV. Ophir, cuius meminerunt sacræ literæ, videtur fuisse aurea Cherfonesus. Sic tradit Iosephus lib. 8. antiq. Est autem nobis aurea Cherfonesus omnis ea ora, quæ Pegusiis, Malacâ & Samotrâ continetur. Iosephus d.l. in India orientali ponit, & terram auream suo tempore vocatam addit. Eupolemus apud Eusebium lib. 9. præpar. evang. c. 4. Vrephen appellat, & dicit insulam maris rubri esse. Goropius, Postellus, Arias Montanus, & alij Peruanam regionem in America esse putant. Quod si ita est, Scriptura ex quatuor illis mundi partibus, Asia, Africà,Europâ,& Americâ,loca quædam inseruit historiæ sacræ. Alij existimant Cephalam Æthiopicam esse ipsissimā Ophir. Tradit enim Thomas Lopezius in suâ Indicâ navigatione, Cephalæs habere libros patriâ linguâ scriptos, in quibus legitur Salomonē regem hinc tertio quoque anno aurum tulisse. Abundatque hæc regio etiamnù hodie aurifodinis, adeo vt nihil præter aurù exteris mercatoribus communicet, vt Lusitanorum peregrinationes testantur. Edidit tamen Gaspar Varrerius Lusitanus nuper opusculum de Ophirâ regione, in quo constanter asseuerat, multisque argumentis persuadere conatur, sacræ Scripturæ Ophiram esse auream Cherfonesum, aut potius omnem eam oram, quæ Pegusiis, Malacâ & Samotrâ continetur. Cæterùm de Ophir vide 1. Reg. 9. v. vlt. c. 10. v. 11.
units.tr: XV. Ophir, which the sacred letters mention, seems to have been the Golden Chersonese. So Josephus lib. 8. antiq. teaches: the whole coast contained by Pegu, Malacca and Samotra is for us the Golden Chersonese. Josephus, in the same place, places it in eastern India, and adds that it was called the Golden Land in his own time. Eupolemus, in Eusebius lib. 9. praep. evang. c. 4., calls it Urphe and says it is an island in the Red Sea. Goropius, Postellus, Arias Montanus and others think it is the Peruvian region in America. If that is so, Scripture has introduced places into sacred history from all four parts of the world: Asia, Africa, Europe and America. Others suppose that Ethiopian Sofala is the very Ophir. For Thomas Lopez, in his account of the Indian voyage, relates that the people of Sofala have books written in their native language, in which it is read that King Solomon brought gold from there every third year. This region still today abounds in gold mines, so much so that it trades nothing with foreign merchants except gold, as the voyages of the Portuguese attest. Nevertheless, the Portuguese Gaspar Varrerius recently published a little work on the region of Ophir, in which he steadfastly asserts, and tries to persuade by many arguments, that the Ophir of Sacred Scripture is the Golden Chersonese, or rather the whole coast contained by Pegu, Malacca and Samotra. Moreover, for Ophir see 1. Reg. 9. v. vlt. c. 10. v. 11.

units.la: XVI. Multae partes Europae commemoran- tur in Scripturis.
units.tr: XVI. Many parts of Europe are mentioned in the Scriptures.

units.la: Nominatim multa loca Graeciae, & Italiae. De his itaque aliquid attingemus. Ad Graeciam pertinent hae provinciae, 1. Thracia; cuius urbes celebriores sunt Nicopolis, Philippi, Philippopolis, Adrianopolis, Heraclea, & Constantinopolis, ῥίζα πόλεων [?] Thraciae. 2. Cherfonesus Thraciae; in qua est Calliopolis. 3. Macedonia; in qua Thessalonica, Neapolis, Berrhoea, Apollonia, Dyrrhachium. 4. Epirus, nunc Albania; in qua Nicopolis. 5. Achaia, diuisa in nouem regiones, e quibus insigniores sunt Doris, Phocis (in qua Delphi) Attica (in qua Athenae) Corinthia regio (in qua Corinthus, emporium) & Laconica, in qua Lacedaemon. 6. Peloponnesus, nunc Morea. Eius oppidum celebre sunt Cenchreae. Ex partibus Italiae commemorantur in S. literis Roma, Neapolis, Puteoli, Syracusae, Rhegium, Forum Apij, Tres tabernae. Porro etiam fit mentio Dalmatiae: denique quarundam insularum, vt Cypri, Melitae, Cretae: de quibus vide infra in Chronologia Itinerarium B. Pauli.
units.tr: Many places in Greece and Italy are named specifically. Therefore we shall touch on some of them. The following provinces belong to Greece: 1. Thracia, whose more notable cities are Nicopolis, Philippi, Philippopolis, Adrianople, Heraclea and Constantinople, the root of the cities [ῥίζα πόλεων] of Thrace. 2. Thracian Chersonese, in which is Callipolis. 3. Macedonia, in which are Thessalonica, Neapolis, Berrhoea, Apollonia and Dyrrachium. 4. Epirus, now Albania, in which is Nicopolis. 5. Achaia, divided into nine regions, of which the more notable are Doris, Phocis (in which is Delphi), Attica (in which is Athens), the Corinthian region (in which is Corinth, the trading centre) and Laconia, in which is Lacedaemon. 6. Peloponnesus, now Morea. Its famous town is Cenchreae. Among the parts of Italy mentioned in the Holy Letters are Rome, Naples, Puteoli, Syracuse, Rhegium, Appii Forum and Three Taverns. Further, mention is made of Dalmatia, and finally of certain islands, such as Cyprus, Malta and Crete, concerning which see below, in the Chronology, the Itinerary of St Paul.

units.la: XVII. Dimensio aquae singulariter spectatur in mari, lacubus, & fluminibus.
