units.tr: XVII. The extent of water is considered especially in the sea, in lakes, and in rivers.

units.la: Mare est triplex, Oceanum, Mediterraneum, & Caspium. Mare Oceanum est, quod totam terram instar cinguli ambit. Hoc diuiditur in varios sinus & freta. Ex sinubus in S. literis celebratur Arabicus, qui appellatur mare rubrum, mare iunci siue carecti, mare Aegypti, & mare Erythraeum. Et quidem mare iunci, seu caricis, siue algae appellatur, quia eiusmodi planta in litore crescit: rubrum vero & Erythraeum dicitur ab Erythro rege, hoc est, ab Edom siue Esau, qui principatum in illis locis tenuit: non vero a colore: caeruleum namque est. Mare mediterraneum est, quod ab occasu per medias terras irrumpens ex Oceano, versus ortum & septentrionem diffunditur, & Africam ab Europa disterminat. In sacris appellatur mare magnum, item mare occidentale, respectu terræ sanctæ: item, mare Tharsis, quod fuit nomen filij Iauanis Gen. 10. verf. 4. Ab eo appellata fuit Cilicia hoc nomine
units.tr: The sea is threefold: the Ocean, the Mediterranean, and the Caspian. The Ocean is the sea that encircles the whole earth like a girdle. It is divided into various bays and straits. Among the bays, the Arabian is celebrated in Holy Scripture, and it is called the Red Sea, the sea of reeds or sedge, the sea of Egypt, and the Erythraean Sea. It is called the sea of reeds, or of sedge, or of seaweed, because such a plant grows on its shore. It is called Red and Erythraean from King Erythras, that is, from Edom or Esau, who held power in those places, and not from its colour, for it is in fact blue. The Mediterranean Sea is the sea that bursts in from the Ocean on the west through the midst of the lands, spreads out towards the east and north, and separates Africa from Europe. In the sacred books it is called the Great Sea, also the Western Sea, with respect to the Holy Land; also the Sea of Tarshish, which was the name of a son of Javan (Gen. 10:4). From him Cilicia was called by this name

units.la: 2. Chron. 9. v. 21. & Tarsus eius metropolis: & quia ea ad mare sita erat, ipsum mare Esa. 2. Ion. 1. v. 3. Proprie itaq; maris mediterranei pars, quæ est ad Ciliciam, appellata fuit Tharsis: sed per synecdochen totum mare mediterraneum à Iudæis ita fuit appellatum. Nam quia illa ipsa pars Iudæis erat notissima, appellatio ipsius ad totum mare mediterraneum fuit extensa. Hoc est mare, in quo Paulus tot pericula sustinuit, vt ex Actis apost. constat. Mare Caspium, siue Hircanum, est situm in Asia, remotum ab Oceano, & mari mediterraneo. Lacus multi sunt in orbe terrarum. In Iudæa sunt tres, e quibus duo posteriores notissimi sunt in sacra historia. Primus lacus est Samachonitis, alijs Maron, & Aqua Maronitica. Maginus ait, esse potius stagnum quàm lacu. Efficitur enim à Iordane in valle quadam, præsertim tempore resolutionis niuium à Libano fluentium: quod quidem stagnum æstate vt plurimum exsiccatur, crescentibus ibi arbustis & herbis, in quibus leones, & aliæ bestiæ latitant. Secundus est lacus Gene[?]areth, seu, mare Tiberiadis & Galilæa. Nomen habet ab amoenitate. Nam regio vicina dicitur Genezareth & Genesar q.d. Gan-far i.e. hortus principis: quia terra ista fuit cultissima & amoenissima. Tertius est lacus Asphaltites, sic dictus à bitumine ἀσφάλτῳ. Dicitur etiam mare salsum in S. literis, & vulgo mortuum. Sequuntur insignia flumina, quorum Scriptura meminit. Et primò se offerunt quatuor flumina paradisi: Gen. 2, ver. 10, hoc modo. Eden est Auranitis, h.e. suprema Chaldæ æ pars, cuius ager non solum totius Orientis, sed terrarum etiam o bis est amoenissimus & fertilissimus; & videtur dicta Auranitis quasi Audanitis, seu Edenitis. Ex hoc terræ tractu procedit fluuius, Euphrates, qui se diuidit in quatuor capita. Euphrates enim quadripartitus est. Primum caput Euphratis est Pison, qui dicitur Euphrates inferior, item Pallitigris, q.d. Piso-Tigris, Miscetut enim cum Tigri ad Apameam. Secundum caput est Githon, vulgo Maharsares, quasi Naharsares, fluuius principis. Tertium est Chiddekel, i. e. Tigris, qui hodie appellatur Tiglath. Quartum caput retinet nomen Euphratis, qui mediam Babylonem permeat. Euphrates Hebraice dicitur פרת [?] i.e. vmbilicus, duabus de causis: tum, quòd tractus Euphrateus nostrum hemisphærium ferme medium secat, & orientem ab occidente discriminat: tum, quia gentes ex hoc quasi centro versus omnes mundi plagas dispersæ sunt. Gen.11. Quibus causis potest addi tertia, quòd ex isto loco superstitio Babylonica in totum orbem vna cum hominibus sit disseminata. Quod hic dicitur de Euphrate, ipsum esse vmbilicum terræ, id intelligendum est de terra habitabili veteribus cognita, itemque sensu laxiore. Nam & Ierusalem dicitur vmbilicus terræ. Sphæram inspice, & ini rationem septem climatum, quæ sola veteribus erant cognita: videbis Ierusalem, & totum vicinum tractum esse quasi vmbilicum terræ habitabilis, veteribus cognitæ. Sunt, qui Hierosolymam dicunt non in medio terræ, sed Iudææ sitam esse, quomodo Delphi in medio Græciæ erant siti. Deinde celebris est Iordanis fluuius, qui mediam Palæstinam secat. Oritur in montis Libani radicibus à duobus fontibus, Ior & Dan. Cursu suo efformat duos lacus, nempe Samachonitidem & mare Tiberiadis, tandemque in mare mortuum se exonerat. Apud Ezechielem occurrit fluuius Chobar, siue Chebar c.1 [?]. qui multis postea cœlestibus revelationibus & diuinis apparitionibus, eidem prophetæ propter illum exhibitis, est nobilitatus. Iunius existimat esse Chaboram Ptolemaeiin Mesopotamia influentem in Euphratem. Scaligero est Tigris, qui dictus est ποταμὸς βασιλικὸς [?], flumen regium, Chald. Nehar-malca: ita vt sit dictus Chobar à præfecto, qui diduxit, ne præcipiti cursu Babyloniam infestaret; regium flumen, à rege, qui diduci iussit.
units.tr: 2. Chron. 9. v. 21. and its metropolis Tarsus. And because that city lay by the sea, the sea itself was so called (Isa. 2; Jonah 1:3). Properly, then, the part of the Mediterranean that lies off Cilicia was called Tarshish, but by synecdoche the Jews applied that name to the whole Mediterranean Sea. For since that very part was best known to the Jews, its name was extended to the whole sea. This is the sea in which Paul endured so many dangers, as is clear from the Acts of the Apostles. The Caspian Sea, or Hyrcanian, lies in Asia, remote from the Ocean and the Mediterranean. There are many lakes in the world. In Judea there are three, of which the last two are the best known in sacred history. The first lake is Samachonitis, by others Maron, and the Waters of Maron. Maginus says it is more a pool than a lake. It is formed by the Jordan in a certain valley, especially when the snows flowing from Lebanon melt. This pool for the most part dries up in summer, while shrubs and herbs grow there, in which lions and other beasts lie hidden. The second is the lake of Gennesaret, or the Sea of Tiberias and Galilee. It takes its name from its pleasantness, for the neighbouring region is called Gennesaret and Genesar, as if Gan-sar, that is, the garden of the prince, because that land was most cultivated and most pleasant. The third is the lake Asphaltites, so called from bitumen [ἀσφάλτῳ]. In Scripture it is also called the Salt Sea, and commonly the Dead Sea. Next come the notable rivers, which Scripture mentions. And first there present themselves the four rivers of paradise, in the following way (Gen. 2, ver. 10). Eden is Auranitis, that is, the highest part of Chaldea, whose land is the most pleasant and fertile not only of the whole East but of the whole earth; and Auranitis seems so called as if it were Audanitis, or Edenitis. From this tract of land a river proceeds, the Euphrates, which divides into four heads. For the Euphrates is fourfold. The first head of the Euphrates is Pison, which is called the Lower Euphrates, and also Pallitigris, as if Piso-Tigris, for it mingles with the Tigris at Apamea. The second head is Githon, commonly Maharsares, as if Naharsares, the river of the prince. The third is Chiddekel, that is, the Tigris, which today is called Tiglath. The fourth head keeps the name Euphrates, and it flows through the middle of Babylon. The Euphrates is called in Hebrew [פרת], that is, navel, for two reasons: first, because the Euphratean tract cuts our hemisphere almost in the middle and separates east from west; second, because the peoples were scattered from this centre, as it were, towards all the regions of the world (Gen. 11). To these reasons a third may be added: that from this place Babylonian superstition was spread abroad over the whole world together with men. What is said here of the Euphrates, that it is the navel of the earth, is to be understood of the inhabited earth known to the ancients, and in a looser sense. For Jerusalem too is called the navel of the earth. Look at the sphere and consider the seven climates, which alone were known to the ancients: you will see that Jerusalem and the whole neighbouring region lie as it were at the navel of the inhabited earth known to the ancients. There are some who say that Jerusalem is not in the middle of the earth but is situated in Judea, just as Delphi was situated in the middle of Greece. Next, the river Jordan is famous, which cuts through the middle of Palestine. It rises at the foot of Mount Lebanon from two springs, Ior and Dan. In its course it forms two lakes, namely Samachonitis and the Sea of Tiberias, and at last it empties itself into the Dead Sea. In Ezekiel there occurs the river Chobar, or Chebar (Ezek. 1), which was afterwards made famous by many heavenly revelations and divine appearances shown to that prophet beside it. Junius thinks it is the Chaboras of Ptolemy, flowing into the Euphrates in Mesopotamia. For Scaliger it is the Tigris, which is called the royal river [ποταμὸς βασιλικὸς], a royal river, in Chaldee Nehar-malca; so that it was called Chobar from the prefect who diverted it, lest with its headlong course it should harass Babylonia, and royal river from the king who ordered it to be diverted.

units.la: XV. OPTICA SACRA.
units.tr: XV. Sacred Optics

units.la: I. Optica sacra est bene videndi scientia ex S. literis illustrata. Latinis dicitur Perspectiua. Est autem specialis quædam geometria, sicut Musica, specialis arithmetica. Hinc Optica dicitur esse geometria in visu, luce, colore, & umbrâ: Musica, arithmetica in auditu.
units.tr: I. Sacred optics is the science of seeing well, illustrated from the Holy Scriptures. In Latin it is called Perspective. It is a special kind of geometry, just as music is a special kind of arithmetic. Hence optics is said to be geometry applied to sight, light, colour and shadow, while music is arithmetic applied to hearing.

units.la: II. Eius partes duæ sunt: una de visibili, altera de visione.
units.tr: II. It has two parts: one concerning the visible, the other concerning vision.

units.la: III. Visibile est corpus radians. Intellige radium opticum, qui est species visibilis, in oculum incidens.
units.tr: III. The visible is a radiating body. By this I mean the optical ray, which is the visible species falling into the eye.

units.la: IV. Visibile est per se, vel per accidens. Illud per se & immediatè radiat: hoc, mediante alio.
units.tr: IV. The visible is either per se or per accidens. The former radiates directly and immediately; the latter radiates through something else.

units.la: V. Visibile per se est primarium, vel secundarium. Primarium est, quod primò præcipueque radiat, ut lux: secundarium, quod in luce radiat, ut color.
units.tr: V. The visible per se is either primary or secondary. The primary is that which radiates first and above all, such as light; the secondary is that which radiates in light, such as colour.

units.la: VI. Lux est visibile, quod per se videtur, & quod facit ut cætera visibilia videantur. Atque hæc est causa, quòd Deus primo die creauerit lucem Genenef. 1. verf. 3. Lux enim est prima gratia domus, ut ait Ambrosius lib. 2. hexaem. cap. 9. quæ si desit, tota domus deformi horret incultu, ut idem ait. Augustino dicitur colorum regina: & ipsi definitur, quòd & alia demonstret, & seipsam tract. 35. in Iohan. Quam definitionem elegantèr expressit apostolus Eph. 5. verf. 13. πᾶν τὸ φανερούμενον φῶς ἐστι, lux est, quod omnia manifestat. Neque enim φανερούμενον passiuâ, sed mediâ formâ ponitur: quia mens apostoli est, docere, quemadmodum lux corporalis φανεροποιεῖ, manifesta reddit, corporalia, ita lucem spiritualem verbi Dei φανεροποιεῖν, manifestare, opera impura tenebrarum, ut homines illorum pudeat. Porrò triplex est lux corporalis': infundens & non infusa, vt in sole: infundens & infusa, vt in luna & igne: non infundens, sed infusa, vt in aëre. Et sic est spiritualis lux, infundens & non infusa, in Deo: infundens, & infusa, in doctoribus: non infundens, sed infusa, in discipulis & auditoribus.
units.tr: VI. Light is the visible that is seen per se, and that causes other visible things to be seen. This is why God created light on the first day, Gen. 1, v. 3. For light is the first grace of the house, as Ambrose says, Hexaemeron, book 2, ch. 9, and without it the whole house lies in an unsightly, bare state, as the same writer says. Augustine calls it the queen of colours, and it is defined as that which both reveals other things and reveals itself, Tractate 35 on John. The apostle expressed this definition elegantly in Eph. 5, v. 13: everything that is made manifest is light [πᾶν τὸ φανερούμενον φῶς ἐστι], that is, light is that which manifests all things. For made manifest [φανερούμενον] is put in the middle voice, not the passive, because the apostle's meaning is to teach that just as bodily light makes manifest [φανεροποιεῖ], that is, renders manifest, bodily things, so the spiritual light of God's Word makes manifest [φανεροποιεῖν], that is, reveals, the impure works of darkness, so that people are ashamed of them. Moreover, bodily light is threefold: pouring out and not poured in, as in the sun; pouring out and poured in, as in the moon and fire; not pouring out but poured in, as in the air. So too spiritual light is: pouring out and not poured in, in God; pouring out and poured in, in teachers; not pouring out but poured in, in disciples and hearers.

units.la: VII. In luce spectatur effectum & oppositum eius.
units.tr: VII. In light one considers its effect and its opposite.

units.la: Effectum lucis est lumen: oppositum, vmbra. Lumen est splendor à lucente corpore emissus. Sic lux est in corpore solis : lumen fluit à corpore solis. Vtrumque Graecè φῶς dicitur. Sed Latini hic sunt exquisitiores. Nam lux ab illis dicta est vis, quae est in corpore lucido. At huius sive speciem, sive effectum, lumen appellarunt, vt ait Scaliger exerc. 71. f. 1. Indoles eius est eadem cum parente, iuxta illud tritum: Qualis causa, talis effectus. Hinc in Scripturis praecipua mysteria, nunc lucis, nunc luminis similitudine explicantur: puta mysterium aeternae generationis Heb. 1. regenerationis Iohan. 1. item natura Dei 1. Iohan. 1. & similia. Huc pertinet Vrim Exod. 28. & Leuit. 8. Vmbra est priuatio lucis: eaque totalis, vel partialis. Vmbra totalis est nox: vnde tenebras putant dici, quòd teneant vmbram, & definiunt eas priuationem totius lucis. Hinc vt res sublimes, mysticae, & laetae in sacris literis nomine lucis insigniuntur, ita res humiles, turpes, aduersae, & similes appellantur tenebrae: puta afflictiones, sepulchrum, miseria in inferno, peccatum, caecitas spiritualis in mente &c. Vide Iob. 17. v. 12. Psal. 88. ver. 13. Matth. 8. v.12. 1.Iohan. 1. & 2. Vmbra partialis est deminutio luminis: vt quam parietes & viridaria faciunt, cum recti lucis radii auertuntur, & obliqui obscurius micant. Quibusdam vmbra eleganter definitur affectio aëris lumine aliquo priuati. Varia sunt eius effecta & adiuncta, puta desam esse vel minus de[?]sam, refrigerare, exhilarare vel cotristare, seruire dimesioni corporis &c. Vnde vmbra in Scripturis nunc ꝑ refrigerio & ꝑtectione, nunc ꝑ figura quę Christum venturum veluti depinxit, nunc pro re tristi ponitur. Iud. 9. v.15. Psal. 17. v.8. Coloss. 2. v.17. Iob. 3. v.5. Ratio harum similitudinum petitur ex his aphorismis. 1. Vmbra est humida & frigida. 2. Pictores faciunt vmbras, vt imagines, quae planae sunt, solidae videantur: quod dicunt adumbrare. 3. Vmbra sequitur figuram corporis. 4. Vmbra diuturnior & crassior est ingrata. Caeterum varia sunt vmbrae magisteria, inter quae in vsu quotidiano primas facile tenet Gnomonica, quae docet fabricare sciotherica siue solaria. Nam gnomon in medio amusio collocatur ad vmbras inuestigandas, vt illarum beneficio horae indagentur. Prout enim incidunt vmbrae vel in medium, vel ad dextram, vel ad sinistram, ita iudicantur horae, vel meridiana, vel ante, vel post meridiem. Vmbra meridiana est breuissima, vmbra ante meridiem semper decrescit, post meridiem semper accrescit. Hinc Iudic. 9. v.36. vmbra montis, sole praecipitante, dicitur longe maxima. In Scripturis est celebre horologium solarium Achabi, in quo Deus reduxit vmbram decem gradibus, hoc est, decem semihoris. 2. Reg. 20. verf. 1. Esa. 38. v.8. Ita dies, qui duodenas horas aequales continebat, septendecim horarum effectus est. Neque enim verum est, quod scribunt nonnulli Hebraei, vmbram retroceflisse, procedente tamen sole, nec secutam esse vmbram motum solis. Hoc, inquam, falsum est: quia ex Esa. 38. vers. 8. colligere licet, vmbram retroceflisse pariter retrocedete sole. Sed videamus breuiter fabricam solarij Achabi. Erant in eo gradus singuli [?] ad semihoras notandas constituti. Solarium enim diurnum apud Iudaeos indicabat horas duodenas. Iam vero Deus per prophetam ita dicit Achabo: Hoc ipsum tibi esto signum a Iehoua, factum esse Iehouam rem, quam locutus est: abeatne ista vmbra decem gradibus, an retrocedat decem gradibus. Quae duplicatio numeri denarij euincit gradus fuisse [?], h. e. solarium indicasse semihoras vicenas quaternas, quarum gradus totidem commatis fuerint distinct[?], ita vt vmbra per sciatheram siue gnomona secundum solis cursum peruaserit omnia commacommata, siue, vt propheta appellat, gradus solarij.
units.tr: The effect of light is lumen; its opposite is shadow. Lumen is the splendour emitted from a shining body. Thus light is in the body of the sun, and lumen flows from the body of the sun. Both are called φῶς in Greek. But the Latins are more precise here: they called light the power that is in a luminous body, and they called its species or effect lumen, as Scaliger says, Exercitations 71, f. 1. Its nature is the same as its source, according to the common saying: such is the cause, such is the effect. Hence in Scripture the chief mysteries are explained sometimes by the likeness of light, sometimes by that of lumen: for example, the mystery of eternal generation, Heb. 1; regeneration, John 1; likewise the nature of God, 1 John 1, and similar passages. To this belongs the Urim, Exod. 28 and Lev. 8. Shadow is the privation of light, and it is either total or partial. Total shadow is night, whence people think darkness is so called because it holds back the shadow, and they define it as the privation of all light. Hence, just as lofty, mystical and joyful things are marked in the sacred writings by the name of light, so humble, base, adverse and similar things are called darkness: for example, afflictions, the sepulchre, misery in hell, sin, spiritual blindness of mind, and so on. See Job 17, v. 12; Ps. 88, v. 13; Matt. 8, v. 12; 1 John 1 and 2. Partial shadow is a diminishing of light, as that which walls and shady groves make when the straight rays of light are turned aside and the oblique ones shine more dimly. Some define shadow elegantly as an affection of the air deprived of some light. Its effects and attributes are various: to be shady or less shady, to cool, to cheer or sadden, to serve the size of a body, and so on. Hence in Scripture shadow is sometimes used for refreshment and protection, sometimes for a figure that as it were portrayed the coming Christ, and sometimes for a sorrowful thing. See Judg. 9, v. 15; Ps. 17, v. 8; Col. 2, v. 17; Job 3, v. 5. The reason for these likenesses is drawn from the following aphorisms. (1) Shadow is moist and cold. (2) Painters make shadows so that images, which are flat, appear solid; this is called shading. (3) Shadow follows the shape of the body. (4) A shadow that lasts longer and is thicker is unpleasant. Besides this, there are various arts of shadow, of which the one most easily holding first place in daily use is gnomonics, which teaches how to make sundials, or solaria. For the gnomon is placed in the middle of the dial to trace the shadows, so that the hours may be found by their help. For as the shadows fall either in the middle, or to the right, or to the left, so the hours are judged to be noon, or before noon, or after noon. The noon shadow is very short; the shadow before noon always shortens; after noon it always lengthens. Hence in Judg. 9, v. 36 the shadow of the mountain, when the sun is sinking, is called very long indeed. In Scripture there is the famous sundial of Ahaz, on which God turned the shadow back ten degrees, that is, ten half-hours. 2 Kings 20, v. 1; Isa. 38, v. 8. Thus the day, which had twelve equal hours, became one of seventeen hours. For it is not true, as some Hebrews write, that the shadow went back while the sun still advanced, nor that the shadow followed the motion of the sun. This, I say, is false, because from Isa. 38, v. 8 it may be gathered that the shadow went back in the same way as the sun went back. But let us briefly look at the construction of Ahaz's sundial. It had individual steps set up to mark the half-hours. For the daytime dial among the Jews showed twelve hours. Now God speaks through the prophet to Ahaz thus: This shall be a sign to you from Jehovah, that Jehovah will do the thing he has spoken: shall this shadow go forward ten degrees, or go back ten degrees? This doubling of the number ten proves that the steps were [?], that is, that the dial marked twenty-four half-hours, whose steps were distinguished into as many divisions, so that the shadow, through the gnomon or style, passed over all the divisions according to the course of the sun, or, as the prophet calls them, the steps of the dial.

units.la: VIII. Color est visibile, quod speciem sui in luce immediatè diffundit. Vitelloni eleganter dicitur lux incorporata. Est autem color simplex, vel mixtus. Color simplex est, qui non componitur ex alio colore, & ex quo reliqui omnes componuntur. Dicitur aliàs primarius & extremus. Eiusmodi sunt albedo & nigredo. In illa est plus lucis, in hac plus umbrae. Hinc albedo in sacris est symbolum iustitiae & lętitiae Apoc. 1. 3. 4. 6. 7. nigredo peccati & afflictionis Cant. 1. verf. 5. 6. Color mixtus est, qui componitur ex simplicibus. Dicitur aliàs compositus, secundarius, & intermedius. Eiusmodi sunt rubedo, flauedo, & reliqui omnes praeter album & nigrum.
units.tr: VIII. Colour is the visible that immediately spreads its species in light. Vitellio elegantly calls it embodied light. Colour is either simple or mixed. A simple colour is one that is not composed of another colour, and from which all the rest are composed. It is also called primary and extreme. Such are whiteness and blackness: white has more light, black has more shadow. Hence in Scripture whiteness is a symbol of righteousness and joy, Rev. 1, 3, 4, 6, 7; blackness of sin and affliction, Song 1, v. 5, 6. A mixed colour is one composed of simple colours. It is also called compound, secondary and intermediate. Such are redness, yellowness, and all the others except white and black.

units.la: IX. Visibile per accidens est, quidquid per lucem & colorem videtur. Eiusmodi sunt magnitudo, numerus, continuitas, separatio, distantia, & situs, in praedicamento quantitatis: figura, identitas, aequalitas, similitudo, diuersitas, inaequalitas, dissimilitudo, asperitas, laeuitas, raritas, densitas, pulchritudo, diaphanitas, in praedicamento qualitatis: motus, in praedicamento actionis & passionis: denique visibilia priuatiua, vt umbra, obscuritas, quies, deformitas.
units.tr: IX. The visible per accidens is whatever is seen through light and colour. Such are magnitude, number, continuity, separation, distance and position, in the category of quantity; shape, identity, equality, likeness, difference, inequality, unlikeness, roughness, smoothness, rarity, density, beauty, transparency, in the category of quality; motion, in the category of action and passion; and finally privative visibles, such as shadow, obscurity, rest, deformity.

units.la: X. Visio est actio videntis, & passio visi.
units.tr: Vision is the action of the one who sees and the undergoing of the thing seen.

units.la: XI. Visio consideratur in genere, & in specie.
units.tr: Vision is considered in general and in particular.

units.la: XII. Visio in genere consideratur ratione causae efficientis & formae. Causa efficiens visionis (quantum quidem ad Opticam) est medium perspicuum, radius visivus, & figura optica. Medium perspicuum, vulgo diaphanum, est corpus pellucidum, radiis peruium: puta aer, aqua, vitrum, crystallus, cornu, glacies, & gemmae quaedam. Hic merito admiramur sapientiam Dei opificis, qui aërem ita creauit, vt infinitas rerum species seruare posset impermixtas. Radius visivus est species intentionalis siue imago rei visibilis, per medium perspicuum transiens. Huius radij velocitas, qua fertur in instanti, subtilitas, quâ non impletaërem, egregiè oculos ponit naturam spirituum.Figura optica est pyramis,cuius vertex est in centro oculi,basis in re visibili.Dicitur pyramis, non quòd semper sit talis, sed quòd cum ista figura semper habeat cognationem. Forma visionis est applicatio ad oculum,omnibus rectè se habentibus:ita nempe ut oculus sit sanus, magnitudo rei visibilis sit conueniens, distantia proportionata, medium purum & illuminatum, denique visibile rectè collocatum ante sensorium.Hæc visionis natura egregiè illustrat res spirituales & mentales. Unde in sacris literis cognitio,prouidentia Dei,beatitudo, & similia figurantur hoc nomine. Ita Deus vidit sua opera esse bona Gen.1. videt res nostras Psalm.33. videtur à sanctis in cœlo 1. Cor.13.
units.tr: In general, vision is considered with respect to its efficient cause and its form. The efficient cause of vision (as far as optics is concerned) is the transparent medium, the visual ray, and the optical figure. A transparent medium, commonly called diaphanous, is a pellucid body permeable to rays, such as air, water, glass, crystal, horn, ice, and certain gems. Here we rightly admire the wisdom of God the Maker, who created the air so that it could preserve the infinite species of things unmixed. The visual ray is an intentional species, or image of the visible thing, passing through the transparent medium. The speed of this ray, by which it travels in an instant, and its subtlety, by which it does not fill the air, vividly sets forth the nature of spirits. The optical figure is a pyramid whose apex is at the centre of the eye and whose base is on the visible thing. It is called a pyramid not because it is always such, but because this figure always has an affinity with it. The form of vision is the application to the eye when all things are rightly disposed: namely, that the eye is sound, the size of the visible thing is suitable, the distance is proportionate, the medium is clear and illuminated, and finally the visible object is rightly placed before the sense organ. This nature of vision admirably illustrates spiritual and mental realities. Hence in the sacred letters knowledge, the providence of God, blessedness, and similar things are figured by this term. So God saw that his works were good (Gen. 1.); he sees our affairs (Ps. 33.); he is seen by the saints in heaven (1 Cor. 13.).

units.la: XIII. Visio in specie est vera vel falsa,& utraque simplex vel composita. Visio vera est, qua visibile, vti est, percipitur. Sic corpus Christi post resurrectionem vere fuit visum à discipulis Luc.24. Iohan.20. Visio salsa est, qua visibile percipitur non ita vt est. Sic præstigiatores Pharaonis Exod.7. oculos Ægyptiorum mentesque præstiguebant, id est, obtenebrabant, ut non possent ipsorum impofturas videre & animaduertere. Huc quoq; pertinent præstigiæ circulatorum,quæ agilitate manuum procurantur. Visio simplex est, quæ fit per radium rectum, qui dicitur perpendicularis & incidentiæ. Ita videmus solem, lunam,arbores, animalia. Atque hæc visio est magistra eruditionis certissima. Psal.8. Visio composita est, quæ fit per duos radios, unum rectum,alterum obliquum. Estque reflexa, vel refracta. Visio reflexa est, quæ fit per radium repercussum in idem medium. Ea est obscurior, vel manifestior. Illa est, cùm reflectitur tantum lux & color, ut quando radij solis à terra reflectuntur, & lux in angulis medium repercutitur: hæc est, cùm præter lucem & colore reflectitur imago, ut in speculo: quod ita dictum est, quia in eo speculamur imaginem. Speculum est naturale, ut oculus, stella, gemma, chalybs, crystallus, marmor, aqua, & aër aer densus: vel artificiale, quod fit ex vitro vel metallo, puta ære. Speculorum æneorum mentio fit Exod. 38. v. 8. vbi dicitur labrum chalybeum altaris holocausti fuisse factum e speculis mulierum turmatim conuenientium, & af-ferentium specula sua pro munere spontaneo tabernaculi. Vsus speculorum est ciuilis, militaris, & moralis. Vsus ciuilis est, vt contemplemur faciem in speculis, & rite nos ornemus. Iacob. 1. verf. 23. Vsus militaris est, vt speculis ad hunc finem paratis incendamus res hostium. Vius moralis est, vt animam nostram contemplemur in speculo proprietatum Dei & vitæ Christi, atque ita ex ipsâ faciamus speculum virtutis, in quo resplendeat sacrosancta Trinitas: item, vt creaturas Dei habeamus pro speculis maiestatis eius: denique vt meminerimus, cognitionem, quâ Deum cognoscimus in hac vita, fieri velut in speculo & vmbrâ. 1. Cor. 13. v. 12. Huc pertinet, quod Sap. 7. verf. 26. dicitur de sapientiâ: Ἀπαύγασμα γὰρ ἐστιν φωτὸς ἀϊδίου, καὶ ἔσοπτρον ἀκηλίδωτον τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνεργείας, καὶ εἰκὼν τῆς ἀγαθότητος αὐτοῦ, Splendor enim est lucis æterna, atque speculum virtutis Dei, nullâ maculâ aspersum, eiusq; imago bonitatis. Neque etiam illud hoc loco est silentio prætereundum, speculorum mirabilem reflexionem aliquo modo nos docere, quomodo ideæ omnium rerum sint in Deo. Nam quemadmodum in paruo speculo imagines infinitarum & maximarum rerum sine aliquâ speculi vel compositione, vel læsione, vel contaminatione, distinctè ac eleganter relucent: ita in Deo, tanquam speculo magno huius mundi, resplendent ideæ rerum omnium modo eminentissimo. Visio refracta est, quæ fit per radium repercussum in diuersum medium: vt cùm pomum vel litera videtur per vitrum siue conspicillum. Hæc visio docet nos naturam præconceptæ opinionis. Nam quemadmodum res visæ per duplex medium videntur maiores, & assumunt colorem medij, puta vitri viridis aut rubicundi: sic præconceptæ opiniones faciunt, vt nostra nobis Helena videatur formosissima. Cæterum refractionis exemplum longè pulchercherrimum habemus in iride tum solari, tum lunari. Nam iris est species lucis radiantis, quæ à vario fiue diuerso medio varié obliquata varium colorem repræfentat, ita vt in eâ fit miftio reflexionis & refractionis, eaque longè pulcherrima.Sunt autem tres primarij colores iridis, purpureus seu puniceus, viridis, & cœruleus. Ex his purpureus notat conflagrationem mundi per ignem; viridis, paradisum cœlestem; cœruleus, aquam diluuij, vt piæ antiquitati placuit. Quoties itaque arcum illum versicolorem intuemur, nobis in mentem veniet trium istorum. Quâ quidem obseruatione Opticam sacram concludimus, & studiosum rerum Opticarum hoc studiosè monemus, vt diligentem instituat collationem huius scientiæ cum rebus supernaturalibus, spiritualibus & moralibus, adeoque cum theologiâ, pneumaticâ, & ethicâ.
units.tr: In particular, vision is either true or false, and each is either simple or compound. True vision is that by which the visible thing is perceived as it is. Thus the body of Christ after the resurrection was truly seen by the disciples (Luke 24; John 20). False vision is that by which the visible thing is perceived not as it is. Thus the sorcerers of Pharaoh (Exod. 7.) bewitched the eyes and minds of the Egyptians, that is, darkened them, so that they could not see and notice their deceptions. To this also belong the tricks of jugglers, which are accomplished by the agility of the hands. Simple vision is that which occurs through a straight ray, called perpendicular and incident. Thus we see the sun, the moon, trees, and animals. And this vision is the most certain teacher of learning (Ps. 8.). Compound vision is that which occurs through two rays, one straight and the other oblique, and it is either reflected or refracted. Reflected vision is that which occurs through a ray thrown back into the same medium; it is either more obscure or more manifest. The former is when only light and colour are reflected, as when the rays of the sun are reflected from the earth, and light is thrown back into the corners of a medium; the latter is when, besides light and colour, an image is reflected, as in a mirror, which is so called because in it we behold an image. A mirror is either natural, such as the eye, a star, a gem, steel, crystal, marble, water, and dense air; or artificial, made of glass or metal, such as bronze. Mention of bronze mirrors is made in Exodus 38:8, where it is said that the brazen laver of the burnt offering was made from the mirrors of women who gathered in companies and brought their mirrors as a voluntary offering for the tabernacle. The use of mirrors is civil, military, and moral. The civil use is that we may contemplate our face in mirrors and adorn ourselves properly (Jas. 1:23). The military use is that, with mirrors prepared for this purpose, we may set fire to the enemy's things. The moral use is that we contemplate our soul in the mirror of the perfections of God and the life of Christ, and so make of it a mirror of virtue in which the most holy Trinity may shine; likewise, that we regard the creatures of God as mirrors of his majesty; and finally, that we remember that the knowledge by which we know God in this life is, as it were, in a mirror and in a shadow (1 Cor. 13:12). To this belongs what is said of wisdom in Wisdom 7:26: "For she is the brightness of eternal light, and the unspotted mirror of the power of God, and the image of his goodness" [Ἀπαύγασμα γὰρ ἐστιν φωτὸς ἀϊδίου, καὶ ἔσοπτρον ἀκηλίδωτον τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνεργείας, καὶ εἰκὼν τῆς ἀγαθότητος αὐτοῦ]. Nor is it to be passed over in silence here that the wonderful reflection of mirrors teaches us in some way how the ideas of all things are in God. For just as in a small mirror the images of infinite and very great things shine forth distinctly and elegantly, without any alteration, injury, or contamination of the mirror, so in God, as in the great mirror of this world, the ideas of all things shine forth in a most eminent manner. Refracted vision is that which occurs through a ray thrown back into a different medium, as when an apple or a letter is seen through glass or a spectacle. This vision teaches us the nature of preconceived opinion. For just as things seen through a double medium appear larger and take on the colour of the medium, such as green or red glass, so preconceived opinions make our own Helen seem most beautiful to us. Moreover, we have a most beautiful example of refraction in the rainbow, both solar and lunar. For the rainbow is a kind of radiant light which, being variously bent by a varied or different medium, presents a varied colour, so that in it there is a mixture of reflection and refraction, and a most beautiful one. The rainbow has three principal colours: purple or scarlet, green, and blue. Of these, the purple signifies the conflagration of the world by fire; the green, the heavenly paradise; the blue, the water of the flood, as pious antiquity has held. Whenever therefore we gaze upon that many-coloured arch, these three things will come into our mind. With this observation we conclude sacred optics, and we earnestly advise the student of optical matters to make a diligent comparison of this science with supernatural, spiritual, and moral things, and so with theology, pneumatic theology, and ethics.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: MVSICA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED MUSIC.

units.la: I. Musica sacra est ars bene canendi ex S. literis illustrata.
units.tr: I. Sacred music is the art of singing well, as illuminated by the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: II. Estque vocalis, vel instrumentalis. Musica est ars canendi, fiue instrumentis naturalibus, vt pulmonibus, gutture, lingua, palato, dentibus, labris: fiue artificialibus, vt quæ tactu, pulsu, vel flatu sonant. Vtrobique igitur sunt instrumenta. Verùm quando musica diuiditur in vocalem & instrumentalem, vox opponitur instrumentis fiue organis artefactis. Cæterùm hæc musicæ dichotomia fundata est hinc inde in Psalmis, vbi שיר significat odam fiue canticum voce canendum, מזמור Psalmum fiue canticum organo canendum. Vide Pfal. 3. & 45. Sæpe miscetur musica vocalis cum instrumentali. Vnde quidam Psalmi habent hanc inscriptionem מזמור שיר ψαλμος ωδής, vt reddunt LXX. i. e. Psalmus cantici. Alibi inuertuntur hæ voces. Ex Horatio dices verba sociadachordis[?], qualia erant carmina lyrica. Vide Pfalm. 30. 48. Quidam Hebræi sic adnotant ad hos psalmos. Psalmus est sonus organi cessante voce humana: Canticum est modulatio vocis sine concinente organo: Canticum Psalmi est, cùm vox humana sequitur concentum organi: Psalmus cantici, vbi contra.
units.tr: II. Music is either vocal or instrumental. It is the art of singing either with natural instruments, such as the lungs, throat, tongue, palate, teeth and lips, or with artificial instruments, which sound by touch, striking or blowing. Instruments are therefore found in both kinds. But when music is divided into vocal and instrumental, the voice is set against instruments, that is, against artificial organs. This division of music is founded, here and there, in the Psalms, where שיר [shir] means an ode or song to be sung with the voice, and מזמור [mizmor] a psalm or song to be sung with an instrument. See Ps. 3 and 45. Vocal music is often mixed with instrumental. So some Psalms bear the inscription מזמור שיר [mizmor shir], ψαλμος ωδής [psalmos ōdēs], as the Septuagint render it, that is, a psalm of song. Elsewhere the words are reversed. From Horace you may gather words joined to the strings, such as were the lyric poems. See Ps. 30 and 48. Some Hebrews make these remarks on these Psalms: a psalm is the sound of an instrument with the human voice silent; a song is the modulation of the voice without an accompanying instrument; a song of psalm is when the human voice follows the harmony of the instrument; a psalm of song is the reverse.

units.la: III. Musica vocalis est, quæ docet canere ore. Qualis hæc fuerit apud Iudæos, non est memoriæ proditum. Suidas in historia ὑποκριτικός[?] scribit, Musicam circa Arcadij tempora concidisse, cùm quidem Hebræorum Musica multò ante cum ipsa politia Iudaica exoleuisset. Cum hac quoque, metri, quod in Psalmis Dauidis & aliis libris sacris adhibitum fuit, rationem omnem amissam esse non est dubium. Interim tamen vt in Poetica, sic quoque in Musica possunt probabiliter quædam colligi ex sacris literis, & quidem hoc modo. 1. Vetustissimus fuit mos præcinendi & accinendi, & quidem carmen amœbeum. Id colligere est ex cap. 15. Exod. vbi Moses præcinuit canticum, virorum choro succinente; & Maria soror Mosis præcinuit idem canticum, mulieribus accinentibus. 2. Inter musicos debet esse princeps siue præcentor & director. Hic in Psalmis hinc inde appellatur מנצח[?] i.e. victor, præfectus cantorum, magister symphoniæ. 3. Symphonia est acuta, vel grauis. Symphonia acuta musicis dicitur alta & superior. Veteres vocabant sonos synemmenos, diazeugmenos, & hyperbolæos: qui soni optimè vocibus virginum referuntur. Vnde Hebræi symphoniam istam eleganter appellant virginea. 1. Chron. 15. v. 20. Psal. 46. v. 1. בנבלים על עלמות[?] in na-blijs super virgines, h.e. cum nablijs virgineæ siue acutæ symphoniæ. Hoc genus Musices Dores vocarunt παρθένεια. Symphonia grauis musicis nostratibus dicitur ballus & tenor, veteribus, hypate & mese, id est, imus & medius sonus. Hebræi elegantèr vocant על־השמינית לנצח[?] 1. Chron. 15. verf. 21. Psal. 6. verf. 1. super octauam ad vincendum, i.e. ad obtinendum siue praeualendum in cantu, siue, adattollendam vocem ita vt vincantur alij. Eodem sensu musicis dicitur octaua, & diapason. Prius genus pleumque[?] in Chromate positum est secundo genere musices: posterius, tertio. Hac de re accipe sequentem typum. Media seu minuscula Superacuta g f e Acuta vel Attinales d c b a Infima seu maiuscula Finales G F E D Graues C A G F
units.tr: III. Vocal music is that which teaches singing with the mouth. What it was among the Jews has not been handed down to memory. Suidas, in his entry on hypocritic [ὑποκριτικός], writes that music declined around the time of Arcadius, although Hebrew music had long before fallen into disuse along with the Jewish polity. Nor is there any doubt that the whole system of metre used in the Psalms of David and other sacred books has been lost. Meanwhile, as in poetry, so also in music, some things can probably be gathered from Scripture, and in this way. 1. The most ancient custom was for one part to lead and the other to answer, and this was an antiphonal song. This may be gathered from Exodus 15, where Moses led the song while the choir of men answered, and Miriam, the sister of Moses, led the same song while the women answered. 2. Among the musicians there must be a chief or precentor and director. Here in the Psalms he is called, here and there, מנצח [menatseach], that is, victor, prefect of the singers, master of the symphony. 3. A symphony is either high or low. A high symphony is called by musicians "high" and "superior". The ancients called these sounds synemmenos, diazeugmenos and hyperbolaeos, and these sounds are best referred to the voices of virgins. Hence the Hebrews elegantly call that symphony "virginal": 1 Chron. 15:20; Ps. 46:1, בנבלים על עלמות [binevalim al alamoth], that is, with harps upon virgins, that is, with the harps of the virginal or high symphony. The Dorians called this kind of music parthenia. A low symphony is called by our musicians "bass" and "tenor"; by the ancients hypate and mese, that is, the lowest and the middle sound. The Hebrews elegantly call it על־השמינית לנצח [al-hashminit lenatseach], 1 Chron. 15:21; Ps. 6:1, upon the eighth, to conquer, that is, to obtain or prevail in the singing, or to raise the voice so that others are surpassed. In the same sense musicians call it the octave and the diapason. The former kind is mostly placed in the chromatic of the second genus of music, the latter in the third. On this matter, take the following diagram: CLAVES. Excellent, supreme and doubled: aaa gg ff ee dd cc bb aa. Hyperbolaean: 5. Middle or small: g f e. Superacute: g f e. Acute or attinales: d c b a. Lowest or large: Finals G F E D. Grave: C A G F.

units.la: Hoc schema est fundamentum musicae vtriusque, tum vocalis, tum instrumentalis. 4. Ad cantum rite instituendum requiruntur certi modi. Tales vulgo numerantur duodecim, e quibus sex sunt principes, puta Dorius, Phrygius, Lydius, Mixolydius, Aeolius, & Ionicus: & totidem subditi, vt puta Hypodorius, Hypophrygius, Hypolydius, Hypomixolydius, Hypoaeolius, & Hypoionicus. Hi modi sunt certissimus canon cantilenae cuiusque. Existimarim Hebræos habuisse aliquid simile, hoc modo. In Psalmis hinc inde occurrunt certæ inscriptiones, quæ proculdubio notant initium cantilenæ & tonû musicum, ad cuius melodiam psalmus iste, cui titulus ille præscribitur, sit decantatus. e. g. Psalmus quintus habet istã inscriptionem : [?]למנצח אל הנחילות מזמור Magistro symphoniæ super Nechiloth Psalmus q. d. Psalmus traditus magistro symphoniæ, vt decantetur iuxta tonum siue modum Nechiloth, id est, cantionis, quæ sic incipit, & ita dicitur à sono apum, quem imitari debet, sicut si aliquis bombum appellet. Psalmus sextus ita inscribitur : למנצח בנגינות על השמינית מזמור Magistro symphoniæ fidium super octauam Psalmus q. d. Psalmus traditus præsecto symphoniæ seu præcentori (dem Kapellenmeister) vt decantetur iuxta modum octauæ. Octauus autem sonus in musica est intentissimus. Psalmus septimus ita inscribitur שגיון לדוד Odeerratica, siue varia, Dauidis. h. e. Psalmus decantandus tono instabili : ita vt Siggaion sit nomen cantionis certæ speciei, ad varios & instabiles modos siue tonos factæ, quæ vsurpabatur in magnis animi perturbationibus & angustiis, vbi vni rei, sermoni & tono non insistitur, sed ab alio ad alium transcurritur. Psalmus octauus talem habet epigraphen למנצח על הגתית מזמור h. e. Victori seu magistro symphoniæ super Haggitthith Psalmus. q. d. Psalmus decantandus iuxta melodiam quæ Gitthith dicitur. Confer Psal. 81. 84. Psalmus nonus ita inscribitur : למנצח על־מות לבן מזמור h.e. Victori super Muthlabben psalmus. q. d. Psalmus decantandus ad modos cantilenæ, quæ dicitur Muthlabben. Psalmus decimussextus inscribitur ita : מכתם לדוד Michtam Dauidi i. e. Psalmus decantandus iuxta modulos cantilenæ, quæ incipit Michtam. Psalmus 22. talem habet titulum : למנצח על איילת השחר מזמור id est, Magistro symphoniæ super ceruam matutinam Psalmus. q. d. Psalmus datus magistro symphoniæ, vt decantetur ad modos cantilenæ vulgaris, cuius initium erat, Cerua matutina. Psalmus 32. ita inscribitur: לדוד משכיל Dauidis erudiens h. e. Psalmus decantandus ad modos carminis & harmoniæ, cuius nomen est Mascil. Psalmus 38. sic inscribitur : מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד לְהַזְכִּיר Psalmus Dauidis ad commemorandum h. e. decantatus ad modos carminis vulgaris, cuius initium fuit להזכיר[?] Vide quoq; Pf.70. Psalmus 45. inscribitur : עַל שׁוֹשַׁנִּים Super Schoschannim; quæ vox fuit principium cantici alicuius vulgaris, ad cuius modulos decantatus fuit iste Psalmus. Confer Pfal.69. & 80. Psalmus 35. inscribitur עַל מַחֲלַת Super Machalath: quæ vox fuit initium cantilenæ vulgaris, ad cuius modos decantatus fuit hic Psalmus. Additur autem מַשְׂכִּיל, ut significetur melodiam huius Psalmi fuisse mixtam siue compositam ex Machalath & Mascil. Confer Pfal.88. Idem iudicium est de Psalmo 56. qui fuit decantatus ad melodiam compositam ex cantilena Ionath Elem h. e. columbæ taciturnæ, & Michtam, h. e. insignis aureoli. Idem quoque iudicium est de Psalmo 57. qui fuit decantatus ad melodiam cantilenæ Al-Tascheth, Neperdas, & Michtam. Confer cum Psal 58.59. Similiter Psalmus 60. fuit decantatus ad modos cantilenæ Sufan Ngeduth, i.e. Rosa testimonij, & Michtam. Porrò Psalmus 75. fuit decantatus ad modos cantilenæ tritæ, cuius initium fuit, Al Tascheth, Neperdas. Sunt etiam Psalmi, qui incipiunt ab Haleluiah, ut Psal. 106. 111. & alij. Quo innuitur illos esse decantatos ad modulos cantilenæ sic incipientis. Denique sunt quindecim Pfalmi a 120. usque ad 135. qui inscribuntur Maaloth i.e. ascensionum siue graduum. Quo significatur, Psalmos istos effe [?]decantatos ad numeros cantionis, cuius initium fuit Maaloth. Et hæc est nostra sententia de inscriptionibus Psalmorum. Alij putant, his vocibus denotari certa instrumenta musica, super quæ decantati fuerint isti Pfalmi alij alia comminiscuntur. Sed nostra sententia est simplicissima, & doctissimis interpretibus approbata. Oportet autem illud non ofcitanter tenere: videl. nomina modorum exprimere naturam melodiæ & rerum decantandarum, e. g. Nechiloth exprimit sonum apum : Scheminith, sonum acutum octauæ: Siggaion, varietatem toni: Haggittith, melodiam in vrbe Gath celebrem: Muthlabben, epinicion super morte improbi alicuius hostis prostrati decantatum: Michtam, melodiam cantilenæ instar auri pretiosæ &c. 5. Melodia Hebræorum videtur gubernata fuisse accentibus. Ita statuit Elias in Masforeth. Sicut enim in Romanis ecclesiis hymni iuxta dispositionem characterum siue notularum cantantur: ita verisimile est, Hebræos loco istorum apicum vsos fuisse accentibus. Neque est, quòd aliquis obiiciat, accentus à Masforitis demum fuisse inuentos. Cum enim in libro Zohar (qui omnium Hebræorum consensu ante Masforitas & editum Talmud conscriptus est) fiat mentio punctorum & accentuum, vt sunt Chirek, Cholem, Schurek, Sagol, Tzere, Scheua, Segolta, Makkaph, Sarka, Schopharholech: necesse est puncta & accentus longe antiquioris esse profapiæ. Cæterum sunt, qui talem accentuum tenorem commemorant:
units.tr: This diagram is the foundation of both kinds of music, vocal and instrumental. 4. For singing to be properly taught, certain modes are required. Usually twelve are counted, of which six are principal: Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian and Ionian; and as many subordinate: Hypodorian, Hypophrygian, Hypolydian, Hypomixolydian, Hypoaeolian and Hypoionian. These modes are the surest rule of any melody. I would suppose the Hebrews had something similar, in this way. In the Psalms, here and there, occur certain inscriptions, which doubtless indicate the beginning of a melody and the musical mode to which the psalm bearing that title was sung. E.g. Psalm 5 has this inscription: למנצח אל הנחילות מזמור [lamenatseach el hanechiloth mizmor], to the master of the symphony, upon Nechiloth, a psalm, that is, a psalm handed to the master of the symphony to be sung according to the mode or tune Nechiloth, that is, of the song which begins thus, and is so called from the sound of bees, which it ought to imitate, just as if one were to call it a buzzing. Psalm 6 is inscribed: למנצח בנגינות על השמינית מזמור [lamenatseach binginot al hashminit mizmor], to the master of the stringed symphony, upon the Sheminith, a psalm, that is, a psalm handed to the prefect of the symphony or precentor (the Kapellmeister) to be sung according to the mode of the octave. The eighth sound in music is the most intense. Psalm 7 is inscribed שגיון לדוד [shiggaion ledavid], Shiggaion of David, that is, a psalm to be sung in an unstable tone, so that Shiggaion is the name of a certain species of song, made to varied and unstable modes or tones, which was used in great perturbations of mind and in distress, where one does not dwell on one matter, word or tone, but runs from one to another. Psalm 8 has the epigraph למנצח על הגתית מזמור [lamenatseach al hagittith mizmor], to the master of the symphony, upon the Gittith, a psalm, that is, a psalm to be sung to the melody called Gittith. Compare Ps. 81 and 84. Psalm 9 is inscribed: למנצח על־מות לבן מזמור [lamenatseach al-mut labben mizmor], to the master, upon Muthlabben, a psalm, that is, a psalm to be sung to the modes of the song called Muthlabben. Psalm 16 is inscribed מכתם לדוד [mikhtam ledavid], Michtam of David, that is, a psalm to be sung to the measures of the song which begins Michtam. Psalm 22 bears this title: למנצח על איילת השחר מזמור [lamenatseach al ayelet hashachar mizmor], to the master of the symphony, upon the morning hind, a psalm, that is, a psalm given to the master of the symphony to be sung to the modes of a common song whose beginning was the morning hind. Psalm 32 is inscribed לדוד משכיל [ledavid maskil], of David, a maskil, that is, a psalm to be sung to the modes of a song and harmony whose name is Maskil. Psalm 38 is inscribed מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד לְהַזְכִּיר [mizmor ledavid lehazkir], a psalm of David, to bring to remembrance, that is, sung to the modes of a common song whose beginning was להזכיר [lehazkir]. See also Ps. 70. Psalm 45 is inscribed עַל שׁוֹשַׁנִּים [al shoshannim], upon Shoshannim, which word was the beginning of some common song, to whose modes this psalm was sung. Compare Ps. 69 and 80. Psalm 35 is inscribed עַל מַחֲלַת [al machalath], upon Machalath, which word was the beginning of a common song, to whose modes this psalm was sung. But the word מַשְׂכִּיל [maskil] is added, to signify that the melody of this psalm was mixed or composed of Machalath and Maskil. Compare Ps. 88. The same judgment holds for Psalm 56, which was sung to a melody composed of the song Jonath-elem-rechokim, that is, the silent dove, and Michtam, that is, a notable golden piece. The same judgment holds for Psalm 57, which was sung to the melody of the song Al-tashheth, Do not destroy, and Michtam. Compare Ps. 58 and 59. Likewise Psalm 60 was sung to the modes of the song Shushan Eduth, that is, the rose of testimony, and Michtam. Further, Psalm 75 was sung to the modes of a well-known song whose beginning was Al-tashheth. There are also Psalms that begin with Hallelujah, such as Ps. 106, 111 and others, by which it is implied that they were sung to the modes of a song beginning in that way. Finally there are fifteen Psalms, from 120 to 135, inscribed Maaloth, that is, of ascents or steps. By this it is signified that these Psalms were sung to the measures of a song whose beginning was Maaloth. This is our opinion on the inscriptions of the Psalms. Others think these words denote certain musical instruments on which those Psalms were sung, and others devise other explanations. But our view is the simplest, and it is approved by the most learned interpreters. It is necessary, however, not to hold it carelessly: namely, that the names of the modes express the nature of the melody and of the things to be sung. E.g. Nechiloth expresses the sound of bees; Sheminith, the high sound of the octave; Shiggaion, the variety of the tone; Gittith, a melody famous in the city of Gath; Muthlabben, a victory song sung over the death of some wicked enemy laid low; Michtam, a melody like a precious piece of gold, and so on. 5. The melody of the Hebrews seems to have been governed by accents. So Elias decided in the Masora. For just as in the Roman churches hymns are sung according to the arrangement of characters or notes, so it is probable that the Hebrews used accents in place of those marks. Nor should anyone object that the accents were first invented by the Masorites. For since the book Zohar, which by the common consent of the Hebrews was written before the Masorites and the edited Talmud, mentions points and accents, such as Chirek, Cholem, Shurek, Sagol, Tzere, Sheva, Segolta, Makkaph, Sarka and Shofarholech, it follows that the points and accents are of far greater antiquity. Moreover, there are those who record such a tenor of accents:
