units.la: Hæc, inquam, traditur à quibusdam fuisse ratio melodiæ Hebraicæ. Verùm enimuerò nimis incondita, & proinde grauitate, amplitudine, suavitate & sanctitate librorum sacrorum indigna videtur hæc musica.
units.tr: This, I say, is by some accounts the principle of Hebrew melody. But this music seems far too crude, and therefore unworthy of the gravity, grandeur, sweetness and holiness of the sacred books.

units.la: IV. Musica instrumentalis est, quæ docet canere organis hanc ad rem aptis. Moses Gen.4.v.21. nominibus citharæ & organi (synecdochicè comprehendit omnia instrumenta musica; tum ψαλφατα, quæ alijs dicuntur ἔνχορδα & κρουστά, quæ fidibus constant & manu tanguntur, ut citharæ, nablia, tympana: tum πνευματικά sive ἐμπνευστά, quæ digitis ventone mouentur, ut tubæ, buccinæ, tibiæ, & similia organa. Apparatus huiusmodi instrumentorum est infinitus. Confer Psalm. 150. cum 1. Chron. 15. vers. 16. & seqq. Dan. 3. v. 10. Passim quoque fit mentio buç inæ: ut Exod.19. Levit. 25. Ios.6. Vsus organorum istorum, ut & totius musicæ, debet esse triplex. Primum & præcipuus est, ut Deus celebretur voce & organis. Acque hæc causa fuit, quòd in cultu legali adhibita fuerunt diuersa organa: vt admonerentur non in aliis rebus frivolis & ineptis, vt mundus facere solet, sed in celebratione beneficiorum Dei oblectationes animorum esse quærendas, atque huc studium omne esse referendum Psal. 148. Et quemadmodum sunt varia Dei beneficia: sic nostrum est subinde nova & varij generis carmina condere, & concinere, tum voce, tum organis, in laudem & honorem Dei, & domi, & in templo, & in campo.
units.tr: IV. Instrumental music is that which teaches playing on instruments suited to this purpose. Moses, in Genesis 4:21, by the names "cithara and organ" comprehends by synecdoche all musical instruments: first the psalteria [ψαλτήρια], which others call enchorda and krousta [ἔγχορδα, κρουστά], which consist of strings and are touched by the hand, such as the cithara, nabla and tympana; then the pneumatic instruments, or empneusta [πνευματικά, ἐμπνευστά], which are moved by the fingers or by breath, such as trumpets, horns, pipes and similar organs. The variety of such instruments is endless. Compare Psalm 150 with 1 Chronicles 15:16ff. and Daniel 3:10. The horn (bucina) is also mentioned here and there, as in Exodus 19, Leviticus 25 and Joshua 6. The use of these organs, as of all music, should be threefold. The first and chief use is that God be celebrated with voice and instruments. For this reason various instruments were employed in the legal worship, so that men might be reminded not to seek the delights of their souls in other frivolous and foolish things, as the world usually does, but in celebrating God's benefits; and that all our zeal should be directed to this, Psalm 148. And just as God's benefits are various, so it is our task to compose and sing from time to time new songs of various kinds, both with voice and with instruments, in praise and honour of God, at home, in the temple and in the field.

units.la: Neque vero hoc modo paedagogia & infantia veteris populi veluti postliminio introducitur. Non enim apparatum Leuiticæ musicæ in templa nostra inuehimus, sed quantum excitandis animis satis est adhiberi volumus. Coloss.3.v.16. Deinde musica debet seruire moderatæ hilaritati, & profligandæ melancholiæ. 1. Sam. 16.v.16.23. Denique harmonia musica debet nobis in memoriam redigere harmoniam illam mundi, quæ cernitur inter cœlum & elementa, inter facultates animæ, inter corpus & animam, inter qualitates corporis: item egregiam illam harmoniam, quæ fuit in homine, & inter hominem atq; reliquas creaturas ante lapsum, quæque erit in altera vita. Vide quæ sub finem Poeticæ disseruimus ex Athanasio de utilitate numerorum poëticorum. Uno verbo: Musica & harmonia, quæ cernitur in cantilenis, organis musicis, & vocibus auicularum musicarum, nos admonere debet de harmonia precum & virtutum.
units.tr: Nor in this way is the childhood and infancy of the old people brought back, as if by right of return. For we do not import into our churches the apparatus of Levitical music, but we wish only as much to be used as is sufficient to stir up souls. Colossians 3:16. Next, music ought to serve moderate cheerfulness and to drive away melancholy, 1 Samuel 16:16, 23. Finally, musical harmony ought to bring back to our memory that harmony of the world which is seen between heaven and the elements, between the faculties of the soul, between body and soul, and between the qualities of the body; likewise that excellent harmony which existed in man, and between man and the other creatures, before the fall, and which will exist in the next life. See what we discussed at the end of the Poetics, from Athanasius, on the usefulness of poetic numbers. In a word: music and harmony, which are seen in songs, in musical instruments and in the voices of musical birds, ought to remind us of the harmony of prayers and virtues.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: ARCHITECTONICA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED ARCHITECTONICS.

units.la: I. ARchitectonica sacra est bene ædificandi scientia ex S. literis illustrata.
units.tr: I. Sacred architectonics is the science of building well, illuminated from holy Scripture.

units.la: II. Eius partes duæ sunt: prima, de affectionibus, altera, de exemplari operis extruendi. Oportet enim in omni opere hæc duo expendere: quale debeat esse, & cui exemplari debeat esse conforme.
units.tr: II. It has two parts: the first concerns the qualities of a work, the second concerns the pattern on which it is to be built. For in every work two things must be weighed: what it ought to be like, and to what pattern it ought to conform.

units.la: III. Affectiones operis extruendi sunt tres: videl. Firmitas, Symmetria, & Eurythmia. Firmitas est, qua opus est stabile & diuturnum. Symmetria est, qua partes cum toto & inter se certa proportione congruunt. Eurythmia est, qua singulæ partes habent venustum commodumque aspectum. Hæc tria occurrunt in vasto illo mundi opificio & singulis eius partibus. Videmus enim cœlum & terram, omniaque corpora in iis contenta, ita esse à Deo creata, ut sint stabilia, & certa proportione prædita, & deniq; venusta specie oblectent aspectum. Vide Gen.1.
units.tr: III. The qualities of a building are three, namely firmness, symmetry, and eurythmy. Firmness is that by which a work is stable and lasting. Symmetry is that by which the parts agree with the whole and with one another in a fixed proportion. Eurythmy is that by which each part has a graceful and fitting appearance. These three occur in that vast workmanship of the world and in each of its parts. For we see that heaven and earth, and all the bodies contained in them, were created by God so as to be stable, endowed with a fixed proportion, and finally to delight the eye with a pleasing form. See Gen. 1.

units.la: IV. Exemplar operis extruendi est partim naturale, partim artificiale.
units.tr: IV. The pattern for building is partly natural and partly artificial.

units.la: V. Exemplar naturale est vniuersus hic mundus. Deus siquidem ita architectatus est hunc mundum aspectabilem, ut in eo nihil possit desiderari. Merito itaq; opus hoc omnibus numeris absolutum habetur pro exemplari, in quod intueri debet quilibet architectus. Neque dubium est, primos architectos ex intuitu admirandi huius operis devenisse ad artis suæ rudimentum & complementum. Videmus enim artem in omnibus imitari naturam.
units.tr: V. The natural pattern is this whole visible world. For God so designed this visible world that nothing in it can be wanted. Rightly, therefore, this work, complete in every respect, is taken as a pattern which every architect ought to contemplate. Nor is there any doubt that the first architects arrived at the beginnings and perfection of their art by gazing on the admirable work. For we see that in all things art imitates nature.

units.la: VI. Exemplar artificiale est opus certo quodam artis ductu extructum: cuiusmodi exemplaria in Scripturis sunt multa: videlicet arca Noë, tabernaculum Moisis, urbs Hierosolyma, templum Salomonis, templum Ezechielis mysticum, & cœlestis Hierosolyma in Apocalypsi. Hæc enim ita sunt comparata, ut in singulis aliquid occurrat, quod architecto possit esse utile. Nos itaque percurremus singula, & illa habebimus loco quinque columnarum, quæ vulgo id sunt architectis, quod modi sunt musicis, & carminum genera poëtis.
units.tr: VI. The artificial pattern is a work built under a certain guidance of art. Of this kind there are many patterns in Scripture: namely Noah's ark, the tabernacle of Moses, the city of Jerusalem, the temple of Solomon, Ezekiel's mystical temple, and the heavenly Jerusalem in the Apocalypse. For these are so constituted that in each something occurs which can be useful to an architect. We shall therefore go through them one by one, and will take them in place of the five columns, which are to architects what modes are to musicians and kinds of verse to poets.

units.la: VII. Arca Noë est primum exemplar, in quo notanda sunt tria: videl. magnitudo, forma exterior, & interior ipsius dispositio. Magnitudo, sive mensura, his verbis describitur Gen. 6. v. 15. Trecentorum cubitorum erit longitudo eius, quinquaginta cubitorum latitudo eius, & triginta cubitorum altitudo ipsius. Et talis (inquit Augustinus lib. 15. de civitate Dei cap. 26.) est humani corporis supinè iacentis proportio: siquidem longitudo eius est sexcupla ad latitudinem, decupla verò ad altitudinem seu profunditatem, si rectâ lineâ longitudinem eius dimetiamur à summo vertice ad pedum plantas, latitudinem ab extremitate alterius humeri ad alterum, & profunditatem à summitate pectoris ad dorsi superficiem. Hic incidit quaestio, quales cubiti hoc loco intelligantur, num geometrici, vel humani? Ego existimo fuisse humanos seu vulgares, & aio cubitum talem complecti digitos transversales 24. ita ut sit sesquipedalis: quâ de re vide supra in Geometricis. Hac ratione arca neque nimis vasta, neque nimis angusta fuisse deprehendetur. Etenim si multiplices 300. longitudinis cubitos per 50. latitudinis, resultabunt quindecim millia cubitorum quadratorum in basi arcae, ita ut τὸ ἐπίπεδον[?], planum, sive area, cuiusque contignationis fuerit eius magnitudinis. Quod sane spatium est amplissimum. Rursus si 15000. isti cubiti multiplicentur per 30. cubitos altitudinis, efficiet summam quadringentorum quinquaginta millium cuborum, seu quadratorum solidorum. Quod spatium procul dubio poterat abunde sufficere pro cunctis illis animalibus, escisque ipsorum commodè continendis. Forma, sive figura, arcae fuit κεκοσμημένη[?] seu καμαρῳ[?], camerata, ita ut tectum altitudine unius cubiti assurrexerit supra 30. cubitos altitudinis, & subgrunda similiter omni ex parte in cubitum unum proiecta extiterit, ad arcendas ab arca fenestrisque illius pluuias. Id probatur ex verf. 16. In cubiti longitudinem consummato eius tectum superne, ostiumque arca in latere ipsius ponito. Per fubgrundam intellige partes tecti prominentes.Dispositio arca interior fuit trium cænaculorum fiue mānfionum principalium verf.16. è quibus infima proculdubio fuit destinata animalibus quadrupedibus, mediana hominibus & omnis generis commeatui, suprema auibus.Singulæ istæ contignationes mansiones fuerunt subdiuisæ in mansiunculas complures fiue septa varia, quæ Græcis dicuntur καλιαί. verf.14. Tota denique arca fuit feneftrata luculentiffimè verf.16.Quæritur etiam de ligno Gopher, materiâ arcæ, qualenam illud fuerit? Probabile autem videtur plerisq; interpretibus, fuisse cupressum vel cedrum, & quidem cupressum potiús quàm cedrum: quia cupressus non sentit vetustatem, rimam fiffuramq; non capit,denique teredines propter innatam amaritudinem non patitur. In eximiam hanc cupressinæ materiæ perpetuitatem apprime conuenit, quod Epiphanius aduerf. hæref. lib. 1. scribit, reliquias arcæ Noëad suam vfqueætatem visendas perduraffe.
units.tr: VII. Noah's ark is the first pattern, and three things are to be noted in it: namely its size, its outward form, and its inward arrangement. Size, or measurement, is described in these words: Gen. 6. v. 15. The length of it shall be three hundred cubits, the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits. And such (says Augustine, De civitate Dei, book 15, chapter 26) is the proportion of a human body lying on its back: for its length is six times its breadth and ten times its height or depth, if we measure the length in a straight line from the top of the head to the soles of the feet, the breadth from the tip of one shoulder to the other, and the depth from the front of the chest to the surface of the back. Here the question arises, what kind of cubits are meant in this place, geometrical or human? I think they were human or common cubits, and I maintain that such a cubit takes in twenty-four transverse fingers, so that it is a foot and a half long; on this matter see above under Geometry. By this reckoning the ark will be found neither too vast nor too narrow. For if you multiply the 300 cubits of length by the 50 of breadth, there result fifteen thousand square cubits in the base of the ark, so that the floor, or area, of each deck was of that size. This space is certainly very ample. Again, if these 15,000 cubits are multiplied by the 30 cubits of height, they make a sum of four hundred and fifty thousand cubic, or solid square, cubits. That space could undoubtedly have sufficed abundantly for all those animals and for holding their food conveniently. Form, or shape, of the ark was vaulted [κεκοσμημένη] or arched [καμαρῳ], arched, so that the roof rose one cubit above the thirty cubits of height, and the eaves likewise projected one cubit on every side, to keep the rain off the ark and its windows. This is proved from verse 16: Finish it to a cubit upward, and set the door of the ark in the side thereof. By eaves understand the projecting parts of the roof. The inward arrangement of the ark was three storeys or principal dwellings (verse 16), of which the lowest was undoubtedly assigned to the four-footed animals, the middle to men and all kinds of provisions, and the highest to birds. Each of these storeys was subdivided into several small dwellings or compartments, which the Greeks call kaliai (verse 14). Lastly, the whole ark was most brightly furnished with windows (verse 16). There is also a question about the gopher wood, the material of the ark: what kind of wood was it? It seems probable to most interpreters that it was cypress or cedar, and indeed cypress rather than cedar: because cypress does not feel age, does not admit a crack or fissure, and finally, because of its innate bitterness, is not attacked by woodworms. What Epiphanius writes in his work against heresies, book 1, fits very well with the remarkable durability of cypress wood: that the remains of Noah's ark lasted to be seen down to his own time.

units.la: VIII. In tabernaculo fœderis, à Mose fabricato, oportet considerare magnitudinem & partes in eo contentas. Magnitudo tabernaculi quibusdam videtur fuisse figuræ quadratæ, ita vt in longitudine, latitudine, & altitudine habuerit decem cubitos. Nobis autem videtur fuisse talis.Longitudo fuit 30. cubitorum, latitudo 10. altitudo itidem 10. ita vt fuerit tota longitudo tripla ad eius latitudinem. Exod.26. v. 16. vnde sic colligo. Si tabulæ omnes erectæ habebant altitudinis 10. cubitos, vtique tabernaculi altitudo fuit 10. tantum cubitorum. Et, fi tabulata lateralia habebant singula viginti tabulas, latas 1½. cubitum, sanè tota longitudo tabernaculi fuit 30. cubitorum.Latitudo fine dubio fuit æqualis altitudini, vt effet conueniens proportio. Interpretes huic rationi e textu petitæ addunt, Salomonem diuino instinctu templum suum, non quidem ad mensuram, sed tamen ad proportionem tabernaculi, quod erat templum quoddam portatile, ad peregrinantis populi commodum, extruxisse. Nam sicut in tabernaculo tripla fuit tota longitudo ad eius latitudinem, ita in templo eadem fuit observata proportio. Templum enim erat longitudinis 60. cubitorum, latitudinis vero 20. Fuit itaque tum longitudo, tum latitudo templi dupla ad longitudinem, & latitudinem tabernaculi. Partes contentae, erant vel in anteriori parte, quae communiter Sanctum dicitur, vel in posteriori, quae Sanctum sanctorum appellatur. Partes in his duobus locis contentae, fuerunt tanta magnitudine, quantam & decoris ratio, & magnitudo rerum iis imponendarum vel includendarum requirebat.
units.tr: VIII. In the tabernacle of the covenant, made by Moses, one must consider its size and the parts contained in it. Size of the tabernacle seems to some to have been square, so that it had ten cubits in length, breadth, and height. But to us it seems to have been as follows. The length was thirty cubits, the breadth ten, and the height likewise ten, so that the whole length was triple its breadth. Exod.26. v. 16. Whence I conclude thus: if all the upright boards were ten cubits high, then the height of the tabernacle was surely only ten cubits. And if the side walls had twenty boards each, each 1½ cubits broad, then surely the whole length of the tabernacle was thirty cubits. The breadth was without doubt equal to the height, so that the proportion would be fitting. The interpreters add to this reasoning, drawn from the text, that Solomon, by divine inspiration, built his temple not to the same measure but yet to the proportion of the tabernacle, which was a kind of portable temple for the convenience of the people on pilgrimage. For just as in the tabernacle the whole length was triple its breadth, so in the temple the same proportion was observed. For the temple was sixty cubits long but twenty broad. Thus both the length and the breadth of the temple were double those of the tabernacle. The parts contained were either in the front part, commonly called the Sanctum, or in the rear, which is called the Sanctum sanctorum. The parts contained in these two places were of such size as the requirement of seemliness and the size of the things to be placed or enclosed in them demanded.

units.la: IX. In vrbe Hierosolymā occurrunt ista tria: locus naturā & arte munitus, amplitudo, & magnificentia. Hinc toties fit huius vrbis mentio in sacris. Vide prolixas ipsius descriptiones apud alios.
units.tr: IX. In the city of Jerusalem three things occur: a place fortified by nature and by art, its extent, and its magnificence. Hence this city is so often mentioned in the sacred books. See its lengthy descriptions in other writers.

units.la: X. In templo Salomonis spectatur magnitudo & ornatus. Magnitudo templi ex partibus colligitur, quae fuerunt numero tres. Prima pars appellatur Porticus & Vestibulum: secunda post Porticum, Domus exterior, Templum, & Sanctum: tertia, omnium intima, Oraculum, Sanctum sanctorum, & Domus sanctissima. Ex his partibus tertia in longitudine & latitudine erat 20. cubitorum, & totidem in altitudine, quantum ad partem internam. 1.Reg. 6.v. 20. Sanctum itaque sanctorum intrinsecus fuit quadratum. Extrinsecus autem altitudo eius vulgo putatur fuisse cubitorum 120. quae dicitur fuisse altitudo porticus 2. Chron. 3. v. 4. ita vt sanctum sanctorum & sanctum fuerint eiusdem cum porticu altitudinis: nisi malis cum quibusdam dicere porticum ante templum suisse veluti turrim quandam editissimam, ita vt sanctum & sanctum sanctorum non fuerint eiusdem altitudinis cum porticu. Secunda erat longitudinis 40. cubitorum, latitudinis 20. altitudinis iuxta opinionem communem extrinsecùs, 30. intrinsecùs. 1. Reg. 6. v. 2. Prima erat longitudinis 20. cubitorum, & latitudinis 10, 1. Reg. 6. ver. 3. altitudinis 120. 2. Chron. 3. verf. 4. Porrò hîc intelligendi sunt cubiti sacri fiua primarij: quia illorum vsus erat in dimetiendis aedificijs sacris. 2. Chron. 3. v. 3. Ex his intelligere est, solum templi habuisse figuram ἐπηρομήκης i.e. oblongi, & quidem talis oblongi, cuius longitudo triploerat maior quàm latitudo. De atrijs quaeritur, quot fuerint? Sunt enim qui quatuor commemorant. Sed ex 2. Reg. 21. v. 5. liquidò liquet, duo fuisse atria, quorum vnum fuit exterius & maius, pro populo, alterum interius & minus, pro sacerdotibus. 1. Reg. 6. Ornatus templi fuit longè magnificentissimus, & hodiè ἀµίµητος[?].
units.tr: X. In Solomon's temple one observes its size and its adornment. The size of the temple is gathered from its parts, which were three in number. The first part is called the Portico and Vestibule; the second, after the Portico, the outer house, the Temple, and the Holy Place; the third, innermost of all, the Oracle, the Holy of Holies, and the most holy house. Of these parts the tertia was in length and breadth twenty cubits, and as many in height, as far as the inner part. 1.Reg. 6.v. 20. The Holy of Holies within was therefore square. Outwardly, however, its height is commonly thought to have been 120 cubits, which is said to have been the height of the portico, 2. Chron. 3. v. 4. so that the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies were of the same height as the portico; unless you prefer to say with some that the portico in front of the temple was like a very lofty tower, so that the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies were not of the same height as the portico. The second was forty cubits long and twenty broad, and in height, by the common opinion, thirty cubits outwardly and thirty inwardly. 1. Reg. 6. v. 2. The first was twenty cubits long and ten broad, 1. Reg. 6. ver. 3. and 120 in height. 2. Chron. 3. verf. 4. Moreover, the cubits to be understood here are sacred or primary cubits, because their use was for measuring sacred buildings. 2. Chron. 3. v. 3. From these things it may be gathered that the temple alone had the figure of an oblong [ἐπηρομήκης], that is, oblong, and indeed of such an oblong whose length was three times greater than its breadth. Concerning the courts it is asked how many there were, for some mention four. But from 2. Reg. 21. v. 5. it is clear that there were two courts, one outer and larger, for the people, the other inner and smaller, for the priests. 1. Reg. 6. The adornment of the temple was by far the most magnificent, and even today is inimitable [ἀµίµητος].

units.la: XI. Templum Ezechielis ( vt & vrbs ipsius) totam architectonicen ponit ob oculos. Vide Ezech. 40. vsque ad finem libri, & obserua proportionem elegantissimam, firmitatem longè maximam, ornatum excellentissimum, & denique varietatem domunculaṙu in templo, vrbisque amplitudinem. Tametsi enim hæc omnia sunt figura corporis Christi, hoc est, ecclesiæ ipsius: tamen nihil impedit, quo minus etiam artificium architectonicum inde possit peti.
units.tr: XI. The temple of Ezekiel (like the city itself) sets the whole architecture before our eyes. See Ezek. 40. to the end of the book, and observe its most elegant proportion, its very great firmness, its outstanding ornament, and finally the variety of the small chambers in the temple and the vastness of the city. For although all these things are a figure of the body of Christ, that is, of the Church itself, nothing prevents us from also drawing architectural instruction from them.

units.la: XII. Hierosolyma [illegible, ~8 letters] Apoc. 21. sequentia documenta architectonica exhibet.
units.tr: XII. Jerusalem [illegible, about 8 letters] in Rev. 21. presents the following architectural lessons.

units.la: 1. Res, quae proposita est architecto, debet esse iustae magnitudinis, vt scil. sit accommodata iis vsibus, quibus destinatur. verf. 10. 2. Requiritur ornatus conueniens. v. 11. itemque lux. ibid. 3. Oportet adesse debitam proportionem, munditiem, & firmitatem. v. 11. 12. 4. Quadrata figura valde conuenit iis rebus, quae debent esse immota, vel stabilia. verf. 16. Vbi nec illud est silendum, quadro inesse suam perfectionem: vnde illae loquendi formulae, Redigere in quadrum, Quadrare, Quadratus. Æqualitas laterum etiam commendat quadratum. Capacitas quoque eximiâ inuenitur in huiusmodi figurâ. Sic d. l. dicitur lôgitudo cœlestis Hierosolymæ esse 12000. stadiorum, latitudo similiter 12000. stad. & altitudo totidem. Area itaque ipsius complectitur stadia 144000000. quæ multiplicata per stadia 12000. exhibent 1728000000000. cubica stadia, è quibus singula sufficerent continendis alicuius prouinciæ satis populosæ incolis. Unde intelligere est, cœlestem Hierosolymam abundè sufficere ad excipiendum omnes omnino electos.
units.tr: 1. The thing proposed to the architect ought to be of the right size, that is, suited to the uses for which it is intended. v. 10. 2. Fitting ornament is required, v. 11. and likewise light. ibid. 3. There must be due proportion, neatness, and firmness. v. 11, 12. 4. The square figure is very well suited to things that must be fixed or stable. v. 16. Nor must we pass over here that the square has its own perfection, whence those forms of speech: reducing to a square, to square, squared. The equality of its sides also recommends the square. Great capacity is also found in a figure of this kind. Thus the said passage says that the length of the heavenly Jerusalem is 12,000 stadia, its breadth likewise 12,000 stadia, and its height as much. Its area therefore comprises 144,000,000 stadia, which multiplied by 12,000 stadia yields 1,728,000,000,000 cubic stadia, each of which would be enough to hold the inhabitants of a fairly populous province. From this it is to be understood that the heavenly Jerusalem is amply sufficient to receive all the elect without exception.

units.la: XIII. Praxis eorum, quæ hactenus sunt tra- dita, continetur his aphorismis.
units.tr: XIII. The practice of the things handed down so far is contained in the following aphorisms.

units.la: 1. Architectus sibi proponat schemata siue typos arcæ Noë, tabernaculi Mosis, vrbis Hierusalem, templi Salomonis, tepli Ezechielis, & cœlestis Hierosolymæ: prout figuræ istæ à doctissimis viris sunt editæ, putà à Villalpando, Torniello, Lauatero, & similibus. Proponat, inquam, sibi, & ichnographiam, <bl>den Grund</bl> / & orthographiam, <bl>den Aufriß</bl>.
units.tr: 1. Let the architect set before himself the diagrams or types of Noah's ark, the tabernacle of Moses, the city of Jerusalem, the temple of Solomon, the temple of Ezekiel, and the heavenly Jerusalem, as these figures have been published by very learned men, such as Villalpando, Tornielli, Lavater, and others of that kind. Let him set before himself, I say, both the ground plan (den Grund) and the elevation (den Aufriß).

units.la: 2. Accurate obseruet proportiones, ornatum, amplitudinem, & similia, prout in sacris literis describuntur.
units.tr: 2. Let him observe carefully the proportions, ornament, size, and similar features, as they are described in the sacred letters.

units.la: 3. Partes contentas & ornatum quoque diligenter obseruet, atque super istis rebus varias doctorum sententias expendat. Sic v.g. 1. Reg. 6. v. 4. defeneftris templi legimus, Salomonem illas fecisse [Hebrew]. Quidam vertunt, prospectui accommodas, clausas, & priorem vocem interpretantur, è lato contractas vtrinque vsque ad mediam crassitiem muri, vt eâ ratione lux commodius vtrinque immitteretur: posteriorem vocem ita explicant, vt dicant, fuisse vitreas. Alij vertunt, apertas clausas, siue prospectuum clausorum, i. e. laxiores intrinsecus, quàm extrinsecus, seu latas intrinsecus, angustas extrinsecus. Sunt, qui reddunt, obliquas, h. e. introrsum angustiores, extrorsum verò latiores, vt multum lucis accipientes in templum inueherent. Alij verò fenestras intelligüt fa-ctas in modum retis, hoc est, reticulatas, quales solent esse cancelli. Lutherus ad hunc locum sic adnotat: Die Fenster so inwendig weit/ vnnd außwendig enge sind / da kan man nicht wol noch viel hinein sehen / aber sehr wol vnnd viel herauß sehen. Solches reimet sich fein mit dem mysterio, Spiritualis homo iudicat omnia, & ipse a nemine iudicatur. Ein geistlicher Mensch kennet alles / vnnd siehet wol auß / aber niemandt kennet jhn. Das ist meines achtens / daß der Text spricht / die Fenster am Hauße waren offen vnnd zu / mir hinnen sind sie offen / dir draussen sind sie zu.
units.tr: 3. Let him also diligently note the parts contained and the ornament, and weigh the varied opinions of the learned on these matters. Thus, for example, at 1 Kings 6:4 we read concerning the windows of the temple that Solomon made them [Hebrew]. Some translate this as "suited to a view, closed", and explain the former word as "narrowed from wide on both sides to the middle thickness of the wall, so that light might be let in more conveniently from both sides"; they explain the latter word as meaning that they were glazed. Others translate it "open closed", or "of closed views", that is, wider on the inside than on the outside, or wide inside and narrow outside. Some render it "oblique", that is, narrower on the inside but wider on the outside, so that they would bring more light into the temple. Others understand the windows to have been made in the manner of a net, that is, latticed, like the screens that are usually found. Luther, on this passage, annotates thus: "The windows which are wide on the inside and narrow on the outside: one cannot well see in there, but one can see out very well and much. This agrees nicely with the mystery: the spiritual man judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one. A spiritual man knows everything and sees out well, but no one knows him. This, in my judgment, is what the text says: the windows in the house were open and closed; for me they are open within, for you they are closed without."

units.la: 4. Postquam architectus satis expendit sacra exemplaria, delineet suum opus. Delineatio ista vsitatè[?] appellatur graphis, cuius partes sunt numero tres. Prima est ichnographia, quæ est a area[?] iacentis descriptio, futuri operis specimen exhibens. Vulgo appellant formam planam, Itali plantam, Germani den Grundriß. Hinc phrasis, in Grund legen. Ichnographia ista fit ope circini & regulæ. Secunda graphidis pars est orthographia, quæ est frontis ipsius, hoc est, ædificij frontem attollentis, siue subrecti, delineatio, externam operis dispositionem oboculos ponens. Italis dicitur fronte, Germanis der Aufriß. Tertia pars graphidis est sciagraphia, seu scenographia, quæ est internæ partis delineatio. Italis dicitur profilo.
units.tr: 4. When the architect has sufficiently weighed the sacred models, let him draw up his own work. This drawing is commonly called graphis, of which there are three parts. The first is the ichnography, which is the description of the area lying flat, showing a specimen of the future work. Commonly they call it the flat form; the Italians call it the plan, and the Germans den Grundriß. Hence the phrase to lay in the ground. This ichnography is made with the help of compass and ruler. The second part of the graphis is the orthography, which is the delineation of the front itself, that is, of the front of the building rising upright, or its elevation, setting the external arrangement of the work before the eyes. The Italians call it fronte, the Germans der Aufriß. The third part of the graphis is the sciagraphy, or scenography, which is the delineation of the internal part. The Italians call it profilo.

units.la: 5. Architectonicæ studiosus & magister sic versetur in contemplatione tum exemplarium sacrorum, tum aliorum operum, vt illa transferat ad institutionem moralem & spiritualem: ita nempe, vt dispiciat, quomodo ædificia & similia opera pulchrè extructa nos admoneant partim de studio virtutis & pietatis, vt simus templa Spiritus sancti & tabernacula, in quibus inhabitet Dominus 1. Cor. 3. vers. 16. & cap. 6. vers. 19. 1. Cor. 6. v. 16. partim de ecclesiæ militantis & triumphatis perfectione & pulchritudine 1. Cor. 5. v. 1. Heb. 13. v. 14. Sic v. g. ex cap. 40. Ezech. hæc monita spiritualia possunt desumi. Vir, qui metitur longitudinem, latitudinem & altitudinem murorum est Christus, qui spiritu suo ordinat longitudinem, latitudinem & altitudinem ecclesiæ, facitq; vt illa nunc angustior, nunc latior existat, singulisq; membris sua dona secundum mensuram largitur. Murus quadratus significat stabilem esse conditionem ecclesiæ. Abatriis ascenditur in templi interiora, hoc est, à primis fidei elementis fit progressus ad altiora mysteria. Quidam manent in atrijs, quidam penetrant interiora templi, h. e. vni plus incognitione mysteriorum tribuitur quàm alteri. Hostiæ mactantur ad portæ Aquilonaris latus, h. e. affectus nostri iugulandi sunt vento septentrionali aspero i. e. cruce.
units.tr: 5. Let the student and master of architecture so occupy himself in contemplating both the sacred models and other works, that he transfers them to moral and spiritual instruction; namely, so that he sees how buildings and similar works, finely constructed, admonish us partly about the pursuit of virtue and piety, that we may be temples of the Holy Spirit and tabernacles in which the Lord dwells (1 Cor. 3:16; and 1 Cor. 6:19; 1 Cor. 6:16), and partly about the perfection and beauty of the militant and triumphant Church (1 Cor. 5:1; Heb. 13:14). Thus, for example, from Ezek. 40 these spiritual admonitions may be drawn. The man who measures the length, breadth, and height of the walls is Christ, who by his Spirit orders the length, breadth, and height of the Church, and makes it now narrower, now wider, and bestows his gifts on each member according to measure. A square wall signifies that the condition of the Church is stable. One ascends from the outer courts into the inner parts of the temple; that is, from the first elements of faith there is progress to the higher mysteries. Some remain in the courts, some penetrate the inner parts of the temple, that is, more knowledge of the mysteries is given to one than to another. The sacrifices are slaughtered at the side of the north gate, that is, our affections are to be put to death by the harsh north wind, that is, by the cross.

units.la: XVIII. ETHICA SACRA.
units.tr: XVIII. SACRED ETHICS.

units.la: I. EThica sacra est doctrina viuendi ex præscripto virtutis, sumta ex sacris literis.
units.tr: I. Sacred ethics is the teaching of how to live according to the rule of virtue, taken from the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: II. Virtus est conuenientia cum lege. Peccatum est ἀνομία, id est, discrepantia à lege, vt definit Spiritus sanctus 1. Iohan. 3. ver. 4. Itaque virtus est ἐννομία, id est, conuenientia cum lege. Intellige legem archetypam & ectypam. Lex archetypa est ipsa Dei natura, siue sanctitas illa, quæ ab æterno in æternum durat, & immutabilis manet. Unde Deus dicit, Sancti estote, quia ego sanctus sum. Leuit. 11. verf. 44. 45. cap. 19. v. 2. cap. 21. v. 8. Lex ectypa est tum naturæ, tum positiva. Lex naturæ impressa est cordibus nostris: & eleganter ab apostolo appellatur δικαίωμα τοῦ θεοῦ. Rom. 2. v. 14. 15. Lex positiva est, quæ fertur à superiore. Estque diuina, vel humana. Lex diuina Deum habet authorem. Estque æterna & immutabilis, vel temporalis & mutabilis. Ibi sunt leges morales & quædam iudiciales siue forenses apud Mosen: hic sunt leges ceremoniales & quædam iudiciales apud eundem. Lex humana est, quæ ab hominibus est profecta: cuiusmodi sunt leges XII. tabularum apud Romanos, & apud alias gentes aliæ. Omnes hæ leges sunt norma virtutis, quatenus nempe consentiunt cum lege archetypâ & lege naturæ. Cæterùm conuenientia illa virtutis cum lege philosophis dicitur mediocritas, siue medium inter duo extrema, excessum nempe & defectum.
units.tr: II. Virtue is agreement with the law. Sin is ἀνομία [anomia], that is, disagreement with the law, as the Holy Spirit defines it in 1 John 3:4. Therefore virtue is ἐννομία [ennomia], that is, agreement with the law. Understand the law as archetypal and ectypal. The archetypal law is the very nature of God, or that holiness which endures from eternity to eternity and remains unchanging. Hence God says: Be holy, for I am holy, Lev. 11:44, 45; 19:2; 21:8. The ectypal law is both natural and positive. The natural law is written on our hearts, and the apostle elegantly calls it τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ θεοῦ [to dikaiōma tou theou], the righteous requirement of God, Rom. 2:14, 15. The positive law is that which is issued by a superior. It is either divine or human. Divine law has God as its author, and it is either eternal and unchangeable or temporal and changeable. Among these are the moral laws and certain judicial or forensic laws in Moses; and the ceremonial laws and certain judicial laws in the same Moses. Human law is that which has come forth from men, such as the Laws of the Twelve Tables among the Romans, and other laws among other peoples. All these laws are the norm of virtue, insofar as they agree with the archetypal law and the law of nature. Moreover, philosophers call this agreement of virtue with the law the mean, or the middle between two extremes, namely excess and deficiency.

units.la: III. Virtus consideratur in genere & in specie. IV. Virtus in genere habet suas affectiones & summa capita.
units.tr: III. Virtue is considered in general and in particular. IV. Virtue in general has its own affections and chief heads.

units.la: V. Affectiones virtutis sunt sinceritas & constantia. Omni liquidem virtuti haec duo insunt. Quod patet ex summa legis Deut. 6. v. 5. & Matth. 22. v. 37. 38. 39. Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex tota anima tua, & ex tota cogitatione tua. Iflud est primum & magnum mandatum. Secundum autem simile est huic, Diliges proximum tuum vt te ipsum. Sane qui debet diligere Deum ex toto corde, ex tota anima, & ex tota cogitatione, & proximum sicut seipsum, is tenetur vtrumque diligere sincere & constanter. Sinceritas est affectio virtutis, qua fit vt ipsi nihil simulatum fictumue infit.Haec est illa simplicitas columbina, quam Christus nobis commendat Matth. 10. v. 16. Haec est illa infantulorum rectitudo, quam iubet imitari Christus Matth. 18. v. 3. Amen dico vobis, nisi vos conuerteritis, & fiatis vt pueruli, nequaquam ingrediemini in regnum coelorum. Confer 1. Petr. 2. v. 2. De hac quoque praecipit apostolus Rom. 12. Dilectio esto minime simulata. Huic affectioni opponitur hypocrisis, quam Deus grauiter odit & detestatur. Matth. 6. v. 5. 16. 6. 23. v. 28. Constantia est affectio virtutis, qua fit vt eodem modo & perpetuo fimus sinceri. Hanc Deus commendat Abrahamo Gen. 17. v. 1. Ego sum Deus fortis omnipotens, indesinenter ambula coram me, & esto integer. Huic affectioni opponitur leuitas & pertinacia. Illius exemplum est Iudas Iscariotes, deficiens a Christo Matt. 26. huius, Israelitae Ier. 44. verf. 16. 17. Caeterum hae duae assectiones insunt omni virtuti, sed inaequaliter. Nam insunt in gradu vel excellenti, vnde virtus dicitur heroica, qualis fuit in Simfone, Elia, Iohanne Baptista, Christo: vel remisso, vnde virtus dicitur vulgaris.
units.tr: V. The affections of virtue are sincerity and constancy, for both of these belong to every virtue. This is clear from the sum of the law: Deut. 6:5 and Matt. 22:37, 38, 39: You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with your whole mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. Indeed, whoever must love God with the whole heart, soul and mind, and his neighbour as himself, is bound to love both sincerely and constantly. Sincerity is the affection of virtue by which nothing feigned or pretended is found in a person. This is that dovelike simplicity which Christ commends to us, Matt. 10:16. This is that innocence of little children which Christ bids us imitate: Matt. 18:3: Verily I say to you, unless you turn and become as little children, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven. Compare 1 Pet. 2:2. The apostle also enjoins this in Rom. 12: Let love be without hypocrisy. Hypocrisy is opposed to this affection, and God hates and detests it severely. Matt. 6:5, 16; 6:23; 23:28. Constancy is the affection of virtue by which we are sincere in the same way and perpetually. God commends this to Abraham, Gen. 17:1: I am God Almighty; walk before me continually and be perfect. Levity and obstinacy are opposed to this affection. An example of the former is Judas Iscariot, who fell away from Christ, Matt. 26; of the latter, the Israelites, Jer. 44:16, 17. Moreover, these two affections belong to every virtue, but unequally. For they are present either in an excellent degree, whence virtue is called heroic, as it was in Samson, Elijah, John the Baptist and Christ; or in a slack degree, whence virtue is called common.

units.la: VI. Summa capita virtutis sunt prudentia & iustitia vniuersalis. Nam hae duae virtutes adeo sunt gencgenerales, vt reliquas dirigant, vt patebit in explicatione. Hinc quibusdam vocantur virtutes dirigentes; quia reliquas gubernant. Et ideo reliquę virtutes dicuntur speciales & directæ.
units.tr: VI. The chief heads of virtue are prudence and universal justice. For these two virtues are so general that they direct the rest, as will be shown in the explanation. Hence some call them directing virtues, because they govern the others. And for this reason the other virtues are called special and directed.

units.la: VII. Prudentia est virtus recte ponderans circumstantias. Hanc Christus commendat Matt.10. v.16. Estote prudentes vt serpentes. Intellige prudentiam Spiritus, non carnis. Nam prudentia carnis est mors, prudétia autem spiritus vita & pax. Rom.8. v.6. Et in corde hominis tali prudentia prædit requiescit sapientia[?]. Prou.14. vers.33. Prudentiæ spiritualis exemplum est in quinque virginibus Matth. 25. & in fideli atque prudenti seruo Matth.24. v.45. Luc.12. v.42. Prudentiæ carnalis exempla passim sunt obuia in filijs huius seculi, de quibus Christus pronuntiat, illos esse prudentiores filijs lucis. Luc.16. v.8. Imprudentiæ exemplum sunt quinque fatuæ virgines Matth.25. Veræ prudentiæ etiam opponitur opinio prudentiæ, quâ multi turgent, de quâ apostolus Rom.12. v.16. Ne estote prudentes apud vosmetipsos. Cæterum prudentiæ vis in eo est posita, vt omnia quadrent ad circumstantias, de quibus est versus,
units.tr: VII. Prudence is the virtue that rightly weighs circumstances. Christ commends this in Matt. 10:16: Be wise as serpents. Understand the prudence of the Spirit, not of the flesh. For the prudence of the flesh is death, but the prudence of the Spirit is life and peace, Rom. 8:6. And wisdom rests in the heart of a man who has such prudence, Prov. 14:33. An example of spiritual prudence is in the five wise virgins, Matt. 25, and in the faithful and wise servant, Matt. 24:45; Luke 12:42. Examples of carnal prudence are everywhere to be found among the sons of this age, of whom Christ declares that they are more prudent than the sons of light, Luke 16:8. An example of imprudence is the five foolish virgins, Matt. 25. Opposed to true prudence also is the opinion of prudence, in which many swell with pride, of which the apostle says, Rom. 12:16: Do not be wise in your own eyes. Moreover, the force of prudence lies in this, that everything is fitted to the circumstances, of which there is a verse:

units.la: Quis, quid, vbi, quibus auxilijs, cur, quomodo, quando.
units.tr: Who, what, where, by what aids, why, how, when.

units.la: Nisi enim istarum circumstantiarum, in primis personæ, loci, & temporis accurata & circumspecta habeatur ratio, nihil potest fieri, quod laudem mereatur, vel gratiam habeat, vel utilitatem nobis aut alijs adferat.
units.tr: For unless a careful and circumspect regard is had to these circumstances, above all of person, place and time, nothing can be done that deserves praise, or finds favour, or brings usefulness to us or to others.

units.la: IX. Iustitia universalis est virtus obligans hominem ad obedientiam erga omnes leges. Intellige leges iustas, quales sunt, quæ cum decalogo non pugnant. De hac iustitiâ apostolus pronuntiat Rom.13. v.10. Charitas, siue dilectio, est impletio legis. Et eleganter monet author concordantiarum Biblicarum iustitiam esse cogitationem & actionem cum lege Dei congruentem. Unde passim in Scripturis iustitia ponitur pro omni virtute: vt Psal.4. v.6. Sacrificate sacrificia iustitiæ. Hos.10. v.12. Semina te vobis in iustitia. Heb. 1. ver. 9. Dilexisti iustitiam, & odisti iniquitatem. De hac iustitia loquitur vulgatus versus.
units.tr: IX. Universal justice is the virtue that binds a man to obedience towards all laws. Understand just laws, such as are not at odds with the Decalogue. Of this justice the apostle declares, Rom. 13:10: Charity, or love, is the fulfilling of the law. And the author of the Biblical Concordances elegantly remarks that justice is thought and action agreeing with the law of God. Hence in the Scriptures justice is often put for every virtue, as in Ps. 4:6: Offer the sacrifices of justice; Hos. 10:12: Sow to yourselves in justice; Heb. 1:9: You have loved justice and hated iniquity. The common verse speaks of this justice:

units.la: Ἐν δὲ δικαιοσύνῃ συνέχη[?] πᾶσαι ἀρεταί.
units.tr: In justice all virtues are held together [En de dikaiosynē synechei pasai aretai].

units.la: Iustitia in sese virtutes continet omnes.
units.tr: Justice contains all the virtues within itself.

units.la: Continet, inquam, in se omnes virtutes, quatenus est universalis obedientia Deo debita, congruens ad normam totius decalogi, seu legis naturae divinitus insitae mentibus nostris, & nos convincens iustum & aequum esse, ut Deo serviamus iuxta omnes leges ab ipso praescriptas. Huc facit praefatio, quam Deus praemisit decalogo Exod. 20. v. 2. Ego sum Ichoua Deus tuus, qui eduxi te ex terra Ægypti, è domo seruorum. q.d. Ego sum Dominus ille, qui ab aevo in aevum est, & a quo sunt omnia, quae sunt. Iustum itaque & aequum est, ut omnia mea mandata servetis[?]. Deinde ego sum Deus tuus, qui te adoptavi in filium, & omnis generis bonis te mihi obstrinxi. Ergo & hoc nomine teneris observare praecepta mea, ne vno quidem excepto.
units.tr: It contains, I say, all the virtues within itself, insofar as it is the universal obedience owed to God, agreeing with the norm of the whole Decalogue, or of the law of nature divinely implanted in our minds, and convincing us that it is just and right that we should serve God according to all the laws he has prescribed. To this points the preface which God placed before the Decalogue, Exod. 20:2: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. That is to say: I am that Lord who is from age to age, and from whom all things that are, are. It is therefore just and right that you keep all my commandments. Further, I am your God, who have adopted you as my son and bound you to me with every kind of good. Therefore you are bound also on this account to observe my precepts, not one of them excepted.

units.la: X. Virtus in specie est dilectio Dei & proximi.
units.tr: X. Virtue in its species is love of God and neighbour.

units.la: Haec divisio sumta est ex Matth. 22. v. 37. 38. 39. ubi Christus v. 40. ait, Ab iis duobus mandatis tota lex & prophetae pendent. Quam in sententiam apostolus Rom. 13. v. 9. pronuntiat omnia mandata ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται[?], i.e. summatim compleri, hoc sermone, Diliges &c. & Gal. 5. v. 14. ait, totam legem hoc uno verbo πληροῦσθαι[?], compleri. Quam ab causam haec lex dicitur regia Iacob. 2. v. 8. Ex his ita licet colligere. Si virtus est ἐννομία, sive convenientia cum lege, & vero lex cōtinetur dilectione Dei & proximi, necesse est virtutem quoque esse dilectionem Dei & proximi, seu virtute erga Deum, aut erga proximum. Utriusq; norma perfectissima est decalogus Exod. 20. & Deut. 5. In hoc siquidem amplissima & inexhausta sapientia ita continetur, ut ille sit regula vitae piorum, ad quam omnia sua consilia, actiones, & studia accommodare, atque ita Deo grata dicere & facere debent: item norma vitae in externis actionibus, ut mores honeste regantur: item fons omnium honestarum legum, quae dicuntur positivae: item vinculum & nervus omnium imperiorum, & totius civilis societatis, utpote cuius salus & tranquillitas ex observatione legum depender[?]: fons denique & eruditissima epitome atq; summa omnium scriptorum philosophicorum, oratoriorum, & poeticorum, quibus doctrinam ethicam, œconomicam, & politicam homines sapientes complexi sunt. Quæ cum ita sint, optima proculdubio methodus Ethicæ sacræ, sive Christianæ, censeri debet, quæ virtutes omnes ordine in præcepta decalogi distributas recenset atque explicat. Fundamentum itaque nostræ Ethicæ sit decalogus, qui ita sonat Exod. 20.
units.tr: This division is taken from Matt. 22. v. 37, 38, 39., where Christ at v. 40 says, On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. To the same effect the apostle at Rom. 13. v. 9 declares that all the commandments are summed up [ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται], that is, briefly fulfilled, in this saying, "You shall love," etc. At Gal. 5. v. 14 he says that the whole law is fulfilled [πληροῦσθαι], made complete, in this one word. For this reason the law is called royal, Jas. 2. v. 8. From this we may infer as follows. If virtue is lawfulness [ἐννομία], that is, agreement with the law, and the law is contained in love of God and neighbour, then virtue must also be love of God and neighbour, or virtue towards God or towards neighbour. The most perfect rule of both is the Decalogue, Exod. 20. and Deut. 5. In it such ample and inexhaustible wisdom is contained that it is the rule of life for the pious, to which they ought to accommodate all their plans, actions and pursuits, and so speak and do what is pleasing to God; likewise the norm of life in outward actions, so that morals may be honourably governed; likewise the fount of all honourable laws, which are called positive; likewise the bond and sinew of all government and of the whole civil society, since its safety and tranquillity depend on the observance of laws; and finally the fount and most learned epitome and summary of all philosophical, oratorical and poetical writings, in which wise men have embraced ethical, economic and political teaching. Since this is so, beyond doubt the best method of sacred or Christian ethics ought to be judged to be the one that recounts and explains all the virtues, distributed in order under the precepts of the Decalogue. Let the Decalogue therefore be the foundation of our ethics, which reads as follows, Exod. 20.

units.la: Præfatio.
units.tr: Preface.

units.la: Vers.1. Tum elocutus est Deus omnia hæc verba, dicendo:
units.tr: Verse 1. Then God spoke all these words, saying:

units.la: 2. Ego sum Iehova Deus tuus, qui eduxi te è terrâ Ægypti, è domo servorum:
units.tr: 2. I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage:

units.la: Primum præceptum.
units.tr: The First Commandment.

units.la: 3. Ne esto tibi ullus deorum alienorum ante faciem meam.
units.tr: 3. Thou shalt have no other gods before me.

units.la: Secundum præceptum.
units.tr: The Second Commandment.

units.la: 4. Ne facito tibi sculptile, aut ullam imaginem eorum quæ sunt in cœlis supra, aut quæ in terra infra; aut quæ in aquis infra terram:
units.tr: 4. Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the waters under the earth:

units.la: 5. Ne incurvans te honorem exhibeto eis, neque colito ea: nam ego, Iehova Deus tuus Deus fortis Zelotes sum, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in nepotes, & in abnepotes, in eos qui odio prosequuntur me:
units.tr: 5. Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, upon the third and upon the fourth generation of them that hate me;

units.la: 6. Exercens vero benignitatem in millesimos eorum, qui diligunt me, & qui observant mandata mea.
units.tr: 6. And shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me and keep my commandments.

units.la: Tertium præceptum.
units.tr: The Third Commandment.

units.la: 7. Ne assumito nomen Iehova Dei tui in vanum: nam non relinquet impunem Iehova eum, qui assumserit nomen suum in vanum.
units.tr: 7. Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain: for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

units.la: Quartum præceptum.
units.tr: The Fourth Commandment.

units.la: 8. Recordare diei sabbati, ut sanctifices illum:
units.tr: 8. Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.

units.la: 9. Sex diebus operaberis, & facies omne opus tuum:
units.tr: 9. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work:

units.la: 10. Dies vero septimus sabbatum est Iehoua Deo tuo: ne facito ullum opus tu, aut filius tuus, aut filia tua, seruus tuus, aut ancilla tua, aut jumentum tuum, aut peregrinus tuus qui est intrapor-tas tuas.
units.tr: 10. But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates.

units.la: 11. Nam sex diebus perfecit Iehoua cœlum, & terram, mare, & quidquid est in eis, quievit vero die illo septimo: idcirco benedixit Iehoua diei sabbati, & sanctificauit illum.
units.tr: 11. For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day and hallowed it.

units.la: Quintum præceptum.
units.tr: The Fifth Commandment.

units.la: 12. Honora patrem tuum, & matrem tuam; ut prolongent dies tuos super terram illam, quam Iehoua Deus tuus dat tibi.
units.tr: 12. Honour thy father and thy mother, that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.

units.la: Sextum præceptum.
units.tr: The Sixth Commandment.

units.la: 13. Ne occidito.
units.tr: 13. Thou shalt not kill.

units.tr: The Seventh Commandment.

units.la: 14. Ne scortator.
units.tr: 14. Thou shalt not commit fornication.

units.la: Octauum præceptum.
units.tr: The Eighth Commandment.

units.la: 15. Ne furator.
units.tr: 15. Thou shalt not steal.

units.la: Nonum præceptum.
units.tr: The Ninth Commandment.

units.la: 16. Ne proferto contra proximum tuum testimonium falsum.
units.tr: 16. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.

units.la: Decimum præceptum.
units.tr: The Tenth Commandment.

units.la: 17. Ne concupiscito domum proximi tui: ne concupiscito vxorem proximi tui, aut seruum eius, aut ancillam eius, aut bouem eius, aut asinum eius, denique quidquid est proximi tui.
units.tr: 17. Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house; thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything that is thy neighbour's.

units.la: Hæc sunt decem illa verba, ut appellantur Deut. 4.v.13. Decem itaque erunt classes siue ordines virtutum, quas explicabimus. Quemadmodum autem verba ista decem inscripta fuerunt duabus tabulis lapideis, ut est d.l. ita virtutes referuntur ad primam, vel secundam decalogi tabulam. Illarum summum genus est pietas, harum, probitas. Pietas est, qua de vero Deo recte sentimus, eundemque rite colimus. Hæc est fundamentum omnis felicitatis 1. Tim. 4. ver. 8. Norma ipsius est præcepto 1. 2. 3. & 4. hoc modo.
units.tr: These are the ten words, as they are called (Deut. 4.v.13). There will therefore be ten classes or orders of virtues, which we shall explain. Just as these ten words were inscribed on two tables of stone, as in d.l., so the virtues are referred to the first or the second table of the decalogue. Their highest genus is piety, and of the second table, probity. Piety is that by which we think rightly of the true God and worship him duly. It is the foundation of all happiness (1. Tim. 4. ver. 8). Its rule lies in the first, second, third and fourth precepts, as follows.

units.tr: Virtues of the First Commandment.

units.la: 1. Cognitio siue Agnitio Dei.
units.tr: 1. Knowledge or acknowledgement of God.

Obedientia erga Deum & studium placendi Deo. 11. Perseuerantia. 12. Inuocatio Dei in corde, siue interna illa. 15 13. Gratiarum actio interna Deo debita. 14. Zelus pro gloria Dei.
units.tr: 2. Faith or trust in God. 3. Adoration of the heart. 4. Patience. 5. Hope. 6. Repentance and resipiscence. 7. Love of God. 8. Fear of God. 9. Humility toward God. 10. Obedience toward God and zeal to please God. 11. Perseverance. 12. Invocation of God in the heart, or that inward invocation. 13. Inward thanksgiving due to God. 14. Zeal for the glory of God.

units.tr: 3. Outward thanksgiving due to God. 4. Religious use of oaths. 5. Religious use of vows. 6. Religious use of lots. 7. Confession of divine truth.

units.tr: 2. Reverence for the ecclesiastical ministry.

units.la: Probitas est, quâ de homine sentimus vt par est, ipsum-que rectè diligimus. Ea est posita in dilectione sui ipsius & proximi iuxta præceptum 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. hoc modo.
units.tr: <hi>Probity</hi> is that by which we think of man as is fitting and love him rightly. It is founded on the love of oneself and of one's neighbour, according to the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth and tenth precepts, as follows.

units.la: Atque hæ sunt virtutes particulares siue speciales numero LXIV, quibus si addantur duæ affectiones, & totidem virtutes generales siue universales, paulò ante explicatæ, collegium Ethicum constabit LXVIII. cameris, in quibus anima fidelis se oblectare debet cum angelis & sanctis hominibus tanquam suis collegis suauissimis. Sed iam videamus singulas virtutes.
units.tr: These are the particular or special virtues, sixty-four in number. If to them are added two affections and as many general or universal virtues, explained a little earlier, the ethical college will consist of 68 chambers, in which the faithful soul ought to delight itself with the angels and holy men as its most pleasant colleagues. But now let us look at the individual virtues.

units.la: I. Cognitio Dei est studium cognoscendi
units.tr: I. The knowledge of God is the zeal for knowing

units.la: Deum, sicut se patefecit. Haec est prima pars pietatis, ex qua cæteræ partes oriuntur. Si enim aliquis sciat & firmiter statuat, Deum esse veracem, omnipotentem, summè iustum, summè bonum, summâ maiestate præditum, protinus fiduciam suam in Deo collocat, ipsum adorat, patienter ipsius voluntati se submittit &c. Hinc rectè dicitur, Claritas notitiæ in intellectu parit firmitatem actionis in voluntate. Sedulò itaque demus operam, ut Deum rectè cognoscamus, idque ex libro naturæ & scripturæ, ex lege & euangelio, ex V. & N.T. ex Bibliis paruis & magnis: ut, inquam, cognoscamus ipsius tum essentiam unam, spiritualem, æternam & omnipotentem, in quâ verè & realiter distinctæ sunt tres personæ: tum opera, puta creationem, redemptionem, sanctificationem, & glorificationem: tum denique voluntatem in verbo revelatam. Ier. 9. v. 24. Iohan. 6. v. 39. 40. 6. 17. v. 3. Haec est notitia Dei Christiana, multùm differens à philosophicâ, quâ etiam gentiles fuerunt præditi. Rom.1.&2. Agamus itaq; Deo gratias, quòd nos vocauerit & transtulerit è tenebris in lucem, & dederit nobis Filium suum vnigenitum, per quem cognoscimus Patrem, & in quo sunt absconditi omnes thesauri sapientiæ & cognitionis. Iohan. 1. v. 9. & 18. c. 14. v. 6. 7. Coloss. 2. v. 3. Diligenter etiam scrutemur Scripturas, ex quibus solis peti potest salutaris notitia Dei. Iohan. 5. v. 39. Rom. 10. v. 8. & 17. Deniq; quia nemo potest discere mysteria verbi Dei, nisi ab ipso Deo doceatur, oremus ipsum, vt nobis largiatur Spiritum sanctum, qui aperiat nobis Scripturas. Luc. 24. v. 32. c. 11. v. 13. Ioh. 6. v. 44.45. Cum hac Dei notitia pugnant Ignoratio Dei & omnes opiniones erroneæ de ipsius essentia & voluntate. Psal. 14. Act. 17. v. 23.
units.tr: God, as he has revealed himself. This is the first part of godliness, from which the other parts arise. For if someone knows and firmly holds that God is true, almighty, supremely just, supremely good, and endowed with supreme majesty, he at once places his trust in God, adores him, patiently submits himself to his will, and so on. Hence it is rightly said: "Clarity of knowledge in the intellect produces firmness of action in the will." Let us therefore take care diligently to know God rightly, and to know him from the book of nature and from Scripture, from the law and from the gospel, from the Old and New Testaments, from the small Bibles and the large: that is, to know his essence, which is one, spiritual, eternal and almighty, in which three persons are truly and really distinct; his works, namely creation, redemption, sanctification and glorification; and finally his will as revealed in the Word. Jer. 9. v. 24. John 6. v. 39, 40. 17. v. 3. This is the Christian knowledge of God, differing greatly from the philosophical knowledge which even the Gentiles possessed. Rom. 1 and 2. Let us therefore give thanks to God, who has called us and brought us out of darkness into light, and has given us his only-begotten Son, through whom we know the Father, and in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. John 1. v. 9; 18; 14. v. 6, 7. Col. 2. v. 3. Let us also search the Scriptures diligently, for from them alone can saving knowledge of God be sought. John 5. v. 39. Rom. 10. v. 8, 17. Finally, since no one can learn the mysteries of the Word of God unless he is taught by God himself, let us pray him to grant us the Holy Spirit, who may open the Scriptures to us. Luke 24. v. 32. 11. v. 13. John 6. v. 44, 45. Ignorance of God, and all erroneous opinions about his essence and will, are at odds with this knowledge of God. Ps. 14. Acts 17. v. 23.

units.la: II. Fides siue fiducia in Deo est, quâ homo pius agnoscens potentiam & misericordiam Dei in eo firmiter acquiescit contra omne periculū. Non intelligitur hoc loco fides in Christo mediatore iuxta promissionem euangelij acquiescens, & certò statuens sibi peccata remitti propter ipsius satisfactionem: sed fiducia illa, quâ Deo tribuimus laudem veritatis, potentiæ, & benevolentiæ erga nos, & ideo in ipso acquiescimus, etsi omnibus rebus destituti simus. Psal.2.v.vlt.&11.v.1.& 25.v.2.&57.v.2.& 118. v.18. Esa.31.v.1.c.36.v.7. Cum hac fiducia pugnant, diffidentia; confidentia, siue præsumtio confidens proprijs viribus, sapientia, iustitia &c. item fiducia præsidiorum humanorum; idololatria & superstitio confidens in idolis, bonis operibus, ritibus magicis &c.
units.tr: II. Faith, or trust in God, is that by which a godly man, recognising the power and mercy of God, rests firmly in him against every danger. Here is meant not faith resting in Christ the mediator, in accordance with the promise of the gospel, and firmly holding that its sins are forgiven on account of his satisfaction; but that trust by which we ascribe to God the praise of truth, power and goodwill towards us, and therefore rest in him, even if we are deprived of all things. Ps. 2 (last v.), 11. 1, 25. 2, 57. 2, 118. 18. Isa. 31. 1; 36. 7. Distrust is at odds with this trust; and confidence, or presumption, which relies on one's own powers, wisdom, righteousness and so on; likewise trust in human protections; and idolatry and superstition, which trust in idols, good works, magical rites and the like.

units.la: III. Adoratio cordis est reuerentia erga Deū, quâ fit vt homo illum propter summam ipsius maiestatem, suamque propriam indignitatem, summâ cum animi demissione reuereatur. Vide exemplum Abrahami Gen. 18. vers. 27. Iacobi Gen 32. v. 10. Dauidis 2. Sam. 7. vers. 18. & seqq. & Pauli Rom. 11. v. 33. & seqq.Cum hâc adoratione pugnat Spiritualis superbia coram Deo. Luc. 18.v.11.12.
units.tr: III. Reverence of heart is the reverence towards God by which a man, on account of God's supreme majesty and his own unworthiness, revers him with the deepest humility of spirit. See the examples of Abraham, Gen. 18. v. 27; of Jacob, Gen. 32. v. 10; of David, 2 Sam. 7. v. 18ff.; and of Paul, Rom. 11. v. 33ff. Spiritual pride before God is at odds with this reverence. Luke 18. v. 11, 12.

units.la: IV. Patientia est virtus primæ tabulæ, quâ obedimus Deo in tolerandis malis. Ita nempe, vt non faciamus aliquid contra ipsius mandata, nec illi irascamur; sed ex fide vera agnoscamus eum nobis propitium esse, & expectemus ipsius auxilium, mitigationem aut liberationem, & hac fide & spe dolorem leniamus. Rom.8 & c.15.verf.4.Luc.21.v.19.1.Cor.10.v.10. Heb. 10. v.36.
units.tr: IV. Patience is a virtue of the first table, by which we obey God in bearing evils: namely, so that we do nothing against his commands, and do not grow angry with him; but from true faith acknowledge that he is favourable to us, and await his help, relief or deliverance, and by this faith and hope we ease our pain. Rom. 8; 15. v. 4. Luke 21. v. 19. 1 Cor. 10. v. 10. Heb. 10. v. 36.

units.la: Hæc patientia Christiana differt à philosophica illâ, quæ est vtcunque obedire rationi in ferendis aduersis, ita vt nihil contra iustitiam, constantiam, modestiam, aut alias virtutes facias. Exempla Christianæ patientiæ habemus in Christo, Abele, Dauide, Iobo, Ieremiâ, Iohanne Baptistâ, Paulo &c. Ipsi opponuntur impatientia irascens Deo in ærumnis, & hypocritica tolerantia.
units.tr: This Christian patience differs from that philosophical patience which consists in obeying reason in bearing adversity in some way, so that you do nothing against justice, constancy, modesty or the other virtues. We have examples of Christian patience in Christ, Abel, David, Job, Jeremiah, John the Baptist, Paul and others. Opposed to it are impatience, which rages against God in distress, and hypocritical toleration.

units.la: V. Spes est certa expectatio omnium bonorum ex manu Dei. Eleganter diuiditur in spem venia, seu remissionis peccatorum: gratia, seu bonorum corporalium & spiritualium: & gloria, seu resurrectionis & vitæ æternæ. Spes siquidem est placida expectatio, quâ mes-pia agnoscens Dei veritatem, eiusque in se amorem, præsentiam & auxilium diuinum in omnibus expectat, quantum ad remissionem peccatorum, mitigationem pœnarum, & donationem bonorum iuxta consilium Dei, & deniq; vitam æternam. Iob.13.v.15. Psal.37.v.3.4.5.6.7. Hæc spes non confundit Rom.5.v.5. & proinde dissimilis est spei mundanæ & fallaci, de quâ Aristoteles pronuntiat, quòd sit somnium vigilantis. Cum spe Christiana pugnant desperatio, & præsumtio sperans sine verbo Dei, & sine vocatione, & confidens propriis viribus. Prioris vitij exemplum est in Saule, posterioris in Petro.
units.tr: V. Hope is the sure expectation of all good things from the hand of God. It is neatly divided into hope of pardon, that is, of the forgiveness of sins; hope of grace, that is, of bodily and spiritual goods; and hope of glory, that is, of the resurrection and eternal life. For hope is a calm expectation by which a sorrowful yet godly man, acknowledging the truth of God and his love towards himself, expects the divine presence and help in all things, as far as the forgiveness of sins, the mitigation of punishments and the bestowal of goods according to God's counsel, and finally eternal life. Job 13. v. 15. Ps. 37. v. 3-7. This hope does not disappoint, Rom. 5. v. 5, and so it is unlike worldly and deceptive hope, of which Aristotle pronounced that it is the dream of one awake. Despair is at odds with Christian hope, and so is presumption, which hopes without the Word of God and without a call, and trusts in its own powers. An example of the former fault is Saul, of the latter Peter.

units.la: VI. Pœnitentia est dolor, quo quis dolet se offendisse Deum, propterea quòd intelligit id esse iniustum, quodq; Deum diligit, ac proinde ab omnibus honorari eum cupit. Huiusmodi dolor fuit in Dauide Psal. 51. & in Petro Matth. 26. v. vlt. & v. trique profuit. Dicitur in Scripturis dolor secundum Deum. 2.Cor. 7. v. 9. Hic dolor est initium vitæ æternæ, & ex se parit Resipiscentiam, quæ est conuersio ad Deum, consistens in mortificatione veteris & viuificatione noui hominis. Rom. 6. Gal. 5. Coloss. 2. Psal. 34. v. 15. & 37. v. 27.
units.tr: VI. Repentance is the sorrow by which someone grieves that he has offended God, because he understands that this was wrong, and because he loves God and therefore wishes him to be honoured by all. Such sorrow was in David, Ps. 51, and in Peter, Matt. 26, last v., and it benefited both. Scripture calls it sorrow according to God, 2 Cor. 7. v. 9. This sorrow is the beginning of eternal life, and of itself produces amendment, which is conversion to God, consisting in the mortification of the old man and the quickening of the new. Rom. 6; Gal. 5; Col. 2; Ps. 34. v. 15; 37. v. 27.

units.la: VII. Amor Dei est incendium cordis, quo homo cognoscens Dei bonitatem & amorem erga se, ipsum vicissim amat super omnia. Ita nempe, vt feruet omnia Dei mandata cum quâdam lætitiâ acquiescente in ipso. Hæc siquidem dilectio non est otiosa, sed operosa Ioh. 23. v. 11. Iohan. 14. v. 23. 1. Ioh. 5. v. 2. 3. Huic opponitur odium Dei & amor Dei simulatus, qualis ferme regnat inter Christianos, qui labijs suis præferunt amorem Dei, sed re ipsa testantur merum ipsius & mandatorum eius odium. VIII. Timor Dei est affectus filialis, quo homo agnoscens Dei misericordiam & iustitiam, offensionem ipsius veretur vt summum malum. Veretur, inquam, ne offendat Deum, non tam quòd sentiat se ab eo punitum iri, si offenderit ipsum, quàm quòd indignum & iniquum iudicet, offendere illum, qui summâ maiestate est præditus, & plurimis maximisque beneficijs nos affecit, quibus declarauit se paterne affectum esse erga nos. Hunc timorem nobis commendat Scriptura Leuit. 19. v. 14. Deut. 6. v. 13. Psal. 2. v. 11. Prou. 1. & 3. Esa. 8. v. 13. Hebr. 12. v. 28. Ipsi opponitur securitas carnalis, qua fit vt homo viuat sine timore Dei & iudicij diuini, sine pœnitentiâ, fide, & dilectione Dei & proximi: item superstitio trepidans timore, vbi non est timor, vt Psal. 14. dicitur. IX. Humilitas erga Deum est virtus, qua nostram indignitatem coram Deo agnoscimus, omnemque fiduciam virium& virtutum nostrarum abijcimus, solique Deo omnia nostra bona accepta ferimus. Hæc virtus inter alia facit, vt agnitione propriæ infirmitatis non appetamus maiora voca5 tione nostrâ, sed nos contineamus intra metas vocatio- nis, & faciamus nostri muneris officia, fiduciâ diuini auxilij, nec alia Dei organa despiciamus. 1. Cor. 4. v. 7. Iob. 1. vers.21.1. Chron. 29. v.12.14.17. Deut. 6. v.13. c.10. v.12.20. Mich. 6. v. 8. Iac. 4. v.10. Luc. 1. v.50. Matth. 11. v. 29. Phil. 2. v. 5. & seqq. 1. Petr. 5. v.5. 6. Cum hac virtute pugnant ficta humilitas, & superbia, quæ est, sine timore Dei, & sine agnitione propriæ infirmitatis, sese admirari & supra alios extollere, propter certas dotes, & propriâ sapientiâ, sanctitate, & viribus confidere, & alios despicere; & cùm ad10 uersa accidunt, irasci Deo tanquam iniustè punienti.
units.tr: VII. The love of God is the burning of the heart, by which a man, recognising God's goodness and love towards himself, loves him in return above all things. So much so that he delights, with a certain joyful acquiescence in him, in all God's commandments. For this love is not idle but active. John 14. v. 11, 23. 1 John 5. v. 2, 3. Opposed to it are hatred of God, and feigned love of God, such as largely reigns among Christians, who profess the love of God with their lips, but in fact testify to their hatred both of him and of his commandments. VIII. The fear of God is the filial affection by which a man, recognising God's mercy and justice, dreads offending him as the greatest evil. He dreads, I say, lest he offend God, not so much because he feels that he will be punished by him if he offends him, as because he judges it unworthy and wrong to offend him who is endowed with supreme majesty and has bestowed upon us very many and very great benefits, by which he has shown that he is fatherly disposed towards us. Scripture commends this fear to us: Lev. 19. v. 14. Deut. 6. v. 13. Ps. 2. v. 11. Prov. 1 and 3. Isa. 8. v. 13. Heb. 12. v. 28. Opposed to it are carnal security, by which a man lives without the fear of God and of divine judgement, without repentance, faith and love of God and neighbour; and likewise superstition, which trembles with fear where there is no fear, as is said in Ps. 14. IX. Humility towards God is the virtue by which we acknowledge our unworthiness before God, cast away all confidence in our own strength and virtues, and ascribe all our good things solely to God as received from him. Among other things, this virtue makes it so that, recognising our own weakness, we do not aim higher than our calling, but keep ourselves within the limits of our vocation, perform the duties of our office trusting in the divine help, and do not despise the other instruments of God. 1 Cor. 4. v. 7. Job 1. v. 21. 1 Chron. 29. v. 12, 14, 17. Deut. 6. v. 13; 10. v. 12, 20. Mic. 6. v. 8. James 4. v. 10. Luke 1. v. 50. Matt. 11. v. 29. Phil. 2. v. 5ff. 1 Pet. 5. v. 5, 6. Opposed to this virtue are feigned humility and pride, which consist in admiring oneself without the fear of God and without recognition of one's own weakness, in exalting oneself above others on account of certain gifts, in trusting in one's own wisdom, holiness and strength, in despising others; and, when adversity comes, in being angry with God as though he punished unjustly.

units.la: X. Obedientia erga Deum est virtus, quâ quis promtus est ad seruandum omnia Dei mandata. Huius obedientiæ adiunctum inseparabile est Studium placendi Deo. Neque enim aliter placere Deo possumus, quàm obediendo mandatis eius. Quam obedientiam quò studiosius & alacriùs ei præstamus, eò magis il- li placemus. Hinc obedientia dicitur esse melior sacrificio. 1. Sam. 15. v. 22. 23. Confer Exod. 23. v. 21. 22. Deut. 28. v.1. & seqq.
units.tr: X. Obedience towards God is the virtue by which someone is ready to keep all God's commandments. Inseparable from this obedience is the eagerness to please God. For we cannot please God except by obeying his commands. The more eagerly and readily we render this obedience, the more we please him. Hence obedience is said to be better than sacrifice. 1 Sam. 15:22, 23. Compare Exod. 23:21, 22; Deut. 28:1ff.

units.la: XI. Perscuerantia est virtus pe-manens in dilectione Dei. In ipsius nempe vera agnitione, fiducia, adoratione cordis, patientia, & similibus virtutibus. Absque hac fit, & virtutes nil nisi larua quædam erunt. Matt. 24. v. 13. Apoc. 2. v. 10.
units.tr: XI. Perseverance is the virtue of remaining in the love of God. That is, in the true knowledge of him, trust, reverence of heart, patience and similar virtues. Without it, the virtues are nothing but masks. Matt. 24:13; Rev. 2:10.

units.la: XII. Inuocatio Dei interna est elevatio metis ad Deum, quâ petimus dari nobis necessaria. Hæc nobis passim mandatur Matth. 7. vers. 7. c. 26. vers. 11. Psal. 50. v. 15. Luc. 18. v. 1. Colos. 4. v. 2. 1. Thes. 5. v. 17. Cum hac virtute pugnant omissio inuocationis & inuocatio ethnica atque superstitio.
units.tr: XII. Internal invocation of God is the lifting up of the mind to God, by which we ask that the things necessary be given to us. This is commanded us everywhere: Matt. 7. v. 7; Matt. 26. v. 11; Ps. 50. v. 15; Luke 18. v. 1; Col. 4. v. 2; 1 Thess. 5. v. 17. Against this virtue fight the omission of invocation, and heathen invocation and superstition.

units.la: XIII. Gratiarum actio interna, Deo debita,
units.tr: XIII. Internal thanksgiving, owed to God

units.la: est agnoscere & confiteri mente, Deum solum esse authorem & datorem omnis boni, & nos gratiâ Dei esse plane indignos; ideoque Deum laudare, & ipsi vota nuncupare atque exsoluere. Hanc nobis commendat Scriptura Psal.107.v.1. Esa.12.v.1[?]. Coloss.4.v.2. 1.Thess.5.v.17.18. Quia vero admodum difficulter à nobis impetramus, ut Deo gratias agamus ita ut par est, non ab re fuerit quotidie beneficiorum Dei catalogum quasi texere, hoc fere modo. Beneficia spiritualia sunt patefactio Dei, electio ecclesiae, missio Filij, donatio euangelij, remissio peccatorum, donatio Spiritus sancti, novitas vitae, liberatio à tyrannide Diaboli & à morte æternâ, vita æterna, imò Deus ipse, qui erit omnia in omnibus, & suâ luce, sapientiâ, iustitiâ, vitâ, lætitiâ, & gloriâ nos in omni æternitate complebit. Beneficia corporaliafunt vita, honesta disciplina, victus, cibus, potus, pax, bona valetudo, successus in administratione politica & œconomica, defensio liberorum & bonorum fortunæ seu possessionum, bona fama, honestus locus, & alia innumera.
units.tr: is to acknowledge and confess in the mind that God alone is the author and giver of every good, and that we are altogether unworthy of God's grace; and therefore to praise God and to make and pay our vows to him. Scripture commends this to us Psal.107.v.1. Esa.12.v.1[?]. Coloss.4.v.2. 1.Thess.5.v.17.18. But since we very hardly bring ourselves to give thanks to God as we ought, it will not be out of place to weave, as it were, a daily catalogue of God's benefits, roughly in this way. Spiritual benefits are the revelation of God, the election of the Church, the mission of the Son, the gift of the gospel, the remission of sins, the gift of the Holy Spirit, newness of life, deliverance from the tyranny of the Devil and from eternal death, eternal life; indeed God himself, who will be all in all, and will fill us to all eternity with his light, wisdom, righteousness, life, joy and glory. Bodily benefits are life, honest discipline, sustenance, food, drink, peace, good health, success in public and household affairs, the protection of children and of goods and possessions, a good name, an honourable station, and countless others.

units.la: XIV. Zelus pro gloriâ Dei est ardens animi studium tuendi & propagandi gloriam Dei, & iustus dolor atque indignatio aduersus ea, quæ contra gloriam Dei fiunt. Oportet autem vt hic Zelus consentiat cum vocatione nostrâ, & coniunctus sit cum rectâ cognitione, ne nobis obijciatur illud apostoli Rom. 10. verf. 2. Ζῆλ[?]ο οὐ κατ᾽ ἐπίγνωσιν[?]. De legitimo Zelo vide Iohan. 2. v. 14. & seqq. Psal. 68. v. 10. 1. Reg. 19. v. 10, Act. 17. v. 16. Num. 25. v. 11. 2. Cor. 7. v. 7. Hic Zelus hodiè est admodum rara auis. Nostrum itaque est orare Deum, vt nobis largiatur Spiritum feruoris, qui consumat stipulas & spinas peccatorum vbique subolescentium.
units.tr: XIV. Zeal for the glory of God is the ardent desire of the mind to defend and spread the glory of God, and a just grief and indignation against whatever is done against the glory of God. This zeal ought to agree with our calling and be joined with right knowledge, lest that saying of the apostle be thrown at us: Rom. 10. v. 2. Zeal, but not according to knowledge [Ζῆλος οὐ κατ᾽ ἐπίγνωσιν]. On lawful zeal see John 2:14ff.; Ps. 68:10; 1 Kings 19:10; Acts 17:16; Num. 25:11; 2 Cor. 7:7. Such zeal is today a very rare bird. It is therefore our task to pray God to grant us the spirit of fervour, which may consume the stubble and thorns of sin springing up everywhere.

units.la: XV. Religio circa ritus & ceremonias est, quâ quis ita obseruat ritus & ceremonias sacras, vt illæ ancillentur fidei, spei & charitati. Religio vera est interna, vel externa. De religione internâ sic pronuntiat apostolus Iacobus c. 1. v. vlt. Religio pura & incontaminata apud Deum & Patrem, hæc est, inuisere orphanos & viduas in afflictione ipsorum, & immaculatum sese seruare a mundo. Ex quâ definitione intelligimus, religionem veram & internam complecti dilectionem Dei & proximi, adeoque totum Christianismum. Religio vera externa consistit in obseruatione ceremoniarum a Deo præscriptarum: cuiusmodi in V. T. fuerunt sacrificia, conuiuia sacra, certæ lotiones, abstinentia a certis cibis, jeiunia, adoratio coram arcâ fœderis & versus templum, circumcisio, & agnus paschalis: in N.
