T. prædicatio & auscultatio verbi Dei so-lennis, & usurpatio sacramentorum prout a Christo sunt instituta. Horum rituum obseruatio hactenus probatur Deo, si ancillētur fidei, spei & charitati. Psalm. 50. Esa. 1. cap. 29. v. 1. 13. c. 58. v. 4. c. 66. v. 3. Matth. 15. v. 7. 8. Hicautem prohibentur, repræsentatio Dei per imagines, approbatio externæ idololatriæ, magici ritus & illorum approbatio.
units.tr: XV. Religion concerning rites and ceremonies is that by which someone observes the sacred rites and ceremonies in such a way that they serve faith, hope and charity. True religion is either internal or external. The apostle James pronounces thus on internal religion: c. 1. v. last. Pure and undefiled religion before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unspotted from the world. From this definition we understand that true and internal religion embraces the love of God and of neighbour, and so the whole of Christianity. True external religion consists in the observance of the ceremonies prescribed by God: of which in the Old Testament there were sacrifices, sacred feasts, certain washings, abstinence from certain foods, fasts, worship before the ark of the covenant and towards the temple, circumcision and the paschal lamb; in the New Testament, the solemn preaching and hearing of God's Word, and the use of the sacraments as Christ instituted them. The observance of these rites is so far pleasing to God, if they serve faith, hope and charity. Ps. 50; Isa. 1; Isa. 29:1, 13; Isa. 58:4; Isa. 66:3; Matt. 15:7, 8. Here are forbidden the representation of God by images, the approval of external idolatry, magical rites and the approval of them.

units.la: XVI. Societas cum religionis studiosis est, quando cum iis conuersamur, qui Deum colunt ritibus cum verbo ipsius non pugnantibus. Huc pertinent connubia, fœdera, conuiuia, & similia.2.Chron. 15. vers. 10. c. 19. vers. 2. Mal. 2. vers. 11. 1. Cor. 6. v. 1. & seqq. c. 10. v. 27. 28.
units.tr: XVI. Fellowship with the devout in religion is when we associate with those who worship God with rites that do not conflict with his Word. To this belong marriages, alliances, feasts and the like. 2 Chron. 15:10; 19:2; Mal. 2:11; 1 Cor. 6:1ff.; 10:27, 28.

units.la: XVII. Sanctificatio nominis Dei est, qua vtimur nomine Dei sancte: hoc est, cum celebratione, veracitate, reuerentiâ, & circumspectione, vt sermo noster exprimat virtutes primi præcepti. Deut. 8. vers. 8. c. 10. v. 8.1. Sam. 2. v. 20. Sanè cum auiculæ omnesq; aliæ creaturæ sonent laudem Dei, & pro modulo quæque suo gloriam eius enarrent, foedissimum fuerit, si nos hanc musicam & harmoniam ingrato stridore violemus. Psal. 19. & 29. & 148. Quemadmodum enim si in testudine vnica chorda dissonet, totus concentus turbatur: ita si in catholicâ illâ nominis Dei celebratione homo non tantùm non faciat suum officium, sed etiam vitium inspergat, nō potest non male sonare hæc musica. Demus itaque operaram, vt titulos Dei nonnisi in re graui, summâ cum reuerentiâ vsurpemus. Deut. 18. v. 18. Rom. 9. v. 5.
units.tr: XVII. Sanctification of the name of God is when we use the name of God holily: that is, with celebration, truthfulness, reverence and circumspection, so that our speech expresses the virtues of the first commandment. Deut. 8:8; 10:8; 1 Sam. 2:20. Indeed, since the little birds and all other creatures sound the praise of God, and each in its measure declares his glory, it would be most shameful if we were to break this music and harmony with ungrateful discord. Ps. 19, 29 and 148. For just as if a single string on a lyre is out of tune, the whole concert is disturbed, so if in that universal celebration of God's name a man not only fails to do his duty but also mixes in a fault, this music cannot but sound badly. Let us therefore take care to use the titles of God only in serious matters and with the greatest reverence. Deut. 18:18; Rom. 9:5.

units.la: XVIII. Inuocatio Dei externa est, quando clarâ voce Dei opem imploramus. Siue id fiat cantu, siue voce non cantante. Vide passim psalmos, qui inscribuntur Cantica & Psalmi, & iubent cantare Deo canticum nouum: vt Psal. 18. 67. 68. 96. 96. 149. item dicta Scripturæ, vbi sancti dicuntur clamasse ad Dominum: vt, Exod. 8. vers. 12. c. 14. vers. 10. Num. 12. v. 13. Iudic. 3. v. 9. 1. Sam. 7. vers. 8. 1. Reg. 17. vers. 20. 21. Psal. 3. 4. 17. 18. 22. 15 28. &c.
units.tr: XVIII. External invocation of God is when we implore God's help with a clear voice. Whether this is done by singing or by speaking without song. See throughout the psalms that are headed Songs and Psalms, which bid us sing a new song to the Lord, such as Ps. 18, 67, 68, 96, 149; likewise the passages of Scripture where the saints are said to have cried to the Lord, as Exod. 8:12; 14:10; Num. 12:13; Judg. 3:9; 1 Sam. 7:8; 1 Kings 17:20, 21; Ps. 3, 4, 17, 18, 22, 28, etc.

units.la: XIX. Gratiarum actio externa, Deo debita, est voce suâ celebrare Dei maiestatem & opera. Vide titulum præced. & infrà in Poeticis indicem Canticorum in sacris occurrentium.
units.tr: XIX. External thanksgiving, owed to God, is to celebrate with one's voice the majesty and works of God. See the preceding heading, and below, under Poetics, the index of the canticles occurring in the sacred books.

units.la: XX. Religio circa iuramentum est virtus, quâ confirmamus veritatem in re controuersâ, Deo teste inuocato. Vide Deut. 6. vers. 13. c. 10. v. 20. Hebr. 6. ver. 16. 1. Cor. 1. v. 23. Comites siue adiunctâ legitimi iuramenti debent esse veritas, iudicium, & iustitia. Ier. 4. v. 2. Pugnantia sunt, sophisticæ & calumniiosæ interpretationes iuramentorum, iuramenta impia, & periuria, quibus tota vita plena est.
units.tr: XX. Religion concerning the oath is the virtue by which we confirm the truth in a disputed matter, calling God to witness. See Deut. 6:13; 10:20; Heb. 6:16; 1 Cor. 1:23. The companions or accompaniments of a lawful oath ought to be truth, judgement and righteousness. Jer. 4:2. Contrary to these are sophistical and calumnious interpretations of oaths, impious oaths, and perjuries, with which the whole of life is full.

units.la: XXI. Religio circa votum est virtus, quâ Deo aliquid promittimus, officij gratiuæ animi testâdi causâ. Ita nempe, vt exercitium aliquod corporis eligamus, vltrò & feriò, ad alendam vel excitandam resipiscentiam & gratitudinem nostram erga Deum. Gen. 28. §§ vers. 20.
units.tr: XXI. Religion concerning the vow is the virtue by which we promise something to God, for the sake of testifying a dutiful and grateful mind. Namely, by choosing some bodily exercise, freely and deliberately, to nourish or stir up our repentance and our gratitude towards God. Gen. 28:20.

units.la: XXII. Religio circa fortes est virtus, quâ fortes adhibemus vt lites componantur, & seditiones caueantur. In diuidendis nempe patrimonijs & facultatibus, & idoneis personis ad certa officia eligendis. Prou. 16. verf. 33. cap. 18. verf. 18. Iof.[?] 14. & 15. 1. Sam. 10. Act. 1.
units.tr: XXII. Religion concerning lots is the virtue by which we use lots so that disputes may be settled and seditions avoided. Namely, in dividing inheritances and goods, and in choosing suitable persons for particular offices. Prov. 16:33; 18:18; Josh. 14 and 15; 1 Sam. 10; Acts 1.

units.la: XXIII. Confessio veritatis diuinae est, quâ veritatem verbi Dei constanter, quando opus est, profitemur. Nefcil. illam vel abnegemus, vel abijciamus propter terrores, odia, supplicia, vel alia pericula. Finis autem nobis debet esse propositus, vt Deo obtemperetur, & ne vera ipsius notitia in terris extinguatur.De hac virtute vide Matth. 10. verf. 32. 1. Pet. 3. v. 15. Ipsi repugnant negotio veritatis diuinae, & impia pertinacia fanaticorum & male instituorum in religione.
units.tr: XXIII. Confession of divine truth is the virtue by which we steadfastly profess the truth of God's Word whenever the need arises. We must not deny or abandon it out of fear, hatred, torture or other dangers. Our aim ought to be set before us: that God may be obeyed, and that the true knowledge of him may not be extinguished on earth. On this virtue see Matth. 10. v. 32. 1. Pet. 3. v. 15. Those who oppose the business of divine truth, and the impious obstinacy of fanatics and of men ill-taught in religion, are opposed to it.

units.la: XXIV. Religio circa dies sacros est, quando vacamus cultui Dei solenni, in aliquâ congregatione, tempore diuinitus lancito. Scriptura appellat sanctificationem sabbati, quae absoluitur officijs communibus & proprijs. Officia communia sunt, orare Deum, ipsique gratias agere, sacramenta venerari, conferre eleemosynam, verbum Dei meditari, cum alijs colloqui de doctrina Christiana, aegrotos inuisere. Officia propria sunt varia: vt ministrorum verbi, praedicare verbum Dei, administrare sacramenta, recitare preces; auditorum, verbum praedicatum audire, preces tacito suspirio subsequi: magistratus, parentum & praeceptorum, prohibere & punire violationem sabbati, & promouere e contrario ipsius sanctifi-cationem, &c. Exod. 31. ver. 13. 14. 15. Deut. 5. v. 12. Ier. 17. verf. 22. Neh.[?] 13. verf. 16. Haec vero omnia debent coniungi cum sabbato interno, quo anima quiescit à peccatis, & in Deo quietem suam quaerit & inuenit.
units.tr: XXIV. Religion concerning holy days is when we devote ourselves to the solemn worship of God in some assembly at a time divinely appointed. Scripture calls this the sanctification of the sabbath, and it is carried out by common and particular duties. Common duties are: to pray to God and give him thanks, to reverence the sacraments, to bestow alms, to meditate on the Word of God, to talk with others about Christian doctrine, and to visit the sick. Particular duties vary: for ministers of the Word, to preach the Word of God, to administer the sacraments, and to recite the prayers; for hearers, to listen to the preached Word and to follow the prayers with silent sighs; for magistrates, parents and teachers, to forbid and punish violation of the sabbath, and conversely to promote its sanctification, etc. Exod. 31. ver. 13. 14. 15. Deut. 5. v. 12. Ier. 17. verf. 22. Neh. 13. verf. 16. All these things ought indeed to be joined with the inner sabbath, in which the soul rests from sins and seeks and finds its rest in God.

units.la: XXV. Veneratio ministerij ecclesiastici est, quâ recte de illo sentimus & loquimur, & res ad illius fuftentationem requisitas libenter & liberaliter conferimus. Vide Gal. 6. verf. 6. Hebr. 13. verf. 17. Matth. 10. v. 40. 41. 42. Gal. 4. v. 15. 19. 1. Thess. 2. v. 13. c. 5. v. 12. 13. 1. Cor. 4. v. 15. 1. Tim. 4. v. 16.
units.tr: XXV. Reverence for the ecclesiastical ministry is the virtue by which we think and speak rightly of it, and gladly and generously contribute what is required for its support. See Gal. 6. verf. 6. Hebr. 13. verf. 17. Matth. 10. v. 40. 41. 42. Gal. 4. v. 15. 19. 1. Thess. 2. v. 13. c. 5. v. 12. 13. 1. Cor. 4. v. 15. 1. Tim. 4. v. 16.

units.la: XXVI. Officiositas est virtus, quâ commodis aliorum libenter feruimus, prudenti oblatione, & iucundâ præstatione nostrorum officiorum. Hæc virtus vulgo dicitur esse triplex: Spontanea, cùm quis alicui gratificatur non rogatus: efflagitata, cùm quis rogatus officium præstat, idque hilariter & citò: denique compensans, cùm quis officium officio compensat. Exemplum officiositatis vide Gen. 23. v. 6. vbi Hethæi offerunt Abrahamo locum sepulturæ: & c. 24. v. 18. vbi Rebecca bibendum dat feruo Abrahami.
units.tr: XXVI. Courtesy is the virtue by which we gladly serve the advantage of others, through a prudent offering and a pleasant performance of our duties. This virtue is commonly said to be threefold: spontaneous, when someone does a kindness to another without being asked; solicited, when someone performs a duty when asked, and does so cheerfully and promptly; and finally reciprocal, when someone repays a duty with a duty. For an example of courtesy see Gen. 23. v. 6., where the Hittites offer Abraham a place of burial, and c. 24. v. 18., where Rebekah gives drink to Abraham's servant.

units.la: XXVII. Philoftorgia est virtus, quæ liberis & parentibus, cæterisque sanguine iunctis, tribuit debitum amorem & honorem. Eius itaque pars est pietas erga parentes, cuius simulacrum cernere est in ciconijs. Vide de hac virtute in œconomicis.
units.tr: XXVII. Natural affection is the virtue which gives due love and honour to children and parents and other blood relations. Its part is therefore piety towards parents, the image of which may be seen in storks. On this virtue see under the household duties.

units.la: XXVIII. Iustitia distributiua præmiorum est, quâ discernimus præmia virtuti debita. Iustitia est virtus, quæ suum cuique tribuit: estque vniuersalis, vel particularis. Iustitia vniuersalis est obedientia erga omnes leges, vt paulo ante ostendimus.Iustitia particularis est, quæ suum cuique tribuit in certâ materiâ: estque distributiua, vel commutatiua. Iustitia distributiua est præmiorum, vel pœnarum. Illa est huius loci: hæc pertinet ad præceptum sextum. Iustitia commutatiua pertinet ad præceptum octauum. Iustitia præmiorum est, quæ discernit gradus personarum, officiorum, & præmiorum, vt in iis seruetur proportio geometrica. Ea tribuit suum viuis & mortuis. Iustitia viuis suum tribuens est, quâ singulis conuenientem locum, honorem, & similia distribuimus. Rom. 13. verf. 7. Iustitia mortuis suum tribuens est, quâ facimus iusta defun&is, siue praestamus ipsis ultima pietatis officia: moderatè scil. ipsos lugendo, & corpora ipsorum honestè sepeliendo, gratamque ipsorum memoriam usurpando. Gen. 23.1. Thess. 4. v. 13.
units.tr: XXVIII. Distributive justice of rewards is that by which we distinguish the rewards due to virtue. Justice is the virtue which gives each his own, and it is either universal or particular. Universal justice is obedience to all laws, as we showed a little earlier. Particular justice is that which gives each his own in a definite matter, and it is either distributive or commutative. Distributive justice concerns either rewards or punishments. The former belongs to this place; the latter pertains to the sixth precept. Commutative justice pertains to the eighth precept. The justice of rewards is that which distinguishes the degrees of persons, offices and rewards, so that a geometrical proportion is kept in them. It gives what is due to the living and to the dead. Justice giving what is due to the living is that by which we distribute to each the place, honour and the like that suit him. Rom. 13. verf. 7. Justice giving what is due to the dead is that by which we perform funeral rites for the departed, or render them the last duties of piety: namely, by mourning them with moderation, burying their bodies honourably, and keeping their memory in grateful remembrance. Gen. 23. 1. Thess. 4. v. 13.

units.la: XXIX. Gratitudo est, quâ retribuimus bene de nobis meritis iucundam accepti beneficij memoriam[?], signis tum voluntatis, tum facti declaratam. Hanc Scriptura nobis commendat Coloss. 3. v.15. Exemplum vide in Dauide 2. Sam. 2. v. 6.
units.tr: XXIX. Gratitude is that by which we repay with good those who have deserved well of us, keeping a pleasant memory of a benefit received, and declaring it by signs both of the will and of deeds. Scripture commends this to us in Coloss. 3. v. 15. An example is seen in David, 2. Sam. 2. v. 6.

units.la: XXX. Gravitas est virtus, quâ habitus & gestus hominis in conversatione ad decorum sanctum cuiuis conueniens componuntur. Scriptura appellat honestam conuersationem. Hebr. 13. v. 18. 1. Petr. 1. v. 15.
units.tr: XXX. Gravity is the virtue by which a person's bearing and gestures in conduct are arranged to a holy decorum suited to everyone. Scripture calls it honest conduct. Hebr. 13. v. 18. 1. Petr. 1. v. 15.

units.la: 1. Petr. 2. v. 12. Honestas illa in eo est posita, ut gestus actionesque nostrae congruant cum ordine naturae, locorum, personarum, & temporum.
units.tr: 1. Petr. 2. v. 12. That honesty consists in this: that our gestures and actions agree with the order of nature, of places, of persons and of times.

units.la: XXXI. Modestia est virtus, quâ honores nobis conuenientes decorè appetimus, prosequimur, & tuemur. Haec nihil est aliud quàm humilitas erga homines, quae nos frenat, ne in opinione de nobis, aut sermone, aut actionibus, supra nostras vires nos efferamus,nec extra vocationem aliquid suscipiamus, sed in timore Dei diligenter nostra officia faciamus, sic tamen ut gloriam honestam, & bonam famam appetamus. Phil. 2. vers. 3.
units.tr: XXXI. Modesty is the virtue by which we becomingly seek, pursue and maintain the honours fitting to us. This is nothing other than humility towards men, which restrains us so that we do not, in our opinion of ourselves, or in our speech or actions, raise ourselves above our strength, nor take on anything beyond our calling; rather we diligently perform our duties in the fear of God, yet in such a way that we seek honest glory and a good reputation. Phil. 2. vers. 3.

units.la: 1. Petr. 5. v. 5. 1. Cor. 15. v. 7. 9. Rom. 1. v. 1. 1. Cor. 1. v. 1. & passim in epistolarum inscriptionibus.
units.tr: 1. Petr. 5. v. 5. 1. Cor. 15. v. 7. 9. Rom. 1. v. 1. 1. Cor. 1. v. 1. and throughout the superscriptions of the epistles.

units.la: XXXII. Reuerentia est honor erga superiores. Eius proprium est, dona Dei in alijs agnoscere & magnificere, & conscientiâ propriae infirmitatis se illis subij-cere, & hanc subiectionem externis significationibus declarare. Rom. 12. v. 10. 2. Cor. 8. v. 22. 23.
units.tr: XXXII. Reverence is honour towards superiors. Its proper task is to recognise and magnify the gifts of God in others, to submit oneself to them, mindful of one's own weakness, and to declare this submission by outward signs. Rom. 12. v. 10. 2. Cor. 8. v. 22. 23.

units.la: XXXIII. Fidelitas est, quae in mutuâ beneuolentiâ & omnibus officiis alicui debitis seruat constantiam, in rebus secundis & aduersis. Huius fidelitatis exempla sunt seruus Abrahami Gen. 24. Iosephus. Gen. 39. & 41. Moses Hebr. 2. v.5.
units.tr: XXXIII. Fidelity is that which keeps constancy in mutual goodwill and in all the duties owed to someone, in prosperity and in adversity. Examples of this fidelity are Abraham's servant, Gen. 24; Joseph, Gen. 39 and 41; Moses, Heb. 2. v. 5.

units.la: XXXIV. Amicitia est virtus, retribuens amico ex beneuolentia mutuum amorem. Huius tanta est vis, vt animos, in quibus viget vera pietas & virtutis amor, conglutinet in vnum, & quasi vnum cor faciat, vt in Dauide & Ionathane videre est. 1. Sam. 18. v.2. Prou. 17. v.17. Verùm amicitia illa, quae nititur vtilitate, est admodum fragilis, ita vt duplici nomine possit appellari ollaris. Prou. 14. v.20. Esa. 19. v.2. Mich. 7. v.5.
units.tr: XXXIV. Friendship is the virtue which repays a friend with mutual love arising from goodwill. Its power is so great that it binds together into one the minds in which true piety and love of virtue flourish, and makes them as it were one heart, as may be seen in David and Jonathan. 1 Sam. 18. v. 2. Prov. 17. v. 17. But that friendship which rests on advantage is very fragile, so that it may be called by the double name of a pot-friendship. Prov. 14. v. 20. Isa. 19. v. 2. Mic. 7. v. 5.

units.la: XXXV. Fortitudo est virtus docens medium seruare circa formidabilia. Estque togata, vel bellica. Fortitudo togata est, qua perseueramus in honesto proposito iuxta vocationem nostram, & toleramus iniurias propter honestam causam, & excelso animo despicimus pericula, virtutis causa. Eius insigne speculum habemus in Daniele cap. 6. & ipsius sociis cap. 3. Fortitudo bellica est, qua suscipiuntur pericula pro aris & focis. Vide exemplum Abrahami Gen. 14. item Iosuae, Simsonis, Dauidis, & similium.
units.tr: XXXV. Fortitude is the virtue which teaches us to keep the mean in face of frightening things. It is either civil or military. Civil fortitude is that by which we persevere in an honourable purpose according to our calling, endure injuries for an honourable cause, and with a lofty spirit despise dangers for the sake of virtue. We have a remarkable mirror of it in Daniel, chapter 6, and in his companions, chapter 3. Military fortitude is that by which dangers are undertaken for altars and hearths. See the example of Abraham, Gen. 14; likewise of Joshua, Samson, David and similar men.

units.la: XXXVI. Iustitia distributiua poenarum est, quae debitas poenas irrogat iis, qui sunt meriti. Seruat autem proportionem geometricam. Eius fines modumque Deus accurate circumscripsit in lege sua: vt Exod. 21. 22. &c. Vide infra Iurisprudentiam sacram.
units.tr: XXXVI. Distributive justice of punishments is that which inflicts the deserved penalties on those who have merited them. It keeps a geometrical proportion. God himself has precisely defined its limits and measure in his law, as in Exod. 21. 22. etc. See below under sacred jurisprudence.

units.la: XXXVII. Magnanimitas est eminentia quaedam fortitudinis. Excitat enim animum in malorum metu ad res arduas & periculosas necessario suscipiendum & superandum. Eius exemplum est in Simsone Iudit. 14.15.16. & apostolo Paulo Act.21.v.13. Magnanimitas quoque alio sensu est eminentia siue excellens gradus modestiae, faciens, vt appetamus honores eminentes, virtuti heroicae debitos. Eius exemplum est Christus Iohn.[?] 6. v.15.
units.tr: XXXVII. Magnanimity is a certain eminence of fortitude. For it rouses the mind, in fear of evils, to take up and overcome difficult and dangerous things that must be faced. Its example is Samson, Judith 14, 15, 16, and the apostle Paul, Acts 21. v. 13. Magnanimity is also, in another sense, an eminence or excellent degree of modesty, causing us to seek eminent honours that are due to heroic virtue. Its example is Christ, John 6. v. 15.

units.la: XXXVIII. Mansuetudo est virtus moderans vim irascendi, vt nonnisi cum ratione & ex ossicio irascamur. Alias appellatur Longanimitas. Versatur autem hæc virtus circa iram, tanquam obiectum internum; circa pœnam, tanquam obiectum externum. De hac virtute passim concionatur Scriptura, vt Psal. 4. vers. 5. Eccles. 7. v. 10. Matth. 5. v. 22. Eph. 4. v. 25. Gal. 5. v. 23. Eph. 4. ver. 2. Iacob. 3. v. 13. Colos. 3. v. 12. Mansuetudo, si de summo iure remittat, dicitur æquitas, Græcis ἐπιείκεια: quæ valde commendat hominem. {5} ... fieri potest, quantum in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus in pace viuentes. Confer Hebr.12.v.14. Exemplum est Abraham cedens fratri Lotho. Gen.13.
units.tr: XXXVIII. Meekness is the virtue that moderates the force of anger, so that we are angered only with reason and as duty requires. It is otherwise called long-suffering. This virtue is concerned with anger as its inner object, and with punishment as its outer object. Scripture preaches about this virtue throughout, as in Psal. 4. vers. 5. Eccles. 7. v. 10. Matth. 5. v. 22. Eph. 4. v. 25. Gal. 5. v. 23. Eph. 4. ver. 2. Iacob. 3. v. 13. Colos. 3. v. 12. Meekness, if it remits something of its full right, is called equity, in Greek epieikeia [ἐπιείκεια], which greatly commends a man. {5} ... as far as it depends on you, live at peace with all men. Compare Hebr. 12. v. 14. An example is Abraham yielding to his brother Lot, Gen. 13.

units.la: XLII. Misericordia est, quâ afficimur sensu miseriæ aliorum, eamque pro viribus subleuare studemus. Hæc virtus ex se parit eleemosynam, de quâ Daniel pronuntiat, peccata hac virtute abrumpi.c.4.v.14.[?] Ad hanc misericordiæ partem adhortatur nos Christus Luc.11.vers.41.cap.12.v.33. In genere de misericordia vide Luc.6.v.36. 1.Cor.12.v.25.26. 1.Iohan.3.v.17. Coloss.3.v.12. Prou.14.v.21.
units.tr: XLII. Mercy is the feeling by which we are moved by the misery of others, and we strive to relieve it as far as we can. This virtue gives birth to almsgiving, of which Daniel declares that sins are broken off by this virtue. c.4.v.14.[?] Christ exhorts us to this part of mercy Luc.11.vers.41.cap.12.v.33. On mercy in general see Luc.6.v.36. 1.Cor.12.v.25.26. 1.Iohan.3.v.17. Coloss.3.v.12. Prou.14.v.21.

units.la: XLIII. Humanitas est, quâ sumus facilès, mitès, & tractabiles. Nomen habet ab homine. Nam quia homo inter omnia animalia maximè mitis est, merito humanus pro facili, miti, & tractabili ponitur: & ideò humanitas inter alia significat facilitatem quandam & tractabilitatem beneuolentiamque inter omnes, quam Græci φιλανθρωπίαν vocant, Germani, Leutseligkeit. Eius exemplum iliustre est Christus Luc.2.v.52.
units.tr: XLIII. Humanity is that by which we are easy-going, gentle, and affable. It takes its name from man. For since man is the gentlest of all animals, "humane" is rightly used for easy, gentle, and affable; and so humanity signifies, among other things, a certain easiness, affability, and kindness toward all, which the Greeks call philanthropy [φιλανθρωπία] and the Germans Leutseligkeit. Its striking example is Christ Luc.2.v.52.

units.la: XLIV. Nemesis est zelus, indignè ferens scelera grassari in patriâ, eaque coercens pro virili. Supra considerauimus Zelum pro gloriâ Dei. Hoc loco est sermo de Zelo pro publico bono patriæ: vt cùm Simson amore patriæ, & indignatione aduersus Philistæos, accensus fuit, vt susciperet labores & pericula pro populo suo. Iudic.14.15.16.
units.tr: XLIV. Nemesis is zeal, indignantly bearing that crimes run rampant in one's country, and restraining them to the best of one's ability. Above we considered zeal for God's glory; here the discussion is of zeal for the public good of one's fatherland, as when Samson, kindled by love of his country and indignation against the Philistines, undertook labours and dangers for his people. Iudic.14.15.16.

units.la: XLV. Castitas est puritas animi & corporis, vitans omnes libidines à Deo prohibitas. Ea consideratur in genere, quatenus omnibus hominibus convenit Leuit.18.v.24.c.19.v.2. Deut.23.v.17. Prou.5.vers.8. c.6.v.25. Act.15.v.20. Rom.13.v.13,1. Cor.5.v.9. 2.Cor.7. vers.1.Gal.5.vers.25.Eph.5.ver.3.Phil.4.v.8.Col.3.v.5.8.9. 1.Thess.4.vers.3.4.5.7.1.Tim.3.ver.2.2.Tim.2.v.22.Tit.1. v.18. Hebr.12.v.14.1.Petr.2.v.11.1.Ioh.2.v.16.17.Iud.v.24. Apoc.2.vers.21. Vel in specie, quatenus est virginalis
units.tr: XLV. Chastity is purity of mind and body, avoiding all lusts forbidden by God. It is considered in general, insofar as it belongs to all men Leuit.18.v.24.c.19.v.2. Deut.23.v.17. Prou.5.vers.8. c.6.v.25. Act.15.v.20. Rom.13.v.13,1. Cor.5.v.9. 2.Cor.7. vers.1.Gal.5.vers.25.Eph.5.ver.3.Phil.4.v.8.Col.3.v.5.8.9. 1.Thess.4.vers.3.4.5.7.1.Tim.3.ver.2.2.Tim.2.v.22.Tit.1. v.18. Hebr.12.v.14.1.Petr.2.v.11.1.Ioh.2.v.16.17.Iud.v.24. Apoc.2.vers.21. Or in particular, insofar as it is virginal

units.la: 1. Cor. 7. vel coniugalis Hebr. 13. v. 4. vel vidualis 1. Tim. 5. v. 5. 6. 1. Cor. 7.
units.tr: 1. Cor. 7. vel coniugalis Hebr. 13. v. 4. vel vidualis 1. Tim. 5. v. 5. 6. 1. Cor. 7. (That is, as it is conjugal, 1. Cor. 7.; or as it is marital, Hebr. 13. v. 4.; or as it is widowly, 1. Tim. 5. v. 5. 6. 1. Cor. 7.)

units.la: XLVI. Verecundia est virtus, quæ metuit cōspectum Dei & angelorum, itemque infamiam comitantem delicta, & metu iudicij diuini coercet cupiditates, habitumque corporis ita regit, vt conueniat ordini naturæ, personarum, & locorum. Cernitur hæc virtus in vultu & oculis Iob. 31. ver. 1. Gen. 24. v. 64. Prou. 7. v. 13. in verbis honestis Gen. 4. verf. 1. Psal. 51. verf. 1. Esa. 7. v. 20. paucis item & submissis. Matth. 12. verf. 19. Prou. 10. v. 19. denique in vestitu Tit. 2. verf. 3.
units.tr: XLVI. Modesty is a virtue which fears the sight of God and of the angels, likewise the infamy that accompanies sins; by fear of divine judgment it restrains desires, and it governs bodily bearing so that it agrees with the order of nature, of persons, and of places. This virtue is seen in the countenance and eyes Iob. 31. ver. 1. Gen. 24. v. 64. Prou. 7. v. 13.; in honest words Gen. 4. verf. 1. Psal. 51. verf. 1. Esa. 7. v. 20.; also in few and humble words Matth. 12. verf. 19. Prou. 10. v. 19.; and finally in clothing Tit. 2. verf. 3.

units.la: XLVII. Temperantia est virtus, quæ moderatur appetitum cibi & potus. Eius partes sunt Abftinentia & Sobrietas; è quibus illa seruat modum naturæ conuenientem in sumendo cibo, hæc in potu. Vide Luc. 21. verf. 34. Rom. 13. verf. 13. Prou. 20. verf. 1. cap. 23[?] verf. 26.
units.tr: XLVII. Temperance is the virtue which moderates the appetite for food and drink. Its parts are abstinence and sobriety; of which the former keeps the measure proper to nature in taking food, the latter in drink. See Luc. 21. verf. 34. Rom. 13. verf. 13. Prou. 20. verf. 1. cap. 23[?] verf. 26.

units.la: XLVIII. Sedulitas est, quâ quis diligenter facit labores vocationis suæ. Vide Gen. 3. v. 19. 1. Cor. 7. v. 24. Prou. 6. v. 4. & seqq.
units.tr: XLVIII. Diligence is that by which someone carefully performs the labours of his calling. See Gen. 3. v. 19. 1. Cor. 7. v. 24. Prou. 6. v. 4. & seqq.

units.la: XLIX. Studium honestè rem parandi est virtus, quæ docet ita laborare, vt in vocatione nostra conuenientes facultates paremus. Itanempe vt cœlestem benedictionem expectemus à Deo, quem piis precibus vitâque sanctâ nobis conciliamus. Psal. 127. & 128. 1. Cor. 3. v. 7. 8.
units.tr: XLIX. Zeal for honestly acquiring property is a virtue which teaches us to labour so that we acquire means fitting to our calling; namely, so that we expect heavenly blessing from God, whom we win over to ourselves by pious prayers and a holy life. Psal. 127. & 128. 1. Cor. 3. v. 7. 8.

units.la: L. Parsimonia est, quâ bona recte parta recte custodimus ad vsus in vitâ quotidianâ necessarios. Vide Esa. 65. v. 8. Eccles. 19. v. 1. Iohan. 6. v. 12.
units.tr: L. Thrift is that by which we rightly keep goods rightly acquired, for the uses necessary in daily life. See Esa. 65. v. 8. Eccles. 19. v. 1. Iohan. 6. v. 12.

units.la: LI. Sufficientia est, quâ vnusquisque suo demenso & sorte contentus est. Puta bonis, statu, honore, opibus, & similibus. 1. Tim. 6. v. 6. & seqq. Psal. 37. v. 16.
units.tr: LI. Contentment is that by which each person is content with his measure and lot; say, with goods, station, honour, wealth, and the like. 1. Tim. 6. v. 6. & seqq. Psal. 37. v. 16.

units.la: LII. Frugalitas est, quâ quis proprias facultates refert ad usus à Deo ordinatos. Ita nempe, ut iis utatur ad Dei gloriam, suam ipsius & aliorum utilitatem. Eccles. 9. v. 9. Psal. 104. v. 15. & 128.
units.tr: LII. Frugality is that by which someone refers his own resources to the uses ordained by God; namely, that he uses them for God's glory and for his own and others' benefit. Eccles. 9. v. 9. Psal. 104. v. 15. & 128.

units.la: LIII. Iustitia commutatiua in contractibus, seu commutatione rerum, seruat aequalitatem Arithmeticam. Regulas ipsius vide Leuit. 25. verf. 14. Matth. 7. v. 12. 2. Cor. 8. v. 3. Deut. 23. v. 20.
units.tr: LIII. Commutative justice in contracts, or in the exchange of goods, preserves arithmetical equality. For its rules see Leuit. 25. verf. 14. Matth. 7. v. 12. 2. Cor. 8. v. 3. Deut. 23. v. 20.

units.la: LIV. Liberalitas, siue beneficentia, est virtus, quâ pro viribus nostris communicamus bona nostra. Vide Hebr. 13. verf. 16. Luc. 6. verf. 35. Gal. 6. verf. 9.10.
units.tr: LIV. Liberality, or beneficence, is the virtue by which we share our goods according to our means. See Hebr. 13. verf. 16. Luc. 6. verf. 35. Gal. 6. verf. 9.10.

units.la: LV. Hospitalitas est, quâ hospites, & inprimis exules, officiis hospitalibus complectimur. Officia hospitalia sunt posita in rectè excipiendo, tractando siue recreando, & dimittendo. Vide de hac virtute Rom. 12. v. 13. 1. Petr. 4. v. 13.
units.tr: LV. Hospitality is that by which we embrace guests, and especially exiles, with hospitable duties. Hospitable duties consist in receiving them rightly, treating or refreshing them, and dismissing them. On this virtue see Rom. 12. v. 13. 1. Petr. 4. v. 13.

units.la: LVI. Veracitas est, quâ rem, sicut se habet, iuxta cordis sensum, & rationis dictamen, proferimus. Vide Zach. 8. verf. 16. Matth. 5. verf. 37. Iacob. 5. vers.12.
units.tr: LVI. Veracity is that by which we state a thing as it is, in accordance with the sense of the heart and the dictate of reason. See Zach. 8. verf. 16. Matth. 5. verf. 37. Iacob. 5. vers.12.

units.la: LVII. Eulalia est, quâ veritatem proferimus sono conveniente. Ita nempe, ut gratia fit in sermone nostro. Psal.45.v.2.3.
units.tr: LVII. Eulalia is that by which we utter the truth in fitting sound; namely, so that there is grace in our speech. Psal.45.v.2.3.

units.la: LVIII. Docilitas est, quâ facile cedimus melioris sententiæ. Ne scil. philautiâ aut arrogantiâ pertinaciter amplectamur falsas opiniones, sed ut alios meliora docentes libenter audiamus & sequamur. 2.Tim.3. vers.15.
units.tr: LVIII. Docility is that by which we readily yield to the better opinion: lest from self-love or arrogance we obstinately cling to false opinions, but rather gladly hear and follow those who teach better things. 2.Tim.3. vers.15.

units.la: LIX. Taciturnitas est moderatus linguæ usus. Neque enim sic dicitur, quòd doceat nos semper tacere, sed quòd linguam coërceat fidei & charitatis sanctæ repagulis. Iacob.3.v. & seqq. Psal.34.v.14. & 39.v.2.
units.tr: LIX. Taciturnity is the moderate use of the tongue. For it is not so called because it teaches us always to be silent, but because it restrains the tongue with the bars of faith and holy charity. Iacob.3.v. & seqq. Psal.34.v.14. & 39.v.2.

units.la: LX. Affabilitas est, quâ faciles sumus & moderati in alloquendo. Vide Matth. 10. v. 12.
units.tr: LX. Affability is that by which we are easy and moderate in addressing others. See Matth. 10. v. 12.

units.la: LXI. Comitas est virtus, quâ in sermone suavitatem erga alios declaramus. Ita nempe, vt in loquendo, audiendo, respondendo, salutando &c. benevolétiam nostram cum sale aliquo testatam faciamus: 2.Tim.3.v.10.1.Cor.13.v.4.Coloss.3.v.12.c.4.v.6.Matt.10.v.12.
units.tr: LXI. Courtesy is a virtue by which we show kindness toward others in our speech; namely, that in speaking, listening, answering, greeting, and so on, we make our goodwill evident with a certain seasoning of wit. 2.Tim.3.v.10.1.Cor.13.v.4.Coloss.3.v.12.c.4.v.6.Matt.10.v.12.

units.la: LXII. Urbanitas est, quâ ornatur sermo cum decoro. Huiusmodi ornamenta sunt ænigmata, tropi urbaniusculi, sales decori & non mordaces, & similia ornamenta, quibus alij admonentur, leniuntur, vel irritantur. Iudic. 14. v. 15.
units.tr: LXII. Urbanity is that by which speech is adorned with decorum. Such ornaments are riddles, witty tropes, pleasant and non-biting jests, and similar embellishments by which others are admonished, soothed, or provoked. Iudic. 14. v. 15.

units.la: LXIII. Puritas cordis est sancta ordinatio & moderatio, cogitationum, cupiditatum & assectuum. Hanc Deus requirit in omnibus nostris viis & operibus. 1.Tim.1.vers.5.1.Thes.5.vers.23.Eph.4.v.23.
units.tr: LXIII. Purity of heart is the holy ordering and moderation of thoughts, desires, and affections. God requires this in all our ways and works. 1.Tim.1.vers.5.1.Thes.5.vers.23.Eph.4.v.23.

units.la: LXIV. Lucta adversus pravas cogitationes & appetitus est, quando resistimus quàm acerrimè omni inordinatæ motioni. Hanc graphicè describit apostolus Rom.7.
units.tr: LXIV. The struggle against wicked thoughts and appetites is when we resist with the utmost vehemence every disordered motion. The apostle describes this vividly in Rom.7.

units.la: Atque hæc est Ethica sacra, cuius finis & norma debet esse lux illa pura, plena, infinita, fontalis, & vitalis, quæ est Deus, itemque Christus in carne patefactus: subiectū informationis debet esse anima deiformis, hoc est, illa, quæ cupit Deo magis magisque fieri similis: media denique debent esse tres viæ sive semitæ splendidæ; videl. via purgativa, quâ vitium expurgemus, avertendo mentem, voluntatem, & affectum à vanitate huius mundi, & convertendo illa ad Deum: via illuminativa, quâ lux illa divina illabatur animo purgato à sordibus: & via unitiva, quâ mens divinâ speculatione atque amore velut ignea essecta relinquat cuncta creata, & Deo per sapientissimam ignorantiam rerum nauci, in splendidissimâ abysso uniatur. Atqː hæ tres viæ in qualibet virtute debent expendi.
units.tr: And this is sacred ethics, whose end and norm ought to be that pure, full, infinite, fontal, and vital light which is God, and also Christ manifested in the flesh; the subject of formation ought to be the deiform soul, that is, the soul which desires to become more and more like God; the means finally ought to be three shining ways or paths. Namely: the purgative way, by which we purge vice, turning mind, will, and affection away from the vanity of this world and toward God; the illuminative way, by which that divine light flows into the soul cleansed of its filth; and the unitive way, by which the mind, through divine contemplation and love made as it were fiery, leaves behind all created things and, by a most wise ignorance of things, counted as nothing, is united to God in the most splendid abyss. And these three ways must be weighed in every virtue.

units.la: XIX. OECONOMICA SACRA.
units.tr: XIX. Sacred Economics.

units.la: I. OEconomica sacra est prudentia recte cu-randi domum, ex sacris literis collecta.
units.tr: I. Sacred economics is the prudent art of governing the household, drawn from the holy Scriptures.

units.la: II. Domus est communitas familiae, reique familiaris. Duae ig. sunt partes domus: videl. familia, & res familiaris. 1. Reg. 4.
units.tr: II. The household is the community of a family and of its property. For there are two parts of a household, namely the family and the family's property. 1 Kings 4.

units.la: III. Familia est societas personarum domestici conuictus iure deinctarum. Dici possunt personae oeconomicae seu domesticae.
units.tr: III. A family is the society of persons bound together by the law of domestic living together. These persons may be called economic or domestic persons.

units.la: IV. Personarum oeconomicarum spectatur societas & officium. Graece dices συζυγίαν ἡ πρόσωπον[?].
units.tr: IV. The society and the duty of economic persons are to be considered. In Greek you may say syzygia [συζυγία] or prosopa [πρόσωπα].

units.la: V. Societas personarum oeconomicarum est mutua illarum obligatio ad praestandum sibi invicem debita familiae officia.
units.tr: V. The society of economic persons is the mutual obligation by which they owe one another the duties of the family.

units.la: VI. Societas ista est triplex: coniugalis, patria & herilis. Eph. 5. & 6. Coloss. 3.
units.tr: VI. This society is threefold: conjugal, paternal and servile. Eph. 5 and 6; Col. 3.

units.la: VII. Societas coniugalis dicitur coniugium, quod est unius viri & foeminae indiuidua coniunctio. Tam arcta est haec vnio, vt duo fiant vna caro. Gen. 2. v. 23. 24. Matth. 19. v. 5. Vna, inquam, caro iure naturae seu primae creationis, & iure vocationis siue officij. Est autem coniugium, vel primum, inter duas personas, quae antea non vixerunt in coniugio, vt Gen. 11. v. 29. 1. Reg. 3. vel secundum, inter duas personas, e quibus alterutra, vel vtraque antehac vixit in coniugio, & peruenit ad statum viduitatis. Vsitate appellant secundas nuptias, & secunda vota: quorum ius probatur exemplo Abrahami Gen. 25. & Moßs. Num. 12. & authoritate apostolica. Rom. 7. v. 2. 3. 1. Cor. 7. v. 8. 9. 1. Tim. 5. v. 14. Iniqua ig. est sententia Tertulliani, qui patrocinium viniuratus ita iuscepit, vt secundas nuptias damnauerit. Deinde coniugium est sterile, vel fœcundum, vt in Lea & Rahele videre est Gen.30. Tertiò coniugium est felix & tranquillum, vel infelix & turbulentum. Sic Abrahami coniugium cum Sarâ erat felix Gen. 21. Iobi infelix ex parte vxoris Iob. 2. Abigailis infelix ex parte mariti Nabalis. 1. Sam. 25.
units.tr: VII. The conjugal society is called marriage, which is the indivisible joining of one man and one woman. This union is so close that the two become one flesh. Gen. 2:23–24; Matt. 19:5. One flesh, I say, by the law of nature or of the first creation, and by the law of calling or office. A marriage is either a first marriage, between two persons who have not previously lived in marriage (as Gen. 11:29; 1 Kings 3), or a second marriage, between two persons of whom one or both have previously lived in marriage and have come to the state of widowhood. They are commonly called second nuptials and second vows. The right to these is proved by the example of Abraham (Gen. 25) and of Moses (Num. 12), and by apostolic authority (Rom. 7:2–3; 1 Cor. 7:8–9; 1 Tim. 5:14). Unjust, indeed, is the opinion of Tertullian, who, having taken up the cause of the wine-drinkers, so received it that he condemned second marriages. Next, a marriage is either barren or fruitful, as may be seen in Leah and Rachel (Gen. 30). Thirdly, a marriage is either happy and peaceful, or unhappy and turbulent. Thus the marriage of Abraham with Sarah was happy (Gen. 21); that of Job was unhappy on the wife's side (Job 2); that of Abigail was unhappy on the husband's side, with Nabal (1 Sam. 25).

units.la: VIII. Societas patria est, quâ parentes & liberi inter se devinciuntur. Huc pertinet fratrum & sororum mutua affectio & coniunctio in eâdem familia. Gen. 25. Eph. 6. Coloss. 3.
units.tr: VIII. The paternal society is that by which parents and children are bound to one another. To this belongs the mutual affection and union of brothers and sisters in the same family. Gen. 25; Eph. 6; Col. 3.

units.la: IX. Societas herilis est, quâ herus & servus inter se devinciuntur. Sub hero hera, sub feruo serua intelligitur. Pertinet huc feruorum inter se mutua assectio & coniunctio in eâdem familiâ. Gen. 24. Eph. 6. Coloss. 3.
units.tr: IX. The servile society is that by which master and servant are bound to one another. Under master is understood mistress, and under servant, maidservant. To this belongs the mutual affection and union of servants with one another in the same family. Gen. 24; Eph. 6; Col. 3.

units.la: X. Officium œconomicum est, ad quod præstandum obligantur personæ œconomicæ. Estq; aliud internum, quod personæ istæ præstare tenentur erga se mutuò: aliud externum, quod erga alios, puta vicinos & similes, præstare debent.
units.tr: X. The economic duty is that which economic persons are bound to perform. And there is one duty that is internal, which these persons are obliged to render to one another, and another that is external, which they ought to render to others, such as neighbours and the like.

units.la: XI. Officium œconomicum internum est coniugale, patrium, vel herile.
units.tr: XI. The internal economic duty is conjugal, paternal or servile.

units.la: XII. Officium coniugale est, ad quod præstandum obligantur coniuges, iisque aut inituri coniugium, aut qui iam inierunt.
units.tr: XII. The conjugal duty is that which spouses are bound to perform, both those who are about to enter marriage and those who have already entered it.

units.la: XIII. Inituri coniugium faciant officium suum præparando, eligendo, promittendo, & convenientem solennitatem adhibendo. Præparatio est pia juvenum & puellarum compositio, quâ student pietati & castitati, Deumque orant vt omnibus ipsorum laboribus & cogitationibus benedicat, discunt deniq; ea, quæ per universam vitam prosunt in coniugio. 1. Tim. 4. vers. 8. 6. 5. v. 22. Eph. 4. v. 28. Exempla vide Isaaci, Jacobi, Rebeccæ, Rahelis, & filiarum sacerdotis Midian. Gen. 14 & 29. Exod. 2. Electio est, quâ deligitur persona diligenda; vbi primò requiruntur preces ad Deum, deinde prudens consideratio donorum, è quibus alia principaliter, alia minùs principaliter sunt spectanda. Principaliter spectari debet pietas, castitas, peritia œconomica, & paritas religionis. Prou. 11. v. 16. c. 31. v. 11. & seqq. Eccles. 26. v. 1. 2. Deut. 7. v. 3. 4. Gen. 24. v. 3. Iudic. 14. v. 4. c. 3. v. 6. 1. Reg. 11. v. 1. Minùs principaliter spectari debet dos & forma. Ni si principaliter hæc duo spectentur, nulla sperari potest benedictio à Deo. Eccles. 25. v. 25. 26. c. 26. v. 1. 2. 3. 4. Promissio coniugii non debet esse clandestina, sed parentibus, vel iis qui sunt loco parentum, cognita: non sophistica, lubrica & fallax, sed plana, firma & certa Exod. 20. v. 11. Gen. 24. Tob. 5. Huc pertinent Sponsalia, quæ ita debent celebrari, vt fiant vtrinque pia vota, quibus omnia fausta nouis coniugibus exoptentur; item vt conuiuio lætoexhilarentur propinqui, & acta sponsaliorum literis confignentur; denique vt noui coniuges ad sincerum & mutuum amorem incitentur, protectioni & tutelæ Dei commendentur, ipsisque omnia pietatis & humanitatis ossicia deferantur. Gen. 24. Tob. 7. & 8. Solennitas nuptialis consistit in inuitatione, ornatu sponsi & sponsæ, ritibus & conuiuio nuptialibus: in quibus omnibus decorum, consuetudo, & conditio nostra spectanda. Gen. 29. Iudic. 14. Psalm. 45. Esa. 62. verf. 1. 7. Tob. 8. & 9. 1. Maccab. 9. Iohan. 2.
units.tr: XIII. Those about to marry should perform their duty by preparing, choosing, promising, and observing a fitting solemnity. Preparation is the godly composure of young men and maidens, by which they strive for piety and chastity, pray to God that he may bless all their labours and thoughts, and finally learn those things that are useful for the whole of life in marriage. 1 Tim. 4:8; 5:22; Eph. 4:28. For examples see Isaac, Jacob, Rebekah, Rachel, and the daughters of the priest of Midian: Gen. 14 and 29; Exod. 2. Choice is the selection of the person to be loved, in which prayers to God are first required, and then a prudent consideration of the gifts, of which some are to be regarded chiefly and others less so. Piety, chastity, economic skill and agreement in religion ought chiefly to be considered. Prov. 11:16; 31:11ff.; Ecclus. 26:1–2; Deut. 7:3–4; Gen. 24:3; Judg. 14:4; 3:6; 1 Kings 11:1. Dowry and appearance ought to be considered less. Unless these two are considered chiefly, no blessing from God can be hoped for. Ecclus. 25:25–26; 26:1–4. The promise of marriage should not be secret, but made known to the parents or to those who stand in their place; not sophistical, slippery and deceitful, but plain, firm and certain. Exod. 20:11; Gen. 24; Tob. 5. To this belong the betrothal, which ought to be celebrated so that on both sides pious vows are made, by which all happy things are wished for the new spouses; likewise that the relatives be gladdened by a feast, and that the acts of the betrothal be recorded in writing; and finally that the new spouses be stirred to sincere and mutual love, be commended to the protection and guardianship of God, and be shown every office of piety and kindness. Gen. 24; Tob. 7 and 8. The nuptial solemnity consists in the invitation, the adornment of bridegroom and bride, the nuptial rites and the feast; in all of which decency, custom and our condition must be considered. Gen. 29; Judg. 14; Ps. 45; Isa. 62:1, 7; Tob. 8 and 9; 1 Macc. 9; John 2.

units.la: XIV. Qui iam inierunt coniugium, illudq; consummarunt, debent facere officium commune, & proprium.
units.tr: XIV. Those who have already entered marriage and consummated it ought to perform the common and the proper duties.

units.la: XV. Officium commune coniugum est pietatis, mutui amoris, & fidelitatis. Pietatis officium est, quo coniuges Deum amant, timent, honorant, & inuocant assiduis precibus, vt ipsorum coniugium iuuare & ornare velit. Psal. 127. & 128. Tob. 8. Quòd si coniu-gium gium ipsorum sit sterile, vel infelix, ne murmurent adversus Deum, sed patienti sint animo, & instent precibus Gen.25.v.21. Si vero coniugium sit fœcundum, tranquillum & felix, agant Deo gratias, & ita se gerant, ut ille hanc benedictionem ipsis continuet Gen.30.v.20. Ps.128. Officium amoris mutui est, quo coniux alter alterum ita complecti & prosequi debet, ut suam ipsius carnem amar. Gen.2.v.24. Matth.19.v.5.6. Quod si forte contentio & discordia inter coniuges oriatur, ne diu illam alant, sed adhibeant pia media, quibus, quam primum fieri potest, fiat animorum vera reconciliatio. Si enim omnibus Christianis, multo magis pijs coniugibus hoc convenit. Matt.5. v.23,24. Officium fidelitatis consistit in fide coniugali, ut illa servetur salva & illibata Exod.20.v.13. Leuit.20.v.10. Malach.2.ver.14. itemque in cura rei domesticæ. Gen.11. verf.31. Psal.127.& 128. Ecclesiastic. 7.ver.22. 23.24.25.26. Ad fidem coniugalem pertinet mutua coniugum benevolentia. 1.Cor.7.v.2.3.4. Tob.8.v.7.
units.tr: XV. The common duty of spouses is of piety, of mutual love, and of fidelity. The duty of piety is that by which spouses love, fear and honour God, and call upon him with constant prayers, that he may wish to help and adorn their marriage. Ps. 127 and 128; Tob. 8. But if their marriage is barren or unhappy, let them not murmur against God, but be patient in spirit and persist in prayer. Gen. 25:21. If indeed the marriage is fruitful, peaceful and happy, let them give thanks to God, and so conduct themselves that he may continue this blessing to them. Gen. 30:20; Ps. 128. The duty of mutual love is that by which one spouse ought to embrace and cherish the other as their own flesh. Gen. 2:24; Matt. 19:5–6. But if perchance strife and discord arise between spouses, let them not nourish it for long, but employ pious means by which a true reconciliation of minds may be effected as soon as possible. For this is fitting for all Christians, and much more for pious spouses. Matt. 5:23–24. The duty of fidelity consists in keeping conjugal faith safe and unblemished, Exod. 20:13; Lev. 20:10; Mal. 2:14, and likewise in care of the household. Gen. 11:31; Ps. 127 and 128; Ecclus. 7:22–26. To conjugal faith belongs the mutual goodwill of the spouses. 1 Cor. 7:2–4; Tob. 8:7.

units.la: XVI. Officium coniugale proprium est mariti, vel uxoris.
units.tr: XVI. The proper conjugal duty is that of the husband or of the wife.

units.la: XVII. Officium mariti est affirmatiuum & negatiuum. Officium affirmatiuum est, amare uxorem ut corpus & carnem suam. Prou.5.v.18.19. Eph.5.v.25.28.29. recte uti potestate & imperio maritali Gen.3.v.16. Coloss.3. v.19. Eccles.4.v.35. concedere uxori potestatem competentem in liberos, servos & ancillas Gen.16.v.6. prudenter conversari cum uxore 1.Petr.3.v.7. muliebrem imbecillitatem in uxore corrigere suâ mansuetudine 1.Cor.9. v.22. denique morositatem, iracundiam, & fastum, quātum fieri poterit, amicis & gravibus admonitionibus reprimere. Iob.2.v.10. Officium negatiuum est, non pati se per uxorem seduci in superstitionem & errorem 1.Cor.14. verf.34.35. non pati uxorem suam in errore permanere. 1.Tim.2.v.11. non admittere imperium muliebre in se.
units.tr: XVII. The duty of a husband is both affirmative and negative. The affirmative duty is to love his wife as his own body and flesh, Prov. 5.18, 19; Eph. 5.25, 28, 29; to use his marital power and authority rightly, Gen. 3.16; Col. 3.19; Eccles. 4.35; to grant his wife suitable authority over the children and the male and female servants, Gen. 16.6; to live prudently with his wife, 1 Pet. 3.7; to correct the weakness of womanhood in his wife by his own gentleness, 1 Cor. 9.22; and finally, as far as possible, to restrain her peevishness, anger and pride by friendly but weighty admonitions, Job 2.10. The negative duty is not to let himself be seduced by his wife into superstition and error, 1 Cor. 14.34, 35; not to allow his wife to remain in error, 1 Tim. 2.11; and not to admit female rule over himself.

units.la: 1. Tim.2.v.12.13.14. non audire uxorem in publicis nego-
units.tr: 1 Tim. 2.12, 13, 14: not to listen to his wife in public affairs, unless perhaps she offers a faithful admonition.

units.la: tiis, nisi forte fidelem admonitionem suggerat. Gen.21. v.10.12. Esth.7.v.3. & seqq. denique non facile vxori committere arcana. Iud.16.v.17. Mich.7.v.5.
units.tr: in public business, unless perhaps she offers a faithful warning. Gen. 21:10, 12; Esth. 7:3 ff. Finally, not to entrust secrets easily to a wife. Judg. 16:17; Mic. 7:5.

units.la: XVIII. Officium vxoris consistit in dilectione, subiectione, studio virtutum vxori inprimis conuenientium, adiumento, & applicatione. Dilectio debet ita esse comparata, vt vxor solum maritum vnice diligat. 1.Tim.2.ver.15. Tit.2.v.4. idque etiam in rebus aduersis. Gen.12.v.2.7. & seqq. Subiectio est, qua vxor, memor suae infirmitatis, marito suo paret in omni re honesta. Gen.3.v.16. Rom.7.v.1.2. Eph.5.v.22.23.24. 1.Tim.2. v.11.12. Tit.2.v.5. 1.Petr.3.v.1.5.6. Virtutes vxoricum primi conuenientes, sunt modestia, pudicitia, sobrietas, frugalitas &c. 1.Tim.3.v.11. Tit.2.v.3.4.5. 1.Petr.3.v.1.2.3.4.5.6. Officium adiumenti est in eo, vt vxor marito suo auxilium ferat pro viribus. Gen.2.v.20. Tob.8.v.6. Officium applicationis, siue accommodationis, est, quo pia vxor se applicat ad animum ac mores mariti, quantum per religionem & conscientiam fieri potest, eique gratificatur omnibus honestis & licitis modis. Prouerb.31.v.12. Eccles.26.v.16. 17.18.19.20.21.22. Caeterum exemplum bonae mulieris sunt Sara 1.Petr.3.v.6. Abigail 1.Sam.25. Hanna 1.Sam.1. malae, vxor Iobi & Tobiae senioris. Iob.2. Tob.2.
units.tr: XVIII. The wife's duty consists in love, submission, zeal for the virtues especially fitting to a wife, help, and accommodation. Her love should be such that the wife loves her husband alone, and loves him above all others. 1 Tim. 2:15; Titus 2:4, and this even in adversity. Gen. 12:2, 7 ff. Submission is that by which the wife, mindful of her weakness, obeys her husband in every honest matter. Gen. 3:16; Rom. 7:1, 2; Eph. 5:22, 23, 24; 1 Tim. 2:11, 12; Titus 2:5; 1 Pet. 3:1, 5, 6. The virtues especially fitting to a wife are modesty, chastity, sobriety, thrift, and so on. 1 Tim. 3:11; Titus 2:3, 4, 5; 1 Pet. 3:1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The duty of help lies in this, that the wife bring her husband aid according to her strength. Gen. 2:20; Tob. 8:6. The duty of accommodation, or adaptation, is that by which the godly wife fits herself to her husband's mind and manners, as far as religion and conscience allow, and pleases him in every honest and lawful way. Prov. 31:12; Ecclus 26:16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22. Moreover, examples of a good woman are Sarah, 1 Pet. 3:6; Abigail, 1 Sam. 25; Hannah, 1 Sam. 1. Examples of a bad wife are Job's wife, Job 2, and the wife of the elder Tobias (Tobit), Tob. 2.

units.la: XIX. Officium in societate patria est parentum erga liberos, liberorum erga parentes, & liberorum erga se inuicem.
units.tr: XIX. The duty in the paternal society is that of parents toward children, of children toward parents, and of children toward one another.

units.la: XX. Officium parentum erga liberos est commune, vel proprium. Officium commune est vtriusque parentis, & consistit in φιλοστοργία, quâ fit, vt parentes summopere ament suos liberos, illorumque saluti indei[?] momento conceptionis vsque ad eam aetatem, quâ sibi recte consulere possunt, quàm solicitissime prospiciant. Esa.49.v.15. Matth.7.v.9.10. 1.Reg.3.v.26. Effecta huius philostorgiae sunt, infantes recens natos Christo offerre per baptismum Matth.19.v.13.14. in prima pueritia[?] domi suæ docere capita Catechetica & formulas precum Deut. 4. v. 40. c. 6. v. 2. 2. Tim. 3. v. 15. tempestiue iplos mittere in scholam. Hebr. 6. v.1. ducere ipsos ad conciones sacras. Deut. 31. verf. 12. Ioel. 2. v. 16. Matth. 21. v. 15. 16. Luc. 2. v. 46. domi ab illis exigere conciones, & omninò fungi vicem præceptorum domesticorum. Deut. 6. v. 7. Psal. 34. v. 12. Prou. 4. v. 1. 2. 3. & seqq. item potestate patriâ & disciplinâ erga illos rectè uti Prou. 13. v. 24. c. 19. v. 18. c. 23. v. 13. 14. c. 29. verf. 15. Hebr. 12. v. 5. 6. Eccles. 30. v. 1. exploratis ipsorum ingeniis, ipsos ad certum vitæ genus dirigere. Prou. 20. v. 11. colligere ipsis thesauros, quantum possunt illæsâ conscientiâ. Prou. 19. ver. 14. 2. Cor. 12. v. 14. ita nempe, ut simul, & inprimis, relinquant ipsis thesauros in cœlo Matth. 6. verf. 20. Prou. 8. v. 10. 11. Officium proprium est patris, vel matris. Proprium patris officium est tum defensionis, quâ liberos suos pro viribus, quibus præ matre pollet, ab omnibus malis tutos præstat Matth. 2. v. 14. tum authoritatis, quâ ipsos in officio continet Eph. 6. v. 4. tum solicitudinis, quâ ipsos elocat, & post mortem quoque ipsis prospicit de alimentis, tutoribus &c. Gen. 24. & 49. 2. Paral. 21. v. 3. Iohan. 19. v. 26. 27. 1. Maccab. 2. v. 64. & seqq. Proprium matris officium est tum lactationis, tum familiaritatis. Illud in eo consistit, ut mater proprio lacte nutriat infantulum, si per valetudinem possit. Gen. 21. verf. 7. 1. Sam. 1. v. 23. Hoc situm est in materna conuersatione & institutione. Gen. 24. v. 15. 16. c. 29. v. 6. Familiaritas ista temperanda est gravitate, ne degeneret in indulgentiam. Esa. 3. v. 17. Eccles. 42. v. 12.
units.tr: XX. The duty of parents toward children is either common or proper. The common duty belongs to both parents and consists in affection [φιλοστοργία], by which parents love their children exceedingly and care for their welfare, from the moment of conception until the age at which they can look after themselves, with the greatest anxiety. Isa. 49:15; Matt. 7:9, 10; 1 Kings 3:26. The effects of this affection are: to offer newborn infants to Christ through baptism, Matt. 19:13, 14; to teach them at home in early childhood the catechetical heads and formulas of prayer, Deut. 4:40; 6:2; 2 Tim. 3:15; to send them to school in good time, Heb. 6:1; to bring them to sacred sermons, Deut. 31:12; Joel 2:16; Matt. 21:15, 16; Luke 2:46; to require from them at home an account of the sermons, and in general to act in place of domestic teachers, Deut. 6:7; Ps. 34:12; Prov. 4:1, 2, 3 ff.; likewise to use paternal power and discipline toward them rightly, Prov. 13:24; 19:18; 23:13, 14; 29:15; Heb. 12:5, 6; Ecclus 30:1; to direct them to a certain way of life once their natures are known, Prov. 20:11; to gather treasures for them, as far as they can without injury to conscience, Prov. 19:14; 2 Cor. 12:14, namely in such a way that at the same time, and above all, they leave them treasures in heaven, Matt. 6:20; Prov. 8:10, 11. The proper duty belongs to the father or to the mother. The proper duty of the father is threefold: of defence, by which he keeps his children safe from all evils, as far as his strength, which surpasses the mother's, allows, Matt. 2:14; of authority, by which he keeps them in their duty, Eph. 6:4; and of care, by which he settles them in life and, even after death, provides for them with food, guardians, and so on, Gen. 24 and 49; 2 Chron. 21:3; John 19:26, 27; 1 Macc. 2:64 ff. The proper duty of the mother is of two kinds: of nursing and of familiarity. The first consists in this, that the mother nourish her infant with her own milk, if her health allows, Gen. 21:7; 1 Sam. 1:23. The second lies in the mother's conduct and instruction, Gen. 24:15, 16; 29:6. This familiarity must be tempered with gravity, lest it degenerate into indulgence, Isa. 3:17; Ecclus 42:12.

units.la: XXI. Officium liberorum erga parentes est obedientiæ, obseruantiæ, & gratitudinis. In his enim posita est philostorgia liberorum erga parentes. Obedientia est, quâ liberi etiam ad nutus parentum, & interna animi sensa vel coniecturis cognita, prômtè actiones suas ex animo instituunt. Prou. 6. v. 20. c. 15. v. 5. Eph. 6. v. 1. 2. 3. Col. 3. v. 20. Sed cauto hîc est opus, ne ista obedientia sit cœca & nimia, putâ impia & inhonesta. Matt. 10. v. 37. verf. 37. Luc. 14. v. 26. 1. Reg. 2. v. 19. & seqq. Obseruantia est, quâ liberi animum suum honorificum erga parentes aliis etiam declarant: puta comitate in verbis; industria in suscipiendis & peti ficiendis iis, quæ parentib. sciunt honori esse & delectationi; ministeriis denique & officiositate. Leuit. 19. v. 3. Deut. 27. v. 16. Ecclesiastic. 3. v. 2. & seqq. Tob. 4. v. 3. & seqq. Huius obseruantiæ pars magna est regere, & quasi condonare infirmitates parentum, præsertim vbi consenuerunt. Gen. 9. verf. 23. Prou. 20. v. 20. c. 23. ver. 22. c. 30. v. 17. Eccles. 3. v. 13. 14. 15. Gratitudo est, quâ liberi parentes senio confectos, si necessitas postulat, victum alunt ac iuuant, quod Græci eleganter dicunt ἀντιπελαργεῖν[?]. Gen. 47. v. 1. & seqq. 1. Tim. 5. v. 4. Eccles. 3. v. 15. 16. 17.
units.tr: XXI. The duty of children toward parents is one of obedience, reverence, and gratitude. For in these lies the affection of children toward parents. Obedience is that by which children, even at their parents' nod, and at their inner feelings known by the signs of them, promptly shape their actions from the heart. Prov. 6:20; 15:5; Eph. 6:1, 2, 3; Col. 3:20. But here caution is needed, lest this obedience be blind and excessive, that is, impious and dishonourable. Matt. 10:37; Luke 14:26; 1 Kings 2:19 ff. Reverence is that by which children also show to others their respectful attitude toward their parents: for example, courtesy in speech; diligence in undertaking and carrying out those things which they know to be an honour and a delight to their parents; and finally service and dutifulness. Lev. 19:3; Deut. 27:16; Ecclus 3:2 ff.; Tob. 4:3 ff. A large part of this reverence is to bear with and, as it were, pardon the infirmities of parents, especially when they have grown old. Gen. 9:23; Prov. 20:20; 23:22; 30:17; Ecclus 3:13, 14, 15. Gratitude is that by which children, if necessity requires, feed and help their parents worn out with age, which the Greeks elegantly call to repay the care of storks [ἀντιπελαργεῖν]. Gen. 47:1 ff.; 1 Tim. 5:4; Ecclus 3:15, 16, 17.

units.la: XXII. Officium liberorum erga se inuicem consistit in mutuo amore & auxilio. Vide Psal. 133. Gen. 37.
units.tr: XXII. The duty of children toward one another consists in mutual love and help. See Ps. 133; Gen. 37.

units.la: XXIII. Officium in societate herili est dominorum erga seruos, seruorum erga dominos, & seruorum erga se inuicem. Officium dominorum erga seruos est directio seruorum ad exercitia pietatis, & operas vitæ necessarias. Directio ad exercitia pietatis in primis in eo vertitur, vt heri hoc agant vt serui audiant conciones, & sabbatum recte transigant. Exod. 20. v. 10. 1. Sam. 1. v. 21. Ioh. 4. ver. 53. Act. 10. v. 2. Directio ad operas est, qua pater & materfamilias exigunt a seruis pensum ordinarium. Eccles. 33. v. 28. 29. & laborantibus dant competentem cibum & potum iusto tempore. 1. Tim. 5. verf. 18. Matth. 24. v. 45. Eccles. 33. v. 25. & numerant mercedem debitam. Leuit. 19. v. 13. Deut. 24. v. 14. Luc. 10. v. 7. & tuentur seruos contra iniuriam aliorum. Eccles. 33. v. 31. item sequunturproprium consilia bona. Eccles. 10. v. 28. fidelitatem quoq; ipsorum compensant præmiis, procuratione coniugij, curatione valetudinis aduersæ &c. Matth. 25. v. 21. Ecclesiastic. 7. v. 20. 21. fugiunt insuper indulgentiam in seruos, & familiaritatem cum iis. Prou.19. v.19. Eccles.33. v.27.28. neque tamen ideo rigorem adhibent. Eph.6. v. 9. Leuit. 25. v.53. sed debitam seueritatem; puta erga ignauos, contentiosos, temulentos &c. Prou.14. v. vlt. Matth. 20. v. 13. 14. c.24. v. 48. & seqq. Luc. 16. v. 1. 2. Officium seruorum erga dominos est triplex; venerationis, obsequij, & fidelitatis. Veneratio est, qua serui honore debito prosequuntur patrem & matrem familias. 1. Tim. 6. v. 1. 2. dissimiles scil. Hagari. Gen. 16. v. 4. Obsequium est, quo serui ex animo suis dominis obediunt. Psal. 123. v. 2. Gen. 16. v. 9. Eph. 6. v.5.6.7.8. Coloss.3.v.22.23.24. Quòd si domini sint rigidiores & morosiores, patienter ista vitia ferunt. 1. Pet.2. v. 18.19. Fidelitas est, qua serui omnia sua ministeria ad herorum commoda dirigunt, etiam sponte sua. Tit.2. verf. 9.10. Luc. 12. v. 42. c. 16. v. 13. Matth. 6. v. 24. Officium seruorum erga se invicem est amoris & auxilij mutui. Matt. 24. v. 45.49. Luc. 12. v. 42. 45.
units.tr: XXIII. The duty in the household is that of masters toward servants, of servants toward masters, and of servants toward one another. The duty of masters toward servants is to direct the servants to the exercises of piety and to the necessary labours of life. Direction to the exercises of piety consists chiefly in this, that masters see to it that their servants hear the sermons and keep the Sabbath properly. Exod. 20:10; 1 Sam. 1:21; John 4:53; Acts 10:2. Direction to labour is that by which the father and mother of the household require from the servants their ordinary task, Ecclus 33:28, 29, and give the labourers adequate food and drink at the proper time, 1 Tim. 5:18; Matt. 24:45; Ecclus 33:25, and pay the wages due, Lev. 19:13; Deut. 24:14; Luke 10:7, and protect the servants against the wrongs of others, Ecclus 33:31; likewise they follow good counsel of their own, Ecclus 10:28. They also reward the servants' fidelity with prizes, with arranging a marriage, with care of sickness, and so on, Matt. 25:21; Ecclus 7:20, 21. Moreover they avoid indulgence toward servants and familiarity with them, Prov. 19:19; Ecclus 33:27, 28, and yet do not on that account use harshness, Eph. 6:9; Lev. 25:53, but due severity, namely toward the idle, the quarrelsome, the drunken, and so on, Prov. 14 (last verse); Matt. 20:13, 14; 24:48 ff.; Luke 16:1, 2. The duty of servants toward masters is threefold: of reverence, of obedience, and of fidelity. Reverence is that by which servants pay the due honour to the master and mistress of the household, 1 Tim. 6:1, 2; unlike, namely, Hagar, Gen. 16:4. Obedience is that by which servants obey their masters from the heart, Ps. 123:2; Gen. 16:9; Eph. 6:5, 6, 7, 8; Col. 3:22, 23, 24. But if masters are harsher and more peevish, they bear these faults patiently, 1 Pet. 2:18, 19. Fidelity is that by which servants direct all their service to the advantage of their masters, even of their own accord, Titus 2:9, 10; Luke 12:42; 16:13; Matt. 6:24. The duty of servants toward one another is one of love and mutual help. Matt. 24:45, 49; Luke 12:42, 45.

units.la: XXIV. Officium oeconomicum erga vicinos est concordiae & beneficentiae.
units.tr: XXIV. The household's duty towards neighbours consists in harmony and beneficence.

units.la: Concordia est, qua vicini ad mutuam beneuolentiam & pacem propendent. Gen.13. v.8.9. Prou. 27. v. 10. Eccles. 25. v. 2. Beneficentia est officium necessitatis & iucunditatis. Officium necessitatis cernitur in dando mutuo, siue pecuniam, siue supellectilem petat vicinus pius & egens. Deut 15. v. 7. 8. Tob. 1. v. 16. Luc. 6. v. 35. Eccles. 29. v. 2. item in fideiussione prudenti & necessaria. Prou.6. v. 1. 2. 3. Eccles. 29. v. 17. item in commodis vicini promouendis, ita nempe vt vicinus adsit vicino temporibus tristibus, eique condoleat, laetis vero congratuletur. Luc. 1. verf. 58. c. 7. verf. 12. Iohan. 11. v. 19. item hortetur vicini seruos & ancillas ad debitam erga dominum suum fidelitatem, non vero illos alienet aut corrumpat. Exod. 20, verf. 17. Philem. v. 13. 14. denique iumenta, domos, & agros vicini iuuet atque promoueat, non vero laedat, vel auferat. Exod. 22. v. 5. 6. Deut. 22. v. 1. & seqq. c. 27. v. 17. Officium iucunditatis est, quo vicinus erga vicinum benevolentiam & amorem suum interdum moderato conuiuio declarat. Zach. 3. v. 10.
units.tr: Harmony is that by which neighbours incline to mutual goodwill and peace. Gen. 13. v. 8, 9. Prov. 27. v. 10. Ecclus 25. v. 2. Beneficence is a duty of necessity and of pleasantness. The duty of necessity is seen in lending, whether a pious and needy neighbour asks for money or for household goods. Deut. 15. v. 7, 8. Tob. 1. v. 16. Luke 6. v. 35. Ecclus 29. v. 2. Likewise it is seen in prudent and necessary suretyship. Prov. 6. v. 1, 2, 3. Ecclus 29. v. 17. Likewise in promoting the advantages of a neighbour, namely by standing by a neighbour in sad times and grieving with him, and by congratulating him in happy times. Luke 1. v. 58; ch. 7. v. 12. John 11. v. 19. Likewise in urging a neighbour's menservants and maidservants to due fidelity towards their master, and not in estranging or corrupting them. Exod. 20. v. 17. Philem. v. 13, 14. Finally, one should help and advance a neighbour's beasts of burden, houses and fields, and not harm or carry them off. Exod. 22. v. 5, 6. Deut. 22. v. 1 and following; ch. 27. v. 17. The duty of pleasantness is that by which a neighbour declares his goodwill and love towards a neighbour, now and then, by a moderate banquet. Zech. 3. v. 10.

units.la: XXV. Hactenus de familiâ, prima domus parte, sequitur res familiaris, qua tanquam instrumento vtitur dominus familię[?], vt domus fit beata.
units.tr: XXV. So far concerning the household, the first part of the house; there follows the family property, which the master of the household uses as an instrument, so that the house may become blessed.

units.la: Intellige beatitudinem œconomicam.
units.tr: Understand the economic blessedness.

units.la: XXVI. In re familiari consideratur tum acquisitio, tum conseruatio, tum denique difpensatio.
units.tr: XXVI. In family property three things are considered: its acquisition, its preservation, and finally its disposal.

units.la: XXVII. Acquisitio rei familiaris est, qua illa iuste comparatur. Hic videnda est virtus acquisitionis, & modus acquirendi. Virtus acquisitionis est pia & prudens industria. Deut. 28. Psal. 127. In primis hic requiritur vigilantia patris & matris familias 1. Tim. 3. verf. 5. c. 5. v. 8. Prou. 31. v. 10. & seqq. itemque accurata operarum distributio, pro commoditate & ratione temporis. Eccles. 3. Rom. 12. verf. 11. vbi iubemur seruire tempori. Modus acquirendi rem familiarem est naturalis, vel artificialis. Naturalis est, qui ex terra & animantibus docet rem facere: vt est agricultura & pecuaria. Agricultura est antiquissimus acquirendi modus, ipsis patriarchis frequentatus. Gen. 2. v. 5. 8. c. 3. v. 17. & seqq. c. 9. v. 20. Pecuaria est agriculturæ proxima. Gen. 4. v. 2. c. 47. v. 3. Exod. 3. v. 1. Modus acquirendi artificialis est, qui consistit in actionibus ciuilibus, quas artis industria & prudentia regit. Eius species multæ sunt: videl. donatio, hæreditas, venatio, mercatura, operæ locatio &c. Donatio est modus acquirendi facillimus. Gen. 24. verf. 53. 1. Sam. 30. v. 26. Hæreditas similiter. Iof. 17. & 19. Prou. 19. v. 14. Venatio est modus acquirendi, qui facile reddit hominem ferum & agrestem. Gen. 27. v. 5. Mercatura fit navigatione, deuectione, emtione, venditione, permutatione, cambio &c. Gen. 37. 1. Reg. 5. Est autem hic acquirendi modus valde periculosus, non tantum propter iacturam, quam sæpenumero patiuntur mercatores, sed etiam propter multiplices fraudes, quibus id hominum genus est deditum. Eccles. 27. v. 1. 2. 3. Leuit. 19. v. 35. 36. Prou. 11. v. 1. Ezech. 28. v. 18. Inprimis hic Deo displicent flagellatio annonae Leuit. 25. verf. 35. Prou. 11. v. 26. Amos. 5. & 8. & vsura mordax, Leuit. 25. v. 36. 37. Nehem. 5. Psal. 15. Operalocatio est, quando pro mercede opera hominis venditur. Ea fit exercitio artium liberalium & mechanicarum. Gen. 4. v. 21. 22. Exod. 36. v. 1. Eccles. 38. v. 1. 25. & seqq.
units.tr: XXVII. The acquisition of family property is that by which it is justly obtained. Here the virtue of acquisition and the mode of acquiring are to be considered. The virtue of acquisition is pious and prudent diligence. Deut. 28. Ps. 127. Here especially the watchfulness of the father and mother of the family is required. 1 Tim. 3. v. 5; ch. 5. v. 8. Prov. 31. v. 10 and following; likewise the careful distribution of labours according to convenience and the season of time. Eccles. 3. Rom. 12. v. 11, where we are bidden to serve the time. The mode of acquiring family property is either natural or artificial. The natural is that which teaches to make property from the earth and from living creatures, as agriculture and animal husbandry. Agriculture is the most ancient mode of acquiring, practised by the patriarchs themselves. Gen. 2. v. 5, 8; ch. 3. v. 17 and following; ch. 9. v. 20. Animal husbandry is closest to agriculture. Gen. 4. v. 2; ch. 47. v. 3. Exod. 3. v. 1. The artificial mode of acquiring is that which consists in civil transactions, which the industry and prudence of skill govern. It has many kinds, namely gift, inheritance, hunting, trade, the hiring out of labour, etc. Gift is the easiest mode of acquiring. Gen. 24. v. 53; 1 Sam. 30. v. 26. Inheritance likewise. Josh. 17 and 19. Prov. 19. v. 14. Hunting is a mode of acquiring which easily makes a man wild and rustic. Gen. 27. v. 5. Trade is carried on by navigation, carriage, buying, selling, exchange, bills of exchange, etc. Gen. 37. 1 Kings 5. Yet this mode of acquiring is very dangerous, not only on account of the losses which merchants often suffer, but also on account of the manifold frauds to which that class of men is given over. Ecclus 27. v. 1, 2, 3. Lev. 19. v. 35, 36. Prov. 11. v. 1. Ezek. 28. v. 18. Above all, the cornering of the market displeases God. Lev. 25. v. 35. Prov. 11. v. 26. Amos 5 and 8, and biting usury. Lev. 25. v. 36, 37. Neh. 5. Ps. 15. Hiring out of labour is when a man's work is sold for wages. This is done by the practice of the liberal and mechanical arts. Gen. 4. v. 21, 22. Exod. 36. v. 1. Ecclus 38. v. 1, 25 and following.

units.la: XXVIII. Conseruatio rei familiaris est, qua bona legitime parta pie possidentur, & ne dilabantur, prouide custodiuntur. Hanc ad rem primo requiritur αὐτάρκεια, quae facit, vt pater & materfamiliâs facultatibus suis, quas Dei benedictione & honesto suo labore pepererunt, sint contenti. 1. Tim. 6. v. 6. & seqq. Prou. 15. & 16. Deinde oportet, vt adsit parsimonia œconomica, cuius vis est longè maxima in conseruanda & amplificanda re familiari. Iohan. 6. v. 12. Tertiò requiritur laborum continuatio. Prou. 10. v. 4. 5. Quartò luxus est vitandus. Eccles. 19. v. 1. Sextò fiducia in diuitijs non est ponenda. Prou. 11. v. 28. Psal. 62. v. 11. Septimò non oportet insolescere opibus, contra Deum vel proximum. Prou. 30. v. 7. 8. 9. Iacob. 2. v. 1. 2. & seqq. 1. Tim. 6. v. 17.
units.tr: XXVIII. The preservation of family property is that by which goods lawfully gained are piously possessed and carefully guarded lest they slip away. For this purpose, first, contentment (αὐτάρκεια) is required, which makes the father and mother of the family content with their resources, which they have gained by God's blessing and their honest labour. 1 Tim. 6. v. 6 and following. Prov. 15 and 16. Next, there must be economic thrift, whose force is by far the greatest in preserving and increasing family property. John 6. v. 12. Thirdly, continuance in labours is required. Prov. 10. v. 4, 5. Fourthly, luxury is to be avoided. Ecclus 19. v. 1. Sixthly, trust is not to be placed in riches. Prov. 11. v. 28. Ps. 62. v. 11. Seventhly, one ought not to become proud of wealth, against God or neighbour. Prov. 30. v. 7, 8, 9. James 2. v. 1, 2 and following. 1 Tim. 6. v. 17.

units.la: XXIX. Dispensatio rei familiaris est eius vsurpatio legitima ad Dei gloriam, & nostrum, ac aliorum commodu. Hanc suadet pietas erga Deum, vrget charitas erga nos & proximum, moderatur oculus œconomicus iuxta facultatum modum. Oportet autem rem familiarem siue possessionem in tres partes dispescere. Prima pars dispensetur Deo, hoc est, templis, ministris verbi, scholis, & alijs piis vsibus. Exod. 36. v. 4. Mal. 1. v. 7. & seqq. Eccles. 35. v. 5. 11. Secunda pars cedat in tuum tuorumque vsum, ita vt vnà cum tuis vtaris-fruaris bonis Dei cum gratiarum actione & frugalitate. Psal. 104. verf. 15. r. Tim. 4. v. 5. c. 5. v. 23. Tertia pars cedat proximo indigenti operà tuâ 1. Tim. 5. v. 18. Hîc verò duplici opus est cautione: Primò omnibus quidem est benefaciendum, qui indigent, maximè tamen domesticis fidei. Gal. 6. v. 10. Deinde est dandum, ne egrediamur dominio facultatum nostrarum. Proverb. 5. v. 16. 17.
units.tr: XXIX. The disposal of family property is its lawful use for the glory of God and for our own and others' advantage. Piety towards God recommends this, charity towards ourselves and our neighbour urges it, and the economic eye moderates it according to the measure of one's resources. One ought, however, to divide family property or possession into three parts. The first part is to be dispensed to God, that is, to churches, ministers of the Word, schools and other pious uses. Exod. 36. v. 4. Mal. 1. v. 7 and following. Ecclus 35. v. 5, 11. The second part is to go to your own use and that of your household, so that together with your people you may use and enjoy God's goods with thanksgiving and frugality. Ps. 104. v. 15. 1 Tim. 4. v. 5; ch. 5. v. 23. The third part is to go to a needy neighbour by your labour. 1 Tim. 5. v. 18. Here, however, a double caution is needed. First, good must indeed be done to all who are in need, but most of all to the domestics of the faith. Gal. 6. v. 10. Then, one must take care not to go beyond the mastery of one's resources. Prov. 5. v. 16, 17.

units.la: Atque hæc sunt generalia monita œconomica, quæ facili negotio accommodari possunt œconomiæ regiæ, satrapicæ, politicæ, privatæ, Sophoclêæ sive literatæ, splendidæ, mediocri, &c. quarum exempla passim insacris occurrunt: ut regiæ. 1. Reg. 4. & 7. satrapicæ Gen. 41. v. 33. & seqq. privatæ Gen. 13. vers. 5. & seqq. splendidæ Iob. 1. & ult. &c. In his vero omnibus oportet meminisse catholicissimi huius canonis: Decalogus est regula vitæ ethica, œconomica, politica, &c.
units.tr: These are the general economic admonitions, which can be readily adapted to royal, satrapal, political, private, Sophoclean or literary, splendid, middling economies, and so on, examples of which occur everywhere in the sacred writings: royal, 1 Kings 4 and 7; satrapal, Gen. 41. v. 33 and following; private, Gen. 13. v. 5 and following; splendid, Job 1 and last chapter, etc. In all these things, however, one must remember this most catholic canon: the Decalogue is the ethical, economic, political rule of life, etc.

units.la: XX. POLITICA SACRA.
units.tr: XX. Sacred Politics.

units.la: I. Politica sacra est prudentia recte constituendi & administrandi politiam sive rempublicam, e sacris literis hausta.
units.tr: I. Sacred politics is the prudence of rightly establishing and administering a polity or commonwealth, drawn from the sacred writings.

units.la: II. Partes ipsius sunt quatuor: videl. de reip. fundatione, conservatione, amplificatione, & curatione. Si malis dichotomiam, dic primam partem tractare de reip.fundatione sive constitutione, secundam de administratione, quæ cernatur in statu reip. integro & turbato. In statu integro seu bene affecto est reip. conservatio & amplificatio: in male affecto curatio.
units.tr: II. It has four parts, namely concerning the founding, preservation, enlargement, and care of the commonwealth. If you prefer a dichotomy, say that the first part deals with the founding or constitution of the commonwealth, and the second with its administration, which is seen in the commonwealth's state, whether whole or disturbed. In the whole or well-disposed state there is preservation and enlargement of the commonwealth; in the ill-disposed state, cure.

units.la: III. Fundatio reip. est, quâ incipit esse communitas rerum, personarum, & actionum ad vitam civilem pertinentium.
units.tr: III. The founding of a commonwealth is that by which a community of things, persons, and actions pertaining to civil life begins to exist.

units.la: IV. Hic considerantur quatuor 'causæ rempublicam constituentes.
units.tr: IV. Here four causes constituting the commonwealth are considered.

units.la: V. Causa efficiens reip. prima est Deus, secunda consensus mutuus hominum. Et primò quidem Deus est, qui transfert & stabilit regna Dan.2. v.21. c.4.v.14. & ab ipso solo pendet felicitas reip. Deut. 4.v.40. c.6.v.1,8.12.18.c.28.2.Sam.5.v.10.c.6.v.12.c.8.1.Reg.10.v.8.2.
