Reg.18.v.7.2. Chron.27.28.29.31.33.34.36. Psal.37.72.85.144. 147.Deinde consensus hominum mutuus effecit, ut coierint in societatem vitae civilis. Gen. 11. Vide paulò post de successionis cum electione temperatura.
units.tr: V. The first efficient cause of the commonwealth is God; the second is the mutual consent of men. First, God transfers and establishes kingdoms, Dan. 2:21; 4:14, and the happiness of the commonwealth depends on him alone: Deut. 4:40; 6:1, 8, 12, 18; 28:2; 2 Sam. 5:10; 6:12; 8; 1 Kings 10:8; 2 Kings 18:7; 2 Chron. 27, 28, 29, 31, 33, 34, 36; Ps. 37, 72, 85, 144, 147. Then the mutual consent of men brought it about that they came together into a society of civil life, Gen. 11. See a little later on the tempering of succession with election.

units.la: VI. Finis reip. est tranquillitas publica coniuncta cum exercitio publico virtutis, Nam optimè imperandi & parendi praecepta omnia ad unum eò redeunt, ut inter cives pietas & iustitia regnet, & à subditis atque rege domi exerceatur, foris autem, ut subditi ab hostibus externis iustis armis à principe defendantur. Psal.72.v.1.&102.Prou.20.v.8.& 26.
units.tr: VI. The end of the commonwealth is public tranquillity joined with the public exercise of virtue. For all the precepts of governing and obeying well come down to this: that piety and justice reign among the citizens, and are practised at home by subjects and the king, while abroad the subjects are defended by the prince with just arms against external enemies. Ps. 72:1; 102; Prov. 20:8; 26.

units.la: VII. Materia reip. sunt res & personae civiles, ex quibus resp. constat. Res civiles sunt domus, vrbes, nummi, territorium, & similia, quae pertinent ad vitam civilem commodè transigendam Gen. 4.&11.1.Reg.4.&5. Personae civiles sunt magistratus & subditi, & hi pauperes vel diuites, nobiles vel ignobiles, indigenae vel inquilini seu peregrini. Magistratus in rep. est necessarius Rom. 13. Est autem alius summus, alius inferior. Magistratus summus constituitur per electionem, vel successionem. Ita videmus Deum gubernasse populum à se electum, primò ducatu Mosis, qui principio sine iudicibus & magistratibus volentem populum, ac senatum ad consilia vocabat, eisdemque iura reddebat. Postea loceri[?] sui Iethronis consiliis & monitis elegit septuaginta duos seniores, ex fingulis tribubus sex, qui leuiora negotia curarent. Exod. 18. Deinde administrauit Deus eandem remp.opera & minis-terio iudicum, hoc est, gubernatorum. H enim dicebantur iudices, quòd penes eos esset authoritas & potestas dicendi ius, & remp. moderandi, sed nonnisi iuxta ipsius legis datae praescriptum: unde eorum potestas non erat regia[?] & arbitraria, sed iuxta Mosis leges & instituta. Dia[?]mate, aut sceptro, uti reges minime utebantur: hæreditarij non erant, sed partim consilio & authoritate prudentum hominum creabantur, partim singulari Dei vocatione designati eligebantur: bella suscipiebant, gerebant, ius dicebant, sed in omnibus legem Mosis sequebantur: tributa non imponebant. Vide passim in libro Iudicum. Postquam potestas iudiciaria commutata fuitin regiam, reges primò fuerunt electi, ut Saul & Dauid, sed postea Deus voluit, ut successionis iure ex certa quadam familia reges praesent populo. Et ideo hæc gubernationis forma censetur a multis optima, quod Deus illam in populo suo constituerit. Sed hoc tenendum est, Deum probasse non simplicem successionem, sed successionis & electionis quasi temperaturam & mixturam. Hinc lex regia Deut. 17. sic habet: Constitues super te regem, quem elegerit Iehova Deus tuus. Ubi electio regis Deo, constitutio, susceptio, vel comprobatio, populi suffragiis tribuitur. Atque ita etiam, ubi ad reges ventum fuit, observatum legimus. Cum enim populi seniores, qui universum populum repraesentabant, regem a Samuele postularent, consulenti Samueli retegit Deus, Saulem se regem elegisse. Samuel itaque Saulem ungit. Nihilominus tamen comitiis in Mispah indictis a Samuele, quasi re plane adhuc integra & infecta, forte agitur, quae in Saulem cadit, actum demum, populo universo acclamante, Saul rex nominatus dicitur. Sam. 10. v. 17. & seqq. c. 11. v. 14. 15. Saule deinde reprobato, Samuel Dauidem in regem Israel ungit 1. Sam. 16. v. 1. Verum non prius quam Saule mortuo rex exstitit, & universi populi suffragiis, rex Iudae primum, septem autem annis post, universi Israelis consensu, rex Israelis in Hebron ungitur 2. Sam. 2. verf. 4. & 5. v. 1. Salomonem Dauid, senex & aegrotus, ipse regni successorem designat, quibusdam aulae proceribus praesentibus 1. Reg. 1. verf. 30.
units.tr: VII. The matter of the commonwealth is its civil things and civil persons, of which the commonwealth consists. The civil things are houses, cities, money, territory, and similar things that pertain to living a civil life decently (Gen. 4 and 11; 1 Kings 4 and 5). The civil persons are magistrates and subjects, and these may be poor or rich, noble or common, native or resident aliens or strangers. A magistrate is necessary in a commonwealth (Rom. 13). There is, however, one supreme magistrate and another who is inferior. The supreme magistrate is established by election or by succession. Thus we see God governing the people chosen by himself. First, under the leadership of Moses, who at the beginning, without judges and magistrates, called the people and the senate to counsel when they wished, and gave them justice. Afterwards, on the advice and counsel of his father-in-law Jethro, he chose seventy-two elders, six from each tribe, to look after the lesser business (Exod. 18). Then God administered the same commonwealth through the work and ministry of judges, that is, governors. For they were called judges because the authority and power of declaring law and of governing the commonwealth lay with them, but only according to the prescription of the law that had been given; hence their power was not royal and arbitrary, but according to the laws and institutions of Moses. They did not use a diadem or sceptre, as kings did not at all; they were not hereditary, but were created partly by the counsel and authority of prudent men, and partly chosen as designated by a singular calling of God. They undertook and waged wars and gave judgments, but in all things they followed the law of Moses; they did not impose tributes. See everywhere in the book of Judges. After the judicial power was changed into a kingly one, kings were at first chosen, as Saul and David were; but afterwards God willed that kings should be set over the people by the right of succession from a certain family. And therefore this form of government is judged by many to be the best, because God established it among his people. But this must be held: God approved not simple succession but a kind of blending and mixture of succession and election. Hence the royal law in Deut. 17 reads thus: You shall set over yourself a king whom the LORD your God shall choose. Here the choice of the king is ascribed to God, while the establishing, the acceptance, or the confirmation is ascribed to the votes of the people. And we read that this was also observed when they came to kings. For when the elders of the people, who represented the whole people, asked Samuel for a king, God revealed in answer to Samuel's inquiry that he had chosen Saul as king. So Samuel anointed Saul. Nevertheless, when an assembly had been summoned at Mizpah by Samuel, the matter was, as if still wholly unsettled and undone, conducted by lot, which fell on Saul; and finally, with the whole people acclaiming, Saul is said to have been named king (1 Sam. 10:17ff.; 11:14, 15). Then, Saul having been rejected, Samuel anointed David as king of Israel (1 Sam. 16:1). But he did not become king until Saul was dead; by the votes of the whole people he was first anointed king of Judah, and seven years later, by the consent of all Israel, he was anointed king of Israel at Hebron (2 Sam. 2:4, 5; 5:1). David himself, old and sick, designated Solomon as successor to the kingdom, with some of the court nobles present (1 Kings 1:30).

units.la: 1. Chron. 28. verf. 5. Postea tamen Hierosolymis convocat universum Israelis coetum, ubi ab universo populo Salomon rex proclamatur, in regem vngitur, inque Israelis folio collocatur, principibus & optimatibus ei sese[?] iureiurando publice devincientibus. 1. Paral. 29. v. 22. 23. 24.
units.tr: (1 Chron. 28:5.) Afterwards, however, he summoned the whole assembly of Israel to Jerusalem, where Solomon was proclaimed king by the whole people, was anointed king, and was set on the throne of Israel, the princes and nobles publicly binding themselves to him by oath (1 Chron. 29:22, 23, 24).

units.la: Mortuo Salomone universus populus in Sichem venit, 5 ut regem ungerent filium ipsius Roboamum, a quo onerum publicorum alleviatione petunt, quam cum ex sententia non obtinerent, decem tribus ab ipso ad Ieroboamum deficiunt 1. Reg. 12. v. 1. 4. 16. Cæso Amasia, Oziam, sive Azariam, filium ipsius, universus Israel regem constituit. 2. Reg. 14. v. 21. 2. Chron. 26. v. 1. Simile exemplum est in Ioafo 2. Paral. 36. v. 1. & Ioa 2. Reg. 11. v. 12. Insignis hanc in sententiam est locus 2. Sam. 16. v. 17. 18. vbi Husai ait: Eius ero, quem elegit Iehoua, & populus ille, & omnes viri Israel, illius ero, & cum eo manebo. Ex quibus omnibus concludere licet, regnum Israelis hæreditarium fuisse, si stirpem vel familiam spectes, si vero personas, electitium fere. Porro magistratus solet inaugurari, ungi, proclamari, & aliis solennitatibus ornari atque commendari, de quibus passim in libris Samuelis, Regum & Chronicorum. Qualitates summi magistratus quod attinet, illæ summatim describuntur Deut. 17. de quibus vide paulo post. Quæritur etiam hic de imperio muliebri, an illud sit licitum? Resp. Per se non est illicitum, nisi si qua lex publica repugnet, ut patet in exemplo Deborae. Iud. 4.
units.tr: When Solomon died, the whole people came to Shechem to have his son Rehoboam anointed king, and of him they asked for relief from the public burdens; when they did not obtain this as they wished, ten tribes fell away from him to Jeroboam (1 Kings 12:1, 4, 16). When Amaziah was slain, all Israel made Uzziah, or Azariah, his son, king (2 Kings 14:21; 2 Chron. 26:1). A similar example is in Joash (2 Chron. 36:1; and 2 Kings 11:12). A notable passage to this effect is 2 Sam. 16:17, 18, where Hushai says: I will be his whom the LORD and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, and with him I will remain. From all these things it may be concluded that the kingdom of Israel was hereditary if you regard the stock or family, but almost elective if you regard the persons. Moreover, a magistrate is usually inaugurated, anointed, proclaimed, and adorned and commended with other solemnities, of which there is mention everywhere in the books of Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles. As to the qualities of the supreme magistrate, these are summarily described in Deut. 17, concerning which see a little later. It is also asked here whether female rule is lawful. Answer: in itself it is not unlawful, unless some public law opposes it, as is clear from the example of Deborah (Judg. 4).

units.la: Magistratus inferior est, qui pendet a summo, & proinde nullam sine ipsius consensu authoritatem habet. 1. Reg. 4.
units.tr: The inferior magistrate is one who depends on the supreme magistrate, and therefore has no authority without his consent. 1 Kings 4.

units.la: Subditi sunt vel omnino subditi, & mere passiue se habet, ut sunt singuli cives per se & absque ulla dignitate: vel sunt subditi secundum quid, ut populus universus, itemque magistratus inferiores. Nam populus universus ita paret magistratui summo, ut possit in illum animaduertere, illumque deponere, si peccet contra leges fundamentales. 1. Sam. 12. v. 4. c. 13. v. 14. 2. Reg. 14. v. 19. Populum autem repræsentant Ordines sive Ephori alicuius regni & provinciæ. Magistratus quoque inferiores possunt pro modo suę[?] iurisdictionis resistere magistratui summo, fi tyrannus euadat, qui corrigi non possit. Iud. 3. v. 19. c. 9. v. 21. Cæterum inter subditos alij sunt diuites, alij pauperes. Deut. 15. v. 4. 6. 7. & rursus alij nobiles, alij ignobiles Num. 1. v. 16. Esa. 3. v. 5. 1. Sam. 9. v. 6. Act. 17. v. 4. alij indigenæ, alij peregrini Deut. 15. alij ciues nati, alij scripti. Act. 22. v. 28.
units.tr: Subjects are either subjects absolutely, who stand in a purely passive relation, as individual citizens do in themselves and without any dignity; or they are subjects in a certain respect, as the whole people is, and likewise the inferior magistrates. For the whole people obeys the supreme magistrate in such a way that it can take action against him and depose him if he sins against the fundamental laws. 1 Sam. 12:4; 13:14; 2 Kings 14:19. The estates or ephors of some kingdom or province represent the people. Inferior magistrates too can, according to the measure of their jurisdiction, resist the supreme magistrate if he becomes a tyrant who cannot be corrected. Judg. 3:19; 9:21. Moreover, among subjects some are rich and others poor, Deut. 15:4, 6, 7; and again some are noble and others ignoble, Num. 1:16; Isa. 3:5; 1 Sam. 9:6; Acts 17:4; some are native and others foreigners, Deut. 15; some are citizens by birth and others by enrolment. Acts 22:28.

units.la: VIII. Forma reip. est vnio rerum & personarum ciuilium in virtute ciuili. Estque vel monarchia, vel polyarchia. Monarchia est, in qua maiestas vnius est. Dan. 2. & 4. Polyarchia est, cum maiestas pluribus inest. Estque aristocratia, vel democratia. Aristocratia est, in qua maiestas optimatibus inest. Iudic. 1. 2. 3. 4. &c. Democratia est, in qua maiestas populo inest, ita nempe ut pars bona ciuium imperio præsideat. Omnibus his formis opponitur Anarchia, cuius mala sunt infinita: unde merito appellatur lerna & Ilias calamitatum publicarum & priuatarum. Iudic. 17. v. 6. c. 18. v. 7. c. 19. v. 1. c. 21. v. 25. Monarchiæ opponitur Tyrannis, quæ à Nimrodo cœpit, & ab illo tempore infelici propagatione & successione ad nostra usque tempora peruenit. Gen. 10. Iudic. 9. 1. Reg. 12. Aristocratiæ opponitur Oligarchia, quando ad paucos astringitur forma, quæ pluribus optimatibus debebatur: item Timocratia, quando habetur ratio pomposæ dignitatis, diuitiarum, & similium. Democratiæ opponitur Ochlocratia, quando plebs, bellua illa multorum capitum, tumultuarie sedet ad clauum reip. Quæritur hoc loco, Quænam ex tribus reip. formis sit optima? Resp. Illa, quæ est ita mixta, ut conueniat genio populi. Huiusmodi mixtio potest esse multiplex. In Scripturis inueniuntur duo ipsius modi. Et primò quidem ratio reipublicæ, qua per iudices populus Israëliticus regebatur, fuit mixta ex Aristocratia & Democratia. Nam unus quidem præficiebatur tanquam optimus, sed promiscuè ex populo, qui toti reipublicæ præerat: at monarcha, siue rex non erat, quia non arbitratu suo, sed legis præscripto omnia facere debebat. Et quia isti iudices electione populi, vel saltem eius consensu, creabantur, eatenus erat quodammodo Democratia, qua ex populo quidam praeficiuntur, modo hi, modo illi. Rursus quia nonnisi probi viri in iudices eligebatur, ideo 5 secundum eam partem erat quaedam ratio Aristocratiae, qua boni ratione probitatis & integritatis reip. praesunt. Tum quoque illud fuit aristocraticum, quod iudices e populo electi non potuerunt sine Synedrio ius dicere. Synedrium illud constabat ex LXX. illis senioribus, siue optimatibus & magnatibus, quos Deus adiunxit Mosi, cum solus vniuersum populum ferre non posset, & ipsis de spiritu Mosis dedit Num. 11. v. 14. 24. 25. Ho. seniorum horum Synedrium perpetuum fuit in populo Dei, vsque ad Herodem Ascalonitam, teste Iosepho. Deinde tempore potestatis regiae monarchica reip. forma aristocratia quadam fuit temperata. Nam vnus ad clauum gubernationis ita sedit, vt Senatu illo magno, cuius modo est facta mentio, fuerit stipatus, & ad illius consilia & deliberationes res regni graues & arduas reuocauerit. Sic Roboam habuit seniores illos, qui etiam coram patre ipsius Salomone steterunt. Sed cum horum consilio repudiato, consilium iuuenum, qui cum ipso adoleuerant, audiret, inde regni scissura secuta est. 1. Reg. 12. v. 6. & seqq. Iosaphatus quoq; iudices in regno suo, ad omne negotium regium, constituit. 2. Paral. 19. v. 11.
units.tr: VIII. The form of a commonwealth is the union of things and civil persons under civil authority. It is either a monarchy or a polyarchy. A monarchy is one in which sovereignty belongs to a single person. Dan. 2. & 4. A polyarchy is one in which sovereignty belongs to several. It is either an aristocracy or a democracy. An aristocracy is one in which sovereignty rests with the best men. Iudic. 1. 2. 3. 4. &c. A democracy is one in which sovereignty rests with the people, namely in such a way that a good part of the citizens presides over the government. Opposed to all these forms is anarchy, whose evils are endless; hence it is rightly called the Lerna and Iliad of public and private calamities. Iudic. 17. v. 6. c. 18. v. 7. c. 19. v. 1. c. 21. v. 25. Opposed to monarchy is tyranny, which began with Nimrod and has passed down, by an unhappy line of succession, to our own times. Gen. 10. Iudic. 9. 1. Reg. 12. Opposed to aristocracy is oligarchy, when the rule that was due to many optimates is narrowed to a few; likewise timocracy, when regard is had to showy dignity, wealth and the like. Opposed to democracy is ochlocracy, when the common people, that beast of many heads, sits at the helm of the commonwealth in a tumultuous way. The question here is: which of the three forms of commonwealth is best? Answer: that which is so mixed that it suits the character of the people. A mixture of this kind can take many forms, and two such modes are found in Scripture. First, the constitution by which the people of Israel was governed through judges was a mixture of aristocracy and democracy. For one man was set over the people as the best, but he was chosen indiscriminately from the people, and he presided over the whole commonwealth. Yet he was not a monarch or king, since he had to do everything not at his own pleasure but as the law prescribed. And because these judges were created by the choice of the people, or at least with its consent, so far it was in a way a democracy, in which certain men are set over the people, now this one, now that one. Again, because only upright men were chosen as judges, in that respect there was a certain element of aristocracy, in which good men, by reason of their probity and integrity, preside over the commonwealth. It was also aristocratic that the judges chosen from the people could not give judgment without the Sanhedrin. That Sanhedrin consisted of those seventy elders, or optimates and magnates, whom God joined to Moses when Moses alone could not bear the whole people, and to whom he gave some of the Spirit of Moses. Num. 11. v. 14. 24. 25. This Sanhedrin of elders was perpetual among the people of God, down to Herod the Ascalonite, as Josephus testifies. Then, in the time of royal power, the monarchical form of commonwealth was tempered by a certain aristocracy. For the one sat at the helm of government in such a way that he was surrounded by that great senate of which mention has just been made, and he referred the weighty and difficult affairs of the kingdom to its counsels and deliberations. So Rehoboam had those elders, who had even stood before his father Solomon. But when he rejected their counsel and heard the counsel of the young men who had grown up with him, the kingdom was split. 1. Reg. 12. v. 6. & seqq. Jehoshaphat also appointed judges in his kingdom for every royal business. 2. Paral. 19. v. 11.

units.la: IX. Conseruatio reip. est, qua resp. pergit porro esse. Eius causa est prima, vel secunda. Causa prima est Deus. Prouerb. 8. v. 15. Causa secunda est tum angelus, tum homo. Angelus praeficitur reip. a Deo, vt constat ex Dan. 10. & Act. 16. v. 9. Homo conseruat rempublicam ordinando, administrando, & defendendo. Ordinatio est, qua resp. conformatur ad exemplar magnae illius & mundanae reip. ita vt vbi sint summa, media, & infima, quae certo quodam ordine prudentiae ciuilis ita deuinciuntur, vt inde pulcherrima exstat harmonia. Exod. 18. ver. 20. & seqq. Num. 1. Administratio est, qua resp. gubernatur, ita vt singuli suum faciant officium. Huius administrationis spectanda est tum norma, tum forma. Norma administrationis politica debet esse lex Deut. 17. v. 18, 19. Exod. 21. & seqq. Vide leges de religione, magia, mutuo, & similibus, infra in Iurisprudentia sacra. Forma administrationis consistit in eo, ut omnes faciant officium suum, parendo & obediendo, in genere, & in specie. Et in genere quidem istae virtutes requiruntur ad conseruandum rempublicam. I. Verus veri Dei cultus. 1. Reg. 13. v. 1. c. 14. v. 22. c. 15. v. 13. c. 18. ver. 40. 2. Reg. 10. v. 16. c. 25. v. 29. 31. 33. Psal. 112. 116. 119.
units.tr: IX. The preservation of a commonwealth is that by which it goes on continuing to exist. Its cause is either first or second. The first cause is God. Prov. 8. v. 15. The second cause is both angel and man. An angel is set over a commonwealth by God, as is clear from Dan. 10. & Acts 16. v. 9. Man preserves the commonwealth by ordering, administering and defending it. Ordering is that by which the commonwealth is conformed to the pattern of that great worldly commonwealth, so that there are highest, middle and lowest parts, bound together in a certain order of civil prudence in such a way that a most beautiful harmony results. Exod. 18. ver. 20. & seqq. Num. 1. Administration is that by which the commonwealth is governed, so that each person performs his own duty. In this administration both the norm and the form must be considered. The norm of political administration ought to be the law. Deut. 17. v. 18, 19. Exod. 21. & seqq. See the laws on religion, magic, loans and similar matters, below in Sacred Jurisprudence. The form of administration consists in this, that everyone performs his duty, by obeying and submitting, in general and in particular. In general, these virtues are required for preserving the commonwealth. I. True worship of the true God. 1. Reg. 13. v. 1. c. 14. v. 22. c. 15. v. 13. c. 18. ver. 40. 2. Reg. 10. v. 16. c. 25. v. 29. 31. 33. Psal. 112. 116. 119.

units.la: 2. Sam. 21. v. 6. 17. Prou. 20. v. 28. V. Societas cum vicinis & extraneis populis contracta. Iud. 18. v. 28. 1. Sam. 28. v. 2. c. 29. v. 2. c. 30. v. 2. Iud. 12. v. 1. c. 20. v. 7. 8. c. 21. v. 5. 11. In specie requiruntur officia magistratus & subditorum, hoc modo. I. Officium cuiuslibet magistratus describitur. Chron. 11. v. 19. 2. Chron. 13. v. 16. 24. 26. c. 29. v. 25. Prou. 26. v. 10. 12. c. 29. v. 14. Exod. 2. v. 13. c. 18. v. 21. 25. Deut. 1. v. 13. 14. c. 6. v. 7. c. 11. v. 19. c. 16. v. 19. 20. II. Officium summi magistratus. Ios. 1. v. 7. 2. Sam. 6. v. 1. c. 7. v. 1. 2. Tim. 2. 2. Sam. 23. v. 3. c. 9. v. 1. c. 15. v. 4. c. 17. v. 2. & nominatim Deut. 17. v. 18. & seqq. Vbi describitur lex regia, quam Deus proposuit populo suo, ut illam obseruarent in electione regis. Continetur autem his nouem conditionibus. Prima est, ut rex nonnisi Dei consilio & nutu creetur, ne sit in populo seditio, dum rex eligitur. Secunda, ut non externus, sed Hebraeus rex constituatur, ut hac ratione rex populum sibi subiectum diligat, & vicissim diligatur a populo, & ne ciues inducat ad alias leges, aliamue religionem. Tertia, ut cum regnum acceperit, non multiplicet sibi equos, nec amplum equitatum comparet. Ita voluit Deus, ne esset bellorum amator, sed pacis & quietis studiosus: & omnis ptorsus hac ratione Iudæis sublata fuit occasio eundi in Ægyptum, unde equi comparabantur. Quarta, ne multiplicet sibi vxores: ne hac videl. occasione nimium distrahatur a regni negotiis, & ne filios multiplicando, regno sit oneri. Quinta, ne auri argentiue copiam sibi comparet atque cumulet: ne scil. populum expilet, atque auarus fiat, lucrique cupidus. Sexta, ut curet sibi describi exemplar legis diuinæ quàm castigatissimum, hoc est, ad exéplar legis eorum, qui erant legis periti, quales erant Sacerdotes & Leuitæ; ut sic ille assuescat Deum suum timere ac reuereri, ac discat seruare omnia legis mandata, & quod rectum est, iudicare. Septima, ut exemplar illud legis sic descriptum apud se habeat, & in eo legat cunctis vitæ suæ diebus; nempe ut bene præsit, & remp. administret. Octaua, ne extollat cor suum, contemnendo vexando, & opprimendo subditos. Nona, ne vnquam ab æquo & iusto deflectat[?], ut ita suum cuique ius tribuat. Hæc sunt illa iura regalia, quæ Deus præscripsit, è quibus reliqua facillimo negotio deduci possunt. Exempla piorum regum sunt Dauid, Salomon, Iosaphat, Ezechias, Iosias. Hic incidit quæstio, quid sibi velit ius illud regis 1. Sam.8.v.11.&seqq. Resp. Sunt qui existimant, hæc omnia, quæ ibi referuntur, regibus esse concessa, perinde ac si essent iura regalia; & omnia nostra bona esse regis, ita vt ipse sit dominus omnium nostrorum bonorum mobilium, sè mouentium, & stabilium. Rursus sunt qui putant, ea omnia ibi referri tanquam per ironiam dicta: quasi Deus dicat, rex vester, quem tantopere desideratis, hæc & hæc faciet. Videte ergo quales soleant esse regis mores: his enim moribus, & hac consuetudine vtentur erga vos reges. Alij existimant, hæc locum habere, quando publica necessitas postulat: alioqui tyrannica esse, non regia, ista iura. Nobis ita videtur. Ius regis, quod hoc loco describitur, est partim verum & legitimum, partim vsurpatum & tyrannicum. Et ius verum aut est mite, aut durum, in casu scil. necessitatis. Ius vsurpatum est, quod pugnat cum recta ratione, videlicet cum iure diuino, naturae, & gentium: quale v. g. est id, quod v.14. dicitur, Agros & vineas vestras accipiet. Constat enim, Achabum graviter peccasse, quando vineam Nabotho eripuit. Sed pergamus in recensendis officijs politicis.
units.tr: 2. Sam. 21. v. 6. 17. Prou. 20. v. 28. V. Alliance contracted with neighbouring and foreign peoples. Iud. 18. v. 28. 1. Sam. 28. v. 2. c. 29. v. 2. c. 30. v. 2. Iud. 12. v. 1. c. 20. v. 7. 8. c. 21. v. 5. 11. In specie the duties of magistrates and subjects are required, in this way. I. The duty of any magistrate is described. Chron. 11. v. 19. 2. Chron. 13. v. 16. 24. 26. c. 29. v. 25. Prou. 26. v. 10. 12. c. 29. v. 14. Exod. 2. v. 13. c. 18. v. 21. 25. Deut. 1. v. 13. 14. c. 6. v. 7. c. 11. v. 19. c. 16. v. 19. 20. II. The duty of the supreme magistrate. Ios. 1. v. 7. 2. Sam. 6. v. 1. c. 7. v. 1. 2. Tim. 2. 2. Sam. 23. v. 3. c. 9. v. 1. c. 15. v. 4. c. 17. v. 2. and especially Deut. 17. v. 18. & seqq. There is described the royal law, which God set before his people, that they might observe it in choosing a king. It is contained in nine conditions. The first is that the king should be created only by the counsel and nod of God, so that there be no sedition among the people while the king is being chosen. The second is that the king should be appointed not from outside but as a Hebrew, so that by this arrangement the king may love the people subject to him, and be loved in return by the people, and so that he may not lead the citizens to other laws or another religion. The third is that, once he has received the kingdom, he should not multiply horses for himself nor acquire a large cavalry. God willed this so that he would not be a lover of wars but a seeker of peace and quiet; and by this arrangement the occasion for the Jews to go down to Egypt, whence horses were procured, was entirely removed. The fourth is that he should not multiply wives for himself, lest on this occasion he be too much distracted from the business of the kingdom, and lest by multiplying sons he become a burden to the kingdom. The fifth is that he should not acquire and pile up for himself a store of gold or silver, lest he plunder the people, become greedy and eager for gain. The sixth is that he should take care to have a copy of the divine law written out for himself as correctly as possible, that is, according to the copy kept by those who were skilled in the law, such as the priests and Levites; so that he may learn to fear and revere his God, and to keep all the commandments of the law and to judge what is right. The seventh is that he should keep that copy of the law thus written beside him, and read in it all the days of his life; namely, so that he may govern well and administer the commonwealth. The eighth is that he should not lift up his heart by despising, harassing and oppressing his subjects. The ninth is that he should never deviate from what is equitable and just, so that he gives each his own right. These are those royal rights which God prescribed, from which the rest can be derived with very great ease. Examples of pious kings are David, Solomon, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah and Josiah. Here the question arises, what that right of the king in 1. Sam. 8. v. 11. & seqq. means. Answer: some hold that all the things mentioned there were granted to kings as if they were royal rights, and that all our goods belong to the king, so that he is lord of all our movable, self-moving and fixed goods. Others think that all these things are there said in irony, as if God were saying: your king, whom you so earnestly desire, will do this and that. See therefore what the manners of the king are likely to be: for kings will use these manners and this custom towards you. Others hold that these things apply when public necessity demands it, and that otherwise these rights are tyrannical, not royal. This is my view. The right of the king described in this place is partly true and lawful, partly usurped and tyrannical. And a true right is either mild or harsh, namely in a case of necessity. A usurped right is one that fights against right reason, namely against divine, natural and international law; such as is what is said in v. 14, He will take your fields and vineyards. For it is clear that Ahab sinned grievously when he snatched the vineyard from Naboth. But let us proceed in reviewing the political duties.

De munitionibus & praesidiis vide 2. Chron. 11. v.5. 6. Neh. 7. v.3. c.13. v.19. 1. Reg. 9. v.15. 19. De amicitia cum vicinis & dissitis 2. Sam. 5. verf. 11.

There follows defence, which is made secure in respect of the state by war, fortifications, friendship with neighbours and distant peoples, and by covenants with friends or enemies. On war see below, in the Sacred Polemic. On fortifications and garrisons see 2 Chronicles 11:5, 6; Nehemiah 7:3; 13:19; 1 Kings 9:15, 19. On friendship with neighbours and distant peoples see 2 Samuel 5:11.
1 Kings 4 (last verse); Judges 18:28; 1 Samuel 28:2; 29:2; 30:2. On covenants: Genesis 14:13; 21:27, 32; 26:28; 31:44; Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 9; 24:24.

units.tr: Its first cause is the blessing of God (1 Kings 3:13). Its second cause is manifold, namely: increase of families (Exodus 1; Numbers 1); increase of wealth, flocks and herds, etc. (1 Kings 4 and 10); the surrender of enemies (Joshua 9:3); the conquest of enemies (Joshua 12; 2 Samuel 5 and 8); the metropolis (Nehemiah 7:3; 13:19); commerce with foreigners (2 Chronicles 2:10; Genesis 23:16; Acts 12:20); the sea and naval affairs (2 Chronicles 8:29; 9:21; 1 Kings 9:26); crafts and agriculture (Ecclesiastes 5:8); the care of public roads (Deuteronomy 21:4; Ezra 8:30; 2 Chronicles 15:5; Deuteronomy 23:24); public archives (1 Chronicles, throughout the book); public expenses and revenues (1 Kings 4:7, 20, 25, 26; 10; 9:25); the multitude of the people (1 Kings 4:9; Proverbs 14:28; Nehemiah 3); and lastly public buildings (1 Kings 7:1, 7; 2 Kings 12:5, 9; 22:4; 2 Chronicles 24:3; 34:8, 12).

units.la: XI. Curatio reip. est, qua sanantur morbi ciuiles, qui male afficiunt rempublicam. Hic duo sunt obseruanda: quinam videl. morbi remp. infestent, & quomodo illi morbi curentur. Ad primum quod attinet, certum & ratum esse debet, politiam mutari posse, & saepe solere. Gen.47.verf.21.2.23.Exod.5.ver.20.21.c.14.v.12. 1.Sam.18.v.4.5.c.16.v.1.2.Sam.10.v.18.1.Reg.12.v.4.16.24.25. 28.32. Esa.60.v.12. Esdr.6.v.12. Prou.28.v.28.c.29.v.8.19. Eccles.4.verf.14. Hoc diligenter inculcandum est regibus & principibus, qui interdum sibi persuadent solium & regimen suum fore aeternum, vt in Pharaone & Nebucadnezare videre est. Deinde morbi, qui politias euertunt, aut saltem mutationem illis adferunt, sunt atrocia peccata, quæ attrahunt poenas varias. Peccata hic summatim sunt contemtus Dei. 1. Sam.12. ver.17.27. Exod.8.v.9.c.14. Iof.24. v.11.c.20. Iudic.6.v.6. 1.Reg.11.v.5.c.9.c.22.v.44.c.23.v.8.9.2. Sam.2.v.33.34. mors piorum. 2.Reg.25.v.18.2.Chron.35.v.25. Esa.3.v.5.c.57.v.1. De peccatis & poenis peccatorum coniunctim vide Deut.28. vbi est catholicum prognosticum mutationis & euersionis rerum publ. Videamus nunc secundo loco, quomodo sanentur morbi civiles. Sunt autem hic remedia universalia & particularia. Remedia universalia sunt veluti quaedam panacea: cuiusmodi sunt preces & pia vita. Ion.3.v.11. Remedia particularia sunt varia.
units.tr: XI. The cure of the commonwealth is that by which the civil diseases that afflict the commonwealth are healed. Here two things are to be observed: first, which diseases infest the commonwealth; and second, how those diseases are cured. As to the first, it must be certain and established that a polity can be changed, and that it often is. Genesis 47:21, 23; Exodus 5:20, 21; 14:12; 1 Samuel 18:4, 5; 16:1; 2 Samuel 10:18; 1 Kings 12:4, 16, 24, 25, 28, 32; Isaiah 60:12; Ezra 6:12; Proverbs 28:28; 29:8, 19; Ecclesiastes 4:14. This must be carefully impressed upon kings and princes, who sometimes persuade themselves that their throne and rule will last forever, as may be seen in Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar. Next, the diseases that overthrow polities, or at least bring a change to them, are atrocious sins, which draw various punishments. The sins here, in summary, are: contempt of God (1 Samuel 12:17, 27; Exodus 8:9; 14; Joshua 24:11; 20; Judges 6:6; 1 Kings 11:5; 9; 22:44; 23:8, 9; 2 Kings 3:2; 14:4; 15:4; 23:4; 2 Chronicles 30:13; 31:34); the true religion changed (Joshua 22:11; 2:2, 18, 23, 29, 34; Acts 17:11); the crimes of citizens (Judges 20:1, 2; 2 Samuel 11:8; 22; 13:1, 2, 3, 13, 23; 1 Kings 19:16, 17; 21:7; 2 Kings 17:7, 8, 9; 2 Chronicles 36:14); public cruelty (Genesis 37:27; Judges 1:6; 19:19, 23); the avarice of magistrates (Nehemiah 5:15; Proverbs 29:4; 28:15, 16); sedition of citizens among themselves, or civil war (2 Samuel 3:10, 11, 13; 4:1); conspiracy of subjects against the prince (1 Samuel 30:6); defection of allies (2 Kings 8:20, 22, 28); the tyranny of a prince (Judges 9:56); wicked courtiers (1 Samuel 18:21; 21:8; Psalm 52; 2 Samuel 11:4; 19:3; 2 Kings 9:32; Esther 3 and 7). Moreover, God punishes the sins of king and people, and in punishing He changes or overthrows the polity. To this place belong the multitude of enemies and the excessive power of neighbours (1 Kings 15:17, 18; 2 Kings 14:8; 16:6, 7; 15:37; 19:32, 37); frequent calamities and those often received (2 Kings 19; Psalms 123, 129, 137); the barrenness of women (Genesis 20:17); the impotence of princes (1 Samuel 2:33, 34); the death of the godly (2 Kings 25:18; 2 Chronicles 35:25; Isaiah 3:5; 57:1). On the sins and punishments of sinners taken together see Deuteronomy 28, where there is the universal prognostication of the change and overthrow of public affairs. Let us now consider, in the second place, how civil diseases are healed. Now there are here universal and particular remedies. Universal remedies are, as it were, a kind of panacea: such are prayers and a godly life (Jonah 3:11). Particular remedies are various.

units.la: Nam in bellis civilibus, qui a nobis diffident, comitate ac benignitate ad nos sunt revocandi & quantocyus allicicendi 1.Sam.2.v.7. similiter duces & antesignani bellorum civilium. ibid.v.17.18. in coniurationibus consiliarij nobis sunt conciliandi. 2.Sam.15.verf.14. in tyrannide, refistendum est tyranno ab optimatibus Iudic.9.verf.30.41.51. qui hostes plurimum nobis nocuerunt, iidem summo studio nobis sunt conciliandi. 2.Sam.3.v.20.21.
units.tr: For in civil wars, those who are estranged from us are to be called back to us by courtesy and kindness, and won over as quickly as possible (1 Samuel 2:7). Likewise the leaders and standard-bearers of civil wars (ibid., 17, 18). In conspiracies, counsellors are to be won over to us (2 Samuel 15:14). In tyranny, the tyrant is to be resisted by the nobles (Judges 9:30, 41, 51). Those who have done us the most harm as enemies are to be won over to us with the greatest zeal (2 Samuel 3:20, 21).

units.la: Atque haec est Politica sacra, breviter delineata. Facile iam erit regulas & exempla iuxta methodum hic praescriptam congerere ex libris Moses, Iosuae, Iudicum, Samuelis, Regum, Chronicorum, Esdrae, Nehemiae, Psalmorum & Proverbiorum. Oportet insuper ante oculos habere rationem Politiae Iudaicae, quatenus illa fuit constituta partim a Mose, partim a Davide, & aliis regibus. Occurrunt autem hic ista tria: Consilia, Iudicia, & Magistratus. Consilia erant coetus illi, qui stabuebant res pertinentes ad universum reip. statum. Erant autem numero duo, Concio & Senatus. Concio erat populi congregatio, eaque partim popularis seu universalis, duodecim tribuum Exod.35. Num.37.Deut.9. partim familiaris seu tribulis, singularum tribuum Ios.19.Iud. 12. partim vrbana, siue particularis.1.Par.30.1.Reg.8. Senatus erat congregatio optimatum, & is quoq; triplex: videl.popularis, in quem conueniebant seniores populi vniuersi, numero LXX. Num.15. familiaris, in quem conueniebant seniores singularum tribuum 2.Reg.20. & vrbanus, in quem conueniebant senatores singularum vrbium. Iudic.11.Ruth.4. Iudicia erant coetus illi, qui definiebant singularem aequitatem, quae lege prouideri aut praescribi non potuit. Erant autem alia ciuitatum Exod.18.Deut.1.2.Paral.19. quae exercebantur in porta cuiusque ciuitatis Deut.25. Ios.8.Ruth.3. Prou.22. alia concilij Hierosolymitani, quod inde a Mose vsque ad Herodem durauit, & vsitate appellatur Sanhedrin. Vide Deut. 17.& 19. 2.Paral.19. Magistratus erant togati, vel bellici. Magistratus togati praerant tempore pacis. Erant autem vel vniuersi populi, vt primò iudices, deinde reges, & tertiò post captiuitatem Principes & pontifices: vel singularum tribuum, iique tum phylarchi, principes tribuum Num.1. & 4. tum patriarchae, principes familiarum Num.26. vel singularum ciuitatum, iique chiliarchi, hecatontarchi, pentecontarchi, decarchi. h. e. praefecti 1000.100.50. vel 10. hominibus. Exod.18.Deut.1. Magistratus bellici administrabant rem bellicam. Erant autem praefecti exercitus vel politici, vel templi. Praefecti exercitus politici erant tum princeps militiae, seu imperator, & dux belli 1.Sam.14.v.50. 2.Sam.24.v.2. tum duces inferiores, puta chiliarchi, hecatontarchi &c. 1.Paral.12.&24. 2.Paral.28. Praefecti exercitus templi praerant custodiae templi. 1.Maccab.4. v.vlt.
units.tr: And this is Sacred Politics, briefly outlined. It will now be easy to gather rules and examples, following the method prescribed here, from the books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, the Psalms and Proverbs. It is also necessary to keep before our eyes the constitution of the Jewish polity, insofar as it was established partly by Moses, partly by David and other kings. Three things occur here: counsels, judgements and magistrates. The counsels were those assemblies which deliberated on matters pertaining to the whole state of the commonwealth. There were two of them, the Assembly and the Senate. The Assembly was a gathering of the people, and this was partly popular or universal, of the twelve tribes together (Exodus 35; Numbers 37; Deuteronomy 9); partly familial or tribal, of each single tribe (Joshua 19; Judges 12); and partly urban or particular (1 Chronicles 30; 1 Kings 8). The Senate was an assembly of the nobles, and this too was threefold: namely, the popular, in which the elders of the whole people, seventy in number, met (Numbers 15); the familial, in which the elders of each single tribe met (2 Kings 20); and the urban, in which the senators of each single city met (Judges 11; Ruth 4). The judgements were those assemblies which determined particular equity, which could not be provided for or prescribed by law. Some of these were the courts of the cities, which were held at the gate of each city (Exodus 18; Deuteronomy 1 and 2; 2 Chronicles 19; Deuteronomy 25; Joshua 8; Ruth 3; Proverbs 22). Another was the council of Jerusalem, which lasted from Moses down to Herod, and is commonly called the Sanhedrin (see Deuteronomy 17 and 19; 2 Chronicles 19). The magistrates were either civil (togati) or military (bellici). The civil magistrates presided in time of peace. These were either of the whole people, such as first judges, then kings, and thirdly after the captivity princes and high priests; or of single tribes, and these were either the tribal chiefs, princes of the tribes (Numbers 1 and 4), or the patriarchs, princes of families (Numbers 26); or of single cities, and these were the chiliarchs, centurions, leaders of fifties and of tens, that is, prefects over a thousand, a hundred, fifty or ten men (Exodus 18; Deuteronomy 1). The military magistrates administered military affairs. These were prefects of the army, either of the state or of the temple. The prefects of the state's army were both the commander of the host, or general, and leader of the war (1 Samuel 14:50; 2 Samuel 24:2), and the lower commanders, such as chiliarchs, centurions and so on (1 Chronicles 12 and 24; 2 Chronicles 28). The prefects of the temple's army presided over the guard of the temple (1 Maccabees 4, last verse).

units.la: XXI. SCHOLASTICA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED SCHOLASTICS

units.la: 1. SCholastica sacra est prudentia bene constituendi & regendi scholam ex praescripto S. literarum.
units.tr: 1. Sacred scholastic is the prudence of rightly establishing and governing a school according to the prescription of Holy Scripture.

units.la: II. Eius partes sunt duæ: prima est de exemplari, altera, de modo vtendi hoc exemplari.
units.tr: II. It has two parts: the first concerns the exemplar, the second concerns the manner of using this exemplar.

units.la: III. Exemplar scholæ Christianæ (de illâ enim nobis est sermo) est schola piorum in V. & N. T. §[?] Hoc enim exemplar intueri debent magistratus Christiani, itemque præceptores & discipuli, vt rite constituant, ornent, amplificent vel restituant scholas. Principio autem hic se offerunt scholæ domesticæ & publicæ patriarcharum, inde ab Adamo vsque ad constitutam politiam Mosaicam. Talis fuit schola illa priuata Adami, in quâ instituutus fuit Abel Heb. 11. v. 4. & post hunc Seth. Fides enim cùm sit ex auditu, sanè Abel & Seth instituti fuerint necesse est in schola fidei & pietatis. Talis quoque fuit schola illa publica Adami & Sethi, in quâ nomen Iehouæ coeptum est inuocari, publicè scil. constitutâ ecclesiâ & schola. Gen. 4. ver. 26. cùm antea in familiis tantùm inuocaretur nomen Domini. Cùm enim Adam & Seth animaduerterent, Cainitas passim inualescere, moribusque suis corruptis & corrumpentibus multos inficere, coeperunt pios contrahere in corpus ecclesiæ & scholæ, vt illos prædicatione verbi, institutione catechismi, & exercitatione pietatis ab impietate palam grassante vindicarent. Scholam istam Sethi propagatam fuisse continuâ successione in ecclesiâ[?] constat, quòd Seth mortuus est anno M.1042. Lamec[?]h an. 1651. Mathusalem an. 1656. quodque Noah natus an. M.1056. vixit cum Enos, Cainan, Malaleel, Iared, Mathusalem, Lamech, Sem, Arphaxad, Salah, Heber, Peleg, Regu, Serug, Nahor, Thora & Abraham. Mortuus enim est an. M.2005. Verisimile ig. est Noam propagasse scholam Sethi post Mathusalemum, vsque ad Abrahamum: ita tamen, vt Sem quoque habuerit scholam suam eodem tempore. Is enim mortuus est anno M.2158. De schola Abrahami legimus Gen. 18. ver. 19. vbi Deus facit mentionem priuatæ & catecheticæ institutionis Abrahami. Confer Gen. 20. v. 17. c. 21. v. 33. 34.[?] 22. v. 14. 15. c. 26. v. 5. Scholam Abrahami continuauit Isaac, & posteris suis tradidit. Gen. 25. v. 2. c. 26. v. 25. c. 28. v. 1. 2. 3. 4. Jacob quoque habuit scholam suam priuatam: Gen. 31. v. 11. & seqq. c. 33. v. 20. c. 35. v. 1. & seqq. c. 46. v. 1. 2. c. 48. & 49. Post Jacobum scholae priuatae, siue domesticae institutiones, in Aegypto perdurarunt usque ad mortem Josephi. Gen. 50. v. 23. Post Josephum vero, cum populus Israëliticus mirum in modum augeretur, ita ut domestica institutio sufficere non posset, quaelibet tribus procul dubio habuit scholas suas, non sublatis tamen domesticis scholis. Porrò postquam populus ex Aegypto in desertum fuit eductus, Moses & Aharon fuerunt primi doctores scholae publicae & universalis. Deut. 4. verf. 14. c. 5. v. 1. 7: Confer Exod. 20. & seqq. Interim tamen scholae priuatae domesticae non fuerunt sublatae, sed confirmatae. Deut. 6. v. 6. c. 4. v. 10. c. 11. v. 19. Exod. 12. v. 24. & seqq. Schola Mosis & Aharonis peperit scholas Leuitarum, quae fuerunt ordinariae, & duratunt usque ad excidium Hierosolymitanum per Titum. Act. 13. v. 14. & seqq. Deut. 17. v. 8. c. 18. v. 7. 1. Chron. 13. 14. 15. 17. Praeter has Leuitarum scholas ordinarias fuerunt etiam scholae extraordinariae prophetarum, ut constat ex 1. Sam. 1. v. 25. 26. c. 3. v. 20. 21. c. 19. v. 20. 21. & seqq. 1. Reg. 18. v. 13. 14. Reg. 2. v. 5. 7. 15. 16. 17. c. 4. v. 1. 2. & seqq. c. 6. v. 1. Videamus nunc scholas N. T. ubi praeter scholas Judaeorum, & nominatim Pharisaeorum Matth. 22. v. 15. 16. Johan. 3. v. 10: primo occurrit schola Johannis Baptistae Matth. 11. verf. 2. Joh. 1. v. 28. deinde schola Christi Johan. 18. v. 19. 20. denique scholae apostolorum Act. 13. 15. 20. 2. Tim. 2. & 3.
units.tr: III. The exemplar of a Christian school (for it is of that one that we are speaking) is the school of the godly in the Old and New Testaments, §[?]. Christian magistrates, and likewise teachers and pupils, ought to look to this exemplar, so that they may rightly establish, adorn, enlarge or restore schools. First there present themselves the domestic and public schools of the patriarchs, from Adam down to the establishment of the Mosaic polity. That private school of Adam was such a school, in which Abel was taught, Heb. 11. v. 4. and after him Seth. For faith comes by hearing, so Abel and Seth must certainly have been trained in a school of faith and godliness. That public school of Adam and Seth was also such a school, in which the name of Jehovah began to be called upon, namely when the Church and school were publicly constituted, Gen. 4. ver. 26. whereas before this the name of the Lord was called upon only in families. For when Adam and Seth noticed that the Cainites were spreading everywhere, and with their corrupt morals were corrupting and infecting many, they began to gather the godly into a body, a Church and a school, so that by the preaching of the Word, instruction in the catechism and the practice of piety they might defend them against impiety openly rampant. That the school of Seth was propagated by continuous succession in the Church is clear, because Seth died in the year M.1042, Lamech in 1651, Methuselah in 1656, and because Noah, born in the year M.1056, lived with Enos, Cainan, Mahalalel, Jared, Methuselah, Lamech, Shem, Arphaxad, Salah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah and Abraham. For he died in the year M.2005. It is therefore probable that Noah propagated the school of Seth after Methuselah, down to Abraham, yet in such a way that Shem also had his own school at the same time. For he died in the year M.2158. Concerning the school of Abraham we read Gen. 18. ver. 19. where God makes mention of Abraham's private and catechetical instruction. Compare Gen. 20. v. 17, ch. 21. v. 33, 34, 22. v. 14, 15, ch. 26. v. 5. Isaac continued the school of Abraham and handed it on to his posterity. Gen. 25. v. 2, ch. 26. v. 25, ch. 28. v. 1, 2, 3, 4. Jacob also had his own private school: Gen. 31. v. 11 and following, ch. 33. v. 20, ch. 35. v. 1 and following, ch. 46. v. 1, 2, ch. 48 and 49. After Jacob, private schools, or domestic instruction, continued in Egypt until the death of Joseph. Gen. 50. v. 23. But after Joseph, when the Israelite people increased wonderfully, so that domestic instruction could not suffice, each tribe without doubt had its own schools, though the domestic schools were not abolished. Moreover, after the people had been led out of Egypt into the wilderness, Moses and Aaron were the first teachers of the public and universal school. Deut. 4. ver. 14, ch. 5. v. 1, 7. Compare Exod. 20 and following. Meanwhile, however, the private domestic schools were not abolished but confirmed. Deut. 6. v. 6, ch. 4. v. 10, ch. 11. v. 19, Exod. 12. v. 24 and following. The school of Moses and Aaron gave rise to the schools of the Levites, which were ordinary and lasted until the destruction of Jerusalem by Titus. Acts 13. v. 14 and following. Deut. 17. v. 8, ch. 18. v. 7, 1 Chron. 13, 14, 15, 17. Besides these ordinary schools of the Levites there were also extraordinary schools of the prophets, as is clear from 1 Sam. 1. v. 25, 26, ch. 3. v. 20, 21, ch. 19. v. 20, 21 and following, 1 Kings 18. v. 13, 14, 2 Kings 2. v. 5, 7, 15, 16, 17, ch. 4. v. 1, 2 and following, ch. 6. v. 1. Let us now look at the schools of the New Testament, where, besides the schools of the Jews, and especially of the Pharisees, Matt. 22. v. 15, 16, John 3. v. 10, first appears the school of John the Baptist, Matt. 11. ver. 2, John 1. v. 28, then the school of Christ, John 18. v. 19, 20, and finally the schools of the apostles, Acts 13, 15, 20, 2 Tim. 2 and 3.

units.la: IV. Modus utendi his exemplaribus continetur sequentibus regulis. 1. Patresfamilias & magistratus Christiani debent in hoc incumbere, ut instituant & foveant scholas: exemplo patriarcharum, Mosis, Samuelis, Davidis, & Salomonis. Gen. 18. v. 19. Deut. 4. v. 14.
units.tr: IV. The manner of using these exemplars is contained in the following rules. 1. Heads of households and Christian magistrates ought to labour at this, that they establish and foster schools, after the example of the patriarchs, Moses, Samuel, David and Solomon. Gen. 18. v. 19. Deut. 4. v. 14.

units.la: 1. Sam. 3. v. 20. 1. Chron. 23. & 24. 2. Chron. 8. v. 26. c. 23. v. 8. c. 29. v. 25. & seqq. 2. Scholae aliae sint priuatae & domesticae, aliae publicae. Illae his subserviant, hae illas confirment: Confer Deut.6.v.6.&c.4.v.14. 3. Peculiaria loca affignetur scholis. Ita videmus Leuitas habuisse scholas suas in peculiaribus urbibus, quarum erant quadraginta octo Num. 35. Ios. 21. & postea in singulis civitatibus synagogas. Act. 15.v.21.&c.13. 4. Prouentus sufficientes constituantur docentibus in scholis. Ita videmus Leuitas habuisse amplissimos reditus, vt liberati curis & negotiis huius vitae animalis liberius & commodius docendi muneri & studiosae iuuentuti vacare possent. 5. Distincti sint labores docentium & discentium. Sic Leuitarum quidam difcebant, quidam docebant, h. e. quidam discipuli, quia doctores erant. Discipuli erant primò theorici, hoc est, incumbebant theoriae siue studio legis vsque ad annum vigesimum: ab hoc vsque ad annum 30. erant intermedij: post annum vero trigesimum fiebant practici, h.e. admittebantur ad officia ecclesiastica Num. 4. verf.3.c.8.v.24.1. Chron. 23.v.26. Esdr.3.v.8. 6. Inter docentes sint certigradus. Sic varij erant gradus & ordines Leuitarum. Quidā ex iis populo praelegebant Scripturam, eamque interpretabantur Neh. 8.v.3.&seqq. quidam operabantur sacris.
units.tr: 1 Sam. 3. v. 20. 1 Chron. 23 and 24. 2 Chron. 8. v. 26, ch. 23. v. 8, ch. 29. v. 25 and following. 2. Some schools should be private and domestic, others public. The former should serve the latter, and the latter should confirm the former. Compare Deut. 6. v. 6, etc., ch. 4. v. 14. 3. Particular places should be assigned to the schools. Thus we see that the Levites had their schools in particular cities, of which there were forty-eight, Num. 35. Josh. 21. and afterwards synagogues in each city. Acts 15. v. 21, etc., ch. 13. 4. Sufficient revenues should be provided for those who teach in the schools. Thus we see that the Levites had very ample incomes, so that, freed from the cares and business of this animal life, they might be able to devote themselves more freely and conveniently to the office of teaching and to studious youth. 5. The labours of teachers and learners should be distinguished. So some of the Levites learned, others taught, that is, some were disciples, because they were teachers. The disciples were first theoretical, that is, they applied themselves to the theory or study of the law until the twentieth year; from this until the thirtieth year they were intermediate; but after the thirtieth year they became practical, that is, they were admitted to ecclesiastical offices. Num. 4. ver. 3, ch. 8. v. 24, 1 Chron. 23. v. 26, Ezra 3. v. 8. 6. Among teachers there should be distinct grades. So the Levites had various grades and orders. Some of them read the Scripture publicly to the people and interpreted it, Neh. 8. v. 3 and following; some ministered in sacred things.

units.la: 1. Chron. 23.v.4.5. quidam ferebant arcam, illique minis-trabant. 1.Chron. 15.& 26. quidam pro populo precabantur Num. 9.v.6. quidam erant ianitores. 1. Chron. 23. quidam musici. ibid. Quidam iudices. Deut. 17. v.9.10.11.12. 1.Chron.19.v.8.9. Vide 24. classes Leuitarum, quas constituit Dauid 1. Chron. 23.24.25.27. Huc pertinent tituli illi in N.T. Rabbi, Rabboni, Archisynagogus, Magister in Israël &c. Ioh. 3.v.10. Marc. 5.v.22. Matth. 23.v.7. Luc. 13.v.11. Iohan. 10. verf.16. Act. 13. v.15. c. 18. v.8. 7. Distincta sint in scholis subsellia docentium & discentium. Ita videmus in synagogis Iudaeorum fuisse cathedras superiores & inferiores, quas docentes & discentes, & conferentes inter sese, occupabant. Matth. 23. v. 6. Act. 22. v. 3. 8. Praeceptor induat animum parentis erga discipulum, & discipulus animum filij. Quo pertinet, quod discipuli prophetarum appellantur ipsorum filij. 1.Reg. 20. v. 35. 2.Reg. 2. v. 3. 5. 7. 15. cap. 4. v.38. c.5. v.22. c.6. v.1. 9. 1. v. 1. & quòd in Prouerbiis toties occurrit hæc formula, Fili mi: vt c.1.v.8. 10.15.c.2.v.1. quodq; apostolus Paulus Timotheum appellat filium suũ 1.Tim.1.v.2.c.2.v.1. similiter Titum. Tit.1. v. 4. & Philemonem. Philem.v.10. Confer 1. Petr. 5.v.13. Quemadmodum itaque pater gignit filium, & genito prospicit de necessarijs: ita præceptor debet gignere discipulum, instillando ipsi semen pietatis & eruditionis, & hoc semen fouendo, irrigando, educando &c. vt arborescat. Hoc sensu apostolus lus dicit, se genuisse Philemonem. Philem.v.10. & Corinthios, 1.Cor.4.v.15. Consistit autem hæc generatio in communicatione doctrinæ, & gubernatione morum. Illa est τεχνογονία[?], hæc βιοσοφία[?]. Vtrobique requiritur lenitas paterni affectus, & prudens attemperatio seu accommodatio. 9. A compendiis fiat initium in scholis. Hic enim est cibus ille facilis concoctionis, siue lac, quod optimè conuenit primæ ætati. 1.Pet.2.v.2. Heb. 5. v.12. 13. 10. Præceptores non solùm doceant continuè legendo & explicando, sed etiam interrogando, itemque colloquendo, ita vt discipulis dent facultatem placidè interrogandi de iis, quæ non satis intelligunt, itemque respondendi ad interrogata. Exempla vide Matth. 5. vbi Christus solus loquitur Iohan. 9. vbi à discipulis interrogatur. Matth. 16. vbi discipulos ipse interrogat. Confer Luc. 2. v. 46. 1.Cor.14. 11. Scholæ ficinstituantur, vt omnes discant non scholæ, sed vitæ, id est, vt ex scholis sumi queant, qui publicè sint vtiles in vitâ ecclesiasticâ, politicâ, œconomicâ & scholasticâ. Quid multis? Schola Christi, in quâ fuerunt 12. apostoli, & 70. discipuli, & alij quidam homines frugi, Ioh. 4.v.1.2. Matth.10.v.2. Luc.10.v.1. hæc, inquam, schola semper nobis obuersetur ante oculos tanquam exemplar omni exceptione maius. Nam inde cognoscemus, quanta fidelitas requiratur in præceptore, quàm laboriosa sit hæc functio, quòd non vno impetu doctrina instilletur, quòd sint gradus constituendi inter discipulos, quid deceat discipulos, & denique quid potissimum sit docendum & discendum. Confer hæc cum Didacticâ & Mnemonicâ.
units.tr: 1 Chron. 23. v. 4, 5. Some carried the ark and ministered to it. 1 Chron. 15 and 26. Some prayed for the people, Num. 9. v. 6. some were doorkeepers, 1 Chron. 23. some were musicians, ibid. some were judges, Deut. 17. v. 9, 10, 11, 12, 1 Chron. 19. v. 8, 9. See the twenty-four classes of Levites which David established, 1 Chron. 23, 24, 25, 27. To this belong those titles in the New Testament: Rabbi, Rabboni, archisynagogue, teacher in Israel, etc. John 3. v. 10, Mark 5. v. 22, Matt. 23. v. 7, Luke 13. v. 11, John 10. ver. 16, Acts 13. v. 15, ch. 18. v. 8. 7. In schools the seats of teachers and learners should be distinct. Thus we see that in the synagogues of the Jews there were higher and lower chairs, which the teachers and the learners, conferring among themselves, occupied. Matt. 23. v. 6, Acts 22. v. 3. 8. The teacher should put on the feelings of a parent towards the pupil, and the pupil the feelings of a son. To this pertains the fact that the disciples of the prophets are called their sons. 1 Kings 20. v. 35, 2 Kings 2. v. 3, 5, 7, 15, ch. 4. v. 38, ch. 5. v. 22, ch. 6. v. 1, 9, 1 Sam. 1. v. 1. and that in Proverbs this formula, My son, occurs so often, as in ch. 1. v. 8, 10, 15, ch. 2. v. 1. and that the apostle Paul calls Timothy his son, 1 Tim. 1. v. 2, ch. 2. v. 1, likewise Titus, Titus 1. v. 4, and Philemon, Philem. v. 10. Compare 1 Pet. 5. v. 13. Just as a father begets a son and provides for the begotten what is necessary, so a teacher ought to beget a pupil, instilling into him the seed of piety and learning, and nourishing, watering and bringing up this seed, so that it may grow into a tree, etc. In this sense the apostle says that he begot Philemon, Philem. v. 10, and the Corinthians, 1 Cor. 4. v. 15. This begetting consists, however, in the communication of doctrine and the governance of morals. The former is the begetting of skills [τεχνογονία], the latter the wisdom of life [βιοσοφία]. In both cases gentleness of paternal affection and prudent adjustment or accommodation are required. 9. Instruction in schools should begin from summaries. For this is that food which is easy to digest, or milk, which suits the first age best. 1 Pet. 2. v. 2, Heb. 5. v. 12, 13. 10. Teachers should not only teach by continual reading and explanation, but also by questioning and conversing, so that they give the pupils the opportunity of calmly asking about things they do not sufficiently understand, and of answering what is asked. For examples see Matt. 5, where Christ speaks alone, John 9, where he is questioned by the disciples, Matt. 16, where he himself questions the disciples. Compare Luke 2. v. 46, 1 Cor. 14. 11. Schools should be established so that all learn not for school but for life, that is, so that from the schools there may be taken those who are publicly useful in ecclesiastical, political, domestic and scholastic life. What more need be said? The school of Christ, in which there were twelve apostles, seventy disciples, and certain other sober men, John 4. v. 1, 2, Matt. 10. v. 2, Luke 10. v. 1, this school, I say, should always stand before our eyes as an exemplar greater than any exception. For from it we shall learn how great faithfulness is required in the teacher, how laborious this function is, that doctrine is not poured in with one onslaught, that grades must be established among the pupils, what befits pupils, and finally what above all is to be taught and learned. Compare these things with Didactica and Mnemonica.

units.la: XXII. LEXICA SACRA.
units.tr: XXII. SACRED LEXICONS.

units.la: Lexica sacra est ars de modo adornandi Lexicon Scripturæ sacræ, Simalis, appella Lexicographiam.
units.tr: Sacred lexicography is the art of arranging a lexicon of Holy Scripture; some call it lexicography.

units.la: II. Lexicon Scripturæ sacræ est veteris vel noui testamenti.
units.tr: II. A lexicon of Holy Scripture is either of the Old Testament or of the New Testament.

units.la: III. Lexicon veteris testamenti est Hebraicum. Eius methodus hæc erit. Radices sive voces primæ distinguantur à vocibus ortis, quemadmodum in Concordantiis Hebraicis R. Mordechai Nathan, Thesauro Pagnini, & Lexico Hebraico Buxtorfij factum est. Deinde singulis vocibus, tum primis tum ortis, subiiciatur ea quæ sunt singularia & insignia per totum V.T. canonem. e.g. רָשָׁע[?] est impius, qui est instabilis, nec manet in eadem dispositione, nec conquiescit nisi pravis rebus gestis, quibus alios inquietat. חוֹטֵא[?] est peccator, qui non animo solum & clam, sed etiam nudo, quod aiunt, capite, coram cœlo & Iehova peccatis se commaculat. לֵץ[?] est irrisor, qui sibi strenuè gratulatur de peccato, ita ut Deum & homines insuper habeat. [illegible, ~4 letters] significat eum, in quo est [illegible, ~5 letters] quique adeo est beneficus erga alios. Quòd si voces singulæ, vna cum phrasibus, quæ in V.T. Hebraicæ editionis occurrunt, ita explicetur, non est dubium quin Lexicon Hebraicum sit futurum penu locupletissimum, ex quo disputatores & concionatores possint depromere vberrimam piæ & patheticæ differtationis materiam.
units.tr: III. The lexicon of the Old Testament is Hebrew. Its method will be as follows. Roots, or primary words, are to be distinguished from derived words, as has been done in the Hebrew Concordances of R. Mordechai Nathan, in Pagninus's Thesaurus, and in Buxtorf's Hebrew Lexicon. Then, under each word, both primary and derived, should be placed what is peculiar and notable throughout the whole canon of the Old Testament. For example, רָשָׁע [rasha] is "wicked," one who is unstable, who does not remain in the same disposition, and who finds rest only in wicked deeds by which he disturbs others. חוֹטֵא [chotei] is "sinner," one who defiles himself with sins not only in his mind and in secret, but also, as they say, bare-headed, before heaven and Jehovah. לֵץ [lets] is "scoffer," one who heartily rejoices in sin, so that he holds both God and men in contempt. [illegible] signifies one in whom there is [illegible], and who is therefore beneficent towards others. If the single words, together with the phrases that occur in the Hebrew edition of the Old Testament, were explained in this way, there is no doubt that the Hebrew lexicon would become a most abundant storehouse, from which disputants and preachers could draw a very rich supply of material for a devout and moving discourse.

units.la: IV. Lexicon noui testamenti est Græcum.
units.tr: IV. The lexicon of the New Testament is Greek.

units.la: Eius methodus debet esse eadem cum Lexico V.T. Distinguantur itaque themata, sive voces primitivæ, à derivatis & compositis, & singulis subijciantur ea, quæ sunt singularia & insignia per totum N. T. canonem, e.g. εὐδοκέω est valde c'electior[?], summam voluptatem percipio, ut cum Deus Pater dicit de Christo filio suo dilecto Matt. non satis plenè vertitur In quo acquiesco: quia sæpe acquiescimus in aliquo inuiti. Sic itaq; vertendum fuerit, In quo valde delector, Qui est mea summa voluptas. Ἀναλύω est idem quod resoluo, migro, reuertor. Sic cum apostolus Phil.1.v.23. ait τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἔχων εἰς τὸ ἀνα-λῦσαι[?], hic est illorum verborum sensus, Desiderium habens ad migrandum, vel reuertendum; non autem iste vulgaris, Cupio dissolui. Nam ἀναλύειν[?] hic est, domum redire, in cœlestem videl. patriam. De his & similibus tum vocibus, tum phrasibus vide in nostro Lexico theologico, quod propediem ζωῇ Θεοῦ[?] in lucem proferemus. Interea temporis euolue Lexicon Noui Testamenti authore Georgio Pasore.
units.tr: Its method ought to be the same as that of the lexicon of the Old Testament. Themes, or primitive words, are therefore to be distinguished from derivatives and compounds, and under each are to be placed what is peculiar and notable throughout the whole canon of the New Testament. For example, εὐδοκέω [eudokeo] is to be highly pleased, to take the greatest delight: when God the Father says of his beloved Son Christ, Matt. 3, the rendering "In whom I acquiesce" does not express it fully, since we often acquiesce in something reluctantly. So it should be rendered: "In whom I greatly delight, who is my greatest pleasure." ἀναλύω [analyo] means the same as to depart, to migrate, to return. So when the Apostle says in Phil. 1.23, τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἔχων εἰς τὸ ἀναλῦσαι [ten epithymian echon eis to analysai], the sense of those words is: "having a desire to depart or return"; not the common rendering, "I desire to be dissolved." For ἀναλύειν [analyein] here means to return home, namely to the heavenly fatherland. Concerning these and similar words and phrases, see our theological lexicon, which we shall soon bring to light under the title ζωῇ Θεοῦ [zoe Theou]. Meanwhile, consult the Lexicon of the New Testament by George Pasor.

units.la: XXIII. GRAMMATICA SACRA.
units.tr: XXIII. Sacred Grammar.

units.la: I. GRammatica sacra est ars purè loquendi verbis Scripturæ.
units.tr: I. Sacred grammar is the art of speaking purely with the words of Scripture.

units.la: II. Estque duplex, una Hebraica pro V. T. altera Græca pro nouo. Quemadmodum plenum Lexicon tum Hebraicum, tum Græcum, adornari potest ex canone V. & N. T. ita quoque Grammatica omnibus numeris absoluta, tum Hebraica, tum Græca, ex eodem canone, plenis præceptis & infinitis exemplis instrui potest. Vide Thesaurum Hebraicæ Grammaticæ Buxtorfij. Grammaticam Græcam N. T. nondum licuit videre. Ut vero huic compendio inseratur, non patitur studium breuitatis. Itaque sufficiat indicasse modum operis.
units.tr: II. It is twofold: one Hebrew, for the Old Testament, the other Greek, for the New. Just as a full lexicon, both Hebrew and Greek, can be compiled from the canon of the Old and New Testaments, so too a grammar complete in every respect, both Hebrew and Greek, can be drawn from the same canon and furnished with full rules and countless examples. See the Thesaurus of Hebrew Grammar by Buxtorf. A Greek grammar of the New Testament I have not yet been able to see. But the pursuit of brevity does not allow it to be inserted into this compendium. It will therefore suffice to have indicated the method of the work.

units.la: XXIV. RHETORICA SACRA.
units.tr: XXIV. Sacred Rhetoric.

units.la: I. RHetorica sacra est ars ornatè loquendi, verbis Scripturæ.
units.tr: I. Sacred rhetoric is the art of speaking ornately, using the words of Scripture.

units.la: II. Eius partes duæ sunt: prima est de elocutione, secunda de actione.
units.tr: II. It has two parts: the first concerns elocution, the second delivery.

units.la: III. Elocutio est exornatio orationis. Estque tropus, vel figura. Quæ duo sæpe concurrunt.e.g.in exclamatione metonymicâ,metaphoricâ.
units.tr: III. Elocution is the adornment of speech. It is either a trope or a figure, and these two often coincide, for example in a metonymic or metaphorical exclamation.

units.la: IV. Tropus est mutatio nativæ significationis.
units.tr: IV. A trope is a change of a word's native meaning.

units.la: V. In eo spectantur affectiones & species.
units.tr: V. Two things are considered in it: its affections and its species.

units.la: VI. Affectiones troporum sunt quinque:emphasis, catachresis, hyperbole, allegoria & concursus. Emphasis est, quâ tropus est insignis: ut emphatica est illa metaphora, quâ Christus discipulos suos appellat sal terræ. Matth. 5. v. 13. Catachresis est, cùm tropus est durior ut Heb. 11. v. 5. Per fidem Enoch fuit translatus,ne videret mortem, i.e. ne sentiret seu experiretur. Hyperbole est, cùm tropus est audacior in augendo, vel minuendo: ut Exod.13.Dabo vobis terram fluentem lacte & melle. Iob.25. vers. 6. Quanto minus mortalis, vermis? & filius hominis, lumbricus? Allegoria est continuatio tropi: ut Matth. 3. v. 10. Arbor mala, quæ fructus bonos non fert, exciditur, & in ignem conijcitur. & v. 12. Cuius ventilabrum in manu ipsius, & permundabit aream suam, & coget triticum in horreum suum, paleam autem exuret igni inextinguibili. Huc pertinent parabolæ Christi, quæ nihil sunt aliud quàm metaphoræ allegoricæ: item apologi, ut Iudic. 9. & ænigmata, ut Iudic. 14. De comedente exiit sonus, & de forti egressa est dulcedo: & proverbia, ut Matth.23. Excolatis culicem, camelum autem deglutitis. 1. Cor.5. Modicum fermenti totam massam inficit. 2. Petr. 2. Canis reuersus est ad vomitum, & sus lota ad volutabrum cœni. Concursus troporum est, quando duo vel plures tropi in vna voce concurrunt: vt, Gen.14. v.21. Da mihi animam: hic est synecdoche membri geminæ: quia primum positus est singularis pro plurali, deinde anima pro homine. Psal.16. v.10. Non derelinques animam meam in sepulchro: hic est synecdoche membri & integri: quia anima ponitur pro Dauide, & Dauid pro corpore ipsius. Gen. 21. v.1. Iehova visitauit Saram: hic Deus dicitur visitare per metaphoram, quæ appellatur ἀνθρωποπάθεια[?]: & visitare ponitur pro benefacere, cum sua natura sit vocabulum μεῖζον[?] siue generale, quod specialiter nunc bonam, nunc malam in partem accipitur.
units.tr: VI. The affections of tropes are five: emphasis, catachresis, hyperbole, allegory and concurrence. Emphasis is that by which a trope is striking, as the metaphor is emphatic by which Christ calls his disciples the salt of the earth. Matt. 5:13. Catachresis is when the trope is harsher, as in Heb. 11:5. By faith Enoch was translated so that he should not see death, that is, so that he should not feel or experience it. Hyperbole is when the trope is bolder in magnifying or diminishing, as in Exod. 13: I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey. Job 25:6. How much less is mortal man, a worm? and the son of man, a maggot? Allegory is a continuation of a trope, as in Matt. 3:10. A tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire. And v. 12: whose winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly clean his threshing floor, and gather the wheat into his barn, but burn the chaff with unquenchable fire. To this belong the parables of Christ, which are nothing other than allegorical metaphors; likewise fables, as in Judg. 9, and riddles, as in Judg. 14: Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness; and proverbs, as in Matt. 23: You strain out the gnat and swallow the camel. 1 Cor. 5: A little leaven leavens the whole lump. 2 Pet. 2: The dog has returned to his vomit, and the washed sow to her wallowing in the mire. Concurrence of tropes is when two or more tropes meet in one word, as in Gen. 14:21: Give me the soul. Here is a synecdoche of the double member: first the singular is put for the plural, then soul for man. Ps. 16:10: You will not leave my soul in the grave. Here is a synecdoche of part and whole, since soul is put for David, and David for his body. Gen. 21:1: Jehovah visited Sarah. Here God is said to visit by a metaphor which is called anthropopatheia [ἀνθρωποπάθεια]; and to visit is put for to do good, although by its nature it is a more general word [μεῖζον] that is taken now in a good sense and now in a bad one.

units.la: VII. Species troporum sunt quatuor: metonymia, ironia, metaphora, & synecdoche.
units.tr: VII. There are four species of tropes: metonymy, irony, metaphor and synecdoche.

units.la: VIII. Metonymia est causæ & effecti; subiecti & adiuncti; antecedentis, connexorum, & consequentis. Metonymia causæ est efficientis, finis, materiæ, & formæ. Metonymia efficientis est, cum efficiens ponitur pro effecto: vt Christus pro beneficiis ipsius Gal. 3. v.29. Spiritus sanctus pro donis ipsius. Ioel. 2. v. 28. Israel pro Israelitis Exod. 5. ver. 2. membra corporis Deo tributa, pro actionibus, quæ proficiscuntur ab iis membris, vt oculus pro prouidentia. Psal. 33. v.18. sic affectus[?], pro effectibus affectuum, vt ira Dei pro vindicta. Psal. 6. v.1. Metonymia finis est, cum finis ponitur pro finito seu destinato: vt, 1. Cor. 11. v.10. Propter hoc debet mulier potestatem habere in capite propter angelos, id est, velamen in signum potestatis, hoc est, quòd potestati viri sit subiecta. Metonymia materiæ est, cum ex materia significatur materiatū: vt, terra, cinis & puluis pro ipso homine. Gen. 3. & 18. aurum & argentum pro nummis aureis & argenteis Matt. 10. v.19. semen pro filijs & posteris. Gen. 3. Psal. 18. Metonymia formæ est, cum ex forma intelligitur formatum: vt Gen. 6. v.11. Terra impleta erat violentia, id est, hominibus violentis. Metonymia effecti est, cum ex effecto causa intelligitur: vt, 2. Reg. 4. v. 40. Mors est in olla, id est, res mortifira. Luc. 11. verf. 14. Eiecit Christus daemonium, quod erat mutum, id est, quod hominem, quem possidebat, reddebat mutum; 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. Christus est nobis factus a Deo sapientia, & iustitia, & sanctificatio, & redemtio, hoc est, illarum rerum author seu effector. Pertinet huc metonymia destinati, cum finitum ponitur pro fine: vt, Gen. 20. ver. 16. ait rex Abimelech ad Saram de Abrahamo: Ipse tibi est operimentum oculorum, id est, maritus. Nam propter maritum velatur vxor in signum subiectionis. Metonymia subiecti est, cum ex subiecto significatur adiunctum: vt, Gen. 3. verf. 1. Serpens locutus est cum Eua; id est, diabolus in serpente. Genes. 6. verf. 11. Terra corrupta erat; id est, homines in terra. Iohan. 3. verf. 16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, id est, homines electos in mundo. Matth. 5. verf. 29. Si oculus tuus dexter te scandalizat, erue eum, & abijce abs te; id est, resiste libidini, quae se in oculo exerit, eamque extingue. Huc pertinet metonymia signati: vt, Gen. 40. verf. 12. Tres illi palmites, tres dies sunt, id est, significant tres dies. Similiter verf. 18. Tria canistra illa, tres dies sunt. Sic Gen. 41. verf. 26. Septem illae vaccae bonae, septem anni sunt &c. Metonymia adiuncti est, cum ex adiuncto significatur subiectum: vt, Rom. 11. Electio assecuta est, id est, electi. Hos. 9. verf. 16. Etiamsi genuerint, tamen occidam ventris ipsorum desideria, h. e. delideratissimos eorum liberos. Huc pertinet metonymia signi: vt, Gen. 49. Non recedet sceptrum a Iuda, id est, potestas. Matth. 10. verf. 34. ait Christus, Non veni mittere pacem, sed gladium, id est, discordiam, cuius signum est gladius. Metonymia antecedentis est, cum ex antecedente intelligitur consequens: vt Gen. 4. Adam cognovit vxorem. Quod etiam est exemplum tropi verecundi. Metonymia consequentis est, cum ex consequente intelligitur antecedens: vt, Deut. 34. verf. 5. Mortuus itaque est Moses, iubente Iehova, id est volente. Metonymia connexorum est, quando connexa inter se permutantur; vt, Iud. 3. verf. 24. Pedes tegere, id est, aluum leuare. Quod ipsum etiam est exemplum tropi verecundi.
units.tr: VIII. Metonymy is of cause and effect, of subject and adjunct, of antecedent, of connected things and of consequent. Metonymy of cause is of the efficient, the end, the matter and the form. Metonymy of the efficient is when the efficient is put for the effect, as Christ for his benefits, Gal. 3:29; the Holy Spirit for his gifts, Joel 2:28; Israel for the Israelites, Exod. 5:2; and the members of the body attributed to God for the actions that proceed from those members, as the eye for providence, Ps. 33:18; so also affections [affectus] for the effects of the affections, as the anger of God for vengeance, Ps. 6:1. Metonymy of the end is when the end is put for the thing ended or intended, as in 1 Cor. 11:10: Because of this the woman ought to have authority on her head because of the angels, that is, a veil as a sign of authority, that is, because she is subject to the authority of her husband. Metonymy of the matter is when the thing made is signified by its matter, as earth, ashes and dust for man himself, Gen. 3 and 18; gold and silver for golden and silver coins, Matt. 10:9; seed for children and descendants, Gen. 3; Ps. 18. Metonymy of the form is when the thing formed is understood from its form, as in Gen. 6:11: The earth was filled with violence, that is, with violent men. Metonymy of the effect is when the cause is understood from the effect, as in 2 Kings 4:40: Death is in the pot, that is, a deadly thing. Luke 11:14: Christ cast out a demon which was mute, that is, which made the man it possessed mute. 1 Cor. 1:30: Christ was made to us by God wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption, that is, the author or effector of those things. To this belongs the metonymy of the intended, when the thing ended is put for the end: as in Gen. 20:16, where King Abimelech says to Sarah about Abraham: He is to you a covering of the eyes, that is, a husband, for on account of the husband the wife is veiled as a sign of subjection. Metonymy of the subject is when the adjunct is signified by the subject, as in Gen. 3:1: The serpent spoke with Eve, that is, the devil in the serpent. Gen. 6:11: The earth was corrupt, that is, the men on the earth. John 3:16: So God loved the world, that is, the elect men in the world. Matt. 5:29: If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you, that is, resist the lust which shows itself in the eye, and quench it. To this belongs the metonymy of the thing signified, as in Gen. 40:12: Those three branches are three days, that is, they signify three days. Similarly v. 18: Those three baskets are three days. So Gen. 41:26: Those seven good cows are seven years, etc. Metonymy of the adjunct is when the subject is signified by the adjunct, as in Rom. 11: The election has obtained, that is, the elect. Hos. 9:16: Even if they bear children, I will slay the dear desires of their womb, that is, their most beloved children. To this belongs the metonymy of the sign, as in Gen. 49: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, that is, power. Matt. 10:34: Christ says, I did not come to bring peace, but a sword, that is, discord, of which the sword is the sign. Metonymy of the antecedent is when the consequent is understood from the antecedent, as in Gen. 4: Adam knew his wife. This is also an example of a modest trope. Metonymy of the consequent is when the antecedent is understood from the consequent, as in Deut. 34:5: So Moses died at the command of Jehovah, that is, at his will. Metonymy of connected things is when things connected with one another are exchanged, as in Judg. 3:24: to cover the feet, that is, to relieve the bowels. This too is an example of a modest trope.

units.la: IX. Ironia est, cùm ex contrario significatur contrarium,
units.tr: IX. Irony is when the opposite is signified by means of the contrary.

units.la: Eius genera sunt varia, hoc modo. 1. Antiphrasis; cum vox affirmatiua ponitur pro negatiuâ: vt, Iob. 1. verf. 5. Peccauerunt filij mei, & benedixerunt Deum, id est, non benedixerunt. 2. Mimesis; cùm dictum alterius illusoriâ quâdam imitatione exprimimus: vt, Psal. 22. v. 9. Deuoluit se ad Iehouam, liberet eum, eripiat eum, quandoquidem delectatur eo. 3. Sarcasmus; qui est hostilis irrisio, per contrarium alicui in praesentissimo periculo conuitium faciens: vt, Matth. 28. v. 29. Aue rex Iudaeorum. 4. Ironia nuda, cùm simpliciter, sine antiphrasi, mimesi, sarcasmo, vel simili modo, significatur contrarium ex contrario: vt, Gen. 3. v. 22. ait Deus de Adamo & Eua, Ecce homo euasit sicut vnus ex nobis. Matth. 26. v. 45. Christus ad discipulos ait: Dormite quod superest, & requiescite. 1. Cor. 4. v. 8. Paulus ad ambitiosos quosdam sic ait: Iam saturati estis, iam ditati estis, absque nobis regnum adepti estis. Marc. 7. v. 9. Christus Scribis & Pharisaeis ait: Sane bene abrogatis mandatum Dei, vt traditionem vestram seruetis.
