units.tr: Its kinds are various, as follows. (1) Antiphrasis, when an affirmative word is put for a negative: as in Job 1:5, My sons have sinned and blessed God, that is, have not blessed him. (2) Mimesis, when we express another's words by a kind of mocking imitation: as in Ps. 22:9, He committed himself to Jehovah; let him deliver him, let him rescue him, since he delights in him. (3) Sarcasmus, which is hostile mockery, insulting someone by means of the contrary while he is in the greatest danger: as in Matt. 28:29, Hail, King of the Jews. (4) Bare irony, when the contrary is signified by the contrary simply, without antiphrasis, mimesis, sarcasm or some similar figure: as in Gen. 3:22, where God says of Adam and Eve, Behold, the man has become like one of us. Matt. 26:45, Christ says to the disciples, Sleep on now, and take your rest. 1 Cor. 4:8, Paul says to certain ambitious people, Now you are full, now you are rich, you have reigned without us. Mark 7:9, Christ says to the scribes and Pharisees, Full well you set aside the commandment of God, that you may keep your tradition.

units.la: X. Metaphora est, cùm ex simili significatur simile.
units.tr: X. Metaphor is when a likeness is signified by a likeness.

units.la: Gen. 2. v. 1. Itaque perfecti sunt caeli & terra, & omnis exercitus eorum. Gen. 4. ver. 10. Ecce vocem sanguinum fratris tui, clamantium ad me de terra. Gen. 15. verf. 1. dicit Deus Abrahamo, Ego sum tibi clypeus. Gen. 22. verf. 1. Deus tentauit Abrahamum. Huc itaque pertinet ἀνθρωποπάθεια [?], qua Deo tribuuntur membra, affectus, sensus, passiones, & similia. Quanquam haec exempla etiam possunt subiici metonymiae causae efficientis. Porro & haec sunt metaphorica. Matth. 16. v. 6. Cauete à fermento Pharisaeorum & Sadducaeorum. Iohan. 11. v. 11. Lazarus amicus noster dormit, id est, mortuus est. 1. Cor. 3. v. 16. An nescitis vos esse templum Dei, & Spiritum Dei habitare in vobis. Iohan. 1. v. 1. In principio erat λόγος.
units.tr: Gen. 2:1, Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all their host. Gen. 4:10, Behold, the voice of your brother's blood, crying to me from the ground. Gen. 15:1, God says to Abraham, I am your shield. Gen. 22:1, God tested Abraham. To this belongs anthropopatheia [ἀνθρωποπάθεια], by which members, affections, senses, passions and the like are attributed to God. Although these examples could also be placed under metonymy of the efficient cause. Further, these are also metaphorical. Matt. 16:6, Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. John 11:11, Our friend Lazarus sleeps, that is, has died. 1 Cor. 3:16, Do you not know that you are God's temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? John 1:1, In the beginning was the Word [λόγος].

units.la: XI. Sy-
units.tr: XI. Sy-

units.la: XI. Synecdoche est totius vel partis. Ibi est Synecdoche integri & generis, hic membri & speciei.
units.tr: XI. Synecdoche is of the whole or of the part. There the synecdoche is of the whole and the kind, here of the member and the species.

units.la: Synecdoche integri est, cum ex integro intelligitur membrum: vt, Gen.16. v. 2. Sara ait, Occlusit me Iehoua, id est, vterum meu.
units.tr: Synecdoche of the whole is when the member is understood from the whole: as in Gen. 16:2, Sarai says, Jehovah has shut me up, that is, my womb.

units.la: Per hunc tropum pluralis ponitur pro singulari: vt, Gen. 21.v.7. Certò lactabit filios Sara, id est, filium. Huius loci est κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων, quæ sic dicitur theologis: vt Iohan.3. v.13. Nemo ascendit in cælum, nisi qui descendit è cælo, Filius hominis, qui est in cælo. Sic 1.Cor.2.v.8. Dominum gloriæ crucifixerunt. Et, Act.20. v.29. Deus ecclesiam acquisiuit proprio sanguine. Theologi dicunt hæc prædicari de Christo κατ᾽ ἄλλο.
units.tr: By this trope the plural is put for the singular: as in Gen. 21:7, Sarah will surely nurse sons, that is, a son. To this place belongs the communicatio idiomatum [κοινωνία ἰδιωμάτων], as it is called by the theologians: as in John 3:13, No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven. So too 1 Cor. 2:8, They crucified the Lord of glory. And Acts 20:28, God acquired the Church with his own blood. The theologians say that these things are predicated of Christ according to the other [κατ᾽ ἄλλο].

units.la: Synecdoche generis est, cum ex genere significatur species: vt Gen.31.v.21. Iacob traiecit flumen, id est, Euphratem.
units.tr: Synecdoche of the genus is when the species is signified by the genus: as in Gen. 31:21, Jacob crossed the river, that is, the Euphrates.

units.la: Huc pertinent ea dicta, in quibus vocabulo Dei (quod generale & tribus personis commune est) intelligitur vna aliqua persona Trinitatis: interdum Pater, idque frequentissimè, propter principatum originis: vt, Iohan.3. ver.16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum. Gal.4. v. 4. Cùm venit plenitudo temporis, emisit Deus Filium suum. ibid. v.6. Quoniam estis filij, emisit Deus Spiritum Filij sui in corda vestra: interdum Filius; vt Act.20 v.28. Deus acquisiuit suo sanguine ecclesiam: interdum Spiritus S. vt Act.5. verf.4. Non es mentitus hominibus, sed Deo. Synecdoche membri est, cùm ex membro significatur integrum: vt, Gen.6.v.12. Corruperat omnis caro viam suam. Ezech.18. v.20. Anima, quæ peccat, ipsa morietur. Per hunc tropum numerus singularis pro plurali ponitur Gen.12.v.3. Erat Cananæus in eâ regione. Synecdoche speciei est, cùm ex specie intelligitur genus: vt Gen.3. v.19. In sudore vultus tui vescéris pane tuo. Gen.4.v.20. Iabal fuit pater degentium in tentoriis. Gen.14.v. 14. Cùm audisset Abraham, captiuum esse fratrem suum, id est, agnatum suum Loth. Per hunc tropum numerus certus pro incerto ponitur: vt, Gen.33.verf.3. Iacob versus fratrem suum Esau incurvabat se in terram septies, id est, multoties. Gen.31.v.7. ait Iacob, Labanem mutasse mercedem suam decies.
units.tr: To this belong those sayings in which by the word God (which is general and common to the three persons) one particular person of the Trinity is understood: sometimes the Father, and this very frequently, on account of the principle of origin: as in John 3:16, So God loved the world. Gal. 4:4, When the fullness of time came, God sent forth his Son. Ibid. v. 6, Because you are sons, God sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts. Sometimes the Son: as in Acts 20:28, God acquired the Church with his own blood. Sometimes the Holy Spirit: as in Acts 5:4, You have not lied to men but to God. Synecdoche of the member is when the whole is signified by a member: as in Gen. 6:12, All flesh had corrupted its way. Ezek. 18:20, The soul that sins, it shall die. By this trope the singular number is put for the plural: Gen. 12:3, The Canaanite was in that land. Synecdoche of the species is when the genus is understood from the species: as in Gen. 3:19, In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread. Gen. 4:20, Jabal was the father of those who dwell in tents. Gen. 14:14, When Abraham heard that his brother was taken captive, that is, his kinsman Lot. By this trope a definite number is put for an indefinite: as in Gen. 33:3, Jacob bowed himself to the ground seven times before his brother Esau, that is, many times. Gen. 31:7, Jacob says that Laban changed his wages ten times.

units.la: XII. Figura est habitus sermonis elegantior, Estque dictionis vel sententiae.
units.tr: XII. A figure is a more elegant form of speech, and it is of word or of sentence.

units.la: XIII. Figura dictionis est artificiosa verborum collocatio. Estque primaria, vel secundaria.
units.tr: XIII. A figure of word is an artful arrangement of words. It is either primary or secondary.

units.la: XIV. Figurarum dictionis primariarum genera sunt decem, hoc ordine. I. Ἐπιζεύξις est, cum idem sonus continuè iteratur, in eadem sententia: vt, Esa. 6.v.3. Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus Iehova Zebaoth. Psal. 22. vers. 1. Deus meus, Deus meus, quare deseruisti me? II. Anadiplosis est, qua idem sonus repetitur in fine praecedentis, & initio sequentis sententiae: vt, Psal. 121. v.1. Leuo oculos meos ad montes, unde veniat auxilium meum: auxilium meum à Iehova, qui fecit caelum & terram. Psal. 98. v.4.5. Iubilate Iehovae tota terra, vociferamini, & psallite: psallite Iehovae in cithara: in cithara & voce cantus. III. Climax est, qua idem sonus repetitur ad connectendum varia gradatim: vt, Rom. 8.v.28. vbi nectitur aurea salutis catena: Quospradecreuit, hos & praedestinauit: quos praedestinauit, hos & vocauit: quos vocauit, illos & iustificauit: quos iustificauit, illos etiam glorificauit. Hic sunt quinque gradus, nimirum πρόγνωσις, προ-θεσις[?], κλῆσις, δικαίωσις, δόξασμός. Rom. 5. v. 3. 4. 5. Vt qui sciamus, quòd afflictio tolerantiam efficiat: tolerantia vero experientiam, experientia autem spem: Porrò spes non pudefacit. 2. Petr. 1. v. 5. 6. 7. Vos autem curam omnem adhibentes, praestate in fide virtutem, in virtute scientiam, in scientiâ abstinentiam, in abstinentia pietatem, in pietate amorem fraternitatis, in amore fraternitatis charitatem. Vide etiam Hosea 2.v.21.22.Iacob.1.v.13. 14.Ioel.1.v.3.4. IV. Anaphora est, cùm idem sonus iteratur in principiis sententiarum: vt, Psal. 118. ver. 8. Melius est confidere in Domino, quàm confidere in homine. Melius est confidere in Domino, quàm in principibus. Ibid. v. 15. 16. Dextra Iehova fecit fortiter. Dextra Iehova excelsa. Dextra Iehova facit fortia. Psal. 148. v. 1. & seqq. Laudate Deum de coelis: Laudate eum in excelsis: Laudate eū omnes angeli eius, &c. Psal.19. per totum fere psalmum repetuntur hæc duo vocabula, Vox Domini. Psal. 150. vers. 1. & seqq. Laudate Deum fortem desanctitate eius : laudate eum de expanso &c. Psal. 118. v. 6. Iehoua mecum, non timebo; quid faciat mihi homo? Iehoua mecum, & ego despiciam inimicos meos. Rom. 8. vers. 33. & seqq. Quis intentabit crimina aduersus electos Dei ? Deus est is, qui iustificat. Quis est qui condemnet? &c. Deut. 28. continuantur hæc duo vocabula: Benedictus, Maledictus. Vide etiam 1. Cor. 13. vers. 4. cap. 12. vers. 10. V. Epistrophe est, cùm idem sonus in clausulis sententiarum iteratur : vt, Psalm. 115. vers. 9. 10. 11. Israel fide Iehouæ : auxilium & clypeus eorum est. Domus Aharon fidite Iehouæ : auxilium & clypeus eorum est. Qui timetis Iehouam, fidite Iehouæ : auxilium & clypeus eorum est. Psalm. 136. in singulis versibus repetitur hæc clausula : Quoniam in seculum misericordia eius: atque adeo sexies vicies ibi occurrit epistrophe. Philem. vers. 11. Quondam tibi inutili, nunc verò tibi & mihi perutili. VI. Symploce est, cùm idem sonus iteratur in principiis, & idem in clausulis : vt, Psalm. 47. vers. 7. Psallite DEO, psallite : psallite regi nostro, psallite. Psalm. 118. vers. 2. 3. 4. Dicat nunc Israel, quòd in seculum misericordia eius. Dicat nunc familia Aharon, quòd in seculum misericordia eius. Dicant nunc qui timent Iehouam, quòd in seculum misericordia eius. Rom. 14. vers. 8. Siue viuimus, Domino viuimus : siue morimur, Domino morimur. Siue igitur viuamus, siue moriamur, Domini sumus. Est etiam hic κατὰ τὸν κύκλον & ἀντιστροφῆς [?]. VII. Epanalepsis est, cùm idem sonus in principio & clausula repetitur: vnde appellari solet circulus oratorius, quia nempe ab vno sono incipit, & facit reuersionem ad eundem. Sic Psalm. 8. versu vltimo Psaltes repetit primum psalmi pronuntiatum κατὰ τὸν κύκλον [?]: Iehoua Domine noster, quàm magnificum est nomen tuum in vniuersa terra. Similiter Psalm. 103. vers. vlt. repetuntur prima verba psalmi: Benedic anima mea Iehoua. Phil. 4. vers. 4. est epaναλεψις in vno & eodem versu: Gaudete in Domino semper. per: rursum, inquam, gaudete. VIII. Epanodus est, cum ordine retrogrado repetuntur soni proxime antegredi\ vt, Esai. 5. verf. 20. Vae dicentibus malum bonum, & bonum malum: qui ponunt tenebras lucem, & lucem tenebras: qui ponunt amarum dulce, & dulce amarum. Marc. 2. Sabbatum propter hominem factum est, non homo propter sabbatum. vide etiam Rom. 3. verf. 21. cap. 2. verf. 1. IX. Paronomasia est commutatio quantitatis, literae, vel syllabae: vt Psalm. 96. verf. 5. dij gentium, [Hebrew, illegible, ~6 letters], dicuntur, [Hebrew, illegible, ~6 letters] quasi dicat, non dij. Habac. 2. verf. 18. Ad faciendum [Hebrew, illegible, ~6 letters] id est, idola, [Hebrew, illegible, ~6 letters] id est, muta. Esaiae 45. verf. 6. Faciet Iehova conuiuium [Hebrew, illegible, ~4 letters] pinguium, conuiuium [Hebrew, illegible, ~6 letters] facium. Roman. 1. verf. 29. est paronomasia in vocibus φθόν@, φόν@: item πνευμα, πνευμάτ: & verf. 31. in vocibus ἀσωτῆς, ἀσυνέτ-ᾱ τυς. X. Polyptoton est, cum repetitur eadem vox in alio casu & tempore: vt, Genes. 2. verf. 7. Moriendo morieris. Genes. 50. verf. 2. Visitando visitabit vos. Hab. 2. verf. 3. Veniendo veniet. Eccles. 1. verf. 1. Vanitas vanitatum. Iob. 21. verf. 2. Audite audiendo. Matth. 18. verf. 22. Dicit ei Iesus, Non dico tibi vsque septies. 1. Thess. 1. verf. 5. ἐν ὑμῖν δ' ὑμᾶς.
units.tr: XIV. There are ten kinds of primary figures of word, in this order. I. Epizeuxis [Ἐπιζεύξις] is when the same sound is repeated continuously in the same sentence: as in Isa. 6:3, Holy, holy, holy is Jehovah of hosts. Ps. 22:1, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? II. Anadiplosis is when the same sound is repeated at the end of the preceding sentence and at the beginning of the following one: as in Ps. 121:1, I lift up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help comes: my help is from Jehovah, who made heaven and earth. Ps. 98:4-5, Shout to Jehovah, all the earth; break forth, and sing praises: sing praises to Jehovah with the harp; with the harp and the voice of song. III. Climax is when the same sound is repeated to connect various things step by step: as in Rom. 8:28, where the golden chain of salvation is linked: Whom he foreknew, these he also predestined; whom he predestined, these he also called; whom he called, these he also justified; whom he justified, these he also glorified. Here there are five steps, namely prognosis [πρόγνωσις], prothesis [πρόθεσις], klesis [κλῆσις], dikaiosis [δικαίωσις], doxasmos [δοξασμός]. Rom. 5:3-5, Knowing that affliction produces endurance, and endurance experience, and experience hope; and hope does not put us to shame. 2 Pet. 1:5-7, But make every effort to supply in your faith virtue, in virtue knowledge, in knowledge self-control, in self-control steadfastness, in steadfastness godliness, in godliness brotherly affection, in brotherly affection love. See also Hos. 2:21-22; James 1:13-14; Joel 1:3-4. IV. Anaphora is when the same sound is repeated at the beginnings of sentences: as in Ps. 118:8, It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man. It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in princes. Ibid. vv. 15-16, The right hand of Jehovah does valiantly. The right hand of Jehovah is exalted. The right hand of Jehovah does mighty things. Ps. 148:1 ff., Praise God from the heavens; praise him in the heights; praise him, all his angels, etc. In Psalm 29 these two words, the voice of the Lord, are repeated through almost the whole psalm. Ps. 150:1 ff., Praise God in his sanctuary; praise him in the firmament of his power, etc. Ps. 118:6, Jehovah is with me; I will not fear: what can man do to me? Jehovah is with me; I will look down on my enemies. Rom. 8:33 ff., Who shall bring a charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns? etc. Deut. 28 continues these two words: Blessed, Cursed. See also 1 Cor. 13:4; 1 Cor. 12:10. V. Epistrophe is when the same sound is repeated at the ends of sentences: as in Ps. 115:9-11, O Israel, trust in Jehovah: he is their help and shield. O house of Aaron, trust in Jehovah: he is their help and shield. You who fear Jehovah, trust in Jehovah: he is their help and shield. In Psalm 136 this closing phrase is repeated in every verse, for his mercy endures forever, and so the epistrophe occurs twenty-six times there. Philem. 11, Once useless to you, but now useful to you and to me. VI. Symploce is when the same sound is repeated at the beginnings and likewise at the ends: as in Ps. 47:7, Sing praises to God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises. Ps. 118:2-4, Let Israel now say that his mercy endures forever. Let the house of Aaron now say that his mercy endures forever. Let those who fear Jehovah now say that his mercy endures forever. Rom. 14:8, Whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord. So whether we live or die, we are the Lord's. Here there is also kata ton kyklon [κατὰ τὸν κύκλον] and antistrophe [ἀντιστροφή]. VII. Epanalepsis is when the same sound is repeated at the beginning and at the end; whence it is usually called the oratorical circle, because it begins from one sound and returns to the same. Thus in Ps. 8, in the last verse, the psalmist repeats the first statement of the psalm, according to the circle [κατὰ τὸν κύκλον]: Jehovah our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth. Similarly in Ps. 103, in the last verse, the first words of the psalm are repeated: Bless Jehovah, O my soul. Phil. 4:4 has epanalepsis within one and the same verse: Rejoice in the Lord always. Again, I say, rejoice. VIII. Epanodos is when sounds that have just gone before are repeated in reverse order: as in Isa. 5:20, Woe to those who call evil good, and good evil; who put darkness for light, and light for darkness; who put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter. Mark 2:27, The sabbath was made for man, not man for the sabbath. See also Rom. 3:21; Rom. 2:1. IX. Paronomasia is a change of quantity, letter or syllable: as in Ps. 96:5, the gods of the nations [Hebrew, illegible] are called [Hebrew, illegible], as if to say, not gods. Hab. 2:18, to make [Hebrew, illegible], that is, idols, [Hebrew, illegible], that is, dumb things. Isa. 45:6, Jehovah will make a feast [Hebrew, illegible] of rich things, a feast [Hebrew, illegible] of dregs. Rom. 1:29 has paronomasia in the words phthonou, phonou [φθόνου, φόνου]; likewise pneuma, pneumatos [πνεῦμα, πνεύματ]; and v. 31, in the words asōtēs, asynetous [ἀσωτῆς, ἀσυνέτους]. X. Polyptoton is when the same word is repeated in another case or tense: as in Gen. 2:17, Dying you shall die. Gen. 50:24, Visiting he will visit you. Hab. 2:3, Coming he will come. Eccles. 1:2, Vanity of vanities. Job 21:2, Hear diligently, hear. Matt. 20:22, Jesus says to him, I do not say to you until seventy times seven. 1 Thess. 1:5, en humin di' humas [ἐν ὑμῖν δ᾽ ὑμᾶς].

units.la: 2. Tim. 3. verf. 13. πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι, Dum & seducunt, & seducuntur.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 3:13. Seducing and being seduced [πλανῶντες καὶ πλανώμενοι]: both deceiving and deceived.

units.la: XV. Figurarum dictionis secundariarum genera sunt XXVI. hoc ordine: Antanaclasis, Ploce, Synonymia, Exergasia, Tautotes, Paregmenon, Antithesis, Antitheta, Antimetathesis, Antistrophe, Synoeceiosis, Oxymoron, Isocolon, Parison, Hendiadys, Tmesis, Synthesis, Homoeocatalecton, Parechesis, Erotesis, Parembole, Parenthesis, Synanteses, Hyperbaton, Hypallage, Hysterologia. Nos illas attingemus, quae in Bibliis saepius occurrunt. I. Antanaclasis est, cum vox eadem repetitur, sed diversa significaficatione. Eius exempla vide Matth.1.v.22.c.5.v.19.c.8.v.11. c.10.v.39.c.12.v.38.49.c.15.v.3.c.16.v.4.18.c.26.v.52. Luc.9. verf.26. 60.c.12.v.8. Ioh.1.v.10.c.2.v.42.c.3. v. 6.13.17.31.c.12. v.44. c.13.v.8.c.19.v.22.c.21.v.18. Rom.2.v.21.28.c.3.v.19.21, 27.c.4.v.18.c.8.v.24.c.9.6.c.11.v.6.7.1.Cor.1.v.21.c.7.v.20.22. c.8.verf.3. 2.Cor.10.v 3. Gal.4.v.9.21. Eph.1.v.3.23.Phil.3.v.12. 1.Thess.5. verf.10. 2.Tim.1.v.18.c.2.9.13. Hebr.6.v.19.c.11.v.35. Iac.3.v.18.c.5.v.12.1.Petr.3.v.9.19.1.Petr.4.v.1.1.Ioh.3.verf.19. Duo ex his exemplis adducam. Ioh.2. vox πιστεύειν diuersi-mode sumitur: πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ, θεωροῦντες τὰ σημεῖα αὐτοῦ, ἃ ἐποίει. Αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς οὐκ ἐπίστευεν ἑαυτὸν αὐτοῖς. i.e. Multi crediderunt in eum visis signis, quaedebat. Ipse autem Iesus non credebat semet iis. Rom.12.apostolus ait, τὴν φιλοξενίαν διώκοντες, Hospitalitatem sectantes: tum subiicit, εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς διώκοντας ὑμᾶς, Benedicite iis, qui vos insectantur. Hic verbum διώκειν significat rem persequi studio obtinendi eam: mox, aliquem persequi animo laedendi. II. Exergasia est, cum orationes idem significantes coniunguntur: vt Ion. 2.v.2.3. Inclamaui ex angustia mea, & exaudiuit me: e ventre sepulchri vociferatus sum, exaudisti vocem meam. Nam proieceras me in profundum, in intimam partem marium. Psal. 117. Laudate Iehovam omnes gentes, celebrate eum omnes populi. Haec figura non est confundenda cum ἐπιμονή: vtpote quae est accurata & continuata eiusdem rei tractatio, qualis est Rom. 9. 10. & 11. Eph. 2.verf.1.Phil.2.v.2. Coloss.1.v.17. III. Antistrophe est, cum positum quippiam retorquemus. Dicitur etiam βίαιον & ἀντιμεταβολή. Exemplum elegans est in responsione Cananitidis, Matth.15. v.26.27. vbi Christus ad illam ait: Non est honestum, sumere panem filiorum, & obijcere catellis. Illa inuertit: Imo, etiam canes comedunt de micis cadentibus a mensis dominorum. Artificium rhetoricum tale est in hoc exemplo: Quia canis es, ait Christus, non conuenit tibi porrigi panem. Imo, inquit Syrophoenissa, Quia canis sum, non denegabis mihi micas de mensa cadentes. IV. Ὀξύμωρον, siue ὀξυμωρολογία, q.d. acutifatuum, aliis ἐναντίωσις [?], est species apparen-tiæ tis contradictionis: vt, Matth. 10. v.39. Qui inuenerit animā suā, perdet eam: & qui perdiderit animam suam meā causā, inueniet eam. 1. Tim. 5. v. 6. Vidua, quæ lasciuit, ea viuens mortua est. Hebr. 11. vers.27. Vt qui videret inuisibilem illum. Iacob. 1.v.9.10.
units.tr: XV. There are twenty-six kinds of secondary figures of diction, in this order: Antanaclasis, Ploce, Synonymia, Exergasia, Tautotes, Paregmenon, Antithesis, Antitheta, Antimetathesis, Antistrophe, Synoeceiosis, Oxymoron, Isocolon, Parison, Hendiadys, Tmesis, Synthesis, Homoeocatalecton, Parechesis, Erotesis, Parembole, Parenthesis, Synanteses, Hyperbaton, Hypallage, Hysterologia. I shall touch on those which occur more often in the Bible. I. Antanaclasis is when the same word is repeated but with a different meaning. For examples see Matt. 1:22; 5:19; 8:11; 10:39; 12:38, 49; 15:3; 16:4, 18; 26:52; Luke 9:26, 60; 12:8; John 1:10; 2:42; 3:6, 13, 17, 31; 12:44; 13:8; 19:22; 21:18; Rom. 2:21, 28; 3:19, 21, 27; 4:18; 8:24; 9:6; 11:6, 7; 1 Cor. 1:21; 7:20, 22; 8:3; 2 Cor. 10:3; Gal. 4:9, 21; Eph. 1:3, 23; Phil. 3:12; 1 Thess. 5:10; 2 Tim. 1:18; 2:9, 13; Heb. 6:19; 11:35; Jas. 3:18; 5:12; 1 Pet. 3:9, 19; 4:1; 1 John 3:19. I will adduce two of these examples. In John 2 the word πιστεύειν is used in different senses: "Many believed in his name, when they saw the signs which he did. But Jesus himself did not trust himself to them" [πολλοὶ ἐπίστευσαν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ, θεωροῦντες τὰ σημεῖα αὐτοῦ, ἃ ἐποίει. Αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ Ἰησοῦς οὐκ ἐπίστευεν ἑαυτὸν αὐτοῖς]. That is: many believed in him when they saw the signs he did; but Jesus himself did not trust himself to them. In Rom. 12 the apostle says, "Pursuing hospitality" [τὴν φιλοξενίαν διώκοντες], and then adds, "Bless those who persecute you" [εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς διώκοντας ὑμᾶς]. Here the verb διώκειν means first to pursue a thing with zeal to obtain it, and then to pursue a person with intent to harm. II. Exergasia is when clauses having the same meaning are joined together, as in Jonah 2:2-3: "I cried out of my distress, and he heard me; out of the belly of the grave I cried, and you heard my voice. For you had cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas." Psalm 117: "Praise the LORD, all nations; extol him, all peoples." This figure is not to be confused with ἐπιμονή, which is the careful and continued treatment of one matter, as in Rom. 9, 10 and 11; Eph. 2:1; Phil. 2:2; Col. 1:17. III. Antistrophe is when we turn back a point that has been put to us. It is also called βίαιον and ἀντιμεταβολή. There is a fine example in the reply of the Canaanite woman, Matt. 15:26-27, where Christ says to her, "It is not right to take the bread of the children and throw it to the little dogs." She turns it back: "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters' tables." The rhetorical device in this example is this: Because you are a dog, says Christ, it is not fitting to give you bread. Yes, says the Syrophoenician woman, because I am a dog, you will not deny me the crumbs falling from the table. IV. Oxymoron, or ὀξυμωρολογία, that is, "sharp foolishness," which some call ἐναντίωσις [?], is a kind of apparent contradiction, as in Matt. 10:39: "He who finds his life will lose it, and he who loses his life for my sake will find it." 1 Tim. 5:6: "She who gives herself to pleasure is dead while she lives." Heb. 11:27: "As seeing him who is invisible." Jas. 1:9-10: "Let the lowly brother glory in his exaltation, but the rich in his humiliation."

units.la: Qui est humilis, glorietur in sublimitate suâ. Contrà qui dies est, in demissione sui. V. Parison est, cùm orationis partes habent totidem dictiones, ac dictiones ipsæ totidem syllabas: vt, Rom.14.v.8. Siue viuimus, Domino viuimus: siue morimur, Domino morimur. VI. Hendiadys, seu ἓν διὰ δυοῖν, est, cùm res vna diuiditur in duas: vt, Matth.4.v.16. Populus positus in tenebris, vidit lucem magnam: & positis in regione & vmbra mortis, lux exorta est; pro, in regione vmbrosa mortis. Sic Matth.20.v.20. Tunc venit ad eum mater filiorum Zebedæi cum filiis suis, adorans & petens aliquid ab eo; i. e. adorando petens. VII. Interrogatio, siue ἐρώτησις[?], est, cùm sermonem ad aliquid inquirendum artificiosè inflectimus: vt, Rom. 8. vers.37. Quis nos separabit à dilectione Christi? num tribulatio? num angustia? &c. Hæc interrogatio maiorem ornatum & motum adfert orationi, quàm si apostolus dixisset, Nulla res nos separabit à dilectione Dei, neq; tribulatio, neque angustia &c. VIII. Hyperbaton est, cùm verba cohærentia transponuntur. Exemplum insigne est Eph. 1. v. 1. vbi verba ista, Et vos, cohærent cum illis verbis v.5. Vnà vivificauit cum Christo. Versus intersecti[?] dicuntur Parembole, quæ in medio orationis circumstantiam aliquam interponit. Similes figuræ, videl. tum hyperbaton, tum parembole, occurrunt Eph. 3. v. 1. vbi enuntiatum primo versu inchoatum, mox versu seq. interrumpitur, & absoluitur demum ver.14. IX. Hypallage est, cùm dictiones interse alternantur ordine inuerso: vt, Matth.8.v.5. Statim igitur purgata fuit eius lepra, id est, purgatus fuit ille à lepra. X. Hysterologia est, cùm id quod primo loco poni debebat, in oratione secundo loco ponitur. Dicitur alio nomine ὕστερον πρότερον, postero-prius. Exemplum est Matth. 11. v. 4. 5. vbi Christus dicit: Renuntiate Iohanni quæ auditis & videtis. Hæc duo deinceps καθ᾽ ὑστέρωσ[?]ιν, ordine inuerso, commemorantur: Cæci vident, surdi audiunt &c.
units.tr: V. Parison is when the parts of a sentence have equal numbers of words, and the words in turn have equal numbers of syllables, as in Rom. 14:8: "Whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord." VI. Hendiadys, or ἕν διὰ δυοῖν, "one through two," is when one thing is divided into two, as in Matt. 4:16: "The people sitting in darkness saw a great light, and for those sitting in the region and shadow of death, light has risen," meaning "in the shadowy region of death." So also Matt. 20:20: "Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came to him with her sons, worshipping and asking something of him," that is, worshipping and asking. VII. Interrogatio, or ἐρώτησις [?], is when we skilfully turn our speech to an inquiry, as in Rom. 8:35: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation? Or distress?" etc. This question brings more ornament and emotion to the speech than if the apostle had said, "No thing shall separate us from the love of God, neither tribulation nor distress," etc. VIII. Hyperbaton is when cohering words are transposed. A notable example is Eph. 1:1, where the words "and you" belong with the words of v. 5, "made alive together with Christ." Verses interrupted in this way are called Parembole, which inserts some circumstance into the middle of a sentence. Similar figures, namely both hyperbaton and parembole, occur in Eph. 3:1, where a sentence begun in the first verse is interrupted in the next verse and is only completed at v. 14. IX. Hypallage is when words alternate with one another in inverted order, as in Matt. 8:5: "Immediately, therefore, his leprosy was cleansed," that is, he was cleansed of his leprosy. X. Hysterologia is when what ought to have been placed first is placed second in the speech. It is also called ὕστερον πρότερον, "last first." An example is Matt. 11:4-5, where Christ says: "Report to John what you hear and see." These two things are mentioned in reverse order, as in "The blind see, the deaf hear," etc.

units.la: XVI. Figura sententiæ est totius orationis ornatus. Estque primaria, vel secundaria.
units.tr: XVI. The figure of sentence is the ornament of the whole speech. It is either primary or secondary.

units.la: XVII. Figurarum sententiæ primariarum genera sunt decem, hoc ordine. 1. Exclamatio est, quâ oratio exornatur per particulam exclamandi, idque explicitè, vel implicitè. Explicitè: vt, Rom. 7. verf. 24. Miser ego homo! quis me liberabit ex isto corpore mortis? Implicitè: vt, Rom. 11. verf. 33. O profundas diuitias tum sapientiæ tum cognitionis Dei! quàm inscrutabilia sunt eius iudicia, & viæ eius imperuestigabiles! Hæc figura est magnum prorsus animi commouendi instrumetum & quidem variorum affectuum: videl. admirationis Psal. 133. v. 1. Matt. 15. v. 28. desperationis, vel acerbissimi doloris. Esa. 1. v. 4. Matt. 27. v. 46. optationis Esa. 64. v. 1. 1. Chron. 11. v. 17. Num. 14. v. 2. indignationis Malach. 1. v. 6. Matt. 17. v. 17. Luc. 24. v. 25. obtestationis 2. Tim. 4. v. 1. 2. commiserationis Ezech. 9. v. 8. 2. Sam. 14. v. 5. 2. Reg. 3. v. 10. Esa. 1. v. 4. execrationis & imprecationis Psal. 69. v. 33-34. & 109. v. 8. Exclamationi subiiciuntur Epiphonema & Licentia. Epiphonema est acclamatio, quæ tractato aliquo argumento subijcitur: vt, 2. Tim. 2. v. 7. Considera quæ dico. Det vero tibi Deus intelligentiam in omnibus. Iob. 18. verf. 21. Profecto ista sunt tabernacula, iniqui; & iste locus viri non agnoscentis Deum fortem. Vide etiam Psal. 46. v. 8. 12. & 109. v. 20. & 111. verf. 9. & 118. v. 4. Licentia, Græcis παρρησία, est, quâ quis confidenter dicit, ita vt rem odiosam libere absque vlla circuitione & occultatione eloquatur. Illustre exemplum est Esa. 1. & Matth. 23. II. Apostrophe est persona commutatio, quâ orator ad aliam se couertit personam: videl. ad Deum. Psal. 33. v. 22. & 82. v. 8. Ioel. 1. v. 19. ad reges Psal. 2. v. 10. ad hostes. Psal. 6. v. 9. ad mortuos 2. Sam. 1. v. 26. ad bestias Ioel. 2. v. 22. ad res sensu destitutas Deut. 32. v. 1. Psal. 114. v. 5. Esa. 1. v. 1. Ioel. 2. v. 21. 1. Cor. 15. v. 55. Luc. 23. v. 3. Matth. 11. v. 21.
units.tr: XVII. There are ten kinds of primary figures of sentence, in this order. 1. Exclamatio is when a speech is adorned by an exclamatory particle, either explicitly or implicitly. Explicitly, as in Rom. 7:24: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?" Implicitly, as in Rom. 11:33: "O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgements, and his ways past finding out!" This figure is a powerful instrument for moving the mind, and indeed of various emotions: of wonder, as in Ps. 133:1; Matt. 15:28; of despair or most bitter grief, as in Isa. 1:4; Matt. 27:46; of desire, as in Isa. 64:1; 1 Chron. 11:17; Num. 14:2; of indignation, as in Mal. 1:6; Matt. 17:17; Luke 24:25; of entreaty, as in 2 Tim. 4:1-2; of compassion, as in Ezek. 9:8; 2 Sam. 14:5; 2 Kings 3:10; Isa. 1:4; of cursing and imprecation, as in Ps. 69:33-34 and 109:8. To exclamation are subjoined the Epiphonema and the Licentia. Epiphonema is an acclamation added to some matter already treated, as in 2 Tim. 2:7: "Consider what I say; and may the Lord give you understanding in all things." Job 18:21: "Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous, and this is the place of the man who does not know God." See also Ps. 46:8, 12; 109:20; 111:9; 118:4. Licentia, in Greek παρρησία [parrhesia], is when someone speaks with confidence, so that he states an offensive matter freely, without any circumlocution or concealment. A famous example is Isa. 1 and Matt. 23. II. Apostrophe is a change of person, by which the speaker turns to another person: namely to God, Ps. 33:22; 82:8; Joel 1:19; to kings, Ps. 2:10; to enemies, Ps. 6:9; to the dead, 2 Sam. 1:26; to beasts, Joel 2:22; to things deprived of sense, Deut. 32:1; Ps. 114:5; Isa. 1:1; Joel 2:21; 1 Cor. 15:55; Luke 23:3; Matt. 11:21.

units.la: III. Prosopopœia est persona commutatio, quâ is qui dicit, eit, mutatur. Eftq; imperfecta, vel perfecta, Prosopopoeia imperfecta est, qua sermo alienæ personæ leuiter & obliquè repræsentatur: vt, Baruch.3. Stella autem dederunt lumen in custodiis suis, & latatæ sunt: vocatæ sunt, & dixerunt, Adsumus. Sic Luc.23. verf.3. Dicent montibus, Cadite super nos; & collibus, Tegite nos. Prosopopoeia perfecta est, qua personam nostram omnino deponimus, & aliam introducimus loquentem: puta Deum Pfal.82.v.2. Pfal.50.v.16. Prou.8. v.4. Luc.12.v.20. hominem Luc.12.v.17. res sensu destitutas Iudic.9.verf.7. & feqq. 2.Reg.14.verf.9. IV. Epanorthosis est, qua antecedens aliquid in oratione corrigitur: vt, Esa.49.v.15. Iohan.16.v.32. 1.Cor.15.v.10. 2.Tim.4.verf.7. Gal.4.verf.9. 1.Ioh.2.v.2. vbi apostolus ait: Ipse est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris. Nec pro nostris solum, sed etiam pro totius mundi peccatis. V. Aposiopesis est, qua sententiæ inchoatæ cursus ita abrumpitur, vt inde pars aliqua eius non dicta subintelligatur: vt, Psalm.6. verf.4. Anima mea turbata est valde: & tu Domine vsquequo? (scil. differs opem. Matth.9. verf.6. Vt autem sciatis, potestatem habere Filium hominis in terra remittendi peccata. Hic est [illegible, ~10 letters]. Nam subaudiendum est consequens hoc: Audite quid sim facturus. Rhetores vocant [illegible, ~12 letters]. Luc.19. verf.41. Videns ciuitatem fleuit super illam, & ait. Si cognouisses in die tua hæc, ea quæ ad pacem tuam: (scil. pertinerent. Gal.1. verf.1. Paulus neque ab hominibus, neque per homines: (scil. vocatus, vel missus. Genes.3. verf.22. Nunc ergo, ne forte mittat manum suam, & sumat etiam de arbore vitæ, & comedat viuatque in sæculum: subintellige, Exturbabo hominem de horto, adituque in eum prohibebo. Psal.95. verf.11. Si introibunt in requiem meam: subaudi, Non ero Deus, aut verax. Talis aposiopesis est Esa.5.v.9. Aposiopesis [illegible, ~12 letters], i.e. indignantis & reprehendentis est Psalm.4. verf.3. Quo vsque gloriam meam in ignominiam? (scil. vertitis. Aposiopesis vehementis amoris est Ruth.1. verf.17. Ita faciat mihi Iehoua, & ita pergat: (scil. nisi fecero quod dixi. VI. Addubitatio est deliberatio nobiscum: vt, Psalm.139. verf.7. & feqq. Quo ibo a Spiritu tuo? & quo a facie tua fugiam? &c. Rom. 7. [?] ver. 24. 52. Miser ego homo? quis me eripiet ex isto corpore mortis? Gratias ago Deo per Iesum Christum. Vide etiam Phil. 1. v. 22.
units.tr: III. Prosopopoeia is a change of person, by which the speaker is changed. It is either imperfect or perfect. Prosopopoeia is imperfect when the speech of another person is represented lightly and indirectly, as in Baruch 3. The stars gave light in their watches, and rejoiced; they were called, and said, Here we are. So too in Luke 23 v. 3. They shall say to the mountains, Fall on us; and to the hills, Cover us. Prosopopoeia is perfect when we altogether lay aside our own person and introduce another speaking: for example God, in Psalm 82 v. 2, Psalm 50 v. 16, Proverbs 8 v. 4, Luke 12 v. 20; a man, in Luke 12 v. 17; and things deprived of sense, in Judges 9 v. 7 and following, 2 Kings 14 v. 9. IV. Epanorthosis is that by which something said earlier in the speech is corrected: as in Isaiah 49 v. 15, John 16 v. 32, 1 Cor. 15 v. 10, 2 Tim. 4 v. 7, Gal. 4 v. 9, 1 John 2 v. 2, where the apostle says: He himself is the propitiation for our sins. And not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. V. Aposiopesis is that by which the course of a begun sentence is so broken off that some part of it is understood though unsaid: as in Psalm 6 v. 4, My soul is greatly troubled: but you, Lord, how long? (understood: you delay help). Matthew 9 v. 6, But that you may know that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins. Here there is [illegible]. For the following must be understood: Hear what I am about to do. The rhetoricians call it [illegible]. Luke 19 v. 41, And when he saw the city, he wept over it, and said, If you had known in this your day the things that belong to your peace (understood: they would have been spared). Gal. 1 v. 1, Paul, neither from men nor through men (understood: called, or sent). Genesis 3 v. 22, Now therefore, lest he put forth his hand and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever: understood, I will drive the man out of the garden and forbid him access to it. Psalm 95 v. 11, They shall not enter into my rest: understood, I will not be God, or true. Such an aposiopesis is in Isaiah 5 v. 9. An aposiopesis of indignation and rebuke is in Psalm 4 v. 3, How long will you turn my glory into shame? (understood: you turn it). An aposiopesis of vehement love is in Ruth 1 v. 17, So may the Lord do to me, and more also (understood: unless I do what I have said). VI. Addubitatio is deliberation with ourselves: as in Psalm 139 v. 7 and following, Whither shall I go from your Spirit? or whither shall I flee from your face? etc. Rom. 7 v. 24: Wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from this body of death? I thank God through Jesus Christ. See also Phil. 1 v. 22.

units.la: VII. Communicatio est deliberatio cum aliis: vt, Ier. 23. v. 23. 24. Numquid Deus de propinquo ego sum, dixit Iehova, & non Deus de longinquo? num occultabit se quispiam in occultis, & ego non videbo eum, dixit Iehova? Sic & verf. 29. Nonne sicut est verbum meum tanquam ignis? Vide quoque Malach. 1. verf. 6. Esa. 58. v. 21. Psal. 94. v. 7. 8. 10. 1. Cor. 10. v. 15. 16. Sic Act. 4. v. 19. Vos ipsi iudicate, an iustum sit in conspectu Dei, vos potius audire quam Deum? Item Act. 9. v. 4. 5. 6.
units.tr: VII. Communicatio is deliberation with others: as in Jeremiah 23 v. 23, 24, Am I a God at hand, says the Lord, and not a God afar off? Can any hide himself in secret places, and I shall not see him, says the Lord? So too v. 29: Is not my word like fire? See also Malachi 1 v. 6, Isaiah 58 v. 21, Psalm 94 v. 7, 8, 10, 1 Cor. 10 v. 15, 16. So Acts 4 v. 19, Judge for yourselves whether it is right in the sight of God to hear you rather than God? Likewise Acts 9 v. 4, 5, 6.

units.la: VIII. Occupatio est, cum alieni consilii interrogationem ita anteuertimus, vt ad eam respondeamus: vt, Rom. 9. verf. 19. 20. Dices ergo mihi, Quid adhuc succensés nobis? nam voluntati illius quis resistit? Imo vero ô homo, tu quis es, qui ex aduersò respondes Deo. Num dicet figmentum fictori, Cur me tale fecisti? Matth. 11. v. 26. Etiam, pater, quia ita placuit tibi. Rom. 9. v. 6. 1. Ioh. 2. v. 1. 2. Cor. 4. verf. 16. Hebr. 5. ver. 8. Rom. 2. v. 17. & seqq. Esa. 49. v. 14. Ezech. 18. verf. 2. Apoc. 3. v. 17. Rom. 11. v. 59.
units.tr: VIII. Occupatio is when we anticipate the objection of an opposing argument so as to answer it: as in Romans 9 v. 19, 20, You will say to me then, Why does he still find fault? For who resists his will? Nay but, O man, who are you who answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to him who formed it, Why have you made me thus? Matthew 11 v. 26, Yes, Father, for so it pleased you. Romans 9 v. 6; 1 John 2 v. 1, 2; 2 Cor. 4 v. 16; Heb. 5 v. 8; Rom. 2 v. 17 and following; Isaiah 49 v. 14; Ezek. 18 v. 2; Rev. 3 v. 17; Rom. 11 v. 59.

units.la: IX. Permissio est, qua permittitur aliquid fieri: vt, Rom. 2. v. 17. & seqq. Ecce, tu cognominaris Iudaeus, & acquiescis in lege, & gloriaris in Deo. Et nosti eius voluntatem &c. Vide etiam Iudic. 10. v. 14.
units.tr: IX. Permissio is that by which something is allowed to be done: as in Romans 2 v. 17 and following, Behold, you are called a Jew, and rest upon the law, and glory in God. And you know his will etc. See also Judges 10 v. 14.

units.la: X. Concessio est, qua dictum aliquod conceditur: vt, Ioh. 5. verf. 31. Si ego testor de meipso: testimonium meum non est verum. Hoc Christus dicit per concessionem. 1. Cor. 1. verf. 23. 25. Nos autem praedicamus Christum crucifixum; Iudaeis quidem offendiculum, Graecis autem stultitiam. Nam stultitia Dei sapientior est, quam homines: & infirmitas Dei robustior est quam homines. Vide etiam Gal. 1. v. 6. Iacob. 2. v. 18.
units.tr: X. Concessio is that by which a statement is granted: as in John 5 v. 31, If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true. Christ says this by way of concession. 1 Cor. 1 v. 23, 25, But we preach Christ crucified; to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Greeks foolishness. For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. See also Gal. 1 v. 6, James 2 v. 18.

units.la: XVIII. Figurarum sententiae secundariarum genera sunt XXVIII. hoc ordine: Auxesis, Digressio, Transitio, Ratiocinatio, Aetiologia, Periphrasis, Extenuatio, Reiectio, Translatio, Dialogismus, Definitio, Distributio, Congeries, Incrementum, Diatyposis, Hypotyposis, Paradigma, Imago, Collatio, Comparatio, Paradoxum, Paromologia, Paradiastole, Anthypophora, Crama, Gnoma, Noema, Chria. Exhis figuris illas attingemus, quarum vsus in Scripturis est paulò frequentior. I. Auxesis elt, cùm gradibus aliquot peruenit ur ad summum: vt, Phil.3.v.5.6.Circumcisus octavo die, ex gente Israelis: tribu Beniamin, Hebraeus ex Hebraeis, religione Pharisaeus. Vide etiam Rom.5.v.7.8. Eph.2.v.11.12.15. Iof. 7.v.1. Eph.1.v.19.20. II. Digressio, παρέκβασις, est alienae rei, sed ad vtilitatem causae pertinentis, extra ordinem excurrens tractatio: vt, 2.Cor.11.v.20. Paulus in suorum pro ecclesia Dei laborum commemorationem excurrit, quam digressionem etiam cap.seq. per sequitur. Vide etiam Gal. 1.v.17.& seqq.c.2.v.2.& seqq.Coloss.3.v.11.Matth.14.v.3 & seq.
units.tr: XVIII. The kinds of secondary figures of sentence are 28, in this order: Auxesis, Digressio, Transitio, Ratiocinatio, Aetiologia, Periphrasis, Extenuatio, Reiectio, Translatio, Dialogismus, Definitio, Distributio, Congeries, Incrementum, Diatyposis, Hypotyposis, Paradigma, Imago, Collatio, Comparatio, Paradoxum, Paromologia, Paradiastole, Anthypophora, Crama, Gnoma, Noema, Chria. Of these figures we shall touch on those whose use in the Scriptures is somewhat more frequent. I. Auxesis is when a thing is brought up by several steps to the highest point: as in Philippians 3 v. 5, 6, Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, as touching the law a Pharisee. See also Rom. 5 v. 7, 8; Eph. 2 v. 11, 12, 15; Joshua 7 v. 1; Eph. 1 v. 19, 20. II. Digressio [παρέκβασις] is a treatment of a matter foreign to the subject, yet pertaining to the usefulness of the cause, running out of the normal order: as in 2 Cor. 11 v. 20, where Paul runs off into a recounting of his own labours for the Church of God; a digression which he also continues into the following chapter. See also Gal. 1 v. 17 and following; Gal. 2 v. 2 and following; Col. 3 v. 11; Matt. 14 v. 3 and following.

units.la: III. Transitio, μετάβασις, qua connectuntur partes orationis: vt, Rom.9.v.10. Neque hoc solum, sed & Rebecca. q.d. Non solum autem hoc accidit quod narraui de duob. filijs Abrahae; sed & Rebecca hoc idem experta est in filiis suis. Quibus verbis Paulus transit à doctrina de iustificatione & sanctificatione ad tractatum de praedestinatione. Phil.3.verf.1. Quod superest, fratres, gaudete. IV. Aetiologia est breuis redditio causae: vt, Gal.3.v.18. Nam si ex lege est hereditas, non iam ex promissione. Coloss.1.v.16. V. Periphrasis est, quâ multis verbis rem obumbramus, sic tamen vt cerni possit: vt, Iohan.3.v.26. Is qui tecum erat trans Iordanem, cui tu testimonium dedisti, ecce baptizat: id est, Iesus baptizat. Iohan.vlt.v20. Conuersus Petrus vidit illum discipulum, quem diligebat Iesus, sequentem; qui & recubuerat in coena super pectus eius, & dixerat, Domine quis est ille qui te prodit? hoc est, videt Iohannem. VI. Definitio, ὁρισμός, est magnifica rei explicatio: vt, Gal.3, verf.24. Lex est paedagogus ad Christum. VII. Congeries est, quando plures coaceruantur species: vt, Gal.5.Manifesta sunt opera carnis, quae sunt fornicatio, immunditia, impudicitia, &c. VIII. Hypotyposis est, quâ rem velut ob oculos ponimus: vt, Psal.7.v.13.14. Deus κατὰ ὑποτύπωσιν depingitur cum arcu & sagittis paratus, & in hostes intentus. IX. Anthypophora est, cùm vnum argumentum conceditur, opposito fortiori. Dicitur alio nomine ἀντικαταλλάξις & ἀντεισαγωγὴ, compensatio. Exemplum insigne est Matth. 21. vers. 23. 24. 25. vbi Christus Pharisæis quærentibus, Quâ potestate hoc facis? respondet, Interrogabo [?]& ego vos quiddam: Baptismus Iohannis vnde erat? ex cœlo an ex hominibus?
units.tr: III. Transitio [μετάβασις] is that by which the parts of a speech are connected: as in Romans 9 v. 10, And not only this, but also Rebecca; that is, not only has this happened which I have related of the two sons of Abraham, but Rebecca also has experienced the same in her sons. With these words Paul passes from the doctrine of justification and sanctification to the treatment of predestination. Phil. 3 v. 1, Finally, brethren, rejoice. IV. Aetiologia is a brief statement of a cause: as in Gal. 3 v. 18, For if the inheritance is of the law, it is no longer of promise. Col. 1 v. 16. V. Periphrasis is that by which we veil a matter in many words, yet so that it can be discerned: as in John 3 v. 26, He who was with you beyond the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, behold, he baptizes: that is, Jesus baptizes. John, last chapter, v. 20, Peter, turning, saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following; who also had leaned on his breast at supper, and had said, Lord, who is it that betrays you? that is, he sees John. VI. Definitio [ὁρισμός] is a splendid explanation of a thing: as in Gal. 3 v. 24, The law is our schoolmaster to bring us to Christ. VII. Congeries is when several kinds are heaped together: as in Gal. 5, The works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness, lewdness, etc. VIII. Hypotyposis is that by which we set a thing, as it were, before the eyes: as in Psalm 7 v. 13, 14, God is depicted by way of hypotyposis [κατὰ ὑποτύπωσιν] as armed with bow and arrows, and bent upon his enemies. IX. Anthypophora is when one argument is granted while a stronger one is set against it. It is also called by another name [ἀντικαταλλάξις, ἀντεισαγωγὴ], compensation. A notable example is Matthew 21 v. 23, 24, 25, where Christ, when the Pharisees ask, By what authority do you do these things? answers, I will also ask you one thing: the baptism of John, whence was it? from heaven or from men?

units.la: XIX. Actio est ornata elocutionis prolatio; conueniente scil. voce & gestu. Vox conueniens est, quæ debitam habet quantitatem & qualitatem. Ratione quantitatis vox est intensa & remissa, item tarda, distincta, expedita, & denique firma, non decrescens, sed sæpe augescens. Ratione qualitatis vox est exilis, flebilis, exultans, aspera, acuta, grauis, horrida, suauis &c. Vtrobique oportet vt vocis sonus sit accommodatus rebus. Sic in miseratione debet esse vox flebilis, flexibilis, plena, & interrupta: in iracundia, acuta, incitata, & crebro incidens: in metu & verecundia, contracta, hæsitans, & lenta: in dolore grauis, pressa & lachrymabilis: in risu & lætitia, clara-pura, & exultans. Esa.58.verf.1.Dan. 6.verf.21.Iud.8.verf.1.& feqq. 2.Reg. 18. v.28. Matth. 23. per totum. Gestus conueniens est, qui rebus, affectibus, voci, & consuetudini est accommodatus. Sic demissio capitis est habitus conueniens luctui, dolori, & humiliationi Esa.58. v.5. Oculi in aliquem conuersi indicant captationem attentionis Luc.6.v.20. Lachrymæ indicant mœrorem. Luc. 19.v.41. Percussio pectoris & deiectio oculorum est signum humilitatis. Luc.18.ver.13. Vide infra Ciuilem conuersationem.
units.tr: XIX. Action is the delivery of ornate speech, with a voice and gesture that suit it. A suitable voice is one that has the due quantity and quality. As to quantity, the voice is loud and soft, and likewise slow, distinct, fluent, and finally firm, not tailing off but often rising. As to quality, the voice is thin, tearful, exultant, harsh, shrill, deep, bristling, sweet, and so on. In both respects the sound of the voice must be fitted to the subject. Thus in pity the voice should be tearful, pliant, full, and broken; in anger, sharp, agitated, and often breaking in; in fear and shame, constrained, hesitant, and slow; in grief, heavy, pressed down, and tearful; in laughter and joy, clear, pure, and exultant. Esa.58.verf.1. Dan. 6.verf.21. Iud.8.verf.1. & seqq. 2.Reg. 18. v.28. Matth. 23. per totum. A suitable gesture is one fitted to the subject, the feelings, the voice, and custom. Thus lowering the head is a bearing suited to mourning, grief, and humiliation Esa.58. v.5. Eyes turned on someone indicate an attempt to win attention Luc.6.v.20. Tears indicate sorrow Luc. 19.v.41. Striking the breast and lowering the eyes is a sign of humility Luc.18.ver.13. See below, Civil conversation.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: LOGICA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED LOGIC.

units.la: 1. LOgica sacra est ars bene differendi exemplo Scripturæ sacræ[?], Bene differere est meditari,inuenire,disponere,disputare,colloqui,& similia rationis munia obire.
units.tr: 1. Sacred logic is the art of reasoning well, by the example of Holy Scripture. To reason well is to meditate, discover, arrange, dispute, confer, and perform the similar duties of reason.

units.la: II. Partes logicæ sunt duæ, inuentio & dispo- sitio.
units.tr: II. The parts of logic are two: invention and disposition.

units.la: III. Inuentio est quâ colligitur materia dissertationis. Estque thematis & argumenti. Hæc duo enim sunt materia omnis dissertationis.
units.tr: III. Invention is that by which the matter of a discourse is gathered. This matter is twofold, the theme and the argument, for these two are the whole matter of every discourse.

units.la: IV. Thema est, de quo disseritur. Ita nempe, vt explicetur, vel probetur. Est autem thema primò simplex, vel compositum. Thema simplex est, quod proponitur explicationis causâ: vt sunt omnia vocabula & omnes res vocabulis istis significatæ, vt Gen.1. cœlum, terra, lux, sol: item omnes quæstiones, ad quas non potest respondéri ita vel non, quales sunt in isto versu:
units.tr: IV. The theme is that about which one discourses, so that it may be explained or proved. A theme is either simple or compound. A simple theme is one proposed for the sake of explanation, such as all words and all things signified by those words, as in Gen. 1: heaven, earth, light, sun. Likewise, all questions to which one cannot answer simply yes or no, such as those in this verse:

units.la: Quis, quid, vbi, quibus auxiliis, cur, quomodo, quando.
units.tr: Who, what, where, by what aids, why, how, when.

units.la: Thema compositum est, quod proponitur demonstrationis causâ: cuiusmodi sunt omnes quæstiones, ad quas responderi potest ita vel non: vt Rom.4. An homo iustificetur fide? Deinde thema est thesis, vel hypothesis. Thesis est thema generale: vt, Omnis homo mendax Psalm.116. Hypothesis est thema speciale: vt sunt omnes historiæ, putà de Adamo, Euâ, Enocho, Mose &c. Huiusmodi themata multa sunt Heb.11. Tertiò thema est theoreticum, vel practicum. Thema theoreticum est, quod cognitionis causâ proponitur: estque didascalicum, vel elencticum. Didascalicum thema est, quod facit ad verum docendum: vt est Psalmus 1. Thema elencticum est, quod facit ad redarguendum falsum: vt est caput 3. ad Galatas. Thema practicum est, quod actionis causâ proponitur. Estque paedeuticum, epanorthoticum, vel paracleticum. Thema paedeuticum est, quod proponitur ad instituendum in bono: vt est caput quintum posterioris epist. Petri. Thema epanorthoticum est, quod proponitur ad vitandum malum: vt est caput 6. Rom. Thema paracleticum est, qp consolationis causâ proponitur: vt 1. Thess.4.v.13.14. Postrema hæc themata diuisio sumta est ex
units.tr: A compound theme is one proposed for the sake of demonstration, such as all questions to which one can answer yes or no, as in Rom. 4: Is a man justified by faith? Again, a theme is either a thesis or a hypothesis. A thesis is a general theme, as "Every man is a liar," Ps. 116. A hypothesis is a particular theme, such as all histories, for example, concerning Adam, Eve, Enoch, Moses, and so on. Many such themes occur in Heb. 11. Thirdly, a theme is either theoretical or practical. A theoretical theme is one proposed for the sake of knowledge; it is either didactic or elenctic. A didactic theme is one that serves to teach truth, as Psalm 1. An elenctic theme is one that serves to refute falsehood, as chapter 3 of Galatians. A practical theme is one proposed for the sake of action; it is either paedeutic, epanorthotic, or paracletic. A paedeutic theme is one proposed for instruction in what is good, as the fifth chapter of the second epistle of Peter. An epanorthotic theme is one proposed for avoiding evil, as chapter 6 of Romans. A paracletic theme is one proposed for the sake of comfort, as 1 Thess. 4:13–14. This last division of themes is taken from

units.la: {2} 2.Tim.3.v.16. & Rom.15.v.4. & est propria thematis theologici. Quoties itaque differendum est de themate sacro, quinque ista genera oportet percurrere, & simul obseruare locum communem theologicum, ad quem thema propositum pertinet. e.g. si differendum sit ex Luc. 1. de angelo Gabriele, thema illud est didascalicum, & pertinet ad locum communem de angelis.
units.tr: {2} 2 Tim. 3:16 and Rom. 15:4, and is proper to theological themes. Whenever, therefore, one is to discourse on a sacred theme, these five kinds ought to be run through, and at the same time one should observe the common theological topic to which the proposed theme pertains. For example, if one is to discourse from Luke 1 about the angel Gabriel, that theme is didactic and pertains to the common topic concerning angels.

units.la: V. Argumentum est, quod facit ad evolutionem thematis. Ita nempe, vt illud declaret, vel demonstret, vel amplificet. Nam haec triplex vis & facultas inest argumento.
units.tr: V. The argument is that which contributes to the unfolding of the theme, so that it either declares it, proves it, or amplifies it. For this threefold power and capacity belongs to an argument.

units.la: VI. In argumento spectantur affectiones & species.
units.tr: VI. In an argument one considers its affections and its species.

units.la: VII. Affectiones argumenti sunt consensio & dissensio, necessitas & contingentia, affirmatio & negatio, vis primitiva vel derivativa, consideratio simplex vel comparatio: quae omnia fundantur in relatione. Omnibus enim argumentis accidit vt sint relata, idque secundum species modo enumeratas, puta consensionem, dissensionem, necessitate &c. Hinc argumenta logica consentiunt vel dissentiunt, idq; vel necessario & immutabiliter, vel contingenter & mutabiliter. Deinde argumenta aliquid affirmant sive ponunt in rerum natura, vel negant sive tollunt. Tertio argumenta sunt originis primae vel ortae. Deniq; considerantur vel simpliciter extra collationem, vel in collatione sive comparatione. Hae affectiones sparguntur per argumenta logica sive loca inventionis non aliter atque sanguis & succus per totum corpus; hoc est ita, vt, quemadmodum singula quidem membra neque sunt exsanguia, neq; exsucca, neque tamen ideo aequaliter sanguine & succo praedita, sic quoque argumenta logica participent de illis assectionibus, sed inaequaliter. Hinc est, quod argumenta quaedam appellantur consentanea, dissentanea, comparata, & orta, quia in illis eminet istiusmodi affectio. Sic v.g. consensio principaliter & primo inest causæ & essecto; subiecto & adiuncto; antecedenti, connexis, & cosequenti; reliquis autem nonnisi propter illa. Quare consensio inter definitionem & definitum erit vel causæ & effecti, vel subiecti & adiuncti &c. Similiter dissensio principaliter & primo inest diversis, disparatis &c. Ideo si dicam inter causam & effectum cerni dissensionem aliquam, oportet ut videam an causa & effectum dissentiant ut diversa, disparata, relata &c. De comparatis & ortis idem est judicium.
units.tr: VII. The affections of an argument are agreement and disagreement, necessity and contingency, affirmation and negation, primitive or derivative force, and simple consideration or comparison. All of these are grounded in relation. For it happens to all arguments that they are related, and this according to the species just enumerated, namely agreement, disagreement, necessity, and so on. Hence logical arguments agree or disagree, and that either necessarily and immutably, or contingently and mutably. Again, arguments either affirm or posit something in the nature of things, or deny or remove it. Thirdly, arguments are either of primary origin or of derived origin. Finally, they are considered either simply apart from comparison, or within a comparison. These affections are spread through logical arguments, or topics of invention, just as blood and juice are through the whole body. That is, just as individual members are neither bloodless nor juiceless, yet are not equally endowed with blood and juice, so also logical arguments partake of these affections, but unequally. Hence some arguments are called consentaneous, dissentaneous, comparative, and derived, because this kind of affection stands out in them. Thus, for example, agreement inheres principally and primarily in cause and effect, in subject and adjunct, in antecedent, connected, and consequent; but in the rest only on account of these. Therefore agreement between a definition and the thing defined will be that of cause and effect, or of subject and adjunct, and so on. Likewise, disagreement inheres principally and primarily in things diverse, disparate, and so on. So if I say that some disagreement is perceived between cause and effect, I must see whether cause and effect disagree as diverse, disparate, related, and so on. The same judgment holds for comparative and derived arguments.

units.la: VIII. Species argumenti sunt, quòd fit insitum vel assumtum. Illud etiam artificiale, hoc inartificiale dicitur,
units.tr: VIII. The species of an argument are that it is either innate or assumed. The former is also called artificial, the latter inartificial.

units.la: IX. Argumentum insitum est, quod sua vi facit ad evolutionem thematis.
units.tr: IX. An innate argument is one that by its own force contributes to the unfolding of the theme.

units.la: X. Estque primum, vel ortum.
units.tr: X. And it is either primary or derived.

units.la: XI. Argumentum primum est suæ originis: Estque simplex, vel comparatum.
units.tr: XI. A primary argument is of its own origin; and it is either simple or compared.

units.la: XII. Argumentum simplex est, quod extra comparationem consideratur. Estque consentaneum, vel dissentaneum.
units.tr: XII. A simple argument is one considered apart from comparison. And it is either consentaneous or dissentaneous.

units.la: XIII. Argumentum consentaneum est, quod cum suo themate consentit. Consentit autem summe, vel remisse.
units.tr: XIII. A consentaneous argument is one that agrees with its theme. It agrees either supremely or in a lesser degree.

units.la: XIV. Argumentum summe consentaneum est causa & effectum.
units.tr: XIV. A supremely consentaneous argument is cause and effect.

units.la: XV. Causa est, cuius vi res est.
units.tr: XV. A cause is that by whose force a thing is.

units.la: XVI. Causa est externa, vel interna. Illa est efficiens & finis, hæc materia & forma.
units.tr: XVI. A cause is either external or internal. The external is efficient and final; the internal is material and formal.

units.la: XVII. Efficiens est causa, à quâ res est. Hæc primò est procreans, vel conseruans. Procreans est, quæ rem facit esse: ut Gen. 1. v. 1. In principio creavit Deus cœlum & terram. Efficiens conferuans est, quæ rem facit porrò esse: vt, Hebr.1.v.3. Christus omnia portat verbo suo potente. Deinde efficiens est solitaria, vel socia[?]. Solitaria, siue totalis, est, quæ sola ad rem efficiendam sufficit: vt Christus solus calcauit torcular Esa.63.v.3. Solus Deus potest remittere peccata Luc.5.v.21. Efficiens socia, siue partialis, est, quæ cum aliis agit. Estque principalis, vel minus principalis. Efficiens principalis agit primario: minus principalis secundario: vt 1.Cor.3.verf.6.7. Ego plantaui, Apollos rigauit: sed Deus dedit incrementum. Itaque neque is qui plantat est aliquid, neque qui rigat: sed Deus, qui dat incrementum. Ad causam minus principalem refertur instrumentum & causa impellens. Instrumentum est, quod à causa principali motum adiuuat actionem: vt 1.Cor.3.v.9. Dei administri sumus. Causa impellens mouet efficientem principalem vel minus principalem. Estque προηγουμένη vel προκαταρκτικὴ[?]. Προηγουμένη est in ipsa efficiente: vt Matth.11.verf.26. Etiam Pater, quia sic placuit tibi. Προκαταρκτικὴ[?] est extra efficientem: vt Rom.8.verf.32. Is quidem qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit eum, qui non etiam cum eo omnia nobis gratificabitur? Tertiò efficiens agit per se, vel per accidens. Efficiens per se agit suâ facultate: estque naturalis vel voluntaria. Naturalis est, quæ agit ex naturæ suæ vi: vt, Genef.1. verf. 11. Proferat terra herbulas. Voluntaria est, quæ agit cum præcognitione & consilio: vt, Psalm.115. verf.3. Deus noster in cœlis est, quidquid placet, facit. Efficiens per accidens est, quæ alterius facultate efficit: vt, 1.Corinth.1. ver.23. Christus crucifixus Iudæis est offendiculum, Græcis stultitia.
units.tr: XVII. The efficient cause is that from which a thing is. This is, first, either creating or conserving. Creating is that which makes a thing to be: as in Gen. 1:1, In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. A conserving efficient is that which makes a thing continue to be, as Heb. 1:3: Christ upholds all things by his powerful word. Next, the efficient is either solitary or associated. The solitary, or total, is that which alone suffices for producing the thing: as Isa. 63:3, I alone have trodden the winepress; and Luke 5:21, God alone can forgive sins. An associated, or partial, efficient is one that acts together with others. It is either principal or less principal. The principal efficient acts primarily, the less principal secondarily, as in 1 Cor. 3:6–7: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. So neither is he who plants anything, nor he who waters, but God, who gives the increase. To the less principal cause there belong the instrument and the impelling cause. An instrument is that which, moved by the principal cause, assists the action, as in 1 Cor. 3:9: We are God's fellow workers. An impelling cause moves the principal or less principal efficient. It is either proēgoumenē [προηγουμένη] or prokatarktikē [προκαταρκτικὴ]. The proēgoumenē is within the efficient itself, as Matt. 11:26: Even so, Father, for so it seemed good in your sight. The prokatarktikē is outside the efficient, as Rom. 8:32: He who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? Thirdly, the efficient acts either per se or per accidens. An efficient per se acts by its own faculty; and it is either natural or voluntary. The natural is that which acts by the force of its nature, as Gen. 1:11: Let the earth bring forth grass. The voluntary is that which acts with foreknowledge and counsel, as Ps. 115:3: Our God is in the heavens; he does whatever he pleases. An efficient per accidens is that which produces its effect by the faculty of another, as 1 Cor. 1:23: Christ crucified is a stumbling block to the Jews, and foolishness to the Greeks.

units.la: XVIII. Finis est cuius gratia res est.
units.tr: XVIII. An end is that for the sake of which a thing is.

units.la: Estq; principalis, vel minus principalis. Finis principalis est, qui primario intenditur ab efficiente. Estque summus, vel summo subordinatus. Finis summus, aliis vltimus, est vniuersalis; vel particularis. Finis summus vniuersalis est, ad quem omnia in vniuerso mundo ordinantur: 1.Cor.10.v.31. Omnia ad Dei gloriam facite. Finis summus particularis est, ad quem omnia referuntur in certa aliqua materia: vt summus finis Logicæ est bene differere. Finis summo subordinatus est, qui tanquam intermedius ad summum refertur: vt Christus 1.Cor.11.v.24.25. præcipit sacram suam cœnā celebrare ad sui recordationem. Finis minus principalis est, qui secundario intenditur ab efficiente: vt, qui seruiunt altari, secundario hoc debet spectare vt viuat de altari 1.Cor.9.v.13.
units.tr: It is either principal or less than principal. A principal end is that which the efficient cause primarily intends. It is either the highest, or subordinate to the highest. The highest end, which is last of all, is either universal or particular. The highest universal end is that to which everything in the whole world is directed: 1 Cor. 10.31: Do all things to the glory of God. The highest particular end is that to which everything is referred within some definite subject matter: thus the highest end of logic is to reason well. An end subordinate to the highest is one that is referred to the highest as an intermediate end: thus Christ, in 1 Cor. 11.24-25, commands that his holy supper be celebrated in remembrance of him. A less than principal end is one that the efficient cause intends secondarily: thus those who serve at the altar ought to look to this secondarily, that they may live from the altar, 1 Cor. 9.13.

units.la: XIX. Materia est causa ex qua res est. Estque præexistens, vel coexistens. Materia præexistens antecedit materiatū: vt Gen.2. Adam ex terra formatus est, & Eua ex costa Adami. Materia coexistens est, ex qua constat materia- tum: vt Gen.2.v.1. exercitus cœli & terræ, i.e. omnes creaturæ, sunt materia ex qua constat mundus. Sic membra corporis sunt eius materia. Eph.4.v.16. XX. Forma est, per quam res est id quod est. Particula per notat intimam ΘΕΑΧΩΡΗΤΟΝ. Est autem forma interna, vel externa. Forma interna est, quæ sensibus non subiicitur. Hanc Deus implantauit omnibus rebus Gen.1. quando illis peculiares & distinctas naturas inseuit. Forma externa est naturalis, vt est forma arboris vitæ Gen.2. vel ar- tificialis, vt forma arcæ Noë Gen.6. XXI. Effectum est, quod a causa existit. Sic a Deo, tanquam efficiente procreante, per Deum, tanquam efficientem conseruantem, & ad Deum, tanquam causam finalem, sunt omnia. Rom.11.v.vlt. Effecta Christi sunt mi- racula varia, vt Iohan.2. aquæ in vinum conuersio. XXII. Argumentum remisse consentaneum est subiectum & adiunctum; antecedens, conne- xum, & consequens. XXIII. Subiectum est, quod alicui subiicitur. Estq; recipiens, vel occupans. Subiectum recipiens est, qui recipit adiunctum vel in se, vt Christus sapientiam Luc.2.v.vlt. vel ad se, vt Christus togam, coronam spineam, & alia eiusmodi. Subiectum occupans est, circa quod versatur adiunctum, vt verus Christianus circa Christi mortem 2.Tim.2.v.8. XXIV. Ad-
units.tr: XIX. Matter is the cause out of which a thing is. It is either pre-existing or co-existing. Pre-existing matter comes before the thing made from it: thus Gen. 2: Adam was formed out of the earth, and Eve out of Adam's rib. Co-existing matter is that out of which the thing made consists: thus Gen. 2.1, the host of heaven and earth, that is, all creatures, is the matter out of which the world consists. So too the members are the matter of the body, Eph. 4.16. XX. Form is that through which a thing is what it is. The particle through denotes the inmost [ΘΕΑΧΩΡΗΤΟΝ]. Form is either internal or external. Internal form is that which is not subject to the senses. God implanted this in all things, Gen. 1, when he gave them their particular and distinct natures. External form is either natural, as the form of the tree of life, Gen. 2, or artificial, as the form of Noah's ark, Gen. 6. XXI. An effect is that which comes into existence from a cause. Thus all things are from God as efficient creator, through God as efficient preserver, and unto God as final cause, Rom. 11, last verse. The works of Christ are various miracles, such as the changing of water into wine, John 2. XXII. An argument, in a loose sense, is a subject and an adjunct; an antecedent, a connection, and a consequent. XXIII. A subject is that to which something is attached. It is either receiving or occupying. A receiving subject is one that receives an adjunct either within itself, as Christ received wisdom, Luke 2, last verse, or upon itself, as Christ received a robe, a crown of thorns, and other things of that kind. An occupying subject is that about which an adjunct is employed, as a true Christian is occupied with Christ's death, 2 Tim. 2.8. XXIV. Ad-

units.la: XXIV. Adiunctum est, quod accedit suo subiecto. Estque receptum, vel occupatum. Adiunctum receptum est, quod subiecto vel inhaeret, ut sapientia Salomoni 1. Reg. 3. vel adhaeret, ut purpura & byssus diuitiepuloni Luc.16. Porro adiunctum receptum est proprium, vel commune. Proprium adiunctum est, quod competit omni subiecto, soli, & semper: ut Deus est omnipotens. Gen. 17. v. 1. Adiunctum commune est, quod cor ingenter inest: ut, Abel erat pastor. Gen. 4. Adiunctum occupatum est, quod versatur circa subiectum: ut Christus Luc. 2. verf. 49. circa ea, quae sunt Patris ipsius; & fides Heb. 11. verf. 1. circa res inaspectabiles.
units.tr: XXIV. An adjunct is that which attaches itself to its subject. It is either received or occupied. A received adjunct is that which either inheres in the subject, as wisdom did in Solomon, 1 Kings 3, or clings to it, as purple and fine linen to the rich man, Luke 16. Further, a received adjunct is either proper or common. A proper adjunct is one that belongs to every subject, to it alone, and always: thus God is almighty, Gen. 17.1. A common adjunct is one that inheres in a thing without being its own: thus Abel was a shepherd, Gen. 4. An occupied adjunct is one that is busied about its subject: thus Christ, Luke 2.49, is busied with the things of his Father; and faith, Heb. 11.1, is busied with things unseen.

units.la: XXV. Antecedens est, quod rem antecedit, non ut causa vel subiectum, sed ut merum antecedens. Sic Gen. 1. primus dies antecessit secundum; & passio Christi ipsius resurrectionem Matth. 27. & 28.
units.tr: XXV. An antecedent is that which comes before a thing, not as a cause or subject, but as a mere antecedent. Thus, in Gen. 1, the first day came before the second; and Christ's passion came before his resurrection, Matt. 27 and 28.

units.la: XXVI. Connexum est, quod simul est cum re. Sic omnia Dei attributa sunt connexa. Exod. 34. verf. 6, 7. item eclipsis & passio Christi Luc. 23.
units.tr: XXVI. A connection is that which is together with a thing. Thus all the attributes of God are connected. Exod. 34.6-7. Likewise the eclipse and the passion of Christ, Luke 23.

units.la: XXVII. Consequens est, quod rem sequitur, non ut effectum vel adiunctum, sed ut merum consequens. Sic Gen. 1. dies secundus sequutus est primum; & Act. 1. ascensio Christi resurrectionem.
units.tr: XXVII. A consequent is that which follows a thing, not as an effect or adjunct, but as a mere consequent. Thus, in Gen. 1, the second day followed the first; and, Acts 1, Christ's ascension followed his resurrection.

units.la: XXVIII. Argumentum dissentaneum est, quod a re dissentit. Deus indidit rebus consensiones, quia omnia voluit pendere ab vno aliquo, & tendere ad vnum aliquid: dissensiones vero, ne multa essent vnum, & hoc non esset illud, & illud non esset hoc.
units.tr: XXVIII. A dissenting argument is that which disagrees with a thing. God gave things agreements because he willed that all things should depend on some one thing and tend toward some one thing; but disagreements, so that many things should not be one, and this should not be that, and that should not be this.

units.la: XXIX. Estque diuersum, vel oppositum.
units.tr: XXIX. It is either different or opposed.

units.la: XXX. Diuersum est, quod dissentit faciendo distinctionem. Hinc diuersa sunt fons omnium bonarum distinctionum. Exemplum huius loci est 2. Cor. 4. v. 8.
units.tr: XXX. A different thing is that which disagrees by making a distinction. Hence different things are the source of all good distinctions. An example of this place is 2 Cor. 4.8.

units.la: 9. Premimur quidem, sed non opprimimur: estuamus, sed non exstuamus [?]; vexamur, sed non deserimur: deiicimur, sed non perimus.
units.tr: 9. We are indeed pressed, but not crushed; we are perplexed, but not despairing; we are persecuted, but not forsaken; we are cast down, but not destroyed.

units.la: XXXI. Oppositum est, quod dissentit faciendo oppositionem, siue repugnantiam. Itaque opposita non possunt tribui eidem, secundum idem, ad idem, & eodem tempore. Si vero quatuor ista sint diuersa, puta subiectum, pars, respectus, & tempus, nulla est oppositio.
units.tr: XXXI. An opposite is that which disagrees by making an opposition or repugnance. Thus opposites cannot be attributed to the same thing, in the same respect, in the same place, and at the same time. If, however, these four are different, namely subject, part, respect, and time, there is no opposition.

units.la: XXXII. Oppositio est disparatorum, relatorum, aduersorum, contradicentium, vel privantium.
units.tr: XXXII. Opposition is of things that are disparate, relative, adverse, contradictory, or privative.

units.la: XXXIII. Disparata sunt, quorum vnum multis pariter opponitur. Sic 1. Petr. 1. v. 18. 19. Non caducutebus[?], auro aut argento, ex vanis moribus patriis estis redemti: sed pretioso sanguine Christi, tanquam agni immaculati. Hic aurum, argentum, & sanguis Christi disparantur.
units.tr: XXXIII. Disparate things are those of which one is opposed to many alike. Thus, 1 Pet. 1.18-19: You were redeemed not with corruptible things, with gold or silver, from your vain conduct inherited from your fathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a spotless lamb. Here gold, silver, and the blood of Christ are set apart from one another.

units.la: XXXIV. Relata sunt, quae amice opponuntur. Sic Christus arguit Matth. 22. verf. 45. Si Christus est dominus Dauidis, non erit eius filius, h.e. potestati subiectus.
units.tr: XXXIV. Relative things are those that are opposed in a friendly way. Thus Christ argues, Matt. 22.45: If Christ is David's lord, he will not be his son, that is, subject to his power.

units.la: XXXV. Aduersa sunt, quae perpetuo diffident. Sic Matth. 6. v. 24. Non potestis Deo seruire & Mammonae. Vide etiam 1. Cor. 10. v. 21.
units.tr: XXXV. Adverse things are those that are always at odds. Thus Matt. 6.24: You cannot serve God and Mammon. See also 1 Cor. 10.21.

units.la: XXXVI. Contradicentia sunt, quorum alterum negat vbique. Sic Rom. 9. verf. 25. Vocabo populum meum: & eam, quae dilecta erat, dilectam.
units.tr: XXXVI. Contradictory things are those of which one denies the other everywhere. Thus Rom. 9.25: I will call my people that which was not my people, and her who was not beloved, beloved.

units.la: XXXVII. Priuantia sunt, quorum alterum negat in subiecto habili. Sic Rom. 6. v. 2. Qui mortui sumus peccato, quomodo adhuc viuemus in eo ? q. d. non viuemus in eo.
units.tr: XXXVII. Privative things are those of which one denies the other in a subject capable of it. Thus Rom. 6.2: We who have died to sin, how shall we still live in it? That is to say, we shall not live in it.

units.la: XXXVIII. Argumentum comparatum est, quod confertur cum suo themate in aliquo tertio. Hoc saepe notis ostenditur: interdum proiecti[?] & apodosi[?] plenius explicatur, vt in exemplis patebit.
units.tr: XXXVIII. A compared argument is one that is set alongside its theme in some third thing. This is often shown by marks; sometimes the protasis and apodosis are explained more fully, as will be clear from the examples.

units.la: XXXIX. Comparatum est in quantitate siue gradu, vel in qualitate extra gradum. Ibi est par & impar, hu[?]simile & dissimile..
units.tr: XXXIX. Things are compared either in quantity or degree, or in quality outside degree. Here belong equal and unequal, like and unlike.

units.la: XL. Par est, quod cum alio confertur in vno eodemque gradu. Sic Philip. 1. v.6. Christus non duxit ra-pinam, parem esse cum Deo. Ita tres personæ sacrosanctæ Trinitatis sunt pares essentiâ & proprietatibus essentiæ 1.Ioh. 5.verf.7.
units.tr: XL. Equal is that which is compared with another in one and the same degree. Thus Phil. 1.6: Christ did not consider it robbery to be equal with God. So too the three persons of the holy Trinity are equal in essence and in the properties of the essence, 1 John 5.7.

units.la: XLI. Impar est, quod cum alio confertur in diuerso gradu, eoque maiori vel minori. Hincimparest maius, vel minus. Maius est, cuius gradus excedit: vt Act. 5. v. 29. Oportet Deo potius obedire quàm hominibus. Minus est, cuius gradus deficit: vt Psal. 89. v. 7. nemo cum lehoua potest comparari. Matt. 6. v. 26. lilia & aues cœli sunt infra hominem longo interuallo.
units.tr: XLI. Unequal is that which is compared with another in a different degree, either greater or less. Hence the unequal is the greater or the less. The greater is that whose degree exceeds: thus Acts 5.29: We ought to obey God rather than men. The less is that whose degree falls short: thus Ps. 89.7: no one can be compared with Jehovah. Matt. 6.26: the lilies and the birds of heaven are far below man.

units.la: XLII. Simile est, quod cum alio confertur in vna qualitate. Sic Psal. 1. v. 3. pius dicitur esse instar arboris iuxta riuos plantatæ. Eph. 5. v. 24. Sicut ecclesia subdita est Christo: sic vxores viris suis sint subditæ.
units.tr: XLII. Like is that which is compared with another in one quality. Thus Ps. 1.3: the godly man is said to be like a tree planted beside streams of water. Eph. 5.24: As the Church is subject to Christ, so let wives be subject to their husbands.

units.la: XLIII. Dissimile est, quod cum alio confertur in diuersa qualitate. Sic Ioh. 10. pastor bonus vitam ponit pro ouibus suis: mercenarius autem fugit. Psal. 1. v. 4. Non sic impij: scilicet vt pij. Esa. 54. v. 10. Montes commouebuntur, & colles contremiscent: fœdus autem pacis meæ non mouebitur in æternum, dicit Dominus.
units.tr: XLIII. Unlike is that which is compared with another in a different quality. Thus John 10: the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, but the hireling flees. Ps. 1.4: The wicked are not so, but like chaff. Isa. 54.10: The mountains shall be moved and the hills tremble, but my covenant of peace shall not be moved for ever, says the Lord.

units.la: XLIV. Argumentum ortum est, quod perinde arguit, sicut primum, à quo oritur. Estque nominale, vel reale. Illud arguit vocem, vt Coniugatum & Notatio. Hoc arguit rem, vt Distributio & Definitio.
units.tr: XLIV. An argument that arises from something argues in the same way as the first thing from which it arises. It is either nominal or real. The former argues a word, as the conjugate and notation do; the latter argues a thing, as distribution and definition do.
