units.la: XLV. Coniugatum est vox à voce deducta Logicè. Sic iustus à iustitiâ est Logicè: contrà iustitia est à iustus Grammaticè. Ioh. 3. v. 31. Qui è terrâ est, terrenus est, & terrena loquitur. 1. Cor. 13. vers.11. Dum puer eram, puerilitèr loquloquebar, puerili-ter sentiebam, puerili-ter cogitabam: sed vir factus, puerilia deleui.
units.tr: XLV. The conjugate is a word derived logically from another word. Thus "just" is logically derived from "justice," whereas conversely "justice" is grammatically derived from "just." John 3:31: He who is of the earth is earthly, and speaks of earthly things. 1 Cor. 13:11: When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I felt as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things.

units.la: XLVI. Notatio est vocis è suâ origine explicatio Logica. Logica dico, non Grammatica. Hæc spestat[?] vocem, quâ vox est: illa, quâ est symbolum rei, & quatenus ad intellectum refertur: vt Adam nomen habet à rubrâ terrâ Genef. 2. notatio est à materiâ. Eua sic dicta est, quòd esset mater viuentium ibid. notatio est ab effecto.
units.tr: XLVI. Notation is the logical explanation of a word from its origin. I say logical, not grammatical. The latter looks at the word as a word; the former looks at it as a sign of the thing and as it relates to the intellect. For example, Adam has his name from red earth, Gen. 2: the notation is from the material. Eve was so called because she was to be the mother of the living, ibid.: the notation is from the effect.

units.la: XLVII. Distributio est resolutio totius in partes. Totum est, quod partes habet. Estq; proprium vel improprium. Totum proprium est, quod habet partes proprie dictas. Estque genus vel integrum. Genus est totum, quod essentiam communicat speciebus: vt, animal est genus hominis & bestiæ. Integrum est totum, quod essentiam accipit à partibus. Estq; essentiale, vel materiale. Integrum essentiale est, quod constat partibus essentialibus: vt homo constat animâ & corpore Gen. 2. Integrum materiale est, q; constat partibus integrantibus: vt hominis corpus variis membris 1.Cor.12.v.14.& seqq. Estq; similare, vel dissimilare. Similare, quod constat partib. homogeneis: vt aqua Gen. 1. Dissimilare, quod constat partibus heterogeneis: vt corpus hominis 1. Cor.12. Totum improprium est, quod habet partes improprie dictas: quale est causa respectu suorum effectorum, & contrà: subiectum respectu adiunctorum, & contrà. Pars est, quæ sub toto continetur. Estque similiter propria, vel impropria. Pars propria est species, indiuiduû vel membrum. Species est pars generi subiecta. Indiuiduum est pars speciei subiecta. Sic Gen. 1. & 2. Deus creauit species & indiuidua. Membrum est, quod constituit integrũ: estq; essentiale, vel integrale. Membrum essentiale est, quod constituit totum essentiale: vt materia & forma. Membrum integrale est, quod constituit totum integrale. Estq; homogeneum seu similare, vel heterogeneũ seu dissimilare: & hoc est principale, vel minus principale. Principale, q; ad totius constitutionem simpliciter est necessarium: vt cor in homine. Minus principale, quod a toto abesse potest citra ipsius interitum: ut digitus in homine. Pars impropria est cum diuiditur causa per effecta, & contra; vel subiectum per adiuncta, & contra. Hinc iam pendet distributionis diuisio, quod sit primaria, vel secundaria. Distributio primaria est totius proprij. Est quod vel generis in species: ut, animal est homo vel bestia Psal. 32. v. vlt. vel integrum membra: ut, hominis partes sunt anima & corpus. Gen. 1. templum Salomonis distribuitur in porticum, sanctum, & sanctum sanctorum. 1. Chron. 3. Distributio secundaria est totius impropij. Estque vel causae in sua effecta, & effecti in suas causas: vel subiecti in sua adiuncta, & adiuncti in sua subiecta. e.g. ex efficiente, Scriptura est partim a prophetis, partim ab apostolis exarata Eph. 2. v. 20. ex materia, Vasa templi Salomonis erant alia ex auro, alia ex argento 1. Reg. 4. ex forma, Vasa sunt quadrata, vel rotunda: ex fine, Omnis Scriptura diuinitus inspirata utilis est ad doctrinam, ad redargutionem, ad correctionem, ad institutionem, 2. Tim. 3. ex effectis, Verbum Dei occidit, vel viuificat 2. Cor. 3. ver. 6. e subiectis, Semen aliud cecidit in viam, aliud in petrosa, aliud in spinas, aliud in terram bonam. Matth. 13. v. 4. ex adiunctis, Ministrorum in ecclesia alii sunt apostoli, alii prophetae, alii pastores, alii doctores. Eph. 4.
units.tr: XLVII. Distribution is the resolution of a whole into its parts. A whole is that which has parts. It is either proper or improper. A proper whole is that which has parts properly so called. It is either a genus or an integral whole. A genus is a whole that communicates its essence to its species, as animal is the genus of man and beast. An integral whole is a whole that receives its essence from its parts. It is either essential or material. An essential integral whole is one that consists of essential parts, as man consists of soul and body, Gen. 2. A material integral whole is one that consists of integrating parts, as the body of man consists of various members, 1 Cor. 12:14 and following. It is either similar or dissimilar. A similar whole consists of homogeneous parts, as water, Gen. 1. A dissimilar whole consists of heterogeneous parts, as the body of man, 1 Cor. 12. An improper whole is one that has improperly so-called parts; such is a cause with respect to its effects, and conversely; a subject with respect to its adjuncts, and conversely. A part is that which is contained under a whole. Parts likewise are proper or improper. A proper part is a species, an individual, or a member. A species is a part subordinate to a genus. An individual is a part subordinate to a species. So Gen. 1 and 2: God created species and individuals. A member is that which constitutes an integral whole; it is either essential or integral. An essential member is that which constitutes an essential whole, as matter and form. An integral member is that which constitutes an integral whole. It is either homogeneous or similar, or heterogeneous or dissimilar; and this is either principal or less principal. A principal member is one that is absolutely necessary to the constitution of the whole, as the heart in man. A less principal member is one that can be absent from the whole without its destruction, as a finger in man. An improper part is when a cause is divided by its effects, and conversely, or a subject by its adjuncts, and conversely. From this depends the division of distribution into primary and secondary. Primary distribution is of a proper whole. It is either of a genus into its species, as animal is man or beast, Ps. 32 last verse; or of an integral whole into its members, as the parts of man are soul and body, Gen. 1. The temple of Solomon is distributed into the porch, the holy place and the holy of holies, 1 Chron. 3. Secondary distribution is of an improper whole. It is either of a cause into its effects, and of an effect into its causes; or of a subject into its adjuncts, and of an adjunct into its subjects. E.g., from the efficient: Scripture was written partly by the prophets, partly by the apostles, Eph. 2:20. From the matter: the vessels of Solomon's temple were some of gold, some of silver, 1 Kings 4. From the form: vessels are square or round. From the end: all Scripture, divinely inspired, is profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction, 2 Tim. 3. From the effects: the Word of God kills or gives life, 2 Cor. 3:6. From the subjects: other seed fell on the path, other on rocky ground, other among thorns, other on good ground, Matt. 13:4. From the adjuncts: among the ministers in the Church some are apostles, some prophets, some ministers, some teachers, Eph. 4.

units.la: XLVIII. Definitio est, qua explicatur quid res sit. Seu, est definiti explicatio. Est autem definitio perfecta, vel imperfecta. Definitio perfecta constat terminis essentialibus: vt, Peccatum est ἀνομία 1. Ioh. 3. Videetiam definitionem fidei Hebr. 11. v. 1. Definitio imperfecta constat terminis non-essentialibus: vt, Gal. 3. v. 24. Lex est paedagogus noster in Christum respiciens.
units.tr: XLVIII. Definition is that by which it is explained what a thing is; or it is the explanation of the thing defined. A definition is either perfect or imperfect. A perfect definition consists of essential terms, as: sin is lawlessness [ἀνομία], 1 John 3. Also see the definition of faith, Heb. 11:1. An imperfect definition consists of non-essential terms, as: the law is our schoolmaster leading us to Christ, Gal. 3:24.

units.la: XLIX. Hucusque expositum est argumentum insitum: restat assumtum, quod vim suam ab alio mutuatur, & dicitur Testimonium. Testimonium est diuinum, vel humanum. Testimonium diuinum est quod Deum authorem habet: estque immediatum, quod Deus protulit sine ministerio creaturae, vt illud Matth. 3. & 17. Hic est filius ille meus dilectus, in quo valde delector. Hunc audite: vel mediatum, ad quod perhibendum Deus aliorum ministerio est vsus Hebr. 1. v. 1. Testimonium humanum est, quod hominem authorem habet. Huc pertinet obligatio, Gen. 44. v. 32. confessio, Iohan. 1. v. 20. iusiurandum, Rom. 1. v. 9. & similia multa.
units.tr: XLIX. So far has the inherent argument been set out; there remains the assumed argument, which borrows its force from another and is called testimony. Testimony is either divine or human. Divine testimony is that which has God as its author; it is either immediate, which God uttered without the ministry of a creature, as in Matt. 3 and 17: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him; or mediate, for the purpose of which God used the ministry of others, Heb. 1:1. Human testimony is that which has a man as its author. To this belong obligation, Gen. 44:32; confession, John 1:20; oath, Rom. 1:9; and many similar things.

units.la: L. Adhuc fuit inuentio, sequitur dispositio, altera Logicae pars, de disponendis thematibus & argumentis, ad bene iudicandum.
units.tr: L. So far there has been invention; there follows disposition, the second part of logic, concerning the arrangement of themes and arguments for sound judgment.

units.la: LI. Estque axiomatica, syllogistica, vel methodica.
units.tr: LI. Disposition is either axiomatic, syllogistic, or methodical.

units.la: LII. Dispositio axiomatica regit compositionem & diuisionem in axiomate, vt discernatur verum a falso.
units.tr: LII. Axiomatic disposition governs the composition and division within an axiom, so that the true may be distinguished from the false.

units.la: LIII. Axioma est, quo vnum de alio enuntiatur.
units.tr: LIII. An axiom is that by which one thing is predicated of another.

units.la: LIV. Axioma consideratur in genere, & in specie.
units.tr: LIV. An axiom is considered in general and in particular.

units.la: LV. Axioma in genere habet partes, diuisiones generales, & affectiones.
units.tr: LV. An axiom in general has parts, general divisions, and affections.

units.la: LVI. Partes axiomatis sunt subiectum & praedicatum, quae vinculo, seu adstrigmento, coaptantur. Subiectum est prior pars axiomatis, de qua aliquid dicitur: alias antecedens. Praedicatum est posterior pars axiomatis, quae de subiecto dicitur: alias consequens. In subiecto itaque quaerendum est thema, idque simplex: in praedicato argumentum, idque declarans. Multiplex autem hic est crypsis, quae facile soluitur, si attendatur natura thematis & argumenti, itemque vis constructionis & articuli Graeci, e.g. Iohan. 1. v. 1. Θεὸς ἡν ὁ λόγος[?]. Articulus a[?] monstrat subiectum. In plenis comparationibus protasis continet argumentum, apodosis thema. Itaque protasis est subiectum, apodosis praedicatum. e.g. Pfalm. 103.v.13 [?]. Vt miseretur pater liberorum, miseretur Iehova timentium ipsum. Analysis logica, expendens naturam themat is & argumenti, sic tollit crypsin, Deus miseretur timentium ipsum, ut pater miseretur liberorum.
units.tr: LVI. The parts of an axiom are the subject and the predicate, which are joined by a link or connecting term. The subject is the first part of the axiom, of which something is said; otherwise called the antecedent. The predicate is the latter part of the axiom, which is said of the subject; otherwise called the consequent. Therefore in the subject we seek the theme, and this a simple one; in the predicate the argument, and this one declaring it. There is a manifold obscurity here, which is easily resolved if one attends to the nature of the theme and the argument, and likewise to the force of the construction and of the Greek article, e.g. John 1:1: the Word was God [Θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος]. The article shows the subject. In full comparisons the protasis contains the argument, the apodosis the theme. Thus the protasis is the subject, the apodosis the predicate. E.g. Ps. 103:13: As a father pities his children, so the LORD pities those who fear him. The logical analysis, weighing the nature of the theme and the argument, removes the obscurity thus: The LORD pities those who fear him, as a father pities his children.

units.la: LVII. Generales diuisiones axiomatis sunt, quod sit affirmatum vel negatum, verum vel salsum, necessarium vel contingens, vniuerlale vel singulare. Axioma affirmatum est, cuius vinculum affirmatur, hoc est, cuius praedicatum cum subiecto coiungitur: vt 1. Cor. 13. verf. 4. Charitas est patiens. Negatum est, cuius vinculum negatur, h. e. cuius praedicatum a subiecto diuellitur: vt 1. Cor. 13. verf. 5. Charitas non quaerit sua. Vtrumque, affirmatum inquam & negatum, est purum, vel modale. Purum est, cuius praedicatum conuenit subiecto sine modo: vt, Deus est spiritus. Iohan. 4. Modale est, quod vnum habet ex his modis, Necesse, contingens, impossibile, possibile: vt Matth. 18. v. 7. Necesse est vt veniant scandala. Axioma verum est, quod pronuntiat vti res est: ita nempe vt consentanea affirmet, & dissentanea neget. Nam quae in rerum natura sunt coiuncta vel disiuncta, in oratione quoque, tum ἐνδιαθέτῳ tum προφορικῇ, oportet coniungere vel disiungere. Axioma falsum est, quod non pronuntiat vti res est: ita nempe vt consentanea neget, & dissentanea affirmet: vt Gen. 3. verf. 4. Dixit serpens mulieri, Non moriemini. Axioma necessarium est, in quo praedicatum tribuitur subiecto immutabiliter: contingens, in quo mutabiliter. In axiomate vero tres sunt gradus necessitatis, videl. κατὰ παντὸς, καθ' αὑτὸ, καθ' ὅλου τῶν ὄντων [?]. Necessarium κατὰ παντὸς est, cuius praedicatum omni subiecto semper inest: vt Iohan. 3. v.16. Omnis qui credit in Christum, habet vitam aeternam. Necessarium καθ' αὑτὸ est, cuius partes inter se sunt essentiales. Estque primi, vel secundi modi. Καθ' αὑτὸ primi modi est, cuius praedicatum est de essentia subiecti: vt, Homo est animal rationale. Καθ' αὑτὸ secundi. fecundi modi est, cuius subiectum est de essentiâ prædicati: vt, Homo est risibilis. In primo modo prædicatur sua[?] essentialis, seu essentiale à priori: in secundo proprium, seu essentiale à posteriori. Necessarium καθ' ὅλου πρῶτον[?] est, cuius prædicatum cum subiecto disponitur reciprocè. Hic τὸ καθ' ὅλου respicit prædicatum, significans illud cum subiecto sic cohærere, vt eo nec sit γενικώτερον, nec εἰδικώτερον: πρῶτον autem conuenit subiecto, indicans illud esse οἰκεῖον & germanum, ratione prædicati, quod illi non ἄλλο, sed immediatè conueniat: vt, Deus est omnipotens.
units.tr: LVII. The general divisions of an axiom are that it is affirmative or negative, true or false, necessary or contingent, universal or singular. An affirmative axiom is one whose link is affirmed, that is, whose predicate is joined to the subject: as 1 Cor. 13:4: Love is patient. A negative one is one whose link is denied, that is, whose predicate is separated from the subject: as 1 Cor. 13:5: Love does not seek its own. Both the affirmative and the negative are either pure or modal. A pure one is one whose predicate belongs to the subject without a mode: as God is spirit, John 4. A modal one is one that has one of these modes: necessary, contingent, impossible, possible: as Matt. 18:7: It is necessary that offences come. A true axiom is one that states things as they are, namely so that it affirms what agrees and denies what disagrees. For what are joined or separated in the nature of things must also be joined or separated in speech, both inward [ἐνδιάθετος] and uttered [προφορική]. A false axiom is one that does not state things as they are, namely so that it denies what agrees and affirms what disagrees: as Gen. 3:4: The serpent said to the woman, You shall not surely die. A necessary axiom is one in which the predicate is attributed to the subject unchangeably; a contingent one is that in which it is attributed changeably. In an axiom there are three degrees of necessity, namely always [κατὰ παντὸς], in itself [καθ' αὑτὸ], and of the whole [καθ' ὅλου] of beings. A necessary axiom always [κατὰ παντὸς] is one whose predicate always belongs to every subject: as John 3:16: Everyone who believes in Christ has eternal life. A necessary axiom in itself [καθ' αὑτὸ] is one whose parts are essential to one another. It is of the first or second mode. The first mode in itself is one whose predicate belongs to the essence of the subject: as Man is a rational animal. The second mode in itself is one whose subject belongs to the essence of the predicate: as Man is capable of laughter. In the first mode the essential is predicated, or the essential a priori; in the second the proper, or the essential a posteriori. A necessary axiom of the whole, first [καθ' ὅλου πρῶτον] is one whose predicate and subject are reciprocally arranged. Here "of the whole" [καθ' ὅλου] regards the predicate, signifying that it so coheres with the subject that it is neither more general nor more specific than it; "first" [πρῶτον] refers to the subject, indicating that the predicate is proper and genuine to it, because it belongs to it not through something else but immediately: as God is almighty.

units.la: Gen. 15.v.1. Axioma vniuersale est, cuius prædicatum tribuitur subiecto vniuersaliter. Estq; generale, vel speciale. Axioma generale est, cuius prædicatum tribuitur omni subiecto: vt, Matt. 15.v.13. Omnis plantatio, quam non plantauit Pater meus cœlestis, eradicabitur. Matt. 6. Nemo potest duob. dominis seruire. Axioma speciale est, in quo prædicatū tribuitur subiecto cuidam: vt, Quidā Pharisæi crediderunt in Christū Iohan. 1. & 3. Nō omnes vocati sunt electi Matt. 20. Axioma singulare, siue proprium est, cuius prædicatū vni duntaxat subiecto tribuitur: vt, Nicodemus credidit in Christū Iohan.3. Memineris axiomata singularia aliter etiā dici quę sunt inusitata philosophis: vt, Deus est homo, Panis est corpus Christi.
units.tr: Gen. 15.v.1. A universal axiom is one whose predicate is attributed to its subject universally. It is either general or special. A general axiom is one whose predicate is attributed to every subject: for example, Matt. 15.v.13. Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Matt. 6. No one can serve two masters. A special axiom is one in which the predicate is attributed to a certain subject: for example, Some Pharisees believed in Christ, John 1 and 3. Not all who are called are chosen, Matt. 20. A singular, or proper, axiom is one whose predicate is attributed to only one subject: for example, Nicodemus believed in Christ, John 3. Note that singular axioms are also called by another name, one that is unusual among the philosophers: for example, God is man; bread is the body of Christ.

units.la: LVIII. Affectiones axiomatis sunt consensio & dissensio vnius axiomatis cum alio.
units.tr: LVIII. The affections of an axiom are the agreement and disagreement of one axiom with another.

units.la: Consensio axiomatis est æquipollentia & cōuersio: dissensio, oppositio. Æquipollentia est cōueniētia axiomatū in sensu, verbis diuersis: vt, Panis est corpus Christi, Panis est sacramentū corporis Christi. 1. Cor. 11. Conuersio est subiecti & prædicati transpositio, saluâ veritate. Fit autem tribus modis. 1. Per simplicē transpositionē: vt, Deus est omnipotens, &, Qui est omnipotens, est Deus. 2. Per trāspositionē & vocularū Omnis & Quidā mutationē: vt, Omnis electus est vocatus, Quidā vocatus est electus. 3. Per trāspositionē, & cōtrapositionē, i.e. permutationē affirmationis & negationis: vt, Omnes electi sunt vocati, Qui nō sunt vocati, nō sunt electi. Oppositio est pugna duorū axiomatū; quib. nempe idem de eodé fecundum idé,ad idé, & eodé tempore affirmatur & negatur. Oppofitio ista est contraria, vel contradictoria. Oppofitio contraria est inter generale affirmatum & negatum. Et hic vtraque pars potest esse falsa: vt, Nullus dies introibit regnum coelorum, Omnis dies introibit regnum coelorum. Oppofitio contradictoria est inter generale assirmatum & speciale negatum, aut contrà; vel singulare affirmatum & negatum: vt, Nihil est ignoscendum, Aliquid est ignoscendum: Paulus fuit apostolus, Paulus non fuit apostolus. Et hic necesse est alteram partem esse veram, alteram falsam. Hinc Scholastici: Contradictio non est in sinu Dei, qui non miscet ea, quæ sunt & non sunt.
units.tr: The agreement of axioms is equipollence and conversion; disagreement is opposition. Equipollence is the agreement of axioms in sense though with different words: for example, Bread is the body of Christ; bread is the sacrament of the body of Christ. 1 Cor. 11. Conversion is the transposition of subject and predicate with the truth preserved. It happens in three ways. (1) By simple transposition: for example, God is almighty, and, Whoever is almighty is God. (2) By transposition together with a change of the words all and some: for example, Every elect person is called; some called person is elect. (3) By transposition and contraposition, that is, by exchanging affirmation and negation: for example, All the elect are called; those who are not called are not elect. Opposition is the conflict of two axioms, in which the same thing is affirmed and denied of the same thing, in the same respect and at the same time. This opposition is either contrary or contradictory. Contrary opposition lies between a general affirmative and a general negative, and here both parts may be false: for example, No day will enter the kingdom of heaven; every day will enter the kingdom of heaven. Contradictory opposition lies between a general affirmative and a special negative, or the reverse, or between a singular affirmative and a singular negative: for example, Nothing is to be forgiven; something is to be forgiven. Paul was an apostle; Paul was not an apostle. Here one part must be true and the other false. Hence the Schoolmen say: "Contradiction is not in the bosom of God," who does not mix together things that are and are not.

units.la: LIX. Axioma in specie diuiditur in simplex, & compositum.
units.tr: LIX. An axiom, considered in its kinds, is divided into simple and compound.

units.la: Axima simplex est, in quo vnum de vno præadicatur: seu, quod continetur vinculo verbi: vt, Christus est filius Dei Iohan. 3. Axioma compositum est, in quo duo minimum simplicia, vinculo coniunctionis, coiunguntur. Estque congregatiuum, vel fegregatiuum. Congregatiuum est, cuius partes coniunctione vinciuntur; fiue consentanea, fiue dissentanea enuntiet. Estque copulatum, vel connexum. Axioma copulatum est, cuius coniunctio est copulatiua: vt, Eccles. 11. v. 3. Bona & mala, vita & mors, pauperta & diuitia à Domino proficiscuntur. Coniunctioni copulatiuæ æquipollent particulæ relatiuæ: vt, Matth. 24. Vbi cadauer, ibi aquilæ. Axioma connexum est, cuius coniunctio est connexiua, seu conditionalis: vt, Gen. 3. v. 3. Si vescemini de fructu arboris, moriemini. Hoc axiomate disponi possunt omnis generis argumenta, exceptis diuersis. Hinc recte procedit ista connexio: Rom. 8. v. 17. Si fumus filij, etiam hæredes: item illa Rom. 11. ver. 6. Si salus est per gratiam, iam non ex operibus. Sed hæc non procedit: Si homo est dies, etiam Deo placet: vel, Si est dies, Deo non placet. Axioma fegregatiuum est, cuius partes coniunctione separantur. Itaque enuntiat tantum dissentanea. Estque discretum, vel disiunctum. Axioma discretum est, cuius coniunctio est difcretiua. Dicitur etiam prolepticum, quia ferme occupat obiectionem. Hoc axiomate sola diuersa enuntiantur: vt, 1. Cor. 8. v. 5. Quanquam multi dicantur dij: nobis tamen vnus est Deus. Axioma disiunctum est, cuius coniunctio est disiunctiua. Enuntiat tantum opposita: vt, Aut fide iustificamur, aut operibus. Rom. 4. Dicitur etiam propositio alternativa.
units.tr: A simple axiom is one in which one thing is predicated of one thing, or which is contained within the bond of a verb: for example, Christ is the Son of God, John 3. A compound axiom is one in which at least two simple axioms are joined by a conjunction. It is either congregative or segregative. A congregative axiom is one whose parts are bound together by a conjunction, whether it states agreeing or disagreeing things. It is either copulative or connective. A copulative axiom is one whose conjunction is copulative: for example, Eccles. 11. v. 3. Good and evil, life and death, poverty and riches come from the Lord. Relative particles are equivalent to copulative conjunctions: for example, Matth. 24. Where the carcass is, there the eagles will be. A connective axiom is one whose conjunction is connective, or conditional: for example, Gen. 3. v. 3. If you eat of the fruit of the tree, you will die. All kinds of arguments can be arranged in this axiom, except the diverse ones. Hence this connection rightly proceeds: Rom. 8. v. 17. If we are sons, then also heirs; likewise that of Rom. 11. v. 6. If salvation is by grace, it is no longer from works. But this does not proceed: If man is a day, he also pleases God; or, If it is day, it does not please God. A segregative axiom is one whose parts are separated by a conjunction. Therefore it states only disagreeing things. It is either discretive or disjunctive. A discretive axiom is one whose conjunction is discretive. It is also called proleptic, because it almost anticipates an objection. Only different things are stated by this axiom: for example, 1 Cor. 8. v. 5. Although there are many who are called gods, yet for us there is one God. A disjunctive axiom is one whose conjunction is disjunctive. It states only opposites: for example, We are justified either by faith or by works, Rom. 4. It is also called an alternative proposition.

units.la: LX. Sic fuit dispositio axiomatica: sequitur syllogistica, quae regit discursum in syllogismo, vt discernatur consequens & inconsequens.
units.tr: LX. Thus is the axiomatic arrangement; there follows the syllogistic, which governs the reasoning in a syllogism, so that what follows and what does not follow may be distinguished.

units.la: LXI. Syllogismus est, quo thema compositum disponitur cum argumento probante, vt positis praemissis sequatur conclusio.
units.tr: LXI. A syllogism is that in which a compound thesis is set alongside a proving argument, so that, with the premises laid down, the conclusion follows.

units.la: LXII. In syllogismo spectantur fundamenta, partes & species.
units.tr: LXII. In a syllogism one considers its foundations, parts and species.

units.la: LXIII. Fundamenta siue principia syllogismi sunt duo. Primum est dictum de omni, & nullo. Dictum de omni est, quando sub subiecto nihil potest sumi, cui non tribuitur praedicatum: vt, Omnis homo est mendax Psal. 116. Ergo & Abraham, & Dauid, & Petrus. Dictum de nullo est, quando sub subiecto nihil potest sumi, de quo non remoueatur praedicatum: vt, Nullus homo est Deus. Ergo nec Herodes. Alterum syllogismi fundamentum est dictum proportionis: Quae conueniunt vel non conueniunt in tertio, inter se conueniunt vel non conueniunt: vt, Christus est omnipotens. Ergo est Deus. Hic Christus & Deus conueniunt in illo tertio, omnipotens. Itaque inter se conueniunt. Homo non est omnipotens. Ergo non est Deus. Hic homo & Deus non conueniunt in isto tertio, omnipotens. Ergo nec inter se conueniunt. Atq; haec sunt principia regulatiua cuiusuis syllogismi.
units.tr: LXIII. The foundations or principles of a syllogism are two. The first is the dictum concerning all and the dictum concerning none. The dictum concerning all is when, under the subject, nothing can be taken to which the predicate is not attributed: for example, Every man is a liar, Psalm 116. Therefore Abraham too, and David, and Peter. The dictum concerning none is when, under the subject, nothing can be taken from which the predicate is not removed: for example, No man is God. Therefore neither is Herod. The other foundation of the syllogism is the dictum of proportion: things which agree or do not agree in a third thing agree or do not agree with one another. For example, Christ is almighty; therefore he is God. Here Christ and God agree in that third thing, almighty, and so they agree with one another. Man is not almighty; therefore he is not God. Here man and God do not agree in that third thing, almighty, and therefore they do not agree with one another either. These are the regulating principles of any syllogism whatever.

units.la: LXIV. Partes syllogismi sunt materia & forma. Materia syllogismi est tum remota, vt sunt tres termini, e quibus duo sunt in conclusione seu quaestione, tertius est ipsum argumentum: tum propinqua, vt duae praemissae, puta maior & minor, seu propositio & assumtio; & conclusio. Forma syllogismi est apta medij termini cum extremis difpositio.
units.tr: LXIV. The parts of a syllogism are matter and form. The matter of a syllogism is partly remote, namely the three terms, of which two are in the conclusion or question, and the third is the argument itself; and partly proximate, namely the two premises, the major and the minor, or proposition and assumption, and the conclusion. The form of a syllogism is the fitting arrangement of the middle term with the extremes.

units.la: LXV. Species syllogismi sunt, quòd alius sit manifestus, alius crypticus. Syllogismus manifestus est, [?] in quo nulla est anomalia. Estque simplex, vel compositus. Syllogismus simplex est, in quo praedicatum quaestionis est in propositione, subiectum in assumtione. Eius figurae sunt tres. Prima figura est, in qua argumentum antecedit in propositione, sequitur affirmatum in assumtione: ut, Rom. 1. & 2.
units.tr: LXV. The species of syllogism are that one is manifest and another cryptic. A manifest syllogism is [?] one in which there is no anomaly. It is either simple or compound. A simple syllogism is one in which the predicate of the question is in the proposition and the subject in the assumption. It has three figures. The first figure is that in which the argument comes first in the proposition, and the affirmative follows in the assumption: for example, Rom. 1. and 2.

units.la: Omnes peccatores sunt rei irae divinae.
units.tr: All sinners are liable to the wrath of God.

units.la: Omnes homines sunt peccatores.
units.tr: All men are sinners.

units.la: Ergo omnes homines sunt rei irae divinae.
units.tr: Therefore all men are liable to the wrath of God.

units.la: Secunda figura est, in qua argumentum semper sequitur, negatum in altera parte: ut, Rom. 8.
units.tr: The second figure is that in which the argument always follows, negated in the other part: for example, Rom. 8.

units.la: Nulli in carne viuentes Deo placent.
units.tr: Those living in the flesh do not please God.

units.la: Omnes iuxta spiritum versantes Deo placent.
units.tr: All who walk according to the Spirit please God.

units.la: Ego nulli iuxta spiritum versantes viuunt in carne.
units.tr: Therefore none who walk according to the Spirit live in the flesh.

units.la: Tertia figura est, in qua argumentum semper antecedit, affirmatum in assumtione: ut, Rom. 8.
units.tr: The third figure is that in which the argument always comes first, affirmed in the assumption: for example, Rom. 8.

units.la: Omnes iustificati glorificantur.
units.tr: All the justified are glorified.

units.la: Omnes iustificati sancte viuunt.
units.tr: All the justified live holily.

units.la: Ergo quidam qui sancte viunt, glorificantur.
units.tr: Therefore some who live holily are glorified.

units.la: Syllogismus compositus est, in quo tota quaestio disponitur cum argumento in propositione. Estque connexus, vel disiunctus. Syllogismus connexus est, cuius propositio est connexa. Estque primi, vel secundi modi. Connexus primi modi est, qui assumit antecedens, & concludit consequens: ut Rom. 8. v. 17.
units.tr: A compound syllogism is one in which the whole question is set out with the argument in the proposition. It is either connective or disjunctive. A connective syllogism is one whose proposition is connective. It is of the first or second mode. The connective of the first mode is one that assumes the antecedent and concludes the consequent: for example, Rom. 8. v. 17.

units.la: Si sumus filij Dei, sumus etiam haeredes regni cœlorum.
units.tr: If we are sons of God, we are also heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: Atqui sumus filii Dei.
units.tr: But we are sons of God.

units.la: Ergo etiam sumus haeredes regni coelorum.
units.tr: Therefore we are also heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

units.la: Connexus secundi modi est, qui tollit consequens, ut tollat antecedens: ut, Gal. 2. v. ult.
units.tr: The connective of the second mode is one that denies the consequent so as to deny the antecedent: for example, Gal. 2. v. last.

units.la: Si per legem iustitia obueniret, Christus frustra effet mortuus.
units.tr: If righteousness came through the law, Christ died in vain.

units.la: Sed Christus non est frustra mortuus.
units.tr: But Christ did not die in vain.

units.la: Ergo iustitia non obuenit per legem.
units.tr: Therefore righteousness does not come through the law.

units.la: Syllogismus disiunctus est, cuius propositio est disiunctiua. Estque primi, vel secundi modi. Disiunctus primi modi est, qui tollit unum, & reliquum concludit. Itaq; habet conclusionem affirmatam: ut, Rom. 4.
units.tr: A disjunctive syllogism is one whose major premise is disjunctive. It is of the first or the second mood. The disjunctive of the first mood denies one part and concludes the other. So it has an affirmative conclusion, as in Rom. 4.

units.la: Aut ex merito Deus nos saluat, aut ex gratia.
units.tr: Either God saves us by merit, or by grace.

units.la: Sed non ex merito nos saluat.
units.tr: But he does not save us by merit.

units.la: Ergo saluat nos ex gratia.
units.tr: Therefore he saves us by grace.

units.la: Disiunctus secundi modi est, qui assumit unum, & reliquum tollit. Itaque habet conclusionem negatam: ut, Matth. 6.
units.tr: The disjunctive of the second mood affirms one part and removes the other. So it has a negative conclusion, as in Matt. 6.

units.la: Aut Deo seruiendum, aut Mammonae.
units.tr: Either God must be served, or Mammon.

units.la: At Deo seruiendum.
units.tr: But God must be served.

units.la: Ergo non Mammonae.
units.tr: Therefore not Mammon.

units.la: Syllogismus crypticus est, qui admittit anomaliam. Estq; defectus, redundans, vel inuersus. Syllogismus defectus est enthymema, exemplum, vel inductio. Enthymema est, in quo deficit propositio, assumtio, vel conclusio: ut 1. Cor. 6. v. 20. Emti estis pretio. Glorificate igitur Deum in corpore vestro. Hic deest propositio. Sic 1. Tim. 6. v.17. Exemplum est, quo hypothesis transfertur ad thesin syllogisticè: ut Rom. 4. Abraham fuit iustificatus fide. Ergo & nos fide iustificamur. Inductio est, qua ex singularibus omnibus rite collectis infertur conclusio vniuersalis: ut Heb 11. Abel, Enoch, Noë, & similes sancti placuerunt Deo per fidem. Ego fieri non potest, ut quisquam Deo placeat sine fide. Syllogismus redundans est sorites & dilemma. Sorites est, in quo coaceruantur plura axiomata, ita ut semper praedicatum praecedentis sit subiectum sequentis, donec conclusio inferatur, in qua praedicatum ultimi axiomatis tribuatur subiecto primi: ut, Rom. 8. v. 29.30.
units.tr: A cryptic syllogism is one that admits an anomaly. It is defective, redundant, or inverted. A defective syllogism is an enthymeme, an example, or an induction. An enthymeme is one in which a premise, an assumption, or the conclusion is lacking, as in 1 Cor. 6:20: "You were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body." Here the major premise is lacking. So also 1 Tim. 6:17. An example is one in which a hypothesis is transferred syllogistically to a thesis, as in Rom. 4: Abraham was justified by faith. Therefore we too are justified by faith. An induction is one in which a universal conclusion is rightly inferred from all the singulars collected, as in Heb. 11: Abel, Enoch, Noah, and similar saints pleased God through faith. But it cannot happen that anyone pleases God without faith. A redundant syllogism is the sorites and the dilemma. The sorites is one in which several axioms are heaped together, so that the predicate of each preceding axiom is the subject of the next, until a conclusion is drawn in which the predicate of the last axiom is attributed to the subject of the first, as in Rom. 8:29-30.

units.la: Quos Deus praenouit, illos praedestinauit.
units.tr: Whom God foreknew, them he also predestined.

units.la: Quos praedestinauit, eos etiam vocauit.
units.tr: Whom he predestined, them he also called.

units.la: Quos vocauit, eos etiam iustificauit.
units.tr: Whom he called, them he also justified.

units.la: Quos iustificauit, eos etiam glorificauit.
units.tr: Whom he justified, them he also glorified.

units.la: Egò quos Deus praenouit, eos glorificauit.
units.tr: Therefore whom God foreknew, them he glorified.

units.la: Si malis, ita enuntia: Omnes praescíti sunt praedestinati, Omnes praedestinati sunt vocati. Omnes vocati sunt iustificati. Omnes iustificati sunt glorificati. E. omnes praescíti sunt glorificati. Dilemma est, in quo ex oppositis immediatis ita concluditur, ut utroque cornu feriatur adversarius; ut Iohan. 18.v.20. est eiusmodi dilemma Christi: Aut male loquutus sum, aut bene. Si male, testare de malo. Sin bene, cur me caedis? Huc etiam pertinet illud. Si homines legem Dei implent, aut damnati, aut electi eam implebunt. Non illi: quia damnantur. Non hi: quia ipsis opus est morte Christi. Syllogismus inuersus est, in quo propositio, assumtio & conclusio vel singulae, vel universae sunt transpositae: ut, Rom.8.v.4.5.9. transponuntur partes syllogismi, quarum ordo naturalis hic est.
units.tr: If you prefer, put it thus: All those foreknown are predestined. All the predestined are called. All the called are justified. All the justified are glorified. Therefore all the foreknown are glorified. A dilemma is one in which a conclusion is drawn from immediate opposites so that the opponent is struck on both horns. Christ's dilemma in John 18:20 is of this kind: either I spoke badly, or well. If badly, bear witness to the evil. But if well, why do you strike me? To this also belongs the following: If men fulfil God's law, either the damned or the elect will fulfil it. Not the damned, because they are damned. Not the elect, because they need the death of Christ. An inverted syllogism is one in which the premise, the assumption and the conclusion, singly or all together, are transposed, as in Rom. 8:4, 5, 9, where the parts of the syllogism are transposed; their natural order is this:

units.la: Qui sunt secundum carnem, ij ambulant secundum carnem.v.5.
units.tr: Those who are according to the flesh walk according to the flesh. v. 5.

units.la: Vos autem non estis secundum carnem.v.9.
units.tr: But you are not according to the flesh. v. 9.

units.la: Ergo vos non ambulatis secundum carnem.v.4.
units.tr: Therefore you do not walk according to the flesh. v. 4.

units.la: Ibidem continetur alius syllogismus eiusdem sententiae in contrariis, hoc modo.
units.tr: In the same passage is contained another syllogism of the same sense, but in contrary terms, as follows.

units.la: Qui sunt secundum spiritum, ij ambulant secundum spiritum.v.5.
units.tr: Those who are according to the Spirit walk according to the Spirit. v. 5.

units.la: Vos estis secundum spiritum. v.9.
units.tr: You are according to the Spirit. v. 9.

units.la: Ergo vos ambulatis secundum spiritum. v.4.
units.tr: Therefore you walk according to the Spirit. v. 4.

units.la: LXVI. Dispositio methodica regit discursum in methodo, ut discernatur ordo & confusio.
units.tr: LXVI. Methodical arrangement governs the discourse within a method, so that order and confusion may be told apart.

units.la: LXVII. Methodus est, quā disponuntur varia axiomata homogenea procedendo à generalibus ad specialia. Axiomata homogenea sunt, quae ad unum scopum tendunt. Generalia vero sunt, quae sine aliis cognosci queunt, & sine quibus alia cognosci non possunt. Sic historia lapsus Gen. 3. non potuit cognosci sine historia creationis Gen. 1. Sed haec sine illa potuit cognosci. Caeterūm methodus est vnica ratione formæ modò expressæ. Sed modi & gradus eius sunt varij. Est enim methodus didascalica, vel historica: exquisita, vel popularis: synthetica, vel analytica. Didascalicæ exemplum est in epistolâ ad Hebræos: historicæ Gen. 1. 2. & seqq. exquisitæ Rom. 9. 10. 11. popularis Rom. 12. 13. 14. 15. 16. syntheticæ Rom. 9. & 10. Eph. 1. analyticæ. Iacob. 2.
units.tr: LXVII. Method is that by which various homogeneous axioms are arranged, proceeding from the general to the special. Homogeneous axioms are those that tend to one aim. General axioms are those that can be known without others and without which others cannot be known. Thus the history of the fall, Gen. 3, could not be known without the history of creation, Gen. 1, but the latter could be known without the former. Method is one in its rational form, as just expressed, but its modes and grades are various. For method is either didactic or historical, exquisite or popular, synthetic or analytic. An example of the didactic is the epistle to the Hebrews; of the historical, Gen. 1, 2 and following; of the exquisite, Rom. 9, 10, 11; of the popular, Rom. 12-16; of the synthetic, Rom. 9 and 10, Eph. 1; of the analytic, James 2.

units.la: XXVI. ORATORIA SACRA.
units.tr: XXVI. Sacred Oratory.

units.la: I. Oratoria sacra est ars copiosè dicendi ad imitationem scripturæ sacræ.
units.tr: I. Sacred oratory is the art of speaking copiously in imitation of Holy Scripture.

units.la: II. Eius partes sunt quinque: Inventio, Dispositio, Elocutio, Memoria, & Pronuntiatio. Si velis, ita revoca ad dichotomiam: Partes oratoriæ facultatis duæ sunt, Formatio orationis, & Promulgatio. Formatio respicit tum res in Inventione & Dispositione, tum verba in Elocutione. Promulgatio est ratione Memoriæ & Pronuntiationis.
units.tr: II. Its parts are five: Invention, Disposition, Elocution, Memory, and Delivery. If you wish, you may reduce these to a dichotomy: the parts of the oratorical faculty are two, the Formation of the speech and its Publication. Formation concerns both the matter, in Invention and Disposition, and the words, in Elocution. Publication concerns Memory and Delivery.

units.la: III, Inventio est, quâ orator cogitat de themate & argumento idoneo. Confer cum Logicis.
units.tr: III. Invention is that by which the orator considers a suitable theme and argument. Compare with the Logicians.

units.la: IV. Thema est illud ipsum, de quo dicendum est oratori.
units.tr: IV. The theme is that very matter about which the orator must speak.

units.la: V. Estque generis demonstratiui, deliberatiui, vel iudicialis: quibus accidit character. Hæc vsitatè dicuntur tria causarum genera.
units.tr: V. It is of the demonstrative, deliberative, or judicial kind, and each of these has its own character. These are commonly called the three kinds of causes.

units.la: VI. Genus demonstratiuum vertitur in didascalia, laudes, & vituperio. Didascalia est, quâ orator docet. Eius exempla sunt Esa. 66. de vero Dei cultu: Matth. 6. de providentia Dei: c. 13. de diligenti auscultatione & meditatione verbi Dei: c. 24. 25. de fine seculi: Rom. 2. 3. 4. de iustificatione: Gal. 3. similiter: 1. Cor. 15. de resurrectione mortuorum: Heb.1.2. de duabus in Christo naturis: c.5.6.7.8.9.10. de abrogatione sacerdotij legalis, & successione sacerdotii æterni Iesu Christi: Laus est persona, rei, vel facti. Personæ: vt Cyri Esa. 42. Iohannis Baptistæ Luc. 7. Rei: vt verbi Dei Psalm. 19. & 119. ecclesiæ Psalm. 87. concordiæ Psal. 133. donorum Dei 1. Cor. 12.13, 14. Ad laudem personæ pertinet doxologia: vt Esa. 12. Psal. 103. & 104. Rom.1. verf.27.1.Tim.1.v.17. Facti: vt Heb.11. Vituperium similiter est personæ, rei, vel facti. Personæ: vt Matth.23. Gal.3.verf.1.Luc.14.v.25. Rei: vt Gal.6. verf.19.20. Facti: vt 1. Cor. 5.
units.tr: VI. The demonstrative kind turns on teaching, praise, and blame. Teaching is that by which the orator instructs. Examples are Isa. 66 on the true worship of God; Matt. 6 on the providence of God; ch. 13 on diligent hearing and meditation on the Word of God; chs. 24 and 25 on the end of the age; Rom. 2, 3, and 4 on justification; Gal. 3 likewise; 1 Cor. 15 on the resurrection of the dead; Heb. 1 and 2 on the two natures in Christ; chs. 5 to 10 on the abrogation of the legal priesthood and the succession of the eternal priesthood of Jesus Christ. Praise concerns a person, a thing, or a deed. Of a person: as Isa. 42 of Cyrus; Luke 7 of John the Baptist. Of a thing: as Ps. 19 and 119 of the Word of God; Ps. 87 of the Church; Ps. 133 of concord; 1 Cor. 12, 13, and 14 of the gifts of God. Doxology belongs to the praise of a person: as Isa. 12; Ps. 103 and 104; Rom. 1:27; 1 Tim. 1:17. Of a deed: as Heb. 11. Blame likewise concerns a person, a thing, or a deed. Of a person: as Matt. 23; Gal. 3:1; Luke 14:25. Of a thing: as Gal. 6:19, 20. Of a deed: as 1 Cor. 5.

units.la: VII. Genus deliberatiuum positum est in institutione, correctione, & consolatione. Hinc thema est vel institutiuum Esa. 40. 49. 55. 56. Ier. 3. 4.18.27.33. Marc. 9.10.11.1.Cor.16. 2.Cor.8. vel correctiuum Esa. 1.28. 58.59. Ier. 2.5.6.7.8.9. Ezech.11. 13.14.16.19.20.22.23.28.34. Hos.1.2.3.4. Matth. 11.12.16.21.23. Marc. 2. 8.11. vel consolatorium Esa.32.35.40. & octo sequ. Ier.29.30.31. Ezech.38.40. Ioh.14. & seqq. Rom.8. Hebr.10.
units.tr: VII. The deliberative kind rests on instruction, correction, and consolation. Hence the theme is either instructive: Isa. 40, 49, 55, 56; Jer. 3, 4, 18, 27, 33; Mark 9, 10, 11; 1 Cor. 16; 2 Cor. 8; or corrective: Isa. 1, 28, 58, 59; Jer. 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9; Ezek. 11, 13, 14, 16, 19, 20, 22, 23, 28, 34; Hos. 1, 2, 3, 4; Matt. 11, 12, 16, 21, 23; Mark 2, 8, 11; or consolatory: Isa. 32, 35, 40, and the eight following chapters; Jer. 29, 30, 31; Ezek. 38, 40; John 14 and following; Rom. 8; Heb. 10.

units.la: VIII. Genus iudiciale positum est in refutatione. Hinc thema est redargutiuum Esa. 8.28.29.31.44. 46.47. Matth.5.6.7.15. Rom.1.2. & seqq. 1. Cor. 8. 9.10.15. Ex his patet esse quinque status thematis, ita vt alius sit ἀδαχλικὸς[?] (sub quo ἐγκωμιαστικὸς ἢ ψεκτικὸς, i.e. laudatiuus & vituperatiuus) παιδευτικὸς, ἐπανορθωτικὸς, παρα-κλητικὸς[?], ἢ ἐλεγκτικὸς. Itaque dispiciat orator in deligendo themate, vt illud sit distinctum, non confusum, aut implicatum. Tametsi enim oratio fere miscet varia themata: tamen semper habet principalem aliquem statum vel doctrinæ, vel institutionis, vel correctionis, vel consolationis, vel refutationis.
units.tr: VIII. The judicial kind rests on refutation. Hence the theme is refutative: Isa. 8, 28, 29, 31, 44, 46, 47; Matt. 5, 6, 7, 15; Rom. 1, 2, and following; 1 Cor. 8, 9, 10, 15. From these it is clear that there are five states of the theme: it is either didactic [διδασκαλικὸς] (under which fall the encomiastic [ἐγκωμιαστικὸς] or laudatory, and the vituperative [ψεκτικὸς]), paedeutic, epanorthotic, paracletic [παρακλητικὸς], or elenctic [ἐλεγκτικὸς]. The orator, therefore, must take care in choosing his theme that it be distinct, not confused or entangled. For although a speech generally mixes various themes, it always has some principal state, whether of teaching, instruction, correction, consolation, or refutation.

units.la: IX. Character thematis est sublimis, medius, vel humilis. Character sublimis est rerum magnarum: quales sunt Deus, vita æterna, pulchritudo & ascensio Christi. Vide Exod. 34. 1. Cor. 2. verf. 9. Act. 1. Psal. 45. Character medium est rerum mediocrium: quales sunt homo, terra, piscis. Gen. 1. Character humilis est rerum minutarum & vilium: quales sunt Cain, Cham, opilio. Triplicem hunc characterem diligenter expendet orator, ut videat qualia argumenta & ornamenta debeat adferre in medium. Si enim v. g. de templo Salomonis sint verba facienda, character sublimis ostendit, qualis debeat esse tractatio argumentosa.
units.tr: IX. The character of the theme is lofty, middling, or low. The lofty character belongs to great things, such as God, eternal life, the beauty and ascension of Christ. See Exod. 34; 1 Cor. 2:9; Acts 1; Ps. 45. The middling character belongs to things of middling rank, such as man, the earth, a fish: Gen. 1. The low character belongs to small and base things, such as Cain, Ham, a shepherd. The orator will weigh this threefold character carefully, so that he sees what kind of arguments and ornaments he ought to bring forward. For if, say, one must speak about Solomon's temple, the lofty character shows that the treatment should be weighty in its arguments.

units.la: X. Argumentum est, quo thema evolvitur.
units.tr: X. The argument is that by which the theme is unfolded.

units.la: Ita nempe ut explicetur vel disputetur.
units.tr: That is, it is explained or disputed.

units.la: XI. Argumentum consideratur in genere, & in specie.
units.tr: XI. The argument is considered in general and in particular.

units.la: XII. In genere argumentum est docens, delectans, vel movens: vel, ut alij loquuntur, logicum, ethicum, & patheticum. Argumentum docens est, quo natura rei ita ponitur ob oculos, ut intelligatur. Estque declarans, probans, vel amplificans. Argumentum declarans est, quo thema simplex explicatur: probans, quo thema compositum demonstratur: amplificans, quo utrumque thema dilatatur. Sumuntur autem haec argumenta ex locis inventionis Logicae. Nam causa, effectum, subiecto &c. faciunt ad declarandum, probandum, & amplificandum. Prae ceteris tamen ad amplificandum faciunt antithesis[?], syncrisis, distributio, & testimonium: Argumentum delectans est, quo conciliatur animus auditoris. Hoc sumitur ex locis ethicis virtutum: videl. a persona dicentis & audientis: si & ille prudentem, si probum, si sui ipsius memorem, si benevolum se oratione probet: & hic se digna audiat, & ætati[?], moribus, & studiis suis convenientia. Rom. 9.v.1 2.3.4.5.1 Iohan.2.v.1. Argumentum movens est, quo excitatur vel sedatur affectus in auditore. Hoc sumitur ex locis affectuum, puta irae, amoris, odij, timoris, pudoris, indignationis, invidiae, aemulationis. Gal.3.v.1.1.Cor.5.
units.tr: XII. In general, the argument is teaching, delighting, or moving; or, as others put it, logical, ethical, and pathetic. An argument that teaches is that by which the nature of the thing is set before the eyes so that it is understood. It is either declaring, proving, or amplifying. A declaring argument is that by which a simple theme is explained; a proving argument is that by which a compound theme is demonstrated; an amplifying argument is that by which either theme is enlarged. These arguments are drawn from the topics of Logical invention. For cause, effect, subject, and so on serve to declare, prove, and amplify. Above all, however, antithesis, syncrisis, distribution, and testimony serve to amplify. An argument that delights is that by which the mind of the hearer is won over. This is drawn from the ethical topics of the virtues, namely from the person of the speaker and of the hearer: whether the speaker shows himself by his speech to be prudent, upright, mindful of himself, and well-disposed; and whether the hearer hears what is worthy of himself and fitting to his age, manners, and studies. Rom. 9:1, 2, 3, 4, 5; 1 John 2:1. An argument that moves is that by which the affection in the hearer is stirred up or calmed. This is drawn from the topics of the emotions, such as anger, love, hatred, fear, shame, indignation, envy, and rivalry. Gal. 3:1; 1 Cor. 5.

units.la: XIII. Argumentum in specie consideratur, quantum ad genera thematis, & speciales affectus. Quantum ad genera thematis, loca praecipua didascalia sunt definitio, distributio, causae, effecta, cognata, & pugnantia: laudis & vituperij, quantum ad personas, genus, natio, natales, educatio, bona malaue animi, corporis, & fortunae; res gestae, earumque praemia & poenae; mors: quantum ad res, causae, adiuncta bona & mala, & effecta: quantum ad facta, honestum & turpe, utile & inutile, facile & difficile. Deinde loca generis instituti praecipua sunt, ab honesto, iusto, aequo, pio, utili, tuto, decoro, laudabili, necessario, facili, possibili, praeceptis & promissionibus Dei, consilio sanctorum prophetarum & apostolorum, exemplis & factis sanctorum, utilitate quae redibit ad nos vel universam ecclesiam, illustratione gloriae Dei, aedificatione aliorum, etiam integrarum ecclesiarum; a gloria expectanda apud Deum, angelos, & homines; a metu ignominiae, certitudine & magnitudine praemiorum.
units.tr: XIII. The argument in particular is considered with respect to the kinds of theme and to the particular affections. With respect to the kinds of theme, the principal topics of teaching are definition, division, causes, effects, things akin and things opposed. Of praise and blame, with respect to persons: birth, nation, parentage, upbringing, good and bad qualities of mind, body, and fortune; deeds done and their rewards and punishments; death. With respect to things: causes, attendant goods and evils, and effects. With respect to deeds: the honourable and the shameful, the useful and the useless, the easy and the difficult. Next, the principal topics of the instructive kind are drawn from what is honourable, just, equitable, godly, useful, safe, becoming, praiseworthy, necessary, easy, possible; from the precepts and promises of God; from the counsel of the holy prophets and apostles; from the examples and deeds of the saints; from the benefit that will return to us or to the whole Church; from the illustration of the glory of God; from the edification of others, even of whole churches; from the glory to be expected before God, the angels, and men; from the fear of disgrace, and from the certainty and greatness of the rewards.

units.la: Tertio loca generis correctiui sunt contraria locis generis praecedentis: e.g. ab inhonesto, iniusto, inutili &c. Quartò praecipua loca generis consolatorij sunt ab honesto, iusto, aequo, utili, inutili, decoro, laudabili, facili, necessario genere malorum, providentia Dei, praesidio sanctorum angelorum, iustitia Dei, rectitudine conscientiae; eo quod credentibus omnia adiumento sint ad bonum; ab effectu afflictionum, promissionibus Dei, necessario signo & effecto divinae electionis, exemplo Christi, exemplis sanctorum, certitudine praemiorum, aedificatione aliorum, praesenti auxilio Spiritus sancti, natura spei & patientiae, effectu meritorum Christi. Quinto praecipua loca generis elencticj sunt ab inutili, iniusto, periculoso, dissentaneis, & dissimilibus. Quantum attinet ad speciales afsectus, ad excitandam solicitudinem adipiscendi salutem aeternam conducunt argumenta ab honesto, a peccatorum turpitudine & magnitudine, ab agnitione humanae fragilitatis, a miseriis internis & externis, quae comitantur vitam peccatis obnoxia; a bonis innumerabilibus, quae a melioris vitae proposito contingunt; a damnis, quae vitae turpitudinè comitantur; à necessario; à facili, v.g. quòd Dei gratiâ opitulante possimus resistere diabolo: ad concitandū odium & detestationem peccati faciunt loci ab authoritate, magnitudine, & diligentiâ piorum; à personarum, quæ vitiis deditæ sunt, vilitate; à vitioi um[?] forma, modo, & reliquis circumstantiis; à magnitudine malorum, quæ ex præsentibus peccatis iam enata sunt, quæque in posterum accedere possunt; ab eo, quòd tam sordidi & abiecti esse non debemus, qui hosti nostro diabolo velimus animos & corpora nostra submittere, ad seruiendum impiis eius suggestionibus; ab eo, quòd perfidiæ, imò & læsæ maiestatis Dei incurrimus crimen, si à Christo deficiamus ad Belial; ab eo, quòd sit summa ingratitudo & crudelitas[?], Christum peccatis suis denuò crucifigere; ab eo, quòd peccatis nos inquinando cõtristamus Spiritum[?] sanctum, sanctosque angelos custodes nostros, itemque vniuersam ecclesiam infamamus; ab eo, quòd si acquiescimus suggestionibus diaboli, nobis ipsis nostræque malitiæ omnis culpa imputabitur, neque vllam prætexere licebit excusationem, & nos ipsi luituri sumus pœnas pro his, quæ suadente diabolo designauerimus: ad excitandum amorem & studium virtutis faciunt loca à religioso, pio, glorioso[?], necessario, circumstantiis, signis, antecedentibus, connexis, consequentibus, exemplis, imitatione Dei, Christi, angelorum & hominum sanctorum: ad imprimendum metum diuini iudicij argumentabimur à nostrâ indignitate, propriâ culpâ, nostrâ imbecillitate; à grauitate pœnarum; ab eo, quòd necessarium sit promissiones & comminationes Dei perfici; ab exemplis eorum, qui iustitiæ vel misericordiæ Dei effecta expertisunt[?]; ab eo, quòd etsi Deus non statim multat, tamen post breue aut longum tempus, vel certè post hanc vitam digna rependit factis supplicia; ab eo, quòd nulla sapientiæ vel industriæ humanæ rima ad euadendum emergendumque ex iudicio Dei patet: ad faciendam spem misericordia Dei faciunt loca, à peccati confessione; à nostri humiliatione & mortificatione; ab assiduâ diuinæ gratiæ implorationc; à virtute Spiritus nos adiuuantis in nostris precationibus; à promissionibus diuinis; ab ingenitâ Dei bonitate, quâ vult rogari,& petita præstare; ab eo, quòd Deus promissis state gaudet, neminemque vult fallere; ab intercessione Christi mediatoris; ab effectu mortis omniumq; meritorum Christi; ab eo, quòd Deus nouit nostras necessitates, etiam antequam petamus; à nostri electione, vocatione, iustificatione; ab eo, quòd Deus nunquam suos prorsus deserit, sed priùs paterno affectu succurrit, quàm extremè periclitemur: ad nobis & aliis imprimendum affectum misericordiæ faciunt argumenta, ab ætate, sexu, conditione, impotentiâ; à vitæ innocentiâ; à priore fortunâ; à genere calamitatis; à magnitudine calamitatis; à comparatione præsentis mali cum aliis incommodis; à loco, tempore, aliisque circumstantijs; à prouidentiâ Dei sapienter omnia ordinate; à dignitate eius, qui affligitur, quòd nimirum fit noster frater, eiusdem regenerationis nobiscum particeps; ab eo, quòd qui calamitate premitur frater noster, non propter sua tantùm peccata, sed magis propter exemplum aliorum patiatur; à metu pariùm malorum nobis impendentium; à præceptis Dei, quæ iubent vt misericordiâ erga alios moueamur; à promissionibus, quæ propositæ sunt iis, qui misericordiam exercuerint; à comminationibus erga imminisericordes; à vitandis contemnendis; insidiis carnis, mundi, & diaboli, qui nos à bene agedo auocant. In aliis affectibus excitandis vel sedandis sumutur argumenta à membris ad caput, à capite ad membra, à comminatione Dei ad effectum, à promissione Dei ad affectum', à personâ vnius pij ad personas omnium piorum, à personâ vnius impij ad personas omnium impiorum, exaggeratione pœnarum & præmiorum, magnifica descriptione attributorum Dei &c.
units.tr: Third, the topics of the corrective kind are the opposites of the topics of the preceding kind: for example, from what is dishonourable, unjust, useless, and so on. Fourth, the principal topics of the consolatory kind are drawn from what is honourable, just, equitable, useful, useless, becoming, praiseworthy, easy, necessary; from the kind of evils; from the providence of God; from the protection of the holy angels; from the justice of God; from the uprightness of conscience, because all things work together for good for those who believe; from the effect of afflictions; from the promises of God; from the necessary sign and effect of divine election; from the example of Christ; from the examples of the saints; from the certainty of the rewards; from the edification of others; from the present help of the Holy Spirit; from the nature of hope and patience; from the effect of the merits of Christ. Fifth, the principal topics of the elenctic kind are drawn from what is useless, unjust, dangerous, discordant, and unlike. As far as particular affections go: to stir up anxiety for obtaining eternal salvation, the following arguments serve: from what is honourable; from the baseness and magnitude of sins; from the recognition of human frailty; from the inward and outward miseries that accompany a life subject to sin; from the countless goods that come from a purpose of a better life; from the losses that accompany the shamefulness of a life of vice; from what is necessary; from what is easy, for example, that by God's helping grace we can resist the devil. To stir up hatred and detestation of sin, the topics serve: from the authority, greatness, and diligence of the godly; from the baseness of persons given over to vices; from the form, manner, and other circumstances of vices; from the magnitude of the evils already born of present sins and of those that may follow in future; from the fact that we ought not to be so base and abject as to wish to submit our minds and bodies to our enemy the devil, to serve the impious suggestions of him; from the fact that we incur the crime of perfidy and even of treason against the majesty of God if we fall away from Christ to Belial; from the fact that it is the highest ingratitude and cruelty to crucify Christ again by our sins; from the fact that by polluting ourselves with sins we grieve the Holy Spirit and bring infamy on the holy angels, our guardians, and likewise on the whole Church; from the fact that if we yield to the suggestions of the devil, all the blame will be imputed to ourselves and to our own malice, and no excuse will be allowed, and we ourselves shall have to pay the penalties for what we have decided upon at the devil's persuasion. To stir up the love and zeal of virtue, the topics serve: from what is religious, godly, glorious, necessary; from circumstances, signs, antecedents, connected things, consequences; from examples; from the imitation of God, of Christ, of the angels, and of the holy men. To impress the fear of divine judgement, we shall argue: from our unworthiness, our own guilt, and our weakness; from the gravity of the punishments; from the fact that it is necessary for God's promises and threatenings to be fulfilled; from the examples of those who have experienced the effects of the justice or mercy of God; from the fact that, even if God does not punish at once, yet after a short or long time, or at least after this life, He repays deeds with deserved punishment; from the fact that no crack of human wisdom or industry lies open for escaping or emerging from the judgement of God. To create hope in the mercy of God, the topics serve: from the confession of sin; from our humbling and mortifying of ourselves; from the constant imploring of divine grace; from the power of the Spirit who helps us in our prayers; from the divine promises; from the innate goodness of God, by which He wills to be asked and to grant what is asked; from the fact that God delights in keeping His promises and wishes to deceive no one; from the intercession of Christ the Mediator; from the effect of the death and of all the merits of Christ; from the fact that God knows our needs even before we ask; from our election, calling, and justification; from the fact that God never utterly forsakes His own, but comes to their aid with a father's affection before they are in extreme danger. To impress the affection of mercy on ourselves and on others, the following arguments serve: from age, sex, condition, helplessness; from innocence of life; from former fortune; from the kind of calamity; from the magnitude of the calamity; from the comparison of the present evil with other misfortunes; from place, time, and other circumstances; from the providence of God, who orders all things wisely; from the dignity of the one who suffers, that is, that he is our brother, a sharer with us in the same regeneration; from the fact that a brother who is crushed by calamity suffers not only for his own sins but rather as an example to others; from the fear of similar evils hanging over us; from the precepts of God, which bid us be moved to mercy towards others; from the promises made to those who have shown mercy; from the threatenings against the unmerciful; from the things to be avoided and despised; from the snares of the flesh, the world, and the devil, who call us away from doing good. In stirring up or calming other affections, arguments are taken: from the members to the head, from the head to the members; from the threatening of God to its effect; from the promise of God to the affection; from the person of one godly man to the persons of all the godly; from the person of one impious man to the persons of all the impious; from the exaggeration of punishments and rewards; from a magnificent description of the attributes of God, and so on.

units.la: XIV. Dispositio est, quâ thema cum suis argumentis aptè distribuitur in sex partes, vt sunt Ex-ordium, ordium, Narratio, Propositio, Confirmatio, Confutatio, & Peroratio. Exordium est orationis principium, animum auditoris ad reliqua praeparans. Eius fines sunt tres, Benevolentia, Attentio, Docilitas: quae petuntur a rebus, vel personis, idq; ex locis inueniendis Logicae. Exempla vide Act. 2. v. 14. 22. 29. c. 13. v. 16. c. 22. v. 1. c. 10. v. 34. c. 24. v. 10. c. 26. v. 2. 26. Rom. 1. v. 8. 1. Cor. 1. v. 4. Coloss. 1. v. 3. Esa. 1. v. 1. 10. Rom. 9. v. 1. c. 10. v. 1. Narratio est rei gestae expositio. Itaque exordio statim subiicitur, si propositio sit inde deducenda; vel praemittitur ei propositio, si hanc declarare possit. Exempla vide Act. 2. v. 22. & seqq. c. 22. v. 3. Apoc. 1. v. 9. & seqq. Propositio est, quae continet thema & summam orationis. Illa si fuerit multiplex, partitio dicitur. Ratio autem in plures quam tres vel quatuor partes debet diuidi. Exemplum partitionis est Apoc. 1. v. 19. Scribe quae vidisti, & quae sunt, & post haec futura sunt. Quibus verbis apocalypsis diuiditur in duo summa capita, videl. tractationem rerum praesentium & futurarum. Confirmatio est argumentorum deductio: vt ne pe propositio recte persuaderi possit. Confutatio est contrariorum argumentorum solutio. Quae confirmationi praemittitur, si auditor sit occupatus insigni praeiudicio. Vtriusque exemplum vide 1. Cor. 15. Peroratio est artificiosus terminus orationis. In hac vt plurimum est ἀναχεφαλαίωσις & παθοποιΐα, h.e. recapitulatio & affectuum concitatio. Vide Philip. 4. v. 1. & seqq. Hebr. 13. v. 20. 21. In confutatione peculiares quidam modi adhibentur: puta regestio Rom. 9. Dices ergo mihi &c. Matth. 21. Nec ego vobis dicam, qua authoritate &c. item reiectio & obiurgatio Rom. 3. Faciamus mala &c. item μίμησις Coloss. 3. Ne tetigeris &c. item oppositio sententiae Dei contra sententiam hominum Matt. 15. Quare vos transgredimini &c. denique germana expositio seu vindicatio Scripturae Matt. 4. Scriptum est &c. Porro in genere correctiuo adhibetur confutatio vel oblique, vt Christus Luc. 13. Herodem vocat vulpem, & eode stratagemate vtitur Nathan 2. Sam. 13. & Esaias c. 5. Ieremias c. 24. Ezechiel c. 17. vel aperte, vt cum Iohannes reprehendit Herodem, Non licet tibi &c. Marc. 6. v. 18.
units.tr: XIV. Disposition is the arrangement by which the theme, with its arguments, is aptly distributed into six parts: the Exordium, the Ordium, the Narration, the Proposition, the Confirmation, the Confutation and the Peroration. The Exordium is the beginning of the speech, preparing the hearer's mind for what follows. Its ends are three: goodwill, attention and teachableness. These are sought from things or persons, by means of the topics of invention found in Logic. For examples see Acts 2:14, 22, 29; 13:16; 22:1; 10:34; 24:10; 26:2, 26; Romans 1:8; 1 Corinthians 1:4; Colossians 1:3; Isaiah 1:1; Romans 9:1; 10:1. Narratio is the exposition of the matter done. So the narration is placed straight after the exordium if the proposition is to be drawn from it; or the proposition is placed before it, if the proposition can be made clear by it. For examples see Acts 2:22ff.; 22:3; Revelation 1:9ff. Propositio is that which contains the theme and the sum of the speech. If it is manifold, it is called a partition. The partition, however, ought not to be divided into more than three or four parts. An example of a partition is Revelation 1:19, "Write the things which you have seen, and the things which are, and the things which shall be hereafter." By these words the Apocalypse is divided into two main heads, namely the treatment of present and of future things. Confirmatio is the drawing out of arguments, so that the proposition may be rightly persuaded, namely by proof. Confutatio is the solution of contrary arguments. It is placed before the confirmation if the hearer is held by some notable prejudice. For an example of each see 1 Corinthians 15. Peroratio is the skilful ending of the speech. In it there is usually ἀνακεφαλαίωσις [anakephalaiōsis] and παθοποιΐα [pathopoiia], that is, recapitulation and the stirring up of the emotions. See Philippians 4:1ff.; Hebrews 13:20, 21. In confutation certain particular modes are employed: for instance, the recital of objections, Romans 9, "You will say to me then..."; Matthew 21, "Neither will I tell you by what authority..."; likewise rejection and rebuke, Romans 3, "Let us do evil..."; likewise μίμησις [mimēsis], imitation of the opponent's speech, Colossians 3, "Touch not..."; likewise the setting of God's sentence against the opinion of men, Matthew 15, "Why do you also transgress..."; and finally the plain exposition or vindication of Scripture, Matthew 4, "It is written..." Moreover, in the corrective kind, confutation is used either obliquely, as Christ calls Herod a fox, Luke 13, and Nathan uses the same stratagem, 2 Samuel 12, and Isaiah ch. 5, Jeremiah ch. 24, Ezekiel ch. 17; or openly, as when John rebukes Herod, "It is not lawful for you..." Mark 6:18.

units.la: XV. Elocutio est, quâ res convenienti stilo ornatur. Quò pertinent tropus, figura, & copia. Tropus est venusta vocis commutatio. Figura est venusta habitus orationis commutatio. Estque dictionis, vel sententiæ. Illa colorem & gratiam, hæc vehementiam & affectum conciliat orationi. Copia est, quâ oratio amplitudinem & magnificentiam aliquam consequitur. Estq; verborum, vel rerum. Copia verborum consistit in synonymis, epithetis, & variatione sententiæ grammaticâ, rhetoricâ & logicâ. Copia rerum consistit in aptâ diuisione materiæ, & singularum partium deductione ex locis inuentionis Logicæ. Exempla elocutionis sunt in toto Scripturæ corpore. Stilus namque Scripturæ non est nisi eloquentissimus, idque hanc ob causam, quòd ἡ ἀφέλεια ἡ πρὸς τὸ ἁπλ- τὸν, h.e. simplicitas & superfluitatis neglectus, veritatis colorem ita conci-ant[?] sermoni Spiritus sancti, vt omnem diligentiam omnemque artem aliorum scriptorum longè superet.
units.tr: XV. Elocution is that by which the matter is adorned with a fitting style. To this belong the trope, the figure and abundance. A trope is a graceful change of a word. A figure is a graceful change in the form of the speech, and it concerns either a word or a sentence. The former gives colour and charm to the speech, the latter vehemence and emotion. Abundance is that by which the speech gains a certain fullness and magnificence. It concerns either words or things. Abundance of words consists in synonyms, epithets, and variation of the sentence grammatically, rhetorically and logically. Abundance of things consists in the apt division of the matter and the development of each part from the topics of invention in Logic. Examples of elocution are found throughout the whole body of Scripture. For the style of Scripture is nothing but most eloquent, and this for the reason that ἡ ἀφέλεια ἡ πρὸς τὸ ἁπλοῦν [hē apheleia hē pros to haploun], that is, simplicity and neglect of superfluity, lends the colour of truth to the speech of the Holy Spirit in such a way that it far surpasses all the diligence and all the art of other writers.

units.la: XVI. Memoria est vis animi, quâ orator rem cognitam, sæpeque repetitam probè meminit. Dico rem cognitam; quia requiritur omnium primò rerum memorandarum intellectio. Addo, sæpe repetitam: quia hoc vno artificio imaginatio, memoria, affectus, totusque adeo homo veluti repletur. Vide Mnemonicam infra.
units.tr: XVI. Memory is the power of the mind by which the orator rightly remembers a matter that is known and often repeated. I say a matter that is known, because the understanding of the things to be remembered is required first of all. I add often repeated, because by this one device the imagination, the memory, the emotions and the whole man, as it were, are filled. See the Mnemonics below.

units.la: XVII. Pronuntiatio est, quâ orator orationem suam aptè enuntiat. Voce scil. clarâ, distinctâ, firmâ, mediocri, æquabili, variâ: & gestu, qui vocem subsequitur, & animo paret unâ cum voce.
units.tr: XVII. Delivery is that by which the orator aptly pronounces his speech: namely with a voice that is clear, distinct, firm, moderate, even and varied, and with gesture, which follows the voice and is prepared together with the voice from the mind.

units.la: XXVII. POETICA SACRA.
units.tr: XXVII. SACRED POETRY.

units.la: I. Poëtica sacra est ars efficiendi poëma ad imitationem Scripturæ.
units.tr: I. Sacred poetry is the art of producing a poem in imitation of Scripture.

units.la: II, Poëma dicitur sensu lato & stricto. Poëmatis nomen non à fingendo, vt putarunt, quia fictis uteretur, sed à faciendo, ποιεῖν[?], dictum est: scil. per excellentiam, vt recte observat Scaliger lib. 1. poët. c. 2. Sumiturautem poësis, & poëmatis, & poëtæ nomen nunc latiùs, nunc strictiùs, vt iam patebit. Idem de hac voce carmen esto iudicium.
units.tr: II. The word "poem" is used in a broad and a narrow sense. The name poema comes not from feigning (fingendo), as some have thought, because poems use fictions, but from making (faciendo) [ποιεῖν], that is, by way of eminence, as Scaliger rightly observes, lib. 1, Poetics, ch. 2. The words poesis, poema and poeta are taken now more broadly, now more strictly, as will soon become clear. The same judgment should be made of the word carmen.

units.la: III. Poëma sensu lato est oratio charactere poëtico animata, h. e. oratio soluta, quæ stilo est pathetico, qualis poëticus, etsi non numerosò. Et hoc laxo sensu theologi numerant quinq; libros poëticos, Iobum, Psalmos, Prouerbia, Ecclesiasten, & Canticum canticorum. Eodé sensu multa cantica sacra, multæ conciones propheticæ, & maximè threni Ieremiæ ad scripta poëtica reuocantur.
units.tr: III. A poem in the broad sense is a speech animated by a poetic character, that is, a prose speech written in a passionate style such as poetry uses, though without metre. In this loose sense theologians count five poetic books: Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs. In the same sense many sacred canticles, many prophetic sermons, and especially the Lamentations of Jeremiah are reckoned among poetic writings.

units.la: Huius loci sunt ista cantica. I. Canticum siue carmen εὐχαριστικὸν[?] Mosis, Exod. 15. quod Moïse diuinitùs dictata præfante, hinc quidem succinente virorum choro, inde verò præeuntem Mosis sororem Mariam prophetissam, insecutis & amœbeum carmen repetentibus mulieribus, popâ[?] certè longè celeberrimâ, decantatum fuit. II. Carmen Mosis προφητικὸν[?], Deut. 32. Hebræi scribunt, canticum istud esse summarium totius legis: vt pote in quo Moses faciat mentionem de magnificentiâ Dei, de creatione mundi, de vno Deo colendo, de generatione diluuij, de diuisione linguarum & terrarum, de electione populi Israelitici, de beneficiis in deserto exhibitis, de futurâ mortuorum resurrectione, & vocatione gentium illarumque consociatione cum Israele restituto, vt interpretatur apostolus Rom. 15. v. 10. vt verè affirmari posset prophetas, qui sunt Mosis ætatem secuti, nihil aliud fuisse, quàm istius cantici interpretes, prout ipsis idem Spiritus peculiarem, & temporum, personarum, ac locorum circumstantiis accommodatam, eorum quæ hic vniuersaliter scripta sunt, explicationem suggessit. III. Canticum ἐπινίκιον[?] Deboræ, ab ipsâ & Baraco decantatum, Iudic. 5. quo celebratur insignis victoria, quam Baracus de Iabino Cananæorum rege reportauit. Hoc carmen, præterquam quòd tum propter ipsius argumenti dignitatem, tum ob elegantiam ac diuinam plane μεγαλοπρεπέστατον[?] dignissimum est, quod omnes assidue legant & admirentur; doctrinam etiam continet, hisce præsertim temporibus admodum necefsariam. IV. Canticum Hannæ matris Samuelis, εὐχαριστήριον[?] simul & διδακτικὸν & προφητικὸν, 1.Sam. 2. Hoc carmine oftendit prophetissa, quæ & quantæ sint Dei opt. Max. vires, elegantissima simul & certissima illarum descriptione : & graphicè describit rerum humanarum vicissitudinem: denique insignem propheriam extremo cantico apponit de Christo, ita vt Mariæ virgini tot seculis posteà nascituræ, totidem pene verbis præiuisse videri possit. V. Carmen lugubre Dauidis, super cæde Saul & Ionathan, & populi Dei, 2. Sam.1. Hac lamentatione nihil flebilius, neque θρηνητικώτερον cogitari potest. Eiusmodi etiam exemplum, quamuis in re dissimili, præbent Psal 39. & 88. VI. Canticum εὐχαριστήριον Dauidis, 2. Sam. 7. In hoc carmen Dauid erupit, postquam per os Nathanis accepit promissionem de Messiæ ex ipsius posteris nasciturò. VII. Canticum Dauidis eucharisticum 1. Chron. 16. quod cantauit in deportatione arcæ. VIII. Canticum Esaiæ ἐπιλυμνήτ[?]ν ἡ προφητικὸν, Esa. 5. Hoc carmen Esaias suis obiurgationibus insenuit, quò facilius audientium animis infigeretur, & memoriæ mandaretur: Mosis in ea re exemplum, & verba pene ipsa secutus Deut. 32. atque adeò tum illius, tum Asaphi Psal. 80. interpres. IX. Canticum Esaiæ ϰαταχθονιστικὸν[?] προφητικὸν, Esa. 26. Hoc canticum Esaias appolsuit concionis præcedentis capitis tanquam sigillum, vt facilius pijres tantas memoriæ mandarent, quibus sese, tum in exilio, ipse reditus sui, consolarentur, tum post reditum, certa venturi Messiæ expectatione sustentarent. X. Canticum Ezechiæ regis, εὐχαριστήριον, Esa. 38. Hoc carmine rex piissimus comp[?]ellitur miseriam suam, & mirificam liberationem, & gratiarum actionem: quæ tria continent summam doctrinæ Christianæ. XI. Canticum Iona εὐχαριστήριον, Ion. 2. Mirabile prorsus est hoc carmen : quippe quod Ionas composuit & recitauit in ventre ceti positus. XII. Canticum εὐχαριστήριον Habacuc prophetæ, Habac. 3. Hoc carmen in primis hodiè nobis est vsurpandum, vbi sub cruce plus quàm Babylonicâ ingemiscunt pij. XIII. Canticum beatæ virginis Mariæ εὐχαριστήριον, Luc. 1. verf. 46. & seqq. XIV. Canticum εὐχαριστήριον ἐν τῷ προφητικῷ [?] Zachariæ sacerdotis & prophetæ Luc. 1. v. 68. & seqq. XV. Canticum Simeonis εὐχαριστήριον ἐν τῷ θεοφιλεῖ [?], Luc. 2. v. 19. & seqq. His adde ex Apocryphis, Canticum Iudithæ. Iudith. 16. & Hymnum trium puerorum. Adiect. ad Daniel. Atque hæc omnia cantica vsitatè appellantur carmina, latè sumto vocabulo, non quòd sint ἔμμετρα [?], sed μετῳδίη [?], vt ita dicam.
units.tr: These canticles belong to this place. I. The thanksgiving canticle or song of Moses, Exod. 15.
