It was sung when Moses, with words dictated by God, led the choir of men singing in response on one side, while on the other side Miriam, Moses' sister, the prophetess, went before, and the women followed, repeating the antiphonal song, a procession certainly by far the most famous. II. The prophetic song of Moses, Deut. 32. The Hebrews write that this canticle is a summary of the whole law, since in it Moses makes mention of the greatness of God, of the creation of the world, of worshipping the one God, of the generation of the flood, of the division of tongues and lands, of the election of the people of Israel, of the benefits bestowed in the wilderness, of the future resurrection of the dead, and of the calling of the Gentiles and their union with the restored Israel, as the apostle interprets it, Rom. 15. v. 10. Hence it could truly be affirmed that the prophets who followed the age of Moses were nothing other than interpreters of this canticle, since the same Spirit suggested to them an explanation of what is written here in general terms, one peculiar to them and adapted to the circumstances of times, persons and places. III. The victory song of Deborah, sung by her and by Barak, Judg. 5. It celebrates the notable victory which Barak won over Jabin, king of the Canaanites. This poem, besides being most worthy that everyone read it constantly and admire it, both on account of the dignity of its subject and on account of its elegance and plainly divine most magnificent [μεγαλοπρεπέστατον] character, also contains doctrine which is especially necessary in these times. IV. The canticle of Hannah, mother of Samuel, at once a thanksgiving, a teaching and a prophecy, 1 Sam. 2. In this song the prophetess shows, with a most elegant and at the same time most accurate description, how great and what kind of powers belong to God, the best and greatest; she vividly describes the vicissitudes of human affairs; and finally she adds to the end of the canticle a remarkable prophecy about Christ, so that she seems to have foretold, in almost the same words, the Virgin Mary, who was to be born so many centuries later. V. David's lament over the slaughter of Saul and Jonathan and of the people of God, 2 Sam. 1. Nothing more mournful [θρηνητικώτερον] can be imagined than this lamentation. Psalms 39 and 88 provide a similar example, though on a different subject. VI. David's thanksgiving song, 2 Sam. 7. In this song David broke out after receiving through the mouth of Nathan the promise of the Messiah who would be born from his posterity. VII. David's eucharistic canticle, 1 Chron. 16., which he sang when the ark was carried in. VIII. Isaiah's reproachful [ἐπιτιμητικὸν] or prophetic canticle, Isa. 5. Isaiah wove this song into his rebukes, so that it might more easily be fixed in the minds of his hearers and committed to memory. In this he followed the example and almost the very words of Moses, Deut. 32., and so was the interpreter of both Moses and Asaph, Ps. 80. IX. Isaiah's subterranean [καταχθονιστικὸν] and prophetic canticle, Isa. 26. Isaiah appended this canticle to the sermon of the preceding chapter as a seal, so that the godly might more easily commit to memory such great things, by which they might console themselves, both in exile and after their return, and sustain themselves after the return with the sure expectation of the coming Messiah. X. The canticle of King Hezekiah, a thanksgiving, Isa. 38. In this song the most pious king sets forth his misery, his wonderful deliverance and his thanksgiving; these three contain the sum of Christian doctrine. XI. The thanksgiving canticle of Jonah, Jonah 2. This song is truly wonderful, since Jonah composed and recited it while placed in the belly of the whale. XII. The thanksgiving canticle of the prophet Habakkuk, Hab. 3. This song is above all to be used by us today, when the godly groan under a cross more than Babylonian. XIII. The thanksgiving canticle of the blessed Virgin Mary, Luke 1. v. 46 and following. XIV. The thanksgiving canticle in the prophetic manner [ἐν τῷ προφητικῷ] of Zechariah, priest and prophet, Luke 1. v. 68 and following. XV. The thanksgiving canticle of Simeon in the God-loving manner [ἐν τῷ θεοφιλεῖ], Luke 2. v. 19 and following. To these add from the Apocrypha the Canticle of Judith, Judith 16, and the Hymn of the Three Children, Additions to Daniel. All these canticles are commonly called poems, the word being taken broadly: not because they are metrical [ἔμμετρα], but because they are sung to music [μετῳδίη], as I may say.

units.la: IV. Poëma, siue carmen, strictè, est oratio numerosa: eaque tum rhythmus, tum metrum, siue versus.
units.tr: IV. A poem, or carmen, strictly speaking, is a numerous speech (oratio numerosa); and this is either rhythm or metre, that is, verse.

units.la: V. Rhythmus est modulatio sine ratione metrorum pedum. Scaliger lib. 2. poët. c. 2. valde commendat definitiones rhythmi authore Bedâ. Illæ sic habent: Rhythmus est metris consimilis verborum modulata compositio, non metricâ ratione, sed numero syllabarum ad iudicium aurium examinata, vt sunt carmina vulgarium poëtarum. Et quidem rhythmus sine metro esse potest, metrum vero sine rhythmo esse non potest. Item: Metrum est ratio cum modulatione: rhythmus modulatio sine ratione. Plerumque tamen casu quodam inuenies etiam rationem in rhythmo, non artificì moderatione seruatam, sed sono & ipsâ modulatione ducente, quem vulgares poëtæ necesse est faciant rusticè, docti faciunt doctè. Hæc Beda, quo nemo veterum melius explicauit quid sit rhythmus, vt ait Scaliger d. l. Idem ibidem hæc habet. Solum canticum Mosis extremo Deuteronomio, Prouerbia Salomonis, & totus fere liber Iob, quâdam rhythmi necessitate cohibentur, qui rhythmus est instar duarum dimetriarum iambicarum, & tinnulus accidit ad aures. Sed aliquando pauciorum sunt syllabarum, aliquando plurium, quales Græcorum στίχοι[?] καταληκτικοί[?], βραχυκαταληκτικοί[?], ὑπερμέτροι[?]: non vtique quòd compensatio fiat κατὰ ἰσοχρονίαν[?], vt in Græcis solet: neque enim hoc exprimi potest idiomate Hebraico: sed quantum sententia postulat, rhythmus nunc longior, nunc brevior est. Et paulò post: Politici Græcorum versus, qui syllabarum numero, non temporum ratione constant, nihil aliud quàm rhythmi sunt. Sic liber Iob, proverbia Salomonis, mere rhythmus est, non metrica modulatio: in quibus & plurimùm versus sunt duo dimetri iambica, aliquando tres dipodia, aliquando mira est inaequalitas, vt ne rhythmi quidem legem sequantur. Ibidem de libro Iobi ait: Pura puta poësis rhythmica est, non metrica, generosa, & mascula, & supra omnes Pindaricos modos. Neque verò putaueris, genus illud rhythmi, quo Proverbia & liber Iob constant, esse simile, quod Iudaeis hodie est in vsu. Nam hodierni versus Iudaici sunt plane rhythmi nostri vulgares, ὁμοιοτάτωτοι[?] & ὁμοιοτέλευτοι[?]: quod à nobis Christianis ante annos 500. didicerunt, nos autem ex leoninis hexametris, qua vocant, eos effinximus: quanquam & Iudaei habent aliud genus, in quo non numeri syllabarum, sed similis definentia ratio habetur. Aliquando enim versus antecedens longior est dimidio: in ὁμοιοτελεύτοις autem καὶ ὁμοιοτάτωτοις tantum conueniunt, quas desinentias in Hebraismo, Syriasmo, & Arabismo non est operosum reperire. Sponte enim occurrunt etiam aliud agentibus. Quare critici Arabici, qui cola & casa in Alcorano dissignarunt, ij nunquam ea terminant, nisi, vbi occurrit verbum similiter definens, vt finis antecedentis. Vnde factum, vt cola siue commata Alcorani sint admodum inaequalia. Ibidem: Versus Iob & Salomonis sunt quatuor dipodia, aut quasi duo dipodia, sed aliquando decurtata, aliquando productiores, prout sententia postulat. A metro enim sententia legem accipit, à sententiâ rhythmus: & propterea metrum nunquam excedit legem suam, rhythmus excedit, cùm sententia postulat. Ex his Scaligeri verbis patet, rhythmum, qui in libro Iob & Prouerbiis occurrit, non esse positum in simili definentia, sed in numero syllabarum citra mensuram pedum. Priori enim modo nulla pars Scripturæ rhythmicè est composita.
units.tr: V. Rhythm is modulation without the rule of metrical feet. Scaliger, lib. 2, Poetics, ch. 2, greatly commends the definitions of rhythm given by the author Bede. They run as follows: Rhythm is a modulated composition of words similar to metre, not governed by metrical rule but judged by the ear according to the number of syllables, as are the songs of vernacular poets. Rhythm can indeed exist without metre, but metre cannot exist without rhythm. Likewise: Metre is rule with modulation; rhythm is modulation without rule. Yet by some chance you will often find a rule in rhythm too, kept not by artistic regulation but led by sound and modulation itself; vernacular poets necessarily produce this crudely, learned poets produce it learnedly. Thus Bede, than whom none of the ancients explained better what rhythm is, as Scaliger says in the passage cited. The same writer has the following in the same place: Only the canticle of Moses at the end of Deuteronomy, the Proverbs of Solomon, and almost the whole book of Job are held together by a certain necessity of rhythm, which is like two iambic dimeters, and falls tinkling on the ears. But sometimes the lines have fewer syllables, sometimes more, like the Greek catalectic [στίχοι καταληκτικοί], brachycatalectic [βραχυκαταληκτικοί] and hypermetric [ὑπερμέτροι] verses; not at all because compensation is made by equal time [κατὰ ἰσοχρονίαν], as is usual in Greek, for this cannot be expressed in the Hebrew idiom; rather, the rhythm is longer or shorter as the sense demands. And a little later: The political verses of the Greeks, which consist of a number of syllables rather than a rule of times, are nothing other than rhythms. So the book of Job and the Proverbs of Solomon are pure rhythm, not metrical modulation; in them for the most part the verses are two iambic dimeters, sometimes three dipodies, and sometimes there is such remarkable inequality that they do not even follow the law of rhythm. In the same place he says of the book of Job: It is pure rhythmic poetry, not metrical, noble and manly, and above all the Pindaric modes. Nor should you think that the kind of rhythm of which the Proverbs and the book of Job consist is similar to what the Jews use today. For today's Jewish verses are plainly our common rhythms, homoioptota [ὁμοιοτάτωτοι] and homoeoteleuta [ὁμοιοτέλευτοι], which they learned from us Christians about 500 years ago; we, however, formed them from the leonine hexameters, as they are called. Yet the Jews also have another kind, in which the rule is not the number of syllables but a similar ending. For sometimes the preceding verse is longer by half; but they agree only in homoeoteleuta and homoioptota, and such endings are not hard to find in Hebrew, Syriac and Arabic, for they occur spontaneously even to those busy with other things. Hence the Arab critics, who marked off the cola and casa of the Koran, never end them except where a verb with a similar ending occurs, as the end of the preceding one. Whence it happens that the cola or commata of the Koran are very unequal. Likewise: The verses of Job and Solomon are four dipodies, or as it were two dipodies, sometimes shortened, sometimes lengthened, as the sense demands. For the sense takes its law from metre, and rhythm from the sense; so metre never exceeds its law, but rhythm exceeds it when the sense demands. From these words of Scaliger it is clear that the rhythm which occurs in the book of Job and in the Proverbs does not consist in a similar ending, but in the number of syllables without the measure of feet. For in the former way no part of Scripture is composed rhythmically.

units.la: VI. Metrum est ratio certa pedum mensurâ constans cum modulatione. Huiusmodi metra in Scripturis occurrere asserit Hieronymus, non uno loco. Prologo 1. in Iob sic ait: A principio itaque voluminis usq; ad verba Iob, apud Hebraeos profana oratio est. Porro a verbis Iob, in quibus ait, Pereat dies, in qua natus sum, & nox, in qua dictum est, Conceptus est homo: usque ad eum locum, ubi ante finem voluminis scriptum est, Idcirco ipse me reprehendo, & ago poenitentiam in fauilla & cinere: hexametri versus sunt dactylo spondaeoque currentes, & propter linguae idioma, crebro recipientes & alios pedes, non earundem syllabarum, sed eorundem temporum. Interdum quoque ipse rhythmus dulcis & tinnulus fertur numeris pedum solutus: quod metrici magis quam simplex lector intelligunt. A supradicto autem versu usque ad finem libri, parvum comma quod remanet, prosa oratione contexitur. Quod si videtur cui incredulum, metra scilicet esse apud Hebraeos, & in morem nostri Flacci, Graecique Pindari, & Alcaei, & Sapphus, vel Psalterium, vel Lamentationes Ieremiae, vel omnia fere Scripturarum cantica comprehendi, legat Philonem, Iosephum, Origenem, Caesariensem Eusebium, & eorum testimonio me verum dicere comprobabit.
units.tr: VI. Metre is a fixed arrangement of feet, measured with a regular rhythm. Jerome asserts that metres of this kind occur in Scripture, and not in just one place. In the first Prologue to Job he says: From the beginning of the volume down to the words of Job, the speech among the Hebrews is ordinary prose. But from the words of Job, where he says, "Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said, A man is conceived," down to the place near the end of the book where it is written, "Therefore I reprove myself, and repent in dust and ashes," the lines are hexameters running in dactyls and spondees, and, because of the idiom of the language, they often admit other feet too, not of the same syllables but of the same times. Sometimes too the rhythm itself is sweet and resonant, carried along in loosened metrical feet, which metrists understand better than a plain reader. From the verse just mentioned to the end of the book, the short remaining clause is woven in prose. If anyone finds it hard to believe that there are metres among the Hebrews, in the manner of our Horace and the Greek Pindar, Alcaeus and Sappho, or that the Psalter, or the Lamentations of Jeremiah, or almost all the canticles of Scripture are composed in verse, let him read Philo, Josephus, Origen, and Eusebius of Caesarea, and their testimony will prove that I speak the truth.

units.la: Idem praefat. in chronic. Eusebij ait: Psalterium in morem Flacci & Pindari nunc iambo currit, Alcaico personat, nunc Sapphico tumet, nunc semipede ingreditur. Ad haec verba Scaliger lib. 2. poët. c. 2. sic adnotat: Pindari poësim iambico & Alcaico metro aut Sapphico currere, credent fortasse, qui nunquam Pindarum legerunt, aut nesciunt, quid sit iambicum, Alcaicum, Sapphicum metrum. Idem leges & in praefatione in Iob.
units.tr: In the preface to the Chronicle of Eusebius he says the same: The Psalter, in the manner of Horace and Pindar, now runs in iambics, now sounds in Alcaics, now swells in Sapphics, now moves in half-feet. On these words Scaliger, in book 2, chapter 2 of his Poetics, comments as follows: Those who have never read Pindar, or do not know what an iambic, Alcaic, or Sapphic metre is, will perhaps believe that Pindar's poetry runs in iambic and Alcaic or Sapphic metre. You will read the same in the preface to Job.

units.la: De Psalterio magis miror, cum neque in eo, neque in threnis, ullum canticum sit metricis legibus astrictum, sed mere soluta sit oratio, charactere poetico animata. Quin Esaiae, & aliorum prophetarum, oratio instar poësios aliquando figurata est, quam tamen propterea poësim non recte dixeris. Et paulo post ait: Vt in Hebraico, Syriaco, Arabico, & Abyssino idiomate ulla metrispecies concipi possit, nemo efficere possit, quia id natura sermonis non patitur. Itaq; praefatione in Iob nulla ratione nititur, quod ait, versus illius li-bri hexametros esse, dactylo spondaeoque currentes, & propter linguae idioma crebro recipientes & alios pedes, non earundem syllabarum, sed eorundem temporum, id est, οὐχ ἰσοσυλλάβους, ἀλλὰ ἰσοχρόνους: nos negamus, tale quid in eo libro extare: imo contra dicimus, ne metra quidem esse, sed metrorum instar. Itaque librum Iobi constare hexametro carmine non magis concesserim, quam, quod postea adjicit, eum librum esse mixtum ex Hebraismo, Syriasmo, & Arabismo: quod miror homini Hebraice perito excidisse. Merus enim Hebraismus est, quanquam pura puta[?] poësis rhythmica est, &c. Idem Scaliger ibidem ait: Hebraismus, Syriasmus, & Arabismus nullo modo ad Graecorum & Latinorum regulam revocari possunt, etiamsi coelum mari misceatur. Et paulo infra de eodem Hieronymo ita scribit: In epistola ad Paulam Vrbicam tetrametra melius vocat, quae hic hexametra. Nam versus Iob & Salomonis sunt quatuor dipodiae, aut quasi duae dipodiae &c. Nos in re intricata paucis aphorismis complectemur nostrum iudicium de poësi librorum sacrorum. 1. In lingua Hebraica V.T. & Graeca N.T. est poësis tripliciter: primo, sublimitate stili tantum, ut in omnibus canticis paulo ante recitatis, excepto primo & secundo: deinde sublimitate stili & membris orationis rhythmice temperatis, ut in cantico secundo, prouerbiis Salomonis, & libro Iob: denique sublimitate stili & membris orationis metrice temperatis, ut in cantico primo & libro psalmorum. 2. Sublimitas stili poetici, sive character poeticus, facit, ut scriptum possit appellari poeticum laxo sensu. Non itaque probamus illud Scaligeri, quod paulo ante recitavimus: Esaiae & aliorum prophetarum oratio interdum poësios aliquando figurata est, quam tamen propterea poësim non recte dixeris. Quasi vero non recte dicatur, quod late dicitur. 3. Rhythmus & metrum in omnibus linguis locum habere possunt: etsi non sit eadem ratio, facilitas, & copia in omnibus linguis. Sic quia Graeci & Latini abundant vocibus breuium & longarum syllabarum varietate constantibus, diversa metrorum genera ibi locum habent. At Hebraea lingua plurimas syllabas longas habet, ut & Germanica. Non itaque tanta metri varietas ibi ceini[?]tur. 4. Rhythmus, qui Deut. 32. in libro Iob, & Prouerbiis Salomonis occurrit, non consistit in simili definentia, sed in dimetriâ & dipodiâ, h.e. non cernitur in ὁμοίοιστοτω[?] ἢ ὁμοιοτελευτῳ[?], vt in nostris rhythmis fit, sed in duabus dimetriis iambicis catalecticis, brachycatalecticis, & hypermetris, cuiusmodi dimetria siue dipodia cernitur in istis versibus iambicis:
units.tr: I am more surprised about the Psalter, since neither it nor the Lamentations contains any canticle bound by metrical laws, but the speech is purely prose, animated with a poetic character. Indeed, the speech of Isaiah and of the other prophets is sometimes figured in the manner of poetry, though for that reason you would not rightly call it poetry. And a little later he says: Since no metrical form can be conceived in the Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, or Abyssinian idiom, no one can achieve it, because the nature of the language does not allow it. Therefore Jerome's preface to Job rests on no reason when he says that the verses of that book are hexameters, running in dactyls and spondees, and because of the idiom of the language often admitting other feet, "not of the same syllables but of the same times" [οὐχ ἰσοσυλλάβους, ἀλλὰ ἰσοχρόνους]. We deny that anything of the kind is found in that book; on the contrary we say that there are not even metres, but only something in the manner of metres. So I would no more concede that the book of Job consists of hexameter verse than I would concede what he adds afterwards, that the book is a mixture of Hebraism, Syriacism and Arabism. That a man skilled in Hebrew should have let this slip surprises me. For it is pure Hebraism, although it is indeed rhythmic poetry, etc. The same Scaliger says in the same place: Hebraism, Syriacism and Arabism cannot in any way be brought back to the rule of the Greeks and Latins, even if heaven were mixed with the sea. And a little below, he writes of the same Jerome thus: In his letter to Paula Urbica he calls them tetrameters better than what he here calls hexameters. For the verses of Job and Solomon are four dipodies, or as it were two dipodies, etc. We shall set out, briefly in a few aphorisms, our judgement on the poetry of the sacred books in this intricate matter. 1. In the Hebrew language of the Old Testament and the Greek of the New, poetry exists in three ways: first, by elevation of style alone, as in all the canticles recited just above, except the first and second; second, by elevation of style together with the members of the speech tempered rhythmically, as in the second canticle, in the Proverbs of Solomon and in the book of Job; and finally, by elevation of style together with the members of the speech tempered metrically, as in the first canticle and in the book of Psalms. 2. The elevation of poetic style, or the poetic character, makes it possible to call a writing poetic in a loose sense. We therefore do not accept Scaliger's statement that we quoted a little above: The speech of Isaiah and of the other prophets is sometimes figured in the manner of poetry, though for that reason you would not rightly call it poetry. As if it were not rightly said, because it is said loosely! 3. Rhythm and metre can have a place in all languages, although the ease and the abundance are not the same in all languages. Thus, because the Greeks and Latins abound in words made up of a variety of short and long syllables, different kinds of metre have a place there. But the Hebrew language has very many long syllables, as does German. Therefore so great a variety of metre is not to be found there. 4. The rhythm that occurs in Deuteronomy 32, in the book of Job, and in the Proverbs of Solomon does not consist in like endings, but in dimeter and dipody, that is, it is not seen in homoeoptoton or homoeoteleuton [ὁμοιόπτωτον ἢ ὁμοιοτελευτον], as happens in our rhythms, but in two iambic dimeters, catalectic, brachycatalectic and hypermetric. A dimeter or dipody of this kind is seen in these iambic verses:

units.la: Hei hei paterna terra! Bello fero succumbere Te cerno, proh dolor, pudorque!
units.tr: Alas, alas, paternal land! I see you forced to yield to war, alas, for grief and for shame!

units.la: Aliquando etiam sunt quatuor dipodiae vt in iambicis tetrametris. 5. In libris sacris occurrunt carmina hexametra, iambica, spondaica, & similia, etsi non sunt similia Graecis & Latinis. Iosephus libro 2. antiq. Iud. cap. 14. facit mentionem hexametri, quo vsum esse Mosen in sua ode post Israelitarum ex Aegypto egressum & Pharaonis interitum testatur. Sed nequaquam istud metri genus conuenit cum ratione, quae Graecis & Latinis est visitata. Idem libr. 7. c. 12. & 15. meminit non tantum organorum musicorum, quae a Dauide instituta sint, sed hymnos quoque vario metro ab eo compositos fuisse affirmat: rationem tamen neque compositionis, neque diuersitatis vllam ostendit, nisi quòd alios quidem trimetros, alios vero pentametros fuisse refert. Hoc Iosephi testimonium non temere est reijciendum. Tametsi enim verum est, Hebraeos nevnum[?] quidem hexametrum posse condere more Latinorum & Graecorum: non tamen ideo concludendum est, ipsos nulla ratione posse effingere carmen hexametrum. Sane argumentum a negatione modi ad negationem rei est ἀνυλλόγιστον[?]. Ideo non recte fecit Scaliger, quòd Hieronymi sententiam de hexametris, lyricis, iambicis, Sapphicis, & Alcaicis Scripturae metris reprehendit. Docuit enim hoc Hieronymus ex authoritate Philonis, Iosephi, Origenis & Eusebij Caesariensis, quos citat. Et vero quam certas leges, quibus isti Scripturæ versus ligentur[?], neque Hieronymus, neque alij vel ante vel post eum adnotauerint & ad nos transmiserint: non tamen desperandum est ingenio excitato de aliquâ saltem veteris poëticæ in libris sacris demonstratione. Sic. v. g. Psal.118. v.25. occurrit metrum elegantissimum:
units.tr: Sometimes there are also four dipodies, as in iambic tetrameters. 5. Hexameters, iambics, spondees and similar metres occur in the holy books, although they are not the same as Greek and Latin metres. Josephus, Jewish Antiquities book 2, chapter 14, mentions the hexameter, and attests that Moses used it in his ode after the Israelites went out of Egypt and Pharaoh perished. But that kind of metre does not agree at all with the system that was in use among the Greeks and Latins. In book 7, chapters 12 and 15, the same author mentions not only the musical instruments that David established, but also affirms that the hymns David composed were in various metres. He does not, however, show any principle either of their composition or of their variety, except that he reports some were trimeters and others pentameters. This testimony of Josephus should not be rejected rashly. For although it is true that the Hebrews could not compose a hexameter in the manner of the Latins and Greeks, it does not follow that they could not in any way produce a hexameter verse. Certainly an argument from the denial of a method to the denial of the thing is illogical [ἀσυλλόγιστον]. So Scaliger did not act rightly in finding fault with Jerome's opinion that the hexameter, lyric, iambic, Sapphic and Alcaic metres occur in Scripture. Jerome taught this on the authority of Philo, Josephus, Origen and Eusebius of Caesarea, whom he cites. Indeed, although neither Jerome nor others, either before or after him, have noted down and handed on to us what certain laws bind these verses of Scripture, nevertheless we must not despair that, with our intellect roused, some demonstration of ancient poetry in the holy books may at least be found. Thus, for example, Psalm 118, verse 25, presents a most elegant metre:

units.la: אנא יהוה הושיעה נא אנא יהוה הצליחה נא
units.tr: Ana Adonai hoshia na; ana Adonai hatzlicha na. [אנא יהוה הושיעה נא אנא יהוה הצליחה נא]

units.la: 6. Totum Psalterium carminibus comprehenditur, seu numeris includitur. Cuius rei hæ videntur potissimum esse causæ. Primo nullum est scriptum in veteri canone, in quo de omnibus articulis fidei nostræ tam multa & illustria extent testimonia, quàm in Psalmis. Quare vt testimonia illa certa & incorrupta extarent, & transmitterentur ad posteros, Spiritus sanctus voluit hanc doctrinam numeris includi. Nam quæ numeris comprehensa sunt, ita cohærent, itaque mutuo nexu colligata sunt, vt si vel syllabam mutes, vel dictionem demasaut transponas, moxerre[?]deprehendatur. Turbatur enim harmonia, quam mens humana vt facile agnoscit, ita mirabiliter eâ capitur, & quasi constringitur, vt discedere abeâ nequeat. Vt igitur firma, certa, & deprauationibus minimè obnoxia traderentur doctrinæ Christianæ testimonia, Spiritus sanctus quasi ex omnibus scriptis propheticis collecta hæc embammata his numeris inclusit, & ecclesiæ commendauit. Nec dubium est diabolum, vt est operum Dei insidiosus μιμητὴς, hanc ipsam ob causam oracula sua versibus seu numeris inclusisse, vt scilicet authoritatem scriptis suis conciliaret, & sciscitatum missis occasionem vel mutandi vel deprauandi responsa præcideret. De Sibyllarum versibus idem est iudicium. Altera causa est, quia propter concinnitatem numerorum multum iuuant memoriam, nec ita facile effluunt, quæ numeris adstricta sunt, quàm soluta oratio. Vt igitur facilius comprehendi hæc doctrinà[?] vulgo, & ad posteros propagari posset, hoc quasi adminiculo fulcire imbecillitatem ingenij humani, & confulere perpetuitati voluit Spiritus sanctus. Videmus enim cantilenas per multa secula durare in vulgo, etiam cum res ipsæ aut historiæ amplius non sunt notæ. Hic vero deploranda est, tum miseria gentis Iudaicæ, tum vero ex parte aliquâ etiam nostra infelicitas, quòd rationem metri, quæ huius carminis propria est, ignoramus. Ea enim cum politiâ Iudaicâ, sicut alia multa, concidit. Sane nullum est dubium, quin si ratio metri nobis constaret, dulcius multò & commodatius nobis futurum esset hoc poema. Tertia causa est apud Athanasium epistolâ ad Marcellinum de interpretatione psalmorum, his verbis: Non ad delectationem aurium aut animorum scripta sunt, aut publicè in templis decantantur hæc poemata, vt pleraque Græcorum aut Latinorum olim in panegyribus recitabantur: sed potius, vt de harmoniâ omnium actionum in vitâ nos commonefaciant. Sicut enim harmonia tibias committens unum concentum efficit: ita quoque in animâ variis motionibus cogitandi, cupiendi, noscendi agitatâ, unde membris initium operandi desumitur, ratio postulat, hominem sibi consonum esse, neque ipsum à seipso dissidere, non vt optima quidem cogitet, pessima tamen faciat, quemadmodum Pilatus, qui cum diceret, Nullam causam mortis in eo invenio, Iudæorum tamen sententia suffragatus est: aut vt concupiscat mala, sed perpetrandi facultate destituatur, quales erant senes illi adversus Susannam: aut vt quidem ab adulterio abstineat, à furto non abstineat: aut vt à furto se purum servet, ab homicidio non servet. Et paulò post: Qui secundùm prædictam rationem concinunt, vt melodia verborum ex numeris vocum cum spiritus harmoniâ congruat, ipsi psallunt & lingua & mente, nec se ipsos solùm, sed etiam alios, qui audire volunt, mirificè adiuuant. Et rursus: Modulatim recitare psalmos nequaquam studium est concinnioris voculationis, sed argumentum cogitationum animi apte in harmoniâ consonantium. Et numeris adstricta lectio signum est concinna quietaque in animo affectionis. Quâ sententiâ Poëticam hanc sacram obsigno.
units.tr: 6. The whole Psalter is comprehended in verses, or enclosed in measures. The chief causes of this seem to be these. First, there is no writing in the Old Canon in which so many and such clear testimonies to all the articles of our faith are found as in the Psalms. Therefore, so that those testimonies might exist certain and uncorrupted and be handed down to posterity, the Holy Spirit willed this doctrine to be enclosed in measures. For things that are comprehended in measures cohere so closely and are bound together by such a mutual bond that, if you change even a syllable, or omit or transpose a word, the disturbance is detected at once. For the harmony is disturbed, which the human mind recognises easily, and is so wonderfully captured by it, and as it were bound, that it cannot depart from it. So, in order that the testimonies of Christian doctrine might be handed down firm, certain and least liable to corruption, the Holy Spirit, as it were gathering these sayings from all the prophetic writings, enclosed them in these measures and commended them to the Church. Nor is there doubt that the devil, as the crafty imitator of God's works, enclosed his oracles in verses or measures for this very reason: namely, to win authority for his writings, and to cut off from those who consulted them the opportunity either of altering or of corrupting the responses. The same judgement holds concerning the verses of the Sibyls. The second cause is that, on account of the harmony of measures, things bound by measure help the memory greatly, and those things that are bound by measure do not slip away so easily as loose prose. So, in order that this doctrine might be more easily grasped by the common people and propagated to posterity, the Holy Spirit willed to prop up the weakness of the human intellect with this kind of support, and to provide for the lasting of the teaching. For we see that songs endure among the common people for many centuries, even when the things themselves or the histories are no longer known. Here, however, both the misery of the Jewish nation and, in some measure, our own misfortune must be lamented, because we do not know the rule of metre that is proper to this song. For it perished together with the Jewish polity, as many other things did. Certainly there is no doubt that if the principle of the metre were known to us, this poem would be far sweeter and more convenient for us. The third cause is found in Athanasius, in his letter to Marcellinus on the interpretation of the Psalms, in these words: These writings were not composed for the delight of the ears or of the minds, nor are these poems sung publicly in the temples, as many of the Greek or Latin panegyrics were once recited; but rather so that they may remind us of the harmony of all actions in life. For just as harmony, joining the pipes, produces one concord, so also in the soul, which is stirred by various motions of thinking, desiring and knowing, from which the limbs take their beginning of acting, reason requires that man be consonant with himself, and not at odds with himself: not that he thinks the best things and yet does the worst, as Pilate did, who, when he said, "I find no cause of death in him," nevertheless yielded to the opinion of the Jews; or that he desires evil things but is deprived of the power of carrying them out, as were those old men against Susanna; or that he abstains from adultery but does not abstain from theft; or that he keeps himself pure from theft but does not keep himself from homicide. And a little later: Those who harmonise according to the aforesaid reason, so that the melody of the words agrees with the rhythm of the voices and the harmony of the spirit, they sing psalms both with the tongue and with the mind, and they help not only themselves but also others who wish to hear, wonderfully. And again: To recite psalms in modulated fashion is by no means a pursuit of more elegant vocalisation, but a display of the thoughts of the mind fittingly in agreement with harmony. And a reading bound by measure is a sign of a feeling in the mind that is harmonious and at rest. With this opinion I seal this Sacred Poetics.

units.la: XXVIII. MNEMONICA SACRA.
units.tr: XXVIII. THE SACRED MNEMONICS.

units.la: 1. MNemonica sacra est ars bene recordandi ex præscripto S. literarum.
units.tr: 1. The sacred mnemonics is the art of remembering well, according to the precept of the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: II. Eius partes duæ sunt: prima est de subiecto recordante, altera de obiecto, cuius oportet recordari: id est, de memoria, & rebus memoriæ mandandis.
units.tr: II. It has two parts: the first concerns the subject who remembers, the second the object which we ought to remember; that is, concerning memory and the things to be committed to memory.

units.la: III. Memoria est vis mentis, quâ memores sumus: id est, seruamus & retinemus, quæ cognouimus, ut promtè occurrant cogitantibus. Eius bonitas pendet à sequentibus. Primò requiritur bonum temperamentum cerebri & totius corporis: quod nempe non fit nimis siccum, neque nimis humidum, sed inter hæc duo medium siue temperatum. Deinde necessaria est abstinentia à voluptatibus. Nam voluptates ingenium & memoriam obtundunt, totumque corpus eneruant. Pertinet huc quod apostolus de immoderato vini visu præcipit Eph. 5. verf. 18. Ne inebriamini vino, in quo est ἀσωτία, id est, luxuria, salutem animi & corporis tollens. Hæc fuit causa Platoni, ut inter præceptiones, quas discipulis suis inculcabat, primam collocaret eam, ut à voluptatibus abstinerent. Tertiò requiritur perturbationum carentia. Nam scientia non potest percipi, nisi mente quiescente: unde etiam ἀπηγμένην[?] ἀπὸ τῆς παθήσεως deduxerunt. Quarto requiritur, ut animus memoriosi, τὰ μνήμονα[?], à curis & sollicitudinibus peregrinorum negotiorum sit vacuus. Hoc fuit primum præceptum, quod Origenes dedit Gregorio, qui postea cognominatus est Thaumaturgus. Quinto habenda est ratio loci & temporis. Et loci quidem ita, ut quæramus sceffum[?]: temporis autem ita, vt inprimis excolamus memoriam in pueritiâ & adolescentiâ , itemque tempore matutino & vespertino. Hic solet moueri quæstio, Cur Plato in Academiam, locum insalubrem, secesserit? Resp. Vt eximiam illam corporis habitudinem, quâ erat præditus, retunderet. Nam valetudo corporis, quæ in summo est, non leue adfert impedimentum inter studendum. Atque ita intelligendi sunt scriptores illi, qui tradunt aduersam valetudinem non leue pondus habere ad studia. Vide Basilium homil. de leg. libr. gent. Naζianζ. epist ad Eudoxum, & Philoponum lib. 3. de anima.
units.tr: III. Memory is the power of the mind by which we are mindful, that is, we keep and retain what we have learned, so that it comes readily to mind when we think. Its goodness depends on the following. First, a good temperament of the brain and of the whole body is required, namely one that is neither too dry nor too moist, but a mean or balance between the two. Next, abstinence from pleasures is necessary. For pleasures dull the wit and the memory and weaken the whole body. To this belongs what the apostle commands concerning the immoderate sight of wine: Eph. 5. verse 18. Do not be drunk with wine, wherein is excess (ἀσωτία, that is, luxury), which destroys the health of soul and body. This was Plato's reason for placing first among the precepts he impressed on his disciples that they should abstain from pleasures. Thirdly, freedom from disturbing passions is required. For knowledge cannot be grasped unless the mind is at rest; hence they also drew the word for "detached" from "passion". Fourthly, it is required that the mind of one who would remember be free from the cares and anxieties of foreign business. This was the first precept that Origen gave to Gregory, who was afterwards surnamed Thaumaturgus. Fifthly, account must be taken of place and time. As for place, we should look for a quiet spot; as for time, we should above all cultivate the memory in childhood and youth, and likewise at morning and evening. Here a question is usually raised: why did Plato withdraw to the Academy, an unhealthy place? Answer: to blunt that remarkable bodily constitution with which he was endowed. For a body in the highest state of health brings no small hindrance to study. And so those writers are to be understood who report that poor health is no small burden to studies. See Basil, homily on the books of the pagans, Gregory of Nazianzus, letter to Eudoxius, and Philoponus, book 3 on the soul.

units.la: IV. Obiectum, cuius oportet recordari, consideratur quantum ad qualitates suas, & media recordandi.
units.tr: IV. The object which we ought to remember is considered with respect to its qualities and the means of remembering.

units.la: V. Qualitates siue conditiones obiecti sunt duæ. Ac primò quidem res memoriæ commendanda debet esse amabilis. Sicut enim amor rerum omnium est principium, vt aiebat Parmenides, ita & memoriæ. Deinde illa ipsa res debet esse admirabilis. Admirabilis inquam vel excellentiâ & dignitate, vel vtilitate. Quæ duo fiadfint, nunquam non se ingeret animo res illa, quam volumus aut debemus memoriæ imprimere.
units.tr: V. The qualities or conditions of the object are two. First, the thing to be commended to memory ought to be lovable. For just as love is the beginning of all things, as Parmenides said, so it is of memory. Next, the thing itself ought to be admirable. I say admirable either for its excellence and worth, or for its usefulness. When both of these are present, that thing which we wish or ought to impress on memory will never fail to press itself upon the mind.

units.la: VI. Media siue adminicula recordandi ex Scripturis sacris colliguntur ista. Principio requiritur crebra repetitio. Sicut enim Deus in gubernatione mundi eandem actionem semper reperit, dando nobis coelitus pluuias, ac tempora edendis fructibus apta Act. 14. verf. 17. ita nos in omnibus nostris actionibus rectis & salutaribus debemus rem vnam & eandem sæpe repetere. Hinc dici solet in scholis: Actio sæpe iterata facit habitum. Hæc est causa, quòd Deus Deuteronom. 6. verf. 6. 7. legis suæ præcepta vult toties iterari: Et erunt verba ista, quæ ego præcipio tibi hodie, in corde tuo: eaque acute ingeres filiis tuis, at loac loqueris de eis, cum sedes domi tuae, & cum ambulas per viam, cum cubas, & cum surgu. Vbi notanda est emphasis in verbis acute ingeres, seu acuesea. Per translationem utitur hac voce Deus, metaphora ducta a cultro, qui dum acuitur, saepius impellitur ad cotem. Innuit studium & diligentiam, qua identidem repetenda & inculcanda sunt pueris praecepta legis. Huc pertinet quintus liber Mosis, qui est δευτερώσις τῆς νόμου[?], repetitio legis. Hanc artem repetitionis longe utilissimam nos etiam docet apostolus Phil. 3. verf. 1. Eadem scribere vobis, mihi quidem haud piget, vobis autem tutum est. O utinam praeceptores & discipuli meminerint huius aureae sententiae apostoli! Ego profecto alta voce dico, nihil esse, quod artem memoriae perficiat in principio, medio & fine, praeterquam repetitionem. Et quemadmodum animalia ista munda fuerunt iudicata, quae ruminat Leuit. 11. & Deut. 14. ita studiosos illos & doctores pronuntiatio frugi, qui assueuerunt crebrae repetitioni, eique horariae, diurnae, hebdomadariae, menstruae, bimestri, trimestri &c. Deinde consulitur memoriae per compendia. Hic modus instituendi, inde ab initio ecclesiae v.t. in populo Dei fuit visitatus. Nam Deus ipse Gen. 3. v. 15. euangelium contraxit in hanc summam: Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis. Idem Exod. 20. totam legem naturae reuocauit ad decem praecepta. Et Christus Matth. 6. & Luc. 11. in compendium redegit artem precandi. Idem Matth. 22. summam legis duobus hisce capitibus contineri docuit: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum &c. Hunc instituendi modum observarunt etiam apostoli: nominatim Paulus 1. Cor. 3. v. 2. vbi ait, se Corinthios rudes aluisse lactis potu, & non esca siue[?] solido cibo. Per lactis potum intelligit prima Christianismi principia, quae catechismum vocant: Per solidum cibum, pleniorem & accuratiorem doctrinam. Nimirum ut adolescebant Corinthij, ita eos aluit apostolus, initio lacte, post autem solido cibo, quae non re, sed tradendi modo differebant. Confer 1. Petr. 2. v. 2. Catecheticae istius, id est, compendiosae, institutionis mentio etiam fit. Luc. 1.
units.tr: VI. The means or aids of remembering are gathered from the Holy Scriptures as follows. First, frequent repetition is required. For just as God, in governing the world, always carries on the same action, giving us rain from heaven and seasons suited to bearing fruit (Acts 14:17), so in all our right and salutary actions we ought often to repeat one and the same thing. Hence it is commonly said in the schools: an action often repeated makes a habit. This is the reason why God wills that the precepts of his law be repeated so often (Deut. 6:6, 7): And these words which I command you this day shall be in your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, when you lie down and when you rise up. Here the emphasis is to be noted in the words "teach diligently", or literally "sharpen". God uses this word by a figure taken from a knife, which, while it is being sharpened, is pressed often against the whetstone. It signifies the zeal and diligence with which the precepts of the law are to be repeated and impressed again and again on children. To this belongs the fifth book of Moses, which is the deuteronomy (δευτερώσις τοῦ νόμου), that is, the repetition of the law. The apostle also teaches us this art of repetition, by far the most useful: Phil. 3. verse 1. To write the same things to you is not irksome to me, but for you it is safe. O that teachers and disciples would remember this golden saying of the apostle! I for my part say aloud that nothing perfects the art of memory at beginning, middle and end except repetition. And just as those animals which chew the cud were judged clean (Lev. 11, Deut. 14), so those scholars and teachers are rightly called fruitful who have accustomed themselves to frequent repetition, and to it at hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, bimonthly, quarterly intervals, and so on. Next, memory is aided by summaries. This method of teaching was in use among the people of God from the beginning of the Church. For God himself (Gen. 3:15) condensed the gospel into this summary: The seed of the woman shall bruise the head of the serpent. Likewise in Exodus 20 he reduced the whole law of nature to ten precepts. And Christ (Matt. 6, Luke 11) reduced the art of prayer to a summary. Again (Matt. 22) he taught that the sum of the law is contained in these two heads: You shall love the Lord your God, and so on. The apostles also observed this method of teaching, especially Paul (1 Cor. 3:2), where he says that he fed the Corinthians, who were unskilled, with milk to drink and not with solid food. By drinking milk he means the first principles of Christianity, which are called the catechism; by solid food, a fuller and more exact teaching. Clearly, as the Corinthians grew, the apostle fed them first with milk and afterwards with solid food, which differed not in substance but in the manner of teaching. Compare 1 Peter 2:2. A mention is also made of this catechetical, that is, summary, instruction (Luke 1:4; Rom. 4; 1 Cor. 14:19; Acts 21:24; Acts 18:25; Gal. 6:6). To this belong the various creeds, such as the Apostles', the Nicene, the Athanasian, and similar ones, which are nothing other than a summary of the articles of faith. From these one may gather how useful and necessary is this method of teaching which is carried on by summaries. And this catechetical method of teaching has prevailed not only in the Church, but has also found a place among all nations and among the teachers of all subjects. Hence Hermes wrote his Emerald Tablet; hence Hippocrates published his aphorisms; hence Euclid handed down the Elements; hence Justinian had the Institutes of law drawn up. Let it therefore remain that among the aids to memory it is not the least to begin from a summary. I say begin. For one must not always remain in the summary, but must proceed from the summary to a fuller treatment of the matter summarised, in accordance with the apostle's words (Heb. 6:1): Therefore, leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us go on to perfection. That is to say: once the heads of the catechism have been known as first principles, which indeed embrace the sum of the whole gospel doctrine but briefly and summarily, as they say, let us advance in the doctrine of salvation, going on to fuller instruction and understanding, lest that saying from 2 Tim. 3:7 be thrown at us:

units.la: verf. 4. Rom.[?]4.1.Cor.14.v.19.Act.21.v.24.c.18.v.25.Gal.6.v.6. Pertinent huc varia symbola, puta apostolicum, Nicenum, Athanasij, & similia, quae nihil sunt aliud, quam compendium articulorum fidei. Ex his colligere est, quam utilis & necessaria sit haec instituendi ratio, quae fit per compedia. Neque solum in ecclesia obtinuit haec catechetica docendi ratio, sed inter omnes quoque gentes & omnium facultatum doctores locum inuenit. Hinc est, quod Hermes scripsit suam tabulam smaragdinam: hinc est, quod Hippocrates aphorismos edidit: hinc est, quod Euclides elementa tradidit: hinc est, quod Iustinianus Institutiones iuris conscribi curauit. Maneat itaque, inter subsidia memoriae nō infimum esse, siquis à compendio incipiat. Dico, incipiat. Non enim oportet semper versari in compendio, sed oportet à compendio pergere ad diexodicam rei in compendio traditae tractationem, iuxta illud apostoli Heb.6.v.1. Quapropter omisso, qui in Christo rudes inchoat sermone, ad perfectionem feramur. q.d. Capitibus catechismi, quae summam quidem totius euangelicae doctrinae complectuntur, sed paucis, & summarie, ut loquuntur: his, inquam, capitibus cognitis tanquam rudimentis, prosiciamus in doctrina salutis, pergendo ad pleniorem institutionem & comprehensionem, ne nobis obijciatur illud ex 2.Tim.3.v.7.
units.tr: vers. 4. Rom.[?]4.1.Cor.14.v.19.Act.21.v.24.c.18.v.25.Gal.6.v.6. To this belong the various creeds, such as the Apostles' Creed, the Nicene, the Athanasian, and similar ones, which are nothing other than a summary of the articles of faith. From these one can gather how useful and necessary is this method of teaching, which is carried out by means of summaries. Nor has this catechetical method of teaching prevailed only in the Church; it has also found a place among all nations and among the teachers of every discipline. Hence Hermes wrote his Emerald Tablet; hence Hippocrates published his Aphorisms; hence Euclid handed down his Elements; hence Justinian had his Institutes of law compiled. Let it therefore remain that, among the aids to memory, it is no small one to begin from a summary. I say, to begin. For one ought not always to remain within the summary, but ought to proceed from the summary to a fuller treatment of the matter handed down in brief, in keeping with the apostle's words in Heb. 6.v.1: Therefore leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us go on unto perfection. That is to say: once the heads of the catechism, which indeed contain the sum of the whole gospel teaching but in few words and in summary fashion, as they say, have been known as the rudiments, let us advance in the doctrine of salvation, proceeding to a fuller instruction and understanding, lest that saying of 2.Tim.3.v.7 be applied to us.

units.la: Semper discentes, sed nunquam proficientes. Confer Hebr.5. v.12.13.14. Tertium memoriae subsidium est dilucida rei explicatio, qua fit ut res velut oculis subijciatur. Ita Galatis Christus κατ' ὀφθαλμούς προεγεγράφη[?], ob oculos fuit depictus, id est, ita egregie ac perspicue fuit propositus, ut quasi oculis eorum repraesentata fuerit viua ipsius imago, ac si apud ipsos esset crucifixus. Huiusmodi graphica alicuius rei descriptio efficaciter ferit sensum, intellectum, & memoriam. In id ergo simus intenti, ut perspicuitati studeamus, eique tum αἰσθητικὴ[?], tum νοητικὴ, ut loquuntur. Hoc Graeci vocant περὶ ὀμμάτων ποιεῖν[?], Latini, ob oculos ponere. Quartum adminiculum memoriae positum est in signis mnemonicis, quæ vocant μνημόσυνα, memorialia. Eiusmodi signa sunt multa. Et primò quidem sunt signa appensa membris corporis, de quibus Exod.13.v.16. Et erit in signum super manum tuam, & in frontalia inter oculos tuos: & Deut.6.verf.8. Ligabisque ea in signum in manu tua, & erunt in frontalia inter oculos tuos: h.e. facies laminas, vel membranulas, quibus inscribes legem meam, & laminas istas, vel membranulas habebis inter brachialia & frontalia, quæ obuersabuntur oculis tuis, vt iugiter tibi redeant in memoriam. Signa iltiusmodi Chaldaicè vocantur [?] philin, Græcè Φυλακτήρια Matth. 23. verf. 5. Talia signa hodie possunt constitui in manibus, annulis, vestibus, & rebus similibus, vt memoriam nostram iuuent. Confer Prouerb.3.v.3.&c.7.v.2. Deinde sunt signa in tabulis, parietibus, postibus, libris, columnis &c. expressa. Sic Deut.6. v.9. ait Dominus: Scribes quoque illa in postibus domus tuæ, & in portis tuis. Hoc præcipiebat Dominus, vt quotiescunq; quis ingrederetur domum, intueretur illa, & reminisceretur. Potest itaque & hodie hæc memoriæ βακτηρίαι adhiberi. Tertiò sunt signa solenniter erecta aliquo in loco. Sic Iacob Gen.28. v.18.22. erexit lapidem in titulum siue statuam, vt esset monumentum visionis. Confer Gen.31. verf.45. Sic Deut.27.v.2.3. ait Dominus: Erit autem die, quâ transferitis Iordanem, vt eatis ad terram, quam Iehoua Deus tuus dat tibi, eriges tibi lapides magnos, quos linies calce, & scribes in illis omnia verba legis huius &c. Hoc postea factum est Iof.4. verf.2. & seqq. Quintò sunt signa certis ritibus & actionibus constantia: qualia sunt sacrificia v.t. & omnino sacramenta v. & n.t. quorum finis inter alia est, in memoriam nobis redigere beneficia Dei Exod. 13. verf.9.1. Corinth.11. verf.24. Quæ omnia eo spectant, vt videamus, quot modis Deus contuluerit memoriæ nostræ, & inde discamus, nos nihil absurdi committere, fiabsque κατὰ ζηλίᾳ imitemur hunc modum in aliis materijs. Quintum subsidium labilis memoriæ est ἀνάμνησις. Visus enim ad cognitionem, apprehensionem, & impressionem rei estaptissiptissimus: quia magis mouet imaginationem, & vehementius ei imprimit quod percepit, quàm sensus cæteri: vnde tenacius inhærent memoriæ, quæ visu percepta sunt. Hinc est, quòd Psal. 34. verf.9. ait Dauid, Gustate & videte, quòd bonum Iehoua. Sextum adminiculum est viua vox, adeoque ἀκροάσις[?], auditio. Nam auditus maximè conducit ad scientiam comparandam, quia disciplinæ percipiuntur per auditum. Ergò vt visu discimus à nobis, ita auditu discimus ab alijs. Rectè igitur Albertus Magnus 1.metaph.c.1. hunc sensum maximè disciplinalem appellauit. Hinc est, quòd Deus toties inculcat illud, Audi, Audite. Vbi singulare est, quòd Psal.45.v.11. coniunguntur ista duo, Audi & vide. De institutione, quæ fit viuâ voce, vide paulò ante loca Scripturæ de catechetica docendi formâ. Nam catechesis significat ista duo: institutionem compendiosam, quæ fit viua voce. Septimum subsidium est scriptio. Hæc enim adeò mouet imaginationem, mentem, & memoriam, vt videri possit potior viuâ loquentis voce. Nam etsi viua vox semper habet aliquid latentis energiæ: tamen citò præteruolat, neque ita manet vt scriptura. Quæ etiam causa est, quòd Deus verbum suum scriptis mandauit. Rom.15.v.4. Octauum memoriæ adminiculum est ordo. Ordo, inquam, quo membra tractationis ita inter se cohærent, vt se inuicem capiant & contineant, vt in catenâ annulus annulum. Huiusmodi ordo non solùm in singulis sacrorum librorum capitibus, sed etiâ in ipsismet libris, quantum ad cohærentiam capitum, est obseruatus: vt ex analyticis sacrarum literarum interpretibus est manifestum. Nonum adminiculû est varietas prudens in docendo. Cùm autem tradendarum disciplinarum in scholis plures sint & diuersi modi; duo præcipui cùm à philosophis antiquis, tum ab omnibus fidelibus præceptoribus reperiuntur vsurpati: vnus, quando solus loquitur, qui docet; alter, quando interrogationes & responsiones adhibetur, & vel præceptor suos discipulos interrogat, vel discipuli præceptore. His docendi modis optimum doctorem Christum esse vsum, historia euangelistarum non obscure significat. Solus loquitur Christus saepissime, ut in concionibus suis Matth. 5. & alibi. Interdum a discipulis interrogatur, ut Iohan. 9. v. 2. Est quando suos ipse discipulos interrogat. Matth. 16. Marc. 8. Luc. 9. Prudentis itaque praeceptoris est, varietate hac prudenti, grata & vtili, partim excitare, partim exhilarare discipulum torpentem. Decimum subsidium est oratio ligata: quae quomodo in sacris literis sit adhibita vide in Poetica. Id solùm hìc observa, rhythmos & versus occultam habere cognationem cum memoriâ. Vndecimum memoriae adminiculû est artificium literarium, quo fit, ut res aliqua elegantiartificio iuxta ordinem literarum digeratur. Quod quidem artificium parui esse momenti nemo audebit dicere, qui meminerit Spiritum sanctum in pluribus psalmis, puta Psal. 25. 34.37. 111.112.145. praesertim autem in omnium longissimo, & ad vitam pie instituendam omnium maximè necessario, id est, Psalm. 119. infirmitati nostrae hac in parte non dedignatum esse succurrere; sed illa sacra carmina vario artificio, secundum ordinem literarum Hebraicarum in eum praecipuè finem digessisse. Confer Proverb. 31. & Thren. 1. 2. 3. 4. De psalmo 119. illud quoque est adnotandum, contineri in illo viginti duos octonarios pro numero literarum Hebraicarum, quorum singuli versus, iuxta Hebraicae linguae elegantiam, incipiunt ab vnâ & eâdem litera: nullum denique esse versum, praeter vnum centesimum vigesimum secundum, qui non habeat, si non plures, vnam saltem ex his decem vocibus: תורה lex, חקים statuta, מצוה praeceptum, פקודים obseruationes, עדות testimonia, משפטים iudicia, אמרה sermo, דבר verbum, צדק iustitia, דרך via. Atque haec etiam sunt adminicula memoriae, quae in S.
units.tr: Always learning, but never making progress. Compare Heb. 5.12–14. The third aid to memory is a clear explanation of the matter, by which the thing is set, as it were, before the eyes. So Christ was placed before the Galatians [κατ' ὀφθαλμούς προεγεγράφη], that is, he was portrayed before their eyes: he was set forth so vividly and plainly that the living image of him seemed to be presented to their eyes, as if he had been crucified among them. A graphic description of this kind strikes the senses, the understanding and the memory with force. Let us therefore aim at clarity and strive for it, both sensible [αἰσθητικὴ] and intelligible [νοητικὴ], as they say. The Greeks call this to make before the eyes [περὶ ὀμμάτων ποιεῖν], the Latins to put before the eyes. The fourth aid to memory consists in mnemonic signs, which they call memorials [μνημόσυνα], memorialia. There are many such signs. First, there are signs attached to parts of the body, of which Exod. 13.16 says: And it shall be a sign upon your hand, and frontlets between your eyes. And Deut. 6.8: And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes. That is, you shall make plates or little membranes on which you will inscribe my law, and you shall have these plates or membranes between your arm-bands and your frontlets, where they will be before your eyes, so that they constantly come back to your memory. Such signs are called in Chaldee philin, in Greek phylacteries [Φυλακτήρια] (Matt. 23.5). Such signs can today be made for the hands, rings, garments and similar things, to help our memory. Compare Prov. 3.3 and following, and 7.2. Second, there are signs written on tablets, walls, doorposts, books, columns and so on. Thus the Lord says in Deut. 6.9: You shall also write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates. The Lord commanded this so that whenever anyone entered the house, he would look at those words and remember them. So these staffs of memory [βακτηρίαι] may be used today too. Third, there are signs solemnly set up in some place. So Jacob set up a stone as a title or monument, a memorial of the vision (Gen. 28.18–22). Compare Gen. 31.45. Thus the Lord says in Deut. 27.2–3: And it shall be on the day when you pass over the Jordan into the land which the Lord your God gives you, that you shall set up for yourselves great stones, and plaster them with lime, and write on them all the words of this law, etc. This was afterwards done in Josh. 4.2 and following. Fifth, there are signs consisting of fixed rites and actions, such as the sacrifices of the Old Testament and, in general, the sacraments of the Old and New Testaments, whose purpose is, among other things, to bring to our remembrance the benefits of God (Exod. 13.9; 1 Cor. 11.24). All of these aim at our seeing in how many ways God has provided for our memory, and so learning that we should commit nothing absurd, and that out of zeal [κατὰ ζῆλον] we should imitate this method in other matters. The fifth aid to a slippery memory is reminding [ἀνάμνησις]. For sight is most apt for knowing, grasping and impressing a thing, since it moves the imagination more and imprints on it what it has perceived more forcefully than the other senses; hence what has been perceived by sight clings more tenaciously to the memory. This is why David says in Ps. 34.8: Taste and see that the Lord is good. The sixth aid is the living voice, and so hearing [ἀκροάσις], listening. For hearing contributes most to acquiring knowledge, since the disciplines are grasped through hearing. Therefore, as we learn from sight by ourselves, so we learn from hearing from others. Rightly therefore Albertus Magnus (in his Metaphysics 1, ch. 1) called this the most disciplinary sense. This is why God so often inculcates the words Hear, hear. It is remarkable that in Ps. 45.11 the two are joined: Hear and see. Concerning instruction given by the living voice, see above the passages of Scripture on the catechetical form of teaching; for catechesis signifies these two things: a compendious instruction given by the living voice. The seventh aid is writing. For this so moves the imagination, the mind and the memory that it may seem more powerful than the living voice of a speaker. For although the living voice always has some hidden energy, yet it flies past quickly and does not remain as writing does. This is also the reason why God committed his word to writings (Rom. 15.4). The eighth aid to memory is order: I mean the order by which the parts of a treatment cohere with one another so that they take hold of and contain each other, like a ring in a chain. Such order has been observed not only in the individual chapters of the sacred books but also, as far as the coherence of the chapters goes, in the books themselves, as is clear from the analytical interpreters of the sacred letters. The ninth aid is prudent variety in teaching. Since there are several different methods of teaching the disciplines in schools, two principal ones are found used both by the ancient philosophers and by all faithful teachers: one, when the teacher alone speaks; the other, when questions and answers are employed, either the teacher questioning his pupils or the pupils questioning the teacher. That Christ, the best teacher, used these methods the history of the evangelists makes clear enough. Christ speaks alone most often, as in his sermons (Matt. 5) and elsewhere. Sometimes he is questioned by his disciples (John 9.2). Sometimes he himself questions his disciples (Matt. 16; Mark 8; Luke 9). It is therefore the part of a prudent teacher, by this pleasing and useful variety, partly to rouse and partly to cheer a sluggish pupil. The tenth aid is bound speech [oratio ligata], on how this is used in the sacred letters see under Poetics. Note only here that rhythms and verses have a hidden kinship with memory. The eleventh aid to memory is the literary artifice by which some matter is arranged elegantly according to the order of the letters. No one will dare to say that this artifice is of little importance who remembers that the Holy Spirit did not disdain to help our weakness in this respect in several psalms, for instance Pss. 25, 34, 37, 111, 112, 145, and especially in the longest of all, and the one most necessary of all for devoutly instructing life, that is Ps. 119; but arranged those sacred songs with varied artifice, according to the order of the Hebrew letters, chiefly for this purpose. Compare Prov. 31 and Lam. 1–4. Concerning Ps. 119 it is also to be noted that it contains twenty-two eight-line stanzas, according to the number of the Hebrew letters, each of whose verses, according to the elegance of the Hebrew language, begins with one and the same letter; and finally that there is no verse, except the one hundred and twenty-second, which does not have, if not more, at least one of these ten words: law [תורה], statutes [חקים], precept [מצוה], observances [פקודים], testimonies [עדות], judgments [משפטים], saying [אמרה], word [דבר], righteousness [צדק], way [דרך]. These too are aids to memory, which occur in the Holy

units.la: Literis occurrunt.
units.tr: Letters.

units.la: XXIX. IURISPRUDENTIA SACRA.
units.tr: XXIX. Sacred Jurisprudence.

units.la: I. Iurisprudentia sacra est doctrina æqui & boni ex sacris literis petita. Et quia ex Mose, divino illo legislatore, colligitur, Mosaica dici potest. Huius iurisprudentiae tanta est dignitas, ut merito habeatur pro regulâ & normâ iurisprudentiae Romanæ.Et spes magna me tenet, pios ICtos cunctas leges suas ad ius diuinum per Mosem traditum tandem aliquando reuocaturos, dissimiles Thomae Linacro, qui lecto illo Christi Matth. 5. vers. 44. Diligite inimicos vestros, librum in terram proiecit, his verbis additis: Aut hæc vera non sunt, aut Christiani non sumus.
units.tr: I. Sacred jurisprudence is the doctrine of what is right and good, drawn from the sacred writings. Since it is gathered from Moses, that divine lawgiver, it may be called Mosaic. Its dignity is so great that it deservedly counts as the rule and standard of Roman jurisprudence. And I have a strong hope that the pious jurists will at last refer all their laws back to the divine law handed down through Moses, unlike Thomas Linacre, who, on reading that saying of Christ, Matth. 5. vers. 44. Love your enemies, threw the book on the ground, adding these words: Either these things are not true, or we are not Christians.

units.la: II. Iurisprudentiae sacrae partes sunt duæ: prima, de collatione iuris Romanicum decalogo; secunda, de legum Mosaicarum forensium explanatione.
units.tr: II. Sacred jurisprudence has two parts: the first is the comparison of Roman law with the Decalogue; the second is the explanation of the forensic laws of Moses.

units.la: III. Prima pars continetur hac regulâ. Leges iuris Romani referantur ad præcepta decalogi, hoc fere modo.
units.tr: III. The first part is contained in this rule: the laws of Roman law are to be referred to the precepts of the Decalogue, roughly in this way.

units.la: Adpraceptumprimum. De summâ Trinitate & fide catholicâ: de hæreticis & Manichæis.
units.tr: To the first precept. On the holy Trinity and the catholic faith; on heretics and Manichaeans.

units.la: Adsecundum. De signo salvatoris Christi non sculpendo vel pingendo.
units.tr: To the second. On not carving or painting the image of the Saviour Christ.

units.la: Ad tertium. De iuramento, testibus &c.
units.tr: To the third. On oaths, witnesses, etc.

units.la: Ad quartum. De sacrosanctis ecclesijs, de diebus festis, &c.
units.tr: To the fourth. On sacred churches, on feast days, etc.

units.la: Adquintum. De libertate, seruitute, ingenuis, libertinis, manumissione, seruis, filijsfamiliâs, adoptione, patriâ potestate, tutelâ, curâ, curatoribus, satisdatione, excusatione, tutore, actione coram iudice, interdicto, litigantibus, procuratore, in ius vocatione, armis litigantium, poena temeritatis, officio iudicis, iudicio publico & priuato, terminis iudicialibus, sententia, appellatione, magistratu, de episcopis & clericis, de episcopali audientia.
units.tr: To the fifth. On liberty, slavery, freeborn persons, freedmen, manumission, slaves, sons under power, adoption, paternal power, guardianship, care, curators, security, excuse, tutor, action before a judge, interdict, litigants, proxy, summons to court, the arms of litigants, penalty for rashness, the office of a judge, public and private judgment, judicial time-limits, sentence, appeal, the magistrate, on bishops and clergy, on the episcopal hearing.

units.la: Ad sextum. De homicidio, iniuriis realibus &c.
units.tr: To the sixth. On homicide, on injuries to the person, etc.

units.la: Ad septimum. De sponsalibus, nuptiis, matrimonio, cognatione, affinitate, polygamia, diuortio, adulterio, spuriis, liberis, fratribus, sororibus.
units.tr: To the seventh. On betrothal, marriage, wedlock, kinship, affinity, polygamy, divorce, adultery, illegitimate children, children, brothers, sisters.

units.la: Ad octauum. De postliminio, bonorum diuisione, dominio, thesauro, traditione, seruitutibus, vsu, vfufructu, habitatione, vsucapione, donatione, alienatione, peculio, haereditate, prodigo, legato, repraesentatione, bonorum possessione, obligatione, contractu, mutuo, indebito, commodato, deposito, pignore, emtione & venditione, locatione, emphyteufi, societate, mandato, solutione, acceptilatione, nouatione, contraria voluntate, furto, poena furti, rapina, damno, testamento, codicillo.
units.tr: To the eighth. On postliminy, division of goods, ownership, treasure, delivery, servitudes, use, usufruct, habitation, usucaption, gift, alienation, peculium, inheritance, the prodigal, legacy, representation, possession of goods, obligation, contract, loan, what is owed by mistake, loan for use, deposit, pledge, buying and selling, letting and hiring, emphyteusis, partnership, mandate, payment, acceptilation, novation, contrary will, theft, penalty for theft, robbery, damage, testament, codicil.

units.la: Ad nonum. De fideiuffione, chirographo, teste, actore, reo, aduocato.
units.tr: To the ninth. On suretyship, handwriting, witness, plaintiff, defendant, advocate.

units.la: Ad decimum. Tria iuris principia, Honeste viuere, Neminem laedere, suum cuique tribuere.
units.tr: To the tenth. The three principles of law: to live honestly, to harm no one, to give each his due.

units.la: IV. Secunda pars iurisprudentiae sacrae explanat leges Mosaicas forenses reuocatas ad singula decalogi praecepta, hoc modo.
units.tr: IV. The second part of sacred jurisprudence explains the forensic laws of Moses, referred to each precept of the Decalogue, in this way.

units.la: Ad primum praeceptum.
units.tr: To the first commandment.

units.la: 1. Lex de puniendo falso propheta. Deut. 13. & 18.
units.tr: 1. The law on punishing a false prophet. Deut. 13. and 18.

units.la: 2. Lex de puniendis illis, qui contumaciter respuerint iudicium sacerdotum. Deut. 17. v. 12. 13.
units.tr: 2. The law on punishing those who stubbornly refuse to obey the judgment of the priests. Deut. 17. vers. 12, 13.

units.la: 3. Lex de integris vrbibus exscindendis, si suaserint defectionem à Deo. Deut. 13. v. 12. & seqq.
units.tr: 3. The law on utterly destroying whole cities if they have persuaded people to fall away from God. Deut. 13. vers. 12 and following.

units.la: 4. Lex de magis, ariolis &c. vbi tenendum, species artium magicarum & illarum amatorum nouem apud Mosen recenseri: videl. traductionem per ignem, diuinationes, planetarios, auguria, praestigias, incantatioaes[?],pythonicos,sortilegos,necyomantiam. Exod. 22. v. 18. 20. Levit. 20. v. 2. 6. 27. Deut. 18. v. 10.
units.tr: 4. The law on magicians, diviners, etc. Here it must be noted that Moses lists nine kinds of magical arts and of those who practise them: namely, passing through fire, divinations, astrologers, augury, illusions, enchantments, pythonists, soothsayers, and necromancy. Exod. 22. vers. 18, 20. Lev. 20. vers. 2, 6, 27. Deut. 18. vers. 10.

units.la: 5. Lex de puniendis Cyclopibus illis, qui nec Deum, nec homines metuunt, quiq; aperte & elata manu Deum blasphemando alios in eandem audaciam pertrahunt. Num. 15. v. 30. 31.
units.tr: 5. The law on punishing those reckless men who fear neither God nor men, and who, blaspheming God openly and with a high hand, draw others into the same audacity. Num. 15. vers. 30, 31.

units.la: 6. Lex de poena, si quis neglecta prohibitione fermentum miscuerit cum paschate[?]. Num. 12. v. 15. c. 19. v. 19.
units.tr: 6. The law on the penalty if anyone, disregarding the prohibition, mixes leaven with the Passover. Num. 12. vers. 15; ch. 19. vers. 19.

units.la: 7. Lex vt bellagerant sub auspiciis Dei, eiusque auxilio confisi ducem sequantur, nihil territi potentia hostium. Deut. 20. v. 1. 2. 3. 4.
units.tr: 7. The law that they go to war under the auspices of God, and, trusting in his help, follow the leader, not terrified at all by the power of the enemy. Deut. 20. vers. 1, 2, 3, 4.

units.la: 8. Lex de tubis argenteis, quae collectionis signum dabant, vt populus semper ad Dei vocem & nutum intentus esset. Num. 10. v. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: 8. The law on the silver trumpets, which gave the signal for assembly, so that the people might always be attentive to the voice and nod of God. Num. 10. vers. 1 and following.

units.la: Ad secundum praeceptum.
units.tr: To the second commandment.

units.la: 1. Leges de idololatria externa: puta de imaginibus idololatricis, templis idololatricis, altaribus item, excelsis, & lucis idololatricis. Exod. 23. verf. 24. c. 34. verf. 13. 17. Num. 33. verf. 52. Deut. 7. verf. 5. 25. cap. 12. verf. 3. cap. 27. verf. 15.
units.tr: 1. Laws on external idolatry: namely, on idolatrous images, idolatrous temples, likewise altars, high places, and idolatrous groves. Exod. 23. vers. 24; ch. 34. vers. 13, 17. Num. 33. vers. 52. Deut. 7. vers. 5, 25; ch. 12. vers. 3; ch. 27. vers. 15.

units.la: 2. Lex de vitandis & exstirpandis infidelibus, qui tanquam flabella magis ac magis accendunt idololatriam. Exod. 23. verf. 31. 32. 33. cap. 34. verf. 11. 12. 15. 16. Deut. 7. verf. 1. 2. 3. 4.
units.tr: 2. The law on shunning and rooting out unbelievers, who, like fans, kindle idolatry more and more. Exod. 23. vers. 31, 32, 33; ch. 34. vers. 11, 12, 15, 16. Deut. 7. vers. 1, 2, 3, 4.

units.la: 3. Lex de admittendis alienigenis. Deut. 23. verf. 3. & seqq.
units.tr: 3. The law on admitting foreigners. Deut. 23. vers. 3 and following.

units.la: Ad tertium praeceptum.
units.tr: To the third commandment.

units.la: Huius praecepti appendix est lex illa Leu. 24. v. 15. 16. vbi poena capitis statuitur aduersus peccatum blasphemiae.
units.tr: An appendix to this precept is that law in Lev. 24. vers. 15, 16, where the penalty of death is laid down against the sin of blasphemy.

units.la: Ad quartum praeceptum.
units.tr: To the fourth commandment.

units.la: Huius loci est lex de poena sabbati violatoribus irrogandâ. Exod. 31. v. 14. 15. Num. 15. v. 36. item de bonis ecclesiasticis Leuit. 27. v. 30. Num. 18. v. 21. 24. Deut. 14. v. 22. 28. c. 16. ver. 11. denique de obseruatione anni sabbatarij. Exod. 23. v. 10.
units.tr: This place contains the law concerning the penalty to be inflicted on those who violate the Sabbath: Exod. 31. 14, 15; Num. 15. 36. It also covers the ecclesiastical goods: Lev. 27. 30; Num. 18. 21, 24; Deut. 14. 22, 28; ch. 16, verse 11. Finally, it covers the observance of the sabbatical year: Exod. 23. 10.

units.la: Ad quintum praeceptum.
units.tr: To the fifth commandment.

units.la: Appendices politicae huius praecepti sunt leges de illis, qui
units.tr: The civil appendices to this commandment are the laws concerning those who

units.la: ʃ Marks in the left margin and at the line "blasphemando" are doubtful printed marks, transcribed only as a note. qui parentibus vim vel atrocem iniuriam inferunt: quales sunt parricidae, parentum percussores, parentibus maledicentes, parentibus rebellantes: item de poenis illorum, qui in magistratum, & ecclesiae ministros sunt iniurii. Exod. 21. v. 11. 15. 17. c. 22. v. 28. Deut. 17. v. 12. c. 21, v. 18. 6.27.v.16.[?] Pertinet quoque huc lex regia Deut. 17.
units.tr: who do violence or grievous wrong to their parents: such as murderers of fathers, strikers of parents, those who curse their parents, and those who rebel against their parents. Also the penalties for those who insult the magistrates and the ministers of the Church: Exod. 21. 11, 15, 17; ch. 22, verse 28; Deut. 17. 12; ch. 21, verse 18; ch. 27, verse 16[?]. The royal law of Deut. 17 also belongs here.

units.la: Ad sextum praeceptum.
units.tr: To the sixth commandment.

units.la: 1. Leges de homicidio voluntario & involuntario. Exod. 21. v. 12.13.18.20. 21.Levit. 24. v. 17. 18. Num. 35. v.16. Deut. 27. v. 24. c. 19. v. 4.
units.tr: 1. Laws concerning voluntary and involuntary homicide: Exod. 21. 12, 13, 18, 20, 21; Lev. 24. 17, 18; Num. 35. 16; Deut. 27. 24; ch. 19, verse 4.

units.la: 2. Leges de mutilationibus & percussionibus. Exod.21. vers. 22. 26. quò pertinet lex talionis.
units.tr: 2. Laws concerning mutilations and blows: Exod. 21, verses 22, 26. To this belongs the law of retaliation (lex talionis).

units.la: 3. Lex de reperto occisi cadauere. Deut. 21. v. 1.
units.tr: 3. The law concerning a corpse found slain: Deut. 21. 1.

units.la: 4. Lex de bove cornupetâ laedente hominem. Exod.21. v.28.32.
units.tr: 4. The law concerning an ox that gores a man: Exod. 21. 28, 32.

units.la: 5. Lex de numero plagarum alicui infligendarum. Deut.25.v.2.
units.tr: 5. The law concerning the number of stripes to be inflicted on anyone: Deut. 25. 2.

units.la: 6. Lex de non lædendis peregrinis. Exod.22.v.21.c.23. v.9. Leuit.19.v.33.
units.tr: 6. The law that strangers are not to be harmed: Exod. 22. 21; ch. 23, verse 9; Lev. 19. 33.

units.la: 7. Lex de servo profugo ob sævitiam heri. Deut.23.v.15. vers.15.
units.tr: 7. The law concerning a slave who flees from the cruelty of his master: Deut. 23. 15, verse 15.

units.la: 8. Lex de nido avium[?] reperto. Deut.22.v.6.
units.tr: 8. The law concerning a bird's nest found: Deut. 22. 6.

units.la: 9. Lex de non comedendo sanguine bestiæ. Leuit.7. v.26.c.17.v.10.c.19.v.26. Deut.12.v.15.20.
units.tr: 9. The law forbidding the eating of an animal's blood: Lev. 7. 26; ch. 17, verse 10; ch. 19, verse 26; Deut. 12. 15, 20.

units.la: 10. Leges polemicæ, sive bellicæ: cuiusmodi sunt, de 25 concione sacerdotis antequam prælium ineatur Deut.20. vers.1. de personis, à bello immunibus, quæ non debent proficisci in militiam. Deut.20.v.5.7.8. de ætate in militiam adscribendorum Num.1. vers.3.c.26.v.2. de transitu militum per terras fratrum. Num.20.v.17. Deut.2. vers.4. 30 de exploratoribus, eorumque missione. Num.13.v.3.19. Deut.1.ver.22. de munditiæ castrorum. Deut.23.v.9.12. de ducibus in primâ acie constituendis. Deut.20.v.9. de arboribus frugiferis non excindendis. Deut.20.v.19. de pace offerendâ, vel non offerendâ. Deut.20.v.10. de prædâ 35 ritè distribuendâ. Num.31.v.26.
units.tr: 10. Laws of war, or martial laws, of which the following are examples: concerning the priest's address to the assembly before battle is joined, Deut. 20, verse 1; concerning persons exempt from war, who ought not to go out to military service, Deut. 20. 5, 7, 8; concerning the age at which men are enrolled for military service, Num. 1, verse 3; ch. 26, verse 2; concerning the passage of soldiers through the lands of brethren, Num. 20. 17; Deut. 2, verse 4; concerning spies and their sending out, Num. 13. 3, 19; Deut. 1, verse 22; concerning the cleanliness of the camp, Deut. 23. 9, 12; concerning the appointment of leaders in the front line, Deut. 20. 9; concerning not cutting down fruit trees, Deut. 20. 19; concerning whether or not peace is to be offered, Deut. 20. 10; concerning the proper distribution of booty, Num. 31. 26.

units.la: Ad septimum præceptum.
units.tr: To the seventh commandment.

units.la: 1. Lex de coniugiis prohibitis. Leuit. 18. & 20. Vetantur autem coniugia inter tredecim personarum consanguinitate vel affinitate coniunctarum genera: videl. cum matre; cum vxore patris siue nouercâ; cum sorore, siue ex patre, siue ex matre; cum nepte ex filiâ; cum filiâ vxoris patris, h. e. cum filiâ nouercae; cum sorore patris, h. e. cum amitâ; cum sorore matris, h. e. cum matertera; cum vxore patrui; cum nuru; cum vxore fratris; cum filiâ vxo-ris, h. e. cum priuignâ; cum nepte ex filiâ vel filio vxoris; cum sorore vxoris.
units.tr: 1. The law concerning forbidden marriages. Lev. 18 and 20. Marriage is forbidden between persons joined by thirteen kinds of kinship or affinity, namely: with a mother; with the wife of one's father, that is, a stepmother; with a sister, whether by father or by mother; with a granddaughter through a daughter; with the daughter of one's father's wife, that is, the daughter of a stepmother; with one's father's sister, that is, an aunt; with one's mother's sister, that is, a maternal aunt; with an uncle's wife; with a daughter-in-law; with a brother's wife; with the daughter of one's wife, that is, a stepdaughter; with a granddaughter through a daughter or son of one's wife; with a wife's sister.

units.la: 2. Lex de coitu cum muliere menstruatâ. Leuit. 18. v. 19. c. 20. v. 18.
units.tr: 2. The law concerning intercourse with a menstruating woman. Lev. 18, verse 19; ch. 20, verse 18.
3. The law concerning sodomy. Lev. 18, verses 22, 23; ch. 20, verses 13, 15, 16; Exod. 22, verse 19; Deut. 27, verse 21.

units.la: 4. Lex de poenâ adulterij. Leu. 20. verf. 10. Deut. 22. verf. 22.
units.tr: 4. The law concerning the penalty for adultery. Lev. 20, verse 10; Deut. 22, verse 22.

units.la: 5. Lex de coitu cum virgine desponsatâ. Deut. 22. verf. 23. 25.
units.tr: 5. The law concerning intercourse with a betrothed virgin. Deut. 22, verses 23, 25.

units.la: 6. Lex de coitu cum concubinâ alterius. Leu. 19. v. 20.
units.tr: 6. The law concerning intercourse with another man's concubine. Lev. 19, verse 20.

units.la: 7. Lex de nuptiis ancillae, quae est filia. Exod. 21. v. 7.
units.tr: 7. The law concerning the marriage of a female slave who is a daughter. Exod. 21, verse 7.

units.la: 8. Lex de suspectâ virginitate illius, quam aliquis duxit. Deut. 22. v. 13.
