For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God. For we know that the whole creation groans together and suffers the pains of childbirth together until now.

units.la: Apoc. 21. v. 1. Deinde vidi cœlum nouum & terram nouam: primum enim cœlum & prima terra abierat: & [?]mare non amplius extabat. Confer Esa. 65. v. 17. & 66. v. 22.
units.tr: Rev. 21:1. Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth; for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more. Compare Isa. 65:17 and 66:22.

units.la: LOCVS XXIX. De vitâ æternâ.
units.tr: LOCUS XXIX. On eternal life.

units.la: 1. Vita æterna consistit in
units.tr: 1. Eternal life consists in

units.la: a) gloriâ virtutis & beatitudinis consummatæ, seu in communione naturæ Dei in secula.
units.tr: a) the glory of virtue and of consummated blessedness, or in the communion of the nature of God for ever.

units.la: b) pleno & perpetuo, & ineffabili, sensu fauoris Dei.
units.tr: b) the full, perpetual and ineffable sense of the favour of God.

units.la: c) perpetuâ celebratione nominis Dei.
units.tr: c) the perpetual celebration of the name of God.

units.la: a) Dan.12.verf.3. Erudientes splendebunt quasi splendore expansi, & iustificantes multos, ut stella, in sempiterna secula.
units.tr: a) Dan. 12.v.3. Those who teach shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and those who turn many to righteousness shall shine like stars for ever and ever.

units.la: Luc.20. v.36. Pares enim angelis sunt. Confer Matth. 22. verf.30.
units.tr: Luke 20.v.36. For they are equal to the angels. Compare Matt. 22.v.30.

units.la: Rom.2. v.6.7. Deus reddet unicuiq; secundum opera ipsius: Iis quidem, qui per tolerantiam quærunt boni operis gloriam, & honorem, & incorruptibilitatem, vitam æternam.
units.tr: Rom. 2.v.6-7. God will render to each one according to his works: to those who by patience in well-doing seek glory, honour and incorruptibility, eternal life.

units.la: Vide Iohan.3. v.15.16. & c.5. v.24. ubi hæc vita dicitur æterna: & Act.26. v.18. ubi appellatur fors inter sanctos: Co-
units.tr: See John 3.v.15-16 and 5.v.24, where this life is called eternal; and Acts 26.v.18, where it is called a lot among the sanctified; Co-

units.la: loff.i.v.12. ubi vocatur fors sanctorum in luce.
units.tr: Col. 1.v.12, where it is called the lot of the saints in light.

units.la: Rom.8. v.18. Reor minimè pares esse temporis præsentis perpessiones gloriæ in nobis revelandæ.
units.tr: Rom. 8.v.18. I reckon that the sufferings of the present time are in no way equal to the glory to be revealed in us.

units.la: Et v.30. Quos autem iustificauit, eos etiam glorificauit.
units.tr: And v.30. Those whom he justified, them he also glorified.

units.la: 1.Cor.15. v.49. Sicut gessimus[?] imaginem terreni, geremus etjam imaginem cœlestis.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 15.v.49. As we have borne the image of the earthly, so we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.

units.la: Et v.53.54. Oportet corruptibile istud induere incorruptibilitatem, & mortale istud induere immortalitatem. Postquam autem hoc corruptibile induerit incorruptibilitatem, & mortale istud immortalitatem, tum fiet illud, quod scriptum est : Absorpta est mors ad victoriam.
units.tr: And v.53-54. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. But when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall come to pass that which is written: Death is swallowed up in victory.

units.la: 2.Cor.5.v.1. Scimus,nos,si terrestris huius domus nostrae tabernaculum dissolutum fuerit, ædificium ex Deo habituros, domicilium videlicet non manu factum, æternum in cœlis.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 5.v.1. We know that if the earthly house of this tabernacle of ours be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.

units.la: Gal.6.v.8. Qui seminat carni suæ, ex carne metet interitum; qui vero seminat Spiritui, ex Spiritu metet vitam æternam.
units.tr: Gal. 6.v.8. He who sows to his own flesh shall from the flesh reap corruption; but he who sows to the Spirit shall from the Spirit reap eternal life.

units.la: 2.Tim.4.v.8. Reposita est mihi iustitiæ corona, quam reddet mihi Dominus in isto die, iustus ille iudex: non solùm autem mihi, sed & omnibus, qui expetiuerint illustrem illum ipsius aduentum.
units.tr: 2 Tim. 4.v.8. A crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day; and not to me only, but to all who have loved his glorious appearing.

units.la: 2.Petri 1.v.4. Vt per hæc efficeremini participes, κοινωνοὶ[?] diuinæ naturæ.
units.tr: 2 Pet. 1.v.4. That by these you may become partakers [κοινωνοὶ] of the divine nature.

units.la: Hebr.12.v.22.23. Accessistis ad montem Sion, & ciuitatem Dei viui, Hierusalem cœlestem, & myriadas angelorum, conuentum vniuersalem & concionem primogenitorum, qui conscripti sunt in cœlis, & iudicem vniuersorum Deum, & spiritus iustorum consummatorum.
units.tr: Heb. 12.v.22-23. You have come to Mount Sion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to myriads of angels, the universal assembly and congregation of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven, and to God the judge of all, and to the spirits of the perfected righteous.

units.la: Apoc.2.v.11. Qui habet aurem, audiat, quid Spiritus dicat ecclesiis. Qui vicerit, nequaquam laedetur à morte secundâ.
units.tr: Rev. 2.v.11. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. He who overcomes shall not be hurt by the second death.

units.la: Et v.26.27.28. Si quis vicerit, & ad finem vsque obseruauerit opera mea, dabo ei potestatem in gentes: & reget eas virga ferrea, & tanquam vasa fictilia conterentur: sicut & ego accepi à Patre meo. Et dabo ei stellam matutinam.
units.tr: And v.26-28. If anyone overcomes and keeps my works to the end, I will give him power over the nations, and he shall rule them with an iron rod, and they shall be broken like earthen vessels, as I also received from my Father. And I will give him the morning star.

units.la: Et c.3.v.5. Qui vicerit, amicietur vestimentis albis: nequeunquam delebo nomen eius ex libro vitæ, sed agnoscam nomen eius in conspectu Patris mei, & in conspectu angelorum eius.
units.tr: And 3.v.5. He who overcomes shall be clothed in white garments; and I will not blot his name out of the book of life, but I will confess his name before my Father and before his angels.

units.la: Et vers.12. Qui vicerit, faciam, vt sit columna in templo Dei mei: nec foràs egredietur amplius: & inscribam ei nomen Dei mei, & nomen ciuitatis Dei mei, nouæ Hierusalem, quæ descendit è cœlo à Deo meo, & nomen meum nouum.
units.tr: And v.12. He who overcomes, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go out no more; and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down out of heaven from my God, and my new name.

units.la: Et vers.21. Qui vicerit, tribuam ei, vt sedeat mecum in throno meo; vt & ego vici, & sedeo cum Patre meo in throno eius.
units.tr: And v.21. He who overcomes, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne.

units.la: Apoc.21.per totum.
units.tr: Rev. 21 throughout.

units.la: Et c.22.v.5. Nox illic (in ecclesiâ gloriosâ) non erit, neque opus est. opus est ei lumine lucernæ, neq; lumine solis: quoniam Dominus Deus illustrat eos: & regnabunt in secula seculorum.
units.tr: And 22.v.5. There shall be no night there (in the glorious church), nor do they need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, for the Lord God gives them light; and they shall reign for ever and ever.

units.la: 2.Cor.4.v.17. Momentanea levitas afflictionis nostræ, excellenter excellentis gloriæ pondus æternum conficit nobis.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 4.v.17. Our light and momentary affliction works for us an eternal weight of glory, far beyond all comparison.

units.la: b) Psal.16.v.11. Satietas lætitiarum est apud faciem tuam: iucunditates in dexterâ tuâ semper.
units.tr: b) Ps. 16.v.11. In your presence is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures for evermore.

units.la: Psal.17.v.15. Satiabor specie tuâ.
units.tr: Ps. 17.v.15. I shall be satisfied with your likeness.

units.la: Apoc.2.v.7. Qui habet aurem, audiat, quid Spiritus dicat ecclesiis. Victori dabo edere ex arbore illâ vita, quæ est in medio para-disi Dei.
units.tr: Rev. 2.v.7. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To him who overcomes I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God.

units.la: Et v.17. Qui habet aurem, audiat, quid Spiritus dicat ecclesiis. Ei, qui vicerit, tribuam, ut edat ex manna illo occulto, & dabo ei calculum album, & in calculo nomen nouum scriptum, quod nemo nouit, nisi qui accipit.
units.tr: And v.17. He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches. To him who overcomes I will give to eat of the hidden manna, and I will give him a white stone, and on the stone a new name written, which no one knows except him who receives it.

units.la: 1.Cor.2.v.9. Prædicamus, sicut scriptum est, quæ oculus non vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec in mentem hominis venerunt: quæ parauit Deus iis, à quibus ipse diligitur. Confer Esa.64.v.8.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 2.v.9. We preach, as it is written: what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, these things God has prepared for those who love him. Compare Isa. 64.v.8.

units.la: 1.Cor.13.v.12. Cernimus enim nunc per speculum & per aenigma, tunc autem coram cernemus: nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc vero cognoscam prout cognitus fuero.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 13.v.12. For now we see through a mirror, in an enigma, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known.

units.la: Etc.15.v.28. Vt Deus sit omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 15.v.28. That God may be all in all.

units.la: c) Apoc.22.v.4. Sedes Dei & agni erit in ea, & serui eius colent eum. Confer Apoc.5.v.12.13.14.&c.19.v.1.& seqq. vbi turba in cœlo aliquoties ingeminat Halleluia.
units.tr: c) Rev. 22.v.4. The throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it, and his servants shall serve him. Compare Rev. 5.v.12-14 and 19.v.1 and following, where the multitude in heaven repeatedly sings Hallelujah.

units.la: 2. Gloriæ cœlestis erunt quidam gradus.
units.tr: 2. There will be certain degrees of heavenly glory.

units.la: 1.Cor.15.v.41.42. Alia est gloria solis, & alia gloria lunæ, & alia gloria stellarum. Stella enim à stella differt in gloria. Ita & resurrectio mortuorum.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 15.v.41-42. There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead.

units.la: Huc pertinet, quòd vita æterna comparatur paradiso, domui, ciuitati, regno, cœnæ magnæ, nuptiis regalibus, brauio & coronæ, Luc.23.Iohan.14. Apoc.21. Matth.20.c.25. Luc.14.1.Cor.9.2.Tim.4. quæ omnia ita sunt comparata, ut admittant iucundam varietatem.
units.tr: To this belongs the fact that eternal life is compared to paradise, a house, a city, a kingdom, a great supper, a royal wedding, a prize and a crown: Luke 23; John 14; Rev. 21; Matt. 20; 25; Luke 14; 1 Cor. 9; 2 Tim. 4; all of which are so arranged as to admit a pleasing variety.

units.la: Matth.13.v.43. Tunc iusti effulgebunt vt sol, in regno Patrissui: hoc est, splendebunt & coruscabunt radiis solis iustitiæ, quisque videlicet secundùm suum gradum.
units.tr: Matt. 13.v.43. Then the righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father: that is, they will shine and sparkle with the rays of the sun of righteousness, each one, that is, according to his own degree.

units.la: 3. Impij in inferno erunt sub peccatis infelices in omnem æternitatem.
units.tr: 3. The wicked in hell will be wretched under their sins for all eternity.

units.la: Esa.66.v.24. Vermis eorum non morietur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur, eruntque nausea omni carni.
units.tr: Isa. 66.v.24. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, and they shall be an abhorrence to all flesh.

units.la: 1.Thess.1.v.6. & deinceps. Iustum est apud Deum vicissim reddere iis, qui affligunt vos, afflictionem:vobis verò, qui affligimini, relaxationem nobiscum, in revelatione Domini Iesu de cœlo cum angelis suis potentibus, cum igne flammante, infligens vltionem iis, qui Deum nesciunt, neq; auscultant euangelio Domini nostri Iesu Christi: qui poenam pendent aeterni exitij, expulsi à facie Domini & gloria virium ipsius.
units.tr: 1 Thess. 1.v.6 and following. It is just with God to repay affliction to those who afflict you, and to give rest to you who are afflicted, along with us, at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with his mighty angels, with flaming fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ: who shall pay the penalty of eternal destruction, cast out from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his power.

units.la: Apoc.20.vers.14.15. Infernus autem ac Mors coniecti sunt in stagnum ignis: quae est mors secunda. Et qui non inuentus est in libro vitae scriptus, coniectus est in stagnum ignis.
units.tr: Rev. 20.v.14-15. And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.

units.la: Et c.21.v.8. Formidolosis, & incredulis, & execrabilibus, & homicidis, & scortatoribus, & veneficis, & idololatris, & omnibus mendacibus portio assignata est in stagno, vbi ardet ignis & sulphur, quod est mors secunda.
units.tr: And 21.v.8. But for the fearful, the unbelieving, the abominable, murderers, fornicators, sorcerers, idolaters and all liars, their portion is in the lake which burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death.

units.la: Et c.22.v.15. Foris autem erunt canes, & venefici, & scortatores, &c.
units.tr: And 22.v.15. But outside are dogs, and sorcerers, and fornicators, etc.

units.la: 4. In damnatis erunt gradus cruciatuum.
units.tr: 4. Among the damned there will be degrees of torment.

units.la: Matth.10.v.15. Amen dico vobis, Tolerabilior erit conditio terra Sodomorum in die iudicij, quàm vrbis illius:(scil. quæ reiecerit euangelium.
units.tr: Matt. 10.v.15. Amen I say to you, it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment than for that city (namely, the one which rejected the gospel).

units.la: Et c.11.v.20.& deinceps. Vae tibi Chorazin, &c. Tyri & Si- donis tolerabilior erit conditio in die iudicij quàm vestra. Item: Terra Sodomorum tolerabilior erit conditio in die iudicij quàm tua, scil. Capernaum.
units.tr: And 11.v.20 and following. Woe to you, Chorazin, etc. It will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for you. Likewise: It will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment than for you, namely Capernaum.

units.la: XXXII. THEOLOGIA NATURALIS.
units.tr: XXXII. NATURAL THEOLOGY.

units.la: I. Theologia positiva est exposita: sequitur theologia methodica, quæ methodo certâ connectit ea, quæ in Scripturis hinc inde spa-sa[?] occurrunt.
units.tr: I. Positive theology has been set out; there follows methodical theology, which by a sure method connects those things that occur scattered here and there in the Scriptures.

units.la: II. Estq; naturalis,vel supernaturalis.
units.tr: II. It is either natural or supernatural.

units.la: III. Theologia naturalis è Scriptura sacrâ colligit documenta illa,quæ sumuntur à creaturis, beneficio luminis naturæ & quotidianæ experientiæ.
units.tr: III. Natural theology gathers from holy Scripture those proofs which are drawn from creatures, by the benefit of the light of nature and of daily experience.

units.la: Index ipsius hic esto.
units.tr: Let this be its index.

units.la: 1. Angeli,tum boni, tum mali,docent Deum esse,& efse Spiritum omnipotentem & infinitum. Vide historias de angelis Gen.19.21.28. Num. 22. Iud.6.& 13. 2.Sam.24. 1.Reg.13.& 19. 2.Reg.1.& 19.1.Chron.21.Iob.1.& 2.Matt. 1.2.4.28.Luc.1.Iohan.5.12.20.Act.5.8.10.11.12.27.Apoc.5. 6.7.8.9.11.12.15.16.17.18.19.20.21.22.
units.tr: 1. Angels, both good and evil, teach that God exists, and that he is an omnipotent and infinite Spirit. See the histories of angels in Gen. 19, 21, 28; Num. 22; Judg. 6 and 13; 2 Sam. 24; 1 Kings 13 and 19; 2 Kings 1 and 19; 1 Chron. 21; Job 1 and 2; Matt. 1, 2, 4, 28; Luke 1; John 5, 12, 20; Acts 5, 8, 10, 11, 12, 27; Rev. 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22.

units.la: 2. Cœlum enarrat gloriam Dei, Psal.19.v.2.& 104.v.3. Esa.40.v.22.
units.tr: 2. The heavens declare the glory of God, Ps. 19:2; 104:3; Isa. 40:22.

units.la: 3. Sol, luna & catera stella conuincunt nos esse Deum, eumq; sapientissimum,optimum,& omnipotentem. Iob. 9.v.4.7.9.& c.38.v.31.32.33. Psal.8.v.2.4. & 19.v.2.& seqq. &136.v.7.8.9.Ier.31. v.35.36.
units.tr: 3. The sun, the moon and the other stars convince us that God exists, and that he is most wise, best and omnipotent. Job 9:4, 7, 9; 38:31, 32, 33; Ps. 8:2, 4; 19:2 and following; 136:7, 8, 9; Jer. 31:35, 36.

units.la: 4. Vicissitudo temporis testatur de prouidentia Dei, Genef.8.& 9.Psal.19.& 65.
units.tr: 4. The changing of the times bears witness to the providence of God: Gen. 8 and 9; Ps. 19 and 65.

units.la: 5. Elementa docent Deum esse, qui curet omnia.
units.tr: 5. The elements teach that there is a God who cares for all things.

units.la: Huc pertinent,vis consumens & fouens in igne,1.Reg. 18. v. 38:commoda & incommoda quæ habemus ab aëre, Deut.28:vers.22.1.Reg.8.v.37:beneficia quæ habemus ab aquâ & terrâ,Gen.1.v.11.20:item, quòd Deus decreto circinauit superficiem aquarum, vt terram nô obruant, Iob. 26.v.10.c.38.v.8.9.10. 11.Psal.104.v.6.7.8.9. Ier.5.v.21.22. 23. denique quòd Deus terram fundauit super maria,Ps. 24.v.1.2.&136. v. 6. 2.Petri 3.v.5.
units.tr: To this belong: the consuming and cherishing force in fire, 1 Kings 18:38; the benefits and harms we have from air, Deut. 28:22, 1 Kings 8:37; the benefits we have from water and earth, Gen. 1:11, 20; likewise that God by decree has set a bound to the surface of the waters, so that they do not overwhelm the earth, Job 26:10; 38:8, 9, 10, 11; Ps. 104:6, 7, 8, 9; Jer. 5:21, 22, 23; and finally that God founded the earth upon the seas, Ps. 24:1, 2; 136:6; 2 Pet. 3:5.

units.la: 6. Meteora sunt specula prouidentiæ Dei. Nam Deus ligat aquas in nubibus, & illas in aëre suspendit, Iob.26.v. 8.9.c.37.v.15.Psal.104.v.3.& 105.v.29.Ier.51.v.16.Idem facit stillare nubes ad fœcundandum hæc inferiora[?], Iob.36. v.27.28. Idem edicit niui & pluuia, vt decidant in terram, Iob.37.v.5.c.38.v.28. Idem per pluuiam fœcundat terram, ingentes calores æstiuos mitigat, homines & animalia recreat, Leuit.26.v.3.4. Deut.11.v.13.14.c.28.v.12.Iacob.5. v.18.Esa.30.v.23.Psal.104.v.13.14.15.16.Act.14.v.17. Idem gignit guttas roris, quo terra mirum in modum fœcundatur,Iob.38.v.28.Prou.3.v.20.Genes.27.v.30.Deut.33.v. 13.28.Zachar.8.v.12.Idem deiicit grandinem e cœlo, Psalm. 147.v.17. Iob.38.v.22.23. Exod.9.verf.17.18.19.22.&seqq. Iof.10.v.11.Psal.78.v.47.48. Idem e thesauris suis producit ventos,Psal.135.v.6.7.Ierem.10.v.13.c.51.v.16.Exod.10.v.13. 19.Num.11.v.31. Amos.4.v.13.Ion.1.v.4. Idem volat super alas venti, Psalm.18.v.11.&104.v.3. Idem creat fulgetrum, tanquam anteambulonem suæ maiestatis, Psal.18.v.13.& 50.v.3. Idem edit vocem suam fortissimam,tonitru, Psalm. 29.Exod.19.v.16.c.20. v.18. 1.Sam.12.verf.18. 19.20.Iob. 40.verf.3.4. Idem creat terræmotum, Psal.18.verf.8. Matth. 28.verf.2.
units.tr: 6. Meteors are mirrors of the providence of God. For God binds the waters in the clouds and suspends them in the air, Job 26:8, 9; 37:15; Ps. 104:3; 105:29; Jer. 51:16. He likewise causes the clouds to drop to make the lower things fruitful, Job 36:27, 28. He likewise commands the snow and rain to fall to the earth, Job 37:5; 38:28. He likewise by the rain makes the earth fruitful, mitigates the great summer heats, and refreshes men and animals, Lev. 26:3, 4; Deut. 11:13, 14; 28:12; James 5:18; Isa. 30:23; Ps. 104:13, 14, 15, 16; Acts 14:17. He likewise produces the drops of dew, by which the earth is made fruitful in a wonderful manner, Job 38:28; Prov. 3:20; Gen. 27:30; Deut. 33:13, 28; Zech. 8:12. He likewise casts down hail from heaven, Ps. 147:17; Job 38:22, 23; Exod. 9:17, 18, 19, 22 and following; Josh. 10:11; Ps. 78:47, 48. He likewise brings forth the winds from his storehouses, Ps. 135:6, 7; Jer. 10:13; 51:16; Exod. 10:13, 19; Num. 11:31; Amos 4:13; Jonah 1:4. He likewise flies upon the wings of the wind, Ps. 18:11; 104:3. He likewise creates lightning, as the forerunner of his majesty, Ps. 18:13; 50:3. He likewise utters his most mighty voice in thunder, Ps. 29; Exod. 19:16; 20:18; 1 Sam. 12:18, 19, 20; Job 40:3, 4. He likewise creates earthquakes, Ps. 18:8; Matt. 28:2.

units.la: 7. Mineralia, siue fossilia, id est, lapides vulgares & pretiosi, metalla, succi item & terræ metallares, partim maiestatem, partim beneficia & iudicia Dei nobis ponunt ob oculos. Iob.28.v.13. & seqq. Exod.28. Genes.19.v.24. 25.&c.14.v.3.
units.tr: 7. Minerals, or fossils, that is, common and precious stones, metals, and also juices and metallic earths, set before our eyes partly the majesty and partly the benefits and judgments of God. Job 28:13 and following; Exod. 28; Gen. 19:24, 25; 14:3.

units.la: 8. Planta, seu stirpes, sunt documenta paternæ Dei curæ, Gen.1.v.29.30.c.2.v.16.Psal.104.v.14.15.
units.tr: 8. Plants, or stems, are proofs of the fatherly care of God: Gen. 1:29, 30; 2:16; Ps. 104:14, 15.

units.la: 9. Volatilia testantur de potentia, sapientia & providentia Dei. Iob.39.v.2.16.17.&seqq. Matth.6.v.26.
units.tr: 9. Birds bear witness to the power, wisdom and providence of God. Job 39:2, 16, 17 and following; Matt. 6:26.

units.la: 10. Aquatilia narrant nobis sapientiam, potentiam,& providentiam Dei, Iob.12.v.8. Psal.104.v.25. 26.27. Iob.26.v.13. & seqq.
units.tr: 10. Fish declare to us the wisdom, power and providence of God: Job 12:8; Ps. 104:25, 26, 27; Job 26:13 and following.

units.la: 11. Bruta terrestria docent nos Deum esse, & esse sapientem, potentem,& bonum,Iob.12.v.7.
units.tr: 11. Land animals teach us that God exists, and that he is wise, powerful and good: Job 12:7.

units.la: 12. Homo, constans anima rationali & corpore organico, in se habet satis miraculorum & oraculorum,quibus nunquam non admonetur de natura & cura Dei. Gen.2.Iob.10.v.10.11.
units.tr: 12. Man, consisting of a rational soul and an organic body, has in himself enough miracles and oracles by which he is never not reminded of the nature and care of God. Gen. 2; Job 10:10, 11.

units.la: Confer supra cum Physicis, & infra cum ζωοπ[?] θεία[?], &c. Vide quoque theologiam naturalem peculiari volumine à nobis editam.
units.tr: Compare above with the physicists, and below with the [zoopoetic?] divine [ζωοπ… θεία…], etc. See also the natural theology which we have published in a separate volume.

units.la: XXXIII. THEOLOGIA CATECHETICA.
units.tr: XXXIII. CATECHETICAL THEOLOGY.

units.la: I. Theologia supernaturalis, siue arcana, è Scriptura colligit ea, quæ sine speciali reuelatione cognosci non possunt.
units.tr: I. Supernatural, or hidden, theology gathers from Scripture those things which cannot be known without special revelation.

units.la: II. Eius partes sunt numero sex, hoc ordine. Primò se offert theologia Catechetica, de quâ Gal.6.v.6. Hanc sequitur theologia didactica, 1.Tim.3.v.2.Tit.2.verf.9. Tertio loco est theologia polemica, quæ etiam appellatur elenctica, & irenica, de quâ Tit.2. v.9. Quarta pars theologiæ supernaturalis appellatur theologia casuum, siue schola tentationum, 1. Cor.7. Penultimum locum obtinet theologia prophetica, 1.Timoth.3.& Tit.1. & 2: vltimum, theologia acroamatica siue moralis, Tit.2. & 3. Vide etiam 2.Tim.3.v. 16.vbi theologia didactica, elenctica & moralis coniunguntur. Cæterum quoties locus vel titulus occurrit in histheologiæ partibus, oportet recurrere ad theologiam positiuam, tanquam fundamentum & matricem.
units.tr: II. Its parts are six in number, in this order. First comes catechetical theology, of which Gal. 6.6. Next follows didactic theology, 1 Tim. 3.2, Tit. 2.9. Third is polemical theology, which is also called elenctic and irenic, of which Tit. 2.9. The fourth part of supernatural theology is called casuistic theology, or school of temptations, 1 Cor. 7. The second-to-last place belongs to prophetic theology, 1 Tim. 3 and Tit. 1 and 2; the last, acroamatic or moral theology, Tit. 2 and 3. See also 2 Tim. 3.16, where didactic, elenctic and moral theology are joined together. Moreover, whenever a place or title occurs in these parts of theology, one must have recourse to positive theology, as the foundation and mother of them all.

units.la: III. Theologia catechetica est compendium religionis Christianæ in quinque capitibus ab ecclesiâ catholicâ in N. T. receptis.
units.tr: III. Catechetical theology is a compendium of the Christian religion in five chapters, received by the catholic Church in the New Testament.

units.la: IV. Primum caput catechismi est symbolum apostolicum, quod est summa siue compendium eorum, quæ pendium eorum, quæ homini Christiano sunt necessaria creditu ad salutem.
units.tr: IV. The first chapter of the catechism is the Apostles' Creed, which is the sum or compendium of those things which are necessary for a Christian to believe for salvation.

units.la: V. Partes symboli tres sunt. Prima est de Deo Patre, articulo primo: secunda de Filio, articulis sex : tertia de Spiritu sancto, articulis quinque. Hæc trichotomia sumta est ex Matth.28. v.16. Baptizantes eos in nomen Patris, Filij,& Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: V. There are three parts of the creed. The first concerns God the Father, in one article; the second concerns the Son, in six articles; the third concerns the Holy Spirit, in five articles. This threefold division is taken from Matt. 28.16, baptizing them in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: VI. Primus symboli articulus habet duo membra. Primum est commune, in voce CREDO, quâ significatur fides catholica & salutifica, quæ complectitur notitiam, confessionem, & fiduciam, ita ut hæc tria deinceps ad singulos articulos sint repetenda. Alterum est singulare, de prima persona Trinitatis, de quâ prædicantur ista tria: quòd sit DEVS, id est, Iehouaille, cuius esse est per-esse, semper esse, & energeticum esse, ita ut sibi habeat suum esse, & à se atque per se faciat omnia esse & prodesse tum in mundo, tum in ecclesiâ, Exod.6.v.2: quòd sit Pater, scilicet Domini nostri Iesu Christi, non creando aut adoptando, sed generando ipsum sine principio, medio sive suc-cessione[?], & fine, Hebr.1.v.2. quòd denique sit omnipotens creator cœli & terra, qui solo nutu fecit omnia esse & bene esse, illaque facit porrò esse, aut non esse, prout ipsius gloria, & utilitas tum universi, tum ecclesiæ postulat, Gen.1. Act.17.v.25. Atque hic est primus articulus, in quo mentio fit omnipotentiæ potius quàm reliquorum Dei attributorum, tum quia omnipotentia præsupponit infinitam essentiam & sapientiam: tum quia est basis fidei nostræ in sequentibus articulis. Porrò origo rerum tribuitur Patri, quòd ille sit origo & fons Trinitatis: redemptio Filio, quia ius filiationis à Filio Dei, & unio atq; communio cum Deo procurari debebat à persona media inter Patrem & Spiritum sanctum: denique sanctificatio Spiritui sancto, quia ultimum hoc opus peculiari modo efficitur ab ultimâ Trinitatis personâ.
units.tr: VI. The first article of the creed has two members. The first is common, in the word I BELIEVE, by which is signified the catholic and saving faith, which embraces knowledge, confession and trust, so that these three are to be repeated afterwards for each article. The second is particular, concerning the first person of the Trinity, of whom these three things are predicated: that he is GOD, that is, Jehovah, whose being is per-esse, always-being, and energetic being, so that he has his being in himself and through himself makes all things to be and to be well, both in the world and in the Church (Exod. 6.2); that he is Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, not by creating or adopting, but by begetting him without beginning, middle or succession, and without end (Heb. 1.2); and finally that he is the almighty creator of heaven and earth, who by his mere nod made all things to be and to be well, and continues to make them to be or not to be, as the glory of himself and the good of the universe and of the Church require (Gen. 1; Acts 17.25). This is the first article, in which mention is made of omnipotence rather than of the other attributes of God, both because omnipotence presupposes infinite essence and wisdom, and because it is the basis of our faith in the following articles. Moreover, the origin of things is ascribed to the Father, because he is the origin and fountain of the Trinity; redemption to the Son, because the right of sonship had to be procured from the Son of God, and union and communion with God by a person standing between the Father and the Holy Spirit; and finally sanctification to the Holy Spirit, because this last work is accomplished in a special way by the last person of the Trinity.

units.la: VII. Secundus articulus habet quatuor commata. Primum est in copula Et, quæ significat paritatem cultus religiosi, qui æquè defertur Filio atque Patri, Iohan.14.verf.7.10.11. Secundum est in duobus nominibus, è quibus Iesus est proprium in quarto modo, ut loquuntur, si quidem non sumatur typicè, Matth.1.verf.21: Christus est cognomen, additum nomini proprio, idem quod Messias, Iohan.1.verf.41. & significat officium propheticum, sacerdotale,& regium Hebr. 1.v.1.2.3. quod nobis prodest vt medicina,itemq; vt regula,quatenus debem* esse prophetæ,sacerdotes, & reges Christo conformes 1. Petr.2.v.5. 9. quâ in re consistit tota ars imitationis Christi. Tertium est de persona Christi, quod sit Filius eius (Patris) vnigenitus,ab æterno scil.& in æternum manens à Patre, inque ipso manens, ipsi per omnia consubstantialis, Hebr. 1.v.3. Quartum est de ipsius officio,quòd sit dominus noster,iure videl.acquisitionis seu emptionis, coseruationis,defensionis,& plenariæ liberationis,2. Petr.2.v.1.
units.tr: VII. The second article has four clauses. The first lies in the conjunction and, which signifies the equality of religious worship, which is paid equally to the Son and to the Father (John 14.7, 10, 11). The second lies in the two names, of which Jesus is a proper name in the fourth manner, as they say, provided it is not taken typically (Matt. 1.21); Christ is a cognomen added to the proper name, the same as Messiah (John 1.41), and signifies the prophetic, priestly and kingly office (Heb. 1.1–3). This serves us as a medicine, and likewise as a rule, inasmuch as prophets, priests and kings ought to be conformed to Christ (1 Pet. 2.5, 9); in this consists the whole art of imitating Christ. The third concerns the person of Christ, that he is the only-begotten Son of the Father, remaining from eternity and into eternity from the Father and in him, consubstantial with him in all things (Heb. 1.3). The fourth concerns his office, that he is our Lord, by the right, namely, of acquisition or purchase, preservation, defence and full deliverance (2 Pet. 2.1).

units.la: VIII. Tertius articulus agit de conceptio- ne & nativitate Christi.
units.tr: VIII. The third article treats of the conception and birth of Christ.

units.la: Et primo quidem Christus conceptus est ex Spiritu sancto, Luc.1.v.35. qui fecit germinare virginem sine viro, sicut in principio fœcundando terrā informem fecit illam proferre herbas sine sole & semine in ipsius gremium projecto, Gen.1.v.2.12. Hæc talis conceptio seruit consolationi & imitationi: Consolationi, quia mediator noster debuit sanctus esse ratione principii, medii,& finis, vt esset idoneus ad hoc tam nobile officium. Imitationi:quia debemus id operam dare,vt anima nostra ex Spiritu sancto, non autem impuro aliquo genio, concipiat omnis generis cogitationes sanctas.DeindeChristus natus est ex Maria virgine,ita vt illa ante partum,in partu,& post partum manserit intemerata, Matth.1.v.25. Natus autem est Christus ex Maria ita,vt assumserit non personam, sed naturam humanam, eamque totam ratione partium essentialium &integralium,itemque infirmitatum naturalium, Hebr. 2.v.17. Fructus nativitatis idem est, qui conceptionis: vt nempe mediator noster esset sanctus, & vt nos quotidie nascamur,non è libidine carnis&sanguinis, sed ex virgineo spiritu.
units.tr: And first, Christ was conceived of the Holy Spirit (Luke 1.35), who made the virgin to conceive without a man, just as in the beginning, by fertilising the formless earth, he made it bring forth herbs without sun or seed, cast into its bosom (Gen. 1.2, 12). Such a conception serves for consolation and for imitation. For consolation, because our mediator had to be holy by reason of his beginning, middle and end, so that he would be fit for so noble an office. For imitation, because we ought to take care that our soul conceives of the Holy Spirit, and not of some impure spirit, all kinds of holy thoughts. Next, Christ was born of the virgin Mary, so that she remained inviolate before the birth, in the birth, and after the birth (Matt. 1.25). Christ was born of Mary in such a way that he assumed not a person but a human nature, and the whole of it, with respect to its essential and integral parts, and likewise its natural infirmities (Heb. 2.17). The fruit of the nativity is the same as that of the conception: namely, that our mediator should be holy, and that we should be born daily, not of the lust of flesh and blood, but of a virginal spirit.

units.la: IX. Quartus articulus habet quatuor mem- bra.
units.tr: IX. The fourth article has four members.

units.la: E quibus primum est de Passione Christi, sub Pontio Pilato, quæ est maxima omnium passionum Christi inde à prima ipsius infantia. Passionis huius pretium pendet à personæ patientis excellētiâ, innocentiâ, & obedientiâ: modus consistit in varietate & atrocitate, siue longitudine & latitudine, altitudine & profunditate: fructus est partim expiatio peccati, partim edulcatio crucis nostræ. Gal. 3.v.10. Rom.8.v.29. Deinde Christus est crucifixus, vt morte maledictam oppetendo nos liberaret à maledictione, & doceret nos crucifixionem carnis, quâ nos crucifigimur mundo, & mundus crucifigitur nobis: quæ quidem crucifixio est differentia specifica inter Christianum & hypocritam. Gal.3.v.13. Rom.6.v.6. Tertiò Christus est mortuus, morte scilicet prima, quâ separata fuit anima à corpore, & secundâ, quâ ipsius anima ad tempus separata fuit à Deo. Mortuus autem est, triumphando de morte æternâ & temporali, non vero succumbendo vel illi vel isti. Itaq; mors Christi non fuit simplex martyrium, sed sacrificium propitiatorium, Deo acceptum, & omnibus credentibus salutare ratione iustificationis, sanctificationis, & glorificationis. Psalm.22.[?] Hebr.2.v.14. Rom.6.v.8. Denique Christus est sepultus, vt veritatem mortis obitæ testatâ faceret, mortemque persequeretur in speluncam vsque suam, & fanctificaret sepulchra nostra, nostra denique peccata sepeliret. Rom.6.v.4. Sepultus autem est splendidè & regiè, vt hoc ipso significaretur, ipsum non esse mortuum vt scelleratum aliquem, item ipsum resurrecturum magnificè.
units.tr: Of these, the first concerns the Passion of Christ under Pontius Pilate, which is the greatest of all the sufferings of Christ from his earliest infancy onward. The worth of this Passion depends on the excellence, innocence and obedience of the person who suffered. Its manner consists in its variety and atrocity, or its length and breadth, height and depth. Its fruit is partly the expiation of sin and partly the sweetening of our cross. Gal. 3.v.10. Rom.8.v.29. Next, Christ was crucified, so that by undergoing a death under a curse he might free us from the curse, and teach us the crucifying of the flesh, by which we are crucified to the world and the world to us. This crucifixion is indeed the specific difference between the Christian and the hypocrite. Gal.3.v.13. Rom.6.v.6. Thirdly, Christ died, namely with the first death, by which his soul was separated from his body, and with the second, by which his soul was for a time separated from God. He died, however, triumphing over eternal and temporal death, not yielding to either of them. Therefore the death of Christ was not a mere martyrdom, but a propitiatory sacrifice, acceptable to God and saving for all believers with respect to justification, sanctification and glorification. Psalm.22.[?] Hebr.2.v.14. Rom.6.v.8. Lastly, Christ was buried, so that he might bear witness to the reality of his death, pursue death into its own cave, sanctify our graves, and finally bury our sins. Rom.6.v.4. He was buried, moreover, in a splendid and royal manner, so that it might be signified by this very fact that he was not dead as some criminal, and that he would rise again in glory.

units.la: X. Quintus articulus agit de descensu Christi ad inferna, & resurrectione ex mortuis, adeoq; coniungit infimum gradum exinanitionis & primum gradum exaltationis. Primò itaque Christus descendit ad inferna, hoc est, sustinuit mortis dominium, & tum à discipulis, tum ab hostibus suis iudicatus fuit similis iis, qui statum mortuorum experti non redeunt in vitam. Hic descensus opponatur horrifico mortis spectro, & nos consoletur adversus statum mortuorum Eph.4.v.10. Deinde Christus resurrexit tertio die à mortuis: resurrexit, inquam, vere & gloriosè tanquam triumphator mortis, sepulchri, inferni & damnationis, ut nobis partā salutem siue meritum suum efficaciter applicaret, spiritualem resurrectionem ex morte peccatorum nos doceret, inque nobis efficeret, pignum denique resurrectionis suae nobis daret. om.4.v.25.c.6.v.4.8.1.Cor.15.v.20.21.
units.tr: X. The fifth article deals with the descent of Christ into the underworld and his resurrection from the dead, and so joins the lowest step of his humiliation to the first step of his exaltation. First, then, Christ descended into hell, that is, he endured the dominion of death, and was judged both by his disciples and by his enemies like those who, having experienced the state of the dead, do not return to life. This descent is set against the horrible specter of death, and comforts us against the state of the dead. Eph.4.v.10. Next, Christ rose again from the dead on the third day. He rose, I say, truly and gloriously, as a conqueror of death, the grave, hell and damnation, so that he might effectively apply to us the salvation or merit which he had obtained, teach us and work in us a spiritual resurrection from the death of sin, and finally give us a pledge of his own resurrection. Rom.4.v.25. 6.v.4.8. 1 Cor.15.v.20.21.

units.la: XI. Sextus articulus est de ascensione Christi in coelum, & sessione ipsius ad dextram Patris. Et primo quidem Christus ascendit in coelum, ut pignus nostrae ascensionis ibi deponeret, ibique pro nobis intercederet, & inde Spiritum sanctum ad nos mitteret. Eph.2. v.6.Hebr.9.v.24.Ioh.16.v.7. Deinde sedet ad dextram Dei Patris omnipotentis, hoc est, versatur in statu maiestatis quae mediatori soli est propria, & dominatur in medio inimicorum suorum, Psal.110.Eph.1.v.20.22.23. Ascensio itaque Christi confirmat fidem remissionis peccatorum & vitae aeternae fruendae in coelis iam apertis a Christo: itemque accendit spem & charitatem qua sursum habemus corda. Sessio ipsius nos consolatur adversus peccatum & hostes externos: quia Christus in coelo pro nobis intercedit, & inde regnat, vincit atque imperat in medio inimicorum suorum.
units.tr: XI. The sixth article concerns the ascension of Christ into heaven and his sitting at the right hand of the Father. First, indeed, Christ ascended into heaven, so that he might there lay up a pledge of our ascension, there intercede for us, and from there send the Holy Spirit to us. Eph.2.v.6. Hebr.9.v.24. Joh.16.v.7. Then he sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father, that is, he is in the state of majesty which belongs to the Mediator alone, and he rules in the midst of his enemies. Psal.110. Eph.1.v.20.22.23. The ascension of Christ therefore confirms faith in the forgiveness of sins and in the enjoyment of eternal life in the heavens now opened by Christ, and likewise kindles hope and love, by which we lift up our hearts. His sitting at the right hand comforts us against sin and external enemies, because Christ intercedes for us in heaven and from there reigns, conquers and commands in the midst of his enemies.

units.la: XII. Septimus articulus est de reditu Christi ad iudicium universale. In quo Christus, expleto ecclesiae in his terris militantis curriculo, in formā aspectabili cognoscet causam omnium hominum, & sententiā dictā sine morā accingetur ad executionem, quae piis erit initium plenae gloriae ac gaudii in coelis, impiis initium plenae ignominiae & doloris in inferis. Recordatio itaque huius iudicii continebit nos in officio, & eriget adversus omnis generis calamitates. 2.Thess.1.v.7.8. 9.10.Apoc.20.v.10.
units.tr: XII. The seventh article concerns the return of Christ to the universal judgment. In it Christ, when the course of the Church militant on these earth is completed, will know the cause of all men in visible form, and, once sentence has been pronounced, will without delay set about its execution. For the godly this will be the beginning of full glory and joy in heaven, and for the ungodly the beginning of full shame and pain in the underworld. Remembrance of this judgment will therefore keep us in our duty and lift us up against every kind of calamity. 2 Thess.1.v.7.8. 9.10. Rev.20.v.10.

units.la: XIII. Octavus articulus est de Spiritu sancto, his verbis: Credo in Spiritum sanctum. Ubi cultus Spiritus sancti pari gradu coniungitur cum cultu Patris & Filii, & simul indicatur persona atque officium Spiritus sancti. Persona notatur voce Spiritus, officium voce sanctus. Et Spiritus quidem hîc dicitur peculiari ratione, quia spiratur à Patre & Filio, hoc est, procedit ab ijs eo prope modo, quo amor spiratur à voluntate, sicut Filius à Patre emanat eo fere modo, quo ratio ab intellectu promanat. Deinde Pater & Filius spirant Spiritum sanctum in corda nostra. Iohan. 15. v. 26. Gal. 4. v. 6. Quod attinet ad officium Spiritus sancti, illud consistit in fouendo, illuminando, & sanctificando. Nam ille fouet inde ab initio creationis res creatas, Gen. 1. v. 2. & illuminat homines, vel fouendo lumen naturæ, vel accendendo lumen gratiæ: & denique sanctificat seu regenerat nos, ex carnalibus faciendo spirituales, seu eripiendo è regno impuri spiritus, & creando in nobis fidem, spem, & charitatem. Vnde confertur oleo lætitiæ, paracleto, arrhaboni, igni, vento, & aquę. Psal. 45. Iohan. 16. Gal. 4. Act. 2. Ioh. 3. Ezech. 47.
units.tr: XIII. The eighth article concerns the Holy Spirit, in these words: I believe in the Holy Spirit. Here the worship of the Holy Spirit is joined on equal footing with the worship of the Father and the Son, and at the same time the person and the office of the Holy Spirit are indicated. The person is marked by the word Spirit, the office by the word Holy. The Spirit is called such here in a particular sense, because he is breathed out by the Father and the Son, that is, he proceeds from them in much the same way as love is breathed out from the will, just as the Son emanates from the Father in roughly the way reason proceeds from the intellect. Next, the Father and the Son breathe the Holy Spirit into our hearts. Joh.15.v.26. Gal.4.v.6. As for the office of the Holy Spirit, it consists in cherishing, enlightening and sanctifying. For he cherishes created things from the beginning of creation, Gen.1.v.2, and enlightens men, either by cherishing the light of nature or by kindling the light of grace; and finally he sanctifies or regenerates us, making us spiritual from carnal, or rescuing us from the kingdom of the unclean spirit, and creating in us faith, hope and love. Hence he is compared to the oil of gladness, to the Paraclete, to the earnest, to fire, to wind, and to water. Psal.45. Joh.16. Gal.4. Act.2. Joh.3. Ezech.47.

units.la: XIV. Nonus articulus incipit de ijs, quæ credimus.
units.tr: XIV. The ninth article begins, concerning those things which we believe.

units.la: Vbi vox Credo communiter pertinet ad hunc articulum & sequentes. Sunt autem duo membra huius articuli. Primum est de ecclesia sancta & Catholica, hoc est, de cœtu electorum omnium, qui fuerunt, sunt & erunt, sive iam regnent cum Christo in cœlis, sive adhuc militent in terris & deinceps militaturi sint. Col. 1. v. 20. Hic cœtus dicitur sanctus: tum quia sanctitas Christi est ipsius sanctitas, Eph. 4. v. 25. 26. 27. tum quia Spiritus sanctus electos magis magisque efficit sanctos in hac vita, Phil. 3. v. 12. 14. donec tandem in beata æternitate Christo coniuncti deponant omnem imperfectionem, 1. Cor. 13. v. 9. & seqq. Secundum huius articuli membrum est de communione sanctorum, quâ omnes electi in capite suo Christo & inter sese habent communia omnia bona gratiæ & gloriæ, omniaque aduersa in hac vita. Eph. 5. v. 19. 30. Coloss. 2. v. 10. 1. Iohan. 1. v. 3.
units.tr: Here the word Credo commonly applies to this article and the following ones. This article has two parts. The first concerns the holy and catholic church, that is, the assembly of all the elect who have been, are, and will be, whether they now reign with Christ in heaven or still fight on earth and will fight hereafter. Col. 1. v. 20. This assembly is called holy: partly because the holiness of Christ is its own holiness, Eph. 4. v. 25. 26. 27.; partly because the Holy Spirit makes the elect more and more holy in this life, Phil. 3. v. 12. 14.; until at last, joined to Christ in blessed eternity, they put off every imperfection, 1. Cor. 13. v. 9. and following. The second part of this article concerns the communion of saints, by which all the elect, in their head Christ and among one another, have in common all the good things of grace and glory, and all the adversities of this life. Eph. 5. v. 19. 30. Col. 2. v. 10. 1. John 1. v. 3.

units.la: XV. Decimus articulus est de remissione peccatorum.
units.tr: XV. The tenth article concerns the forgiveness of sins.

units.la: Remissio ista est beneficium Dei, quo homini credenti propter Christi meritum omnia peccata condonantur à solo Deo, gratis, perfectè, & efficaciter, ita ut in corde existat gaudium spirituale, & in toto homine fuga peccati. Rom.3.v.24.1.Johan.1.v.7.
units.tr: This forgiveness is a benefit of God, by which, for the merit of Christ, all sins are pardoned to the believing man by God alone, freely, completely and effectually, so that spiritual joy exists in the heart and flight from sin in the whole man. Rom. 3. v. 24. 1 John 1. v. 7.

units.la: XVI. Undecimus articulus est de resurrectione carnis: quâ resurget ad imperium Dei creatoris hæc ipsa caro, eadem numero, sed gradu non eadem. Job.19.v.25.& seqq.1.Cor.15.v.51.52.
units.tr: XVI. The eleventh article concerns the resurrection of the flesh: by which this same flesh will rise at the command of God the creator, the same in number but not the same in glory. Job 19. v. 25 and following. 1 Cor. 15. v. 51. 52.

units.la: XVII. Duodecimus articulus est de vitâ æternâ: quæ est finis fidei, consistens in gloriâ & gaudio ineffabili. Gloria in eo est, quòd carebimus omni malo, & implebimur omni bono. Gaudium consistit in plenâ fruitione Dei & sensu fauoris eius. 1. Cor.2.v.9.Apoc.21.& 22. Atq; hoc est symbolum Apostolicum, quod obsignatur particulâ Amen: quod non est ita accipiendum, quasi fit formula precationis, sed quòd fiduciam nostrâ hoc modo facimus testatam.
units.tr: XVII. The twelfth article concerns eternal life: which is the end of faith, consisting in glory and unspeakable joy. The glory lies in this, that we shall be free from every evil and filled with every good. The joy consists in the full enjoyment of God and the sense of his favour. 1 Cor. 2. v. 9. Rev. 21 and 22. This is the Apostles' Creed, which is sealed by the particle Amen; which is not to be taken as though it were a formula of prayer, but as a way of bearing witness to our confidence.

units.la: XVIII. Secundum caput Catechismi est Decalogus, qui est compendium siue summa eorum, quæ homini credenti sunt necessaria factu ad salutem. Est, inquam, compendium totius legis naturæ à Deo exaratum Exod. 20; & proinde obligat omnes homines, & ediscendum est ab omnibus eo, quo legislator proposuit modo.
units.tr: XVIII. The second chapter of the Catechism is the Decalogue, which is the compendium or summary of those things which are necessary for the believing man to do for salvation. It is, I say, a compendium of the whole law of nature, written down by God, Exod. 20; and therefore it binds all men, and it must be learned by all in the manner in which the lawgiver set it forth.

units.la: XIX. Partes decalogi post præfationem sunt duæ tabulæ: è quibus secunda cedit primæ, & utraque informat & reformat totum hominem, quantum ad spiritum & corpus, facultates animæ & membra corporis, in quolibet statu vitæ humanæ. Quæ omnia in singulis præceptis oportet attendere.
units.tr: XIX. The parts of the Decalogue, after the preface, are two tables: the second of which follows from the first, and both form and reform the whole man, as to spirit and body, the faculties of the soul and the members of the body, in every state of human life. All these things must be noted in each precept.

units.la: XX. Præfatio decalogi continet tria argumenta suadentia obedientiam. Primum est à ma-iestate legislatoris, qui est Jehoua: secundum à bonitate ipsius, quòd sit Deus noster, qui vi fœderis gratuiti se quidem dat nobis fruendum, suavero bona vtenda-fruenda: tertium ab omnipotentia, quòd nos è domo servitutis, rebus omnibus conclamatis, ὑπὸ μηχανῆς[?] eductos beneficiis accumulet.
units.tr: XX. The preface of the Decalogue contains three arguments urging obedience. The first is from the majesty of the lawgiver, who is Jehovah; the second from his goodness, in that he is our God, who by the force of the free covenant gives himself to us to be enjoyed, and gives good things to be used and enjoyed; the third from his omnipotence, in that he has led us out of the house of bondage, when all things were despaired of, as if by a deus ex machina [ὑπὸ μηχανῆς], and heaps us with benefits.

units.la: XXI. Primum praeceptum prohibet, ne habeamus deos alienos: hoc est, ne in aliquo fiduciam collocemus vel supra, vel iuxta, vel infra Deum: sed illum solum habeamus pro summo nostro bono, cui adhaereamus fide, spe & charitate in rebus secundis & adversis, detestati omnem idololatriam internam.
units.tr: XXI. The first precept forbids us to have other gods: that is, that we should not place our trust in anything above, beside, or below God, but should hold him alone as our highest good, cleaving to him in faith, hope and love in prosperity and adversity, and detesting all internal idolatry.

units.la: XXII. Secundum praeceptum prohibet externam idololatriam: ne scilicet repraesentemus Deum ulla imagine, aut veneratione aliqua religiosa prosequamur imaginem aliquam sive Dei, sive creaturae: sed cultum Dei externum ita instituamus, ut respondeat spirituali eius naturae. Quia vero homines licenter hic peccant, Deus addit sanctionem, qua testatur, se peccata patrum punire in filiis, qui oderunt ipsum, hoc est, peccata patrum faciunt sua; & facere misericordiam millibus eorum qui diligunt ipsum, custodiendo praecepta ipsius, nominatim hoc secundum, cuius neglectus introducit ἰδωλο[?]ποιΐαν[?], qua introducta necesse est paulatim collabi totam rationem cultus Dei tum interni, tum externi.
units.tr: XXII. The second precept forbids external idolatry: namely, that we should not represent God by any image, nor pay any religious veneration to an image of God or of a creature; but that we should so institute the external worship of God that it corresponds to his spiritual nature. Because men sin here readily, God adds a sanction, by which he testifies that he visits the sins of the fathers upon the children who hate him, that is, they make their fathers' sins their own; and that he shows mercy to thousands of those who love him and keep his precepts; especially this second, the neglect of which introduces idol-making [ἰδωλοποιΐαν], and once this is introduced, the whole system of the worship of God, both internal and external, must gradually collapse.

units.la: XXIII. Tertium praeceptum similiter constat prohibitione & sanctione. Prohibet enim, ne nomen Dei quantum ad essentiam, personas, opera & voluntatem ipsius irreligiose vsurpemus, sed sancte, humiliter, & reuerenter de maiestate ipsius sentiamus, loquamur, scribamus, & loquentes audiamus, ac scribentes legamus. Quia vero homines fere pro leui ducunt hoc peccatum, Deus addit sanctionem, qua testatur non impune laturum, qui peccato blasphemiae aut periurij se obstrinxerit.
units.tr: XXIII. The third precept likewise consists of a prohibition and a sanction. For it forbids us to use the name of God irreverently, with respect to his essence, persons, works and will, but bids us think, speak, write, and, when speaking, listen, and when writing, read, with holiness, humility and reverence concerning his majesty. Because men commonly count this sin a trifle, God adds a sanction, by which he testifies that he will not leave unpunished those who bind themselves by the sin of blasphemy or perjury.

units.la: XXIV. Quartum praeceptum constat quatuor partibus. Prima imperat folicitiffimam sabbati sanctificationem, hoc est, fegregationem vnius è septimanâ diei, quem nonnisi folenni cultui Dei impendamus. Secunda exprimit substantiam praecepti, Sex diebus operaberis, & facies omne opus tuum, quasi dicat, sex diebus facies opus tuum, & septimo die facies opus Dei, pari fcilicet folicitudine vt tuum. Tertia exprimit circumstantiam diei septimi. Quarta est sanctio ab exemplo Dei cessantis ab opere creationis die septimo, & illum benedicentis atque sanctificantis, hoc est, peculiarem benedictionem promittentis omnibus iis, qui diem hunc, ab ipso deftinatum non nisi rebus sanctis, ita transigunt vt ipse praecepit. Caeterum vt Deus diem septimum sanctificauit quiefcendo ab opere creationis: ita Christus diem primum sanctificauit resurgendo à mortuis, & diem septimum suftulit, quiescendo in sepulchro, atque ita finem imponendo huic ceremoniae, quae figurauit ipsius quietem. Itaque Christus transtulit benedictionem à die septimo in primum. Apoc.1.v.10. Act.20.v.7.
units.tr: XXIV. The fourth precept consists of four parts. The first commands the most careful sanctification of the Sabbath, that is, the setting apart of one day of the week, which we are to devote to nothing but the solemn worship of God. The second expresses the substance of the precept, Six days you shall labour, and do all your work, as if to say: on six days do your work, and on the seventh day do the work of God, with the same care, namely, as your own. The third expresses the circumstance of the seventh day. The fourth is a sanction drawn from the example of God, who ceased from the work of creation on the seventh day, and blessed and sanctified it, that is, promised a special blessing to all those who spend this day, appointed by him, only on holy things, and in the manner he has commanded. Moreover, as God sanctified the seventh day by resting from the work of creation, so Christ sanctified the first day by rising from the dead, and abolished the seventh day by resting in the tomb, thus putting an end to this ceremony, which prefigured his rest. Therefore Christ transferred the blessing from the seventh day to the first. Rev. 1. v. 10. Acts 20. v. 7.

units.la: XXV. Praeceptum quintum constat man- dato & sanctione.
units.tr: XXV. The fifth precept consists of a command and a sanction.

units.la: Mandatum praecipit iis qui sunt in statu subiectionis, vt patrem & matrem, hoc est, omnes qui sunt in statu eminentae, & habent rationem parentum, ita vt sint instar vel etiam loco ipsorum, in statu oeconomico, ecclesiastico, scholastico, & politico: vt, inquam, illos honorent amore, more, ore, & re, ita vt honor iste complectatur rectum in intellectu iudicium de persona & officio ipsorum; in voluntate propensionem ad illos amandum & filialiter timendum, illorumq; naevos tolerandum quatenus bona conscientia fieri poterit; modestiam insuper in gestu, reuerentiam in sermone & scriptis, obsequium & seruitium in factis, denique studium implendi studij in occasionibus. Ex his pendent officia correlatiua eorum qui sunt in statu eminentiae, erga inferiores, quos debent habere loco filiorum, & illos amare & iuuare per omnes numeros ϛνρχῆς, meritorum, exercitiorum, & coercitionum. Cæterùm quia hoc præceptum est fundamentum politiæ, quæ sine distinctione officiorum est nulla, ideo non tantùm est primum in secundâ tabulâ, sed etiam sanctione munitum, quâ dicitur, parentes prolongare vitam filiorum frugi, precibus nempe, redâqʒ; institutione. Intelligitur autem sub prolongatione vitæ benedictio, etiam æterna, cuius typus erat terra Canaan.
units.tr: The command is addressed to those who are in a state of subjection, that they honour father and mother; that is, all who hold a position of eminence and stand in the place of parents, so that they are like parents, or even in their place, in the household, the Church, the school and the state. They are to honour them, I say, in love, in manner, in speech and in deed. This honour embraces a right and sound judgement in the understanding about their person and office; in the will, an inclination to love them and to fear them as children fear a father, and to bear with their faults as far as a good conscience allows; further, modesty in bearing, reverence in speech and writing, obedience and service in deeds, and finally, zeal to fulfil their wishes whenever occasion arises. From this follow the correlative duties of those in a position of eminence towards their inferiors, whom they ought to hold in the place of children, and whom they ought to love and help in every way, by rewards, by instruction and by correction. Moreover, since this precept is the foundation of civil order, which cannot exist without a distinction of duties, it is therefore not only first in the second table but is also backed by a sanction, in which it is said that parents will lengthen the lives of their children who are upright, namely by prayers and by sound instruction. Now the prolonging of life is understood to include also the blessing of eternal life, of which the land of Canaan was a type.

units.la: XXVI. Sextum præceptum vult, ne occidamus: scil. vel mente, parui faciendo vitam proximi; vel voluntate & affectibus, ipsum odio habendo, priuatæ vindictæ cupiditate flagrando, & iræ præcipiti atqʒ iniustæ frænalaxando; vel gestibus toruis & austeris; vel sermone virulento; vel reipsâ; vel denique captandoaut præbendo occasionem: sed vitam & valetudinem ipsius defendamus, & mansuetudini, concordiæ, humanitati, placabilitati, misericordiæ, &c. studeamus. De propriæ valetudinis & vitæ defensione idem est iudicium. XXVII. Præceptum septimum vult, ne committamus adulterium: videlicet intellectu, prauè sentiendo de coniugio; vel voluntate & affectibus, fouendo cogitationes impuras; vel gestibus & habitu inuerecundo; vel sermone Fescennino; vel ipso facto; vel captatione aut præbitione occasionis: sed studeamus castitati extra coniugium & in coniugio, castitati, inquam, virginali, coniugali, & viduali. Cæterùm sub adulterio continetur fornicatio, stuprum, incestus, & omnis illicitus modus amoris. XXVIII. Octauum præceptum vult, ne committamus furtum: siue illud sit plagium, siue abigeatus, siue sacrilegium, siue furtum rei profanæ, idqʒ; simplex vel coniunctum, occultum vel manifestarium, paruum vel magnum: ne, inquam, furtum committamus intellectu, male sentiendo de distinctione dominiorum, vel voluntate & affectibus, invidendo proximis dona ipsorum; vel gestibus avaris, invidis & fallacibus; vel sermone fallente, aut tacente vitium in contractibus; vel ipsomet opere; vel captatione aut praebitione occasionum, quibus bona proximi mobilia vel immobilia damnum & vitium capiunt: sed, ut modis acquirendi legitimis studeamus, adeoque nostram rem augendo non diminuamus rem proximi.
units.tr: XXVI. The sixth precept requires that we do not kill: that is, neither by setting little store by our neighbour's life in the mind, nor by hating him in the will and affections, nor by burning with a desire for private revenge, nor by giving free rein to hasty and unjust anger; nor by grim and harsh gestures; nor by venomous speech; nor by actual violence; nor finally by seeking or offering an occasion for it. Rather, let us defend his life and health, and let us strive for gentleness, harmony, humanity, placability, mercy, and so on. The same judgement holds concerning the defence of our own health and life. XXVII. The seventh precept requires that we do not commit adultery: that is, in the understanding, by thinking wrongly of marriage; in the will and affections, by nursing impure thoughts; in gestures and bearing, by immodesty; in speech, by lewd talk; in the deed itself; or by seeking or offering an occasion. Rather, let us strive for chastity outside marriage and within it, chastity, I say, of virgins, of married people and of widows. Moreover, adultery includes fornication, debauchery, incest, and every unlawful form of love. XXVIII. The eighth precept requires that we do not commit theft: whether it be kidnapping, cattle-rustling, sacrilege, or the theft of profane property, and whether simple or aggravated, secret or open, petty or great. That is, we must not commit theft in the understanding, by thinking wrongly of the distinction of ownership; in the will and affections, by envying our neighbours their gifts; in gestures that are greedy, envious and deceitful; in speech that deceives, or that conceals a fault in dealings; in the deed itself; or by seeking or offering occasions by which the movable or immovable goods of our neighbour suffer loss and harm. Rather, let us strive for lawful ways of acquiring, and so by increasing our own property let us not diminish our neighbour's.

units.la: XXIX. Praeceptum nonum vult, ne dicamus falsum testimonium : vel iudicio sinistro[?], vel propensione malâ, vel gestib. ironicis, vel sermone mendace, vel actionibus fallacibus, vel occasionibus, simulationi & dissimulationi hypocriticae viam sternendo: sed studeamus veracitati, ut illâ vel eloquamur, vel celemus, prout gloria Dei, & salus publica & privata, animi & corporis, exigit.
units.tr: XXIX. The ninth precept requires that we do not bear false witness: whether by a sinister judgement, by an evil disposition, by mocking gestures, by a lying speech, by deceitful actions, or by occasions that pave the way for hypocritical pretence and concealment. Rather, let us strive for truthfulness, so that we speak it or keep silent as the glory of God and the public and private welfare, of soul and of body, require.

units.la: XXX. Praeceptum decimum prohibet concupiscentiam inordinatam: hoc est, pravitatem cogitationum & cupiditatum, sive illae sint formatae sive informes, sive consensum eliciant sive non, sive sint morosae sive subitaneae; quae cum sint specie unę, non rectè hoc praeceptum à quibusdam in duo discerpitur. Caeterùm pravitati cogtationum & cupiditatum opponitur sanctitas ipsarum, & lucta adversus omnem impurum motum.
units.tr: XXX. The tenth precept forbids disordered concupiscence: that is, the perversity of thoughts and desires, whether these are formed or unformed, whether they elicit consent or not, whether they are lingering or sudden. Since they are of one kind, this precept is wrongly divided into two by some. Moreover, the holiness of thoughts and desires is opposed to their perversity, and a struggle against every impure motion.

units.la: XXXI. Tertium caput Catechismi est Oratio dominica, quae est compêdium sive summa eorum, quae homini rectè credenti & viuetinunquam non sunt petenda à Deo. Praescriptū est hoc compendium à Christo, Matth.6.Luc.11.
units.tr: XXXI. The third part of the Catechism is the Lord's Prayer, which is a compendium, or summary, of those things which a man who rightly believes and lives ought never to fail to ask of God. This compendium was prescribed by Christ, Matth. 6, Luke 11.

units.la: XXXII. Eius partes sunt tres; praeparatio, sex petitiones, & confirmatio.
units.tr: XXXII. Its parts are three: the preparation, the six petitions, and the confirmation.

units.la: XXXIII. Praeparatio sive praefatio continet tres causas impulsivas & exemplares precationis. Nam quia Deus est Pater, affectu & effectu, {Greek}ςῳγῇ ἢ ἐγῷ[?], debemus illum inuocare libenter, frequenter, ex fide, spe, & charitate. Deinde quia est Pater noster, non solum debemus ipsum inuocare pro nobis, sed etiam pro aliis; & non soli nos oramus, sed etiam alii unà nobiscum, ita ut communi operà & uno veluti ore &corde totam Ecclesiâ Catholicam orare meminerimus, quâdo dicimus Pater noster. Deniq; quia Pater ille noster est in cœlis, maiestas, omnipotentia, & sanctitas eius debet nos inuitare ad sanctè, humiliter[?], & fiducialiter orandum.
units.tr: XXXIII. The preparation, or preface, contains three impelling and exemplary causes of prayer. For because God is Father, in affection and in effect, we ought to call upon him willingly, frequently, and in faith, hope and love. Next, because he is Our Father, we ought to call upon him not only for ourselves but also for others; and we do not pray alone, but others pray along with us, so that we remember, when we say Our Father, to pray with common labour and with one mouth and heart, as it were, for the whole Catholic Church. Finally, because that our Father is in heaven, his majesty, omnipotence and holiness ought to invite us to pray holily, humbly and confidently.

units.la: XXXIV. Sex petitiones diuiduntur in duas veluti tabulas: ita nempe, ut prima complectatur tres petitiones spectantes Deum, ut indicat pronomen tuum, quod occurrit in singulis: secunda cotineat reliquas tres, quæ spectant nos, ut indicat pronomen noster & nos.
units.tr: XXXIV. The six petitions are divided into two tables, as it were: namely, the first embraces three petitions concerning God, as the pronoun tuum indicates, which occurs in each of them; the second contains the remaining three, which concern us, as the pronouns noster and nos indicate.

units.la: XXXV. Prima petitio est regula omnium actionum nostrarum. In universâ siquidem vitâ nostra id nobis debet esse propositum, ut nomen D E I Patris nostri cœlestis, hoc est, gloria eius ratione essentiæ, personarum, & operum sanctificetur, id est, separetur & vindicetur ab omni obliuione & abusu ad sanctum usum in cogitationibus, sermonibus & operibus nostris, secundum quatuor præcepta primæ tabulæ decalogi.
units.tr: XXXV. The first petition is the rule of all our actions. For throughout our whole life this ought to be our purpose: that the name of GOD our heavenly Father, that is, his glory in respect of his essence, persons and works, be sanctified, that is, set apart and vindicated from all forgetfulness and abuse, to holy use in our thoughts, words and deeds, according to the four precepts of the first table of the Decalogue.

units.la: XXXVI. Secunda petitio est summa defideriorum nostrorum. In universâ siquidem vitâ nostra id unicè debemus optare, ut destructo regno Satanæ, regnum gloriæ adueniat, partim in hac vitâ, per inchoationem, procedendo de gradu in gradum; partim post hanc vitam, per consummationem, evehendo in supremum gradum.
units.tr: XXXVI. The second petition is the sum of our desires. For throughout our whole life we ought to wish for this above all: that, the kingdom of Satan being destroyed, the kingdom of glory may come, partly in this life, by a beginning, advancing from degree to degree, and partly after this life, by its consummation, being raised to the highest degree.

units.la: XXXVII. Tertia petitio est norma abnegationis nostri ipsorum. In universâ siquidem vitâ nostra debemus unicè acquiescere in voluntate Dei, & simul facere voluntatem eius patefactam in lege & Evangelio, idq; exemplo sanctorum Angelorum in cœlis, qui acquiescunt in voluntate D E I sine murmure, & faciunt voluntatem eius totam, libenter, cito, & fideliter.
units.tr: XXXVII. The third petition is the rule of self-denial. For throughout our whole life we ought to rest wholly in the will of God, and at the same time to do his will as revealed in the law and the Gospel; and this by the example of the holy angels in heaven, who acquiesce in the will of GOD without murmuring, and do his whole will, gladly, promptly and faithfully.

units.la: XXXVIII. Quarta petitio docet, quomodo debeamus petere bona huius vitæ, & βιωτικά[?]: nimirum ita, ut petamus dari, siue donari, panem satietatis, sanitatis, & tranquillitatis: deinde panem nostrum, qui vocationi nostræ congruat, qui appellatur panis charitatis: tertio panem quotidianum, siue panem diei, qui in præsentem diem ad nostri sustentationem sufficiat, unde appellari solet panis frugalitatis: denique hodie, hoc est, singulis diebus, quibus viuimus hanc vitam breuem & caducam, ita ut sit panis sufficientiæ.
units.tr: XXXVIII. The fourth petition teaches how we ought to ask for the goods of this life and for things pertaining to living. Namely, we ask to be given, or granted, bread of satiety, of health and of tranquillity; then our bread, which fits our calling, and which is called the bread of charity; thirdly, daily bread, or the bread of the day, which suffices for our sustenance for the present day, whence it is usually called the bread of frugality; and finally today, that is, on each of the days in which we live this brief and fleeting life, so that it may be the bread of sufficiency. [βιωτικά]

units.la: XXXIX. Quinta petitio respicit sensum iustificationis seu remissionis peccatorum. Hicenim petimus, ut Deus remissionem peccatorum magis magisque nobis ingeneret atque obsignet per placabilitatem, quæ est insignis fructus fidei, & iustificationis signum infallibile. Nam Christus promisit, patrem in cœlis remissurum peccata omnibus iis, qui proximo remittunt offensas animo sincero.
units.tr: XXXIX. The fifth petition regards the sense of justification, or the remission of sins. For here we ask that God may engender and seal in us the remission of sins more and more, through a forgiving spirit, which is a notable fruit of faith and an infallible sign of justification. For Christ promised that the Father in heaven will remit sins to all those who forgive offences to their neighbour with a sincere heart.

units.la: XL. Sexta petitio respicit sanctificationem nostri, & est bipartita. Proponitur enim in forma axiomatis discreti. Pars prima est negatiua, qua petimus, ne Deus nos inducat in tentationem, deserendo nos, & permittendo ut ab ipso deserti superemur à diabolo, mundo, & carne. Altera pars est affirmatiua, qua petimus liberari à malo, hoc est, à diabolo & omnibus eius technis & artibus malis, quibus ille tanquam mille-artifex vitur, ut vel malum culpæ nobis suggerat, vel malum pœnæ nobis acerbum reddat, vel denique bonum virtutis & felicitatis conuertat in malum.
units.tr: XL. The sixth petition regards the sanctification of ourselves, and it has two parts. It is put forward in the form of a distinct axiom. The first part is negative, in which we ask that God may not lead us into temptation, by forsaking us and allowing us, once forsaken by him, to be overcome by the devil, the world and the flesh. The other part is affirmative, in which we ask to be delivered from evil, that is, from the devil and all his wicked devices and arts, by which he, as the thousand-artificer, works, so as either to suggest to us the evil of guilt, or to make the evil of punishment bitter to us, or finally to turn the good of virtue and happiness into evil.

units.la: XLI. Confirmatio complectitur columnas & sigillum fidei. Columna fidei sunt tres: videlicet regnum, potentia & gloria Dei, eaque omnia sempiterna. Sigillum fidei est particula Amen, qua optamus asseuerádo, & asseueramus optando. Hic itaque est sensus: Hæc omnia à te petimus,quia tu es rex summè gloriosus, qui omnia in omne ævum potes atque vis, quæ ad gloriam nominis tui pertinent. Nos itaq;, filii tui, hoc firmiter persuasum habemus, te non frustraturum fiduciam nostram, quam in te collocamus. Fiat itaque, fiat, fiat, quod rectè petiuimus.
units.tr: XLI. The confirmation contains the pillars and the seal of faith. The pillars of faith are three: namely the kingdom, power and glory of God, and all of these are everlasting. The seal of faith is the particle Amen, by which we wish while affirming, and affirm while wishing. The sense is this: we ask all these things of you, because you are the most glorious King, who can and will do all things for evermore that pertain to the glory of your name. We, therefore, your children, hold this firmly persuaded, that you will not disappoint the trust we place in you. So let it be, let it be, let it be, what we have rightly asked.

units.la: XLII. Quartum Catechismi caput est Institutio baptismi: Ea describitur Matth. 28. & Marc.16.
units.tr: XLII. The fourth chapter of the Catechism is the Institution of baptism. It is described in Matt. 28 and Mark 16.

units.la: XLIII. Institutio baptismi est formula rectè administrandi sacramentum spiritualis generationis in N.T. complexa verbum præceptionis, promissionis, & comminationis. Verbum præceptionis est quo Christus iubet Apostolos ire per totum terrarum orbem; & ibi discipulos facere per prædi-cationem euangelii; & hos discipulos baptizare, siue aquâ consecratâ & cœlestem vocationem gerente lauare, in nomen, hoc est, in cultum, tum Patris, qui nobis dedit Filium; tum Filii, qui nos effecit Patri suo filios dilectos; tum denique Spiritus sancti, qui nobis salutem à Filio partam applicat. Intellige cultum fidei, obedientiæ, & inuocationis. Verbum promissionis est ipsissimum vinculum, quo signū & signatum, id est, res terrestris & cœlestis, vniuntur per fidem promissioni respondentem eâq; nitentem. Verbum comminationis est fulmen, quo hypocritæ consternuntur, & electi excitantur, vt scueritatem Dei in alieno subiecto intuiti discant religiosè tractare sacramentum.
units.tr: XLIII. The institution of baptism is a formula for rightly administering the sacrament of spiritual generation in the New Testament, comprising a word of command, a word of promise, and a word of threatening. The word of command is that by which Christ bids the apostles go through the whole world, make disciples there by the preaching of the gospel, and baptize these disciples, that is, wash them with consecrated water bearing a heavenly calling, in the name, that is, into the worship, of the Father, who gave us the Son; of the Son, who made us beloved sons of his Father; and finally of the Holy Spirit, who applies to us the salvation obtained by the Son. Understand the worship of faith, obedience and invocation. The word of promise is the very bond by which the sign and the thing signified, that is, the earthly and the heavenly thing, are united through faith, which answers to the promise and rests upon it. The word of threatening is the thunderbolt by which hypocrites are struck down and the elect are roused, so that, seeing the severity of God in another's case, they learn to handle the sacrament reverently.

units.la: XLIII. Quintum & vltimum Catechismi caput est Institutio sacræ cœnæ. Ea describitur Matt. 26. Marc. 14. Luc. 22. 1. Cor. 11.
units.tr: XLIII. The fifth and last chapter of the Catechism is the Institution of the holy supper. It is described in Matt. 26, Mark 14, Luke 22, and 1 Cor. 11.

units.la: XLIV. Institutio sacræ cœnæ est formula rectè administrandi sacramentum spiritualis nutritionis in N.T. complexa quatuor istas partes. Prima est de circumstantiis, vt sunt persona instituens, & tempus institutionis: quæ duo plurimum nobis commé-
units.tr: XLIV. The institution of the holy supper is a formula for rightly administering the sacrament of spiritual nourishment in the New Testament, comprising these four parts. The first concerns the circumstances, such as the person instituting it and the time of institution; these two things especially commend this sacrament to us.

units.la: ʃ dant hoc sacramentum. Secundapars est consecratio panis quem Christus accepit, prout nempe in usu erat apud Iudaeos pascha celebrantes: & gratiis actis ipsum sanctificauit, ordinando ad usum mysticum, & ipsi imponendo sublime officium: postea fregit, ac dixit, Hoc est corpus meum, id est, Panis iste & corpus meum in legitimo usu sacramentaliter uniuntur & offeruntur homini vera fide memoriam Christi in hoc mysterio recolenti. Tertiapars est consecratio vini, quod Christus eodem modo tractauit vt panem. Neque enim phrasis illa, qua dicit, Poculum esse nouum foedus per suum sanguinem, est diuersa ab illa, qua dixit, Panem esse corpus suum: sed vtriusque vna est ratio, putas sacramentalis, ita vt panis in eucharistia sit corpus Christi sacramentaliter, & poculum in eucharistia sit foedus nouum sacramentaliter, h.e. medium, quo nobis significatur, obsignatur & exhibetur Christus, quatenus est mediator N. T. per oblationem corporis & sanguinis sui. Quartapars est veluti celeusma, quo excitamur ad mortem Christi, tanquam summum beneficium, in hoc symbolo annunciandum vera fide, spe, & charitate, idque vsque quo venerit, h. e. quamdiu Ecclesia in his terris militat. Plura vide in Theologia catechetica peculiari volumine.
units.tr: The second part is the consecration of the bread which Christ took, namely as it was in use among the Jews celebrating the Passover. Having given thanks, he sanctified it, ordaining it for mystical use and laying upon it a sublime office. Afterwards he broke it and said, "This is my body", that is, this bread and my body are sacramentally united and offered in lawful use to the man who, with true faith, recalls the memory of Christ in this mystery. The third part is the consecration of the wine, which Christ handled in the same way as the bread. For that phrase by which he says, "The cup is the new covenant in his blood", is not different from that by which he said, "The bread is his body"; rather, there is one reasoning for both, namely the sacramental one, so that the bread in the eucharist is the body of Christ sacramentally, and the cup in the eucharist is the new covenant sacramentally, that is, the means by which Christ is signified, sealed and exhibited to us, insofar as he is mediator of the New Testament, through the offering of his body and blood. The fourth part is, as it were, a shout of encouragement, by which we are roused to proclaim, in this symbol, the death of Christ as the highest benefit, with true faith, hope and charity, and that until he comes, that is, for as long as the Church wages war in these lands. See more in the separate volume on Catechetical Theology.

units.la: XXXIV.
units.tr: XXXIV.

units.la: THEOLOGIA DIDACTICA.
units.tr: DIDACTIC THEOLOGY.

units.la: I. Theologia didactica plene explicat locos communes sacros ex Scriptura sacra.
units.tr: I. Didactic theology fully explains the sacred common places from Holy Scripture.
