That is, we shape our manners according to right reason and propriety, which the Greeks call τὸ πρέπον [to prepon], so that they fit the circumstances of persons, places, times and things, and so express charm, harmony and beauty, with symmetry and grace, in civil conduct. James 3:13; Rom. 12:3–4, 6; 15:2; 1 Cor. 13:5–6; 11:4–5.

units.la: III. Conuersatio ciuilis est communis, vel propria.
units.tr: III. Civil conduct is either common or particular.

units.la: IV. Conuersatio ciuilis communis posita est in eo, vt cum cuiusuis conditionis & status hominibus rite conuersemur.
units.tr: IV. Common civil conduct consists in dealing fittingly with people of every condition and rank.

units.la: V. Ea cernitur in recto vsu sermonis, & gestu seu habitu conueniente.
units.tr: V. It is seen in the right use of speech and in a fitting bearing and demeanour.

units.la: VI. Rectus sermonis vsus est in conceptione & pronunciatione verborum.
units.tr: VI. The right use of speech lies in the forming and the uttering of words.

units.la: VII. Conceptio verborum est, qua animi nostri cogitata aliis, quibuscum conuersamur, significanda, praemeditamur, vt conuenientibus verbis illa enuntiemus. Eph.4.v.29. Cùm enim verba sint indicia animi, & veluti character interioris hominis, multum refert, vt illa recte proferantur ex bono thesauro cordis. Matth.12.verf.34. 35.36. Luc.6.v.45. Iacob.3. Prov.4.v.23. c.18.v.20.21.
units.tr: VII. Forming words means considering beforehand what we must signify to those with whom we converse, so that we may express those thoughts in fitting words. Eph. 4:29. For since words are indications of the mind, and as it were the mark of the inner man, it matters greatly that they be brought forth rightly from the good treasure of the heart. Matt. 12:34–36; Luke 6:45; James 3; Prov. 4:23; 18:20–21.

units.la: VIII. Conceptio verborum legitima est, quae recte perpendit qualitatem rerum, personarum, & verborum. Rerum, de quibus; personarum, coram quibus; verborum, quibus sermonem instituere & habere conuenit.
units.tr: VIII. Legitimate forming of words is that which weighs rightly the quality of things, persons and words: of the things we speak about, of the persons before whom we speak, and of the words with which it is fitting to begin and carry on speech.

units.la: IX. In rebus de quibus sermonem instituere volumus, videndum est, quas decorum & honestum sit proferre, & quas tacere. Hic itaque tradenda est ars loquendi & tacendi, vt ita dicamus.
units.tr: IX. Regarding the matters on which we wish to speak, we must consider which it is seemly and honourable to bring forward and which to pass over in silence. Here, then, the art of speaking and of keeping silent, so to speak, must be taught.

units.la: X. Ars loquendi continetur his regulis, Loquendum est de rebus cognitis, conuenientibus, vtilib. necessariis, & veris. Ephef. 4.v.29.1. Cor. 14.v.19. Prov.10. v.20.21. Eccl.20.v.4. 5.c. 3.v.23.c.4.v.27. Iacob.3.v.10. Huc pertinent exempla Christi, & aliorum sanctorum hominum, qui nonnisi de rebus sanctis, piis, vtilibus & necessariis locuti & collocuti leguntur in sacris literis. 2. Materia sermonis est de Deo, vel nobis ipsis, vel proximo. De Deo ita est loquendum, ut ipsius nomen sanctè usurpetur & religiosè tractetur. Exod.20.v.7. De nobismet ipsis nihil est dicendum, quod ad laudem intempestiuam & nimiam, vel vituperium pertinet. Prou.27. v.2. De proximo si dicendū, oportet considerare an causa sit bona vel mala. In bonâ prompte veritati testimonium est perhibendum. 3.Iohan. v.12. In malâ nihil est dicendum, nisi propria conscientia & vocatio vrgeat, aut postulet: si nempe iubeat magistratus, si charitas Christiana imperet admoneri proximum, si aedificatio aliorum hoc requirat, deniq; si pericula possint praecaueri per nostram indicationem. Gen. 37. v.2.2. Leg.6.v.9.1.Cor.1.v.11. Act.23.v.20.21.22.3. De arcanis & dubiis non oportet finistrè & in malam partem iudicare 1. Cor.13.v.5.c 4.v.5. Cogitandum hic est vetus dictum: Favores sunt ampliandi, odia restringenda. 4. Sermo est gratiosus & acceptus, si habeat quatuor comites: prudetiam in discretione circumstantiarum Prou.25.v.11. veritatem Pf. 15.v.2. lenitatem, siue humanitatem Coloss.4.v.6. Prou.15.v. 1.1.Sam.25.verf. 10.24. denique grauitatem & pondus Tit. 2.verf.7.
units.tr: X. The art of speaking is contained in these rules: one must speak of things known, fitting, useful, necessary and true. Eph. 4:29; 1 Cor. 14:19; Prov. 10:20–21; Eccl. 20:4–5; 3:23; 4:27; James 3:10. To this belong the examples of Christ and other holy men, who are read in the sacred writings to have spoken and conversed only of holy, pious, useful and necessary things. 2. The matter of speech concerns God, ourselves, or our neighbour. Of God one must speak so that his name is used holily and treated reverently. Exod. 20:7. Of ourselves nothing is to be said that tends to untimely and excessive praise or blame. Prov. 27:2. Of a neighbour, if one must speak, one must consider whether the cause is good or bad. In a good cause one should readily bear witness to the truth. 3 John 12. In a bad cause nothing is to be said unless one's own conscience and calling urge it or demand it: namely, if the magistrate commands it, if Christian charity requires the neighbour to be admonished, if the edification of others requires it, or finally if dangers can be averted by our disclosure. Gen. 37:2; Lev. 6:9; 1 Cor. 1:11; Acts 23:20–22. 3. About secrets and doubtful matters one should not judge sinisterly and in the worse sense. 1 Cor. 13:5; 4:5. Here the old saying must be kept in mind: favours are to be enlarged, hatreds restricted. 4. Speech is gracious and welcome if it has four companions: prudence in discerning circumstances (Prov. 25:11); truth (Ps. 15:2); gentleness or humanity (Col. 4:6; Prov. 15:1; 1 Sam. 25:10, 24); and finally gravity and weight (Titus 2:7).

units.la: XI. Ars tacendi gubernatur his regulis. 1.Quaedam sunt omnino tacenda, quaedam aliquatenus. 2. Omnino tacenda sunt res inconuenientes, alienae, impertinentes, foedae, turpes, impiae, & nobis non satis cognitae. Psal. 141.v.3. Iacob.3.v.26.c.3. Coloss.3.v. 8.1. Tim.5.v.13. 2.Tim.2.v. 23.Tit.3.v.9. Eph.4.v. 29.5.v.3.4. Psal.50.v.16.19. Matth.12.v. 36.37.3.Qua aliquatenus sunt tacenda, illa sic sunt comparata, vt in iis sermo sit silentio temperandus: puta in assensu & dissensu, in commendatione, in mentione aliorum facienda, in iocis, in irrisione, in censura, in reprehensione & increpatione, deniq; in contentione: idq; iuxta seqq. regulas 4. In assensu & dissensu non debet esse leuitas, vel vitiosus pudor; neque etiâ malitiosa affectatio & obstinatio. Leuitas est in eo, si quis inconsiderate omnia approbet, improbet, damnet, neget, concedat &c. Vitiosus pudor est, cum quis ex vanâ suspicione & metu cuiusdam probri, vel obimaginationem existimationis offensæ & præsumtionem mali, postulantibus nihil recusat, vel pollicetur quæ præstare non potest. Malitiosa affectatio est, cum assectamus τῶν δυσκόλων[?] mores. Obstinatio est in var â contradictione & pertinacia. Prov.12.v.13. Gal 6.v.3. Eccles.7.v.23. 1.Sam.15.v.3.17.5. Commendatio est vel suiipsius, velaliorum. Commendatio sui ipsius tum demum est propter, quando est necessaria. 2.Cor.3.v.1.2.3.c.4.v.12. Ioh.8.v.14. In isto ve- rò casu sic est instituenda, vt Deo tribuamus gloriam, infirmitate nostrâ confiteamur, facta nostra extenuemus,[?] & deniq; laudes nost as mitigemus. 1.Cor.15.2. Cor.12.1. Sam. v.5.1. Cor.9.v.1.2.2.Cor.9.v.11. Extra hunc casu, & absq; bis cautelis[?] commendatio sui ipsius est ridicula, impudens & superba. Prov.27.v.2. Eccl.9.v.21.2. Cor.10.v.18. Commendatio aliorum debet esse ꝑ peculab adulatione. 1.Sam.28.& 29.1. Thes.1 2.v.3.4.5.6. Ps.5.12.140.6. Mentio aliorum sic est facienda, vt absit maledicentia Colos.3.v.8. 9.1. Tim.3.v.2.1. Sam.14.v. 10. vt vi ia proximi dissimulentur, quantum licet. 1.Pet.4.v.8. vt secreta, præsertim amici, non reuelentur. Prov.10. v.19.c.25.v.9. Matt.18.v.15.c.1.v.19.7. Ioci debent esse subtiles, faceti, faciles & iucundi: non longè repetiti, rustici, tædiosi, molesti, scurriles, aculeati, impij &c. 1.Reg.18.v.27. Esa.14.v.11. Prov.17.v.5. Psal.35.v.16.8. Irrisio non facilè locum apud nos inueniet. Certè non debet proficisci ira, despicientiâ & ignominiâ. Eccles.7.v.10.c.8.v.5. Psal.11 v.7.8. Matth.17.v.29. Prov.22.v.10. Gen.21.v.9. Alias irrisio sestiua omninò probari debet, & quandoq; est necessaria. 1.Reg.18.v.17. Esa.44. & 46.9. Exprobratio tum demum est ciuilis, quando fit ob ingratitudinem, vel maleficium. Prov.17.v.9.1.Cor.13.v.4.2. Petr.1.v.6.7. 1.Sam.1.v.6.14.c.25. v.10.11.12. 10.Censura non est ciuilis, nisi fiat iustè & exnecessitate officij. Iacob.3.v.1.c.4.v. 11.Matth.7.v.1.2. Ioh.1.v.9. 11.Act.18.v.4.11. Contentio non est licita, nisi pro veritate; ita tamen vt fiat prudenter & moderatè. 1.Tim.6.v.4.204. 5.v.13.Phil.2.v.3.Tit.3.v.9.
units.tr: XI. The art of keeping silent is governed by these rules. 1. Some things must be kept silent altogether, others only to some degree. 2. Things to be kept altogether silent are those that are unseemly, alien, irrelevant, foul, shameful, impious, and not sufficiently known to us. Ps. 141:3; James 1:26; 3:6; Col. 3:8; 1 Tim. 5:13; 2 Tim. 2:23; Titus 3:9; Eph. 4:29; 5:3–4; Ps. 50:16, 19; Matt. 12:36–37. 3. Things to be kept silent to some degree are so constituted that speech in them must be tempered by silence: namely in assent and dissent, in commendation, in the mention of others, in jests, in mockery, in censure, in rebuke and reproof, and finally in contention; and this according to the following four rules. In assent and dissent there must be neither levity, nor faulty shame, nor malicious affectation and obstinacy. Levity consists in approving, disapproving, condemning, denying, conceding everything without thought. Faulty shame is when someone, from vain suspicion and fear of some disgrace, or from an imagined offence to his reputation and a presumption of evil, refuses nothing to those who ask, or promises what he cannot perform. Malicious affectation is when we affect the manners of the morose. Obstinacy is vain contradiction and pertinacity. Prov. 12:13; Gal. 6:3; Eccl. 7:23; 1 Sam. 15:3; 17:5. Commendation is either of oneself or of others. Self-commendation is proper only when it is necessary. 2 Cor. 3:1–3; 4:12; John 8:14. In that case it must be done so that we give glory to God, confess our weakness, play down our deeds, and finally moderate our praises. 1 Cor. 15:2; 2 Cor. 12:1; 1 Sam. 5:1; 1 Cor. 9:1–2; 2 Cor. 9:11. Outside this case, and without these precautions, self-commendation is ridiculous, impudent and proud. Prov. 27:2; Eccl. 9:21; 2 Cor. 10:18. The commendation of others must be free of crafty flattery. 1 Sam. 28–29; 1 Thess. 2:3–6; Ps. 5:12; 140:6. The mention of others is to be made so that slander is absent, so that the faults of neighbours are concealed as far as possible, and so that secrets, especially those of friends, are not revealed. Col. 3:8–9; 1 Tim. 3:2; 1 Sam. 14:10; 1 Pet. 4:8; Prov. 10:19; 25:9; Matt. 18:15; 1:19. Jokes should be subtle, witty, easy and pleasant: not drawn out at length, rustic, tedious, troublesome, buffoonish, barbed, impious and so on. 1 Kings 18:27; Isa. 14:11; Prov. 17:5; Ps. 35:16; 8. Mockery will not easily find a place among us. Certainly it should not proceed from anger, contempt and disgrace. Eccl. 7:10; 8:5; Ps. 11:7–8; Matt. 17:29; Prov. 22:10; Gen. 21:9. Otherwise, mockery that is sportive must altogether be approved, and it is sometimes necessary. 1 Kings 18:17; Isa. 44, 46:9. Reproach is civil only when it is made on account of ingratitude or wrongdoing. Prov. 17:9; 1 Cor. 13:4; 1 Pet. 1:6–7; 1 Sam. 1:6, 14; 25:10–12. Censure is not civil unless it is done justly and out of the necessity of office. James 3:1; 4:11; Matt. 7:1–2; John 1:9; Acts 18:4, 11. Contention is not lawful unless it is for the truth; yet it must be done prudently and moderately. 1 Tim. 6:4; 5:13; Phil. 2:3; Titus 3:9.

units.la: XII. Cum illis loquendum est, cum quibus
units.tr: XII. With whom one must converse

units.la: conuersari necessitas & utilitas nos urget, & cum quibus ex officio tenemur. Principio autem debemus uti affabilitate & comitate erga quosuis. Rom. 12.ver.15.2.Tim.3.v.2.1.Cor.13.v.4.5.6. Deinde commercium & collatio sermonis cum iis esse debet, quorum conuersatio nos potest reddere meliores. Prou.13.v.20Eccl.9.v.19.& quos nostra conuersatio potest facere meliores, vt sunt indocti, infideles, infirmi, & similes, qui sunt tractabiles, ita vt sit Spes ædificationis & emendationis. 1. Cor. 9.v.22. Extra hunc cœtum non licet conuersari cum infidelibus. 2.Cor.6.v.14.15.16. neque cum sultis Prou. 23.v.9. neque cum verbosis Eccles.8.v.20. 22. neque cum rixosis. Eccles.18.v.10.11.1.Sam.25.v.9.10. 11. neq; cum irrisoribus. Prou.9.v.7.8.c.10.v.8.
units.tr: Those with whom necessity and usefulness oblige us to associate, and with whom duty binds us, are the ones we must speak to. First, we ought to show courtesy and kindness towards everyone. Rom. 12 ver. 15; 2 Tim. 3 v. 2; 1 Cor. 13 v. 4, 5, 6. Next, our dealings and conversation ought to be with those whose company can make us better: Prov. 13 v. 20; Eccl. 9 v. 19; and with those whom our company can make better, such as the untaught, the unbelieving, the weak and the like, who are teachable, so that there is hope of building them up and correcting them: 1 Cor. 9 v. 22. Outside this group it is not lawful to associate with unbelievers, 2 Cor. 6 v. 14, 15, 16; nor with fools, Prov. 23 v. 9; nor with the talkative, Eccl. 8 v. 20, 22; nor with the quarrelsome, Eccl. 18 v. 10, 11; 1 Sam. 25 v. 9, 10, 11; nor with scoffers, Prov. 9 v. 7, 8; ch. 10 v. 8.

units.la: XIII. Verbis utendum est elegantibus, modestis, & iucundis. Ita primo videmus Scripturæ sacræ stilum esse contextum ex verbis elegantiæ plenis. Deinde modestia commendat sanctorum orationes, colloquia, increpationes & hinc inde in sacris. Denique iucunditas commendat colloquia Christi cum discipulis & aliis.
units.tr: XIII. We must use words that are elegant, modest and pleasant. First, we see that the style of Holy Scripture is woven of words full of elegance. Next, modesty commends the prayers, conversations and rebukes of the saints, here and there in the sacred books. Finally, pleasantness commends the conversations of Christ with his disciples and with others.

units.la: XV. Pronunciatio recta est, quâ fit, vt verba concepta, tempestiuè, & decenti sono proferamus. Duo itaque sunt requisita pronuntiationis. Et primo quidem debet illa esse tempestiua, hoc est, eiusmodi, quæ auscultanti adferat commodum, & dicenti conciliet gratiam. Prou.25.v.11.c.15.v.23. Esa.50. vers.4. Eccles.22.v.6.s. 32.v.6.7. Eccles.3.v.4. Roman.12.v.15. Deinde requiritur in pronuntiatione conueniens vocis sonus, qui rebus & ipsarum naturæ sit accommodatus. Eccl.17.v.7.c.40.v.21.1.Cor.14. v.7.8.9.Dan.6.v.21.Prou.18.v.23.Gal.6.v.1.2.Esa.42.vers.2.11. Ier.25.v.30.2.Reg.18.v.28.
units.tr: XV. Delivery is correct when we utter the words we have framed at the right time and with a fitting tone. There are therefore two requirements of delivery. The first is that it be timely, that is, of such a kind as brings advantage to the hearer and wins favour for the speaker: Prov. 25 v. 11; ch. 15 v. 23; Isa. 50 vers. 4; Eccl. 22 v. 6; ch. 32 v. 6, 7; Eccl. 3 v. 4; Rom. 12 v. 15. Next, a fitting sound of voice is required in delivery, one adapted to the matters themselves and to their nature: Eccl. 17 v. 7; ch. 40 v. 21; 1 Cor. 14 v. 7, 8, 9; Dan. 6 v. 21; Prov. 18 v. 23; Gal. 6 v. 1, 2; Isa. 42 vers. 2, 11; Jer. 25 v. 30; 2 Kings 18 v. 28.

units.la: XVI. Gestus hominis in ciuili conuersatione est hominis loquentis, audientis, vel silentis: lentis: & rursus est in singulis membris, vel in toto corpore: itrem in motu, vel vestitu: deniq; est ordinarius, vel extraordinarius: idq; iuxta has regulas. 1. Talem quis fe habitu gestuque exhibeat, qualis videri cupit: & talis reuera intus fit, qualis apparere extrinsecus cupit. Matth. 6. & 23. 2. Habitus fit decorus & fecundum naturā. 1.Cor.11.v.13.14.15.c.14.v.40. 3. Habitus fit virilis in masculo, muliebris in fœmina. 1.Cor.11.v.13.14. 4. Inter loquentem & audientem debet esse conueniens proportio: ita nempe, vt vterque alteri fe recte accommodet. Vide passim disputationes & conciones Christi. Luc. 2.v.46.c.5.v.3. 5. Habitus fit accomodatus ipsi rei: vt, velatio capitis est habitus & gestus hominis tristitia affectā. 2.Sam.15.v.30. capitis demissio est signum luctus, doloris, & humiliationis. Esa. 58. v.5. Gen. 4. v.6. capitis eleuatio est habitus victoris Esa. 35.v.10. frons dura significat obftinationem & impudentiā. Esa. 48. v.4. &c. 6. Inceflus debet esse honestus, lentus, decorus & ciuilis. Esa. 3. verf.17. Deut. 28. v.56. 7. Vestitus fit decorus & honestus, ita nempevt fit necessarius, conformis & aptus corpori, deniqueconueniens vocationi, ætati, & personæ vtentis. Tit.2.verf.3.1. Tim.2.v.9.1.Petr.3.v.3.4. 8. Habitus cósentiat cum vulgatâ consuetudine hominum. Sic apud Iudæos falutationebat osculo Luc.15.v.20. saccus erat habitus lugentium. Ia. 48.v.37. peculiaris erat habitus sacerdotum. Exod.28.prophetarum. 1.Reg.19.v.19. regum Efth.8.v.3. 1.Reg.10. 9. Habitus arbitrarius, fi fit rationabilis, ita vt ex ratione aliquâ probabili fit susceptus, gratiam habet. Tales erant habitus portentofi prophetarum. 2.Reg.3.v.15.c.4.v.34.c.13.v.15.1.10 Reg.18, verf.42. Iohan.9.verf.6.7.1.Sam.19.v.23.24. Matth.3 verf.4.
units.tr: XVI. A man's gesture in civil conversation belongs to him as speaking, listening or silent; and again it belongs to single limbs or to the whole body; to movement or to dress; and finally it is ordinary or extraordinary. This is governed by the following rules. (1) Let someone present himself in bearing and gesture as he wishes to be seen; and he will truly become inwardly what he wishes to appear outwardly: Matt. 6 and 23. (2) Bearing should be becoming and according to nature: 1 Cor. 11 v. 13, 14, 15; ch. 14 v. 40. (3) Bearing should be manly in a man and womanly in a woman: 1 Cor. 11 v. 13, 14. (4) Between the speaker and the listener there ought to be a fitting proportion, namely that each adapt himself rightly to the other. See throughout the disputations and sermons of Christ: Luke 2 v. 46; ch. 5 v. 3. (5) Bearing should be suited to the matter itself: thus, a veiled head is the bearing and gesture of a man feigning sadness: 2 Sam. 15 v. 30; a bowed head is a sign of mourning, grief and humiliation: Isa. 58 v. 5; Gen. 4 v. 6; a raised head is the bearing of a victor: Isa. 35 v. 10; a hard brow signifies obstinacy and shamelessness: Isa. 48 v. 4, etc. (6) Gait should be honourable, unhurried, becoming and civil: Isa. 3 vers. 17; Deut. 28 v. 56. (7) Dress should be becoming and honourable, that is, such as is necessary, suited and fitting to the body, and finally agreeing with the calling, age and person of the one wearing it: Titus 2 vers. 3; 1 Tim. 2 v. 9; 1 Pet. 3 v. 3, 4. (8) Bearing should agree with the common custom of men. Thus among the Jews greeting was done with a kiss: Luke 15 v. 20; sackcloth was the dress of mourners: Jer. 48 v. 37; a distinctive dress belonged to priests, Exod. 28; to prophets, 1 Kings 19 v. 19; to kings, Esth. 8 v. 3; 1 Kings 10. (9) A bearing chosen at will has grace provided it is reasonable, that is, adopted for some probable reason. Such were the remarkable bearings of the prophets: 2 Kings 3 v. 15; ch. 4 v. 34; ch. 13 v. 15; 1 Kings 18 vers. 42; John 9 vers. 6, 7; 1 Sam. 19 vers. 23, 24; Matt. 3 vers. 4.

units.la: XVII. Conuersatio ciuilis propria est, quæ conuenit statui cuiusque proprio, idque inna&u conuiuiali, vel extra illum.
units.tr: XVII. Civil conversation is of two kinds: that which suits each person's own station, and this either at a banquet or outside one.

units.la: XVIII. Conuersatio cuiusque statui conveniens est personarum vel imparium,earumque digniorum aut viliorum,vel parium;iuxta has regulas. 1.Firmiter nobis debet esse persuasum,inter homines alium alio esse praestantiorem. Phil.2.v.3.29. Act.5.v.34.2.Chron.10.Rom.12.v.10. Etsi enim omnes sumus conditi ad imaginem Dei: tamen imago illa certos habet gradus,sive spectemus naturae dotes.1. Cor.12.v.4, 5.6 sive civilem dignitatem Rom.13.v.1. sive denique eruditionem, & similia, quae proprio studio nobis prae aliis comparauimus 1.Thess.5.verf.12.13.Prou.28.v.6. 2.Qui aliis sunt digniores,ita se gerant,ut dignitati suae nullam aspergant labem, ne aliis occasionem praebeant se contemnedi.Eph.4.v.1.2.3. Inter plures praestantes dignior & honoratior habetur is, in quem plures causæ dignitatis concurrunt.Eccl.9.v.17.18.19. 4.Digniores debent se accommodare vilioribus, & hi illos reuereri. Rom.15.v.1.2, Coloss. 3.v.11.1.Corint.9.v.19.&seqq. 5.Digniores ita debent erga inuicem se gerere, vt inter se certent officio honoris, Rom.12.v.10.Phil.2.v.3. 6.Inferiores ita se gerat in morib. reuerentialibus & obsequialibus erga superiores,ne peccent in excessu vel defectu, h.e. ne sint in istiusmodi moribus vel nimii & prodigi,vel nimis parci &tenaces,1.Pet. 3.v.1.2.1.Tim.2.v.9 10.11.12. Caeterum mores isti reuerentiales &obsequiales sunt varii:vt puta mentio de superiore honorifica,commendatio virtutis excellentioris,primus accubitus siue locus superior & dignior, decessio è via,&similia,de quibus passim in Scriptura. 7. Superiores ita se debent gerere erga inferiores,vt honorem sibi oblatum benigne suscipiant,grauitati studeant, liberalitate erga inferiores exerceant,honores sibi non competentes recusent &c.Luc.7.verf.44.&seqq. Matt.7.v.29.Tit.2.v.15.1. Sam.9.v.19.25.26.Deut.17.v.12.20.Rom.12.v.16.Act.12.verf. 22. 8. Couersatio inter pares talis esse debet, qualem sibi par a paritribui vellet.Philip.2.v.3.Eph.5.v.[?].Rom.12.v.19, 1.Petr.2.v.17.Gal.5.v.13.14.
units.tr: XVIII. Conversation suited to each station is with persons who are superior, equal or inferior, and with those who are more worthy or less worthy, or equal; according to these rules. (1) We must firmly be persuaded that among men one is more excellent than another: Phil. 2 v. 3, 29; Acts 5 v. 34; 2 Chron. 10; Rom. 12 v. 10. For although we are all created in the image of God, that image nevertheless has certain degrees, whether we consider the endowments of nature: 1 Cor. 12 v. 4, 5, 6; or civil dignity: Rom. 13 v. 1; or finally learning and the like, which we have acquired for ourselves by our own study beyond others: 1 Thess. 5 vers. 12, 13; Prov. 28 v. 6. (2) Those who are more worthy than others should so conduct themselves that they cast no stain upon their dignity, lest they give others occasion to despise them: Eph. 4 v. 1, 2, 3. Among several excellent persons, the one in whom several grounds of dignity concur is held more worthy and more honourable: Eccl. 9 v. 17, 18, 19. (3) The more worthy ought to accommodate themselves to the less worthy, and the latter to revere the former: Rom. 15 v. 1, 2; Col. 3 v. 11; 1 Cor. 9 v. 19 and following. (4) The more worthy ought to conduct themselves towards one another so as to vie in the duty of honour: Rom. 12 v. 10; Phil. 2 v. 3. (5) Inferiors should so conduct themselves in reverential and obsequious manners towards their superiors that they do not sin by excess or by defect; that is, that they be neither too lavish nor too sparing and grudging in such manners: 1 Pet. 3 v. 1, 2; 1 Tim. 2 v. 9, 10, 11, 12. Moreover, these reverential and obsequious manners are various, such as speaking of a superior with honour, commending an excellent virtue, the first place at table or a higher and more honourable seat, giving way on the road, and the like, of which there is frequent mention in Scripture. (6) Superiors ought to conduct themselves towards inferiors so as to receive kindly the honour offered to them, to strive for gravity, to exercise liberality towards inferiors, and to refuse honours not due to them: Luke 7 vers. 44 and following; Matt. 7 v. 29; Titus 2 v. 15; 1 Sam. 9 v. 19, 25, 26; Deut. 17 v. 12, 20; Rom. 12 v. 16; Acts 12 vers. 22. (7) Conversation between equals ought to be such as an equal would wish to be shown to himself by an equal: Phil. 2 v. 3; Eph. 5 v. [?]; Rom. 12 v. 19; 1 Pet. 2 v. 17; Gal. 5 v. 13, 14.

units.la: XIX. Conversatio conviuialis guber-natur his regulis. 1.Conviuator, sive procurator conviuij, invitet conviuas humaniter, prudenter & temperatiue Esth.5.vers.3.4.5.8. Luc.14. vers.17.23. procuret omnia necessaria 2.Reg.6 v.22. locum amoenum & satis capacem eligat. Luc.14 v.8. 1.Sam.9.v.21. excipiat conviuas decore. Luc.12.v.36. Gen.6.43.v.24. illos recte collocet. Luc.14. bene tractet eosdem Eccles.32.vers.2.3. denique tempestiueipsos dimittat. 2.Conviua invitatus ne recusēt invitatione fine causa probabili. Luc.14. v.18. tempestiue se sistat ibid. rite se paret animo & corpore. 1.Corinth.10. vers.31. fumat cibum & potum cum hilaritate, sobrietate & prudentia. Roman.13.vers.vltim. 1.Thess.5.vers.6.7.8. Prov.23. vers.19.& seqq. Eccles.37.vers.32.& seqq. denique pie, tempestiue & decore discedat. Eccles.32.vers.14. Deut.8.v.10.11.
units.tr: XIX. Conversation at a banquet is governed by these rules. (1) The host, or steward of the banquet, should invite the guests courteously, prudently and moderately: Esth. 5 vers. 3, 4, 5, 8; Luke 14 vers. 17, 23. He should provide all things necessary: 2 Kings 6 v. 22. He should choose a pleasant place, large enough: Luke 14 v. 8; 1 Sam. 9 v. 21. He should receive the guests becomingly: Luke 12 v. 36; Gen. 43 v. 24. He should seat them properly: Luke 14. He should treat them well: Eccl. 32 vers. 2, 3. Finally, he should dismiss them at the right time: 2 Kings... (2) An invited guest should not refuse the invitation without a probable cause: Luke 14 v. 18. He should present himself at the proper time, ibid. He should prepare himself rightly in mind and body: 1 Cor. 10 vers. 31. He should take food and drink with cheerfulness, sobriety and prudence: Rom. 13 vers. last; 1 Thess. 5 vers. 6, 7, 8; Prov. 23 vers. 19 and following; Eccl. 37 vers. 32 and following. Finally, he should take his leave piously, at the right time and becomingly: Eccl. 32 vers. 14; Deut. 8 v. 10, 11.

units.la: XLIV. POLEMICA SACRA.
units.tr: XLIV. SACRED POLEMICS.

units.la: I. Polemica sacra est institutio de ratione belligerandi, e sacris literis collecta. Est aut pars Politicæ. Hæc enim diuiditur in εἰρηνικὴν, & πο-λεμικὴν. Illam supra ex sacris literis delineauimus: hanc nunc delineaturi in memoriam nobis revocamus quod insignis quidam belli dux aliquando dixit magna cum voluptate mea, artem militarem in Mose & Iosua ita esse traditam, vt ex hoc fonte manare oporteat rivulos, qui non sint turbidi in re militari.
units.tr: I. Sacred polemics is the teaching about the conduct of war, gathered from the sacred letters. It is a part of Politics, for Politics is divided into eirenikē [εἰρηνική] and polemikē [πολεμική]. We have already set out the former from the sacred letters; now, in order to set out the latter, we recall to mind what a certain famous commander once said, to my great delight: that the military art was so handed down in Moses and Joshua that streams should flow from this source which are not muddied in matters of war.

units.la: III. Tres sunt eius partes: prima debelli susceptione; secunda, de eius gestione; tertia, de eiusdem euentu.
units.tr: III. It has three parts: first, the undertaking of war; second, its conduct; third, its outcome.

units.la: IV. De belli susceptione sunt hæ regulæ. Cauendum est magistratui, ne quod bellum temere moveat. Qua in re peccauit Achab 1.Reg.22.& Amasias 2.Reg. 14.item Iosias 2.Reg.23. Magistratus ne suscipiat bellū[?], nulli nisi persuasus sit esse legitimum. Legitimum autem bellum est, quod habet mandatum Dei generale vel speciale. Mandatum generale est illud Leuit. 19. v. 18. Diliges proximum tuum, sicut teipsum. Quam dilectionem suam erga subditos etiam tum exercet magistratus, cum eos defendit contra vim iniustam. Quippe gladium non temere gestat. Rom. 13. v. 4. Mandatum speciale de bello suscipiendo est arcanum, vel expressum. Mandatum arcanum est impulsus ille, quo Deus olim incitavit atque excitavit animum quorundam ad vindicandum a vicinis hostibus populum suum. Ita Deus excitavit Othnielem Iudic. 3. v. 10 & Ehudem ibi. v. 15. & Simsonem ibid. c. 13. & seqq. Expressum Dei mandatum datum est vel immediate Iof. 6. 8. 10. 11, vel mediate, idque vel per Vrim & Thummim. Iudic. 1. v. 1. 2.
units.tr: IV. These are the rules concerning the undertaking of war. The magistrate must take care not to start any war rashly. Ahab sinned in this matter (1 Kings 22), and so did Amaziah (2 Kings 14), likewise Josiah (2 Kings 23). The magistrate should not undertake a war unless he is persuaded that it is lawful. A war is lawful, however, when it has a general or a special command of God. The general command is that of Leviticus 19:18: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself." The magistrate exercises this love towards his subjects even when he defends them against unjust violence; for he does not bear the sword in vain (Romans 13:4). A special command to undertake war is either hidden or expressed. The hidden command is that impulse by which God formerly stirred and roused the minds of certain men to avenge his people against neighbouring enemies. So God raised up Othniel (Judges 3:10), and Ehud (ibid. v. 15), and Samson (ibid. ch. 13 and following). God's expressed command was given either immediately (Joshua 6:8, 10, 11), or mediately, and this either through the Urim and Thummim (Judges 1:1, 2),

units.la: 1. Sam. 30. v. 7. 8. 2. Sam. 5. v. 19. vel per ministerium alicuius creaturae, puta angeli Iudic. 6. vel prophetae Iudic. 4. 1. Sam. 15. v. 3. vel integri alicuius coetus, ut quando populus, vel ultro sibi ducem eligit Iudic. 11. vel opem principis sui implorat 1. Sam. 11. vel principi operam suam offerenti assentitur. 1. Maccab. 2. 3. 4. & 13. Porro bellum nititur mandato Dei vel expresso, quo pertinent exempla iam commemorata: vel tacito, ut quando bellum est iustum & necessarium, sive sit defensiuum, sive offensiuum. Pertinet huc regula: Bellum sit iustum causa, fine, & modo. Vide Gen. 14. v. 4. c. 16. v. 20. & 34. Deut 2. v. 5. 9. 25. c. 20. v. 1. 10. Iof. 5. v. 13. 1. Sam. 15. v. 28. 2. Chron. 20. v. 15. Iudic. 15. v. 3. 2. Reg. 14. v. 25.
units.tr: (1 Samuel 30:7, 8; 2 Samuel 5:19), or through the ministry of some creature, for instance an angel (Judges 6), or a prophet (Judges 4; 1 Samuel 15:3), or of some whole assembly, as when the people either chose a leader for themselves of their own accord (Judges 11), or implored the help of their prince (1 Samuel 11), or assented to a prince offering his services (1 Maccabees 2, 3, 4 and 13). Moreover, a war rests on God's command either expressed, to which belong the examples already mentioned, or tacit, as when the war is just and necessary, whether it is defensive or offensive. To this belongs the rule: "Let a war be just in cause, aim and manner." See Genesis 14:4; 16:20; 34; Deuteronomy 2:5, 9, 25; 20:1, 10; Joshua 5:13; 1 Samuel 15:28; 2 Chronicles 20:15; Judges 15:3; 2 Kings 14:25.

units.la: 2. Sam. 5. v. 25. 2. Chron. 13. v. 4. iii. Magistratus antequam bellum, etiam legitimum, suscipiat, aut certe antequam proelium ineat, pacificationem cum hoste tentet, eumque a bello inferendo aut continuando dehortetur. Iudic. 11. 2. Chron. 13. 2. Reg. 14. iv. Magistratus, antequam bellum suscipiat, consultet. Prou. 20. v. 18. c. 24. v. 6. Luc. 14. v. 31. 32. Consultationis istius variae sunt partes: ut puta de sumtibus & commeatu, de opportunitate loci & temporis, de milite idoneo & exercitato, & similibus. Plura vide in Iurisprudentia sacra.
units.tr: (2 Samuel 5:25; 2 Chronicles 13:4.) iii. Before the magistrate undertakes a war, even a lawful one, or at least before he joins battle, he should attempt a peace with the enemy and dissuade him from waging or continuing the war (Judges 11; 2 Chronicles 13; 2 Kings 14). iv. Before undertaking a war the magistrate should take counsel (Proverbs 20:18; 24:6; Luke 14:31, 32). The parts of this deliberation are various: for instance, concerning expenses and supplies, the suitability of place and time, a fit and trained soldiery, and similar matters. See more in Sacred Jurisprudence.

units.la: V. De gestione belli sunt variæ regulæ, è quibus aliæ pertinent ad belli ducem, aliæ ad reliquum exercitum. Dux belli obseruet has regulas.
units.tr: V. There are various rules concerning the conduct of war, some of which pertain to the commander of the war, others to the rest of the army. The commander of war should observe these rules.

units.la: 1. Ne dux belli confidat armis, sed auxilio & protectione Dei Psal.33.v.16.17. & 147.v.10. Huius fiduciæ exemplum illustre proponitur in Dauide. 1.Sam.17.v.45. & c.22.v.33. & seqq. Ps.18.v.30. ite[?] in Ionathane[?]1. Sam.14.v.6. & in Iudâ Maccabæo 2.Maccab.8.v.23.
units.tr: 1. The commander of war should not trust in arms, but in the help and protection of God (Psalm 33:16, 17; 147:10). A famous example of this trust is set before us in David (1 Samuel 17:45; 22:33 and following; Psalm 18:30). Likewise in Jonathan (1 Samuel 14:6), and in Judas Maccabeus (2 Maccabees 8:23).

units.la: II. Dux belli præliũ initurus, auxilium Dei imploret. Hoc fecisse legitur pius ille rex Asa.2.Chron.14. & Iosaphatus.2.Chron.20. & Iudas Maccabæus.2.Maccab.8.
units.tr: II. A commander about to join battle should implore the help of God. This is read of the godly king Asa (2 Chronicles 14), and of Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20), and of Judas Maccabeus (2 Maccabees 8).

units.la: III. Etsi precibus ad Deum pro auxilio conceptis, in bona causâ, bene sperandum est, euentus tamen prælij[?] bonæ & sanctæ voluntati Dei est committendus, exemplo Ioabi 2.Sam.10.
units.tr: III. Although, in a good cause, one should hope well, with prayers offered to God for help, the outcome of the battle nevertheless must be committed to the good and holy will of God, as in the example of Joab (2 Samuel 10).

units.la: IV. Dux belli, antequâm præliũ ineat, milites suos recenseat. 1.Sam.15. 1.Reg.20. 2.Reg.3.
units.tr: IV. A commander, before joining battle, should review his soldiers (1 Samuel 15; 1 Kings 20; 2 Kings 3).

units.la: V. Dux belli antequam præliũ ineat, curet milites per ministrum verbi diuini moneri de officio. Id quod fecisse legitur Iudas Maccabæus. 2.Maccab.8. Quin & ipse milites suos ad fortiter dimicandum exhortari debet. Id quod fecisse legitur Hiskias 2.Chron.32. & Iosaphatus 2. Chron.20. ite Iudas Maccabæus 2.Maccab.8.
units.tr: V. A commander, before joining battle, should see to it that the soldiers are admonished of their duty by a minister of the divine Word. This is read to have been done by Judas Maccabeus (2 Maccabees 8). Indeed he himself ought also to exhort his soldiers to fight bravely. This is read to have been done by Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 32), and Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20), likewise Judas Maccabeus (2 Maccabees 8).

units.la: VI. Dux militibus strenuè pugnaturis promittat præmia: exemplo Calebi Iudic.1. Saulis 1.Sam.17. Dauidis 2.Sam.5. 1.Chron.11. vii.
units.tr: VI. A commander should promise rewards to soldiers who are going to fight vigorously: the example of Caleb (Judges 1), of Saul (1 Samuel 17), of David (2 Samuel 5; 1 Chronicles 11). vii.

units.la: VII. Dux belli hostem aggrediatur, si fieri potest, ex improuiso. Id q; fecit Abraham.Gen.14. & Saul 1.Sam.11. & Dauid 1.Sam.30. viii.
units.tr: VII. If possible, a commander should attack the enemy by surprise. Abraham did this (Genesis 14), and Saul (1 Samuel 11), and David (1 Samuel 30). viii.

units.la: VIII. Dux belli hostem adoriatur, si id commodè fieri potest, ex partibus diuersis: exemplo Abrahami Gen. 14. Iofuæ Iof.8. Saulis 1.Sam.11. ix.
units.tr: VIII. A commander should attack the enemy, if this can conveniently be done, from different sides: the example of Abraham (Genesis 14), of Joshua (Joshua 8), of Saul (1 Samuel 11). ix.

units.la: IX. Dux belli vtatur stratagematis, ad hostem fallendum Iof.8. & 10.v.24. Iudic.3.v.28. c.7. & 20. x.
units.tr: IX. A commander should use stratagems to deceive the enemy (Joshua 8 and 10:24; Judges 3:28; 7 and 20). x.

units.la: X. Dux belli adhibeat celeritatem in hoste persequendo: exèplo Saulis 1.Sam.11. & Dauidis 1.Sam.30. xi.
units.tr: X. A commander should use speed in pursuing the enemy: the example of Saul (1 Samuel 11) and of David (1 Samuel 30). xi.

units.la: XI. Dux belli sibi caueat à securitate: quippe quæ cum periculo aut damno semper est coniuncta. Iudic.8.1.Sam.30. xii.
units.tr: XI. A commander should guard himself against complacency, since this is always joined with danger or loss (Judges 8; 1 Samuel 30). xii.

units.la: XII. Dux belli vrbem aliquam oppugnaturus, priùs pacè eì offerat. Deut.20.v.10. xiii. Dux belli vrbem aliquam obsidens, non corrumpat arbores fructiferas. Deut.20.v.19. v.19. xiv. Castra feruětur munda, corporaliter & spiritualiter. Deut.23.v.12.14. & constent eleganti ordine. Exod. 14.Num.1.& 2. In reliquo exercitu sunt legati in bello & exploratores Iof.1.v.14.1.Sam.14.v.7. capitanei. 1.Sam.14. v. 33.c.18.v.7.c.20.v.28.c.12.v.28.29.c.23.v.8. milites. Iof.14.v. 13.c.17.v.17.18.Iud.10.v.18.Deut.20.v.5.c.24.v.5.2.Sam.5.v. 8.c.2.v.5.c.3.v.38.c.1.v.13.18.c.4.c.11.v.11.c.19.v.14.c.20.v.4.5. Luc.3.v.14. proditores. 2.Sam.4.v.11.c.15.v.32.
units.tr: XII. A commander who is about to assault some city should first offer it peace (Deuteronomy 20:10). xiii. A commander besieging some city should not destroy its fruit trees (Deuteronomy 20:19, 19). xiv. The camp should be kept clean, bodily and spiritually (Deuteronomy 23:12, 14), and should be arranged in a fitting order (Exodus 14; Numbers 1 and 2). In the rest of the army there are: (1) envoys in war and scouts (Joshua 1:14; 1 Samuel 14:7); (2) captains (1 Samuel 14:33; 18:7; 20:28; 12:28, 29; 23:8); (3) soldiers (Joshua 14:13; 17:17, 18; Judges 10:18; Deuteronomy 20:5; 24:5; 2 Samuel 5:8; 2:5; 3:38; 1:13, 18; 4; 11:11; 19:14; 20:4, 5; Luke 3:14); (4) traitors (2 Samuel 4:11; 15:32).

units.la: VI. Euentus belli aut est secundus, aut ad- uersus. Ille victoria, hic clades nominatur.
units.tr: VI. The outcome of war is either favourable or adverse. The favourable outcome is called victory; the adverse, defeat.

units.la: De victoriâ sunt hæ regulæ. 1. Duxagat Deo gratias pro victoriâ. Exod.15. Iudith.5. 11. Nō est sæuiendum in victos. Deut.20. verf.14. si nempe non sit specialis & virgens aliqua causa, qualis est Deut.20.v.17.& 1.Sam.15. 111. Præda hosti detracta rectè est distribuenda; ita nempe vt pars cedat bellatoribus, pars vniuersitati, & ex vtraque illa parte aliquid offeratur Deo. Genef.14.Num.31. Ios.22. 1.Sam 30.2. Maccab.8. iv. Princeps parta victoriâ militibus, qui præ caeteris fortiter pugnarunt, det præmia: Iudic.1. v. Victoriam oportet persequi. Iudic.7.v.25.cap.8.verf.11.c.28.1.Sam. 14.verf.7.Ios.10.v.19.2.Sam.8.verf.6. vi. Insignium victoriarum à Deo nobis concessarum monumenta sunt relinquenda posteris, ad Dei gloriam. Ios.3.& 4.Iud.5.verf.1.2. Sam.22. vii. Bello feliciter confecto, si nō sit metuendum aliud periculum, milites non sinit frustrà in armis retinendi, ne otiosi vel seditionem moueant, vel latrocinia exerceant. Ios.22.v.4. viii. Etsi ius victoriæ est magnum, non tamen in eo modus est excedendus: quia victoria insolens & crudelis Deo displicet, & valde quoque est periculosa. Sic etsi hostem victum victor non tantum bonis exuere, sed etiam tota regione multare potest, & in alienam ditionem transferre, imò & vita priuare Iud.11.v.21.2.Sam. 9.v.11.2.Reg.14.verf.13.14. non tamen hoc semper est faciendum, aut etiam sine discrimine Deut.20.verf.17. De clade sunt hæ regulæ.1. Qui cladem accepit, statum quidem rerum suarum deplorare, veruntamen in Domino Deo suo sese confirmare, deque vindictâ in hostem exercendâ cogitare & consultare debet. Jos.7.Judic.20.1.Sam.30. ii.In magnis cladibus opus est extraordinariis precibus, ieiuniis, & animi conversione ad Deum. Jud.20.v.23.
units.tr: On victory these are the rules. (1) The commander should give thanks to God for victory. Exod.15. Iudith.5. (2) One should not rage against the conquered, Deut.20. verf.14. unless there is some special and compelling cause, such as Deut.20.v.17.& 1.Sam.15. (3) Plunder taken from the enemy is rightly to be divided: part goes to the fighters, part to the whole community, and some of each portion is offered to God. Genef.14.Num.31. Ios.22. 1.Sam 30.2. Maccab.8. (4) The prince, once victory is won, should give rewards to the soldiers who fought most bravely beyond the rest. Iudic.1. (5) Victory must be pursued. Iudic.7.v.25.cap.8.verf.11.c.28.1.Sam. 14.verf.7.Ios.10.v.19.2.Sam.8.verf.6. (6) Monuments of the notable victories granted to us by God are to be left to posterity, for the glory of God. Ios.3.& 4.Iud.5.verf.1.2. Sam.22. (7) When the war has been successfully concluded, and no other danger is to be feared, soldiers are not to be kept under arms in vain, lest they, being idle, either stir up sedition or take to plundering. Ios.22.v.4. (8) Although the right of victory is great, it must not be pushed beyond measure, because an insolent and cruel victory displeases God and is also very dangerous. Thus, although a victor may not only strip the defeated enemy of his goods but also punish his whole region, transfer it under another's rule, and even deprive him of life, Iud.11.v.21.2.Sam. 9.v.11.2.Reg.14.verf.13.14. this is not always to be done, nor done even without discrimination. Deut.20.verf.17. On defeat these are the rules. (1) He who has suffered defeat should indeed lament the state of his affairs, but he ought to strengthen himself in the Lord his God, and think and take counsel about exacting vengeance on the enemy. Jos.7.Judic.20.1.Sam.30. (2) In great defeats there is need of extraordinary prayers, fasting, and conversion of heart to God. Jud.20.v.23.

units.la: iii.Qui victi sunt semel atque iterum in bonâ causâ, tandem triumphatores evadent, si animum non despondeant. Judic. 20.v.33.
units.tr: (3) Those who have been defeated once or twice in a good cause will at last become triumphant, provided they do not lose heart. Judic. 20.v.33.

units.la: iv. In consternatione publicâ princeps ostendat animum imperterritum. 1.Sam.19.v.10.
units.tr: (4) In a public consternation the prince should show an undaunted spirit. 1.Sam.19.v.10.

units.la: XLV. PATHOLOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: XLV. SACRED PATHOLOGY.

units.la: I. PAthologia sacra est doctrina de corrigendis & regendis affectibus, ex præscripto [?] sacrarum literarum. Est autem farrago quaedam ex physicis, ethicis, & theologicis monitis constans.
units.tr: I. Sacred pathology is the doctrine of correcting and governing the affections, according to the prescription of the sacred letters. It is, moreover, a kind of medley made up of physical, ethical and theological admonitions.

units.la: II. Affectus est appetitus, motu cordis & spirituum excitatus ab obiecto externo. Proprie itaque competit animali tantum, homini videlicet & bestiis. Deo quidem & angelis, itemque animæ separatæ, etiam tribuuntur affectus, sed eminenti quadam ratione. Unde affectus, qui sunt in Deo, & angelis bonis, debent esse norma nostrorum affectuum.
units.tr: II. An affection is an appetite, aroused by the motion of the heart and spirits from an external object. Properly, then, it belongs only to animals, namely man and the beasts. Affections are also attributed to God, to angels and to separated souls, but in an eminent manner. Hence the affections that are in God and in good angels ought to be the rule of our affections.

units.la: III. In affectu spectantur hæc tria: generatio, divisio, & regimen.
units.tr: III. Three things are considered in an affection: its generation, its division, and its regulation.

units.la: IV. Generatio affectuum ita habet. Primò se nobis offert obiectum. Hoc deinde movet sentiendi facultatem, quæ excitata ab obiecto, illud cognoscit. Cognitio ista tertiò vim imaginandi attingit, quæ obiectum illud judicat ut bonum vel malum. Quartò obiectum judicatum excitat appetitum in corde pro adeptione & sugâ. Tum spiritus alterantur, atque alterati certo modo corpus afficiunt. Exemplum est in Eva Gen.3. & in filiis Dei, qui videntes filias hominum esse bonâ formâ eligebant eas in[?] uxores Gen.6.
units.tr: IV. The generation of affections proceeds as follows. First, an object presents itself to us. Second, this object stirs the faculty of sense, which, aroused by the object, perceives it. Third, this perception reaches the power of imagination, which judges the object to be good or evil. Fourth, the judged object stirs up appetite in the heart, either to pursue it or to shun it. Then the spirits are altered, and, being altered, affect the body in a certain way. An example is Eve in Gen.3., and the sons of God who, seeing that the daughters of men were fair, chose them as wives, Gen.6.

units.la: V. Diuisio affectuum est multiplex. Sumuntur autem differentiae affectuum à forma siue qualitate, quantitate, vel motu. A forma affectus est simplex vel mixtus, bonus vel malus. Affectus simplex est, qui unam retinet naturam, vt spes, tristitia &c.; mixtus, qui variam induit naturam, vt ira, odium &c. Aliter etiam affectus simplex dicitur, qui non est compositus, vt amor; & mixtus, qui est ex aliis affectib. compositus, vt zelus ex amore, odio, ira. Affectus bonus est talis vel physicè tantùm, vt gaudium quâ tale; vel physicè & ethicè simul, vt gaudium ortum ex cognitione Dei. Similiter affectus malus est talis vel physicè tantùm, vt tristitia quâ talis; vel physicè & ethicè simul, vt tristitia orta ex alterius felicitate. Priori modo affectus sunt communes homini & bestiæ: posteriori sunt hominis proprii. A quantitate affectus sunt moderati vel immoderati, subditi vel durabiles, lenes vel vehementes.
units.tr: V. The division of affections is manifold. Differences among affections are drawn from their form or quality, their quantity, or their motion. By form, an affection is either simple or mixed, good or bad. A simple affection is one that keeps a single nature, such as hope, sadness and so on; a mixed one takes on a varied nature, such as anger, hatred and so on. In another sense an affection is called simple if it is not compounded, like love, and mixed if it is compounded of other affections, like zeal, which is made up of love, hatred and anger. A good affection is such either physically alone, like joy as such, or physically and ethically at once, like joy arising from the knowledge of God. Similarly a bad affection is such either physically alone, like sadness as such, or physically and ethically at once, like sadness arising from another's happiness. In the former sense affections are common to man and beast; in the latter they are proper to man. By quantity, affections are moderate or immoderate, sudden or lasting, gentle or vehement.

units.la: Affectus moderatus est, qui non recedit à rectâ ratione, idcoque est secundùm naturam, & illam conseruat: immoderatus est, qui à rectâ ratione, siue à medio, recedit, secundùm plus & minus, ita vt rationem perturbet, corpusque alteret vt à naturali temperie illud deiiciat: subitus est qui citò fit & desit, durabilis contrà: lenis est, qui æquabiliter decurrit, vehemens contrà. Ex motu diuiduntur affectus bifariam. Nam considerantur ratione principii, medii, & finis: vel ratione centri. A principio ad finem sunt metus & audacia, amor & odium: in fine lætitia & tristitia, voluptas & dolor: in medio desiderium & fuga, spes & desperatio, itemque ira. Ex his affectibus quidam sunt homini communes cum bestiis, vt amor, tristitia &c. quidam proprii, vt spes: & rursus quidam sunt in facultate concupiscentiæ, vt amor, odium, desiderium, fuga, delectatio, tristitia; alii in facultate irascente, vt spes, desperatio, ira, timor, audacia. Ratione centri affectus habent & excitant motum vel à centro ad circumferentiam, vt gaudium &c. vel à circumferenti ad centrum, vt tristitia &c. vel vtroque modo, vt spes.
units.tr: A moderate affection is one that does not depart from right reason, and so it is according to nature and preserves it. An immoderate affection is one that departs from right reason, or from the mean, by excess or defect, so that it disturbs reason and alters the body, throwing it down from its natural temperament. A sudden affection is one that arises quickly and quickly passes; a lasting one is the opposite. A gentle affection flows along evenly; a vehement one the opposite. Affections are divided by motion in two ways. For they are considered either by reason of beginning, middle and end, or by reason of the centre. From beginning to end are fear and boldness, love and hatred; at the end are joy and sadness, pleasure and pain; in the middle are desire and aversion, hope and despair, and likewise anger. Of these affections some are common to man and beast, such as love, sadness and so on; some are proper to man, such as hope. Again, some are in the concupiscible faculty, such as love, hatred, desire, aversion, delight and sadness; others are in the irascible faculty, such as hope, despair, anger, fear and boldness. By reason of the centre, affections either have and produce a motion from the centre to the circumference, as joy does, or from the circumference to the centre, as sadness does, or in both ways, as hope does.

units.la: V. Regimen affectuum continetur his regulis. 1. Deus, Christus, & boni angeli sint specula bonorum affectuum. Et primò quidem Deus non tantùm debet esse finis & obiectum affectuum, quatenus ad ipsius gloriam debet affectus nostri tendere, vel circa ipsum occupati (e. g. Deum debemus amare, & quidquid amamus extra ipsum, propter ipsum debet nobis esse amabile: ipsum non debemus odisse, sed quidquid ipsi aduersatur &c.) sed etiam debet esse regula & norma affectuum. Etsi enim in Deo non sunt affectus animi, qui sunt appetitus sensus: sunt tamen in ipso actus voluntatis affectibus similes. Amat enim Deus bonos, odit malos, gaudet benefactis &c. Hanc Dei naturam imitemur, & vt hoc possimus, imploremus ipsius gratiam, vt nobis largiatur spiritum bonum intelligentiæ, prudentiæ, fortitudinis &c. Esa. 11. verf.1. Deinde Christus in manu suâ habebat affectus, eosq; contrahebat & laxabat suo nutu & arbitratu, ita vt illi nunquam rationis imperium detrectauerint & recusauerint, vel rationem victam ad se pertraxerint, vel illam deseruerint. Quoties itaque occurrit obiectum aliquod patheticum, intueamur Christum,& ipsum imitemur. Phil.2.v.5. Deniq; boni angeli etsi carent affectibus, qui pertinent ad appetitum sensus, habent tamen nihilominus affectus, qui pertinent ad appetitum rationis, id est, ad voluntatem, eosque conformes voluntati Dei. Oremus itaque Deum, ut nobis largiatur praesidium sanctorum angelorum, qui regant nostros affectus. 2. Affectus ex modo & obiecto fiunt boni vel mali moraliter. Ex modo: quia quando sunt {3}immodici atque rationi aduersantur, mali sunt & culpae imputantur; quando vero sunt temperati, sunt boni & secundum naturā. Oportet itaque affectus virtute regi, cohiberi, & sedari. Ex obiecto: quia usuenire solet, ut affectus suā naturā indifferens fiat bonus vel malus prout se habet {3}ipsius obiectum, quod ipsum occupat. Sic odisse bonos, malum est, odisse malos, bonū: amare turpia, malum est, amare bona, bonum: irasci bonis, malum est, irasci malis, bonum: odium personae seu inimicitiae, malum est, odium rei turpis seu odium abominationis, est bonum: dolor secundum Deum est bonus, secundum mundum, malus. 3. In regimine affectuum haec sit cura, ut imaginatio rem obiectam ita percipiat, uti recta ratio illam iudicat. Imaginationem itaque corrigat ratio. 4. Affectus variant pro ratione subiecti recipientis. Sic in filios Dei cadit timor filialis, in reprobos, seruilis: spes nostra est spiritualis, mundi, mundana. 5. Qui vult affectus suos recte temperare, accurate cognoscat suum temperamentum, & operam det, ut cordis atque sanguinis temperiem bonam procuret moderata diaeta. Affectus enim oriuntur excommotione spirituum vitalium in corde, quorum indoles sequitur temperamentum sanguinis. Huc etiam facit ieiunium.
units.tr: V. The regulation of affections is contained in the following rules. 1. God, Christ and the good angels should be the mirrors of good affections. And first, God ought to be not only the end and object of our affections, insofar as our affections ought to tend to his glory or be occupied with him (for example, we ought to love God, and whatever we love apart from him ought to be lovable on his account; we ought not to hate him, but whatever is opposed to him, and so on), but he ought also to be the rule and norm of our affections. For although there are no affections of the soul in God, since these are sensory appetites, nevertheless there are in him acts of will that are similar to affections. God loves the good, hates the wicked, rejoices in good deeds, and so on. Let us imitate this nature of God, and that we may be able to do so, let us implore his grace, that he would bestow on us the good spirit of understanding, prudence, fortitude and so on, Esa. 11, verf.1. Then, Christ held the affections in his hand, contracting and relaxing them at his nod and by his will, so that they never refused or rejected the command of reason, nor drew reason, once conquered, over to themselves, nor deserted it. Whenever, therefore, some passionate object occurs, let us look upon Christ and imitate him, Phil.2.v.5. Finally, the good angels, although they lack the affections that belong to sensory appetite, nevertheless have affections that belong to rational appetite, that is, to the will, and these conform to the will of God. Let us therefore pray God to grant us the protection of the holy angels, who may govern our affections. 2. Affections become morally good or evil from their manner and from their object. From manner: because when they are immoderate and oppose reason, they are evil and are imputed as sin; but when they are temperate, they are good and according to nature. It is necessary, therefore, that the affections be governed by virtue, restrained and calmed. From object: because it commonly happens that an affection, indifferent in its own nature, becomes good or evil according as the object that occupies it is. Thus to hate good men is evil, to hate evil men is good; to love base things is evil, to love good things is good; to be angry with good men is evil, to be angry with evil men is good; hatred of a person, or enmity, is evil, hatred of a base thing, or hatred of abomination, is good; grief according to God is good, grief according to the world is evil. 3. In the governing of the affections this should be the care: that the imagination should perceive the object as right reason judges it. Let reason, therefore, correct the imagination. 4. Affections vary according to the disposition of the receiving subject. Thus in the sons of God there falls filial fear, in the reprobate servile fear; our hope is spiritual, the hope of the world is worldly. 5. Whoever wishes to temper his affections rightly should know his own temperament accurately, and take care to procure a good temperature of heart and blood by moderate diet. For affections arise from the agitation of the vital spirits in the heart, whose quality follows the temperament of the blood. Fasting also contributes to this.

units.la: XLVI. LITHOLOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: XLVI. SACRED LITHOLOGY.

units.la: I. Lithologia sacra est doctrina de gemmis, quarum fit mentio in sacris literis. Pertinet autem partim ad physicam, partim ad ethicam & theologiam.
units.tr: I. Sacred lithology is the doctrine of the gems mentioned in the sacred writings. It belongs partly to natural philosophy and partly to ethics and theology.

units.la: II. Partes ipsius duae sunt: generalis, & specialis.
units.tr: II. It has two parts: the general and the special.

units.la: III. Pars generalis explicat de gemmis communia illa, quae hinc inde in sacris literis occurrunt. Sic v.g. Esa.54. verf.11. & 12. Deus promittit ecclesiae afflictae, se cum ornamento collocaturum lapides eius, & ipsam fundaturum sapphiris, & dispositurum pyropo specularia eius &c. Quibus verbis hoc significatur, fundamentum ecclesiæ fore firmum & politum instar sapphiri, & specularia ipsius repletum iri fulgore præsentiæ Dei. Sic Matth.13. v.45. doctrina euangelij confertur cum pulchris margaritis, idq; propter splendorem, ornatum, pretium, & virtutem. Huiusmodi multa sunt in Scripturis. Vide Concordantias Biblicas ad titulos gemmarum.
units.tr: III. The general part explains those common matters about gems which occur here and there in the sacred writings. For example, in Isa. 54:11–12 [Esa.54. verf.11. & 12.], God promises the afflicted Church that he will lay its stones in order, found it on sapphires, and set its windows with carbuncles, and so on. By these words it is signified that the foundation of the Church will be firm and polished like a sapphire, and that its windows will be filled with the brightness of God's presence. Likewise in Matt. 13:45, the doctrine of the gospel is compared to fine pearls, on account of their splendour, their beauty, their value and their power. There are many such things in the Scriptures. See the biblical concordances under the headings for gems.

units.la: IV. Pars specialis explicat ordinem gemmarum qui est Exod.28. & Apoc.21.
units.tr: IV. The special part explains the order of the gems, which is found in Exodus 28 and Revelation 21.

units.la: V. Ordo gemmarum Exod.28.conuenit cū nominibus duodecim filiorum Israel. Confer Exod.28.v.17.18.19.20.21.cum Gen.49. Significatio mystica hæc est, iuxta sententiam Hugonis Brugthoni. Sardius habuit insculptum nomen Rubenis: quia lapis ruberestari debebat de bellis abeo gerendis contra hostes, pro fortis & terræ suæ defensione. Topazius lapis Simeonis, palliditate sua transparente optime conuenit huic patriarchæ iracundo. Smaragdus tributus fuit Leui, qui doctrinâ sua splendere & lucere debebat
units.tr: V. The order of the gems in Exodus 28 corresponds to the names of the twelve sons of Israel. Compare Exod. 28:17–21 with Genesis 49. The mystical meaning is this, according to the opinion of Hugo Brugthonus. The sardius bore the name of Reuben, because the stone ought to be red, from the wars to be waged by him against enemies, for the defence of the strong and of his land. The topaz, the stone of Simeon, with its pale transparent colour, fits this quick-tempered patriarch very well. The emerald was assigned to Levi, who ought to shine and glow by his teaching.

units.la: Phœbus vt in folio claris lucente smaragdis.
units.tr: Phoebus, as in a leaf gleaming with bright emeralds.

units.la: Carbunculus gessit nomen Iudæ, ex quo Christus, sol iustitiæ, ortus est. Sapphirus fuit lapis Ischaris[?], qui fuit fortis. Sardonyx decoratus fuit nomine Zebulonis, qui habitauit ad mare. Hyacinthus, est lapis Danis, monumentum astutiæ. Chrysoprasus fuit lapis Naphthali, habitantis ad mare, cuius aspectus splendens est instar Chrysoprasi. Amethystus, lapis Gadis, fuit monumentum ipsius fortitudinis bellicæ, quam notat lapis purpureus. Chrysolithus, lapis Aferis, erat monumentum copiæ & fertilitatis terræ, quæ ipsius tribui cedere debebat. Beryllus, lapis Iosephi, fuit signum pietatis, qua Ioseph vicit reliquos, ita vt de ipso dici possit,
units.tr: The carbuncle bore the name of Judah, from whom Christ, the sun of righteousness, arose. The sapphire was the stone of Issachar, who was strong. The sardonyx was adorned with the name of Zebulun, who dwelt by the sea. The hyacinth is the stone of Dan, a monument of shrewdness. The chrysoprase was the stone of Naphtali, who dwelt by the sea, whose appearance is bright like a chrysoprase. The amethyst, the stone of Gad, was a monument of his warlike courage, which the purple stone signifies. The chrysolite, the stone of Asher, was a monument of the abundance and fertility of the land, which ought to fall to his tribe. The beryl, the stone of Joseph, was a sign of the piety by which Joseph surpassed the rest, so that it may be said of him:

units.la: Vincit vulgares, vincit beryllus arenas.
units.tr: He surpasses common ones; the beryl surpasses the sands.

units.la: Iaspis, lapis Beniaminis, fuit monumentum ingenij ad varia bella propendentis, quemadmodum iaspis est verficolor.
units.tr: The jasper, the stone of Benjamin, was a monument of a mind inclined to various battles, just as the jasper is variegated in colour.

units.la: VI. Ordo gemmarum Apoc.21. conuenit cum nominibus duodecim apostolorum, hoc modo. Primus apostolus collegit per ministerium verbi iaspides, hoc est, perpetuò virentes & florentes fide verâ Christianos: secundus cœruleos sapphiros, hoc est, fideles, qui cœlestibus donis ornati, vanitates huius seculi insuper habent: tertius chalcedonios splendentes, hoc est, zelosos & victoriosos confessores: quartus virides smaragdos, id est, florentes & laetos Christianos: quintus sardonyces puros, id est, castitatis studiosos: sextus sardios rubicundos, id est, Christianos sanguine Christi lotos: septimus chrysolithos, id est, constantes & veste iustitiae albicantes Dei filios: octauus beryllos, id est, virentes & lucentes fide ac pietate Christianos: nonus topaζios, hoc est, dominantes affectibus, carnemque suam crucifigentes: decimus chrysoprasos, id est, amatores coelestis thesauri: vndecimus hyacinthos purpureos, id est, Christianos purpurâ Christi vestè regiâ amictos: duodecimus amethystos, id est, temperantiae & castimoniae studiosos. Hinc patet, Ethicam hieroglyphicam ex his posse confici.
units.tr: VI. The order of the gems in Revelation 21 corresponds to the names of the twelve apostles, in this way. The first apostle gathered, through the ministry of the Word, jaspers, that is, Christians who are always green and flourishing in true faith; the second, blue sapphires, that is, faithful people who, adorned with heavenly gifts, despise the vanities of this age; the third, shining chalcedonies, that is, zealous and victorious confessors; the fourth, green emeralds, that is, flourishing and joyful Christians; the fifth, pure sardonyxes, that is, those devoted to chastity; the sixth, ruddy sards, that is, Christians washed in the blood of Christ; the seventh, chrysolites, that is, steadfast children of God who are clothed in white garments of righteousness; the eighth, beryls, that is, Christians green and bright in faith and piety; the ninth, topazes, that is, those who master their passions and crucify their flesh; the tenth, chrysoprases, that is, lovers of the heavenly treasure; the eleventh, purple hyacinths, that is, Christians clothed in the purple of Christ's royal robe; the twelfth, amethysts, that is, those devoted to temperance and chastity. From this it is clear that a hieroglyphic ethics can be built from these.

units.la: XLVII. BIOGRAPHIA SACRA.
units.tr: XLVII. SACRED BIOGRAPHY.

units.la: I. Biographia sacra est doctrina de vita, collecta ex sacris literis. Constat autem monitis physicis, ethicis, œconomicis, politicis & theologicis.
units.tr: I. Sacred biography is the doctrine of life, gathered from the Holy Scriptures. It consists of precepts that are physical, ethical, economic, political and theological.

units.la: II. Vita est actus viuentis, seu est vitalis actionis principium. Est, inquam, actus primus & secundus, quo res est actuosa in se & extra se.
units.tr: II. Life is the act of a living thing, or the principle of vital action. I say it is both first and second act, by which a thing is active within itself and outside itself.

units.la: III. Vita multis modis consideratur. Et primò quidem vita diuiditur vt anima, ita vt sit φυλικὴ, vegetatiua, in plantis; αἰσθητικὴ[?], sensitiua, in animalibus; νοερὰ[?], intellectiua, in Deo, angelis, & hominibus. Prima est vita vegetationis, secunda sensionis, tertia intelligentiæ. Vide Gen.1.v.11.19.20.21.22.27.28.cap.2.verf.7.Ier.44.v.26.Matth. 23.verf.30. Deinde vita est infinita, vel finita. Illa est solius Dei,Deut.31.verf.40. vel finita, quæ est creaturarum viuentium. Est, inquam, finita vel tempore & subiecto simul, vt est hæc vita:vel subiecto tantum, non vero tempore, vt est vita æterna. Gen.3.v.19.Iohan.3.v.16. Si malis, dic vitam increatam & creatam, independentem & dependentem. Tertio vita est prima, vel secunda. Prima est naturalis:secunda,spiritualis.Heb.2.v.4. Vel,plenius,vita est naturalis, ex consortio animæ & corporis, Act.17.v.25. vel carnalis,cum membra seruiunt peccato,Rom.6.v.17.vel spiritualis, cum spiritus dominatur carni,Eph.5.v.14.velæterna, & hæc est vel Dei, vel angeli, vel hominis:& rursus vita æterna hominis aliquando sumitur physicè, & sic quoque in damnatis manet perpetuo, Esa.66.v.44. alias moraliter, pro beato statu, pleno gloriæ & gaudij ineffabilis, Hab.2. v.4.Apoc.21. & 22.Ita quoque est mors naturalis, vt Genef.49. cui opponitur violenta Luc.23.v.42. mors animæ, cum vitiis nos mancipamus,Luc.15.v.vlt. Matth.7.v.1. mors carnis, cum vitiis morimur, Coloss.3. verf.5. mors æterna,cum homo separatur à communione cum Deo,in æternum.Apoc. 21.verf.8. mors crucis & calamitatum, cum βίῳ & est ἀΐδιος [?], id est, vita vitæ expers,propter miseriam multiplicem.Rom. 8.verf.36.1.Cor.5.verf.10. Pertinet quoque huc vsitata illa mortis distinctio, quòd sit prima, vel secunda, siue,est corporalis,vel spiritualis. Mors prima est separatio animæ à corpore.Matth.10.verf.21. Mors secunda est separatio animæ à Deo, seu vitæ æternæ amissio:eaque est vel inchoata in hac vitâ, vel consummata post hanc vitam. Genef.2.verf.17. Apoc.2.verf.11.cap.20.verf.6.14.cap.21.verf.8. Quarto vita est natura, quam viuimus vt homines, siue vt ciues mundi. Gen.2.verf.7.vel gratia,quam viuimus vt homines credentes, siue vt ciues ecclesiæ. Rom.8.verf.1. Gal.2.verf.20. vel gloria, quam viuemus aliquando vt homines translati in patriam,siue vt ciues cœli, Iohan.10.verf.28. Quinto vita est animaanimalis, vel spiritualis. Illa fouetur cibo & potu : hæc non item.Matth.22.verf.30.1.Cor.15.verf.43.44. Sextò vita est contemplatiua, actiua, vel factiua. Vita contemplatiua posita est in speculatione, eaque vel optimâ, vel pessimâ.
units.tr: III. Life is considered in many ways. First, life is divided, as the soul is, so that it is φυλικὴ [phylikē], vegetative, in plants; αἰσθητικὴ [aisthētikē], sensitive, in animals; and νοερὰ [noera], intellectual, in God, the angels and men. The first is the life of growth, the second of sensation, the third of understanding. See Gen. 1.11, 19, 20, 21, 22, 27, 28; Gen. 2.7; Jer. 44.26; Matt. 23.30. Next, life is either infinite or finite. The infinite life belongs to God alone (Deut. 31.40); the finite life is that of living creatures. I say it is finite either in time and in subject together, as this life is, or in subject only and not in time, as eternal life is (Gen. 3.19; John 3.16). If you prefer, call it uncreated and created, independent and dependent. Third, life is either first or second. The first is natural; the second is spiritual (Heb. 2.4). Or, more fully, life is natural, arising from the union of soul and body (Acts 17.25); or carnal, when the members serve sin (Rom. 6.17); or spiritual, when the spirit rules the flesh (Eph. 5.14); or eternal, and this is the eternal life of God, of an angel, or of a man. Again, the eternal life of man is sometimes taken physically, and in this sense it remains forever in the damned (Isa. 66.24); at other times morally, for the blessed state, full of glory and of unspeakable joy (Hab. 2.4; Rev. 21 and 22). So too there is natural death, as in Gen. 49, to which violent death is opposed (Luke 23.42). There is the death of the soul, when we surrender ourselves to vices (Luke 15, last verse; Matt. 7.1). There is the death of the flesh, when we die to vices (Col. 3.5). There is eternal death, when a man is separated from communion with God forever (Rev. 21.8). There is the death of the cross and of calamities, when life is ἀΐδιος [aidios], that is, life bereft of life, because of its manifold misery (Rom. 8.36; 1 Cor. 5.10). To this belongs also the common distinction of death into first and second, or bodily and spiritual. The first death is the separation of the soul from the body (Matt. 10.21). The second death is the separation of the soul from God, or the loss of eternal life; and this is either begun in this life or completed after it (Gen. 2.17; Rev. 2.11; 20.6, 14; 21.8). Fourth, life is nature, which we live as men, or as citizens of the world (Gen. 2.7); or grace, which we live as believing men, or as citizens of the Church (Rom. 8.1; Gal. 2.20); or glory, which we shall sometimes live as men translated into the fatherland, or as citizens of heaven (John 10.28). Fifth, life is animal or spiritual life. The former is nourished by food and drink; the latter is not (Matt. 22.30; 1 Cor. 15.43, 44). Sixth, life is contemplative, active or productive. The contemplative life consists in speculation, and this is either the best or the worst.

units.la: Speculatio optima est cognitio optimi speculabilis, quale est solus Deus. Iohan.17.verf.3. Ierem.9.verf.24. Hæc verò cognitio nō est nuda, sed affectiua siue practica, ita nempe vt consistat in assimilatione cognoscentis & cogniti. Speculatio pessima est vel nuda cognitio, Iacob.2.v.19. vel cognitio siue contemplatio mali. Psal.36.verf.5. Vita actiua est posita in studio virtutis. Iacob.1.verf.25. Vita factiua est posita in exercitio artis alicuius liberalis vel mechanicæ. Sic Paulus fuit doctus artem scenofactoriam, vt loquitur vulgatus interpres, Act.18.verf.3. & artes liberales Act.22.v.3. Nos paulò μεθοδικώτερον persequemur has diuisiones.
units.tr: The best speculation is the knowledge of the best object of speculation, which is God alone (John 17.3; Jer. 9.24). This knowledge, however, is not bare but affective or practical, that is, it consists in the likeness of the knower to the known. The worst speculation is either bare knowledge (James 2.19) or the knowledge, or contemplation, of evil (Ps. 36.5). The active life consists in the pursuit of virtue (James 1.25). The productive life consists in the practice of some liberal or mechanical art. Thus Paul was trained in the art of tent-making, as the Vulgate translator puts it (Acts 18.3), and in the liberal arts (Acts 22.3). We shall pursue these divisions a little more methodically.

units.la: IV. Vita est increata, vel creata.
units.tr: IV. Life is either uncreated or created.

units.la: V. Vita increata est purus putus actus, quo Deus viuit à se & in se, facitq; viuere res extra se. Deus ita viuit, vt sit ipse sua vita, eaque ab æterno in æternum. Est autem hæc vita vel essentiæ diuinæ, vel personarum in essentiâ. Illa est communis Patri, Filio & Spiritui sancto. Deut.32.verf.40. 1.Sam.25.verf.34.Apoc.15.v.7. hæc est propria singularum personarum. Ita Pater viuit à se, Filius à Patre, Spiritus sanctus à Patre & Filio. Iohan.5. verf.26. Filius quidem viuit à se, vt Deus; sed viuit à Patre, vt Filius. Ita Spiritus sanctus viuit à se vt Deus; sed viuit à Patre & Filio, vt est tertia persona procedens à Patre & Filio. Porrò Deus ita viuit, vt aliis quoque det vitam. Genef.1.&2.Act.17.v.28.
units.tr: V. Uncreated life is a pure and simple act by which God lives of himself and in himself, and makes things outside himself to live. God so lives that he is his own life, and this from eternity to eternity. This life is either the divine essence or the persons within the essence. The former is common to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Deut. 32.40; 1 Sam. 25.34; Rev. 15.7); the latter is proper to each person. So the Father lives of himself, the Son of the Father, and the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son (John 5.26). The Son indeed lives of himself as God, but lives of the Father as Son. Likewise the Holy Spirit lives of himself as God, but lives of the Father and the Son as the third person proceeding from the Father and the Son. Moreover, God so lives that he also gives life to others (Gen. 1 and 2; Acts 17.28).

units.la: VI. Vita creata est, quam Deus largitur creaturæ: estq; angelorum, hominis, vel aliarum naturarum, puta bestiarum, plantarum, & totius denique mundi. Nos agemus de vita hominis. De vita angelorum vide in Pneumaticâ, de vita bestiarum, plantarum, & totius mundi, in Physicâ.
units.tr: VI. Created life is that which God bestows on a creature. It belongs to angels, to man, or to other natures, such as beasts, plants and finally the whole world. We shall treat of the life of man. Of the life of angels see in the Pneumatics; of the life of beasts, plants and the whole world, see in Physics.

units.la: VII. Vita hominis est praesentis vel futuri seculi.
units.tr: VII. The life of man belongs either to the present age or to the age to come.

units.la: VIII. Vita praesentis seculi est vel communis, omnium hominum, vel propria, quorundam.
units.tr: VIII. The life of the present age is either common, to all men, or proper, to certain men.

units.la: IX. Vita communis est, quam homo viuit vi naturae siue essentiae suae. Vnde etiam haec vita naturalis & essentialis dicitur. Haec vita est communicans, vel communicata. Vita communicans est animae, eaque immortalis & inseparabilis. Semper enim manet haec vita in statu animae tum corpori unitae, tum a corpore abiunctae, tum denique corpori reunitae. Matth.10.v.28. Memineris hic non esse sermonem de animae vegetatiua & sensitiua, sed de rationali. Diximus enim paulo ante, nos tractaturos de vita hominis, quam scilicet prae bestiis & plantis habet peculiarem. Vita communicata est corporis humani, quatenus humanum est. Haec vita consistit in eo, quod corpus hominis est domicilium & organum animae rationalis. Gen.2.verf.7. Atque haec vita est mortalis: unde in longam & breuem diuiditur. Genef.5.
units.tr: IX. Common life is that which a man lives by virtue of his nature or essence. Hence this life is also called natural and essential. This life is either communicating or communicated. Communicating life belongs to the soul, and it is immortal and inseparable. For this life always remains in the soul, whether it is united to the body, separated from the body, or finally reunited to the body (Matt. 10.28). Bear in mind that here we are not speaking of the vegetative and sensitive soul, but of the rational soul; for we said a little while ago that we would treat of the life of man, which he has apart from beasts and plants. Communicated life belongs to the human body, insofar as it is human. This life consists in this, that the human body is the dwelling and instrument of the rational soul (Gen. 2.7). And this life is mortal; hence it is divided into long and short (Gen. 5).

units.la: X. Vita quorundam hominum propria est, quam homo viuit vi principij extrinsecè superuenientis. Vnde appellari solet vita accidentalis. Non enim vt priorem illam vitam homo viuit vi principij interni, quod est natura ipsi indita: sic etiam res habet in vita illa accidentaria. Est autem haec vita ciuilis, vel spiritualis. Vita ciuilis est, quam homo viuit, vt est ciuis huius mundi. Est q; contemplatiua, actiua, vel factiua. Vita contemplatiua ciuilis vertitur in cognitione veri: vt est vita illorum, qui docent ac discunt artes. Vita actiua ciuilis est, quam homo viuit virtute ciuilis honestatis: vnde & vita honesta dicitur. Eius ratio in eo vertitur, vt viuamus secundum rectam rationem, siue legem naturae, ne degeneremus in sortem brutorum. Vita ista ciuilis est ethica, œco[?]conomica, politica, collegialis, status eminentiæ vel subiectionis, scholastica, &c. Vita ethica est, quæ informatur per virtutes: œconomica, quam homo viuit in societate domestica, siue in familiâ: politica, quam homo viuit in republicâ constitutus: collegialis, quam homo viuit, vt est pars alicuius collegij: scholastica, quam homo viuit, vt est pars scholæ: vita in statu eminentiæ est, quam viuit magistratus, in statu subiectionis, quam viuit subditus. Vita factiua ciuilis est, quâ homo deditus est exercitio alicuius artis liberalis vel mechanicæ. Vita spiritualis est, quam homo viuit, vt est ciuis ecclesiæ catholicæ. De vitâ ciuili vide Genes.4.verf.2. 21.22. de spirituali Rom.8. de vtràque Eccles.44. & aliquot seqq.capp.
units.tr: X. The proper life of certain men is that which a man lives by virtue of a principle coming from outside. Hence it is commonly called accidental life. For a man does not live this life by virtue of an internal principle, which is implanted in him by nature, as he lives the former life; and things are so in this accidental life. This life is either civil or spiritual. Civil life is that which a man lives as a citizen of this world. It is also contemplative, active or productive. Civil contemplative life turns on knowledge of the truth, as is the life of those who teach and learn the arts. Civil active life is that which a man lives by the virtue of civil honesty; hence it is also called the honest life. Its principle is that we live according to right reason, or the law of nature, lest we degenerate into the condition of brutes. This civil life is ethical, economic, political, collegiate, the life of a state of eminence or of subjection, scholastic, and so on. Ethical life is that which is formed by the virtues; economic, that which a man lives in domestic society, or in the household; political, that which a man lives as constituted in a commonwealth; collegiate, that which a man lives as a member of some college; scholastic, that which a man lives as a member of a school; the life in a state of eminence is that which the magistrate lives; in a state of subjection, that which the subject lives. Civil productive life is that in which a man is devoted to the practice of some liberal or mechanical art. Spiritual life is that which a man lives as a citizen of the catholic Church. On civil life see Gen. 4.2, 21, 22; on spiritual life see Rom. 8; on both see Ecclus. 44 and the several following chapters.

units.la: XI. Vita futuri seculi est posita in fruitione Dei sempiternâ, plenâ gloriæ & gaudij ineffabilis. Quam videlicet nec oculus vidit, nec auris audiuit, nec vllus homo cogitatione comprehendit. 1.Corinth.2.verf.9. 2.Cor.5.verf.1. Gal.6.v.8. Atque hæc est delineatio biographiæ, quæ tum demum erit ars bene viuendi, si Christus in nobis viuat per fidem, ita vt possit vnusquisque nostrum dicere cum apostolo: Vnà cum Christo crucifixus sum. Viuo autem non amplius ego, sed viuit in me Christus: & vitam, quam nunc viuo in carne, viuo per fidem illam Filij Dei, qui dilexit me, & tradidit semetipsum pro me. Gal.2.v.20.
units.tr: XI. The life of the age to come consists in the everlasting enjoyment of God, full of glory and of unspeakable joy: which, indeed, neither eye has seen, nor ear has heard, nor has any man comprehended in thought (1 Cor. 2.9; 2 Cor. 5.1; Gal. 6.8). And this is the outline of biography, which will at last be the art of living well if Christ lives in us through faith, so that each of us can say with the apostle: I am crucified with Christ. Yet I no longer live, but Christ lives in me; and the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me. (Gal. 2.20)

units.la: XLVIII.
units.tr: XLVIII.

units.la: HYGIASTICA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED HYGIENE.

units.la: I. HYgiastica sacra est institutio de verâ ratione conseruandæ valetudinis. Nominatim autem Hygiastica sacra est institutio partim ethica siue moralis, partim theologica, partim denique medica, præcipiens de ratione conseruandæ valetudinis, quatenus in Scripturis diuinis eius rei vestigia extant.
units.tr: I. Sacred hygiene is the teaching concerning the true method of preserving health.
