More specifically, sacred hygiene is a teaching that is partly ethical or moral, partly theological, and partly medical, prescribing the method of preserving health insofar as traces of this matter are found in the divine Scriptures.

units.la: II. Institutio moralis & theologica præscribit rationem vitæ sobriæ, hoc est, ordinatæ & temperatæ, illiusq; fructus commemorat,
units.tr: II. The moral and theological teaching prescribes the manner of a sober life, that is, one that is orderly and temperate, and it recounts the fruits of such a life.

units.la: III. Ratio siue modus vitæ sobriæ in eo vertitur, vt debitam in cibo & potu mensuram constanter seruemus, adeoque sanctæ temperantiæ studeamus. De illa mensura vide Exod.16.v.17. Prouerb.30.vers.8.
units.tr: III. The method or measure of a sober life consists in this: that we constantly keep the due measure in food and drink, and so strive for holy temperance. On that measure see Exod. 16.17. Prov. 30.8.

units.la: IV. Mensura ista non est eadem respectu omnium, sed diuersissima, pro diuersâ corporis constitutione, robore, ætate: item pro diuerso vitæ genere. Alia enim conuenit ætati florenti, aliasenili; alia robusto, alia debili; alia sano, alia ægro; alia corpori bilioso, alia pituitoso. Diuersa enim in his est facultas ventriculi: cui facultati hæc mensura exacte, quantum fieri potest, debet esse æqualis & commensa. Hinc fit, vt quod robusto & iuueni est æquale, id debili & seni in duplum vel triplum fit nimium seu inæquale. Nimirum vt in maiori mundo Deus omnia diuerso numero, pondere, & mensurâ disposuit. Sap.11.sic quoque in homine, paruo illo mundo seres habet. Deinde occupationes animi & corporis variæ variam quoque requirunt mensuram. Quia maior, & fere duplo maior mensura cibi potusque congruit illi, qui corporis exercitiis est deditus, quàm ei, qui totus est in studiis, meditatione, oratione, aliisq; mentis functionibus. Functiones enim animi tota vim anin æ sursum trahunt, atque ita suspendunt vires actionum inferiorum, nominatim concoctionis.
units.tr: IV. This measure is not the same for all, but very different according to the body's constitution, strength and age, and likewise according to the kind of life one lives. For one measure suits a flourishing age, another an old age; one suits a robust person, another a weak one; one suits a healthy person, another a sick one; one suits a bilious body, another a phlegmatic one. For the capacity of the stomach differs in these respects, and this measure ought to be made exactly equal and proportionate to that capacity, as far as possible. Hence it happens that what is equal for a robust young man becomes excessive or unequal, two or three times over, for a weak old man. Indeed, just as God has arranged all things in the greater world with diverse number, weight and measure, Wis. 11. so too in man, that little world, there is a similar variety. Moreover, the various occupations of mind and body likewise require various measures. For a larger, nearly double, measure of food and drink suits the one who is devoted to bodily exercise than the one who is wholly given to study, meditation, prayer and the other functions of the mind. For the functions of the mind draw the whole force of the spirit upward, and so suspend the powers of the lower actions, especially digestion.

units.la: V. Mensura cibi & potus inuestigatur certis regulis, hoc modo.
units.tr: V. The measure of food and drink is determined by certain rules, as follows.

units.la: Reg.1. Sitantum ordinarie fumas, vt pofteaparum fis aptu functionibus mentis, puta orationi, meditationi, & studiis literarum, certum est, te mensuram iustam excedere. Natura enim & ij ratio postulat, vt pars vegetans ita foueatur, vt facultas animalis & rationalis non offendatur: quia illa his seruire debet, & esse adminiculo ad earum functiones, non impedimento. Cùm ergo tantum ingeritur pro parte vegetante, vt functionibus superiorum facultatum, nempe sensuum, imaginatricis, intellectus, memoriæ, notabile detur impedimentum, signum est, congruentem mensuram excedi. Prouenit hoc impedimentum ex vaporum è ventriculo, hepate, liene & venis afcendetium[?] copiâ: qui modicè tantùm eò mitterentur, si mensura non excederetur. Experientiâ siquidem constat, cibo potuque nimio assumto non solùm ventriculum, sed etiam hepar, lienem & venas nimium incalescere, & magnam fuliginum vim sursum emittere.
units.tr: Rule 1. If you take so much ordinarily that afterwards you are less fit for the functions of the mind, such as prayer, meditation and literary studies, it is certain that you exceed the just measure. For nature and reason require that the vegetative part be nourished in such a way that the animal and rational faculties are not hindered, because the former ought to serve these and be an aid to their functions, not an obstacle. Therefore, when so much is poured in for the vegetative part that a notable hindrance arises to the functions of the higher faculties, namely the senses, the imagination, the intellect and the memory, this is a sign that the proper measure has been exceeded. This hindrance arises from the abundance of vapours rising from the stomach, liver, spleen and veins, which would be sent up only moderately if the measure were not exceeded. For experience shows that when excessive food and drink are taken, not only the stomach but also the liver, spleen and veins grow too hot, and send up a great quantity of smoky exhalations.

units.la: Reg.2. Si tantum cibi vel potus assumas, vt postea sentias torporem quendam grauitatem, & lassitudinem corporis, cum antea esses agilis & excitatus; signum est, mensuram congruentem excedi:nisi forte ex morbo, vel morbi reliquiis, id proueniat. Cibus enim & potus, naturam viresq; corporis recreare debent, & alacriores reddere, non grauare & opprimere. Qui ergo grauamen sentiunt ex cibi potusq; excessu, iis demensum diurnum sensim minuendū est, donec ad eam mensuram redigatur, ex qua non amplius sentiatur incomodum. Dixi sensim;quia si quis ab inordinatâ viuendi ratione immediatè ac subito trâfeat ad exactam regulam, subita ista mutatio offendet naturam. Quare cõsueta quantitas modicis subtractionibus paulatim minuatur, donec ad eam peruenia-tur mensuram, quæ neruos, spirituum vias, non nimium humectet. Ita fiet, vt Spiritus animalis (à quo tanquam vniuersali & proximo animæ instrumento, omnis vigor corporis in sensu & motu) liberè commeare, & corpus regere queat. Quòd si spiritus ille per vaporum copiam ex cibis intercipiatur, nihil mirum est debilitatem & corporis grauitatem, sensuumque torporem sequi. Germani eleganter ex Iudic.19.v.5. dicunt de vsu cibi & potus, Man muß die Natur stärcken. Et Chri-stus, stus, Luc.21.v.34. abusum cibi & potus in eo ponit, quod grauent cor.
units.tr: Rule 2. If you take so much food or drink that afterwards you feel a certain torpor, heaviness and weariness of body, when before you were nimble and alert, it is a sign that the proper measure has been exceeded, unless perhaps this comes from illness or the remains of illness. For food and drink ought to refresh the nature and strength of the body and make it more lively, not weigh it down and oppress it. Therefore those who feel a burden from an excess of food and drink should gradually reduce their daily amount until it is brought back to the measure at which the discomfort is no longer felt. I say gradually, because if anyone passes at once and suddenly from a disorderly manner of living to the exact rule, this sudden change will injure his nature. Hence the usual quantity should be diminished little by little by modest reductions, until one reaches the measure that does not overly moisten the nerves and the channels of the spirits. In this way the animal spirit (by which, as the universal and immediate instrument of the soul, all the vigour of the body in sensation and motion is carried out) can pass freely and govern the body. But if that spirit is obstructed by an abundance of vapours from food, it is no wonder that weakness, bodily heaviness and torpor of the senses follow. The Germans neatly apply to the use of food and drink the saying from Judg. 19.5: Man muß die Natur stärcken, that is, one must strengthen nature. And Christ, Luke 21.34, places the abuse of food and drink in this, that they weigh down the heart.

units.la: Reg.3. Quilibet explorare debet vires & vasasua[?], ut aequalem mensuram invenire atque observare possit. Communiter post annum aetatis 36. satis esse videntur 12. vel 16. unciae cibi per diem; & totidem vel paulo plures unciae potus. Hoc intellige de iis, qui toti studiis sunt addicti, sive sint debiles, & ad senium vergant, sive robusti & in aetatis flore constituti. Patres sane, qui in eremo vixerant solo pane & aqua, ut est apud Cassianum collat.2. abbatis Mosis cap.19. hanc mensuram observarunt: utpote qui duobus paximaciis, id est, duobus parvulis panibus, vix unius libræ, id est 12. unciarum, pondus habentibus, fuerunt in singulos dies contenti. Quod si Patres illi per longam experientiam satis esse iudicarunt duo paximacia, sive duodecim vncias (singula enim paximacia fuerunt solum sex unciarum, & duo simul iuncta penderunt libram 12. unciarum, qualis fuit apud veteres in usu) & quidem panis sicci absque ullo obsonio: quanto magis satis esse poterunt 6.7.vel 8. unciae panis cum 6.7.vel 8. unciis obsoniorum, quae duplo plus alunt, quam siecus[?] panis. Huc accedit loco aquae, qua illi utebantur, quaeque per se non alit, cerevisia vel vinum, quae multum alimenti præbent. Denique experientia constat, multos esse, quibus longe minus cibi & potus satis sit. Apostolus 1.Tim.5.v.23. monet Timotheum, ut pauculo vino utatur propter crebras infirmitates. Si quis sit valentulus, potest plus vini bibere, quam valetudinarius. Uterque tamen potest etiam bibere ad hilaritatem. Psal.104.15.
units.tr: Rule 3. Everyone ought to test his own strength and vessels, so that he may find and observe the equal measure. Commonly, after the age of thirty-six, twelve or sixteen ounces of food a day seem enough, and as many or a little more ounces of drink. Understand this of those who are wholly given to study, whether they are weak and tending towards old age, or robust and in the flower of their age. Indeed the Fathers who lived in the desert on bread and water alone, as is related in Cassian, Conferences 2, the Abbot Moses, chapter 19, observed this measure, since they were content each day with two paximacia, that is, two small loaves, which weighed scarcely one pound, that is, twelve ounces. If those Fathers judged, through long experience, that two paximacia, or twelve ounces, were enough (for each paximacion weighed only six ounces, and the two together weighed a pound of twelve ounces, which was the custom among the ancients), and that of dry bread alone without any relish, how much more will six, seven or eight ounces of bread with six, seven or eight ounces of relishes be enough, since these nourish twice as much as dry bread? To this must be added, in place of the water they used, which does not nourish of itself, beer or wine, which provide much nourishment. Finally, experience shows that there are many for whom far less food and drink is enough. The Apostle, 1 Tim. 5.23, advises Timothy to use a little wine because of his frequent infirmities. A man who is fairly strong may drink more wine than one who is an invalid. Yet both may drink for cheerfulness, Ps. 104.15.

units.la: Reg. 4. Consultum est, abrumpere prandium vel cœnam, quando cibus & potus incipiunt optime sapere. Certissimum enim hoc est indicium, naturam ventriculi habere obiectum convenientis quantitatis, in quod agat. Huc refer illud Hippocratis in aphorismis: Valetudinem excolunt, citra satietatem vesci cibis, & impigrum esse ad laborem.
units.tr: Rule 4. It is advisable to break off dinner or supper when food and drink begin to taste best. For this is the most certain sign that the nature of the stomach has an object of convenient quantity on which to act. To this refer the saying of Hippocrates in the Aphorisms: Eating without satiety preserves health, and makes one untiring for labour.

units.la: Reg.5. Quod ad qualitatem attinet, omnes pene cibi, communiter vsitati, natura bene constituta conueniunt, si debita in illis quantitas, siue mensura, seruetur. Ab iis tamen, quæ nocent, cauendum: qualia fere sunt pinguia, quæ & stomachum relaxant, eiusq; vires in astrictione sitas dissoluunt, concoctionem reliquorum ciborum impediunt, eosq; semicrudos stomacho excidere faciunt, & fumos in caput copiose emittunt. Literati ergo parce iis vtentur, & sufficienti panis quantitate noxam illorū impedire studebunt.
units.tr: Rule 5. As for quality, almost all foods in common use agree with a well-constituted nature, provided the due quantity or measure is observed. Yet one must beware of those that do harm, such as fatty foods, which both relax the stomach and dissolve its strength, which lies in firmness, impede the digestion of the other foods, cause them to be expelled half-cooked from the stomach, and send up abundant fumes into the head. Scholars, therefore, should use these sparingly, and by a sufficient quantity of bread they will strive to prevent their harm.

units.la: Talia item sunt omnia, quæ experientiâ teste, vel capiti suffusiones, nebulas, vertigines, destillationes aut tusses adferunt; vel ventriculo cruditates, inflationes, tormina, morsus, lancinationes faciunt; vel aliâ ratione statū corporis, aut animi functiones lædunt. Cùm dicitur ab his cauendum, non sic intelligas, quasi ne parce quidem vti liceat, sed ne assumantur notabili copiâ. Exiguâ enim quantitate, vel rarius assumta, nocere non possunt, præsertim si grata appetitui. Imò sæpe quæ magnâ quantitate obsunt, modicâ, naturæ prosunt. Hac cautione obseruatâ, cepæ, brassi-a, caseus, pisa, & fabæ vtiliter adhibentur.
units.tr: Likewise are all those things which, as experience attests, bring on either suffusions, mists, dizziness, catarrhs or coughs in the head; or cause crudities, flatulence, gripings, bites and stabbing pains in the stomach; or otherwise injure the condition of the body or the functions of the mind. When it is said that one must beware of these, do not understand it as if one were not allowed to use them even sparingly, but that they must not be taken in notable quantity. For taken in a small quantity, or more rarely, they cannot harm, especially if they are pleasing to the appetite. Indeed, things that harm in large quantity often benefit nature in moderate amount. With this caution observed, onions, cabbage, cheese, peas and beans are usefully employed.

units.la: Cæterum inter omnia ciborum genera, senibus & debilibus nihil est conuenientius panatellâ, hoc est, pulticulâ ex pane & aquâ aut carnium iusculo simul coc-tis, costante. Hac fere sola cū uno vel altero ouo saluberrimè quis & diutissimè viuere potest. Ratio, cur hæc sit maximè coueniens, est, tum quia concoctu facillima, cùm iam sit instar illius chyli, quem stomachus ex cibis concoctione efficit: tum quia qualitatibus est temperatissima: tum quia putredini & corruptioni minimè obnoxia, vt multi alij cibi, qui in stomacho putrescunt. Præterea copiosus & probus sanguis ex eâ conficitur. Denique facilè aliquid additur, quo vel calidior euadat, vel magis alimentosa.
units.tr: Among all kinds of food, however, nothing is more suitable for the old and the weak than panatella, that is, a little pulp consisting of bread and water or broth of meat cooked together. With this alone, or with one or two eggs, a person can live most healthily and for longest. The reason why this is most suitable is, first, that it is very easy to digest, since it is already like that chyle which the stomach produces from food by digestion; second, that it is most temperate in its qualities; and third, that it is least liable to putrefaction and corruption, unlike many other foods which putrefy in the stomach. Moreover, abundant and good blood is made from it. Finally, something can easily be added to it which makes it either warmer or more nourishing.

units.la: Pertinet huc illud Sapientis, Initium vitæ hominis aqua & panis. Ecclesiast.29.v.28. Quibus verbis significat, vitam hominis his duobus potissimum sulciri & constare, eaq; vitæ conseruandæ esse maximè conuenientia: ne frustrà pretiosæ carnes, aliaque gulæ irritamenta quærantur.
units.tr: Here belongs that saying of the wise man, "The beginning of man's life is water and bread" (Ecclesiasticus 29:28). By these words he signifies that man's life is chiefly sustained by these two things and consists of them, and that these are most suitable for preserving life, so that costly meats and other incitements to gluttony are sought in vain.

units.la: Reg.6. Quibus bona valetudo cura est, iis maxime cauenda ciborum varietas, & exquisita condiendi ratio. Nam præterquam, quòd illa varietas semper nouo modo gulam prouocat, & appetitum excitat, vt nunquam videatur fatis sumsisse, quo fit vt iusta mensura enormiter excedatur: hoc etiam habet incommodi, quòd diuersorum ciborum diuersa natura miras in ventriculo cruditates causatur. Merito itaque laudatur Socrates, qui simplicissimam & tenuissimam diætam amauit: & Zoroaster, qui 2o.annos in deserto vixit solo calcei esu. De Patriarchis quoque, & aliis sanctis viris, testantur sacræ literæ, illos amasse victum simplicem panis & aquæ. Vide Concordantias Biblicas in voce Panis.
units.tr: Reg. 6. Those who care for good health must above all avoid variety of foods and elaborate methods of seasoning. Apart from the fact that such variety always provokes the palate in a new way and excites the appetite, so that one never seems to have eaten enough, and so the proper measure is enormously exceeded, it also has this drawback: the different natures of different foods cause remarkable indigestions in the stomach. Socrates is rightly praised, for he loved the simplest and plainest diet; and so is Zoroaster, who lived twenty years in the desert on nothing but the eating of cabbage. Holy Scripture also testifies that the patriarchs and other holy men loved the simple fare of bread and water. See the Biblical Concordances under the word "Bread."

units.la: Reg.7. Imaginatio est corrigenda iis, qui iustam seruare volunt mensuram in cibo & potu. Nisi enim hoc fiat, imaginatio cibi & potus delectabilis stimulabit appetitum, qui vulgato prouerbio recte dicitur nequam. Quomodo verò, inquiat aliquis, corrigitur imaginatio? Resp. Si nos subducamus ab epularum conspectu, & animo voluamus damna, quæ ex delicatis cibis immoderatè assumtis prouenire solent.
units.tr: Reg. 7. Those who wish to keep the right measure in food and drink must correct their imagination. For unless this is done, the imagination of pleasant food and drink will stir up the appetite, which is rightly called wicked by the common proverb. But how, someone may ask, is the imagination corrected? Answer: if we withdraw from the sight of feasts and turn over in our minds the harms that usually come from immoderately consumed delicacies.

units.la: Reg.8. Hyeme vtendum est siccis & calidus ob copiam pituita, quatunc redundat, & non dissipatur: astate potius humidis & refrigerantibus, quia per calorem aeris ambientis magna fit humorum discussio, & corpus arescit. Hoc autem ita consequemur absque difficultate. Si opus fit diætâ ficciore, vt hyeme, & quando diuturnæ sunt pluuiæ, facile est augere quantitatem panis, & minuere quantitatem potus ac obsoniorum humidorum. Copia enim potus & humidorum, quæ tempore sicco iuuat, eadé si humido & subfrigido aëre peraliquot dies sumatur, nocet, destillationes, raucedines, ac tusses procreans. Quando verò opus est diætâ humidiore, augeri potest mesura potus, addità vino maiore quantitate aquæ; vel loco vini potest assumi tenuis cereuisia.
units.tr: Reg. 8. In winter one should use dry and warm foods, because phlegm then abounds and is not dispersed; in summer one should rather use moist and cooling foods, because the heat of the surrounding air causes a great dissolution of the humours and the body dries up. We shall achieve this without difficulty. If a drier diet is needed, as in winter or when the rains have lasted long, it is easy to increase the quantity of bread and to reduce the quantity of drink and moist dishes. For the amount of drink and moist foods that helps in dry weather harms if it is taken for several days in damp and chilly air, producing catarrhs, hoarseness and coughs. When a moister diet is needed, the measure of drink may be increased by adding a larger quantity of water to the wine; or thin beer may be taken instead of wine.

units.la: Reg.9. Prandium sit Largius cœnâ, vel contrà cœna largiùr prandio, prout cuilibet est commodius. Itaque in prandio poterunt sumi 8. vel 10. vnciæ, vesperi 4. vel 6. aut contrà. Verùm in istis diuturna consuetudo magnam vim habet: similiter corporis dispositio. Nam si ventriculus pituitâ 5 frigidâ & lentâ abundet, magis conducit, ut aliquis semel tantum de die comedat: quia multum temporis requiritur, ut illa concoquatur vel extenuetur. Si tamen refectio in vesperam differatur, proderit meridie modicum quid sumere, præsertim quod iuuet ad nimiam ventriculi hu10 miditatem exliccandam. Vel si meridie prandeatur, tale quid expediet sumere vesperi, verbi gratia, passulas cum pane, vel similia. Maximè enim iis, qui ita affecti, curandum, ut humiditas ista stomachi, quantum fieri potest, corrigatur. quia inde stomachus flatibus, & caput nebulis 15 lentoque phlegmate oppletur. Sapientia, inquit ille, in sicco residet, non in paludibus & lacunis. Et Heraclitus, Anima sicca, anima sapientissima.
units.tr: Reg. 9. Dinner should be larger than supper, or supper larger than dinner, whichever suits each person better. Thus at dinner 8 or 10 ounces may be taken and in the evening 4 or 6, or the reverse. But in these matters long-standing habit has great force, as does bodily constitution. For if the stomach abounds in cold and sluggish phlegm, it is better for a person to eat only once a day, since much time is needed for that phlegm to be digested or thinned. If, however, the meal is put off until evening, it will help to take something small at midday, especially something that helps to dry out the excessive moisture of the stomach. Or if one dines at midday, it will be expedient to take something of the same kind in the evening, for example raisins with bread or similar things. For those so affected must especially take care that this moisture of the stomach is corrected as far as possible, because from it the stomach is filled with wind and the head with mists and sluggish phlegm. "Wisdom," he says, "resides in dryness, not in marshes and pools." And Heraclitus: "A dry soul is the wisest soul."

units.la: Reg. 10. Si forte semel aut iterum excedatur ordinaria cibi & potus mensura, statim ad solitam sobrietatem redire oportet. 20 Cùm enim stomachus ordinariâ diætâ contrahatur, necesse est illum valdè lædi, si supra consuetum distendatur sæpius. Vnus aut alter excessus parum nocet, modò statim ad solitam sobrietatem redeatur.
units.tr: Reg. 10. If by chance the ordinary measure of food and drink is exceeded once or twice, one must at once return to the usual sobriety. For since the stomach is contracted by an ordinary diet, it must be greatly harmed if it is often stretched beyond its usual capacity. One or two excesses do little harm, provided one returns at once to the usual sobriety.

units.la: XI. Non alienum fuerit ab instituto moderatæ diætæ, si voto 25 sancto nos obstringamus ad certam cibi potusque quantitatem. Illud verò est plane necessarium, ut viribus nostris diffidamus, Deumque quotidie rogemus, ut nos regat sancto suo Spiritu, qui nos doceat sobrietatem. Ecclesiast.23.v.6.[?]
units.tr: XI. It would not be out of place in a plan of moderate diet if we bound ourselves by a holy vow to a certain quantity of food and drink. But it is quite necessary that we distrust our own strength and ask God daily to govern us by his holy Spirit, who teaches us sobriety. Ecclesiasticus 23:6 [?]

units.la: Reg. 11. Qui exactam diætam rationem seruare non possunt, iis 30 expedit quotannis bis saltem, nempe in vere & autumno, corpus benepurgare, & humoribus noxiis liberare. Loquor de literarum cultoribus, qui corpus ordinariè non exercent. Porrò ea purgatio fieri debet præuiâ humorum præparatione: neque debet esse valida, & confertim operari, sed sensim 35 per duos vel tres dies assumto medicamento. Sic enim & facile toleratur, & amplius prodest. Nam primo die purgatur gatur prima regio; hoc est, intestina : fecundo hepar:ter­tio, venæ, in quibus maxima prauorum humorum colluuies. Qui enim non sobrie viuunt, singulis diebus aliquid crudi humoris addunt, quod ad venas attractum, per totum corpus veluti per spongiam distribuitur. Itaque intra vnum vel alterum annum tanta sæpe est quantitas praui humoris in corpore, quantum vos ducetarum vnciarum, seu quatuor poculorum, vix capiat. Hi humores tandem temporis tractu putrescunt, & lethales morbos inferunt.
units.tr: Reg. 11. Those who cannot keep an exact rule of diet should at least twice a year, namely in spring and autumn, cleanse the body well and free it from harmful humours. I speak of those devoted to letters, who do not ordinarily exercise the body. Moreover, this purging must be preceded by a preparation of the humours. It should not be violent or act all at once, but gradually, over two or three days, with the medicine taken in stages. For in this way it is easily tolerated and benefits more. On the first day the first region is purged, that is, the intestines; on the second, the liver; on the third, the veins, in which is the greatest washing away of bad humours. For those who do not live soberly add some raw humour each day, which, drawn into the veins, is distributed through the whole body as through a sponge. So within a year or two there is often so much bad humour in the body that it can scarcely be held in two hundred ounces, or four cups. These humours in time putrefy and bring on deadly diseases.

units.la: VI. Fructus vitæ sobriæ sunt varij, è quibus alij corpus, alij animam spectant. Et corpori qui- dem vitæ sobriæ præstat quinque commoda.
units.tr: VI. The fruits of sober living are various: some concern the body, others the soul. Sober living offers the body five benefits.

units.la: 1. Hominem ab omnibus pene morbis liberat ac defendit. Ab illis dico morbis, qui ex cruditate & interna humorum corruptione nafcuntur. 2. Munit nos aduersus externas causas, cuius modi sunt æstus, frigus, labor, & similia. Nam qui corpus purum, & humores temperatos habent, non ita facile lædantur ab æstu, frigore, labore, & similibus incommodis, sicut ij, qui prauis humoribus abundant: &, fi lædantur, facilius & citius curantur. Ita Socrates sua frugalitate effecit, vt quamuis Athenas sæpe pestis vastaret, ipse tamen nunquam ægrotarit. 3. Mitigat morbos incurabiles, vt facile tolerentur, nec magnopere functiones animi impediant. 4. Præstat longæuitatem, & mortem placidam. Nam qui sobrie viuunt, harmoniam humorum egregie tuentur, & cum ex hac vita decedendum, nullos fere vel exiguos dolores sentiunt: quia moriuntur per meram resolutionem. Cum enim per diætam noxios humores euitent, nihilin fe habent, quod temperamentum violente possit destruere, aut calorem naturalem opprimere: ac proinde necesse est, vt viuant, donec humidum primigenium vna cum calore infito fit ita confumtum, vt no sufficiat ad animam in corpore vlterius retinendam. 5. Corpus reddit leue, agile, vegetum, & ad omnes suos motus expeditum. Grauamen enim, naturæ oppressio, & tarditas prouenit ex humorum redundanfundantiâ[?], qui vias spirituum obstruunt, & iuncturas obsident, nimiumque humectant. Itaque sublatâ humorum copiâ per diætam, tollitur causa illius grauaminis & tarditatis, & laxantur viæ spirituum. Deinde per eandem diætam fit, vt concoctio sit bona, & probus conficiatur sanguis, ex quo deinde puri & copiosi suppeditantur spiritus, à quibus omnis vigor & agilitas. His accedit, quod viuus color faciei comitatur vitam sobriam. Dan.1.verf.15. Atque hæc quinque commoda sobrietas adfert corpori Animo similiter præstat quinque. 1. Sensibus externis præstat vigorem. Functiones enim sensuum impediuntur superuacaneis humoribus, quos vita sobria tollit. 2. Mitigat afsectus seu passiones: præsertim iræ & melancholiæ: item appetitum inordinatum cibi, potus & Veneris. Subtrahit enim & corrigit humores, qui illorum causa. 3. Conseruat memoriam. Hæc enim maximè lædi solet ab humore frigido cerebrum occupante, & vias spirituum angustiores obstruendo, & spiritus ipsos refrigerando & torpidos reddendo: quo fit vt apprehensiones sint lentæ, languidæ, & fluxæ, & sæpe in mediâ narratione hominem ita deficiant, vt nesciat quid dixerit, aut quâ de re locutus fuerit, rogetque socios, Quid tractabamus? Totum hoc malum mirificè arcetur, vel curatur diætâ sobriâ & quantum fieri potest, siccâ. Hâc enim fit, vt superflua humiditas vel non generatur, vel genita consumatur. Inprimis abstinendum est à potu calido & fumoso, nisi forte exigua sit quantitas. Etsi enim vinum sit calidum, tamen crebrò & magnâ copiâ haustum, frigidos morbos parit. Nimirum implet caput vaporibus, qui ibidem refrigerati, in frigidam pituitam, quæ est ilias morborum, densatur. 4. Tuetur vigorem ingenij in excogitando, ratiocinando, inueniendo, iudicando; & aptitudinem confert ad diuinas illustrationes suscipiendas. Sobria enim diæta tollit nimiam cerebri humiditatem, vaporum & fuliginum abundantiam, meatuú cerebri obstructionem, nimiam sanguinis copiam, spirituum feruorem à sanguine vel bile prouenientem, vapores biliosos & meIancholicos,& similia speculationis impedimenta. Libidinis impetum extinguit, & tentationes atq; stimulos carnis mirifice sedat, magnamq; carni ac spiritui tranquillitatem conciliat. Sobrietas enim sensim minuit copiam spermatis, copiam item & feruorem spirituum: quibus imminutis sponte cessant libidinosæ imaginationes. Atque hæc sunt eximia illa commoda sanctæ sobrietatis, cuius studiosi cultores illa abundè sunt experti, puta Elias, Elisæus, Daniel, Democritus, Hippocrates, Iohannes Baptista, Bartholus, Cornarus, & alij, de quibus vide Hygiasticon Leonhardi Lessij, scriptum diuinum, ex quo hanc commentationem desumsimus. Tu, homo Dei, ad animum revoca hanc sive commentationem sive commendationem sanctæ sobrietatis, & singulis momentis meditare illud Christi Luc.21.v.34. Attendite vobis ipsis, ne forte grauentur corda vestra crapula & ebrietate, & curæ huius vitæ, & repente in vos superueniat dies ille. Item illud Petri 1.epist.c.5.v.8. Sobrij estote, vigilate: aduersarius vester diabolus, tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem deuoret: cui resistite, fortes in fide. VII. Institutio medica præscribit rationem diætæ & varia medicamenta, quibus sanitas defenditur, & recuperatur. Huius loci sunt præcepta de aëre ambiente, de esculentis & potulentis, de retentione & euacuatione, de variis exercitiis corporis, de somno atque vigilia, de animi perturbationibus, de refectione & confortatione cerebri, cordis, &c. quæ peti possunt è libellis medicis. Sed iis nihil opus est, si nostra monita seruies. Summa enim huc redit:
units.tr: (1) It frees and protects a person from almost all diseases. I mean those diseases that arise from indigestion and the internal corruption of the humours. (2) It fortifies us against external causes, such as heat, cold, labour and the like. Those who have a pure body and temperate humours are not so easily harmed by heat, cold, labour and similar discomforts as those who abound in bad humours; and if they are harmed, they are more easily and quickly cured. So Socrates, by his frugality, ensured that although plague often ravaged Athens, he himself never fell ill. (3) It softens incurable diseases, so that they are easier to bear and do not greatly hinder the functions of the mind. (4) It secures long life and a peaceful death. For those who live soberly keep the harmony of the humours in excellent order, and when they must depart from this life, they feel almost no pain or only a little, because they die by mere dissolution. For since they avoid harmful humours through their diet, they have nothing in themselves that could violently destroy the temperament or overpower the natural heat; and therefore they must live on until the primal moisture, together with the innate heat, is so consumed that it no longer suffices to keep the soul in the body. (5) It makes the body light, nimble, lively, and ready for all its movements. For heaviness, oppression of nature and sluggishness arise from an overabundance of humours, which block the passages of the spirits, besiege the joints and make everything too damp. Therefore, when the quantity of humours is removed by diet, the cause of that heaviness and sluggishness is taken away, and the passages of the spirits are loosened. Moreover, by the same diet, digestion becomes good and the blood is made sound, and from this blood pure and abundant spirits are supplied, from which comes all vigour and agility. To this is added that a healthy colour of face accompanies a sober life. Dan. 1. v. 15. These are the five benefits that sobriety brings to the body. Likewise, it offers five to the mind. (1) It gives vigour to the external senses. For the functions of the senses are hindered by superfluous humours, which sober living removes. (2) It softens the affections or passions, especially anger and melancholy; likewise the disordered appetite for food, drink and sex. For it reduces and corrects the humours that cause them. (3) It preserves the memory. For memory is especially wont to be harmed by cold humour occupying the brain, obstructing the narrower passages of the spirits, cooling the spirits themselves and making them sluggish. The result is that apprehensions become slow, feeble and fleeting, and often in the middle of a narrative a person so fails that he does not know what he has said or what he was speaking about, and asks his companions, "What were we discussing?" This whole evil is wonderfully warded off or cured by a sober diet that is, as far as possible, dry. For by this diet superfluous moisture is either not generated or, once generated, is consumed. Above all, one must abstain from hot and fumy drink, unless perhaps the quantity is small. For although wine is hot, yet when drunk often and in large amounts it produces cold diseases. Indeed, it fills the head with vapours, which, cooled there, are thickened into cold phlegm, which is the source of the whole heap of diseases. (4) It maintains the vigour of the wit in devising, reasoning, discovering and judging, and makes the mind apt to receive divine illuminations. For a sober diet removes excessive moisture of the brain, the abundance of vapours and soot, the obstruction of the passages of the brain, excessive quantity of blood, the fervour of the spirits arising from blood or bile, bilious and melancholic vapours, and similar impediments to contemplation. It extinguishes the impulse of lust, wonderfully calms the temptations and goads of the flesh, and brings great tranquillity to flesh and spirit. For sobriety gradually diminishes the quantity of seed, and likewise the quantity and fervour of the spirits; with these diminished, lustful imaginations cease of their own accord. These are the outstanding benefits of holy sobriety, whose diligent devotees have fully experienced them, namely Elijah, Elisha, Daniel, Democritus, Hippocrates, John the Baptist, Bartholus, Cornarus, and others; on these see the Hygiasticon of Leonhard Lessius, a divine writing, from which we have drawn this discussion. You, man of God, call to mind this discourse, or rather commendation, of holy sobriety, and every moment meditate on that saying of Christ, Luke 21.v.34: Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly. Likewise that saying of Peter, 1 Epist. c.5 v.8: Be sober, be vigilant: your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour; whom resist, steadfast in the faith.

units.la: Si tibi deficiant medici, medici tibi fiant Hæc tria: Mens hilaris, Requies, Moderata diæta.
units.tr: If physicians fail you, let these three become your physicians: a cheerful mind, rest, and a moderate diet.

units.la: VIII. Ad hygiasticam sacram pertinet illa quæstio, Cur Deus Leuit. 11. & Deut. 14. prohibuerit certos cibos, alios vero concesserit. Varij varia hic adferunt. Et primo quidem Porphyrius, apostata, dixit excessum aut defectum caloris aut humoris radicalis dicalis esse in causâ,ꝗ[?] Deus ꝑhibuerit[?] certos cibos,Deinde Doctores ecclesiastici & Scholastici hęc summatim attulerunt. Carnes animalium habentiū ungulam, non tamen divisam, sunt sicci humoris, ac proinde non aptæ ad esum. Rursus carnes animalium habentium ungulam divisam, sed non ruminantium, solent rapto vivere, ac proinde sunt animalia carnivora, & idcirco immunda: item, cum non ruminent, solent cibos integros, non concisos devorare. Cibi itidem ex animantibus, quæ vel reptando, vel serpedo gradiuntur, corporibus sunt noxij, quòd non sint bonæ complexionis. Eâdem ratione mures, & alia id genus animalia, reijciuntur. Nam hos omnes cibos natura ipsâ hominum refugit & detestatur. Præterea aliorum animalium carnes vetantur, quia immundis cibis nutriri solent, tametsi huiusmodi carnes suâ naturâ non sunt humano corpori noxiæ. Et propterea jubet Deus Judæos à carne suilla abstinere, quia porcus volutatur in cœno & luto, & comedit, quidquid in locis immundis invenit. Ex piscibus verò concessit eos,qui pinnulas habet & squamas: eos verò prohibuit, qui squamas aut pinnas non habent: quia prioris generis pisces sunt temperamenti minus phlegmatici. Tertiò sunt,qui Deum nihil horum spectasse scribunt; quòd non sit probabile, Deum his modis medicam rem in rebus sacris curavisse. Aiunt itaque, in hac lege de ciborum delectu illud voluisse Deum, ut animalia, quæ gentibus habebantur pro diis, passim comederentur, sues verò, lepores, cuniculi, & similia immunda censerentur, quia hisce vescebantur Ægyptij, cum cæteris tamquam diis suis parcerent. Ad extremum existimant nonnulli, Deum respexisse patriarcharum consuetudinem, ita ut lege constituerit atque præscripserit illud, quod maiores Israëlitarum in delectu ciborum, more & usu observarunt. Quid mihi videatur in hac materia, paulò fusius dicam. Et primò quidem munditia & immunditia est spiritualis, vel corporalis. Spiritualis munditia & immunditia inter has creaturas inferiores est hominis ꝑpria. Munditia & immunditia corporalis, siue carnalis & materialis, aut est ex natura, aut ex instituto: siue, est φύσεως, vel θέσεως. Ad naturam quod attinet, ex natura creationis, omnia sunt munda Gen.1.v.vlt: sed ex natura corrupta, quatenus illa vitio hominis est vanitati mancipata Rom.8. ea, quae secundum naturam communem, in creatione institutam, sunt bona & munda, contigit esse mala, id est, noxia, & immunda. Hinc fit, vt [?]us & bufo ex natura communi munda, ex natura singulari sint immunda, tum subiectiue, tum effectiue, vt loquuntur. Alioqui certa est apostoli sententia 1. Tim. 4. omnia piis sanctificata esse, & Tit. 1. omnia munda mundis, quemadmodum Deus Petro ostendit Act. 10. Quantum attinet ad institutum, fit vt ea ipsa, quae munda sunt, tamen immunda censeri soleant: vel, quae natura sunt immunda, etiam instituto habentur pro immundis. Instituti autem causae sunt in hoc genere aut naturales, aut morales, aut figurales. Naturales sunt, quae a natura fundamentum habent: vt ad cibum quaedam ex natura adhibentur, & quaedam natura fastidit atque horret, vt quilibet in seipso deprehendit. Morales sunt, quae coniunctam honestatis & aequitatis rationem habent: vt cum Deus iubet Israelitas peregrinantes condere sua excrementa. Deut. 23. Figurales, siue ceremoniales, sunt, quae ad certam aliquam significationem pertinent, quas nec rei natura, nec morum nostrorum ratio simpliciter postulat, sed peculiaris aliqua praecipientis & instituentis intentio circumscribit: vt sunt ceremoniae Mosaicae. Haec iam accommodemus ad nostrum propositum. Triplex immunditia in hoc loco cernitur: in tactu, in cibo, in sacrificio. Quidquid immundum fuit tactu, idem cibo & sacrificio immundum censebatur: in cibo quod immundum fuit, fuit & sacrificio: ad sacrificium maxima munditia desideratur. Has autem munditias & immunditias, vt & priores tres, homines inde a lapsu obseruarunt aliquo modo: naturales & morales, naturae instinctu quodam, sacras, & ad sacrificia pertinentes, singulari revelatione Gen. 6. Erat autem de munditia & immunditiâ naturali aut morali proprie, per se, & principaliter Deus non agit in verbo suo, sed de figurali seu ceremoniali: tamen quin distinctio illa ex causis naturalibus & moralibus aliquo modo illustrari possit non est dubiû.
units.tr: VIII. To sacred hygiene belongs that question: why God, in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14, forbade certain foods and permitted others. Different people bring different answers. First, Porphyry the apostate said that the excess or deficiency of heat or of radical moisture is the cause why God forbade certain foods. Then the ecclesiastical teachers and the Schoolmen summarily offered these reasons. The flesh of animals that have a hoof, but not a cloven one, is of dry humour and therefore not suitable for eating. Again, the flesh of animals that have a cloven hoof but do not chew the cud tends to live by rapine, and therefore such animals are carnivorous and consequently unclean; also, since they do not chew the cud, they tend to devour their food whole, not chewed. Likewise, among the animals that move either by creeping or by crawling, their bodies are harmful as food, because they are not of good constitution. For the same reason mice and other animals of that kind are rejected. For nature itself shrinks from and abhors all these foods. Besides, the flesh of other animals is forbidden because they are usually fed on unclean food, although such flesh is not in its own nature harmful to the human body. And for this reason God commanded the Jews to abstain from swine's flesh, because the pig wallows in mud and filth and eats whatever it finds in unclean places. Among fish, He permitted those that have fins and scales, and forbade those that have neither scales nor fins, because the fish of the former kind are of less phlegmatic temperament. Thirdly, there are those who write that God had regard to none of these things; for it is not probable that God, in sacred matters, should have treated a medical matter in these ways. They say, therefore, that in this law concerning the choice of foods God wished that the animals which were held as gods by the nations should be eaten freely, while swine, hares, rabbits and similar animals should be counted unclean, because the Egyptians fed on them, while they spared the others as their gods. Lastly, some think that God had regard to the custom of the patriarchs, so that He established and prescribed by law what the forefathers of the Israelites had observed in the choice of food by custom and usage. What seems to me on this matter I shall say at somewhat greater length. And first, uncleanness and cleanness is either spiritual or bodily. Spiritual cleanness and uncleanness among these lower creatures is peculiar to man. Bodily cleanness and uncleanness, whether carnal and material, is either from nature or from institution; that is, it is of nature [φύσεως] or of institution [θέσεως]. As far as nature is concerned, by the nature of creation all things are clean (Gen. 1.31); but by corrupted nature, insofar as nature has been subjected to vanity through the fault of man (Rom. 8), those things which are good and clean according to the common nature instituted in creation have come to be evil, that is, harmful and unclean. Hence it happens that the toad and the toad-like creatures, clean by common nature, are unclean by their particular nature, both subjectively and effectively, as they say. Otherwise the apostle's judgment is certain (1 Tim. 4) that all things are sanctified to the godly, and (Titus 1) that all things are clean to the clean, as God showed to Peter (Acts 10). As far as institution is concerned, it comes about that things which are themselves clean are yet customarily regarded as unclean; or things that are unclean by nature are also held to be unclean by institution. Now the causes of institution in this matter are either natural, or moral, or figurative. Natural causes are those that have their foundation in nature: as some things are by nature suited for food, and some nature loathes and abhors, as anyone may discover in himself. Moral causes are those that have a connection with the reason of honesty and equity: as when God commands the Israelites, travelling, to bury their excrement (Deut. 23). Figurative, or ceremonial, causes are those that pertain to some definite signification, which neither the nature of the thing nor the reason of our morals simply requires, but which a particular intention of the one who commands and institutes circumscribes: such are the Mosaic ceremonies. Let us now apply these things to our purpose. Threefold uncleanness is seen in this passage: in touch, in food, and in sacrifice. Whatever was unclean to the touch was likewise regarded as unclean for food and for sacrifice; what was unclean as food was also unclean for sacrifice; and the greatest cleanness is required for sacrifice. Men from the Fall onward have observed these cleannesses and uncleannesses, as well as the earlier three, in some manner: the natural and moral ones by a certain instinct of nature, and the sacred ones, pertaining to sacrifices, by a singular revelation (Gen. 6). Now, God in His word does not treat of cleanness and uncleanness properly, per se and principally, as natural or moral, but of the figurative or ceremonial kind; yet there is no doubt that this distinction between natural and moral causes can be illustrated in some way.

units.la: Sic e. g. Deus lege cauit, ne ederent sanguinem animalium.Gen.9.Leuit.17.Deut.12. Rationem legis addit: Quoniam anima omnis in sanguine est,quasi dicat, quia vita, siue spiritus vitalis, animantium est in sanguine, hoc est, nutritur & sustentatur à sanguine. Nam sanguis est corporis & vitæ alimentum in animantibus: Perinde est ac si diceret, Sicut lychni ignis est in oleo, id est, sustentatur & nutritur ex oleo, sic spiritus vitalis, siue vita animantis, in sanguine consistit. Quare qui edit sanguinem animalis, devorat vitam eius. Prohibuit ergo Deus esum sanguinis, ut ab omni specie crudelitatis, cædibus & iniuriis abstinerent. Sed & aliam rationem subiungit Deus: Et ego dedi illum vobis, ut super altare in eo expietis pro animabus vestris: ac si dicat, Præcipio, ne comedatis sanguinem animalis, quia volui, ut peccata vestra sanguine animalium expietis, & vitam vestram eo sanguine redimatis, eoque veluti manu ducamini ad sanguinem mediatoris. Quare sanguis animalium non nisi ad altare meum, & per sacerdotem, tanquam victima pro peccato, fundendus est.
units.tr: So, for example, God laid down by law that they should not eat the blood of animals (Gen. 9; Lev. 17; Deut. 12). He adds the reason: "For the life of every creature is in the blood," as if to say that the life, or vital spirit, of living creatures is in the blood, that is, it is nourished and sustained by the blood. For blood is the nourishment of the body and of life in living creatures. It is just as if he said: as the fire of a lamp is in the oil, that is, is sustained and nourished by the oil, so the vital spirit, or the life of a creature, consists in the blood. Therefore whoever eats the blood of an animal devours its life. God therefore forbade the eating of blood so that they would abstain from every kind of cruelty, slaughter and injury. But God also adds another reason: "And I have given it to you, that you may make atonement for your souls upon the altar with it". It is as if he said: I command you not to eat the blood of an animal, because I willed that you should atone for your sins with the blood of animals and redeem your lives by that blood, and so be led by the hand, as it were, to the blood of the mediator. Therefore the blood of animals is to be poured out only at my altar, and by the priest, as a victim for sin.

units.la: Prohibebantur itaque Iudæi sanguinem edere, hanc quoque ob causam, quia eum Deus ad sacrificia sibi reseruauerat: & ne occasione ullâ inducerentur ad edendum sanguinem animalium immolatorum, generatim præcepit, ne ullum sanguinem animalium comederent. Ita sc.[?] præcidere voluit omnem peccandi, & perfringendi leges occasionem. Similiter etiam interdixit usum adipis Leuit.3. quia illum sibi ad sacrificia reseruauerat, tanquam pstantiorem[?]: item, quia voluit hac ratione nos docere, non curanda nobis esse cuticula. Ex his patet, ceremonias diuinitus præscriptas non excludere causam naturalem & moralem. Sic in cibis ceremonialiter immundis Deus hoc principaliter spectauit, ut ecclesia hoc modo distingueretura cœtibus gentilium. Quemadmodum enim Æthiopes & Ægyptij obseruationibus suis à Chaldæis, Iudæis & Græcis olim discreti erant: sic Deus ab omnibus aliis gentibus ecclesiam suam discerni voluit singulari obseruatione. Et hæc quidem est communis ratio, ob quam Deus populo suo præscripsit distinctionem illam ciborum mundorum & immundorum. Ad communem istam causam, & figuralem accedit singularis, eaque tum naturalis,tum moralis. Moralis:quia v.g. fciflura vngulæ significat discretionem in rebus sacris, ruminatio meditationem sacram &c. vt antiqui Patres obseruarunt. Naturalis: quia partim natura fastidit quosdam cibos, partim ratio & experientia confirmant, quorundam animalium carnes esse insalubres. Ad has omnes causas accedit vltimo loco singularis & propria illius temporis. Nam quemadmodum Deus populo suo imperauit sacrificia, quæ apud Ægyptios abominationi erant. e.g. boum, ouium, caprarum, turturū &c. quæ apud Ægyptios pro diis habebantur: sic etiam in ratione victus & conuersationis, cum ea nominatim prohibuit, quæ apud Ægyptios finitimasque gentes licebant, tum vero cibum & tactum aut imperauit aut permisit eorum, quę apud illas gentes religio fuit tangere aut vesci: ac proinde singularis hæc fuit in contrariū plane professio, & finitimæ superstitionis detestatio. Sic e.g. Ægyptij vescebantur carne suilla, & quidem fere sola. At hanc Deus prohibet. Vide Theodoretum serm. 7. de Græcorum affectionum curatione. Ex his patet, inter alia quoque causam prohibitionis certorum ciborum fuisse noxam, quam adferunt humano corpori. Ad hygiasticam itaq; & hoc pertinet, non indifferenter vesci cibis.
units.tr: The Jews were therefore forbidden to eat blood, also for this reason: because God had reserved it for his sacrifices. And so that they might not be led by any occasion to eat the blood of sacrificed animals, he commanded in general that they should not eat any blood of animals. In this way he wished to cut off every opportunity for sinning and for breaking the laws. Similarly he also forbade the use of fat (Lev. 3), because he had reserved it for his sacrifices as something more excellent; also because he wished by this means to teach us that the skin is not to be cared for. From these things it is plain that the ceremonies divinely prescribed do not exclude a natural and moral cause. So in the matter of foods that were ceremonially unclean, God principally had this in view: that the Church should be distinguished in this way from the assemblies of the Gentiles. For just as the Ethiopians and Egyptians were once set apart from the Chaldeans, Jews and Greeks by their observances, so God wished his Church to be distinguished from all other nations by a singular observance. And this is indeed the common reason for which God prescribed to his people that distinction between clean and unclean foods. To this common and figurative cause there is added a particular one, both natural and moral. Moral: because, for example, the cleft hoof signifies discernment in sacred matters, and rumination sacred meditation, as the ancient Fathers observed. Natural: because partly nature shrinks from certain foods, and partly reason and experience confirm that the flesh of certain animals is unwholesome. To all these causes there is added last of all a singular cause peculiar to that time. For just as God commanded his people sacrifices that were an abomination among the Egyptians (for example of oxen, sheep, goats, turtledoves, etc., which the Egyptians held to be gods), so too in the matter of diet and way of life he expressly forbade those things which were permitted among the Egyptians and neighbouring nations, and either commanded or permitted the touching and eating of those things which those nations held it sinful to touch or eat. Thus this was a singular profession of the very opposite, and a detestation of the neighbouring superstition. For example, the Egyptians ate pork, and indeed almost only that. But God forbids this. See Theodoret, sermon 7, on the cure of the Greeks' afflictions. From these things it is plain that, among other things, the cause of the prohibition of certain foods was also the harm they bring to the human body. Therefore this also belongs to hygiene, not to eat foods indifferently.

units.la: XLIX.
units.tr: XLIX.

units.la: HISTORICA SACRA.
units.tr: Sacred History

units.la: I. Historica est doctrina de ratione scribendi & legendi historiam.
units.tr: I. History is the doctrine of the method of writing and reading history.

units.la: II. Historia est rerum gestarum narratio. Hæc tàm latè patet, quàm latè patent omnes artes & facultates. Sunt enim historiæ sacræ sive theologicæ, sunt iuridicæ, sunt medicæ, sunt philosophicæ, & hærursus physicæ sive naturales, politicæ sive ciuiles &c. Supellex itaque historica non est unius artis aut facultatis propria, sed cunctis disciplinis est apparata. Hoc vel inde videre est, quòd dantur historiæ sacræ & profanæ, universales & particulares, politicæ & ecclesiasticæ; item historiæ re-gnorum, familiarum, personarum, rerum, actionum, dictorum &c. quæ omnia per varias facultates & artes sunt sparsa.
units.tr: II. History is the narration of things done. It extends as widely as all the arts and disciplines do. For there are sacred or theological histories, there are legal, medical and philosophical histories, and again physical or natural, political or civil histories, and so on. The material of history therefore does not belong to one art or discipline alone, but has been prepared for all the disciplines. This can be seen from the fact that there are sacred and profane histories, universal and particular, political and ecclesiastical; likewise histories of kingdoms, families, persons, things, actions, sayings, etc., all of which are scattered through the various faculties and arts.

units.la: III. Historia consideratur in genere, vel in specie.
units.tr: III. History is considered either in general or in particular.

units.la: IV. In historia in genere spectantur duo: quomodo fit texenda & retexenda, seu scribenda & legenda.
units.tr: IV. Two things are looked at in history in general: how it is to be woven and unwoven, that is, written and read.

units.la: V. Leges scribendæ historiæ sic habent.
units.tr: V. The rules for writing history are as follows.

units.la: 1. In rebus sit varietas & veritas. Varietas, non infinita illa & vaga, sed astricta. Veritas, qua omnia commemorentur sincerè. 2. In stilo sit simplicitas: ne oratoria lumina ossiciant & obstruant lumini historico. 3. Historia, sive historico, duo fines debent esse propositi: unus est ratione rerum praeteritarum, ut illæ ab interitu vindicentur, & transmittantur ad posteros: alter est ratione lectorum, ut illi ædificentur. Utrumque finem eleganter expressit Cicero 2.de orat. his verbis: Historia est testis temporum, nuntia vetustatis, lux veritatis, vita memoria, magistra vita. 4. Historia scribantur vel ex publicis archiuis & instrumentis, vel ex propria experientia. Loquor hic de ordinario scribendi munere. Nam Moses, divinus ille historicus, scripsit extra ordinem, dictante Deo. 5. In historia accurate observentur ista tria: topographia, chronologia, & prosopographia, id est, annotatio recta loci, temporis, & personæ.
units.tr: 1. In matters there should be variety and truth. Variety not that boundless and vague kind, but a restrained one. Truth, so that everything is related sincerely. 2. In style there should be simplicity, so that the ornaments of oratory do not hinder and obstruct the light of history. 3. Two aims should be set before history, or the historian: one, with regard to the things of the past, that they may be saved from oblivion and handed down to posterity; the other, with regard to the readers, that they may be edified. Cicero (De oratore, book 2) expressed both aims elegantly in these words: History is the witness of the ages, the messenger of antiquity, the light of truth, the life of memory, the teacher of life. 4. History is written either from public archives and documents, or from one's own experience. I speak here of the ordinary office of writing. For Moses, that divine historian, wrote outside the ordinary course, at God's dictation. 5. In history the following three things are to be carefully observed: topography, chronology and prosopography, that is, the correct noting of place, time and person.

units.la: VI. Leges in lectione historiæ observentur istæ. 1. Historici authentici præferantur non-authenticis. Historia legantur, si fieri possit, in lingua originali. 3. Si videantur historiæ discrepare, tentetur conciliatio. Quòd si illa non possit locum habere, cogitetur regula: In rebus obscuris oportet sequi id, quod est minimum. 4. Historiæ legantur sine præiudicio. 5. In lectione historiæ attendantur circumstantiæ locorum, temporum, personarum &c. Hoc nisi fiat, sæpenumero accidet, vt historias damnemus falsitatis, quòd non quadrent ad nostram patriam & experientiam. 6. Analysis historicæ prudenter & accuratè instituatur. Pendet autem illa à methodo historicâ & circumstantiis. 7. In lectione historiarum oportet consicere animadversiones historicas, hoc est, axiomata & aphorismos certos, quibus possimus vti in praxi vitæ quotidianæ.
units.tr: VI. The following rules are to be observed in reading history. 1. Authentic historians are to be preferred to non-authentic ones. Histories should be read, if possible, in the original language. 3. If histories seem to disagree, an attempt at reconciliation should be made. But if that cannot be done, the rule should be borne in mind: in obscure matters one must follow what is least. 4. Histories are to be read without prejudice. 5. In reading history, attention should be paid to the circumstances of places, times, persons, etc. Unless this is done, it will very often happen that we condemn histories as false because they do not fit our own country and experience. 6. Historical analysis is to be undertaken prudently and carefully. This depends, however, on historical method and circumstances. 7. In reading histories it is necessary to make historical observations, that is, certain axioms and aphorisms which we can use in the practice of daily life.

units.la: VII. Historia in specie est diuina, vel human- a.
units.tr: VII. History in particular is either divine or human.

units.la: Illa habet Deum authorem, immediatè vel mediatè: hæc proficiscitur ab homine.
units.tr: The former has God as its author, either immediately or mediately; the latter proceeds from man.

units.la: VIII. Historia diuina siue sacra est αὐτόπιστος[?], id est, per se meretur fidem. Hæc itaque antefertur omnibus aliis historiis, neque ad illas exigatur. Institui quidem potest, & vero etiam debet, collatio: verùm ita, vt consensus nos confirmet, dissensio autem non perturbet.
units.tr: VIII. Divine or sacred history is self-credible [αὐτόπιστος], that is, it deserves belief in its own right. It is therefore preferred to all other histories and is not to be judged by them. A comparison may indeed be made, and indeed ought to be made, but in such a way that agreement confirms us and disagreement does not unsettle us.

units.la: IX. Historia diuina V. T. petatur ex libris canonicis. Quod attinet ad libros apocryphos, historia in ipsis prodita non est diuinæ, sed ecclesiasticæ authoritatis.
units.tr: IX. Divine history of the Old Testament is to be sought in the canonical books. As for the apocryphal books, the history related in them is not of divine but of ecclesiastical authority.

units.la: X. Historia diuina N. T. petatur ex libris euangelistarum & apostolorum. Quod attinet ad Canones apostolorum, Pastorem Hermetis, Narrationem Prochori & Lini, Opera Clementis Romani, & similia scripta, non existimandum est omnia illa esse γνῶσις[?]: & si quæ sint γνῶσις[?], non debent æquiparari diuinis. De euangelio Nicodemi, Bartholomæi, & similibus a- pocrypocryphis iam olim reiectis nihil attinet dicere.
units.tr: X. Divine history of the New Testament is to be sought in the books of the evangelists and apostles. As for the Canons of the Apostles, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Narrative of Prochorus and Linus, the works of Clement of Rome, and similar writings, it should not be supposed that all of them are knowledge [γνῶσις]; and if some of them are knowledge, they ought not to be equated with the divine writings. There is no need to say anything about the Gospel of Nicodemus, the Gospel of Bartholomew, and similar apocryphal writings, which were rejected long ago.

units.la: XI. Historia humana in solidum fidem meretur, si historiographus per omnes partes implesse suum munus deprehendatur. Officium istud in tribus est positum, diligentiâ, iudicio, & fide Diligentia poni debet in colligendâ scribendorum materiæ, vt proferantur illa, quæ digna sunt luce. Iudicio opus est, vt videat historicus quibus credat. Fides denique in eo spectatur, vt in narratione historiæ nuda veritas exponatur, siue illa, quæ gesta sunt, probentur scribenti, siue improbentur. Sed accingamur ad scriptionem systematis historiæ sacræ, idque in epitome historico-chronologica, item in prosopographiâ & topographiâ sacrâ. Priùs tamen indicemus modum Chronologiæ sacræ.
units.tr: XI. Human history deserves full credence if the historian is found to have discharged his office in every part. This office consists of three things: diligence, judgement, and good faith. Diligence must be employed in gathering the materials to be written up, so that those things worthy of the light are brought forth. Judgement is needed so that the historian sees whom he should believe. Finally, good faith is looked for in this: that in the narration of history the bare truth is set forth, whether the things that were done are approved or disapproved by the writer. But let us proceed to write out a system of sacred history, namely in a historico-chronological epitome, likewise in sacred prosopography and topography. First, however, we shall set out the method of sacred chronology.

units.la: L. CHRONOLOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: L. SACRED CHRONOLOGY.

units.la: I. CHronologia sacra est temporis notatio historica ex S. literis petita. Proinde, vt historia, sic etiam chronologia, ad varias artes & facultates pertinet. Cæterùm chronologia solet appellari alter historiæ oculus.
units.tr: I. Sacred chronology is the historical notation of time, drawn from the holy Scriptures. Accordingly, like history itself, chronology belongs to various arts and disciplines. It is commonly called the second eye of history.

units.la: II. Eius partes duæ sunt: prima de affectione temporis historici, altera de ipsius partitione. Cum partitione cohæret explicatio.
units.tr: II. It has two parts: the first concerns the attributes of historical time, the second its division. Explanation goes together with division.

units.la: III. Tempus historicum in sacris habet afsectionem analogam & anomalam.
units.tr: III. In the sacred writings, historical time has an analogical and an anomalous affection.

units.la: IV. Affectio analoga temporis sacri est partim ordo & duplicatio, partim rotundatio & variatio. Ordo temporis chronologici in Scriptura sacra est triplex, naturæ, dignitatis, & prudentiæ: siue, vt alii loquuntur, est ordo naturalis, personalis, & historicus. Ordo natura, seu generationis, est, cum id, quod natura & existentiâ est prius, priori loco explicatur. Talis ordo est Gen.1.&1.Chron.3.v.1.2.3.& alibi passim in historiâ V.& N.T.Ordo dignitatis est, cùm id quod dignius est, priorem locum obtinet, licet fuerit posterius naturâ. Sic Gen.48. v. 20. Ephraim praeponitur Manasse. Iunius, & alii putant talem quoque ordinem esse Gen.5.v.24. ubi tres filii Noë commemorantur: quasi Sem non fuerit primogenitus, sed dignitatis causâ ponatur primo loco. Sed infra patebit, ordinem illum esse naturæ. Ordo prudentiæ est, cùm illius rei nomen postremo loco ponitur, à quo historia proximè inceptura est: vt Gen.28.v.5. Esau fratri suo Iacobo postponitur: quia versu 6. historia Esaui sequitur, ad quam transitus ita paratur. Ita 1. Chron.1.v. 27. Ismaelprimogenitus postponitur Isaaco, quia vers. 28. sequitur genealogia Ismaelis. Sic Matth.1.v.1. Abraham postponitur Dauidi, quia v. 2, traditur genealogia ex Abrahami linea.
units.tr: IV. The analogical affection of sacred time consists partly in order and duplication, partly in rounding and variation. The order of chronological time in Scripture is threefold: of nature, of dignity, and of prudence; or, as others put it, it is natural, personal and historical order. The order of nature, or of generation, is when that which is prior in nature and existence is explained in the prior place. Such an order is found in Gen. 1 and 1 Chron. 3:1, 2, 3, and elsewhere throughout the history of the Old and New Testaments. The order of dignity is when that which is more worthy takes the prior place, although it is later in nature. Thus in Gen. 48:20, Ephraim is placed before Manasseh. Junius and others think that Gen. 5:24, where the three sons of Noah are mentioned, is also such an order, as if Shem were not the firstborn but were put first for the sake of dignity. But it will be shown below that this order is that of nature. The order of prudence is when the name of a thing is placed in the last position, which is the one with which the history is about to begin next: as in Gen. 28:5, Esau is placed after his brother Jacob, because in verse 6 the history of Esau follows, and the transition is prepared for it in this way. So in 1 Chron. 1:27, Ishmael, the firstborn, is placed after Isaac, because in verse 28 the genealogy of Ishmael follows. Likewise in Matt. 1:1, Abraham is placed after David, because in verse 2 the genealogy is traced from the line of Abraham.

units.la: Duplicatio temporis est, cùm Scriptura partem temporis præteriti extremam miscet cum primâ futuri. Sic Christus dicitur post tres dies, item tertio die resurrexisse, passim in N.T. At non fuit in sepulchro nisi horis 36. vel circiter. Si duplices partem istam temporis mediam, constabit sibi assertio euangelistarum. Huiusmodi duplicatio in annis regum Iudæ & Israëlis sæpe est adhibita. Rotunditas temporis est, quâ numero vel tempori aliquid additur vel detrahitur, vt fiat numerus exactus, hoc est, definens in ciphram siue denarium. Sic Num. 14. v.34. dicitur: Feretis pœnam iniquitatum vestrarum 40.annos. Hæc verba Israëlitis dicta sunt anno secundo post exitû. Proinde pœnam tulerunt annos 38. ab illo oraculo. Vtitur ergo Spiritus sanctus numero rotundato. Variatio temporis est duplex. Primò, tempus in supputationibus sumitur pro tempore vel completo, vel non completo, sed adhuc currente. Pro completo, vt 1.Reg.15.v.9. Anno itaq; vigesimo Ieroboami regi Israëlis regnauit Asa super Iudam: anno scilicet 20.completo. Nam in eodem cap. v. 25. Nadab dicitur successisse Ieroboamo, anno secundo Asæ. Pro non-completo: vt eodem cap.v.1. dicitur, Decimooctauo anno Ieroboam regnauit Abia super Ierusalem: scil. 18. anno Ieroboami currente vel incipiente coepit regnare Abia. Nam filius eius Asa coepit anno 20. Ieroboami, ut paulo ante est dictum. Deinde initiū & finis temporis interdum inclusiue, interdum exclusiue ponitur in supputationibus: ut si conferas Matth.17.v.1. cum Luc.8.v.28. deprehendes, Matthæum loqui exclusiue, ita ut numeret sex dies intermedios, Lucam inclusiue, ita ut numeret octo dies, quibus primum illum, quo locutus erat Christus, & ultimum, quo transfiguratus est, comprehendit
units.tr: Duplication of time is when Scripture mingles the last part of past time with the first part of the future. Thus Christ is said to have risen after three days, and also on the third day, throughout the New Testament. Yet he was in the sepulchre only for thirty-six hours or thereabouts. If you count that middle part of time twice, the assertion of the evangelists will be consistent. This kind of duplication has often been used in the years of the kings of Judah and Israel. The rounding of time is when something is added to or taken away from a number or a period, so that the number becomes exact, that is, ends in a cipher or a ten. Thus Num. 14:34 says: You shall bear the punishment of your iniquities forty years. These words were spoken to the Israelites in the second year after the exodus. Therefore they bore the punishment thirty-eight years from that oracle. The Holy Spirit therefore uses a rounded number. Variation of time is twofold. First, in reckonings, a time is taken either as complete or as not complete but still running. As complete: thus 1 Kings 15:9: So in the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa reigned over Judah: namely, in the completed twentieth year. For in the same chapter, verse 25, Nadab is said to have succeeded Jeroboam in the second year of Asa. As not complete: thus in the same chapter, verse 1, it is said: In the eighteenth year of Jeroboam, Abijam reigned over Jerusalem: that is, Abijam began to reign in the eighteenth year of Jeroboam, which was running or just beginning. For his son Asa began in the twentieth year of Jeroboam, as was said a little earlier. Second, the beginning and end of a period are sometimes put in reckonings inclusively and sometimes exclusively. If you compare Matt. 17:1 with Luke 9:28, you will find that Matthew speaks exclusively, so that he counts the six intervening days, while Luke speaks inclusively, so that he counts eight days, including both the first day, on which Christ spoke, and the last, on which he was transfigured.

units.la: V. Affectio anomala, siue cryptica, tempo- ris sacri, est partim prolepsis, partim anace-
units.tr: V. The anomalous, or cryptic, affection of sacred time is partly prolepsis and partly anacephalaeosis.

units.la: phalæosis. Prolepsis, seu anticipatio, historica, est narratio posterioris priori loco. Dici potest ὕστερον πρότερον, posterius prius. Prolepsis ista est nominum, vel rerum gestarum. Prolepsis nominum est, cùm nomina longè post rebus imposita, vsurpantur in prioribus historiis. Talis anticipatio est Gen.14.v.7. vbi fit mentio agri Amalekitarum: cùm Amalek tum temporis nondum fuerit natus, vt constat ex Genef.36.v.12. Sic Gen.21.verf.14. Hagar dicitur vagata per desertum Beerseba, id est, putei iuramenti: quod nomen postea impositum est illi loco. Pertinet huc regula vsitata: Historici sacri sæpe narrant vetera nominibus sui temporis. Prolepsis rerum gestarum est, cùm res posteriùs gestæ admiscentur prioribus historiis. Hanc rem confirmant doctores Hebræorum vulgari dicto in commentariis, dicentes, nó esse prius aut posterius in Scriptura, id est, nó semper rationem temporis accuratè in historiis sacris obseruari. Mutatur autem ratio temporis ad commoditatem historiæ; siue memoriam legentium iuuari oporteat, siue ordinem argumetorum obseruari, siue causas, quamuis antecedentes, post factorum historiam explicari. Exemplum huius prolepseos est Iohan.11.verf.2. Maria autem ea erat, qua vnxit Dominum. At sequenti demum capite recensetur ista vnctio. Est itaque postero-prius. Anacephalæosis, seu recapitulatio, historica, est duplex. Primò scriptores sacri loquuntur de rebus prisci secundùm sua tempora: ut, Petrus 1.epist.c.3. v.19. ait, Christum prædicasse spiritibus in carcere, h.e. illis hominibus, qui tempore Petri erant in carcere infernali. Deinde quædam perinde narrantur, quasi sequerentur in ordine temporis, quæ tamen ad priora pertinent. Hæc figura dici potest ὕστερον πρότερον[?], seu πρωθύστερον[?], prioposterius. Sic Gen.2. narratur creatio fœminæ, quasi facta sit post hexaëmeron. Sic historia Michæ & bellum Beniaminiticum, quæ contigerunt sub Pontificatu Pinehæ, attexuntur historiæ Simsonis & Eli, Iud.18.19.&20.
units.tr: Prolepsis, or historical anticipation, is the narration of a later event in an earlier place. It may be called hysteron proteron [ὕστερον πρότερον], "the later before the earlier." This prolepsis concerns either names or deeds. Prolepsis of names is when names given to things long after are used in earlier histories. Such an anticipation is found in Gen. 14:7, where mention is made of the field of the Amalekites, although Amalek had not yet been born at that time, as is clear from Gen. 36:12. So in Gen. 21:14, Hagar is said to have wandered in the desert of Beersheba, that is, the well of the oath, a name given to that place afterwards. The common rule applies here: Sacred historians often relate old things in the names of their own time. Prolepsis of deeds is when things done later are mixed into earlier histories. The doctors of the Hebrews confirm this by a common saying in their commentaries, saying that there is no before or after in Scripture, that is, that the order of time is not always strictly observed in sacred histories. The order of time is altered for the convenience of the history, whether it is necessary to help the memory of the readers, or to preserve the order of the arguments, or to explain causes, even antecedent ones, after the narrative of the deeds. An example of this prolepsis is John 11:2: Now it was Mary who anointed the Lord. Yet this anointing is recounted only in the following chapter. It is therefore later but placed first. Anacephalaeosis, or historical recapitulation, is twofold. First, the sacred writers speak of ancient things according to their own times: thus Peter, 1 Peter 3:19, says that Christ preached to the spirits in prison, that is, to those men who in Peter's time were in the prison of hell. Second, some things are related as if they followed in the order of time, although they belong to earlier events. This figure may be called hysteron proteron [ὕστερον πρότερον], or prohysteron [πρωθύστερον], "prior-later." So Gen. 2 narrates the creation of woman as if it took place after the six days of creation. So the history of Micah and the Benjaminite war, which happened under the high priesthood of Phinehas, is attached to the histories of Samson and Eli, Judg. 18, 19 and 20.

units.la: V I. Partitio temporis sacri est apud varios varia. Nos constituimus decem intervalla temporis in Scripturis definiti inde à creatione mundi usque ad terminum à Daniele & Iohanne in Apocalypsi prædictum. Hæc intervalla volumus esse studiolo sacrarum literatum veluti prædicamenta historico-chronologica, hoc modo.
units.tr: V I. The division of sacred time varies among different writers. We set up ten intervals of time defined in the Scriptures, from the creation of the world down to the terminus foretold by Daniel and John in the Apocalypse. We wish these intervals to serve students of the sacred letters as historical-chronological categories, in the following manner.

units.la: Primum intervallum est à creatione mundi usque ad diluvium, annorum 1656. Gen.7.v.6. Noah autem natus erat sexcentos annos, cum diluvium accidit, aquis exundantibus super terram. Et ibid.vers.11. Anno sexcentesimo vitæ Noachi &c. diffiderunt se omnes fontes abyssi magnæ. Iste annus Noachi fuit à conditu orbis 1656. ut patet è Genes.5.
units.tr: The first interval is from the creation of the world to the flood, 1656 years. Gen. 7:6: Noah was six hundred years old when the flood came, with waters overflowing the earth. And in the same place, verse 11: In the six hundredth year of the life of Noah etc., all the fountains of the great deep were broken up. That year of Noah was 1656 from the founding of the world, as is clear from Genesis 5.

units.la: Secundum intervallum est à diluvio usque ad promissionem Abrahamo factam, annorum 367. Nam promissio ista incidit anno M.2023. Gen.12.v.1. Erat autem Abramnatus septuaginta quinque annos, cum proficisceretur Charane. Iste annus fuit 2023. à conditu mundi, ut patet ex Genes.11.v.10. & seqq.
units.tr: The second interval is from the flood to the promise made to Abraham, 367 years. For that promise fell in the year of the world 2023. Gen. 12:1: Now Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran. That year was 2023 from the founding of the world, as is clear from Genesis 11:10 and following.

units.la: Tertium intervallum est à promissione Abrahamo factâ usque ad exitum ex Ægypto, annorum 430. Exod.12.v.40. 41. Incolatus autem Israelitarum, quo commorati sunt in Ægypto, fuit 430. annorum. Fuit verò exactis 430. annis; fuit, inquam, eodem ipso die, vt egrederentur omnes exercitus Iehoua e terrâ Ægypti. Anni isti peregrinationis, incolatus & seruitutis numerandi sunt à septuagesimo quinto anno ætatis Abrahami, quo ille accepit promissionem. Gal.3.v.17.
units.tr: The third interval is from the promise made to Abraham to the exodus from Egypt, 430 years. Exod. 12:40, 41: Now the sojourning of the children of Israel, who dwelt in Egypt, was 430 years. And it came to pass at the end of the 430 years, on the very same day, that all the hosts of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt. These years of pilgrimage, sojourning and servitude are to be counted from the seventy-fifth year of Abraham's age, when he received the promise. Gal. 3:17.

units.la: Quartum interuallum est ab exitu ex Ægypto vsque ad templum Salomonis inchoatum siue fundatum, annorum 479. Nam anno ab exitu quadringentesimo octauo (ineunte) templum fuit fundatum. 1.Reg. 4.v.1. Deinde fuit anno quadringentesimo octauo ab egressu Israelitarum è terra Ægypti, anno quarto regni Salomonis, vt aedificare inciperet domum Iehoua. Incidit autem is annus in ann. M.2932.
units.tr: The fourth interval is from the exodus from Egypt to the beginning or foundation of the temple of Solomon, 479 years. For the temple was founded in the (beginning of the) four hundred and eighty-first year after the exodus of the Israelites from the land of Egypt. 1 Kings 6:1: And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign, that he began to build the house of the Lord. That year fell in the year of the world 2932.

units.la: Quintum interuallum est à fundatione templi ad captiuitatem Babylonicam, annorum 418. Ier.29.v.10. Sic enim ait Iehoua: nam vbi implebuntur Babylonis septuaginta anni, visitabo vos, & praestabo erga vos verbum meum illud optimum, reducendo vos in hunc locum. Ex quibus verbis colligere licet, captiuitatem Babylonicam arcessendam esse à deportatione Iechoniæ, quæ incidit in annū mundi 3350. Ergo sunt anni 418.à fundatione templi vsque ad initium captiuitatis Babylonicæ. Si malis, hoc interuallum extende vsq; ad excidium templi, quod incidit an.M.3360. Atque ita augebitur hoc interuallum 10.annis, vt fit annorum 428.
units.tr: Quintum interuallum is from the foundation of the temple to the Babylonian captivity, 418 years. Ier.29.v.10.
