He was taken up by Paul and Barnabas for the ministry of the gospel and preached with them here and there. Finally he was made bishop of the church of Alexandria, and from Egypt as far as Pentapolis he taught the gospel in the neighbouring places all round.

units.la: 356. Lucas, natione Antiochenus, professione medicus, fuit sectator Pauli, & omnis peregrinationis eius comes. Scripsit Euangelium & Acta apostolorum.
units.tr: Luke, a native of Antioch and by profession a physician, was a follower of Paul and companion of all his journeys. He wrote the Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.

units.la: 357. Barnabas, hoc cognomentum accepit ab apostolis, lis, quòd esset beneficus erga ecclesiam, Act. 4. v. 36. 37. Fuit Leuita, nomine Ioseph, domo Cyprius. Fuit socius Pauli fidissimus.
units.tr: Barnabas received this surname from the apostles because he was generous towards the church (Acts 4:36-37). He was a Levite, named Joseph, and a Cypriot by birth. He was Paul's most faithful companion.

units.la: 358. Tres fuerunt sectæ Iudæorum præcipuæ, Pharifæi, Sadducæi, & Esseni: Josephus affirmat tres illas sectas, siue, vt ipse appellat, φιλοσοφίας, cognitas fuisse Iudæis ἐκ τοῦ πάνυ ἀρχαίου, a temporibus admodum antiquis. Et verisimile est synagogam templi secundi, simulac desierunt prophetæ, cepisse diuidi in sectas, forte circa annum mundi 3600, & deinceps, inprimis an. 3700. Nam Sadducæi coeperunt authore Sadoco, Pharifæi, Baitho, qui duo fuerunt discipuli Antigoni Socnæi, circa annum mundi 3720. Porrò ex tribus illis sectis, fato omnia tribuebant Esseni; libero arbitrio Sadducæi, fatum inane esse nomen sine re affirmantes. Pharifæi mediam viam sunt ingressi: fato quidem fieri omnia, sed ita, vt hominum liberum arbitrium non tollerent. Potentia Pharifæorum fuit magna: vtpote qui, teste Josepho, regibus potuerunt resistere, illosque bello lacessere. Ipsorum instituta, & veluti regulæ, erant, continentia siue virginitas, assiduitas orandi, afflictio corporis, vt ieiunium; decimatio supra legis præceptum, & obseruatio traditionum, quas Sadducæi repudiabant.
units.tr: There were three principal sects of the Jews: the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the Essenes. Josephus affirms that these three sects, or, as he calls them, philosophies [φιλοσοφίας], were known to the Jews from the very ancient past [ἐκ τοῦ πάνυ ἀρχαίου], from very ancient times. It is likely that the synagogue of the second temple, as soon as the prophets ceased, began to divide into sects, perhaps around the year of the world 3600, and afterwards, especially in 3700. For the Sadducees began under their author Sadoc, and the Pharisees under Baithus; these two were disciples of Antigonus of Socho, around the year of the world 3720. Further, of those three sects, the Essenes attributed everything to fate, while the Sadducees gave everything to free will, asserting that fate is an empty name without a reality. The Pharisees took a middle way: indeed everything happens by fate, but in such a way that they did not remove human free will. The power of the Pharisees was great, since, according to Josephus, they could resist kings and provoke them to war. Their institutions, and as it were their rules, were: continence or virginity, constancy in prayer, mortification of the body such as fasting, tithing beyond the precept of the law, and observance of traditions, which the Sadducees rejected.

units.la: 359. Scribæ fuerunt apud Iudæos ex antiquissimo instituto. Ipsi quippe erant, qui legem populo legebant, in templo & synagogis, ac, si opus esset, interpretabantur. Proptererea in euangeliis Νομικοί, Legis periti, & Νομοδιδάσκαλοι, Legis doctores, appellantur. E corpore Scribarum istorum legalium erant, qui sequerentur Pharisæos, qui Sadducæos, nec non qui Essenos. Errant itaque qui opinantur, Scribas fuisse alteram partem Pharisæorum.
units.tr: The Scribes were among the Jews from the most ancient institution. For they were the ones who read the law to the people in the temple and synagogues and, if there was need, interpreted it. Therefore in the Gospels they are called legal experts [Νομικοί] and teachers of the law [Νομοδιδάσκαλοι]. Of the body of those legal scribes some followed the Pharisees, some the Sadducees, and some likewise the Essenes. Therefore they are wrong who suppose that the Scribes were a second part of the Pharisees.

units.la: 360. Herodiani, Herodem Magnum pro[?] Messia habebant atque colebant.
units.tr: The Herodians held Herod the Great as the Messiah and worshipped him.

units.la: 361. Publicani, apud Romanos erant loco insigni & honesto, sed apud Iudæos non item. Nam eorum nomen, vt ex Iobo & prophetis apparet, erat iam tum terribile & exosum. Inprimis tempore Christi ob graues exactiones male audiebant: unde proverbium Iudæorum, Ne contingat tibi uxor e familia, in qua sit aliquis publicanus; quia sunt omnes publicani, i.e. latrones, scelerati, peccatores, ut nominantur Matth. 9. v. 10.
units.tr: The publicans held an honourable and distinguished place among the Romans, but not so among the Jews. For their name, as appears from Job and the prophets, was already then dreaded and hated. Especially at the time of Christ they were ill spoken of on account of heavy exactions, whence the Jewish proverb: "May a wife not come to you from a family in which there is a publican", because all publicans are robbers, wicked men and sinners, as they are called in Matthew 9:10.

units.la: 362. Augustus, Cæsar, edicto de censu promulgato, famulatur Christo, arcano divinæ providentiæ consilio. Oportebat nimirum Augustum, illum imperatorem & monarcham tantum, metatorem esse hospitii Christo Filio Dei in terras venturo. O infantem admirandum! cui necdum nato, primus omnium mortalium inseruit is, qui tunc, & fere ex omni memoria, in terris fuit monarcha longe maximus, longe potentissimus.
units.tr: Augustus Caesar, by an edict on the census that he published, served Christ by the hidden counsel of divine providence. It was fitting, surely, that Augustus, that emperor and sole monarch, should prepare a lodging for Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world. O admirable infant! For to him, not yet born, the first of all mortals to make arrangements was he who then, and nearly from all memory, was by far the greatest and most powerful monarch on earth.

units.la: 363. P. Sulpitius Quirinus, ab Augusto missus fuit ad censum agendum, quod fuit munus præsidum extraordinarium, & ad ius dicendum provinciæ, quod erat ordinarium præsidum officium.
units.tr: P. Sulpicius Quirinus, sent by Augustus to conduct the census, which was an extraordinary office of governors, and to administer justice in the province, which was the ordinary duty of governors.

units.la: 364. Pontius Pilatus, fuit procurator Iudææ, missus a Tiberio: Antonius Felix, a Claudio: Porcius Festus, a Nerone. Pilatus præsedit annis fere decem: & circiter annum ipsius quartum Christus est passus.
units.tr: Pontius Pilate was procurator of Judea, sent by Tiberius; Antonius Felix by Claudius; Porcius Festus by Nero. Pilate presided for almost ten years, and in about his fourth year Christ suffered.

units.la: 365. Lysanias, est nomen tetrarchæ. Fuerunt autem diversis temporibus tres Lysaniæ, eiusdem principatus tetrarchæ. Primus Lysanias ab Antonio factus est tetrarcha sive regulus Iturææ, sedemque suam collocavit Abilæ, urbe Syriæ. Hic mox ab Antonio est interfectus, in gratiam Cleopatræ. Ab illius morte usque ad 15 annum Tiberii intercedunt anni circiter 63. Secundus Lysanias, fuit primi illius filius, qui patri successit. Hunc excepit Zenodorus quidam, de quo vide Topographiam num. 94. Tertius Lysanias eadem tetrarchia fuit donatus ab Augusto vel Tiberio. Et hic est, quem Lucas cap. 3. appellat tetrarchā Abilenæ, & anno 15 Tiberii vixisse, atque illi parti Cœlesyriæ esse dominatum ostendit.
units.tr: Lysanias is the name of a tetrarch. There were, however, at different times three Lysanias, tetrarchs of the same principality. The first Lysanias was made tetrarch, or petty king, of Ituraea by Antony, and established his seat at Abila, a city of Syria. He was soon put to death by Antony to gratify Cleopatra. From his death to the fifteenth year of Tiberius there lie about 63 years. The second Lysanias was the son of that first one, and succeeded his father. After him came a certain Zenodorus, on whom see the Topography, no. 94. The third Lysanias was granted the same tetrarchy by Augustus or Tiberius. This is the one whom Luke, chapter 3, calls tetrarch of Abilene, and he shows that this man lived in the fifteenth year of Tiberius and ruled that part of Coele-Syria.

units.la: 366. Caiaphas, totos annos septem fuit Pontifex Maximus, & aliquanto amplius. Annas, qui Caiphæ iungitur, fuit ipsius vicarius. Nam Pontifex Maximus habebat suum vicarium, multis de causis, quas inter præcipua fuit feminis profluuium inter dormiendum. Ex omnibus enim pollutionibus huius præcipua semper à Iudæis habita est ratio, maximè à Pontifice Maximo.
units.tr: Caiaphas was high priest for seven full years and a little more. Annas, who is joined with Caiaphas, was his deputy. For the high priest had a deputy for many reasons, chief among which was a nocturnal emission of semen during sleep. For among all the pollutions, this one was always the chief one taken into account by the Jews, especially by the high priest.

units.la: 367. Iudæi, disparabantur posterioribus temporibus in Ἑλληνικῶς[?], Græcanicos, & Ἑβραϊκούς[?], Hebræos. Illi Biblia tantùm legebant Græcè, hi Hebraicè. Aliam Iudæorum distinctionem vide paulò post, num. 397.
units.tr: The Jews were in later times distinguished as Grecians [Ἑλληνικούς] and Hebrews [Ἑβραϊκούς]. The former read the Bible only in Greek, the latter in Hebrew. For another distinction of the Jews, see a little later, no. 397.

units.la: 368. Lazarus, significat inopem, seu ἀβοήθητον[?], qualis fuit mendicus ille Luc. 16. Fuit & alius hoc nomine, frater Mariæ & Marthæ, Iohann. 11.
units.tr: Lazarus means one in need, or helpless [ἀβοήθητον], such as that beggar in Luke 16. There was also another of this name, the brother of Mary and Martha, John 11.

units.la: 369. Magdalena, fuit fœmina, è quâ Christus eiecit septem dæmonia, quæq; fidelem Christo nauauit operam in vitâ & morte ipsius.
units.tr: Magdalene was a woman from whom Christ cast out seven demons, and who faithfully served Christ in his life and in his death.

units.la: 370. Maria, fuit nomen multis mulieribus commune: puta virgini beatæ, de quâ num. 346: Magdalenæ, de quâ paulò ante num. 369: sorori Mariæ virginis, de quâ num. 345: sorori Marthæ, de quâ Iohan. 11: item matri Marci, Act. 12: denique matronæ Romanæ, Rom. 16.
units.tr: Mary was a name common to many women: for instance, the blessed Virgin, of whom see no. 346; Magdalene, of whom see just above, no. 369; the sister of the Virgin Mary, of whom see no. 345; the sister of Martha, of whom see John 11; likewise the mother of Mark, Acts 12; and finally a Roman matron, Romans 16.

units.la: 371. Martha, œconoma fuit bona, Christo dilecta unà cum sorore Mariâ & fratre Lazaro.
units.tr: Martha was a good housekeeper, beloved of Christ together with her sister Mary and her brother Lazarus.

units.la: 372. Simon, fuit nomen multis commune: puta Petro apostolo, Matth. 4: Cananitæ, idem apostolo, Matth. 10: Pharisæo cuidam Hierosolymitano, Luc. 7: leproso cuidâ, Marc. 14: Cyrenæo cuidam, Matth. 27: alutario Ioppensi, Act. 10: prophetæ & doctori Antiocheno, Act. 13: denique infami & famoso mago, Act. 8.
units.tr: Simon was a name common to many: for instance, Peter the apostle, Matthew 4; the Cananaean, the same apostle, Matthew 10; a certain Pharisee of Jerusalem, Luke 7; a certain leper, Mark 14; a certain Cyrenian, Matthew 27; a tanner of Joppa, Acts 10; a prophet and teacher of Antioch, Acts 13; and finally an infamous and notorious magician, Acts 8.

units.la: 373. Barabbas, fuit latro, quem Iudæi Christo præferunt in passione ipsius.
units.tr: Barabbas was a robber, whom the Jews preferred to Christ at his passion.

units.la: 374. Iosephus Arimathæensis, honoratus senator, corpus Christi à Pilato petiit, & sindone inuolutum deposuit in monumento, quod erat excisum è petrâ.
units.tr: Joseph of Arimathea, an honoured senator, asked Pilate for Christ's body, and having wrapped it in a linen cloth, laid it in a tomb that had been hewn out of rock.

units.la: 375. Simeon, senex Hierosolymitanus, vir iustus & religiosus, Christum puerulum recepit in vlnas suas, & primus testimonium ipsi perhibuit.
units.tr: Simeon, an old man of Jerusalem, a just and devout man, received the little child Christ into his arms and was the first to bear witness to him.

units.la: 376. Anna, prophetissa, filia Samuelis, vidua octogintaannorum, puerulo Christo perhibuit testimonium secundum Simeonem.
units.tr: Anna, the prophetess, daughter of Samuel, a widow of eighty years, bore witness to the infant Christ after Simeon.

units.la: 377. Nazarenus, est qui in oppido Nazareth natus, vel educatus est. Ita Christus propter educationem in oppido Nazareth fuit appellatus Nazarenus. Quod Matthaeus c.2.ait praedictum esse à propheta. Quo vero propheta? Resp. Ex Esaiae c.11. hoc debet exponi, itemque ex Zach.11. Etsi enim verbis nusquam scriptum legitur, Christum vocatum iri Nazarenum: inuenitur tamen ἀλλὰ τῶν γεγραμμά[?]τῶν κειμένων, vt loquitur Chrysostomus, id est, rebus[?] ipsis expressum. Nam Esaias expresse Messiam vocat Netser, id est, florem, siue surculum. Quo facit illud Hieroymi ad Marcellam: Ibimus ad Nazareth, & iuxta interpretationem nominis, eius florem videbimus. In loco Zachariae expressis verbis dicitur, nomen Messiae fore Germen. Etsi autem nomina sunt diuersa, surculus, flos, & germen: sunt tamen significatione communia, cuiusmodi nomina saepe solet permutari, vt alterum pro altero ponatur, per metalepsin duplicem, vel etiam triplicem. Porrò Christiani primitus vocabantur à Christo Nazareni, per ludibrium, Act. 24.v. 5. Quàm despecta fuerit vrbs Nazareth, vide Iohan.1.verf. 47.
units.tr: Nazarene is one who was born or brought up in the town of Nazareth. Thus Christ was called a Nazarene on account of his upbringing in the town of Nazareth, which Matthew, chapter 2, says had been foretold by a prophet. Which prophet? Answer: This ought to be explained from Isaiah, chapter 11, and likewise from Zechariah 11. For although it is nowhere written in words that Christ would be called a Nazarene, it is nevertheless found in the things themselves [ἀλλὰ τῶν γεγραμμένων], as Chrysostom puts it, that is, expressed in the things themselves. For Isaiah expressly calls the Messiah Netser, that is, a flower or a shoot. To this agrees that saying of Jerome to Marcella: "We shall go to Nazareth, and according to the interpretation of the name we shall see its flower." In the passage of Zechariah it is said in express words that the name of the Messiah will be Branch. Although the names are different, shoot, flower and branch, they are nevertheless common in meaning; names of this kind are often wont to be interchanged, so that one is put for another, by a double or even triple metalepsis. Further, Christians were at first called Nazarenes after Christ, in mockery, Acts 24:5. How despised the town of Nazareth was, see John 1:47.

units.la: 378. Galilaeus, est qui ex Galilaea oriundus est. Hoc nomine Christus saepe appellatur, vtpote qui in Galilaea à teneris fuit versatus, ibique coepit praedicare verbum euangelii, & discipulos suos ibidem vocauit, qui & ipsi fere Galilaei erant. Post suam resurrectionem, in Galilaea instituit ministerium noui testamenti, Matth. 28.
units.tr: 378. Galilean means a native of Galilee. Christ is often called by this name, since he spent his early life in Galilee, began there to preach the gospel, and called his disciples there, who were themselves mostly Galileans. After his resurrection he established the ministry of the New Testament in Galilee, Matt. 28.

units.la: 379. Zacchaeus, fuit magister siue praefectus publicanorum. Erant enim publicani in societates distributi, vt ex Cicerone apparet. Zacchaeus putatur fuisse gentilis. Sed sine idoneo argumento.
units.tr: 379. Zacchaeus was the master or chief of the tax collectors. For the tax collectors were organised into companies, as is clear from Cicero. Zacchaeus is thought to have been a Gentile, but without a sound argument.

units.la: 380. Nathanael, oriundus è Cana Galilaeae, fuit Israelita simplex & candidus; quo elogio Christus ipsum ornauit, Iohan. 1.
units.tr: 380. Nathanael, a native of Cana in Galilee, was a plain and sincere Israelite, and Christ honoured him with this praise, John 1.

units.la: 381. Nicodemus, erat Pharisaeus, honores seu magistratū gerens in populo Judaico, magnæ vir eruditionis, sed in mysteriis euangelii talpâ cæcior. Institutus fuit à Christo, quem etiam dilexit post mortem, curando ipsius sunus.
units.tr: 381. Nicodemus was a Pharisee who held office or magistracy among the Jewish people, a man of great learning, but in the mysteries of the gospel blinder than a mole. He was taught by Christ, whom he also loved after his death, caring for his body.

units.la: 382. Joseph, cognomento Barsabas & Justus, ab apostolis statuitur unà cum Matthiâ coram facie Dei, ut alteruter in locum Judæ Iscariotis substituatur. Præmissis precibus sors cecidit super Matthiam.
units.tr: 382. Joseph, surnamed Barsabas and Justus, was set up by the apostles together with Matthias before the face of God, so that one of the two might be substituted in the place of Judas Iscariot. After prayer the lot fell on Matthias.

units.la: 383. Ananias, & Sapphira uxor eius, peccant sacrilegio, diffidentiâ & hypocrisi, dum prædium Deo consecrant, & postea partem pretii separant, illudque dissimulant. Quâ de causâ subitò exanimati sunt uterque.
units.tr: 383. Ananias and his wife Sapphira sinned by sacrilege, distrust and hypocrisy, when they consecrated an estate to God and afterwards kept back part of the price and concealed it. For this reason both were struck dead at once.

units.la: 384. Gamaliel, Pharisæus fuit magnæ doctrinæ & existimationis, præceptor Pauli apostoli.
units.tr: 384. Gamaliel, a Pharisee, was a man of great learning and reputation, the teacher of the apostle Paul.

units.la: 385. Septem diaconi eliguntur ab ecclesiâ Hierosolymitanâ. Ex iis fuit Stephanus, protomartyr ecclesiæ ab apostolis plantatæ: item Philippus, qui etiam fuit euangelista: & Nicolaus, proselytus Antiochensis, à quo putantur orti Nicolaitæ, qui scorrationem in rebus adiaphoris numerabant: ita ut Deus permiserit è septem diaconis unum labi, quemadmodum unus è duodecim apostolis est lapsus. Verùm enimvero, quia legimus Act. 6. v. 3. apostolos jussisse, ut adhibitâ inspectione deligerentur viri μαρτυρουμένοι[?], & pleni Spiritu sancto & sapientiâ, non est verisimile Nicolaum diaconum esse authore impuri huius erroris, sed aliumaliquem, fœdum canemaut quiduis potius, quàm hominem.
units.tr: 385. The seven deacons were chosen by the church at Jerusalem. Among them was Stephen, the first martyr of the church planted by the apostles; also Philip, who was also an evangelist; and Nicolas, a proselyte of Antioch, from whom the Nicolaitans are thought to have sprung, who counted lewdness among indifferent things. So God allowed one of the seven deacons to fall, just as one of the twelve apostles fell. Yet since we read in Acts 6:3 that the apostles ordered men to be chosen after inspection, men of good report [μαρτυρουμένοι], full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, it is not likely that the deacon Nicolas was the author of this foul error; it was someone else, a foul dog or anything rather than a man.

units.la: 386. Antipas, fuit celebris martyr in primitivâ ecclesiâ,
units.tr: 386. Antipas was a famous martyr in the primitive church,

units.la: Apoc. 2.
387. Saulus, fuit nomen Pauli apostoli ante conversionem.
units.tr: 387. Saul was the name of the apostle Paul before his conversion.

units.la: 388. Candace, fuit regina Æthiopum, quam Strabo suâ ætate, imperante Tiberio, regnasse scribit, virilem sanè mulierem, sed altero captam oculo. Ab hâc, Candaces nomen, ut Plinius & Suidas scribunt, ad alias Æthiopum reginas derivatū est, & dignitatis haberi cœpit. Theologus gus quidam Hispanus pro reginâ Candace conuertit reginam de Candaciâ, prouinciæ, non fœminæ, Candaces vocabulum ratus.
units.tr: 388. Candace was a queen of the Ethiopians, whom Strabo, writing in his own age under the emperor Tiberius, says reigned: a manlike woman indeed, but blind in one eye. From her, as Pliny and Suidas write, the name Candace was transferred to other queens of the Ethiopians and came to be regarded as a title of dignity. A certain Spanish theologian translated "the queen of Candace" as "the queen from the province of Candacia", thinking Candace was the name of a province, not of a woman.

units.la: 389. Ananias, discipulus Christi apud Damascenos, mittitur ad Paulum recens conuersum, vt ipsum sanet & baptizet.
units.tr: 389. Ananias, a disciple of Christ among the Damascenes, is sent to Paul, newly converted, to heal him and baptise him.

units.la: 390. Æneas, domo Lyddensis, ægritudine paralyticus, ab annis octo, sanatur à Petro apostolo.
units.tr: 390. Aeneas, of Lydda, a paralytic for eight years, was healed by the apostle Peter.

units.la: 391. Tabitha, discipula Christi apud Ioppenses, ex morte suscitatur à Petro.
units.tr: 391. Tabitha, a disciple of Christ at Joppa, was raised from death by Peter.

units.la: 392. Cornelius, pius centurio ex cohorte Italicâ, Cæsareæ, conuertitur ad Christum cum vniuersâ familiâ.
units.tr: 392. Cornelius, a devout centurion of the Italian cohort at Caesarea, was converted to Christ with his whole household.

units.la: 393. Christiani, primùm ita à Christo appellati sunt Antiochiæ, discipuli à doctore, subditi à rege suo, clientes à domino.
units.tr: 393. Christians were first so called by Christ at Antioch: disciples from their teacher, subjects from their king, clients from their lord.

units.la: 394. Agabus, propheta prædicit famem, quæ postea secuta est sub Claudio: item vincula Pauli.
units.tr: 394. Agabus, a prophet, foretold the famine which afterwards came under Claudius, and also the chains of Paul.

units.la: 395. Manahen, collactaneus Herodis Antipæ, fit propheta & doctor ecclesiæ, Act. 13. Similiter Simeon Niger, & Lucius Cyrenæus, e quibus hic fuit cognatus Pauli, & euangelium docuit in Vindelicia, Rhætia, & prouinciis Danubio conterminis.
units.tr: 395. Manaen, foster-brother of Herod Antipas, became a prophet and teacher of the church, Acts 13. Similarly Simeon Niger and Lucius of Cyrene, of whom the latter was a kinsman of Paul, and taught the gospel in Vindelicia, Raetia and the provinces bordering on the Danube.

units.la: 396. Sergius Paulus, proprætor insulæ Paphi, vir prudens, conuertitur à Paulo apostolo, frustrà obsistete Barjesu, pseudoprophetâ & mago, qui etiam appellatus fuit Elymas, Act. 13.
units.tr: 396. Sergius Paulus, proconsul of the island of Paphos, a prudent man, was converted by the apostle Paul, when Barjesus, a false prophet and magician, who was also called Elymas, tried in vain to oppose him, Acts 13.

units.la: 397. Gentes, dicuntur, tum ij, qui adhuc sunt tales, tum isti, qui iam sunt conuersi ad fidem Christi, vt Gal. ii. v. 12. Paulus de Petro ait, μετὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν συνήσθιε, cum gentib. conedebat, Hic Paulus veros Christianos appellat Gentes, non ex eo quòd iam erant, sed quòd fuerant. Eodem sensu, ἀλλόφυλοι, alienigenæ dicuntur, qui vel non erant Iudæi, vel ex alienigenis facti erant Iudæi, ἰουδαϊσμένοι [?]. Posteriori sensu Herodes Magnus dicitur ἀλλόφυλος, alienigena, quia ex Idumæis in Iudæos transscriptus erat. Nam pater ipsius Antipater, & avus Antipas, ex Idumæis facti erant Iudæi, dæi, siue proselyti. Iudæi itaque sunt appellati, & qui verè nascebantur è semine Abrahami, & qui fiebant Iudæi, quos Hellenistæ vocabant proselytos: qui cæteris Iudæis in maximè principalibus iuribus & dignitatibus erant æquales. Hoc solum intererat, inter proselytum & antiquum Iudæum, quòd in synedrium proselytus adoptari non poterat: quia non nisi nobilissimos è sacerdotibus, Leuitis, & reliquo populo, atque in lege exercitatissimos in Synedrium allegebant. Porrò Iudæi appellatio aliquando latius capitur, aliquando angustius. Quando late accipitur, omnes complectitur eiusdem religionis societate iunctos, Hierosolymitanos, Galileos, Peraitas, Idumeos, Alexandrinos, & Babylonios, & omnes qui Philoni & aliis dicuntur οἱ ἐκ τῆς [illegible, ~12 letters], ex dispersione; quæ quidè dispersio contigit tempore captiuitatis Babylonicæ. Cofer Act.2. & Iacob.1. Quando angustius id nomen sumitur, ciues duntaxat Hierosolymitanos complectitur, & illas decem Toparchias, quæ Plinio enumerantur lib. 2. c. 14. & Iosepho lib. 3. belli cap. 4. vbi non decem, sed vndecim recensentur, in quarum medio vrbs sancta eminebat, vt in clypeo vmbilicus. Hinc apud Iosephum non semel opponuntur, ὁ γνή[?]ιος ἐξ αὐτῆς Ἰουδαίας λαός, germanus & purus putus Iudaeorum populus, in ipsâ Iudæâ sic proprie dictâ, vrbe inquam & Toparchiis Hierosolymorum natus, & cæteri Iudæi, putà Galilæi, Idumæi, Hierichuntini &c. Sic sæpe in N. T. Iudæa angustâ significatione capitur, vt Luc.11.verfic.4.& cap.3. verf.1. & in capite 1.verf.5. vbi Herodes Magnus dicitur rex Iudææ, lata significatione accipiendum.
units.tr: 397. The Gentiles are called both those who are still such, and those who have now been converted to the faith of Christ. So in Gal. 2:12 Paul says of Peter that he ate with the Gentiles [μετὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν συνήσθιε], that is, he ate with the Gentiles. Here Paul calls true Christians Gentiles, not because they now are, but because they once were. In the same sense those are called foreigners [ἀλλόφυλοι], aliens, who either were not Jews, or who from being aliens had become Jews [ἰουδαϊσμένοι]. In the latter sense Herod the Great is called a foreigner [ἀλλόφυλος], an alien, because he had been transferred from the Idumeans to the Jews. For his father Antipater and his grandfather Antipas had become Jews from being Idumeans, that is, proselytes. Thus both those who were truly born of the seed of Abraham and those who became Jews, whom the Hellenists called proselytes, were called Jews, and the proselytes were equal to the other Jews in the most important rights and dignities. The only difference between a proselyte and an ancient Jew was that a proselyte could not be admitted to the Sanhedrin, since only the most noble of the priests, the Levites and the rest of the people, and those most skilled in the law, were chosen for it. Moreover, the name Jews is sometimes taken more broadly, sometimes more narrowly. Taken broadly, it embraces all joined in the fellowship of the same religion: the Jerusalemites, Galileans, Peraeans, Idumeans, Alexandrians and Babylonians, and all who by Philo and others are called those of the [...] dispersion [οἱ ἐκ τῆς …], that is, of the dispersion, which happened at the time of the Babylonian captivity. Compare Acts 2 and James 1. Taken more narrowly, the name embraces only the citizens of Jerusalem and those ten toparchies which are listed by Pliny, book 2, chapter 14, and by Josephus, Jewish War, book 3, chapter 4, where eleven rather than ten are counted, in the midst of which the holy city stood out like a navel on a shield. Hence in Josephus the phrase is often opposed: the genuine and pure Jewish people [ὁ γνήσιος ἐξ αὐτῆς Ἰουδαίας λαός], that is, those born in Judaea itself, properly so called, in the city and toparchies of Jerusalem, as against the other Jews, such as the Galileans, Idumeans, Jerichoites and so on. So in the New Testament Judaea is often taken in the narrow sense, as in Luke 1:5, 3:1 and 1:5, where Herod the Great is called king of Judaea, which must be understood in the broad sense.

units.la: 398. Theudas, & Iudas Galilæus, fuerunt duo seditiosi in Iudæâ, Act.5. Caufabonus obseruat, duos fuisse Theudas seditiosos; vnum ante Christum, alterum post, cùm res Imperatoris in Iudæâ procurabat Fadus.
units.tr: 398. Theudas and Judas the Galilean were two seditious men in Judaea, Acts 5. Casaubon observes that there were two seditious men called Theudas: one before Christ, the other after, when Fadus was managing the affairs of the emperor in Judaea.

units.la: 399. Alexander, Hymenæus, & Philetus, à fide desciuerant, docentes nullam esse resurrectionem, & conantes postliminio reuocare ceremonias Mosis. 1.Tim.1.
units.tr: 399. Alexander, Hymenaeus and Philetus had fallen away from the faith, teaching that there is no resurrection, and trying to bring back the ceremonies of Moses by a kind of return of rights. 1 Tim. 1.

units.la: Hermogenes, & Phygellus, fuerunt schismatici, 2.Ti-moth.1.
units.tr: Hermogenes and Phygellus were schismatics, 2 Tim. 1.

units.la: 401. Diotrephes, primatum affectabat in ecclesia, Iohan. epist.3.
units.tr: 401. Diotrephes aspired to primacy in the church, 3 John.

units.la: 402. Timotheus, patria Lystranus, natus patre Græco, matre Iudaeâ fideli, à pueris didicit sacras literas, ab aviâ Loide, & matre Eurica: fuit circumcisus à Paulo propter infirmos fratres, & ab eodem ascitus collega in euangelio Christi.
units.tr: 402. Timothy, a native of Lystra, was born of a Greek father and a faithful Jewish mother; from childhood he learned the holy letters from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. He was circumcised by Paul on account of the weak brethren, and was taken by him as a colleague in the gospel of Christ.

units.la: 403. Titus, natus ex Græcis parentibus gentilibus, conuertitur à Paulo, qui ipsum vocat filium & collegam suum. Docuit in Dalmatiâ.
units.tr: 403. Titus, born of Greek, Gentile parents, was converted by Paul, who calls him his son and colleague. He taught in Dalmatia.

units.la: 404. Silas, fuit allectus à Paulo symmysta & socius peregrinationis euangelicæ.
units.tr: 404. Silas was chosen by Paul as a fellow-worker and companion in his evangelical journeys.

units.la: 405. Iason, ciuis Thessalonicensis pius, hospitio excipit Paulum & Silam, eâque de causâ male mulctatur à suis conciuibus.
units.tr: 405. Jason, a pious citizen of Thessalonica, received Paul and Silas as guests, and for this reason was roughly punished by his fellow citizens.

units.la: 406. Dionysius Areopagita conuertitur à Paulo, Athenis: item Damaris, mulier, & alij quidam Athenienses.
units.tr: 406. Dionysius the Areopagite was converted by Paul at Athens; also Damaris, a woman, and certain other Athenians.

units.la: 407. Gallion, proconsul Achaiæ, reiicit Iudæos accusantes Paulum de religione.
units.tr: 407. Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, rejected the Jews who accused Paul concerning religion.

units.la: 408. Aquila, Iudæus Ponticus, & Priscilla, eius vxor, à Claudio vnà cum aliis Iudæis Româ eiecti, conferunt se Corinthum ad Christianos, ibiq; conficiunt tabernacula ad tempus. Inde se recipiunt Ephesum & Philippos, tandemq; redeunt Romam.
units.tr: 408. Aquila, a Jew of Pontus, and Priscilla, his wife, were expelled from Rome by Claudius along with the other Jews. They went to Corinth to the Christians and there made tents for a time. From there they went on to Ephesus and Philippi, and at last returned to Rome.

units.la: 409. Sosthenes, præfectus Synagogæ Corinthiacæ, conuertitur à Paulo, eaque de causâ cæditur ante tribunal Gallionis à Græcis.
units.tr: 409. Sosthenes, ruler of the Corinthian synagogue, is converted by Paul, and for that reason is beaten by the Greeks before the tribunal of Gallio.

units.la: 410. Apollos, Iudæus Alexandrinus, eloquentiâ & zelo insignis, conuertitur ad fidem Christi, & illam egregiè propagat.
units.tr: 410. Apollos, an Alexandrian Jew, distinguished by eloquence and zeal, is converted to faith in Christ and spreads it very effectively.

units.la: 411. Demetrius, aurifaber templi Dianæ apud Ephesios, concitat suos ciues aduersus Paulum. Fuit etiam pius quidam hoc nomine, cuius meminit Iohannes epist.3.
units.tr: 411. Demetrius, a silversmith of the temple of Diana among the Ephesians, stirs up his fellow citizens against Paul. There was also a godly man of this name, whom John mentions in 3 John.

units.la: 412. Eutychus, adolescens, Troade decidit ex fenestrâ, præ somno, in concione Pauli, qui ipsum ex morte su-scitat.
units.tr: 412. Eutychus, a young man, fell from a window at Troas, overcome by sleep, during Paul's sermon, and Paul raised him from the dead.

units.la: 413. Trophimus, civis pius Ephesi, Paulum comitatur ex Asiâ Hierosolymam. Docuit Arelate in Galliis.
units.tr: 413. Trophimus, a godly citizen of Ephesus, accompanies Paul from Asia to Jerusalem. He taught at Arles in Gaul.

units.la: 414. Lysias, cognomento Claudius, tribunus Hierosolymitanus, Paulum à Iudæis comprehensum, periculo eripit.
units.tr: 414. Lysias, surnamed Claudius, tribune at Jerusalem, rescues Paul from danger when he is seized by the Jews.

units.la: 415. Ananias, Pontifex Maximus, iubet cædere os Pauli apostoli. Tertullus, Ananiæ orator, est similis domino suo.
units.tr: 415. Ananias, the high priest, orders the mouth of the apostle Paul to be struck. Tertullus, Ananias's orator, is like his master.

units.la: 416. Aristarchus, fuit collega, comes & concaptivus Pauli.
units.tr: 416. Aristarchus was a colleague, companion and fellow prisoner of Paul.

units.la: 417. Iulius, centurio cohortis Augustæ, Cæsareæ, Paulum humaniter habitum perducit Romam.
units.tr: 417. Julius, centurion of the Augustan cohort at Caesarea, conveys Paul to Rome, treating him kindly.

units.la: 418. Publius, præfectus Melitæ, Paulum peramicè accipit hospitio.
units.tr: 418. Publius, governor of Melita, receives Paul very kindly into his home.

units.la: 419. Clemens, Pauli collega, docuit Metis.
units.tr: 419. Clement, a colleague of Paul, taught at Metz.

units.la: 420. Philemon, civis pius Thessalonicæ, fuit adiutor Pauli. Archippus, ibidem fuit Pauli commilito.
units.tr: 420. Philemon, a godly citizen of Thessalonica, was a helper of Paul. Archippus, likewise there, was a fellow soldier of Paul.

units.la: 421. Onesimus, servus Philemonis fugitivus, conciliatur hero literis Pauli.
units.tr: 421. Onesimus, the runaway slave of Philemon, is reconciled to his master through a letter of Paul.

units.la: 422. Electa, fuit fœmina præstantis dignitatis, cui Iohannes inscripsit secundam suam epistolam.
units.tr: 422. Electa was a woman of outstanding rank, to whom John addressed his second epistle.

units.la: 423. Gaius, patriâ Derbensis, incolatu Corinthius, fuit pietate & hospitalitate insignis. Huic inscripsit Iohannes tertiam suam epistolam.
units.tr: 423. Gaius, a native of Derbe, resident at Corinth, was distinguished for piety and hospitality. John addressed his third epistle to him.

units.la: 424. Itali, quorum fit mentio Hebr.13. erant sancti quidam in Italiâ, Iudæi procul dubio & Gentes.
units.tr: 424. The Italians, whom Hebrews 13 mentions, were certain saints in Italy, undoubtedly both Jews and Gentiles.

units.la: 425. Phœbe, Epenatus, & alij, quorum mentio fit Rom.16. & illi, qui recitantur 1. Cor.16. Phil.4. Coloss.4. 2. Tim.4.& Tit.3. hi, inquam, ex allegatis locis cognosci possunt quales fuerint.
units.tr: 425. Phoebe, Epaenetus, and the others whose mention is made in Rom. 16, and those who are listed in 1 Cor. 16, Phil. 4, Col. 4, 2 Tim. 4 and Tit. 3: these, I say, can be known from the passages cited, as to what sort of people they were.

units.la: Hic itaque manum de tabulâ prosopographiæ sacræ tollo, eamq; hoc duplici nomine tibi commendatam esse cupio: quòd videlicet insigniter faciat ad facilem recordationem historiarum per universum Scripturæ corpus sparsarum, quatenus quidem illæ unius fere semihorulæ patio in hoc compendio inspici possunt. Quò accedit varietas exemplorum, quibus tum in differtatione, tum in vitæ institutione potes uti, magno cum fructu. Habes enim hic exempla beneficentiæ, charitatis, castitatis, adulationis, ambitionis, animositatis, avaritiæ, crudelitatis, fortitudinis, &c, uno verbo, virtutum ac vitiorum omnium.
units.tr: Here, then, I lift my hand from the tablet of sacred prosopography, and I wish it to be commended to you for a twofold reason. First, it greatly aids the easy recall of the histories scattered through the whole body of Scripture, since these can be surveyed in this compendium in the space of about half an hour. Second, there is the variety of examples, which you may use with great profit both in disputation and in shaping your life. For here you have examples of beneficence, charity, chastity, flattery, ambition, animosity, avarice, cruelty, fortitude, etc.; in a word, of all virtues and vices.

units.la: LIII. TOPOGRAPHIA SACRA.
units.tr: LIII. SACRED TOPOGRAPHY.

units.la: I. TOpographia sacra est pars historiæ sacræ de locis illustribus, quorum passim in Scriptura sit mentio. Eiusmodi loca sunt regiones, urbes, flumina, montes, fontes, templa, & ædificia illustria. Cæterum topographia est alter historiæ oculus.
units.tr: I. Sacred topography is the part of sacred history that deals with the notable places mentioned here and there in Scripture. Such places are regions, cities, rivers, mountains, springs, temples and notable buildings. Topography, moreover, is the other eye of history.

units.la: II. Loca illustria in sacris sic habent, ferè iuxta seriem librorum sacrorum.
units.tr: II. The notable places in the sacred books are set out roughly in the order of the books.

units.la: 1. Eden, est Auranitis, suprema Chaldææ pars: de quâ vide supra in Geographicis. Ibidem vide quatuor flumina paradisi.
units.tr: 1. Eden is Auranitis, the uppermost part of Chaldaea; see on this above under the Geographica. There see also the four rivers of Paradise.

units.la: 2. Terra Nod, est regio Nomadum, in desertâ Arabiâ, Babyloniæ contermina. Quæ regio respectu terræ Canaan est ab oriente Edenem versus, ut est Gen.4.v.16.
units.tr: 2. The land of Nod is a region of nomads in the desert of Arabia, bordering on Babylonia. With respect to the land of Canaan, this region lies to the east, towards Eden, as in Gen. 4:16.

units.la: 3. Ararat montes, sunt celebres propter arcâ Noë, quæ ibi quieuit.Gen. 8. De his rectè scribit Epiphanius:Post diluuium, cùm consedisset arca in montibus Ararat, inter Armenios & Cardueos, nempe in monte quodam Loubar vocato, ibi primùm habitatio hominum post diluuium fieri cæpta est. Montes Cardueï etiam appellantur Gordyæi, Gordi, Cordæi, Cardyei, Cardueni, Gordochi, & Carduchi.
units.tr: 3. The mountains of Ararat are famous because of Noah's ark, which rested there (Gen. 8). Epiphanius writes rightly about them: "After the flood, when the ark had settled on the mountains of Ararat, between the Armenians and the Cardueans, namely on a certain mountain called Loubar, there the habitation of men after the flood first began." The mountains of the Carduchi are also called Gordyaei, Gordi, Cordaei, Cardyei, Cardueni, Gordochi and Carduchi.

units.la: 4. Babylon, antiquissima omnium civitatum à diluvio, habuit ambitum stadiorum 385, authore Strabone. Diodorus ex istâ summâ nonnihil detrahit, & 365 stadia tantum tribuit, secutus fidem Clitarchi, & quorundam, qui cum Alexandro Asiam traiecerunt.
units.tr: 4. Babylon, the most ancient of all cities since the flood, had a circuit of 385 stadia, according to Strabo. Diodorus subtracts something from this sum and allows only 365 stadia, following the account of Clitarchus and certain men who crossed into Asia with Alexander.

units.la: 5. Erec, Edessa vetus ad Euphratem, aliis Arecha in Susiana: Accad, Nisibis Mesopotamiae, in illa eius parte, quae corrupte dicitur A[?]abene, pro Accadene: & Calne, Callinisium, oppidum munitissimum: haec, inquam, oppida eiusdem cum Babylone sunt antiquitatis. Quae omnia condidit Nimrod, Gen.10.v.10.ibiq; primò regnavit.
units.tr: 5. Erech, old Edessa on the Euphrates, by others Arecha in Susiana; Accad, Nisibis of Mesopotamia, in that part of it which is corruptly called A?abene instead of Accadene; and Calneh, Callinicum, a very strongly fortified town. These towns, I say, are of the same antiquity as Babylon. Nimrod founded all of them, Gen. 10:10, and there he first reigned.

units.la: 6. Terra Sinear, est Mesopotamia & Chaldaea, ubi est mons Singaras, imminens Mesopotamiae, & abeo didum oppidum Singara.
units.tr: 6. The land of Shinar is Mesopotamia and Chaldaea, where there is the mountain Singara, overhanging Mesopotamia, and from it the town of Singara, named after it.

units.la: 7. Nineue, Ptolemaeo Ninus, aedificata à Nimrodo in Assyriâ ad Tigrim, fuit longè amplissima, & stupendi pene ambitus. Nam cùm forma esset ἐπιμήκης[?], id est, altera ex parte longior, ita ut duorum laterum inaequalium maius 150 stadia complecteretur, minus 90; totus utiq; ambitus (ἀμβ[?]τος) in unam summam collectus, 480 stadia, hoc est, 60 milliaria, efficiebat. Hinc illud apud Ionam, Nineven videl.esse civitatem longe maximam, triù dierum itinere, hoc est, in circuitu patere itinere triduì: Iter enim unius diei, 20 fere milliaribus aestimari solet. Huc eundem ambitum Plinius Babyloni assignat, quam 60 millia passuum muris amplexam scribit: & Herodotus lib.1. author est, ambitum quatuor laterum eius fuisse stadiorum 480. At Strabo lib.16. Geograph. aperte asseuerat, Nineven multo maiorem fuisse Babylone, quam ait non nisi 380 stadiorum ambitum habuisse. Diodorus quoque minorem habet summam, videl.stadiorum 360. Idem confirmat Clitarchus, & Ctesias Cnidius. Et ultimis hisce potiùs credendum fuerit. Nam & complures sunt, & plerique omnes oculati testes, & ad Scripturae authoritatem propiùs accedunt. Nam à Iona pronuntiatur Nineve fuisse urbs magna Deo, hoc est, summae & admirandae magnitudinis, qualia sunt diuina. Id autem elogium nulli urbium, praeterquam huic soli tribuitur. Dicamus itaque Nineven amplissimam omnium urbium, Babylonem antiquissimam fuisse omnium à diluuio ciuitatum. Gen.10.verf.10.12. Quod utrumque ibi testatur sacra historia.
units.tr: 7. Nineveh, called Ninus by Ptolemy, built by Nimrod in Assyria on the Tigris, was by far the largest, of almost incredible circuit. For since its shape was oblong [epimēkēs], that is, longer on one side, so that the larger of its two unequal sides took in 150 stadia and the smaller 90, the whole circuit, added together into one sum, made 480 stadia, that is, 60 miles. Hence that statement in Jonah, that Nineveh was a very great city, of a three days' journey, that is, that it extended in circuit for a three days' journey: for the journey of one day is usually reckoned at about 20 miles. Pliny assigns the same circuit to Babylon, which he writes was enclosed by walls of 60,000 paces; and Herodotus, Book 1, vouches that the circuit of its four sides was 480 stadia. But Strabo, Book 16 of the Geography, plainly asserts that Nineveh was much larger than Babylon, which he says had a circuit of no more than 380 stadia. Diodorus also gives a smaller sum, namely 360 stadia. Clitarchus and Ctesias of Cnidus confirm the same. Yet we ought rather to believe these last, for they are many, almost all of them eyewitnesses, and they come closer to the authority of Scripture. For Nineveh is pronounced by Jonah to have been "a great city to God", that is, of the greatest and most wonderful size, such as befits divine things. Moreover, this praise is given to no other city but this one alone. Let us say, then, that Nineveh was the largest of all cities, and Babylon the most ancient of all cities since the flood. Gen. 10:10, 12: sacred history bears witness to both.

units.la: 8. Rechobotha, Oroba ad Tigrim: Celachum, Calacines regionis in Assyriâ metropolis, vnde fuit inditum regionis nomen: & Resenum, Resaine[?] oppidum in Mesopotamiâ: hæc, inquam, Nimrod ædificauit post Nineuen, Genes.10. vers.11.
units.tr: 8. Rehoboth-Ir, Oroba on the Tigris; Calah, the metropolis of the region of Calachene in Assyria, whence the region took its name; and Resen, Resaina, a town in Mesopotamia. These, I say, Nimrod built after Nineveh, Gen. 10:11.

units.la: 9. Cananæa, hos terminos habebat tempore Mosis.
units.tr: 9. Canaan: it had these boundaries in the time of Moses.

units.la: Zidon[?] & Gaza, ciuitates maritimæ designabant angulos occidentales à septentrione ad meridiem: Sodoma, Gomorra, Adma, Zeboim & Leschah, angulos orientales à meridie septentrionem versus, contra Moabitarum & Ammonitarum agrum. Gen.10.v.19. Terminos, quibus Deus hanc terram circumscripsit, vide Num.34. Cæterum plerique ex Plinio, Herodoto & aliis historicis, tradunt, Nineuen Tigri fuisse impositam. Sed Strabo lib.16. docet, ad Lycum amnem hanc urbem fuisse extructam. Sunt etiam in sacris literis duo hi termini terræ sanctæ, Chamatha, & fluuius Sihor, nominatissimi: ille septentrionalis, hic australis. Chamatha, siue Emath, fuit urbs Cœlesyriæ, quæ tempore Hieronymi appellata fuit Epiphania. Eluuius Sihor, est riuus Nili, qui dictus est Sihor, teste Hieronymo, quòd aquas turbidas habeat. Atque hinc fortassis μέλας primò Græcis est dictus, & exinde Latinis Melo. Scriptura passim riuum istum Nili vocat נחל מצרים torrentem Ægypti, quandoque etiam flumen Ægypti; non quatenus erat communis limes (sic enim etiam terræ Israelis æquè torres esset ac diceretur) sed quatenus brachiolum erat Nili ipsius, cuius vniuersum corpus erat Ægypti proprium. Porrò idem ille riuus Nahal Mizraim, qui Ægypū à Phœnicia vel terrâ Israelis disterminabat, ab Amoso appellatur torrens deserti, cap.6. v.14: ob desertum nempe Sin, cuius extremitatem Austrum versus attingebat. Cur verò, inquiat aliquis, riuusille Nili, qui omnium proximus erat terræsanctæ, appellatur Esa.13.v.3. Sihor ille qui est ad faciem Ægypti? Resp. Proprium Nili nomen fuit Sihor, aut Sior, aut Sir. Quare idem quoque septem ipsius riuis commune fuisse oportet. Cōsentaneum igitur erat, vt suâ quisque appellatione designaretur, quam ei inderet vrbs aliqua primaria quam alluerat, aut ratio situs, aut quiuis alius respectus idoneus. Hinc factum, vt riuus ille qui omnium proximus erat terræ sanctæ, non Sihor simpliciter (commune quippe erat id & cæterorum nomen) sed Sihor ille qui est ad faciem Ægypti, hoc est, qui à terrâ Israel dirimit anteriorem partem Ægypti, appellaretur.
units.tr: Sidon and Gaza, maritime cities, marked the western corners from north to south; Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboim and Lasha marked the eastern corners from south towards the north, over against the territory of the Moabites and Ammonites. Gen. 10:19. For the limits with which God circumscribed this land, see Num. 34. Moreover, most writers, following Pliny, Herodotus and other historians, hand down that Nineveh was placed on the Tigris; but Strabo, Book 16, teaches that this city was built on the river Lycus. There are also in the sacred letters two most famous boundaries of the holy land, Hamath and the river Sihor: the former northern, the latter southern. Hamath, or Emath, was a city of Coele-Syria, which in Jerome's time was called Epiphania. The river Sihor is a branch of the Nile, and is called Sihor, according to Jerome, because its waters are muddy. Perhaps from this the Greeks first called it melas (black), and afterwards the Latins Melo. Scripture everywhere calls that branch of the Nile nahal Mizraim, "the torrent of Egypt", and sometimes also "the river of Egypt"; not because it was the common boundary (for then the land of Israel too would equally have been called a torrent of Egypt), but because it was an arm of the Nile itself, whose whole body belonged to Egypt. Further, that same stream, nahal Mizraim, which separated Egypt from Phoenicia or the land of Israel, is called by Amos "the torrent of the desert" (Amos 6:14), namely because of the desert of Sin, whose extremity it touched towards the south. But why, someone may ask, is that branch of the Nile, which was nearest of all to the holy land, called "Sihor which is before Egypt" (Isa. 13:3)? Answer: the proper name of the Nile was Sihor, or Sior, or Sir; hence it must be that this name was common to its seven branches. It was therefore fitting that each should be designated by its own appellation, given either by some principal city it watered, or by its situation, or by some other suitable circumstance. Hence it came about that the branch nearest of all to the holy land was called not simply Sihor (for that name was shared with the others too) but "Sihor which is before Egypt", that is, which divides the front part of Egypt from the land of Israel.

units.la: Quam quidem partem, faciem Ægypti appellat propheta, quoniam descendentibus è Cananæâ in Ægyptum, hæc primum ex aduerso statim occurrit, sequeque conspicien-dam præbet, reliquo totius prouinciæ velut corpore nondum apparente. Obiter hic obserua, Nilum ab Hebræo Nahal, unde Phœnicū & Ægyptiorum Neel & Neil, dictum esse, κατ' ἐξοχήν, q. d. fluuium principem.
units.tr: The prophet calls this part "the face of Egypt" because, to those going down from Canaan into Egypt, it is the first thing to present itself directly opposite, and it offers itself to be seen, while the rest of the whole province has not yet come into view as a body. Here note in passing that the Nile was called nahal by the Hebrews, whence the Phoenicians' and Egyptians' Neel and Neil, by way of eminence [kat' exochēn], that is, the chief river.

units.la: 10. Gaza, fuit vrbs Philistæorum satrapia nobilis. Confer Gen.10.v.19. Ios.13.v.3. 1.Sam.6.v.17.
units.tr: 10. Gaza was a noted satrapy of the Philistines. Compare Gen. 10:19; Josh. 13:3; 1 Sam. 6:17.

units.la: 11. Pentapolis fuit regiuncula quinque vrbium, Sodomæ, Gomorrhæ, Adamæ, Zeboim, & Segoris siue Zoharis, è quibus quatuor priores igne & sulphure à Deo sunt deletæ, quinta in gratiam Lothi fuit conseruata. Gen.19.v.22.24. Deut. 29.v.23. Hos.11.v.8. Est & alia Pentapolis, videl. tractus prope Cyrenem, complexus itidem quinque vrbes: nimirum Berenicen, Arsinoen, Ptolemaida, Apollouiam, & ipsam Cyrenen. Hæc differentiæ causâ vocatur: Pentapolis Cyrenaica.
units.tr: 11. Pentapolis was a small region of five cities: Sodom, Gomorrah, Adamah, Zeboim, and Segor or Zoar, of which the first four were destroyed by God with fire and brimstone, while the fifth was preserved for the sake of Lot. Gen. 19:22, 24; Deut. 29:23; Hos. 11:8. There is also another Pentapolis, namely a tract near Cyrene, likewise embracing five cities: Berenice, Arsinoe, Ptolemais, Apollonia, and Cyrene itself. This is called the Cyrenaic Pentapolis, for the sake of distinction.

units.la: 12. Mescha, est regio sub monte Masio, quæ pars est Amani montis, Gen.10.v.29. Masius autem & Mescha nomen habent à Mesch filio Aram.
units.tr: 12. Mesha is a region under Mount Masius, which is part of Mount Amanus, Gen. 10:29. Masius and Mesha have their names from Mesha, son of Aram.

units.la: 13. Sepharum, est oppidum, Ptolemæo Sipphara, ad Euphratem in Mesopotamiâ. Gen.10.v.29.
units.tr: 13. Sepharum is a town, called Sipphara by Ptolemy, on the Euphrates in Mesopotamia. Gen. 10:29.

units.la: 14. Montes orientis, in Scripturis dicuntur montana Chaldææ, quæ Euphratem excipiunt, & ab Arabiâ de-serta[?] sertâ Chaldæam dirimunt. Confer Gen.10.v.29. Num.23. vers.11.
units.tr: 14. The mountains of the East are, in the Scriptures, called the mountains of Chaldaea. They receive the Euphrates and separate Chaldaea from the Arabian desert. Compare Gen. 10:29; Num. 23:11.

units.la: 15. Vr, oppidum Chaldæorum, quod Ammianus eodem nomine appellat, & suo tempore castellum fuisse di-5 cit. Alii historici Orchoen vocant: unde tertia Chaldæorum disciplina fuit Orchoëna dicta, quòd nempe in hoc oppido nata, ibidemque plurimùm exercita esset.
units.tr: 15. Ur, a town of the Chaldeans, which Ammianus calls by the same name, and says was a castle in his time. Other historians call it Orchoe; whence the third school of the Chaldeans was called Orchoena, because, namely, it was born in this town and chiefly practised there.

units.la: 16. Haran, est oppidum præcipuum Mesopotamiæ, quod historici vocant Carras, iuxta quas Crassus, gurges 10 ille avaritiæ, cæsus interiit. In Scriptură V.& N.T. hoc oppidum est nobile habitatione Abrahami patris credentium.
units.tr: 16. Haran is the principal town of Mesopotamia, which historians call Carrhae, near which Crassus, that whirlpool of avarice, was slain and perished. In both the Old and New Testament this town is notable as the dwelling of Abraham, father of believers.

units.la: 17. Sichem, fuit vicina Samariæ, hodiè Neapolis. Iuxta hoc oppidum fuit fons Iacobi, colloquio Christi cum mu5 liere Samaritanâ celebris, Iohan. 4. Alio nomine hoc oppidum appellatum fuit Sichar: etsi[?] Hieronymus diuersa oppida fuisse censet.
units.tr: 17. Sichem, which was near Samaria, is today Neapolis. Beside this town was Jacob's well, famous for Christ's conversation with the Samaritan woman, John 4. The town was also called by another name, Sychar, although Jerome thinks these were different towns.

units.la: 18. Samaria est nomen tum gentis siue regionis, tum ciuitatis. De priori appellatione accipiendus est locus Io10han.4.v.7. Venit mulier de Samaria. Neque enim verisimile est, vrbis Samariæ incolas aquatum ventitasse ad oppidum Sichar, siue Sichem, quod à Samaria vrbe distabat duas lucas. Est igitur Samaria in illo versu, ipsa vrbs Sichar: & de eâdem versus 28 & 30 sunt intelligendi: ac si25 militer vox Samaritanus sæpius in hac historia proSichemita. Videtur autem euangelista hanc potius communem appellationem, quàm propriam vsurpasse, quia odia inter duas illas gentes eâ voce melius exprimebantur: quoad rem cum primis faciebat. Cæterum de Samariâ, 30 tumvrbe, tum regione vide passim in libris regum.
units.tr: 18. Samaria is the name both of a people or region and of a city. The passage John 4:7, A woman came out of Samaria, must be understood in the first sense. For it is not likely that the inhabitants of the city of Samaria went to draw water at the town of Sychar, or Shechem, which was two leagues from the city of Samaria. So in that verse Samaria means the town of Sychar itself, and verses 28 and 30 are to be understood of the same place, just as the word Samaritan in this history often stands for Shechemite. The evangelist seems to have used this common name rather than the proper one, because the hostility between the two peoples was better expressed by that word, which suited his purpose especially. For the rest, on Samaria, both the city and the region, see throughout the books of Kings.

units.la: 15. Ægyptus, fertilissima quidem est regio, sed quæ & ipsa Nili accessu destituta, famem[?] interdum sentiat. Æqui[?] egni[?] vetustate, cum auitâ potentiâ rerumque magnaum[?] memoriâ est celebris. Clarissima ipsius vrbs fuit 35 Alexandria, quam Marcellinus appellat verticem omnium ciuitatum: tum Theba, numero portarum nobilis: Mem-
units.tr: 15. Egypt is indeed a very fertile region, yet, being without the Nile's flooding, it sometimes suffers famine. It is famous for its great antiquity, its former power and the memory of its great deeds. Its most renowned city was Alexandria, which Marcellinus calls the summit of all cities; then Thebes, famous for its number of gates; Memphis, a great royal court and once the greatest city;

units.la: Nn phis, aula regiâ ingens, & maxima olim: item Coptos, Arabicarum, Indicarumque mercium emporium: Abydus, Memnonis regiâ & Osiridis fano insignis: Syene, atque aliæ apud historicos celebratæ. Fuerunt etiam in Ægypto pyramides, quæ ab Israelitis extructæ putantur, cum ab Ægyptiis inter alia onera & hoc ipsis imponeretur tanquam certi temporis pensum.
units.tr: also Coptos, the market for Arabian and Indian goods; Abydos, notable for the royal palace of Memnon and the temple of Osiris; Syene, and others celebrated among the historians. There were also pyramids in Egypt, which are thought to have been built by the Israelites, since the Egyptians imposed this on them among their other burdens, as a task of fixed time.

units.la: 20. Planities Moræ fuit contermina Sichemo, sic dicta à nomine possessoris.
units.tr: 20. The Plain of Moreh bordered on Shechem, and was so called from the name of its owner.

units.la: 21. Bethel, vrbs in tribu Beniamin, primò fuit dicta Luza. Confer Gen.12.v.5. & c.28.v.19. Nuncupata est Bethel, vt memoria patefactionis diuinæ, quæ ibi contigit, propagaretur. Eodem loco Ieroboam vitulum aureum collocauit, vt videretur sequi exemplum Patrum, qui ibi Deum adorauerant. Ea de causa appellata fuit Beth-auen, id est, domus vanitatis, Hos. 4. v.15.
units.tr: 21. Bethel, a town in the tribe of Benjamin, was at first called Luz. Compare Gen. 12:5 and 28:19. It was named Bethel so that the memory of the divine revelation that happened there might be spread abroad. In the same place Jeroboam set up a golden calf, so that he might seem to follow the example of the fathers, who had worshipped God there. For this reason it was called Beth-aven, that is, house of vanity, Hos. 4:15.

units.la: 22. Hai, fuit ciuitas Amorrhæorum trans Iordanem, ad orientalem plagam oppidi Bethel, non longè ab eo distans.
units.tr: 22. Ai was a city of the Amorites beyond the Jordan, on the eastern side of the town of Bethel, not far from it.

units.la: 23. Ellasar fuit Sufiana superior, ad Assyriam pertinens, Gen.14.v.1.
units.tr: 23. Ellasar was Upper Susiana, belonging to Assyria, Gen. 14:1.

units.la: 24. Elam est pars superioris Persiæ, Gen.14.v.1.
units.tr: 24. Elam is part of Upper Persia, Gen. 14:1.

units.la: 25. Bala fuit vrbs in Pentapoli, alio nomine Zohar, siue Segor, item Salissa. Vide num. 11.
units.tr: 25. Bela was a city in the Pentapolis, also called Zoar, or Segor, and likewise Salissa. See no. 11.

units.la: 26. Engadda, fuit vicus prægrandis Iudæorum iuxta mare mortuum: vnde opobalsamum fuit allatum.
units.tr: 26. Engedi was a very large Jewish village beside the Dead Sea, from which balsam oil was brought.

units.la: 27. Dan, fuit oppidum primò Laisch siue Lescem lictu, deinde Dan, tum Cæsarea Paneadis à fonte, postmodum Cæsarea Philippi de nomine illius tetrarchæ qui maximis operibus ornauit eam, postremò Neronia per Agrippam regem ad Neronis honorem appellatum.
units.tr: 27. Dan was a town first called Laish or Leshem, then Dan, then Caesarea Philippi by the spring of Paneas, afterwards Caesarea Philippi after that tetrarch who adorned it with great buildings, and finally Neronias, named by King Agrippa in honour of Nero.

units.la: Salem, vrbs regia Melchisedeci, etiam fuit dicta Iebus à conditore Iebusæo, filio Canaan; item Ierusalem. Diuisa fuit in superiorem & inferiorem. Superior ii vertice Sionis, vnà cum templo in eiusdem montis latere, fita erat, quæ à conditore etiam appellatur ciuitas Lauid. Templo adhærebat inferior ciuitatis pars. Urbs hæc tribus montibus fuit inclyta: monte videl. Sion, Moriâ, & Acrâ. Quo sensu appelletur umbilicus terræ, vide supra in Geographicis. Vulgo traditur & alia vrbs nomine Salem, Gen.33.v.18. Sed alii putant [illegible, ~4 letters] ibi esse nomen appellatiuum, idem quod incolumis.
units.tr: Salem, the royal city of Melchizedek, was also called Jebus, from its founder, the Jebusite, son of Canaan; and likewise Jerusalem. It was divided into an upper and a lower city. The upper city, which lay on the summit of Zion together with the temple on that mountain's side, was also called the city of David after its founder. The lower part of the city adjoined the temple. This city was famous for its three mountains, namely Zion, Moriah and Acra. For the sense in which it is called the navel of the earth, see above in the Geographical section. It is commonly held that there was another town named Salem, Gen. 33:18. But others think that [illegible] there is a common noun, meaning the same as safe and sound.

units.la: 29. Damascus, Syriæ vrbs antiquissima, palmularum fuit feracissima, itemque prunorum, quæ inde vocantur Damascena. Iulianus in epistolis hanc vocat veram Iouis urbem, totiusq; orientis oculum. Hoc in loco Adam vixisse dicitur, unde & nomen Damascus deducunt quidam. Cain ibidem traditur occidisse fratrem.
units.tr: 29. Damascus, the most ancient city of Syria, was very rich in palm trees, and likewise in plums, which are therefore called Damascene. Julian in his letters calls it the true city of Jupiter and the eye of the whole East. Adam is said to have lived in this place, and some derive the name Damascus from this. Cain is said to have killed his brother there.

units.la: 30. Bersheba, erat fons celebris, finisque terminus terræ Israelis ab Austro, ut Iosephus, scriptor vernaculus prodidit. Nomen habet a percussofoedere, quod ibi Abimelech & Abraham confirmarunt iureiurando, Gen.31. verf.31.
units.tr: 30. Beersheba was a famous spring and the southern boundary of the land of Israel, as Josephus, a writer of our own nation, reported. It takes its name from the covenant of the oath, which Abimelech and Abraham there confirmed by an oath, Gen. 21:31.

units.la: 31. Moria, fuit mons a latere Sionis, sic dictus a nobili euentu, qui describitur Gen.22.v.2.14.
units.tr: 31. Moriah was a mountain beside Zion, so called from the noble event described in Gen. 22:2, 14.

units.la: 32. Hebron, ciuitas in terra Canaan, in montanis Iudææ, dicta est & conuallis Mambre, & Arbah, & Ciriatharba, & vrbs Iuda in montanis, Gen.13. & 23. Iof.15. Luc.1. De hac vrbe sic scribit Eusebius: Arbo, hæc est Chebrom, vicus nunc maximus, metropolis olim populorum diuersi generis, & gigantum habitaculum: & postmodo regia sedes Dauidis. Sorte autem obtigit tribui Iuda, & vrbs fuit sacerdotalis, una ex ciuitatibus refugij. Hierosolymis versus Austrum distat milliaribus viginti duobus. Quercus Abraha, & monumentum illic cernitur, & colitur manifeste ab inimicis terebinthus, item ab Abrahamo hospitio suscepti angeli. Cum autem prius vocaretur Arbo, postea vocata est Chebrom, à Chebromo, qui fuit unus e filiis Caleb, ut legitur in libris Paralipomenon. Cur vero appellata fuit Ciriath-arbah? Quidam ab ordine urbium quatuor deductum esse putant nomen, quasi dicas tetrapolim: quo sensu tripolis, pentapolis, & decapolis dicuntur. Aliis placet esse nomen gigantis Arba, qui urbem condiderit. Aliia quatuor patribus nomen loco datum fuisse malunt, qui illic cum vxorib. fuerint sepulti: Adam, Abraham, Isaac, & Iacob.
units.tr: 32. Hebron, a city in the land of Canaan, in the mountains of Judah, was also called the valley of Mamre, and Arbah, and Kiriath-arba, and the city of Judah in the mountains, Gen. 13 and 23; Josh. 15; Luke 1. Eusebius writes of this city thus: Arbo, which is now Chebron, is now a very large village, once the metropolis of peoples of various kinds and the dwelling place of giants, and afterwards the royal seat of David. It fell by lot to the tribe of Judah, and was a priestly city and one of the cities of refuge. It is twenty-two miles south of Jerusalem. The oak of Abraham and his tomb are seen there, and the terebinth, which the enemies openly revere, as well as the place where Abraham received the angels as guests. Although it was formerly called Arbo, it was afterwards called Chebron, from Chebron, who was one of the sons of Caleb, as is read in the books of Chronicles. But why was it called Kiriath-arba? Some think the name is derived from the order of four cities, as if you said tetrapolis; in this sense tripolis, pentapolis and decapolis are also used. Others hold that the name is that of the giant Arba, who founded the city. Others prefer that the place was given its name from four fathers who were buried there with their wives: Adam, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

units.la: Denique sunt, qui existimant, veteres in more positum habuisse, vt insigniores vrbes diuiderent in quatuor partes, e quibus prima fuerit principum, senatus, & sacerdotum: secunda, militum; tertia, agricolarum; quarta, opificum.
units.tr: Finally, there are some who think that the ancients had the custom of dividing their more notable cities into four parts: the first being for princes, senate and priests; the second for soldiers; the third for farmers; the fourth for craftsmen.

units.la: r 33. Chauila est ora maritima, & veluti frons Sufianes inferioris in Perside. Fuit vnus e terminis meridianis terrae Ismaeliticae, vt patet ex Gen.25. v.18. vbi Chauila & Sur desertum sunt termini meridiani, Assyria terminus meridionalis. Qui sane tractus est amplissimus.
units.tr: r 33. Chavilah is a maritime coast, and as it were the front of Lower Susiana in Persia. It was one of the southern boundaries of the land of the Ishmaelites, as is clear from Gen. 25:18, where Havilah and Shur, a desert, are the southern limits, and Assyria the southern boundary. This tract is indeed very extensive.

units.la: 34. Padan est pars Mesopotamiae, a Cebare, siue Chaborâ, fluuio, qui in Euphratem labens regionem dissecat. Huius appellationis, quae saepe in Scripturis occurrit, vestigium certum est nomen Aphadna apud Ptolemaeum duobus oppidis attributum, quorum vnum ad Euphratem, alterum ad Chaboram est situm. Vide supra in geographicis.
units.tr: 34. Padan is a part of Mesopotamia, named from the river Chebar, or Chabora, which flows into the Euphrates and cuts through the region. A certain trace of this name, which often occurs in the Scriptures, is the name Aphadna in Ptolemy, assigned to two towns, one situated on the Euphrates and the other on the Chabora. See above in the geographical section.

units.la: 35. Gerar fuit metropolis Palaestinae, in quâ natus est Isaac. Fuit item nomen regionis, quae postea dicta est Salutaris, teste Hieronymo: olim regnum discretum a Palaestinae satrapiis, & terminus Cananaeae ad plagam Australem.
units.tr: 35. Gerar was the metropolis of Palestine, in which Isaac was born. It was also the name of a region, which was afterwards called Salutaris, according to Jerome; formerly a kingdom distinct from the satrapies of Palestine, and the boundary of Canaan on the southern side.

units.la: 36. Phanuel, siue Panuel, fuit locus iuxta torrentem Iacob, in finibus Amorrhaeorum, vbi Iacob totâ nocte luctatus est cum angelo: ita appellatus, quòd illic vidisset Dominum. Eò loci postea extructa est vrbs, quae Gideonis exercitui negauit panem: quâ de causâ male mulctata est. Hanc vrbem Strabo lib. 16. appellat faciem Dei. Est autem contigua Tripoli, apud eamque mons Libanus definit.
units.tr: 36. Phanuel, or Penuel, was a place beside the brook Jabbok, in the territory of the Amorites, where Jacob wrestled all night with the angel; it was so named because there he had seen the Lord. Later a city was built on that spot, which refused bread to Gideon's army, and for this reason was severely punished. Strabo, book 16, calls this city the face of God. It lies next to Tripoli, and the mountain Lebanon ends near it.

units.la: 37. Tripolis, regio fuit in Phoenicia, sic dicta, quòd tres vrbes, videl. Arcadum, Tyrum, & Sidonem, contineret. Est & Tripolis in Africa. Hinc Tripolis dicitur cum adictione, Syriaca, vel Africana.
units.tr: 37. Tripolis was a region in Phoenicia, so called because it contained three cities, namely Arados, Tyre and Sidon. There is also a Tripolis in Africa. Hence Tripolis is spoken of with an addition, Syrian or African.

units.la: 38. Tetrapolis, fuit regio Syriæ, in quâ fuerunt quatuor insignia oppida. Fuit & Tetrapolis Atticæ, itidem complexa quatuor urbes.
units.tr: 38. Tetrapolis was a region of Syria, in which there were four notable towns. There was also a Tetrapolis in Attica, likewise comprising four cities.

units.la: 39. Decapolis, regio Syriæ, vltra Iordanem sita erat, Galilææ gentium propinqua. Oppida eius à quibusdam ita commemorantur: Damascus, Philadelphia, Scythopolis, Gadara, Hippon, Dion, Pella, Galasa, Canatha, Raphana.
units.tr: 39. Decapolis was a region of Syria lying beyond the Jordan, near Galilee of the Gentiles. Some writers list its towns as follows: Damascus, Philadelphia, Scythopolis, Gadara, Hippon, Dion, Pella, Galasa, Canatha, Raphana.

units.la: 40. Gosen, Ægypti regio & ciuitas. Fuit etiam in tribu Iudâ ciuitas hoc nomine, à quâ tractus circumiacens fuit appellatus terra Gosen. Cæterùm in Gosen, regione Ægypti fuit Rameses, siue, vt alii legunt per metathesin, Raëmses, in optimo & fertilissimo loco, quem Ioseph possidendum & colendum dedit patri & fratribus suis, iussu Pharaonis. Hæc est Heliopolis siue Thebæ: quanquam Hieronymo Rameses, siue vrbs Gosen, est pagus Arsenoitis, in extremis Ægypti finibus.
units.tr: 40. Gosen was a region and city of Egypt. There was also a town of this name in the tribe of Judah, from which the surrounding district was called the land of Goshen. But in Goshen, a region of Egypt, there was Rameses, or, as others read it by metathesis, Raemses, in the best and most fertile place, which Joseph gave to his father and brothers to possess and cultivate, by Pharaoh's command. This is Heliopolis or Thebes. Jerome, however, holds that Rameses, or the city of Goshen, is a district of Arsinoë, at the farthest borders of Egypt.

units.la: 41. Æthiopia, regio Africæ sub Ægypto, Hebræis Cus, q. d. nigredo. Quo nomine tum Æthiopes, tum Asiatici omnes sunt usi, teste Iosepho, qui scribit, Æthiopas tum à seipsis, tum ab Asiaticis omnibus appellatos fuisse Cusaos, siue, Chusaos. Cussii etiamnum hodie appellantur à Lusitanis.
units.tr: 41. Ethiopia, a region of Africa beneath Egypt, is called Cus by the Hebrews, that is, blackness. Both the Ethiopians and all the Asiatics used this name, as Josephus witnesses, who writes that the Ethiopians were called Cusaei, or Chusaei, both by themselves and by all Asiatics. The Portuguese still call them Cussii today.

units.la: 42. Midian, fuit regio, itemque vrbs Æthiopiæ iuxta Arnonem & Ariopolim, cuius nunc ruinæ tantùm demonstrantur. Hic habitauit Iethro, socer Mosis. Est & alia vrbs hoc nomine in Arabiâ, in deserto Saracenorum contra orientem maris rubri, ad meridiem Iudææ. Ex hâc vrbe oriundi fuerunt Midianitæ illi, quibus venditus fuit Ioseph, quique etiam dicuntur Ismaëlitæ, Gen. 37. videlic. propter confusam cum Ismaëlitis habitationem. Alioquin Midianitæ fuerunt posteri Abrahami ex Keturâ, Ismaëlitæ ex Hagarâ. Quare Midianitæ isti fuerunt Midianitæ gente, habitatione Ismaëlitæ: quomodo accidere solet inter mercatores, vt ipsorum cœtus ex variis constent.
units.tr: 42. Midian was a region and also a city of Ethiopia, near the Arnon and Ariopolis, whose ruins alone are now pointed out. Here Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, lived. There is another town of this name in Arabia, in the desert of the Saracens, east of the Red Sea, to the south of Judea. The Midianites to whom Joseph was sold came from this town, and they are also called Ishmaelites (Gen. 37), namely because of their mixed dwelling with the Ishmaelites. Otherwise the Midianites were descendants of Abraham, through Keturah, and the Ishmaelites through Hagar. So these Midianites were Midianites by race and Ishmaelites by residence, as commonly happens with merchants, whose companies are made up of various peoples.

units.la: 43. Gilead, seu Galaad, regio Galilææ ad orientem vltra Iordanem, vbi dimidia tribus Manasses accepit pollef-[?] fionem cum tribubus Ruben & Gad. Fuit sita ad tergum Phœnices & Arabiæ, collibus Libani copulata: extenditur per desertum ad regionem Amorrhæorum. In hac regione fuit nobile emporium hoc ipso nomine, Genef.37. verf.25.
units.tr: 43. Gilead, or Galaad, was a region of Galilee east of the Jordan, where the half-tribe of Manasseh received its possession together with the tribes of Reuben and Gad. It lay behind Phoenicia and Arabia, joined to the hills of Lebanon, and extended through the desert to the region of the Amorites. In this region there was a famous trading post of the same name (Gen. 37:25).

units.la: 44. Horeb, mons siccus & aridus, in quo fuit Sinai, in regione Midianitarum. Vnde hic tractus montanus promiscue appellatur Horeb & Sinai.
units.tr: 44. Horeb is a dry and arid mountain, on which Sinai stood, in the region of the Midianites. Hence this mountain range is called indiscriminately Horeb and Sinai.

units.la: 45. Mansiones Israelitarum, inde à Rameffes ad Iordanem vsq; fuerunt xli. hoc ordine. 1. Ex Ægypto profecti sunt Rameffo Succothas. De priori loco vide paulo ante n. 40. posterior sic dictus est a tabernaculis, siue tuguriis tumultuariis, quæ Israëlitæ in prima ista statione adhibuerunt. Exod. 12. 2. Profecti sunt Succoothis, & castra metati sunt in Etham, fine deserti, Exod.13. Desertum istud eousq; protenditur, quâ Israelitæ fecerunt iterâ traiecto mari: atque hinc composite dictum fuit Pithom, vel Patomus, quasi dicat, os deserti. 3. Castra metati sunt ante fauces montium Chiroth, inter Migdolum, locum munitum, & mare, ante Baalzephon, qui ipse locus fuit etiam munitus. Exod. 14. Hac specie illecti fuerunt Ægyptij ad Israëlitas aggrediendum, ipse retrahendi ipsos in Ægyptum. Inde transierunt per mare. 4. A mari algosio progressi sunt in desertum Sur, quod idem fuit cum deserto Etham. In hoc deserto post tridui iter venerunt ad Mara: quem locum Plinius vocat amaros montes, plane ad genium Hebraici nominis, Exod.15. De mari algosio, sive rubro, vide supra in Geographicis. 6. Venerunt in Elim, vbi erant duodecim fontes, & septuaginta palmæ: qui numerus repræsentat 12 tribus & 70 seniores populi: item 12 apostolos, & 70 discipulos Christi. 7. Profecti ex Elim, castra metati sunt ad mare algosum. Vide sequentes mansiones, seu stationes, Num. 33
units.tr: 45. The stations of the Israelites, from Rameses to the Jordan, were forty-one in this order. (1) They set out from Egypt, from Rameses to Succoth. The earlier place was described above at no. 40; the latter is so called from the tents or makeshift huts which the Israelites used at that first station (Exod. 12). (2) They set out from Succoth and encamped at Etham, at the edge of the desert (Exod. 13). This desert stretched as far as the place where the Israelites crossed the sea on foot; and from this the name Pithom, or Patumus, was formed, as if to say the mouth of the desert. (3) They encamped before the mouths of the mountains of Chiroth, between Migdol, a fortified place, and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon, which place was also fortified (Exod. 14). The Egyptians were lured by this appearance to attack the Israelites, and so to drive them back into Egypt. From there the Israelites passed through the sea. (4) From the Red Sea they advanced into the desert of Shur, which was the same as the desert of Etham. In this desert, after a three days' journey, they came to Marah, which Pliny calls the bitter mountains, a name exactly suited to the Hebrew meaning (Exod. 15). On the Red Sea, or Sea of Reeds, see above in the Geographical section. (5) They came to Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees. This number represents the twelve tribes and the seventy elders of the people, and likewise the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples of Christ. (6) Setting out from Elim, they encamped by the Red Sea. For the following stations, or stopping places, see Num. 33.

units.la: 46. Sin, fuit desertum in terra Edom: alias Kadefchet desertum Pharan[?]. Fuit situm inter Elim & Sinai. In hoc deserto populus Israel annos triginta septem cum dimidio est commoratus: postea dimidium annum in itinere à Kadescho ad vallem Zerodi occupavit. Deut.2.
units.tr: 46. Sin was a desert in the land of Edom; elsewhere called Kadesh, the desert of Paran. It lay between Elim and Sinai. In this desert the people of Israel stayed for thirty-seven and a half years; afterwards they spent half a year on the journey from Kadesh to the valley of Zered (Deut. 2).

units.la: 47. Mare salsum est lacus Alphaltites, seu mare mortuum.
units.tr: 47. The Salt Sea is the lake Asphaltites, or the Dead Sea.

units.la: 48. Chazar-Adar, fuit oppidum geminum, sive coniunctum situ, etsi muro discretum. Hinc Scriptura interdum coniungit hæc duo nomina, ut Num.34. interdum seorsim nominat, ut Ios.15.
units.tr: 48. Hazar-addar was a twin town, or two towns joined in position, though separated by a wall. Hence Scripture sometimes joins the two names, as in Num. 34, and sometimes names them separately, as in Josh. 15.

units.la: 49. Akrabbimi, fuit ascensus montis in deserto siticuloso & scorpionibus referto. Unde quidam appellatiue vertunt ascensum scorpionum, Num.34.v.4.
units.tr: 49. Akrabbim: there was an ascent of a mountain in a dry, thirsty desert, full of scorpions. Hence some translate the name appellatively as "the ascent of scorpions", Num. 34.4.

units.la: 50. Vallis Ægypti in Scriptura dicitur pars Casiotidos, quæ subest monti Casio, cis paludem Sirbonidem: quæ Ægypti propterea dicitur, quòd Ægyptum à Iudæa disterminat.
units.tr: 50. In Scripture the Valley of Egypt is the part of Casiotis that lies beneath Mount Casius, on this side of the Sirbonian marsh. It is called Egyptian because it marks the boundary between Egypt and Judea.

units.la: 51. Mare magnum, in S. literis est mare mediterraneum sive Syrum. Fuit autem ita appellatum ex comparatione aliorum marium, quæ Iudææ adiacent.
units.tr: 51. The Great Sea, in the Holy Letters, is the Mediterranean or Syrian Sea. It was so called in comparison with the other seas that border Judea.

units.la: 52. Hor, est nomen montis, qui etiam dictus fuit Hermon, Sirion, Schenir, & Sion. Num.34. Deut.3. & 4. Ios.13. Caue hic confundas Tzijon cum Sion. Etsi enim vulgo etiam pro Tzijon scribimus Sion: alius tamen fuit ille mons, videl. Hierosolymis; & appellatur mons sanctus, mons Domini, mons congregationis &c. In huius montis vertice erat arx constructa, quæ à Dauide, ciuitas Dauidis est vocata.
units.tr: 52. Hor is the name of a mountain, which was also called Hermon, Sirion, Senir, and Sion (Num. 34; Deut. 3 and 4; Josh. 13). Here take care not to confuse Tzion with Sion. For although in common usage we also write Sion for Tzion, that mountain was a different one, namely at Jerusalem; it is called the holy mountain, the mountain of the Lord, the mountain of the congregation, and so on. On the summit of this mountain stood a citadel, which was called the city of David by David himself.

units.la: 53. Mare Cinnereth, cuius fit mentio Num.34. v.11. est lacus Genezareth.
units.tr: 53. The Sea of Cinnereth, mentioned in Num. 34:11, is the lake of Gennesaret.

units.la: 54. Iordan, fluvius Iudææ, aquas habens suavissimas, Petæam à reliquâ Iudææ disterminans, oritur ad radices Libani, duobus fontibus: alteri nomen est Ior, alteri Dan, qui simul iuncti Iordanem efficiunt.
units.tr: 54. The Jordan, the river of Judea, with very sweet waters, dividing Peraea from the rest of Judea, rises at the foot of Lebanon from two springs. One is named Ior, the other Dan, and joined together they form the Jordan.

units.la: 55. Iericho, civitas opulentissima, in tribu Beniamin, ab Hierosolymis 150, à Iordane 60 distans stadiis. Fuit nobilis palmetis & balsami viridariis. Vnde etiam ciuitas palmarum appellatur Deut.34.
units.tr: 55. Jericho, a very wealthy city in the tribe of Benjamin, lies 150 stadia from Jerusalem and 60 from the Jordan. It was famous for its palm groves and balsam gardens. Hence it is also called the city of palms (Deut. 34).

units.la: 56. Libanus, Syriae mons, à Sidone, Phoenices oppido, vsque ad Smirnam vrbem Cœles Syriae extensus, 150 stadiorum longitudine. Huic exaduerso obtenditur Antilibanus, valle tantùm interiectâ, olim muro illi coniunctus.
units.tr: 56. Lebanon, a mountain of Syria, stretches from Sidon, a town of Phoenicia, to the city of Smyrna in Coele-Syria, a length of 150 stadia. Opposite it lies Antilebanon, separated only by a valley, once joined to it by a wall.
