units.la: 57. Bethlehem, duae sunt: vna in tribu filiorum Zabulon; de quâ Iof. 9. ex quâ oriundus fuit Abezan, iudex: altera in tribu Iudâ, ciuitas Dauid, vbi ille habitauit. Haec fuit patria Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Olim dicta Ephrata, Gen.35. & 48. Vocatur ciuitas Dauid, Luc.2. & Ioban.7.
units.tr: 57. There are two Bethlehems. One is in the tribe of the sons of Zebulun, mentioned in Josh. 19, from which Ibzan the judge came. The other is in the tribe of Judah, the city of David, where he lived. This was the homeland of our Lord Jesus Christ. Formerly it was called Ephrath (Gen. 35 and 48). It is called the city of David (Luke 2 and John 7).

units.la: 58. Bethpeor, fuit ciuitas in tribu Rubenæ[?] cuius regione sepultus est Mose, in terrâ Moabitarum.
units.tr: 58. Beth-peor was a town in the tribe of Reuben, opposite which Moses was buried, in the land of the Moabites.

units.la: 59. Hus, siue Vtz, est regio Trachonitis, sic dicta ab Vtz, filio Amram, Gen.10.v.23. Is enim, teste Iosepho, itemque Hieronymo, Trachonitidem & Damascum condidit. Nam principatum tenuit inter Palæstinam & Cœlesyriam. Huius regio Iob 1. dicitur αὐσῖτις[?] à LXX Interpretibus: alias Ausanitis.
units.tr: 59. Hus, or Uz, is the region of Trachonitis, so called from Uz, son of Aram (Gen. 10:23). For he, according to Josephus and likewise Jerome, founded Trachonitis and Damascus; he held the chief rule between Palestine and Coele-Syria. The region of this name is called in Job 1 Ausitis [αὐσῖτις] by the Septuagint; elsewhere Ausanitis.

units.la: 60. Rama est nomen trium vrbium. Est enim Rama Beniaminis, Rama Naphthali, & Rama Tzophaeorum[?], seu regionis Tzuph, quae 1.Sam.1.v.1. dicitur duplex Rama, quòd in duas ciuitates diuisa esset.
units.tr: 60. Rama is the name of three towns. For there is Rama of Benjamin, Rama of Naphtali, and Rama of the Zuphites, or of the district of Zuph, which in 1 Sam. 1:1 is called double Rama, because it was divided into two towns.

units.la: 61. Silo, ciuitas in tribu Ephraim, clara tabernaculo, quod ibi vsque ad Dauidis tempora hospitium habuit.
units.tr: 61. Shiloh, a town in the tribe of Ephraim, famous for the tabernacle, which had its dwelling there until the time of David.

units.la: 62. Bethsemes, fuerunt tres vrbes hoc nomine: prima, in tribu Iudâ; secunda, in tribu Naphthali; tertia[?], in forte filiorum Isaschar.
units.tr: 62. There were three towns called Beth-shemesh: the first in the tribe of Judah; the second in the tribe of Naphtali; the third in the lot of the sons of Issachar.

units.la: 63. Gariẑim, mons Samariae iuxta Gilgal, trâ Iordanem, Sichemorum imminet[?] ciuitati. Ibi stab[?]. templum illud Iudaeis tantopere exosum, idq; merito.
units.tr: 63. Gerizim, a mountain of Samaria near Gilgal, beyond the Jordan, overhangs the city of Shechem. There stood that temple, so hateful to the Jews, and rightly so.

units.la: 64. Ekron, fuit vna è quinque ciuitatibus & satrapiis Philistaeorum, de quibus 1.Sam.6.
units.tr: 64. Ekron was one of the five cities and principalities of the Philistines, mentioned in 1 Sam. 6.

units.la: 65. Gilgal, siue Galgal, fuit ciuitas vltra Iordanem, non procul à Iericho.
units.tr: 65. Gilgal, or Galgal, was a city beyond the Jordan, not far from Jericho.

units.la: 66. Gabaon, metropolis Heuæorum, Hierosolymis distans xi. stadiis. Hæc è tribu Beniamin, filiis Aharon adscripta est.
units.tr: 66. Gibeon, the metropolis of the Hivites, was eleven stadia distant from Jerusalem. It belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, and was assigned to the sons of Aaron.

units.la: 67. Labes Gileadis, fuit ciuitas, non procul à Pellâ, pergentibus Gadaram.
units.tr: 67. Jabesh Gilead was a city not far from Pella, on the way to Gadara.

units.la: 68. Salim, est nomen regionis & oppidi. Confer 1. Sam.9.&Iohan.3. Dicitur etiam terra Schualis, 1.Sam.13. non procul à Gilgale ad Iordanem.
units.tr: 68. Salim is the name of both a region and a town. Compare 1 Sam. 9. and John 3. It is also called the land of Shual, 1 Sam. 13., not far from Gilgal towards the Jordan.

units.la: 69. Gabaa, siue Gibea, tres fuerunt vrbes hoc nomine. Prima, filiorû Iuda; secunda, sacerdotis Pinehas, in montanis Ephraim; tertia, tribus Beniamin, 60 stadiis ab Hierosolymis. Et hæc fuit regia Saulis: vnde dicitur domus Saulis, 1.Sam.15.v.22. Fuit etiam hoc nomine collis ad vrbem Kiriath Iearim, amœnus valde. 1.Sam.7. qui etiam dicitur Gibeon, 1.Reg 3.verf.9. Hic obserua quatuor sedes regias in populo Dei. Prima fuit Gibea, Saulis: secunda Hebron, Dauidis, qui inde transtulit sedem, Hierosolymam, vbi habitarunt reges Iudæ: quarta, Samaria, sedes regum Israël.
units.tr: 69. Gibeah, or Gibea, was the name of three cities. The first belonged to the sons of Judah; the second to the priest Phinehas, in the mountains of Ephraim; the third to the tribe of Benjamin, sixty stadia from Jerusalem. This last was the royal seat of Saul, whence it is called the house of Saul, 1 Sam. 15:22. There was also a hill of this name near the city of Kiriath-jearim, very pleasant, 1 Sam. 7., which is also called Gibeon, 1 Kings 3:9. Here observe four royal seats among the people of God. The first was Gibeah, of Saul; the second Hebron, of David, who afterwards moved his seat from there to Jerusalem, where the kings of Judah lived; the fourth was Samaria, the seat of the kings of Israel.

units.la: 70. Assyria, regio maioris Asiæ, Ptolemæo terminatur ab ortu Mediæ parte, ab occasu Mesopotamiâ, à septentrione parte minoris Armeniæ, iuxta Niphatem montem, à meridie Susianâ. Plinius autem lib.5.c.12. Assyriam docet Syriæ partem esse, quæ postea vocata est Adiabene.
units.tr: 70. Assyria is a region of Greater Asia. According to Ptolemy it is bounded on the east by part of Media, on the west by Mesopotamia, on the north by part of Lesser Armenia, near Mount Niphates, and on the south by Susiana. Pliny, however, book 5, chapter 12, teaches that Assyria is a part of Syria, which was later called Adiabene.

units.la: Strabo vero lib.6. longè latiores Assyriæ fines assignat, eo nomine comprehendens Babyloniam, & maximam circumiacentium regionum partem. Eandem & Syria à Græcis vocata est, Herod.lib.7. Iustin.lib.1. quanquam multò latiores Syriæ fines fuerunt, quàm Assyriæ. Dicta est autem Assyria ab Assur, filio Sem, & olim complexa fuit 18 regna.
units.tr: Strabo, book 6, assigns much wider limits to Assyria, including under that name Babylonia and the greater part of the neighbouring regions. The Greeks also called the same region Syria, Herodotus book 7, Justin book 1, although the limits of Syria were much wider than those of Assyria. Assyria is named after Asshur, son of Shem, and once embraced eighteen kingdoms.

units.la: 71. Syria, est regio Asiæ, quæ ab oriente terminatur fluuio Euphrate, ab occidente mari mediterraneo & Ægypto, à septentrione habens Ciliciam & partem Cappadociæ, à meridie Arabiam. Eius ciuitates insigniores apud Ptolemæum sunt, Laodicea, Hierapolis, Antiochia, Apamea, Palmyra, Heliopolis, Ptolemais, Sidon, Tyrus, Berytus, Botrys, Tripolis, Seleucia, Cafarea, & Damascus: montes clari, Carmelus, Cafius, Libanus: fluuij, Euphrates, Chryforrhoas, Singas: regiones, Phœnice, Palæstina, Iudæa, Idumæa, Comagena, Samaria, & Syria cœle. Sunt qui quadripartitam faciunt diuisionem,in Syros, Assyrios, Leucosyros, & Cœlesyros. Plinius Mesopotamiam quoq; & Babyloniam Syriæ attribuit: totiusq; Syriæ partem facit Assyriam. Multi confundunt, vt Herodotus, qui Syros à Græcis dictos, Assyrios à barbaris dici scribit, & illis Chaldæos adnumerat. Et sane multi sunt, qui eam, quæ nunc Syria dicitur, olim Assyriam dictam scribunt, detracta solum syllaba. Quidam diuidunt Syriam in quinque partes, videlicet Comagenam, Seleucidem, Cœlesyriam, Phœniciam, & Iudæam. Hebræis Syria dicitur Aram: quæ de re supra in geographicis. Porrò Syria etiam diuiditur in maritimam & mediterraneam. Mediterraneam Syriam cum Assyriâ sæpe confundi certum est.
units.tr: 71. Syria is a region of Asia, bounded on the east by the river Euphrates, on the west by the Mediterranean Sea and Egypt, on the north it has Cilicia and part of Cappadocia, and on the south Arabia. Its more notable cities, according to Ptolemy, are Laodicea, Hierapolis, Antioch, Apamea, Palmyra, Heliopolis, Ptolemais, Sidon, Tyre, Berytus, Botrys, Tripolis, Seleucia, Caesarea, and Damascus. Its famous mountains are Carmel, Casius, and Lebanon; its rivers the Euphrates, Chrysorrhoas, and Singas; its regions Phoenice, Palestine, Judaea, Idumaea, Commagene, Samaria, and Coele-Syria. Some make a fourfold division into Syrians, Assyrians, White Syrians, and Coele-Syrians. Pliny also attributes Mesopotamia and Babylonia to Syria, and makes Assyria a part of the whole of Syria. Many confuse the matter, as Herodotus does, who writes that the Syrians were so called by the Greeks, the Assyrians by the barbarians, and counts the Chaldeans among them. And indeed many write that what is now called Syria was formerly called Assyria, with only a syllable removed. Some divide Syria into five parts, namely Commagene, Seleucis, Coele-Syria, Phoenice, and Judaea. The Hebrews call Syria Aram, a matter treated above in the geographical section. Furthermore, Syria is also divided into maritime and inland. It is certain that inland Syria is often confused with Assyria.

units.la: 72. Phœnicia, regio Syriæ maritima, Galilææ contermina. Eius præcipuæ vrbes post Ptolemaida fuerunt Tyrus & Sidon, & quæ cum his Tripolim efficit, Aradus. Inter Tyrum & Sidonem sita fuit Sarepta.
units.tr: 72. Phoenicia is the maritime region of Syria, bordering on Galilee. Its chief cities, after Ptolemais, were Tyre and Sidon, and Aradus, which with these makes up Tripolis. Between Tyre and Sidon lay Zarephath.

units.la: 73. Syrophœnicia, dicta est quidquid Phœniciæ trans Libanum à Syriâ circumfunditur: à quo confinio nomen ortum est, quomodo dicimus Celtiberos, Gallogræcos & Mysomacedonas.
units.tr: 73. Syrophoenicia is the name given to whatever part of Phoenicia is bordered by Syria beyond Lebanon. The name arose from this boundary, just as we speak of the Celtiberians, the Gallogreeks, and the Mysomacedonians.

units.la: 74. Iudæa, non vno modo sumitur. Vide supra in geographicis, & paulò ante in prosopographiâ, nu.397. Quibus adde sequentia ex nonnullis historicis. Iudæa est regio Syriæ in Asiâ maiore, ad orientem habens mare mortuum, vltra quod est Iordanis fluuius, qui mare mortuum ingreditur: deinde Amorrhæi habitant. Post quos Moabitæ terram occupant: deinceps Ammonitæ & magnus Euphrates. Vltra illos Babylon atque Chaldæorum regio. Persia deinceps inchoat. Ad Aquilonem Galilæa cubat, in cuius tergo Libanus mons, terminus Iudææ, e-minet. minet. Damascus deinde, & Euphrates: ultra quem Syria & Assyria sitæ sunt, quæ respiciunt orientalem plagam. Ulterius Sidon & Tyrus occidentem versus declinant, itemque Palæstina, quæ dicitur Allophylorum terra, ultra quam est mare mediterraneum, quod inde dicitur mare Palæstinorum. Ad meridiem Amalekitæ habitant: post quos Seir mons, & Edomitæ: ultra illos Midianitæ sedent: deinde est mare rubrum: ultra quod Ægyptus sita est ad occidentem Iudææ. Porrò Iudæa aliquando tota terra xii tribuum appellatur: aliquando duæ tantum tribus, Iuda & Beniamin, hoc nomine censentur, ad distinctionem Galilææ & Samariæ, aliarumque in Iudæa late dictâ terrarum. Hinc est, quòd Samaria & Galilæa nunc partes Iudææ statuuntur, nunc ab ipsâ disparantur. De aliis Iudææ partibus idem iudicium.
units.tr: 74. Judaea is not taken in only one sense. See above in the geographical section, and a little before in the prosopography, no. 397. To these add the following from certain historians. Judaea is a region of Syria in Greater Asia, having on the east the Dead Sea, beyond which is the river Jordan, which enters the Dead Sea. Then the Amorites dwell. After them the Moabites occupy the land; next the Ammonites and the great Euphrates. Beyond these lie Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans. Persia then begins. To the north lies Galilee, behind which rises Mount Lebanon, the boundary of Judaea. Then Damascus and the Euphrates; beyond which lie Syria and Assyria, which face the eastern quarter. Further on, Sidon and Tyre tend towards the west, as does Palestine, which is called the land of the Philistines, beyond which is the Mediterranean Sea, which for that reason is called the Sea of the Philistines. To the south dwell the Amalekites; after them Mount Seir and the Edomites; beyond these sit the Midianites; then is the Red Sea, beyond which Egypt lies to the west of Judaea. Moreover, Judaea is sometimes called the whole land of the twelve tribes; sometimes only the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, are reckoned under this name, to distinguish them from Galilee and Samaria and other lands included in the broad sense of Judaea. Hence it is that Samaria and Galilee are sometimes counted as parts of Judaea, and sometimes separated from it. The same judgement holds for the other parts of Judaea.

units.la: 75. Idumæa, regio Syriæ, sic dicta fuit ab Edom sive Esau. Hæc per Alexandrum Regem effecta est pars Iudææ, ita ut Idumæi Hierosolyma vocarent metropolin atque patriam suam, & κοινὴν[?] πόλιν, sibi & universo nomini Iudaico communem: cùm ante id tempus essent hostes Iudæorum, & ἀλλόφυλοι. Atque hinc est, quòd apud Iosephum Herodes dicitur fuisse genere Iudæus: quodque idem Herodes in concione ad proceres Iudæos, ita illos compellat, ἄνδρες ὁμόφυλοι[?], viri eiusdem gentis: quia nempe à primâ quidem stirpe Idumæus erat, sed cuius maiores facti essent Iudæi. Præcipuæ urbes Idumæorum erant Marefa, Gaza, Agrippias, Ascalon & Azotus.
units.tr: 75. Idumaea, a region of Syria, was so named from Edom or Esau. Through King Alexander it became a part of Judaea, so that the Idumaeans called Jerusalem their metropolis and homeland, and a city koinēn polin [κοινὴν πόλιν], common to themselves and to the whole Jewish name. Before that time they had been enemies of the Jews and allophyloi [ἀλλόφυλοι], foreigners. Hence it is that in Josephus Herod is said to have been a Jew by birth; and that the same Herod, addressing the Jewish nobles in an assembly, calls them andres homophyloi [ἄνδρες ὁμόφυλοι], men of the same race: because, of course, he was an Idumaean by first descent, but his ancestors had become Jews. The principal cities of the Idumaeans were Marisa, Gaza, Agrippias, Ascalon, and Azotus.

units.la: 76. Media, Asiæ regio latissima, diuiditur in maiorem & minorem. Illi{9} caput est Achmetha seu Ecbatana: hæc dicitur Atropatia. Terminatur hæc regio à septentrione, mari Hyrcano; ab occasu, Assyriâ & maiori Armeniâ: à meridie Persidem, ab ortu Hyrcaniam habens & Parthiam.
units.tr: 76. Media, the broadest region of Asia, is divided into Greater and Lesser. Its capital is Achmetha, or Ecbatana; this region is also called Atropatene. It is bounded on the north by the Hyrcanian Sea, on the west by Assyria and Greater Armenia, on the south by Persis, and on the east it has Hyrcania and Parthia.

units.la: 77. Persia, amplissimas olim regiones fuit complexa, ut & hodiè. Nam omnem eum Asiæ tractum, qui est inter Tigrim fluuium, sinum Persicum, mare Indicum (quod olim rubrum) Indum, & Iaxartem, fluuios, & Caspium mare, nostrâ ætate à Sophis, Persiæ regibus, possidetur. Superior Persiæ pars in sacris appellatur Elam.
units.tr: 77. Persia once embraced very extensive regions, and still does today. For the whole tract of Asia lying between the river Tigris, the Persian Gulf, the Indian Sea (formerly the Red Sea), the Indus, the river Jaxartes, and the Caspian Sea is possessed in our age by the Sophis, the kings of Persia. The upper part of Persia is called Elam in the sacred books.

units.la: 78. India orientalis, tam vasta est, vt eam tradant esse tertiam partem omnium terrarum. Pomponius scribit, tantum spatium litoris eam occupare, quantum per 6o dies noctèsque velificantibus cursus est. Author est Strabo, in India fuisse 5oooo oppidorum, quorum nullum fuerit minus Co Meropide. Huius Indiæ fit mentio Esth.1.
units.tr: 78. Eastern India is so vast that some report it to be a third part of all the lands. Pomponius writes that it occupies as much coastline as a voyage of sixty days and nights under sail would cover. Strabo is the authority that India had 50,000 towns, none of which was smaller than Co, the Meropian. Mention of this India is made in Esther 1.

units.la: 79. Susa, vrbs nobilissima, Persarum olim regia, vnde tota regio dicta est Susiana. Dicta autem putatur Susa,à liliorum copiâ, quæ illorum lingua dicuntur Susa.
units.tr: 79. Susa, a most noble city, once the royal seat of the Persians, from which the whole region was called Susiana. Susa is thought to have been named from the abundance of lilies, which in their language are called susa.

units.la: 80. Vlai, est fluuius Elamitidos, id est, superioris Persiæ, qui geographis dicitur Eulæus. Ad hoc flumen obiecta est Danieli illa visio, quæ describitur Dan. 8. De fluvio Cebar, ad quem Ezechieli oblata est visio c.1, vide supra in geographicis.
units.tr: 80. Ulai is a river of Elymais, that is, of upper Persia, which geographers call the Eulaeus. The vision described in Daniel 8 was revealed to Daniel by this river. About the river Chebar, by which the vision was shown to Ezekiel, chapter 1, see above in the geographical section.

units.la: 81. Terra Gog & Magog, sunt Asia minor & Scythia. Et Gog quidem est Asia minor, vt restantur nomina Gyges, qui fuit rex; Gygades, qui fuerunt populi; Gygæus lacus; & Gygarta, vrbs. Magog autem est Scythia, siue Sarmatia, cuius incolæ olim, tempore Ezechielis, obtinebant Mediam. Hodie adhuc in Tartaria sunt regiones Gog & Magog, quas illi Gug & Mungug appellant. Plinius ait, Hierapolim Syris appellari Magog: quando scil. Sarmatæ siue Scythæ populati sunt Asiam. Apocalypsis coniungit hæc duo nomina, Gog & Magog, vbi de hostibus ecclesiæ agit.
units.tr: 81. The land of Gog and Magog comprises Asia Minor and Scythia. Gog is indeed Asia Minor, as the names remaining seem to show: Gyges, who was a king; Gygades, who were a people; the lake Gygaeus; and Gygarta, a city. Magog, however, is Scythia, or Sarmatia, whose inhabitants once, in Ezekiel's time, held Media. Even today in Tartary there are regions of Gog and Magog, which they call Gug and Mungug. Pliny says that Hierapolis is called Magog by the Syrians, namely when the Sarmatians or Scythians laid waste Asia. The Apocalypse joins these two names, Gog and Magog, where it speaks of the enemies of the Church.

units.la: 82. Bethulia, est vrbs, in historia Iudith celebris.
units.tr: 82. Bethulia is a town famous from the story of Judith.

units.la: 83. Asdod, siue Azotus, insignis Palestinæ vrbs inter Ascalonem & Ioppem, in tribu Dan, in quâ gigantes habitarunt, capta à Iosuâ. Fuit vna e quinque ciuitatibus Allophylorum, templo idoli Dagon nobilitata. Est & Azotus vrbs Achaiæ.
units.tr: 83. Asdod, or Azotus, a notable city of Palestine between Ascalon and Joppa, in the tribe of Dan, where giants lived, captured by Joshua. It was one of the five cities of the Philistines and was famous for the temple of the idol Dagon. There is also an Azotus, a city of Achaia.

units.la: 84. Arabia est triplex: Petræa, sic dicta à Petrâ, vetustissimo oppido, alias Nabathæa : Deserta, Straboni Scenetis, quòd gens vaga & sine ædificiis habitet ἐν ταῖς σκηνοῖς[?], in tentoriis; deniq; Felix, inter sinum Arabicum & Persicum. In Arabia est mons Sinai, qui & Horeb: etsi propter diversum genium & tractum longiorem habentur etiam pro duobus montibus.
units.tr: 84. Arabia is threefold: Petraea, so called from Petra, a very ancient town, otherwise Nabathaea; Deserta, which Strabo calls Scenetis, because its people wander and dwell without buildings [ἐν ταῖς σκηνοῖς], in tents; and finally Felix, between the Arabian and Persian Gulfs. In Arabia is Mount Sinai, which is also Horeb, although on account of its different character and its longer range it is regarded by some as two mountains.

units.la: 85. Palaestina, provincia Syriae, Arabiae contermina, dicta à Philistim, urbe metropoli. In eâ, inquit Plinius, quinque civitates continebantur, Gaza, Ascalon, Geth, Acaron, & Azotu. Herodotus Syriam vocat altera Palaestina. Palaestina etiam, inquit Stephanus, Phoenicia dicebatur. Est & altera Phoenicia, prope Phaeacian. Deniq; Palaestina etiam dicitur tota terra Canaan, Iudaeam, Samariam, & Galilaeam complexa: tametsi Iudaeae nomine tota Palaestina saepius accipiatur. Ea ab ortu habet Libanum montem, ab occasu mare Phoenicium, à septentrione Phoenicen, à meridie Arabiam Petraeam. Hieronymus in locis Hebraicis ait, esse notandum apud historicos, quod Iudaea ad Palaestinam, Galilaea vero & Samaria ad Phoenicen pertinent.
units.tr: 85. Palaestina, a province of Syria bordering on Arabia, was named from the Philistines, whose chief city it was. Pliny says that it contained five cities: Gaza, Ascalon, Geth, Acaron, and Azotus. Herodotus calls Syria the second Palaestina. Stephanus says that Palaestina was also called Phoenicia. There is also another Phoenicia, near Phaeacia. Finally, Palaestina is also the name for the whole land of Canaan, embracing Judaea, Samaria and Galilee, although the name Judaea is more often used to mean all Palestine. It has Mount Lebanon to the east, the Phoenician sea to the west, Phoenicia to the north, and Arabia Petraea to the south. Jerome, in the Hebrew Places, says that it should be noted in the historians that Judaea belongs to Palestine, but Galilee and Samaria belong to Phoenicia.

units.la: 86. Thabor, vulgo Saron, Graecis Itabyrius & Asabyrius, mons est in medio Galilaeae campo, mirâ sublimis rotunditate, & transfiguratione Christi clarus. Eius altitudo, iuxta Iosephum & Hegesippum, est 3o. stadiorum, Polybio 15[?] stadiorum. Quod ita conciliat Casaubonus: Fieri potest, ut de diuersis partibus montis senserint Polybius & Iosephus. Non enim unâ solùm ex parte adiri solent montes.
units.tr: 86. Thabor, commonly called Saron, by the Greeks Itabyrius and Asabyrius, is a mountain in the middle of the plain of Galilee, remarkable for its wonderful rounded height and famous for the transfiguration of Christ. Its height, according to Josephus and Hegesippus, is 30 stadia; according to Polybius, 15[?] stadia. Casaubon reconciles this thus: it may be that Polybius and Josephus meant different sides of the mountain, for mountains are not usually approached from only one side.

units.la: 87. Nazareth, viculus Galilaeae, in edito loco iuxta mōtem Thabor, in quo fuit nutritus Iesus Christus.
units.tr: 87. Nazareth, a village of Galilee, on a high spot near Mount Thabor, where Jesus Christ was brought up.

units.la: 88. Galilaea, Syriae regio, ad septentrionem Iudaeae sita, quae ab solis occasu Prolemaide civitate, & Carmelo monte disterminatur. Ab oriente terminos habet Iop-pen & Gadoram: à meridie, Scythopolim & Samariam, ita ut ultra Iordanem non extendatur: denique à septentrione Tyrum, ut ex Hegesippo & Iosepho constat. Est autem duplex Galilaea, superior & inferior. Galilaea superior, iuxta Tyrum, Sidonem, & Caesaream Philippi est sita. Dicitur Galilaea gentium, vel quia illic gentes usque ad Salomonis tempora habitarint, vel quòd Hiramo Tyriorum regi oblata sit. Fuit sita in tribu Naphthali. Galilaea inferior circa Tiberiadem & stagnum Genezareth in tribu Zabulon fuit sita. Christus vocatur Galilaeus Matth. 26, tum quòd frequenter sit versatus in Galilaea, tum quia Nazarethi educatus fuit, & in urbe Capernaumo habitavit, Matt. 4.
units.tr: 88. Galilee, a region of Syria, lying north of Judaea, which on the west is bounded by the city of Ptolemais and Mount Carmel. On the east its limits are Joppa and Gadora; on the south, Scythopolis and Samaria, so that it does not extend beyond the Jordan; and finally on the north, Tyre, as is clear from Hegesippus and Josephus. There are two Galilees, upper and lower. Upper Galilee lies near Tyre, Sidon and Caesarea Philippi. It is called Galilee of the Gentiles, either because the Gentiles lived there until the time of Solomon, or because it was given to Hiram, king of the Tyrians. It lay in the tribe of Naphtali. Lower Galilee lay around Tiberias and the lake of Gennesaret, in the tribe of Zebulun. Christ is called a Galilaean in Matthew 26, both because he often stayed in Galilee, and because he was brought up at Nazareth and lived in the city of Capernaum, Matthew 4.

units.la: 89. Bethsaida, fuit civitas Galilaeae, ex qua Petrus, Andreas, & Philippus, apostoli, oriundi. Hoc etiam nomine fuit piscina Hierosolymis, quae vocabatur probatica, q.d. pecualis: quia hostias in ea quondam sacerdotes lavabant.
units.tr: 89. Bethsaida was a town of Galilee, from which the apostles Peter, Andrew and Philip came. Under this same name there was also a pool at Jerusalem called Probatica, that is, "of sheep," because the priests once washed the sacrifices in it.

units.la: 90. Chorazin, non longe abfuit à Bethsaidâ. Fuit & Magdalum, in eodem tractu, inter lacum & montem Thabor, castellum, à quo Magdalena vulgò putatur dicta. Quam sententiam Casaubonus irridet. Summa ipsius sententiae huc redit. Stupor illorum castigandus est, qui ex Ioannis undecimo capite, ἐκ τῆς κώμης Μαρίας καὶ Μάρθας [?], à castello Mariae & Marthae, castellum Magdalum finxerunt, cuius hae essent dominae, & à quo Magdalena inuenisset nomen. Sanè putare, Magdalenam à castello aut turri dictam fuisse, quia Hebraeis Migdal est turris, non minus est absurdum, quàm existimare, omnes qui Mosis nomine sunt appellati, ab aquis fuisse extractos; qui Abrahami, patres fuisse multorum populorum; qui Isaaci, propter risum matris ficelle dictos.
units.tr: 90. Chorazin was not far from Bethsaida. There was also Magdalum, a fortress in the same district, between the lake and Mount Thabor, from which Mary Magdalene is commonly thought to have taken her name. Casaubon mocks this opinion. The sum of his view comes to this. Those people deserve rebuke who, from the eleventh chapter of John, [ἐκ τῆς κώμης Μαρίας καὶ Μάρθας], "from the village of Mary and Martha," invented a fortress of Mary and Martha, of which they were the ladies, and from which Magdalene is supposed to have got her name. Certainly to think that Magdalene was named from a fortress or tower, because in Hebrew Migdal means tower, is no less absurd than to suppose that all who bear the name of Moses were drawn out of the water, that all who bear the name of Abraham were fathers of many peoples, or that all who bear the name of Isaac were named from their mother's laughter.

units.la: 91. Gadara, erat urbs Graecanica, quam Iudaei suam fecerant per vim. Pompeius ademit Iudaeis ἐκ τῶν Ἑλληνίδων πόλεων [?], vt author est Iosephus, i.e. urbes Graecanicas, quae nempe erant in Coele Syria. Quas inter fuit Gadara, teste eodem Iosepho. Ex urbe ista fuit orta magna clarorum philosophorum, philologorum & oratorum copia, circa Herodis Magni tempora. Eorum meminerunt multis locis Graeci Romaniq; scriptores, Cicero, Strabo, Quintilianus, Ausonius. Hinc solui poterit dubitatio, quae multos incessit, quomodo in agro Gadareno fuerit grex porcorum, cum populi illi essent Iudaici. Quae causa quia falsa est, desinant illi dubitationis. Et vero, si maximè Gadara fuisset civitas Iudaica, nihilominus tamen Romani milites, qui praesidii causâ erant in Iudaeâ, potuissent porcos alere.
units.tr: 91. Gadara was a Greek city, which the Jews had seized by force. Pompey took from the Jews, [ἐκ τῶν Ἑλληνίδων πόλεων], "from the Greek cities," as Josephus records, that is, the Greek cities which were in Coele-Syria. Gadara was among them, according to the same Josephus. From this city came a great number of famous philosophers, philologists and orators around the time of Herod the Great. Greek and Roman writers mention them in many places: Cicero, Strabo, Quintilian, Ausonius. Hence the doubt which has troubled many can be resolved, how there could be a herd of pigs in the territory of Gadara, since those people were Jews. Since that reason is false, let them cease their doubt. Indeed, even if Gadara had been wholly a Jewish city, the Roman soldiers who were stationed in Judaea as a garrison could still have kept pigs.

units.la: 92. Aenon & Aenan, sunt duo loca separata, non vero eiusdem loci nomina. Aenon siquidem fuit vicina Scythopoli, ad alteram Iordanis ripam sita, non longe ab ipso flumine remota: vbi baptizauit Iohannes. Aenan vero fuit prope Diospolim, siue Lyddam, ab ea parte Iordanis, quae respicit mare. Hinc recte Eusebius: Aenon, quae sita est in transitu Thamna, desertus nunc locus est &c. Aenon, prope Salem, vbi baptizabat Iohannes, &c. monstratur adhuc locus, octo miliis Scythopoli distans.
units.tr: 92. Aenon and Aenan are two separate places, not names of the same place. Aenon was near Scythopolis, on the other bank of the Jordan, not far from the river itself, where John baptized. Aenan was near Diospolis, or Lydda, on that side of the Jordan which faces the sea. Hence Eusebius rightly says: Aenon, which lies on the way to Thamna, is now a deserted place, etc. Aenon, near Salem, where John was baptizing, etc. The place is still pointed out, eight miles distant from Scythopolis.

units.la: 93. Trachonitis, pars Iudaeae, inter Libanum montem & lacum Tiberiadis sita: cuius tetrarches fuit Philippus. Iosephus scribit, eam esse regionem Syriae Palaestinae. Straboni vocatur Ituraea, propter viciniam. Alioquin Ituraea & Trachonitis fuerunt distinctae regiones, Luc. 2. Trachonitis Hegesippo est Peraea: etiam propter viciniam. Saepenumero enim fit, vt locus vicinus nomine vicini loci appelletur. Alias Peraea est Iudaeae pars vlterior, Arabiae & Aegypto proxima, aspetis dispersa montibus, & a caeteris Iudaeis amne Iordane discreta.
units.tr: 93. Trachonitis, a part of Judaea, lying between Mount Lebanon and the lake of Tiberias, whose tetrarch was Philip. Josephus writes that it is a region of Palestinian Syria. Strabo calls it Ituraea because of its neighbourhood. Otherwise Ituraea and Trachonitis were distinct regions, Luke 3. Hegesippus says that Trachonitis is Peraea, also because of its neighbourhood. For it often happens that a neighbouring place takes the name of the neighbouring place. Otherwise Peraea is the farther part of Judaea, nearest to Arabia and Egypt, rough and scattered with mountains, and separated from the rest of Judaea by the river Jordan.

units.la: 94. Abilena, fuit provincia & vrbs Syriae, quae in euangelio appellatur, tetrarchia Lysaniae. Cuius nomenclaturae haec est causa. Ante natalem Domini quadraginta circiter annis, viuebat in Syria Ptolemaeus Mennæi F, tetrarcha, siue regulus Ituraeae, regionis paruae in confinio Syriae & Arabiae. Strabo author est, paruisse huic regulo montana Ituraeae, Marsyan, Heliopolim, & Chalcidem vrbe Syriae, a qua nomen habuit Chalcidene Plinii. Lysanias iste fuit interfectus ab Antonio. Hunc Lysaniâ filius excepit, factus Ituraeae rex ab Antonio, & ipse mox ab eodem, vt Cleopatrae gratificaretur, occisus. Isti enim dynastiae precario obtinebat suas dominationes, quamdiu gratum erat rerum potientib. Romae. Porro Lysanias F, dominationis suae sedem collocauit Abilae. Ita vocabatur vrbs quaedam Syriae, quam [?]linius[?] facit vnam è sex Tetrarchiis, quæ erant immixtæ urbibus Decapoleos. Cum autem plures essent in Syriâ Abilæ, huic datum est cognomen Lysaniæ, ut ab aliis separaretur. Datú a.est non à posteriore, sed à priore. Tempore Aug. Zenodorus quidam conduxit ditionem Lysaniæ, pactus annuam certæ pecuniæ pensionem. Quamdiu Zenodorus iste in potestate habuit Lysaniæ tetrarchiam, dicta fuit Zenodori tetrarchia: quâ Augustus postea donauit Herodi; quo mortuo, idem Augustus partem aliquam istius tetrarchiæ attribuit Philippo, Herodis F. Pars reliqua & præcipua tetrarchiæ Zenodori, quæ fuerat olim Lysaniæ, dono cessit cuidam Lysaniæ, gratiâ Tiberii vel Augusti. Et hic est Lysanias, cuius meminit Lucas cap.3.
units.tr: 94. Abilena was a province and city of Syria, which is named in the Gospel as the tetrarchy of Lysanias. The reason for this name is as follows. About forty years before the birth of the Lord, there lived in Syria Ptolemy, son of Mennaeus, a tetrarch or petty king of Ituraea, a small region on the border of Syria and Arabia. Strabo records that the mountain country of Ituraea, Marsyas, Heliopolis and Chalcis, a city of Syria, from which Pliny's Chalcidene got its name, obeyed this petty king. This Lysanias was killed by Antony. His son Lysanias succeeded him, made king of Ituraea by Antony, and he himself was soon killed by the same man, in order to gratify Cleopatra. For these dynasts held their rule only on sufferance, as long as it pleased those who held power at Rome. Further, Lysanias the son established the seat of his rule at Abila. This was the name of a certain city of Syria, which Pliny makes one of the six tetrarchies that were mixed with the cities of the Decapolis. Since there were several Abilas in Syria, this one was given the surname Lysaniae, so that it might be distinguished from the others. It was given that name not from the later man but from the earlier one. In the time of Augustus a certain Zenodorus took the lease of the domain of Lysanias, agreeing to pay a fixed yearly sum. As long as this Zenodorus held the tetrarchy of Lysanias, it was called the tetrarchy of Zenodorus; Augustus later gave it to Herod, and when he died, the same Augustus assigned part of this tetrarchy to Philip, son of Herod. The remaining and chief part of Zenodorus's tetrarchy, which had formerly been Lysanias's, was by the gift of Tiberius or Augustus transferred to a certain Lysanias. This is the Lysanias whom Luke mentions in chapter 3.

units.la: 95. Syrtes, duo sinus periculosissimi in mari Libyco, quâ Africam proprie dictam alluit. Eorum alter, qui Carthagini est propinquior, appellatur Syrtis minor: alter, qui in Cyrenaicam vergit, maior. Utraque Syrtis navigantib. est periculosissima, quòd mare ibi vadosum sit, arenæ vehens cumulos, qui loci faciem vicissim immutant, dorsaque & breuia in alia atque alia loca transferunt.
units.tr: 95. Syrtes, two very dangerous bays in the Libyan Sea, which wash the coast of Africa proper. The one nearer Carthage is called the Lesser Syrtis; the other, which lies towards Cyrenaica, is the Greater. Both are very dangerous to sailors, because the sea there is shallow, and the sand, driven into heaps, keeps changing the appearance of the place and shifting the sandbanks and shoals from one spot to another.

units.la: 96. Cyrenaica regio, pertinet ad Africam: quanquam ab Ægypti regibus aliquando gubernata est. Urbs in eâ celeberrima, & quæ Cecropis Archenarum regis ætate condita esse creditur, fuit, nomine Cyrene, æmula quondam Carthaginis, & clarorum virorū memoriâ celebris. Habuit synagogam peruetera, Iudæis iam olim à Tyglatphalasere in hanc Lybiæ partem translatis. Fuerunt & aliæ in hoc tractu urbes, nominatim quatuor, quæ unà cum Cyrene constituebant Pentapolin, de quâ suprà n.11.
units.tr: 96. Cyrenaica regio, belongs to Africa, although at times it was governed by the kings of Egypt. The most famous city in it, which is believed to have been founded by Cecrops in the reign of King Archenaris, was called Cyrene. It was once a rival of Carthage and is well known for the memory of illustrious men. It had a very ancient synagogue, since Jews had been moved to this part of Libya long before by Tiglath-pileser. There were also other towns in this district, four by name, which together with Cyrene made up the Pentapolis, of which see above, n. 11.

units.la: 97. Libya, nunc totam significat Africam, nunc eam Africæ regionem, quæ ab occasu Ægypto imminet.
units.tr: 97. Libya now signifies the whole of Africa, and now that region of Africa which lies to the west, facing Egypt.

units.la: 98. Saba, fuit urbs regia Æthiopiæ: item metropolis Arabum, in monte sita. Inde Sabæi populi, qui felicem Arabiam incolunt, dicti.
units.tr: 98. Saba was the royal city of Ethiopia, and also the metropolis of the Arabs, situated on a mountain. From it are named the Sabaean peoples, who inhabit Arabia Felix.

units.la: 99. Hierosolyma, tempore Christi inprimis clara erant templo, ab Herode instaurato; domo Herodis; ædibus Pontificum, itemq; Præsidum prouinciæ domibus, quæ prætoria dicebantur: præterea foris, tribunalibus, & Lithostroto illo sublimi, in quo Pilatus sedit, quando sententiam de Christo pronunciauit. Huc refer piscinas, quæ in urbe fuerunt complures, itemque fontes eximios: qualis fuit fons Siloha, item piscina Siloha, & piscina probatica, quæ dicta fuit Bethesda. Mons oliueti proximus urbi imminebat, prope medius profunda valle fissus, quà torrens Cedron perfluebat. Ab hoc monte Christo itum est ad crucis ignominiam: ab eodem itum est ad gloriam. Ad eius radices fuit Gethsemane, locus, in quo ante passionem Christus orauit. Nec procul ab hoc monte fuit vicus Bethphage, item Bethania. Locus autem ille, vbi Christus est passus, proximus urbi fuit, nomine Golgotha, ad partem aquilonarem montis Sion. Sic autem dictus est hic locus à calvariis hominum, de quib. esset simplicium: etsi Nonnus, poëta vetustissimus, scribit, nomen huic loco fuisse inditum, à calvaria Adami, ibi sepulta. Proximè hunc locum fuit Ager sanguinis. E remotioribus autem ab urbe locis fuit Aritmathia: tum Lydda, quæ postea Diospolis dicta. Huic proximus locus campestris Assaron, pro quo Hieronymus legit Saron. Emaus sexaginta stadiis ab urbe abfuit; cui Romani post deuictam Iudæam nomen mutarunt, à victoriâ Nicopolin appellatas. Diospoli vicina fuit Ioppe, à quâ Ioppica toparchia cognominata. His omnibus clarior fuit Cæsarea, ante turris Stratonis appellata. Porrò Iudææ oppida etiam fuerunt Gaza, Bethlehem, Chebron, olim Cirioth-arbe, Bethabara, Rama, Iericho, & Antipatris, ita dicta ab Antipatro patre Herodis M, qui eam in honorem patris condidit. Ab urbe Hierosolymâ distabat Samaria, vnius diei itinere. Vicina Samariæ fuit Sichem, quæ post Neapolisest dicta. Contra urbem Samariam, meridiem versus, visebantur duo oppida, Salem & Aenon, vtrumque ad Iordanem: inter cuius fontes duos situm fuit oppidum Paneas, quod Philippus, Herodis tetrarchæ frater in Augu\sti honorem, à quo eas terras acceperat, ornatissimè extruftum, Cæsaream vocauit, & Cæsarea Philippi postea cognominatum est, ad differentiam eius, quam in Iudæâ rex Herodes extruxerat.
units.tr: 99. In the time of Christ, Hierosolyma was especially famous for the temple, restored by Herod; the house of Herod; the residences of the high priests; and the houses of the governors of the province, which were called praetoria. Besides these, there were the outer courts, the tribunals, and that raised pavement, the Lithostroton, on which Pilate sat when he pronounced sentence on Christ. To this belong the pools, of which there were many in the city, and also its remarkable springs: such as the fount of Siloam, the pool of Siloam, and the sheep pool, which was called Bethesda. The Mount of Olives, nearest the city, overhung it; in its middle it is split by a deep valley through which the torrent Kidron flowed. From this mountain Christ went to the shame of the cross; from the same mountain he went to glory. At its foot was Gethsemane, the place where Christ prayed before his passion. Not far from this mountain were the village of Bethphage and also Bethany. The place where Christ suffered lay near the city and was called Golgotha, on the northern side of Mount Zion. This place was so named from the skulls of men, as simple people hold; although Nonnus, a very ancient poet, writes that the name was given to this place from the skull of Adam, who was buried there. Next to this place was the Field of Blood. Of the places further from the city there was Arimathea; then Lydda, afterwards called Diospolis. Next to it was the level plain Assaron, for which Jerome reads Saron. Emmaus was sixty stadia from the city; after Judea was conquered the Romans changed its name, and it was called Nicopolis from the victory. Near Diospolis was Joppa, from which the toparchy of Joppa took its name. More famous than all these was Caesarea, earlier called Strato's Tower. Moreover, the towns of Judea also included Gaza, Bethlehem, Hebron, formerly Kiriath-arba, Bethabara, Rama, Jericho, and Antipatris, so called after Antipater, father of Herod the Great, who founded it in his father's honour. Samaria was a day's journey from the city of Jerusalem. Near Samaria was Sichem, which was afterwards called Neapolis. Opposite the city of Samaria, towards the south, two towns could be seen, Salem and Aenon, both by the Jordan. Between its two sources stood the town Paneas, which Philip, the tetrarch and brother of Herod, in honour of Augustus, from whom he had received those lands, adorned with magnificent buildings and named Caesarea. It was afterwards called Caesarea Philippi, to distinguish it from the one King Herod had built in Judea.

units.la: 100. Mare Genefar, five Genefareth, dictum fuit ab Herodetetrarchâ lacus Tiberiadis ab oppido, quod Herodes in honorem Tiberii nomine Cæsaris appellauit. In huius lacus litore fuit inter alia oppida, Capernaum. Supra Capernaumum Bethsaida, ad ripam Iordanis sita, à Philippo multis ædificiis ornata fuit, & appellata Iulias, à Iuliâ Augusti filiâ. Non longe à Bethsaidâ fuit Dalmanutha. Inter Galilææ oppida etiam fuit Nain, itemque Cana, quæ differentiæ causâ vocatur Cana Galilææ, item Cana maior. Fuit enim etiam Cana minor, in tribu Zabulon, quod nomen Zabulon quoq; fuit ciuitatis, non tantùm tribus. Memoratur & Sion inter oppida Galilææ, itemque Sephor. Trans lacum primæ laudis ager est Genefareth dictus, qui lacui dedit nomen. Eius oppida fuerunt Gamala, Gadara, à quâ Gadareni, & Gergesa, à quâ Gergeseni.
units.tr: 100. Mare Genefar, five Genefareth, was called by Herod the tetrarch the Lake of Tiberias, from the town which Herod named in honour of Tiberius Caesar. On the shore of this lake, among other towns, was Capernaum. Above Capernaum was Bethsaida, situated on the bank of the Jordan, adorned with many buildings by Philip, and named Julias after Julia, daughter of Augustus. Not far from Bethsaida was Dalmanutha. Among the towns of Galilee there was also Nain, and likewise Cana, which for distinction is called Cana of Galilee, or Greater Cana. For there was also Cana minor, in the tribe of Zebulun; the name Zebulun was also that of a city, not only of a tribe. Sion is also mentioned among the towns of Galilee, and likewise Sephor. Across the lake lies the land of highest renown, called Genefareth, which gave its name to the lake. Its towns were Gamala, Gadara, from which came the Gadarenes, and Gergesa, from which came the Gergesenes.

units.la: 101. Antiochia, celebris vrbs Syriæ, & insignis hoc potissimum nomine, quod Christianorum nomen ibi cœ-pit.
units.tr: 101. Antiochia, a famous city of Syria, and notable chiefly for this reason: that the name of Christians began there.

units.la: 102. Parthia, Asiæ regio, ab occasu vicina Mediæ.
units.tr: 102. Parthia, a region of Asia, lying to the west next to Media.

units.la: 103. Pontus, est nomen maris & regionis.
units.tr: 103. Pontus is the name both of a sea and of a region.

units.la: 104. Cappadocia, attingit vtramque Armeniam & Comagenam, & complectitur montana Ciliciæ.
units.tr: 104. Cappadocia borders on both Armenias and Commagene, and embraces the mountainous parts of Cilicia.

units.la: 105. Lycaonia, excipit Cappadociam ab Euxino venientem, complexa Iconium, Derbam, & Lystram.
units.tr: 105. Lycaonia receives Cappadocia coming from the Black Sea, and embraces Iconium, Derbe, and Lystra.

units.la: 106. Cilicia, regio minoris Asiæ, modò Caramania, habuit Tarsum, Pauli apostoli patriam.
units.tr: 106. Cilicia, a region of Asia Minor, now Caramania, had Tarsus, the homeland of the apostle Paul.

units.la: 107. Paphlagonia, regio minoris Asiæ supra Galatiam.
units.tr: 107. Paphlagonia, a region of Asia Minor above Galatia.

units.la: 108. Galatia, vulgo Pera, fuit regio minoris Asiæ, Phrygiæ contermina, sic dicta à Gallis, qui relictâ patriâ sedes ibi fixerant. Eius incolæ appellati sunt Galatæ & Gallograeci.
units.tr: 108. Galatia, commonly called Pera, was a region of Asia Minor bordering on Phrygia. It was so named from the Gauls, who, leaving their homeland, settled there. Its inhabitants were called Galatians and Gallo-Greeks.

units.la: 109. Pisidia, Galatiam ab Austro excipit, complexa duodecim vrbes, quas inter fuit Antiochia, dicta Pisidiæ: cuius meminit Lucas Act.14.
units.tr: 109. Pisidia receives Galatia from the south, and embraces twelve cities, among which was Antioch, called Antioch of Pisidia, which Luke mentions in Act.14.

units.la: 110. Pamphylia, regio minoris Asiæ inter Ciliciam & Syriam, inter alia oppida habuit Pergam & Attaliam, de quibus Act.14.
units.tr: 110. Pamphylia, a region of Asia Minor between Cilicia and Syria, had among its other towns Perga and Attalia, of which we read in Act.14.

units.la: 111. Lycia, regio minoris Asiæ, inter Pamphyliam & Cariam sita, quondam complexa fuit sexaginta oppida, è quibus Patara & Myra celebrantur Act.21.
units.tr: 111. Lycia, a region of Asia Minor between Pamphylia and Caria, once embraced sixty towns, of which Patara and Myra are celebrated in Act.21.

units.la: 112. Caria, regio minoris Asiæ, inter Lyciam & Ioniam, habuit Laodiceam, tempore Pauli claram.
units.tr: 112. Caria, a region of Asia Minor between Lycia and Ionia, had Laodicea, famous in Paul's time.

units.la: 113. Ionia, regio minoris Asiæ, inter Cariam & Aeolidem media. Eius duo ocelli fuerunt Miletus, caput regionis, & plusquam octoginta urbium genitrix: & Ephesus, Asiæ lumen olim dicta, ubi fuit templum Dianæ. Fuit & ibi Smyrna, cuius ecclesia ex Apocalypsi est clara.
units.tr: 113. Ionia, a region of Asia Minor, lies midway between Caria and Aeolis. Its two eyes were Miletus, the head of the region and mother of more than eighty cities, and Ephesus, once called the light of Asia, where the temple of Diana stood. Smyrna was also there, whose church is famous from the Apocalypse.

units.la: 114. Aeolis, sive Aeolia, regio minoris Asiæ inter Italiam & Siciliam, complexa septem insulas, quæ dicuntur Vulcaniæ. Inter oppida eius celebrantur Adramyttium, & Assos, de quâ Act.20.
units.tr: 114. Aeolis, or Aeolia, a region of Asia Minor between Italy and Sicily, embraces seven islands, which are called the Vulcanian Islands. Among its towns the notable ones are Adramyttium and Assos, of which we read in Act.20.

units.la: 115. Troas, est regio minoris Asiæ, quam Plinius minorem Phrygiam appellat, Hellespónto adiacens. Præcipua ipsius urbs fuit Troas.
units.tr: 115. Troas is a region of Asia Minor, which Pliny calls Lesser Phrygia, lying next to the Hellespont. Its chief city was Troas.

units.la: 116. Lydia, mediterranea Asiæ regio, ab occasu Ioniam & Aeoliam attingit. Caput eius quondam fuerunt Sardes, regia Croesi. Hæ sunt Sardes, quarum ecclesiam Iohannes Apoc.2. inter septem illas Asiæ præcipuas commemorat. Est & Philadelphia, Lydorum urbs clarissima, cuius ecclesia etiam nota est ex Apocalypsi. A'Philadelphiâ versus occasum iacent Thyatira, plerisque Phrygiæ attributa. Hinc oriunda fuit Lydia purpuraria, Act.16. Nota est ecclesia Thyatirena, Iohanni etiam memorata.
units.tr: 116. Lydia, an inland region of Asia, reaches to Ionia and Aeolis on the west. Its capital was once Sardes, the royal seat of Croesus. These are the Sardes whose church John, Apoc.2., mentions among those seven chief cities of Asia. There is also Philadelphia, the most famous city of the Lydians, whose church is also known from the Apocalypse. To the west of Philadelphia lies Thyatira, which most assign to Phrygia. From here came Lydia the seller of purple, Act.16. The church of Thyatira is well known, and John also mentions it.

units.la: 117. Phrygia, minoris Asiæ regio, Cariæ, Lydiæ, Mysiæ, & Bithyniæ finitima: quarum omnium fines ita coeunt, ut difficulter possint distingui. Phrygia fuit diuisa in maiorem & minorem. Vrbes ipsius celebriores sunt Pergamum, vbi fuit ecclesia, Iohanni memorata, & bibliotheca insignis: Hierapolis, & Colossa.
units.tr: 117. Phrygia, a region of Asia Minor, borders on Caria, Lydia, Mysia, and Bithynia; the boundaries of all of these meet so closely that they can hardly be told apart. Phrygia was divided into Greater and Lesser. Its more famous cities are Pergamum, where there was a church mentioned by John and a notable library; Hierapolis and Colossae.

units.la: 118. Bithynia, alluitur maribus duobus, Propontide & Ponto Euxino.
units.tr: 118. Bithynia is washed by two seas, the Propontis and the Euxine Pontus.

units.la: 119. Insulae & vrbes maris mediterranei, quarum in Scripturis fit mentio, sunt Samothrace, Mitylene, Chios, Creta, hodie Candia; Rhodus, Cyprus, Salamis, Adria, Syracusa, Melita, Gnidus, Salmo, Pulchri-portus, Lafæa.
units.tr: 119. The islands and cities of the Mediterranean Sea that are mentioned in the Scriptures are Samothrace, Mitylene, Chios, Crete, today Candia; Rhodes, Cyprus, Salamis, Adria, Syracuse, Melita, Gnidus, Salmone, Fair Havens, Lasea.

units.la: 120. Patmos, insula vna ex Sporadibus circa mare Ægeum, in qua Iohannes exulans accepit diuinam apoca-lypsim.
units.tr: 120. Patmos, one of the Sporades islands in the Aegean Sea, where John, while in exile, received the divine Apocalypse.

units.la: 121. Harmageddon, vulgo est locus fatalis, destinatus conuentui principum antichristi Apoc.16. Iunius putat sic dictum, quasi Har-Megiddo, seu montem Megidduntis, qui fuit locus non procul a Chazâ, in claustris Ægypti, vbi rex Iosias a Pharaone fuit interfectus, 2. Reg.23. vers.29. ita vt denotetur locus in auspicatus. Sed rectè hæc sententia reiicitur à Grafero, & laudatur Lutheri acumé, qui in notis suis ad hunc locum sic adnotat: Harmageddon) Zuuff Teutsch/verdambte Krieger/verfluchte Rüstung/ oder vn- glückselige Kriegsleut / ab Herem & Gad. Videris hac de renostrum Lexicon theol. quod propediem prodibit.
units.tr: 121. Harmageddon is commonly taken to be a fatal place, appointed for the gathering of the princes of Antichrist (Apoc.16.). Junius thinks it was so called as if it were Har-Megiddo, that is, the mount of Megiddon, a place not far from Chazâ, on the borders of Egypt, where King Josiah was killed by Pharaoh (2 Kings 23:29), so that the name signifies an unlucky place. But this view is rightly rejected by Grafer, who praises the acuteness of Luther, who in his notes on this passage comments as follows: Harmageddon: "A doomed army, cursed armour, or unhappy soldiers," derived from Herem and Gad. You will see this matter discussed in our Theological Lexicon, which will appear shortly.

units.la: LIV. HIEROGLYPHICA SACRA.
units.tr: LIV. SACRED HIEROGLYPHICS.

units.la: I. Hieroglyphica sacra sunt simulachra fiue notæ rerum insignium, ex sacris literis collecta. Huiusmodi notæ apud Ægyptios erant uisitatissimæ: ut, canis erat hieroglyphicum fidelitatis; formica, industriæ: serpens, prudentiæ; serpens capite mordens caudam, anni. Potes etiam appellare Emblemata.
units.tr: I. Sacred hieroglyphics are images or marks of notable things, gathered from the Holy Scriptures. Such marks were very common among the Egyptians: thus a dog was the hieroglyph of fidelity, an ant of industry, a serpent of prudence, and a serpent biting its own tail of the year. You may also call them Emblemata.

units.la: II. Hieroglyphica diuiduntur in inanimata, & animata, & horum tractatio appellari solet ζωοπαιδεία.
units.tr: II. Hieroglyphics are divided into inanimate and animate, and the study of them is usually called zoopaideia [ζωοπαιδεία].

units.la: III. Hieroglyphica inanimata sic habent.
units.tr: III. The inanimate hieroglyphics are as follows.

units.la: 1. Lux est nota hieroglyphica maiestatis Dei. 1.Iohan.1. v.6. symbolum veritatis,Iohan.3.v.20.21. imago omnium fidelium, Matth.5.v.14. denique prosperitatis, pacis, lætitiæ, consolationis, & omnino status felicis, Iob.18.ver.5.6. Psal.97.v.11.
units.tr: 1. Light is a hieroglyph of the majesty of God, 1.Iohan.1. v.6. a symbol of truth, Iohan.3.v.20.21. the image of all the faithful, Matth.5.v.14. and finally of prosperity, peace, joy, comfort, and of a happy state altogether, Iob.18.ver.5.6. Psal.97.v.11.

units.la: 2. Ignis est hieroglyphicum maiestatis Dei, Exod.3. v.2. c.13.verf.21.22.c.14.verf.24.c.19.v.18.c.24.v.16.17.c.40.v.38. Num.16.v.35.2.Petr.3.v.7. item iræ ipsius omnia consumétis, Deut.4.v.23.24.c.9.v.3.Hebr.12.v.28.29. Porrò est imago Christi, Malach.3.v.2.Apoc.1.v.15.c.2.v.18.c.19.v.12. Spiritus sancti, Matth.3.v.11. verbi Dei, Ierem.5.v.14.& c.23. v.19. Luc.12.v.49. ecclesiæ, Obad.verf.18. doctrinæ falsæ, Apoc.9. v.17.18. denique linguæ malæ, Prou.16.v.27. Iacob.3.v.5.6.
units.tr: 2. Fire is a hieroglyph of the majesty of God, Exod.3. v.2. c.13.verf.21.22.c.14.verf.24.c.19.v.18.c.24.v.16.17.c.40.v.38. Num.16.v.35.2.Petr.3.v.7. likewise of his wrath, which consumes all things, Deut.4.v.23.24.c.9.v.3.Hebr.12.v.28.29. Further, it is the image of Christ, Malach.3.v.2.Apoc.1.v.15.c.2.v.18.c.19.v.12. of the Holy Spirit, Matth.3.v.11. of the Word of God, Ierem.5.v.14.& c.23. v.19. Luc.12.v.49. of the Church, Obad.verf.18. of false doctrine, Apoc.9. v.17.18. and finally of an evil tongue, Prou.16.v.27. Iacob.3.v.5.6.

units.la: 3. Sol est hieroglyphica imago Christi, Malach.4.verf.2. gratiæ Dei, Psal.84.v.12.Esa.60.v.19.20. ecclesiæ catholicæ, Cantic.6.v.7. doctrinæ euangelij, Apoc.8.verf.12.& c.9. v.2. gloriæ & prosperitatis, Ierem.15.v.9. Amos.8.v.9. gloriæ vitæ æternæ, Matth.17.v.2.c.13.v.43.
units.tr: 3. The sun is a hieroglyphic image of Christ, Malach.4.verf.2. of the grace of God, Psal.84.v.12. Esa.60.v.19.20. of the catholic Church, Cantic.6.v.7. of the doctrine of the gospel, Apoc.8.verf.12.& c.9. v.2. of glory and prosperity, Ierem.15.v.9. Amos.8.v.9. of the glory of eternal life, Matth.17.v.2.c.13.v.43.

units.la: 4. Luna est imago ecclesiæ. Cantic.6.v.7. Apoc.12.
units.tr: 4. The moon is an image of the Church. Cantic.6.v.7. Apoc.12.

units.la: 5. Stellæ sunt hieroglyphicum gloriæ futuræ in alterâ vitâ, 1.Cor.15.v.40.41.42. Dan.12.v.3. rectorum reip. Dan.8. v.10. doctorum ecclesiæ, Apoc.1.2.3.& c.8.v.10.11.c.9.verf.1. Nominatim stella matutina est imago mystica Christi, Apoc.22.v.16.c.2.v.28. & stellæ erraticæ sunt imago seductorum, Iudæ v.13. denique Phosphorus seu Lucifer, est symbolum doctrinæ euangelij, 2.Petr.1.v.19. & excellentiæ, quâ quis est prædítus[?], Esa.14.v.12.
units.tr: 5. The stars are a hieroglyph of future glory in the other life, 1.Cor.15.v.40.41.42. Dan.12.v.3. of the rulers of the commonwealth, Dan.8. v.10. of the teachers of the Church, Apoc.1.2.3.& c.8.v.10.11.c.9.verf.1. Specifically, the morning star is a mystical image of Christ, Apoc.22.v.16.c.2.v.28. and wandering stars are an image of seducers, Iudae v.13. Finally, Phosphorus or Lucifer is a symbol of the doctrine of the gospel, 2.Petr.1.v.19. and of the excellence with which someone is endowed, Esa.14.v.12.

units.la: 6. Aqua est hieroglyphicum Spiritus sancti, eiusq; beneficia nobis repræsentat, Esa.12.v.3.c.55.v.1. Ierem.2.v.13. 17. Iob.3.v.5.c.4.v.10.11.14.c.7.v.38. Apoc.7.verf.17.c.21.v.6. c.22.v.17. item euangelii, Ezech.47. Zach.14.v.8. sanguinis Christi, Eph.5.v.26. Hebr.10.v.22.1.Iohan.5.v.6.8. calamitatum, 1.Sam.22.v.17. Psal.32.v.6.c.66.v.12.c.69.v.2. denique numerosæ multitudinis hominum, Ierem.47.v.2. Apoc.17. v.1.15.
units.tr: 6. Water is a hieroglyph of the Holy Spirit, and represents his benefits to us, Esa.12.v.3.c.55.v.1. Ierem.2.v.13. 17. Iob.3.v.5.c.4.v.10.11.14.c.7.v.38. Apoc.7.verf.17.c.21.v.6. c.22.v.17. likewise of the gospel, Ezech.47. Zach.14.v.8. of the blood of Christ, Eph.5.v.26. Hebr.10.v.22.1.Iohan.5.v.6.8. of calamities, 1.Sam.22.v.17. Psal.32.v.6.c.66.v.12.c.69.v.2. and finally of a numerous multitude of men, Ierem.47.v.2. Apoc.17. v.1.15.

units.la: 7. Mare est hieroglyphicum doctrinæ cœlestis, Apoc. 4. & 15. vbi fit mentio maris vitrei.
units.tr: 7. The sea is a hieroglyph of heavenly doctrine, Rev. 4 and 15, where mention is made of the sea of glass.

units.la: 8. Terra est mysticum hieroglyphicum ecclesiæ per Christum renouatæ,& olim glorificandæ,Esa.66.vers.22. & c.65.v.17.
units.tr: 8. The earth is the mystical hieroglyph of the Church renewed through Christ and to be glorified one day, Esa.66.vers.22. and c.65.v.17.

units.la: 9. Emeteoris, nubes sunt hieroglyphica nota doctorum, & quidem ita, vt fœcundæ repræsentent bonos doctores,infœcundæ malos, Prou.25.v.14. Deut.32.v.2. Hebr.12. v.1. pluuia est imago vesbi Dei,eiusque doctrinæ salutaris, Deut.32. v.2.Esa.55.v.10. 11.item hominis salutaria documenta & consilia dantis,Iob. 29. v. 23. inprimis doctorum euangelii. Mich.5.vers.7. item benedictionis, quam Deus nobis confert in Christo, Psal.72.v.6.7. Hose.6.v.3. pluuia impetuosa est imago calamitatis, Eccles.12.vers.2. Matth.7. v.26.27 ros est imago Christi,Hos.14.v.5: verbi Dei,&doctrinæ saluificæ, Deut.32.v.2: multitudinis fidelium in N. T.Ps.110.v.3. doctoru euangelii, Mich.5.v.7.2.Cor.2.ver.15. 1.Cor.3.v.6. donorum diuinitus collatorum, Psal.133.v.3. beneuolentiæ magistratus erga subditos, Prou.19.v.12. infelicitatis hominum impiorum, Hos.13.v.3. & pietatis hypocritarum, Hos.6.v.4. Ventus est hieroglyphicum Spiritus sancti, Iohan.3.v.8: sanctorum angelorum, Zach.6.v.5: publicarum calamitatum, Apoc.7.v.1. doctrinæ cœlestis, ibid. iudiciorum Dei horrendorum. Esa.41.v.16.c.57.v.17. Matth.7.v.27. Ezech.13.v.10.11. Iob.21.v.17. Psal.1.v.4. denique vanitatis, Iob.6.v.26.c.7.v.7.c.15.v.2. Hos.12.v.2.c.8. v.7. tonitru est imago verbi Dei, ac inprimis euangelii, cuius sonus totum terrarum orbem subito peruasit,&corda hominum perculit, vt ad Christum conuerterentur, Apoc.4 v.5.c.14.v.2. item præconum euangelii, Apoc.10.v.3.
units.tr: 9. Clouds, and meteors in general, are hieroglyphic marks of teachers. Indeed they stand for good teachers when they are fruitful, and for bad ones when they are barren, Prou.25.v.14. Deut.32.v.2. Hebr.12.v.1. Rain is an image of the Word of God and of its saving doctrine, Deut.32.v.2. Esa.55.v.10. 11. likewise of one who gives salutary counsel and instruction to men, Iob.29.v.23. above all of the teachers of the gospel, Mich.5.vers.7. likewise of the blessing which God confers on us in Christ, Psal.72.v.6.7. Hose.6.v.3. A violent rain is an image of calamity, Eccles.12.vers.2. Matth.7.v.26.27. Dew is an image of Christ, Hos.14.v.5. of the Word of God and of saving doctrine, Deut.32.v.2. of the multitude of the faithful in the New Testament, Psal.110.v.3. of the teachers of the gospel, Mich.5.v.7. 2.Cor.2.ver.15. 1.Cor.3.v.6. of gifts divinely bestowed, Psal.133.v.3. of the goodwill of the magistrate towards his subjects, Prou.19.v.12. of the unhappiness of wicked men, Hos.13.v.3. and of the piety of hypocrites, Hos.6.v.4. Wind is a hieroglyph of the Holy Spirit, Iohan.3.v.8. of holy angels, Zach.6.v.5. of public calamities, Apoc.7.v.1. of heavenly doctrine, ibid., of the dreadful judgments of God, Esa.41.v.16. c.57.v.17. Matth.7.v.27. Ezech.13.v.10.11. Iob.21.v.17. Psal.1.v.4. and finally of vanity, Iob.6.v.26. c.7.v.7. c.15.v.2. Hos.12.v.2. c.8.v.7. Thunder is an image of the Word of God, and above all of the gospel, whose sound suddenly pervaded the whole circle of the earth and struck the hearts of men, so that they were converted to Christ, Apoc.4.v.5. c.14.v.2. likewise of the heralds of the gospel, Apoc.10.v.3.

units.la: 4. Quam ob causam Iacobo & Iohanni, apostolis fratribus, Christus imposuit nomina Bonaerges, quod est, filii tonitrui, Marc.3.v.17. Est etiam imago comminationum diuinarum, Apoc.6. v.1. & magni consensus atque vehementis contentionis omnium electorum in laudando Deo, Apoc.19.v.6.
units.tr: 4. For this reason Christ gave the apostles James and John, brothers, the name Boanerges [Βοανηργές], that is, sons of thunder, Marc.3.v.17. It is also an image of divine threats, Apoc.6.v.1. and of the great and vehement harmony of all the elect in praising God, Apoc.19.v.6.

units.la: 10. E'fossilibus, aurum est imago hieroglyphica Christi, Cantic.5.ver.10: ecclesiae & singulorum fidelium, Zach.13. verf.9.1.Cor.3.v.12: verbi Dei & fidei veraeac viuae, Apoc.3. v.18.1.Cor.3.v.12: argentum, verbi Dei, Pfal.12.v.7. linguae 5 iusti, Prou.10.v.20: optimatum seu gubernatorum in rep. Esa.1.v.22: verè fidelium, 1. Cor.3.v.12: lapides pretiosi, Christi,* Christianorum & variarum virtutum, Exod.28.1.Cor. 3.v.12. Apoc.21. Vide infra Lithologiam. Sulphur est symbolum doctrinae antichristi: Apoc.9.v.18. & imago poenarum 10 in inferno, Apoc.14.v.10.11.c.19.v.20.c.20.v.10.c.21.v.8. Sal est symbolum incorruptionis in foedere Dei, Leuit.2.v.13. Marc.9.v.49. item hominum piorum, qui doctrinâ & vitae exemplo alios ab interitu conseruant, Matth.5.v.13. Rupes est hieroglyphicum Dei, Psal.18. Petra, Dei 2. Sam.22. 15 & Christi, Matth.16. lapis, Christi Dan.2. Psal.118
units.tr: 10. Among minerals, gold is a hieroglyphic image of Christ, Cantic.5.ver.10. of the Church and of each of the faithful, Zach.13. verf.9. 1.Cor.3.v.12. of the Word of God and of true and living faith, Apoc.3. v.18. 1.Cor.3.v.12. Silver is the Word of God, Pfal.12.v.7. the tongue of the just, Prou.10.v.20. the best men or governors in the commonwealth, Esa.1.v.22. and truly the faithful, 1.Cor.3.v.12. Precious stones are Christ, the Christians, and the various virtues, Exod.28. 1.Cor.3.v.12. Apoc.21. See below, Lithologia. Sulphur is a symbol of the doctrine of Antichrist, Apoc.9.v.18. and an image of the punishments in hell, Apoc.14.v.10.11. c.19.v.20. c.20.v.10. c.21.v.8. Salt is a symbol of incorruption in the covenant of God, Leuit.2.v.13. Marc.9.v.49. likewise of pious men, who by their teaching and example preserve others from destruction, Matth.5.v.13. A rock is a hieroglyph of God, Psal.18. A rock (petra) of God, 2.Sam.22. and of Christ, Matth.16. A stone (lapis) of Christ, Dan.2. Psal.118.

units.la: 11. Explantis, gramen & flos herba est hieroglyphicum commonitorium momentaneae felicitatis impiorum, Psal.92. v.8. & breuitatis vitae mortalium, Psal.103.v.16. palma est imago hominis iusti, Psal.92.v.13. germen, Christi Domini, 20 Ier.23.v.5.c.33.v.14. Zach.3. & 6. absinthium, mortis amarae. Ier.23.v.15. & falsorum doctorum, Apoc.8.v.11. cicuta, mortis perniciosae, Ier.23.v.15. omphax, seu vua immatura, peccati, Ier.31: palea, pseudoprophetarum & falsae doctrinae, Ier.23.v.28: triticum, doctorum verbi & doctrinae salutaris, Ier.23.v.28. item omnium electorum, Matth.3.v.12. c.13.v.30. Zi{ania}, sunt imago reproborum: Matth.13 v.38. arbores virentes, regeneratorum, Apoc.9.v.4. lilium, vitis &c. felicitatis ecclesiae, Hof.14.v.5.6.7. vbi sunt nouem similitudines a plantis desumtae, quibus explicatur felix status 30 ecclesiae per Christum instauratae. Porrò arbor magna & patula est emblema boni magistratus, Dan.4. vitis, Christi, Iohan.15. palmites, electorum, ibid. olea, ecclesiae, Rom.11. v.7: sinapi, doctrinae euangelii, Matth.13.v.32: semen bonum, verbi Dei, Luc.8.v.11. spinae, curarum mundanarum, diuitiarum, & voluptatum, Luc.8.verf.14: cedrus, viri magni, 35 2.Reg.14.v.9. Spina, contemti, ibid.
units.tr: 11. Among plants, grass and flower is a hieroglyphic reminder of the momentary happiness of the wicked, Psal.92.v.8. and of the brevity of mortal life, Psal.103.v.16. A palm is an image of the righteous man, Psal.92.v.13. A shoot (germen) of Christ the Lord, Ierem.23.v.5. c.33.v.14. Zach.3. & 6. Wormwood of bitter death, Ierem.23.v.15. and of false teachers, Apoc.8.v.11. Hemlock of pernicious death, Ierem.23.v.15. Omphax, or unripe grape [ὄμφαξ], of sin, Ierem.31. Chaff of pseudo-prophets and false doctrine, Ierem.23.v.28. Wheat of the teachers of the Word and of saving doctrine, Ierem.23.v.28. and likewise of all the elect, Matth.3.v.12. c.13.v.30. Tares (zizania) [ζιζάνια] are an image of the reprobate, Matth.13.v.38. Green trees of the regenerate, Apoc.9.v.4. Lily, vine, etc. of the happiness of the Church, Hos.14.v.5.6.7. Here there are nine similitudes drawn from plants, by which the happy state of the Church restored through Christ is explained. Further, a great and spreading tree is an emblem of a good magistrate, Dan.4. A vine is Christ, Iohan.15. Branches are the elect, ibid. An olive is the Church, Rom.11.v.17. Mustard is the doctrine of the gospel, Matth.13.v.32. Good seed is the Word of God, Luc.8.v.11. Thorns are worldly cares, riches, and pleasures, Luc.8.v.14. A cedar is a great man, 2.Reg.14.v.9. A thorn is a despised man, ibid.

units.la: IV: Hieroglyphica animata sunt eiusmodi:
units.tr: IV: Animate hieroglyphics are of this kind:

units.la: 1. Ex volatilibus, columba est hieroglyphicum patientiae, mansuetudinis, simplicitatis, sinceritatis, & constantis fideiin coniugio, Matth.10.v.16: ciconia, turtur & hirundo, providae curae, Ier.8.v.7: aquila, regis, Ezech.17.v.3.&seqq. item veræ fideiin Christi mortem intentæ, Matt.24.v.28: ala avis, providentiae Dei, Psal.91.v.4.
units.tr: 1. Among the flying creatures, the dove is the hieroglyph of patience, gentleness, simplicity, sincerity, and constant faithfulness in marriage, Matt. 10:16. The stork, the turtle-dove and the swallow are hieroglyphs of provident care, Jer. 8:7. The eagle is the hieroglyph of a king, Ezek. 17:3ff., and also of true faith looking to the death of Christ, Matt. 24:28. The wing of a bird is the hieroglyph of God's providence, Ps. 91:4.

units.la: 2. Ex aquatilibus, piscesfunt hieroglyphicum hominum, qui degunt in mari huius mundi, & inde extrahuntur in viuarium ecclesiae, Ezech.47.verf.9.10. Vnde apostoli dicuntur piscatores hominum. Matt.4.verf.19. Marc.1.verf. 17.
units.tr: 2. Among the aquatic creatures, fish are the hieroglyph of men who live in the sea of this world and are drawn out from it into the fishpond of the Church, Ezek. 47:9-10. Hence the apostles are called fishers of men, Matt. 4:19; Mark 1:17.

units.la: Quo pertinet etiam parabola lagenae iactae in mare, Matt.13.verf.47. Homines potentes in hoc mundo comparantur balaenis grandibus; populi & exercitus illorum, multitudini piscium adhaerentium squamis balaenarum; tractio illorum ad poenas, iniectioni hamorum in maxillas earum, Ezech.29.verf.3. & deinceps. Pfalm.74.verf.13.14. Esa.27.v.1.
units.tr: To this belongs also the parable of the net cast into the sea, Matt. 13:47. Powerful men in this world are compared to great whales; their peoples and armies are like the multitude of fish clinging to the scales of the whales; their being dragged off to punishment is like hooks put into their jaws, Ezek. 29:3ff.; Ps. 74:13-14; Isa. 27:1.

units.la: 3. Ex bestiis terrestribus, leo, vitulus &c. sunt hieroglyphica angelorum, Ezech.1.& 10. Apoc.4.verf.7. leo rugiens, diaboli, 1.Petr.5.v.8: ovis, est imago Christi, Esa.53.v.7: item hominis errantis, Esa.53.v.6: item hominis verè fidelis, vocemque Christi sequentis, Iohan.10.& Matth.25.v.33: hircus, quatenus sacrificium erat, fuit typus Christi, Leuit.4. 9.&10. quatenus vero petulcum & foetidum est animal, est imago hominis reprobi, Matt.25.v.33. leo est hieroglyphicum Dei, Thren.3.v.10. item Christi, Apoc.5.verf.5: item angeli boni, Ezech.1.&10, vel mali, 1.Petr.5.v.8. item hominis magnanimi & fortis, Gen.49.v.9. Deut.33.v.10. ite hominis crudelis, violenti, & persecutoris, Psal.22.v.22. Psal.7.v.3.&10.v.9. formica, prudentiae & industriae oeconomicae, Prov.6.v.6.&seqq. Confer Prou.30.verf.24.25.26. 29.30.31: serpens, prudentiae erhicae, in omni vitâ necessariae, Matt.10.v.16.
units.tr: 3. Among the land animals, the lion, the calf, etc., are hieroglyphs of angels, Ezek. 1 and 10; Rev. 4:7. A roaring lion is a hieroglyph of the devil, 1 Pet. 5:8. A sheep is an image of Christ, Isa. 53:7; likewise of a wandering man, Isa. 53:6; and of a truly faithful man who follows the voice of Christ, John 10; Matt. 25:33. The goat, insofar as it was a sacrifice, was a type of Christ, Lev. 4:9-10; insofar as it is a butting and foul-smelling animal, it is an image of a reprobate man, Matt. 25:33. The lion is a hieroglyph of God, Lam. 3:10; likewise of Christ, Rev. 5:5; likewise of a good angel, Ezek. 1 and 10, or of an evil one, 1 Pet. 5:8; likewise of a magnanimous and brave man, Gen. 49:9; Deut. 33:20; and of a cruel, violent and persecuting man, Ps. 22:22; Ps. 7:3 and 10:9. The ant is a hieroglyph of prudence and of domestic industry, Prov. 6:6ff. Compare Prov. 30:24-26, 29-31. The serpent is a hieroglyph of the ethical prudence necessary in every life, Matt. 10:16.

units.la: 4. In homine, caput est hieroglyphicum Christi & cuiuslibet superioritatis, 1.Cor.11.v.3.Eph.1.v.20.&seqq.cap.5. v.23. v.23.24:nares, sunt hieroglyphicum irae Dei, 2.Sam.22.v.9. Psal.18.v.9.oculi, providentiae Dei, Psalm.34.v.16. Huc pertinent exempla ἀνθρωποπαθείας [?], quâ Deo tribuuntur aures, manus, brachia, & alia corporis humani membra.
units.tr: 4. In man, the head is the hieroglyph of Christ and of every superior, 1 Cor. 11:3; Eph. 1:20ff.; ch. 5 v. 23. v.23.24: The nostrils, are a hieroglyph of God's wrath, 2 Sam. 22:9. Ps. 18:9. eyes, of God's providence, Ps. 34:16. Here belong the examples of anthropopathy [ἀνθρωποπαθείας] [?], by which ears, hands, arms and other members of the human body are attributed to God.

units.la: Atque hæc sunt hieroglyphica sacra, quæ pertinent inprimis ad theologiam moralem & philosophiam practicam.
units.tr: These are the sacred hieroglyphs, which pertain chiefly to moral theology and practical philosophy.

units.la: LV. GNOMOLOGIA SACRA.
units.tr: LV. SACRED GNOMOLOGY.

units.la: I. GNomologia sacra est pars theologiæ moralis, itemque philosophiæ practicæ, colligens insignes sententias è sacris literis.
units.tr: I. Sacred gnomology is a part of moral theology and likewise of practical philosophy, gathering notable sayings from the sacred letters.

units.la: II. Sententiæ istiusmodi sunt proverbia, ænigmata, apologi, & gnomæ. Proverbia: ut, 2. Petr. 2. v. vltim. Accidit eis, quod proverbio dici solet, Canis reversus est ad suum ipsius vomitum, & Sus lota ad volutabrum cœni. Vide etiā Gen.10.v.9.Num.21.v.27.1.Sam.10.v.12. cap.19. verf.24. c.24.v.19.2.Sam.5.v.8.c.20.v.18.Ezech.12.v.22. 23. ca.16. v.44.c.18.v.2.3.c.24. v.3. Ænigmatis exemplum est Iudic. 14.v.15. Apologi duo sunt in Scriptura, Iudic.9.v.8. & seqq. 2.Reg. 14.v.9. Gnomæ sunt illustria & acuta dicta, quæ tanquam regulæ vitæ nos gubernant in vita oeconomica, politica, ecclesiastica, & scholastica. Has vide in Proverbiis & Ecclesiaste Salomonis, item in libro Sapientiæ & Sirachi.
units.tr: II. Sayings of this kind are proverbs, riddles, fables, and gnomes. Proverbs: for example, 2 Pet. 2, last verse: It has happened to them what is commonly said in a proverb, The dog has returned to his own vomit, and the sow, washed, to her wallowing in the mire. See also Gen. 10.v.9, Num. 21.v.27, 1 Sam. 10.v.12, ch. 19.v.24, ch. 24.v.19, 2 Sam. 5.v.8, ch. 20.v.18, Ezek. 12.v.22-23, ch. 16.v.44, ch. 18.v.2-3, ch. 24.v.3. An example of a riddle is Judg. 14.v.15. There are two fables in Scripture: Judg. 9.v.8 and following, and 2 Kings 14.v.9. Gnomes are illustrious and sharp sayings which guide us as rules of life in domestic, political, ecclesiastical, and scholastic affairs. Look for these in the Proverbs and Ecclesiastes of Solomon, and likewise in the book of Wisdom and in Sirach.

units.la: LVI. CRITICA SACRA.
units.tr: LVI. Sacred Criticism.

units.la: I. CRitica sacra est pars philologiæ sacræ de authoribus librorum sacrorum, reliquaque illorum habitudine quâtum ad verba.
units.tr: I. Sacred criticism is the part of sacred philology concerned with the authors of the sacred books, and with the relation of those books to their words.

units.la: Duas hasce partes Criticæ, adeoque officia critici boni posuerunt veteres: de authoribus veris aut falsis pronun-tiare. tiare, & verba authorum sic illustrare, ut cum antiquitate vera consentiant omnia.
units.tr: The ancients laid down these two parts of criticism, and thus the duties of a good critic: to pronounce on authors as genuine or spurious, and to illustrate the words of the authors so that everything agrees with true antiquity.

units.la: II. Authores librorum sacrorum, sunt vel omnibus recte institutis noti, vel dubii. Sic de authore evangelii Iohannis & epistolae ad Romanos inter omnes constat: de libro psalmorum, Iobi, Estherae, & aliis plurimis in V.T. non item constat. Hic itaque oportet professotem[?] Criticae sacrae adhibere diligentiam, ut statuat id, quod est maxime probabile.
units.tr: II. The authors of the sacred books are either known to all who are rightly instructed, or are doubtful. Thus the authorship of the Gospel of John and of the Epistle to the Romans is certain to everyone; but concerning the Book of Psalms, Job, Esther and many others in the Old Testament, it is not equally certain. Here, therefore, the professor of sacred criticism must apply diligence, so that he may determine what is most probable.

units.la: III. Habitudo librorum sacrorum, quantum ad verba, cernitur partim in varia lectione, partim in vocabulorum rariorum & maximè singularium explicatione. De varietate lectionis in V.T. agit Massora, quae nihil est aliud quàm Critica Hebraeorum, de variis lectionibus N.T. praecipere debet interpretes ipsius philologici. Vocabulorum rariorum explicatio colligenda est ex interpretibus Hebraeis, Graecis, Latinis &c. adhibito proprio iudicio, quod adhaereat textui sacro.
units.tr: III. The relation of the sacred books to their words is seen partly in variant readings, and partly in the explanation of rare words, especially of words occurring only once. The variety of readings in the Old Testament is treated by the Masora, which is nothing other than the criticism of the Hebrews; concerning the variant readings of the New Testament, the interpreters of its philology ought to give instruction. The explanation of rare words is to be gathered from the Hebrew, Greek, Latin and other interpreters, with the application of one's own judgment, which must cling to the sacred text.

units.la: LVII. EPISTOLICA SACRA.
units.tr: LVII. SACRED EPISTLES.

units.la: I. EPistolica sacra est pars Oratoriae de methodo epistolarum in S. literis occurrentium.
units.tr: I. The sacred epistolary art is the part of rhetoric concerned with the method of the letters that occur in the Holy Scriptures.

units.la: II. Ea est communis, vel propria.
units.tr: II. It is either general or particular.

units.la: III. Epistolica communis persequitur partes & affectiones epistolae. Partes epistolae plenae sunt quinque: 1.[illegible, ~10 letters] id est, ea quae epistolis praemitti solent, ut sunt inscriptio, subscriptio, salutatio.
units.tr: III. General epistolary art deals with the parts and qualities of a letter. The parts of a complete letter are five: 1. [illegible, ~10 letters], that is, the things that are customarily placed before letters, such as the address, the subscription and the greeting.

units.la: 2. Exordium. 3. Propositio. 4. Tractatio propositionis. 5. Peroratio. Affectiones epistolae sunt stili simplicitas, Affectuum ingenuitas, Decorum epistolicum, & Sufficiens tractatio argumenti.
units.tr: 2. The exordium. 3. The proposition. 4. The treatment of the proposition. 5. The peroration. The qualities of a letter are simplicity of style, naturalness of the feelings, propriety suited to letters, and a sufficient treatment of the subject.

units.la: IV. Epistolica propria exponit species epistolarum. Sunt autem epistolarum aliae familiares, quales occurrunt apud Esdram & Nehemiam, item in libro Estherae, & libris Maccabaeorum: vt Esdr. 4. v. 11. c. 5. v. 6. c. 7. v. 11. Nehem. 6. Esdr. 3. v. 14. ca. 8. v. 13. 3. Esdr. 6. v. 7. 1. Maccab. 11. v. 31. c. 12. v. 5. c. 13. v. 35. c. 14. v. 19. 2. Maccab. 11. verf. 16. 22. 27. 34: aliae didacticae, quibus explicatur locus communis, vel doctrinae praxis vrgetur in emendatione vitae, & consolatione; quales sunt XIV epistolae Pauli, & VII,reliquo-rum apostolorum, quae dicuntur catholicae.
units.tr: IV. Particular epistolary art sets out the kinds of letters. Some letters are familiar, such as those found in Ezra and Nehemiah, likewise in the book of Esther and the books of the Maccabees: for example, Esdr. 4. v. 11. c. 5. v. 6. c. 7. v. 11. Nehem. 6. Esdr. 3. v. 14. ca. 8. v. 13. 3. Esdr. 6. v. 7. 1. Maccab. 11. v. 31. c. 12. v. 5. c. 13. v. 35. c. 14. v. 19. 2. Maccab. 11. verf. 16. 22. 27. 34. Others are didactic, by which a commonplace is explained or the practice of doctrine is urged for the amendment of life and for consolation. Such are the fourteen letters of Paul and the seven letters of the remaining apostles, which are called catholic.

units.la: LVIII.
units.tr: LVIII.

units.la: LVIII. ARTIFICIUM DISTINGUENDI Sacrum.
units.tr: LVIII. THE SACRED ART OF DISTINGUISHING.

units.la: I. ARtificium bene distinguendi, sumtum e sacris literis, monstrat rectam rationem limitandi. Distinctio est grammatica, vel logica. Illa attendit seriem contextus, & perficitur certis virgulis, puctis commatibus, colis, hypostigmis &c: haec occupatur circa res, quae varietatem aliquam admittunt, & ideo dicitur limitatio, itemque restrictio.
units.tr: I. The art of distinguishing well, drawn from the Holy Scriptures, shows the right method of delimiting. Distinction is either grammatical or logical. The former attends to the sequence of the context and is carried out by certain marks: the virgule, full stop, comma, colon, semicolon and so on. The latter is concerned with things that admit some variety, and for that reason it is called limitation, and likewise restriction.

units.la: II. Limitatio bona vel fit inter res diuersas, vel in vna eademque re attendit aliquam diuersitatem.
units.tr: II. A good limitation either takes place between different things, or, within one and the same thing, notes some diversity.

units.la: III. Limitatio inter res diuersas est, quae certo aliquo signo discernit rem a re, ne duae res pro vna habeantur. Sic Matth. 10. verf. 2. & 4. Simon est nomen duorum apostolorum. Apponitur itaque distinctio, hoc modo: Simon, qui dicitur Petrus. Et v. 4. Simon Cananites. Ibidem, Iacobus est nomen duorum apostolorum. Ideo Ἰακώβου ἵνεκα[?] dicitur, Iacobus filius Zebedaei, v. 2. & Iacobus filius Alphaei, v. 3. Sic Luc. 6. v. 16. Iudas Iacobi F. distinguitur a Iuda Iscariote.
units.tr: III. Limitation between different things is that which, by some certain sign, separates one thing from another, lest two things be taken for one. Thus Matth. 10. vers. 2. & 4. Simon is the name of two apostles. A distinction is therefore added in this way: Simon, who is called Peter. And in verse 4, Simon the Canaanite. In the same place, James is the name of two apostles. Therefore he is called James the son of Zebedee in verse 2, and James the son of Alphaeus in verse 3. So in Luke 6. v. 16. Judas the son of James is distinguished from Judas Iscariot.

units.la: IV. Limitatio, quae fit in una re, discernit vel diuersas partes, vel diuersum respectum, vel diuersa tempora. Diuersas partes: vt Rom.i.v.3. 4. De filio suo, qui ortus est ex semine Dauidis secundum carnem: declaratus autem filius Dei potenter secundum spiritum sanctificationis. Diuersum respectum: vt Matth. 22. vers.45. Si ergo Dauid eum vocat dominum, quomodo filius eius est? Similia exempla vide Luc. 2.v.34. 2.Cor.3.v.16. Diuersa tempora: vt, Phil. 2.vers.7. Christus formam serui accepit: & v.9. Christus in summam euectus est sublimitatem. Hic est sermo de statu diuerso, siue de tempore exinanitionis & exaltationis Christi.
units.tr: IV. Limitation that is made within one thing distinguishes either different parts, or different respects, or different times. Different parts: as in Rom. 1. v. 3, 4.
