Concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and declared to be the Son of God with power according to the Spirit of sanctification. Different respect: as in Matth. 22. vers. 45. If David therefore calls him Lord, how is he his son? For similar examples see Luke 2. v. 34; 2 Cor. 3. v. 16. Different times: as in Phil. 2. vers. 7. Christ took the form of a servant, & v. 9. Christ was exalted to the highest loftiness. Here the discourse concerns a different state, or the time of Christ's humiliation and of his exaltation.

units.la: LIX. PRAEDICAMENTA SACRA.
units.tr: LIX. Sacred Predicaments.

units.la: I. PRædicamenta sacra sunt tabulæ vniuersitatis rerum ex sacris literis illustratæ. Tabulæ istæ monstrant conuenientias & differentias rerum in toto mundo, & sunt veluti loci communes, ad quos potest referri quidquid rerum est in hoc vniuer-so.
units.tr: I. Sacred predicaments are tables of the whole of reality, illustrated from the sacred Scriptures. These tables show the agreements and differences of things in the whole world, and they serve as common places to which whatever exists in this universe can be referred.

units.la: II. Prædicamenta sunt decem, vnum Substantiæ; nouem accidentis, Quantitatis, Qualitatis, Actionis, Passionis, Relationis, Quando, Vbi, Situs, Habitus.
units.tr: II. There are ten predicaments: one of substance, and nine of accident: quantity, quality, action, passion, relation, when, where, situation, and habit.

units.la: III. Substantia est ens per se subsistens. Estque increata, vel creata, vel ex vtraque constans. Substantia increata est Deus, à quo, per quem, & in quem omnia, Rom.11.v.36. Hinc appellatur Iehoua & Eheieh. Substantia creata est spiritus, vel corpus. Spiritus creatus est tũ angelus, tũ anima: de quib. Pneumatica & Theologia præcipiunt. Corpus (cuius consideratio est Physica) est incompletum, vel completum. Corpus incompletum est principium vel passiuum, vt materia, Genef. 2. v. 7. vel actiuum, vt forma siue natura, rebus insita in primâ creatione, Gen. 1. vers.11. Corpus completum est simplex, vel mixtum. Corpus simplex est cœlum, vel elementum: quæ duo coniunguntur 2.Petr.3. v.10. Corpus mixtum est imperfectè, vel perfectè mixtum. Corpus imperfectè mixtum appellatur meteorum, quod generatur vel ex vapore, Gen.2.v.6. vel ex fumo, Psal.18.v.9. Corpus perfectè mixtum est fossile, vegetabile, vel animale. Fossile est vel lapis, isque pretiosus aut vulgaris, Exod.28. 1.Reg.5.v.17. vel metallum, cuius species sex commemorantur Num.31.v.22. vel medium minerale, vt sunt succi&c terræ minerales, puta sal, sulphur &c. Corpus vegetabile, est vel minus, vt herba, vel maius, vt arbor. Gen.1.v.11. Corpus animale est homo, Gen.1.verf.26. vel bestia, eaque volatilis, seu aerea, aquatilis, vel terrestris, Gen.1.v.20.24. Substantia partim increata partim creata est Iesus Christus, Immanuel & Irhiel hanc ob causam dictus, Esa.7. verf.14. Prou.30. verf.1.
units.tr: III. Substance is a being that subsists through itself. It is either uncreated, or created, or made up of both. Uncreated substance is God, from whom, through whom, and unto whom are all things, Rom. 11:36. Hence he is called Jehovah and Eheieh. Created substance is either spirit or body. Created spirit is either an angel or a soul; of these, pneumatics and theology give instruction. Body (whose study belongs to physics) is either incomplete or complete. Incomplete body is either a passive principle, such as matter, Gen. 2:7, or an active principle, such as the form or nature implanted in things at the first creation, Gen. 1:11. Complete body is either simple or mixed. Simple body is either the heavens or an element; these two are joined together in 2 Pet. 3:10. Mixed body is either imperfectly or perfectly mixed. Imperfectly mixed body is called a meteor, which is generated either from vapour, Gen. 2:6, or from smoke, Ps. 18:9. Perfectly mixed body is either a fossil, a vegetable, or an animal. A fossil is either a stone, and that either precious or common, Exod. 28; 1 Kings 5:17; or a metal, whose six kinds are mentioned in Num. 31:22; or a mineral medium, such as mineral juices and earths, for example salt, sulphur and so on. A vegetable body is either smaller, like an herb, or larger, like a tree, Gen. 1:11. An animal body is man, Gen. 1:26, or a beast, and that either flying, or airborne, or aquatic, or terrestrial, Gen. 1:20, 24. Substance partly uncreated and partly created is Jesus Christ, called Immanuel and Irhiel for this reason, Isa. 7:14; Prov. 30:1.

units.la: IV. Quantitas est, à quâ subiectum denominatur quantum, i. e. magnum vel multu. Estque continua, vel discreta. Quantitas continua est, cuius partes communi termino cohærent. Estque magnitudo, vel aliquid magnitudini analogum, vti est tempus, motus, & extensio gradus. Magnitudo est extensio materiæ in corpore naturali: estque linea, superficies, vel corpus: quorum exempla vide in arcâ Noë, Gen. 6. tabernaculo Mosis, Exod.30. & 36. & templo Salomonis, 1.Reg.6. Tempus est continuatio durationis successiua, constans præterito, præsenti & futuro, Psal.19.v.3. Eccl.1.2. & 3. Motus est continuatio actionis & passionis, Gen.1.v.11. Extensio gradus est remissio vel intensio, Ioan.4.v.8. Quantitas discreta est, cuius partes communi termino non continentur: vt est numerus, cuius exempla multa sunt in historiis & prophetiis sacris, vt Num.1. Dan.9. & 12. Apoc.7. & 11.
units.tr: IV. Quantity is that from which a subject is denominated as "quantum," that is, great or many. It is either continuous or discrete. Continuous quantity is that whose parts cohere by a common boundary. It is either magnitude, or something analogous to magnitude, such as time, motion, and the extension of a degree. Magnitude is the extension of matter in a natural body; it is either a line, a surface, or a body. Examples of these may be seen in Noah's ark, Gen. 6; the tabernacle of Moses, Exod. 30 and 36; and the temple of Solomon, 1 Kings 6. Time is the successive continuation of duration, consisting of past, present and future, Ps. 19:3; Eccl. 1:2, 3. Motion is the continuation of action and passion, Gen. 1:11. The extension of a degree is remission or intension, John 4:8. Discrete quantity is that whose parts are not held together by a common boundary, as number is. There are many examples of this in the sacred histories and prophecies, such as Num. 1; Dan. 9 and 12; Rev. 7 and 11.

units.la: V. Qualitas est, à quâ subiectum denominatur quale. Eius species sunt quatuor: Potentia naturalis, Habitus, Qualitas patibilis, & Forma siue figura. Potentia naturalis est propensio naturæ ad aliquid agendum vel patiendum. Eftq; prima, vel secunda.Prima, quæ statim ebullit e forma subiecti, siue sit manifesta, vt est potentia mouendi & quiescendi, appetendi & sentiendi, risibilitas, ϙρρψ, docilitas &c: siue occulta, vt est ιδιοσυγκρασια efficiens sympathiam & antipathiam, vt in magnete est vis trahendi ferrum. Secunda, quæ ex certa organi & temperamenti dispositione pendet: vt est ἀφυια, ingenium, ἀγχινοια. Potentia prima pendet ab ordinariâ creationis lege, quam Deus posuit Gen.1. secunda à peculiari ipsius benedictione, Dan.1. v.4. Potentiæ naturali opponitur impotentia naturalis. Habitus est qualitas introducta in hominem, per quam reddituri habilis ad operationes, quas per solam naturam præstare non potest. Eftq; inchoatus, vel perfectus. Inchoatus est, qui ad persectum disponit: unde dispositio appellatur, quæ est ἀμετα-κολως ἀξιωτις. Talis fuit sapientia & iustitia originalis in homine, Gen.3. Habitus perfectus est, qui complementum suum est adeptus. Eius hæc signa sunt, si quis ειδως, sciens, περιαμβανων, volens; ἀμεταχωτως εχων, constanter; ηδεως, libenter, operetur. Estque infusus, vel acquisitus. Infusus est, qui à Deo singulari gratiâ homini confertur, unde appellatur Θεοδοτος. Eftq; extraordinarius, vt lumen propheticum in V. & N. T. vel ordinarius, vt fides, spes, charitas, 1.Cor.12.&13. Habitus acquisitus est, qui ex sæpius iteratis, vel paucis bene validis actionibus comparatur: estque theoreticus, practicus, vel poeticus. Quo pertinet scientia, ars, virtus, vitium, de quibus vide Sap.7. Galat.5. Qualitas patibilis est affici ens, vel affecta. Qualitas afficiens est, quæ in facultate percipiente passionem efficit. Estque prima, vel orta. Prima: vt lux, calor, frigus, siccitas, humi-
units.tr: V. Quality is that from which a subject is denominated as "such." Its species are four: natural power, habit, passible quality, and form or figure. Natural power is the propensity of a nature to do or suffer something. It is either first or second. The first power, which at once bursts forth from the form of the subject, is either manifest, as the power of moving and resting, of desiring and perceiving, the capacity for laughter, [ϙρρψ], docility, and so on; or hidden, as the idiosyncrasy [ιδιοσυγκρασια] that produces sympathy and antipathy, as in the magnet there is the power of attracting iron. The second power depends on a certain disposition of organ and temperament, as awkwardness [ἀφυια], talent, and quickness of wit [ἀγχινοια]. The first power depends on the ordinary law of creation, which God laid down in Gen. 1; the second on his special blessing, Dan. 1:4. Natural power is opposed by natural impotence. Habit is a quality introduced into a man, by which he is made fit for operations which he cannot perform by nature alone. It is either inchoate or perfect. The inchoate habit is that which disposes towards perfection, and is therefore called a disposition, which is an unfailing fitness [ἀμετακόλως ἀξιωτις]. Such was the original wisdom and righteousness in man, Gen. 3. A perfect habit is one that has attained its completion. Its signs are these: if a man acts knowingly [ειδως], deliberately [περιαμβανων], willingly; if he acts steadily [ἀμεταχωτως εχων], constantly; if he acts gladly [ηδεως], freely. A habit is either infused or acquired. An infused habit is one conferred upon a man by God's special grace, and is therefore called God-given [Θεοδοτος]. It is either extraordinary, such as the prophetic light in the Old and New Testaments, or ordinary, such as faith, hope and charity, 1 Cor. 12 and 13. An acquired habit is one gained from actions often repeated, or from a few actions that are strongly enough performed. It is theoretical, practical, or poetic. To this belong knowledge, art, virtue and vice, on which see Wisd. 7; Gal. 5. A passible quality is a thing that affects, or is affected. The affecting quality is that which produces a passion in a perceiving faculty. It is either first or arising. The first are such things as light, heat, cold, dryness, and humi-

units.la: ditas. Orta est vel magis passiua, vt grauitas & leuitas, raritas & densitas, mollities & duritics, læuitas & asperitas, viscositas & lentor &c. vel magis actiua, vt color, sapor, odor, & sonus. Exempla harum qualitatum vide Exod. 28. 30.36. & seqq.capp. Leuit.1.2.4.8. & 23. Qualitas affecta est, quæ ex effectione qualitatis afficientis existit: vt ira & toruitas, vultus in Caino, Gen.4.v.5. Huc pertinent omnes affectus, boni & mali, simplices & compositi. Forma est qualitas ex certa partium configuratione existens. Estque natiua, vel mechanica. Illius exemplum est in arboribus paradisi, Gen.2.v.9: huius in tabernaculo Mosis, & templo Salomonis, Exod.36. & seqq. 1.Reg.6.
units.tr: dity. The arising qualities are either more passive, such as heaviness and lightness, rarity and density, softness and hardness, smoothness and roughness, viscosity and sluggishness, and so on; or more active, such as colour, taste, smell, and sound. Examples of these qualities may be seen in Exod. 28, 30, 36 and following chapters, and Lev. 1, 2, 4, 8 and 23. An affected quality is one that arises from the effect of an affecting quality: such as anger and sternness, the countenance of Cain, Gen. 4:5. To this belong all the affections, good and bad, simple and compound. Form is a quality arising from a definite configuration of parts. It is either natural or mechanical. An example of the former is in the trees of paradise, Gen. 2:9; of the latter, in the tabernacle of Moses and the temple of Solomon, Exod. 36 and following; 1 Kings 6.

units.la: VI. Actio est actus, quo substantia aliquid dat alicui. Dico substantia: quia actio conuenit solis substantiis. Qualitates dicuntur agere ἀχύρως[?], quamuis substantiis dent ut agant. Est autem actio immanens; vel transiens. Immanens, quæ ipsum agens respicit, vel aliud extra obiectum, ita ut in illo non faciat impressionem. Sic Deus Pater ab æterno gignit Filiū, quomodo sol despargit lumen, Heb.1.verf.2. Transiens, quæ ad aliud, extra agens, obiectum refertur, ita ut in patiente fiat realis mutatio: ut quando Deus gubernat hunc mundum, Psal.104. Deinde actio est intentionalis, vel transmutatiua. Quæ diuisio coincidit cum priori. Tertiò actio est transcendetalis, vel prædicamentalis. De quâ diuisione vide suprà in metaphysicis. Quartò actio est Dei, vel creaturæ. Actio Dei est interna, vel externa. Interna, quæ non terminatur ad creaturas: eaque tum essentialis, ut quando Deus seipsum intelligit & amat; tum personalis, ut generatio & processio diuina. Externa, quæ refertur ad creaturas: eaque vel communis tribus personis, ut creatio, redemtio, & sanctificatio: vel propria certæ personæ, ut missio Filij, assumtio & sanctificatio naturæ humanæ Christi. Actio creaturæ est spiritualis vel corporalis. Spiritualis, ut est motus localis angeli, intellectio & volitio angeli & animæ inorganica, celebratio Dei, tentatio diaboli. Corporalis, ut est illuminatio, generatio, corruptio, alteratio, accretio, diminutio, motus localis, nutritio, sensio, appetitus, affectus, respiratio, progressio, intellectio & volitio organica. Denique actio est naturalis & insita, vel acquisita & habitualis. Naturalis, quæ proficiscitur ex potentia naturali: ut intellectio, loquela, recordatio, fletus, generatio. Acquisita, quæ comparatur exercitio, vt est θεωρία[?] siue contemplatio, πρᾶξις[?] siue operatio, & ποίησις[?] siue effectio.
units.tr: VI. Action is the act by which a substance gives something to something else. I say substance, because action belongs only to substances. Qualities are said to act improperly [ἀχύρως?], although they give substances the power to act. Action is either immanent or transient. Immanent action is that which regards the agent itself, or some other object outside it, without making any impression upon it. Thus God the Father from eternity begets the Son, as the sun sheds its light, Heb. 1:2. Transient action is that which is directed to another object outside the agent, so that a real change takes place in the patient; as when God governs this world, Ps. 104. Further, action is either intentional or transmutative. This division coincides with the previous one. Thirdly, action is either transcendental or predicamental. On this division see above, in the metaphysics. Fourthly, action is either God's or a creature's. God's action is either internal or external. Internal is that which does not terminate upon creatures; and this is either essential, as when God understands and loves himself, or personal, as the divine generation and procession. External is that which refers to creatures; and this is either common to the three persons, such as creation, redemption and sanctification, or proper to a certain person, such as the sending of the Son, and the assumption and sanctification of Christ's human nature. A creature's action is either spiritual or corporeal. Spiritual action is such as the local motion of an angel, the understanding and willing of an angel or of an inorganic soul, the worship of God, the temptation of the devil. Corporeal action is such as illumination, generation, corruption, alteration, accretion, diminution, local motion, nutrition, sensation, appetite, emotion, respiration, progression, and the understanding and willing that are organic. Finally, action is either natural and innate, or acquired and habitual. Natural action proceeds from natural power: such as understanding, speech, recollection, weeping, generation. Acquired action is gained by practice, such as θεωρία [theōria], that is, contemplation; πρᾶξις [praxis], that is, doing; and ποίησις [poiēsis], that is, making.

units.la: VII. Passio est actus, quo aliquid recipit actionem. Estque primò perfectiua, vel destructiua. Persectiua, quae perficit patiens: vt cùm regeneramur à Spiritu sancto, Iohan.3. Destructiua, quae abolet patiens: vt cùm Eua fuit seducta à diabolo. Deinde passio est intentionalis, vel transmutatiua. Intentionalis, cùm nulla fit realis mutatio, sed tantum terminatio actionis: vt cùm Deus à nobis celebratur. Transmutatiua, cùm fit realis mutatio in patiente: vt cùm Deus percussit primogenita Aegypti. Tertiò passio est secundum naturam, vel contra naturam. Illa conseruat rem, vt laetitia: haec corrumpit rem, vt morbus, ira, tristitia.
units.tr: VII. Passion is an act by which something receives an action. It is first either perfective or destructive. Perfective passion perfects the one who undergoes it, as when we are regenerated by the Holy Spirit, John 3. Destructive passion destroys the one who undergoes it, as when Eve was seduced by the devil. Second, passion is either intentional or transmutative. Intentional passion occurs when no real change takes place, but only the terminating of an action, as when God is praised by us. Transmutative passion occurs when a real change takes place in the patient, as when God struck the firstborn of Egypt. Third, passion is according to nature or contrary to nature. The former preserves the thing, as joy does; the latter corrupts it, as sickness, anger and sadness do.

units.la: VIII. Relatio est, quâ vnum refertur ad alterum. In eâ occurrunt conditiones, & diuisiones. Conditiones relationis sunt habere ista quinque: subiectum, cui inest relatio; relatum & correlatum, quae ad se inuicem referuntur; fundamentum, siue rationem & causam referendi; terminum, siue finem: vt in pane sacrae coenae, subiectum est panis, relatum & correlatum sunt panis & corpus Christi, fundamentum est institutio Dei, terminus est mystica significatio, obsignatio, & exhibitio. Diuisiones sunt, quòd relatio sit rationis vel realis, à natura vel instituto, mutua vel non mutua. Relatio rationis est, quae in collatione rerum, quam facit mens nostra, fundamentum habet: vt si quis dextrum & sinistrum in coelo cogitet. Relatio realis est, quae extra rationem in rebus ipsis fundamentum habet. Estq; secundum esse vel dici. Secundum esse, quae nihil absolutae naturae habet: vt paternitas & filiatio. Secundum dici, quae habet absolutam naturam, cui respectus adhaeret: vt cùm columna refertur ad solum cui insistit. Relatio à natura est, quae oritur à natura, vt est consanguinitas. Relatio ab instituto est, quae ab arbitrio Dei vel hominis oritur: aliàs positiua. Huc pertinent relationes variæ in typis, sacrificiis, personis, rebus & actionibus ecclesiasticis in Leuitico. Relatio mutua est inter ea, quæ sunt sub uno genere: vt inter maritum & vxorem, Gen. 2. Relatio non mutua est inter ea, quæ sunt sub diuerso genere: re; vt inter Deum & nos, Psal. 100. v. 3. Christum & Ecclesiam.Eph. 5.
units.tr: VIII. Relation is that by which one thing is referred to another. In it there occur conditions and divisions. The conditions of a relation are these five: the subject, in which the relation inheres; the relate and correlate, which are referred to one another; the foundation, or the reason and cause of referring; the term, or end. For example, in the bread of the Lord's Supper, the subject is the bread, the relate and correlate are the bread and the body of Christ, the foundation is the institution of God, and the term is the mystical signification, sealing and exhibition. The divisions are that a relation is either of reason or real, from nature or by institution, mutual or non-mutual. A relation of reason is one that has its foundation in the comparison of things which our mind makes, as when someone thinks of right and left in the heavens. A real relation is one that has its foundation in the things themselves, outside of reason; and it is either according to being or according to saying. According to being is that which has nothing of an absolute nature, as fatherhood and sonship. According to saying is that which has an absolute nature to which a respect adheres, as when a column is referred to the ground on which it stands. A relation from nature is one that arises from nature, as consanguinity is. A relation by institution is one that arises from the will of God or of man; otherwise it is called positive. To this belong the various relations in types, sacrifices, persons, things and ecclesiastical actions in Leviticus. A mutual relation is that between things which are under one genus, as between husband and wife, Gen. 2. A non-mutual relation is between things which are under different genera, as between God and us, Ps. 100:3, and between Christ and the Church, Eph. 5.

units.la: IX. Quæ sequuntur prædicamenta, sunt secundaria. Exiis Quando est notatio temporis: Vbi est notatio loci: Situs est circumstantia positionis corporum: Habitus est circumstantia vestitus. Exempla primi prædicamenti sunt Psalm. 106: secundi, Num. 34: tertii, Num. 33. Exod. 37. & 38. quarti, Exod. 28.
units.tr: IX. The following predicaments are secondary. Of these, When is the designation of time; Where is the designation of place; Position is the circumstance of the posture of bodies; Habit is the circumstance of clothing. Examples of the first predicament are Ps. 106; of the second, Num. 34; of the third, Num. 33, Exod. 37 and 38; of the fourth, Exod. 28.

units.la: LX.
units.tr: LX.

units.la: COLLATIO LOGICÆ CVM GRAMMATICA EX S. LI- TERIS.
units.tr: A Comparison of Logic with Grammar, from the Sacred Scriptures.

units.la: I. COllatio Logicæ cum Grammaticâ ex sacris literis monstrat exempla, in quibus verba sunt indicia affectionis Logicæ: idq; in locis inuentionis, axiomate, syllogismo & methodo.
units.tr: I. The comparison of Logic with Grammar, drawn from the sacred Scriptures, shows examples in which words are signs of logical affections, and this in the places of invention, the axiom, the syllogism and the method.

units.la: II. In locis inuentionis affectiones rerum certis vocabulis exprimuntur. Et principio quidem genitiuus vim suam spargit per omnes fere locos inuentionis. Notat enim causam efficientem, vt Matth. 25. v. 34. Marc. 1. v. 24. vel causam finalem, vt Iohan. 17. v. 12. Rom. 8. v. 36. 2. Thess. 2. v. 3. vel materiam, vt Act. 2. v. 3. vel formam, vt Leuit. 5. v. 21. vel effectum, vt Gen. 35. v. 18. Luc. 1. v. 69. vel subiectum, vt Gen. 18. v. 21: vel adiunctum, vt Gen. 24. v. 48. vel totum, vt Leuit. 16. v. 5. vel partitionem, vt Gen. 36. v. 15: vel speciem, vt Exod. 29. v. 2. &c. Atque hinc dicitur genitiuus causæ, effecti, subiecti, obiecti, maiorum, minorum, similium &c. Deinde quilibet locus inuentionis peculiaribus vocabulis indicatur. e.g. ex est nota efficientis, Rom. 11. verf. vlt. Exipfo sunt omnia: vel materiæ, vt Gen. 2. & 3. homo sumtus est expuluere terræ: vel antecedentis, vt Deus iussit lucem e tenebris splendescere, 1. Cor. 4. v. 6. Sic pro notat finem, vt Christus pro nobis est mortuus, id est, nostro bono & loco, vt nos redimeret, Rom. 5. verf. 6. 7. v. Quanto magis indicat comparationem imparium, Luc. 11. v. 13. Sed quis omnia recenseat in hoc compendio?
units.tr: II. In the places of invention, the affections of things are expressed by certain words. And first of all, the genitive spreads its force through almost all the places of invention. For it denotes an efficient cause, as Matth. 25. v. 34. Marc. 1. v. 24.; or a final cause, as Iohan. 17. v. 12. Rom. 8. v. 36. 2. Thess. 2. v. 3.; or matter, as Act. 2. v. 3.; or form, as Leuit. 5. v. 21.; or effect, as Gen. 35. v. 18. Luc. 1. v. 69.; or subject, as Gen. 18. v. 21.; or adjunct, as Gen. 24. v. 48.; or whole, as Leuit. 16. v. 5.; or partition, as Gen. 36. v. 15.; or species, as Exod. 29. v. 2. &c. And hence it is called the genitive of cause, of effect, of subject, of object, of greater things, of lesser things, of similar things, and so on. Then, each place of invention is indicated by particular words. E.g. ex is a mark of efficient cause, Rom. 11. last verse: Of him are all things; or of matter, as in Gen. 2 and 3, man was taken out of the dust of the earth; or of antecedent, as God commanded light to shine out of darkness, 1. Cor. 4. v. 6. So pro denotes the end, as Christ died for us, that is, for our good and in our place, so that he might redeem us, Rom. 5. vv. 6, 7. How much more indicates the comparison of unequals, Luc. 11. v. 13. But who could list everything in this compendium?

units.la: III. In axiomate verbum substantiuum, nomina quantitatis, coniunctiones copulati- uæ, connexiuæ, difcretiuæ & disiunctiuæ, par- ticulæ relatiuæ, & similia sunt attendenda.
units.tr: III. In the axiom, the substantive verb, the words of quantity, the copulative, connective, discretive and disjunctive conjunctions, the relative particles, and similar items are to be noted.

units.la: Verbum substantiuum est nota axiomatis simplicis fiue categorici. Huic æquipollent omnia verba actiua & paffiua. Nomina quantitatis sunt omnis, nullus, quidam, nemo, &c. Particulæ relatiuæ sunt vbi, ibi; talis, qualis; tantus, quantus. Coniunctiones copulatiuæ indicant axioma copulatum; connexiuæ, connexum; difcretiuæ, discretum; disiunctiuæ, disiunctum. Exempla vide supra in Logicis.
units.tr: The substantive verb is the mark of a simple or categorical axiom. All active and passive verbs are equivalent to it. The words of quantity are all, none, some, no one, and so on. The relative particles are where and there; such as and of what kind; as great as and as much as. The copulative conjunctions indicate a copulative axiom; connective ones, a connected axiom; discretive ones, a discrete axiom; disjunctive ones, a disjunctive axiom. For examples see above in the Logic.

units.la: IV. In syllogismo attendendæ sunt coniunctiones causales & rationales. Nam illæ indicant argumentum fiue medium terminum, hæc conclufionem fiue quæstionem. Exemplum illustre vide Rom. 3. verf. 20. 23. 28. Hic memineris, coniunctionem causalem semper indicare causam conclusionis fiue consequentiæ, non vero rei fiue essentiæ. e.g. 1. Cor. 10. verf. 5. Plures illorum non approbauit Deus. Probstratienim sunt in deferto. Hic particula enim, fiue nam, non significat causam antecedentem, sed causam illationis. Confer Matth. 25. v. 35. Luc. 7. v. 47. V. In methodo oportet attendere aduerbia ordinis, & omnino particulas connexiles formulasque transitionum. Huc pertinent ista. Roman. 1. verf. 9. Quid igitur? Rom. 4. v. 1. & 6. 6. v. 1. Quid igitur tur dicemus? 1.Cor.12.verf.1. Porrò de spiritualibus donis· 1.Cor.15.v.1. Cæterùm notum facio vobis. Hebr. 11. v.32. Et quid præterea loquor?
units.tr: IV. In the syllogism the causal and rational conjunctions are to be noted. For the former indicate the argument or middle term, the latter the conclusion or question. For a striking example see Rom. 3. v. 20, 23, 28. Here you should remember that a causal conjunction always indicates the cause of the conclusion or consequence, not of the thing or essence. E.g. 1. Cor. 10. v. 5. Many of them God did not approve, for they were overthrown in the desert. Here the particle for, or nam, does not signify a preceding cause but the cause of the inference. Compare Matth. 25. v. 35. Luc. 7. v. 47. V. In method one must attend to adverbs of order and, in general, to connecting particles and formulas of transition. To this belong the following: Roman. 1. v. 9. What then? Rom. 4. v. 1. & 6. v. 1. What then shall we say? 1. Cor. 12. v. 1. Now concerning spiritual gifts. 1. Cor. 15. v. 1. Moreover, I make known to you. Hebr. 11. v. 32. And what more shall I say?

units.la: LXI. CABBALA SACRA.
units.tr: LXI. SACRED CABBALA.

units.la: I. Cabbala sacra est doctrina ex sacris literis colligens arcana philologica, & practica. Cabbalah significat acceptionem, seu doctrinam, aliunde acceptam solo auditu. Est autem, vt Schindlerus in Lexico annotat 1. doctrina patrum, quam accepit vnus de ore alterius, & tradidit posteris ab Adamo vsque ad Mosen, qui legem conscripsit. 2. Lex oretenus tradita seu axiomatica, expositio legis scripta, quam Moses dies 40 & totidem noctes in monte Sinai commoratus, ex ore Dei didicit. De hac sentiunt, quòd Moses eam tradiderit Iosuæ, Iosua septuaginta senioribus, hi prophetis, hi viris magnæ synagogæ, hi suis per multas ætates successoribus vsque ad illud tempus, quo tandem fuit mandata literis & inde confectum Thalmud. 3. vsurpatur de iis mysteriis, quæ Iudæi recentiores in Mosis & prophetarum scriptis vestigant, dum literas & syllabas, præsertim nominum Dei numerant, pro numeris accipiunt, transponunt, & symbolicè mutant. Hæc in speculativam & practicam diuiditur. His adde, quòd Cabbala practica diuiditur in Berefchith & Mercabah. Illa explicat opus creationis, hæc occupatur circa nomina Dei & angelorum, vt adminiculo ipsorum aliquid operetur mirabile. Illa est pars physiologiæ secretioris: hæc labe superstitionis est fœdata.
units.tr: I. Sacred Cabbala is the doctrine that gathers hidden philological and practical matters from the sacred writings. Cabbalah means a reception, or a teaching received from elsewhere by hearing alone. Schindler notes in his Lexicon that it has three senses: (1) the teaching of the fathers, which one man received from the mouth of another and handed on to posterity, from Adam down to Moses, who wrote the law; (2) the law delivered by word of mouth, or the axiomatic law, a written exposition of the law, which Moses learned from the mouth of God while he stayed on Mount Sinai forty days and as many nights; (3) the mysteries which the later Jews seek out in the writings of Moses and the prophets, while they count the letters and syllables, especially the names of God, take them as numbers, transpose them, and change them symbolically. Concerning the second sense, they hold that Moses handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the seventy elders, these to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Synagogue, who passed it to their successors through many ages until the time when at last it was committed to writing, and thence compiled into the Talmud. Cabbala is divided into speculative and practical. To this add that practical Cabbala is divided into Bereshith and Merkabah. The former explains the work of creation; the latter is occupied with the names of God and of the angels, so that by their help one may work some wonder. The former is a part of the more secret physiology; the latter is defiled by the stain of superstition.

units.la: II. Cabbala philologica tribus absoluitur partibus, quæ appellantur פרדס[?], id est, hortus, dictione memoriali.
units.tr: II. Philological Cabbala is completed in three parts, which are called PaRDeS [פרדס], that is, "garden," by a mnemonic word.

units.la: ג[?] significat Gematriā, vt loquuntur Rabbini, hoc est, Arithmologiam, quâ literæ Hebraicæ contextus sacri resoluuntur in numeros. Ꝯleno-[?] tat Notariekun, quando litera ponitur prodiftione. Ea Cabbalæ pars sic dicta est ab apicibus notariorum. Hsignificat[?] Temurah, id est, commutationem elementorum, cum litera pro litera ingeniose ponitur. Primi modi exemplum est Zachar.3.v.8.vbi Messias appellatur germen, quod per Gematriam idem valet quod consolator, quia ex vtriusq; nominis literis resultat numerus 138. Secundi modi exemplum est Gen.21.v.33. vbi complet tria hospitalitatis officia, ita vt notet cibum, potationem, pernoctationem. Tertii modi exemplum est Ierem.25.v.26.vbi per (speciem Cabbalæ Temurae ponitur pro ). Si enim bipertito diuidas alphabetum, & literis literas opponas, litera respondebit , & litera litera . Cæterum huius Cabbalæ usus non tantum est ut sit acutus lusus ingenii, sed etiam ut nobis seruiat in confutandis Iudæis recentioribus. Multa enim Scripturæ V.T. loca per hanc Cabbalam à vetustissimis Iudæis explicantur de sacrosancta Trinitate & Messia, & quidem adeo clare, ut recentiores Iudæi non habeant quod excipiant.
units.tr: The letter ג signifies Gematria, as the rabbis call it, that is, arithmology, by which the letters of a sacred text are resolved into numbers. The letter ... signifies Notarikon, when a letter stands for a word. This part of Cabbala is so called from the abbreviations of the scribes. The letter ... signifies Temurah, that is, the exchange of elements, when one letter is ingeniously put in place of another. An example of the first kind is Zechariah 3:8, where the Messiah is called the "Branch," which by Gematria means the same as "Consoler," because the letters of the two words yield the number 138. An example of the second kind is Genesis 21:33, where the three duties of hospitality are completed, so that it denotes food, drink, and lodging for the night. An example of the third kind is Jeremiah 25:26, where, by the sort of Temurah called Cabbala, one word is put for another, ... If you divide the alphabet into two halves and set letters against letters, the letter ... will answer to ..., and the letter ... to .... Moreover, the use of this Cabbala is not only to be a subtle play of wit, but also to serve us in refuting the later Jews. For many passages of the Old Testament are explained by the ancient Jews through this Cabbala concerning the most holy Trinity and the Messiah, and indeed so clearly that the later Jews have nothing to object.

units.la: III. Cabbala practica duabus continetur partibus.
units.tr: III. Practical Cabbala is contained in two parts.

units.la: Prima versatur circa mysterium siue arcanum naturæ, & tinctura physicorum appellant. Hoc fiquidé arcanum non ita pdiu est literarum monumentis, vt à quolibet inde possit elici vel exsculpi. Exiftimarunt enim adepti, qui dicuntur, philosophi, hoc tantum Dei donum Cabbalisticè duntaxat esse propagandum. Altera huius Cabbalæ pars occupata est circa eam vitæ rationem, qua homo possit sanctorum angelorum præsidium in Iesu Christo sibi conciliare, idque retinere. Quo pertinent precationes Cabbalisticæ Iulii Sperberi, meris Scripturæ verbis adornatæ: itemque præceptiones Henrici Khunrathi de habitu Kabbalistico, & similes pii piorum Cabbalistarum libelli. Quæ omnia Christiano animo velim accipi, ne quis existimet me aperire portam audaciæ Rabbinicæ. Sed manum de hac tabula. Neque enim Cabbaistam agit, qui literis consignat ea, quæ requirunt solum auditum Cabbalisticum. Inspice Cabbalam Reuchlini, eiusque tractatum de verbo mirifico, & deprehendes totam Cabbalæ summam contineri istis Reuchlini verbis in calce verbi mirifici: Sile, cela, occulta, tege, tace, mussa.
units.tr: The first is concerned with the mystery or secret of nature, which the physicists call the tincture. For this secret has not been committed to written records so long ago that anyone can draw it out or extract it from them. The so-called adepts, the philosophers, thought that this gift of God was to be passed on only in a cabbalistic manner. The other part of this Cabbala is occupied with that manner of life by which a man may win for himself the protection of the holy angels in Jesus Christ, and keep it. To this belong the cabbalistic prayers of Julius Sperber, composed of the pure words of Scripture, and likewise the precepts of Henry Khunrath on the cabbalistic disposition, and similar pious little books of pious cabbalists. I would have all these received in a Christian spirit, lest anyone think that I am opening the gate to rabbinic audacity. But I put my hand off this tablet. For he is not acting as a cabbalist who commits to writing those things which require only cabbalistic hearing. Look into the Cabbala of Reuchlin and his treatise on the wonder-working word, and you will find the whole sum of the Cabbala contained in these words of Reuchlin at the end of De verbo mirifico: Be silent, conceal, hide, cover, keep quiet, hush.

units.la: LXII.
units.tr: LXII.

units.la: ALCHYMIA SACRA.
units.tr: SACRED ALCHEMY.

units.la: I. ALchymia sacra est ars separans purum ab impuro, collecta è sacris literis. Non intelligo hic sophistarum diabolicum commentum, quo emungunt loculos aliorum, & de quo rectè dicitur, Alchymia est ars sine arte, pars sine parte, cuius initium est scire, medium mentiri, &finis mendicare. Alia est philosophorum Alchymia, cuius character est innocentia vitæ, & silentium plusquam Harpocraticum. Ista Alchymia est pars physicæ & medicinæ.
units.tr: I. Sacred alchemy is the art of separating the pure from the impure, gathered from the sacred writings. I do not mean here the devilish invention of the sophists, by which they empty the purses of others, and of which it is rightly said: "Alchemy is an art without art, a part without a part, whose beginning is to know, whose middle is to lie, and whose end is to beg." There is another alchemy, that of the philosophers, whose mark is innocence of life and a silence more than Harpocratean. This alchemy is a part of physics and medicine.

units.la: II. Partes Alchymiæ sunt duæ: una de materiâ, altera de præparatione.
units.tr: II. The parts of alchemy are two: one concerns the matter, the other the preparation.

units.la: III. Materia Alchymiæ est universalis, vel particularis.
units.tr: III. The matter of alchemy is either universal or particular.

units.la: IV. Materia universalis est corpus à Deo creatum, ex quo elicitur panacea. De hac rectè pronuntiat philosophus: Una res est à Deo creata, subiectum omnis mirabilitatis, quæ in terris & in cœlis est: ipsa est actu animalis, vegetalis, & mineralis, ubique reperta, à paucissimis cognita, à nullis suo proprio nomine expressa. Quibus verbis quasi digito exserto monstrat materiam philosophicam, de quâ vide tabulam smaragdinam Hermetis, vel potius primum & secundum caput Geneseos. Ibi enim tam clarè describitur hæc materia, ut mirari subeat, nos in tam clarâ luce posse cæcutire. Est autem uno verbo cœlum & terra, id est, cetrum cœli & terræ, seu cœlum philosophorum & terra philosophorum. Confer cum iis, quæ supra in physicis passim disputauimus hac in sententia, & quære centrum omnium centrorum. In illo enim inuenies clauem ad omnes peripherias rerum totius mundi aperiendas. Vide quoque 2. Petr.3.v.5.
units.tr: IV. The universal matter is the body created by God, from which the panacea is drawn. Of this the philosopher rightly pronounces: One thing was created by God, the subject of all the wonders that are on earth and in heaven. It is actually animal, vegetable, and mineral, found everywhere, known by very few, and named by no one by its proper name. In these words he shows the philosophical matter, as if with a finger outstretched. See about it the Emerald Tablet of Hermes, or rather the first and second chapters of Genesis. For there this matter is described so clearly that one is amazed we can grow blind in so clear a light. It is, in a single word, the heaven and earth, that is, the centre of heaven and earth, or the heaven of the philosophers and the earth of the philosophers. Compare it with what we have disputed throughout in physics above on this point, and seek the centre of all centres. For in it you will find the key to open all the circumferences of the things of the whole world. See also 2 Peter 3:5.

units.la: V. Materia particularis est quodlibet corpus minerale, animale, & vegetabile. Verissimum enim est illud philosophema: Quot res, tot medicinæ. Quæ omnes fluunt tanquam riui ex vno fonte. Nam vniuersale illud philosophorum subiectum est spiritus vitæ, qui dum irrepit in lactucæ principia, fit lactuca; dum in rosæ principia irrepit, fit rosa; dum in sal, sulphur & mercurium auri, fit aurum; dum in reliquorum metallorum principia, similiter. De arboribus, brutis, & homine idem est iudicium. Spiritum dico, qui purissimus est in cœlo supremo, & respondet spiritui animali in cerebro: in cœlo mediano non ita est subtilis, & respondet spiritui vitali in corde: in cœlo infimo & aëreo adhuc minus est subtilis, & respondet spiritui nostro naturali in hepate. Hic spiritus in se ipso spectatus, & ab omnibus indiuiduis separatus, nec ignis est, nec aër, nec aqua, nec terra, nec species aliqua ex illis, quæ in sua prædicamenta retulit Aristoteles. Ideo nullo alio nomine appellari posse videtur, quàm quintæ essentiæ. Erit autem anima rationalis essentia sexta. Neque enim illa subiacet huic spiritui catholico, qui extrahitur è chao catholico, & in omnibus corporibus mirabilia efficit. Si vero, inquiat aliquis, hic spiritus inuenitur in omnibus corporibus, perinde est, siue hoc sumatur, siue illud. Resp. Perinde non est: quia habitat in chao vniuersaliter, in reliquis corporibus particulariter. Quare si aliquis quærat medicinam vniuersalem, debet missa facere particularia.
units.tr: V. The particular matter is any mineral, animal, or vegetable body. For that philosophical saying is most true: "As many things, so many medicines." All of these flow like streams from one source. For that universal subject of the philosophers is the spirit of life, which, when it creeps into the principles of lettuce, becomes lettuce; when it creeps into the principles of the rose, becomes a rose; when it creeps into the salt, sulphur and mercury of gold, becomes gold; and likewise when it creeps into the principles of the other metals. The judgment is the same about trees, beasts, and man. I mean the spirit which is most pure in the highest heaven and corresponds to the animal spirit in the brain; in the middle heaven it is not so subtle, and corresponds to the vital spirit in the heart; in the lowest and airy heaven it is still less subtle, and corresponds to our natural spirit in the liver. This spirit, viewed in itself and separated from all individual things, is neither fire, nor air, nor water, nor earth, nor any species of those which Aristotle placed in his categories. Therefore it seems that it can be called by no other name than the quintessence. The rational soul, however, will be a sixth essence. For it is not subject to this universal spirit, which is drawn from the universal chaos and works wonders in all bodies. But if someone should say: "If this spirit is found in all bodies, it makes no difference whether this or that is taken." Answer: It does make a difference, because it dwells in the chaos universally, but in the other bodies particularly. Hence, if anyone seeks a universal medicine, he must set aside the particular things.

units.la: VI. Præparatio materiæ est, quâ ex chao catholico fit sal. Sal, inquam, sapientiæ, quod est principium, medium, & finis operis. Hinc alchymia nomen habet à sale, non sane illo vulgari, quod lippis & tonsoribus est notum, sed philosophico, quod est merus ignis, quo salire oportet ea, quæ à putrefactione debent præseruari. Modus extrahendi illud sal continetur in sacris literis, & quidem adeo clarè in tribus locis, ut nihil possit es5 se clarius. Principio videmus Gen. 1. Deum primo die creasse terram aquis circumfusam, & tertio die aquam separasse à terra, verùm ita, ut aquas diuiserit in superiores & inferiores, quibus terra nunquam non irrigatur & fœcudatur. Tu fac idem, mi philosophe. Imitare Deum, quate10 nus licet. Non potes creare terram, neque verò etiam debes: quia Deus satis superque creauit, quod tuam diligentiam possit occupare. Accipe itaque chaos à Deo creatum: separa ab illo aquam: toties imbue chaos suâ a-quâ, ut elicias sal. Coque, coque: laua, laua: repete, repe15 te. Deinde Gen. 2. legimus Deum creasse fœminam ex costâ viri. Eundem in modum oportet hîc procedere. Sumendus est hermaphroditus, id est, chaos catholicum, & ex Adamo educenda est Eua: vel (ut clariùs dicam ex eodem cap:) sic tractanda est materia, ut vapor ascendat è ter20 ra, qui irriget vniuersam superficiem terræ, per iteratam scil. circulationem. Denique Christus Iohan. 12. v. 24. ait: Amen, amen dico vobis, nisi granum frumenti ceciderit in terram, & mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet: si verò mortuum fuerit, multum adfert fructum. Sic apostolus 1. Cor. 15. v. 36. 37. Demens, quod tu seris, non viuiscit, nisi mortuum fuerit. Et quod seris, non corpus oriturum seris, sed nudum granum, prout inciderit, tritici aut alicuius ex reliquis seminibus. Ex his duobus locis colligere est, putrefactionem esse clauem totius operis, & semen committendum esse terræ, ut ita in primam ma30 teriam reducatur per primam materiam. Si ergo velis metallum, vel aliud corpus resoluere in primam materiam, caue aliquid sumas præter primam materiam. Hæc enim est primum mobile omnium corporum. Unde facile est intelligere, quanto in errore versentur, qui corpus parti35 culare soluunt per aliud particulare. Non ita vah idiotæ, vah sophistæ! Si habeatis particulare corpus, v.g. aurum, soluisoluite illud, non per particulare ( id enim soluet aurum ad Kalendas Græcas ) sed per vniuersale. Sic glacies soluitur in aquam per aquam, primam suam materiam. Sed concludam. Resolue spiritum coagulatum: refolutu sublima: in sublimato resolue aurum, vt habeas medicinam ad homines & metalla. Cur vero aurum potiùs, quàm aliud metallum, vel vegetabile? Resp. Possunt omnis generis corpora fermentari cum spiritu illo catholico à vinculis corporeis liberato. Verùm enim uero aurum est corpus perfectissimum, & ideo resolutum in spiritum non potest non suppeditare præstantiorem tincturam, quàm illa corpora, quæ non peruenerunt ad tantam perfectionem: quia melius meliori potiùs addendum est, quàm bonum meliori.
units.tr: VI. The preparation of the matter is that by which salt is made from the universal chaos: the salt, I say, of wisdom, which is the beginning, middle, and end of the work. Hence alchemy has its name from salt, not indeed that common salt which is known to bleary-eyed men and barbers, but the philosophical salt, which is pure fire, by which those things that ought to be preserved from putrefaction must be salted. The method of extracting that salt is contained in the sacred writings, and indeed so clearly in three places that nothing could be clearer. First, we see in Genesis 1 that God on the first day created the earth surrounded by waters, and on the third day separated the water from the earth, but in such a way that he divided the waters into upper and lower, by which the earth is never not watered and made fruitful. Do the same, my philosopher. Imitate God, as far as you may. You cannot create earth, nor indeed ought you: because God has created more than enough to occupy your diligence. Take, therefore, the chaos created by God; separate the water from it; steep the chaos in its own water so often that you draw out the salt. Boil, boil; wash, wash; repeat, repeat. Next, in Genesis 2 we read that God created the woman from the rib of the man. In the same way one must proceed here. The hermaphrodite, that is, the universal chaos, is to be taken, and Eve is to be brought forth from Adam; or (to speak more clearly, from the same chapter) the matter is to be so handled that vapour rises from the earth, which waters the whole surface of the earth, by repeated circulation. Finally, Christ says in John 12:24: "Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." So the apostle, 1 Corinthians 15:36-37: "Thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die. And that which thou sowest, thou sowest not that body that shall be, but bare grain, it may chance of wheat, or of some other grain." From these two passages it may be gathered that putrefaction is the key to the whole work, and that the seed must be committed to the earth, so that it is thus brought back into the first matter by means of the first matter. If therefore you wish to resolve a metal or other body into the first matter, take care that you add nothing besides the first matter. For this is the prime mover of all bodies. Hence it is easy to understand how far astray those are who dissolve a particular body by means of another particular. Not so, you fools and sophists! If you have a particular body, for example gold, dissolve it, but not by a particular (for that would dissolve the gold at the Greek Kalends), but by the universal. Thus ice is dissolved into water by water, its first matter. But I will conclude. Resolve the coagulated spirit; resolve the sublimate; dissolve gold in the sublimate, so that you have a medicine for men and metals. But why gold rather than some other metal, or a vegetable? Answer: all kinds of bodies can be fermented with that universal spirit once it is freed from its bodily bonds. But gold is the most perfect of bodies, and therefore, once resolved into spirit, it cannot fail to supply a more excellent tincture than those bodies which have not attained such perfection: for the better is rather to be added to the better than the good to the better.

units.la: LXIII. ARS DISPVTANDI EX SACRA Scriptura collecta.
units.tr: LXIII. THE ART OF DISPUTING COLLECTED FROM SACRED Scripture.

units.la: ARs disputandi ex sacra Scriptura collecta præcipit de personis disputantibus, rebus disputandis, & modo disputandi. Pertinet autem ad theologiam, logicam & ethicam.
units.tr: The art of disputing, collected from Holy Scripture, prescribes concerning the persons disputing, the matters to be disputed, and the manner of disputing. It belongs to theology, logic and ethics.

units.la: II. Personæ disputantes sunt duæ, proponens & opponens.
units.tr: II. There are two disputing persons: the proposer and the opponent.

units.la: III. Proponens est, qui propugnat aliquid: opponens, qui oppugnat.
units.tr: III. The proposer is the one who defends something; the opponent is the one who attacks it.

units.la: IV. Utriusque officium est commune, vel proprium.
units.tr: IV. The duty of each is either common or particular.

units.la: V. Officium commune proponentis & opponentis est theologicum, ethicum, & logicū.
units.tr: V. The common duty of proposer and opponent is theological, ethical and logical.

units.la: Officium theologicum est 1. à Deo, omnis veritatis authorre, auxilium implorare, vt in disputando veritas eruatur & elucescat, & falsitas refellatur & fugiatur. 2. ad unius Dei laudem & gloriam omnia referre, non vero ad propriam ingenii aut eloquentiae ostentationem respicere.3. ad Scripturam semper confugere. 4. in disputatione pietatem, modestiam, & aequitatem prae se ferre[?]. Vide passim disputationes Christi cum Pharisaeis, Sadducaeis, discipulis &c. Officium ethicum est, amare candorem & benevolentiam, & fugere sophisticam, morositatem, conuitia, calumnias. Officium logicum est 1. statum controversiae e vestigio constituere, & ad eum omnia referre: nec pati se vel latum ungue a principali illa quaestione abduci. 2. e certis & communibus principiis disputare: ut Christus Matt. 22. cum Sadducaeis disputaturus, e Pentateucho arcessit argumentum, non vero ex reliquis Scripturis, quas illi non admittebant. 3. logice differere, hoc est, breuiter & perspicue. 4. personas non permutare. In summa: Uterque, tum proponens, non opponens, sit veritatis & modestiae amans, & statu controversiae recte cognito, e certis principiis, breuiter ac perspicue suam personam agat. Exemplum vide Matth. 4. Luc. 6. & 20. Iohan. 3.8. & 9. Rom. 3.4.9.10.11. Gal.1.2.
units.tr: The theological duty is: (1) to call upon God, the author of all truth, for help, so that in disputing the truth may be drawn out and shine forth, and falsehood may be refuted and avoided; (2) to refer everything to the praise and glory of God alone, and not to aim at the display of one's own talent or eloquence; (3) always to take refuge in Scripture; (4) to show piety, modesty and fairness in the dispute. See throughout the disputations of Christ with the Pharisees, the Sadducees, his disciples, and others. The ethical duty is to love candour and goodwill, and to shun sophistry, peevishness, abuse and slander. The logical duty is: (1) to set out the state of the controversy at once and refer everything to it, and not to allow oneself to be drawn away from that main question even by a hair's breadth; (2) to dispute from certain and common principles, as Christ, about to dispute with the Sadducees, Matt. 22, takes his argument from the Pentateuch and not from the other Scriptures, which they did not admit; (3) to reason logically, that is, briefly and clearly; (4) not to exchange the roles of the persons. In sum: each of them, both proposer and opponent, should love truth and modesty, and, with the state of the controversy rightly known, should carry on his part briefly and clearly, from certain principles. For examples see Matt. 4, Luke 6 and 20, John 3.8 and 9, Rom. 3.4.9.10.11, Gal. 1.2.

units.la: VI. Officium proprium est tum proponen- tis, tum opponentis.
units.tr: VI. The proper duty belongs both to the proposer and to the opponent.

units.la: Proponentis est certam quaestione constituere, eamque idoneis argumentis confirmare, & argumenta contraria redarguere. Opponentis est oppugnare sententiam aduersariam, ita ut in re seria sophismatis non ludat, sed agnitae veritati cedat. Quia vero uterq; debet esse instructus argumentis, idoneis, proponam hoc loco modum inueniendi argumenta. Is autem uno verbo consistit in deductione thematis per locos inuentionis applicatos materiae theologicae, hoc modo.
units.tr: It is the proposer's task to set up a definite question, to confirm it with suitable arguments, and to refute the contrary arguments. It is the opponent's task to attack the adverse opinion, not playing with sophisms in a serious matter, but yielding to the truth once it is recognised. Since each of them ought to be equipped with suitable arguments, I shall set out here the method of finding arguments. This consists, in a word, in the deduction of the thesis through the topics of invention applied to theological matter, in the following way.

units.la: 1. Ad locum causae efficientis pertinet argumentum a lege cessante; a promissionibus & comminationibus diuinis; a praeceptis & commonitionib. Dei, & reliquis modis docendi, quibus vtitur Scriptura; a causa exemplari, ut a decreto Dei; a causa impellente, instrumentali, & sine qua ne quâ non; à iure ad factum.
units.tr: 1. To the topic of efficient cause belongs the argument from a law that has ceased; from God's promises and threats; from God's precepts and admonitions, and the other modes of teaching that Scripture uses; from the exemplary cause, such as God's decree; from the impelling, instrumental and sine qua non cause; and from right to fact.

units.la: 2. Ad locum finis, argumentum à gloriæ Dei illustratione, aliorum ædificatione, salute animæ & corporis, spe successus, metu ignominiæ, expectatione aliorum, gloriâ expectandâ apud Deum & bonos Christianos in ecclesiâ, virtute finis.
units.tr: 2. To the topic of the end belongs the argument from the illustration of God's glory, the edification of others, the salvation of soul and body, the hope of success, the fear of disgrace, the expectation of others, the glory to be expected before God and good Christians in the church, and the virtue of the end.

units.la: 3. Ad materiam pertinet argumentum à conditione materiæ.
units.tr: 3. To matter belongs the argument from the condition of the matter.

units.la: 4. Ad locum formæ, argumen. à natura & attributis Dei, videlic. eius omnipotentiâ, iustitiâ &c. quæ etiam referri possunt ad locum adiuncti: à naturâ fidei, spei, charitatis, patientiæ &c. à rectitudine conscientiæ; ab æquipollentibus; ab implicito ad explicitum, & vicißim ab implicito ad explicitum, siue ab expresso ad tacitum; à naturâ particularum; à significatione verborum; à vi genitiui; à cessatione rationis, defectu formæ, natura sacramentorum, legis, euangelii &c. ab ideâ id est, naturâ absolutâ rei alicuius.
units.tr: 4. To the topic of form belongs the argument from the nature and attributes of God, namely his omnipotence, justice and so on, which can also be referred to the topic of adjunct; from the nature of faith, hope, charity, patience and so on; from the rectitude of conscience; from equivalents; from the implicit to the explicit, and conversely from the implicit to the explicit, or from the expressed to the tacit; from the nature of particles; from the meaning of words; from the force of the genitive; from the cessation of reason, the lack of form, the nature of the sacraments, of law, of the gospel and so on; and from the idea, that is, the absolute nature of a thing.

units.la: 5. Ad locum effecti, argumentum ab vtili & inutili, iucundo seu delectabili & iniucundo, facili & difficili, beneficiis & iudiciis Dei, præsidio sanctorum angelorum, effecto mortis Christi, intercessione mediatoris, providentiâ Dei, consilio prophetæ vel apostoli, denique à facto ad ius.
units.tr: 5. To the topic of effect belongs the argument from the useful and the useless, the pleasant or delightful and the unpleasant, the easy and the difficult, the benefits and judgements of God, the protection of the holy angels, the effect of Christ's death, the intercession of the Mediator, the providence of God, the counsel of a prophet or apostle; and finally from fact to right.

units.la: 6. Ad locum subiecti, argum. à subiectâ materiâ; à materiâ in quâ, vel circa quam; à re ad modum; à signato ad signum.
units.tr: 6. To the topic of subject belongs the argument from the subject matter; from the matter in which, or about which; from the thing to the manner; from the signified to the sign.

units.la: 7. Ad locum adiuncti, argumen. à proprietate linguæ; à rubro ad nigrum; à phraseologiâ; ab vsurpatione vocis; à certâ locutionis formulâ; à proprietate sermonis; à nomine appellatiuo; à vi numeri; à phrasi Scripturæ; à proprietate rei; à sufficienti; à communiter contingentibus; ab vsitato seu solitis; ab impossibili, vel possibili; ab honesto vel turpi; à consuetudine scriptoris; à necessario vel nonnecessario; à futuro vel non-futuro; à magno vel paruo; à modo siue gradu ad rem; ab ordine; à praxi legis & euangelii; à praxi ecclesiæ; à praxi ministerii ecclesiastici; à figno ad signatum; ab ætate, sexu, vitæ innocentiâ, religiofo, glorioso, pio, iusto, æquo, tuto, decoro, laudabili; à peccati magnitudine & turpitudine, miseriis internis & externis, certitudine & magnitudine præmiorum & pœnarum; ab agnitione humanæ fragilitatis; à personarù, quæ peccant, vilitate; ab authoritate & diligentiâ sanctorum; à dignitate & merito eius qui affligitur; à circumstantiis; à nostrâ imbecillitate, indignitate &c. ab affectu Dei Patris, à laude rei, personæ &c. à nostri electione, vocatione, iustificatione; glorificatione; à necessariâ definitionis diuinæ & prophetiæ veritate.
units.tr: 7. To the topic of adjunct belongs the argument from the propriety of language; from red to black; from phraseology; from the usage of a word; from a fixed form of expression; from the propriety of speech; from the common noun; from the force of number; from the phrase of Scripture; from the property of the thing; from what is sufficient; from what commonly happens; from what is customary or usual; from the impossible or the possible; from the honourable or the base; from the habit of the writer; from the necessary or the unnecessary; from the future or the non-future; from the great or the small; from the mode or degree to the thing; from order; from the practice of law and gospel; from the practice of the church; from the practice of the ecclesiastical ministry; from the sign to the signified; from age, sex, innocence of life, and what is religious, glorious, pious, just, equitable, safe, becoming and praiseworthy; from the greatness and baseness of sin, from internal and external miseries, from the certainty and greatness of rewards and punishments; from the recognition of human frailty; from the baseness of the persons who sin; from the authority and diligence of the saints; from the dignity and merit of the one who is afflicted; from circumstances; from our weakness, unworthiness and so on; from the affection of God the Father; from the praise of the thing, the person and so on; from our election, calling, justification and glorification; and from the necessary truth of the divine definition and of prophecy.

units.la: 8. Ad locum antecedentis, arg. à priori ad posterius; à necessariâ impletione vaticinij.
units.tr: 8. To the topic of the antecedent, the argument from the prior to the posterior; from the necessary fulfilment of a prophecy.

units.la: 9. Ad locum connexorum, arg. à connexis; à verbis antecedentibus & consequentibus, siue à contextu; à cõiunctis ad diuisa; à subiecto ad prædicatum, & vicissim à prædicato ad subiectum; à præmissis ad conclusionem, à generaliad speciale; à primo ad vltimum; à subordinatis; ab antecedente ad consequens, & vicissim à consequente ad antecedens.
units.tr: 9. To the topic of connected things, the argument from connected things; from antecedent and consequent words, or from the context; from things conjoined to things divided; from subject to predicate, and conversely from predicate to subject; from premises to conclusion; from the general to the special; from the first to the last; from subordinate things; from antecedent to consequent, and conversely from consequent to antecedent.

units.la: 10. Ad locum consequentis, arg. ab Est tertii adiecti ad Est secundi adiecti; ab absurdo consequente.
units.tr: 10. To the topic of the consequent, the argument from the is of the third adjunct to the is of the second adjunct; from an absurd consequence.

units.la: 11. Ad locum diuersorum pertinet argum. occupans siue anticipans prolepsim.
units.tr: 11. To the topic of diverse things belongs the argument that occupies or anticipates an objection (prolepsis).

units.la: 12. Ad disparata, arg. à separatis,
units.tr: 12. To disparate things, the argument from things separated.

units.la: 13. Ad relata, arg. à correlatiuis.
units.tr: 13. To related things, the argument from correlatives.

units.la: 14. Ad aduersa, arg. ab incompossibilibus, & ab extremis ad medium.
units.tr: 14. To opposites, the argument from incompatibles, and from extremes to the middle.

units.la: 15. Ad contradicentia, arg. à vi primi principii.
units.tr: 15. To contradictories, the argument from the force of the first principle.

units.la: 16. Ad priuantia, arg. à priuatione ad habitum, & vicissim ab habitu ad priuationem.
units.tr: 16. To privatives, the argument from privation to habit, and conversely from habit to privation.

units.la: 17. Ad locum à pari, arg. ab analogia; à vi masculini generis; ab exemplo; à persona ad personam; à persona ad locum; à persona ad tempus; à tempore ad tempus, ut à tempore legis ad tempus euangelii; à loco ad locum; à contrario sensu; à verisimili seu probabili; à consensu verbi & sacramentorum; à concordia sacramentorum; à concordia V. & N. T.
units.tr: 17. To the topic of like things, the argument from analogy; from the force of the masculine gender; from example; from person to person; from person to place; from person to time; from time to time, as from the time of the law to the time of the gospel; from place to place; from the contrary sense; from what is likely or probable; from the agreement of word and sacraments; from the concord of the sacraments; from the concord of the Old and New Testaments.

units.la: 18. Ad locum à maiori, arg. à vi comparatiui vel superlatiui; à vi geminationis; à futuro actus continui; à comparatione præsentis mali cū aliis malis; à præterito stili prophetici; à capite ad membra; à plenitudine potestatis; à combinatione duorū vel plurium textuum; à magis probabili; à concordantia sacrae & profanae historiae; à concordantia historiae & experientiae.
units.tr: 18. To the topic of the greater, the argument from the force of the comparative or superlative; from the force of repetition; from the future of a continuing act; from comparing a present evil with other evils; from the past tense of prophetic style; from the head to the members; from the fullness of power; from the combination of two or more texts; from what is more probable; from the agreement of sacred and profane history; from the agreement of history and experience.

units.la: 19. Ad locum à minori, argum. à membris ad capita, & à minus probabili. Argumentum à sensu comparato interdum ad maiora, interdum ad minora pertinet.
units.tr: 19. To the topic of the lesser, the argument from the members to the head, and from what is less probable. The argument from a sense compared sometimes pertains to greater things and sometimes to lesser ones.

units.la: 20. Ad similia, arg. à similitudine significationis; à typo ad rem typo significatam; ab externo ad internum; ab interno ad externum; à proportione; à concordantia naturæ & gratiæ; ab allegoria ad genuinam significatiōnem.
units.tr: 20. To similar things, the argument from similarity of signification; from the type to the thing signified by the type; from the external to the internal; from the internal to the external; from proportion; from the concordance of nature and grace; from allegory to the genuine signification.

units.la: 21. Ad dissimilia, arg. à discrimine V. & N. T. & à discrimine legis & euangelii.
units.tr: 21. For dissimilar things, the argument from the difference between the Old and New Testaments, and from the difference between law and gospel.

units.la: 22. Ad coniugata, arg. à persona ad rem.
units.tr: 22. For related things, the argument from the person to the thing.

units.la: 23. Ad notationem, arg. à vi nominis.
units.tr: 23. For the meaning of a term, the argument from the force of the name.

units.la: 24. Ad locum distributionis, arg. à genere ad speciem, & vicissim à specie ad genus; à sententia generali; à thesi ad hypothesin, & vicissim ab hypothesi ad thesin; ab exceptione ad regulam; à parte ad totum, & vicissim à toto ad partem; à generalitate; à diuisis ad coniuncta; à sensu diuiso.
units.tr: 24. For the place of distribution: the argument from genus to species and conversely from species to genus; from a general statement; from thesis to hypothesis and conversely from hypothesis to thesis; from exception to rule; from part to whole and conversely from whole to part; from generality; from divided to conjoined things; and from a divided sense.

units.la: 25. Ad locum definitionis, arg. à definito ad definitionem, & vicissim à definitione ad definitum; à descriptione; ab hypotyposi.
units.tr: 25. For the place of definition: the argument from the defined to the definition and conversely from definition to the defined; from description; and from outline.

units.la: 26. Ad locum testimonij, arg. ab authoritate; à natura, id est, à principiis naturaliter insitis; à communi opinione; ab experientia vniuersali & particulari; à consensu orthodoxo; à traditione rationabili; à consuetudine rationabili. Hanc tabulam inspiciat tum proponens, tum opponens, &,dispiciat, quibus potissimùm argumentis possit uti. Confer supra cum Oratoriâ.
units.tr: 26. For the place of testimony: the argument from authority; from nature, that is, from principles implanted naturally; from common opinion; from universal and particular experience; from orthodox consensus; from reasonable tradition; and from reasonable custom. Let both the proposer and the opponent consult this table and examine which arguments they can chiefly use. Compare above with the rhetoric.

units.la: VII. Res quæ possunt venire in disputationem, debent esse piæ, necessariæ, dubiæ, utiles, cognitu possibiles, perspicuæ, & succinctæ. Pia; quia ea quæ lædunt conscientiam & mores bonos, non sunt in apricum proferenda, sed sepelienda. Necessariæ; quia turpe est ignorare necessaria, & molestû accidit gar- rire de non-necessariis. Dubia; quia de rebus confessis & concessis disputare est superuacaneum. Utiles; quia quæ neque scienti prosunt, neque ignoranti nocent, ex vitâ communi debent excludi. Cognitu possibiles; quia de rebus, quæ captum nostrum superant, neque in verbo Dei revelatæ sunt, superfluum, curiosum, & stultum est disserere. Perspicuæ; quia veritas est clara. Succinctæ; quia amplificationes & excursiones non conueniunt disputationibus, sed orationibus.
units.tr: VII. The matters that may come into dispute ought to be pious, necessary, doubtful, useful, knowable, clear and brief. Pious, because things that injure conscience and good morals are not to be brought into the open but buried. Necessary, because it is shameful to be ignorant of necessary things, and it is tiresome to chatter about unnecessary ones. Doubtful, because to dispute about things admitted and conceded is superfluous. Useful, because things that help neither the one who knows nor harm the one who does not know ought to be excluded from common life. Knowable, because it is superfluous, curious and foolish to discourse about things that exceed our grasp and have not been revealed in the Word of God. Clear, because truth is plain. Brief, because amplifications and digressions suit orations, not disputations.

units.la: VIII. Modus disputandi, sive id scripto fiat, sive vivâ voce, cernitur in oppositione & responsione.
units.tr: VIII. The manner of disputing, whether it is done in writing or by the living voice, consists in objection and response.

units.la: IX. Oppositio est in syllogismo & prosyllogismo. Syllogismus opponentis est principale argumentum, quo ille aliquid oppugnat. Prosyllogismus est argumentum succenturiatum, quo opponens syllogismum principalem, quoties opus est, instando & excipiendo premit.
units.tr: IX. Objection lies in the syllogism and the prosyllogism. The syllogism of the opponent is the principal argument by which he attacks something. The prosyllogism is a supporting argument, by which the opponent, as often as necessary, presses the principal syllogism by insisting and taking up its points.

units.la: X. Responsio fit concessione, vel solutione. Concessione, si argumentum ab adversario oppositum legitimè fit conclusum, & perspicuum, nec thesin infirmet. Solutione contrà. Est autem solutio alia directa, alia indirecta. Solutio directa est, quæ rectà ad formam vel materiam respondet. Ad formam, indicando canonem syllogisticum, in quem peccatur. Ad materiam verò, explicando insolentia & obscura; distinguendo ambigua; negando præmissarum alteram, vel vtramq;, si falsitas infit; reiiciendo consequentiam; limitando, siue distinguendo, q κατὰ τὰ vera sunt; & ad quæstionem, si fuerit peruersa aut mutata, reuocando. Solutio indirecta est, quæ fit retorquendo per βλα[illegible, ~6 letters] que difficile opponendo [illegible, ~5 letters] in obiectione monstrando [illegible, ~5 letters], id est, contradictionem; aut deniq; argumentum omninò reiiciendo [illegible, ~7 letters]. Videamus quædam exempla. Esa. 49. talis obiectio Iudæorum occupatur: Iehova dereliquit me. Deus ad hoc antecedens, vtpote falsum, respondet hunc in modum: Numquid obliuiscetur mulier infantis sui? Et addit: Etiamsi hæc obliuiscatur infantis sui; tamen ego non obliuiscar tui. Qui negationis modus est plane artificiosus. Matth. 25. occupatur serui infidelis obiectio. Noueram te hominem esse durum. Ergo rectè feci, quando talentum mihi abs te cocreditum defodi. Seruator huic obiectioni sic occurrit, vt concesso antecedente, consequens retorqueat in ipsum obiicientem, veluti videlicet infidelem, hoc modo: Si noueras me metere, vbi non seuissem, & inde cogere, vbi non sparsissem, oportuit ergo te tradere pecuniam meam mensariis: & ego, cum venissem, recepisse meum cum fœnore. Aliquando respondetur ad consequentiam per inficiationem, cum illa non est legitima: quomodo respondet apostolus Rom. 9. ad illam obiectionem: Si Deus Iacobum dilexit, & Esauum odio habuit, antequam nati essent, & nec boni, nec mali quidquam fecissent: ergo iniustitia est apud Deum. Apostolus negat consequentiam, & rationem negationis addit ex causa istius iusti iudicii, quæ est voluntas Dei liberrima: nemini obstricta. Aliquando ita negatur consequentia, vt velut ex abundanti negetur & ipsum antecedens: vt Iohan. 8. Iudæi sic obiiciunt Christo: Nos sumus filii Abraham. Ergo nō sumus serui. Respondet Christus, negando consequentiam, quasi dicat: Non sequitur, cum sitis filii Abrahæ secundùm carnem, vos esse liberos, & non habere necesse, vt in libertatem asseramini. Rationem negationis addit: Peccatis subinde. Ergo serui estis. Deinde cùm Iudæi hac responsionem flocci facerent, & suum illud antecedens identidem ingeminarent; Christus etiam antecedes[?] negat, & negationem astruit hoc modo: Si filii Abraham estis[?], opera Abrahami faceretis. Interdum & antecedens & consequens conceditur: consequenti vero aut maius, aut par opponitur, atque obiectionem aduersarii nos nō laedere, aut etiam pro nobis facere, ostenditur. Sic Mat.15. v.2.&feqq. Iudæi obiiciunt Christo: Discipuli tui transgrediuntur traditionem seniorum, dum non lauant manus suas. Ergo peccant. Christus primò respondet, opponendo maius: Et vos transgredimini mandatum Dei per traditionem vestram. Ergo peccatis. Antecedens confirmat v.4.5. Deinde v.10.&feqq. etiam consequentiam negat & confutat. Luc.6.v.1.2. &feqq. Pharisæi accusant discipulos Christi, quod violet sabbatum, vellendo spicas. Christus respondet, Nè hoc quidem legistis, quod fecit Dauid &c. Quæ interrogatio vim habet reprehendendi, idque ἀλογιστικῶς[?], quasi dicat Dominus: Si non legistis, pudeat vos ignorantiæ: si legistis, pudeat vos vel socordiæ, quòd non intellexistis; vel malitiæ, quod intellectum dissimulatis, & de factis similibus dissimile iudicium fertis. Luc.20.v.2.&feqq. Christus non directè seu apertè respondet ad quæstionem sibi propositam, idque non ideò, quòd vellet declinare responsionem ad istâ quæstionem, sed vt responsionem aliquam ad suam quæstionem ex aduersariis eliceret, suamq; responsionem confessione aduersariorum confirmaret. Si enim illi ad quæstionem ipsius verum responsum dedissent, nempe se statuere baptismum Iohannis fuisse è cœlo: Dominus inde deduxisset responsum ad quæstionem sibi propositã, nempe se ea quæ fecerat & adhuc faciat, fecisse & facere potestate diuinitus sibi data: quia nimirum Iohannes dederat ipsi testimonium, quòd ipse sit Christus. Cùm verò aduersarii obmutescerent, Christus argumentatur à pari: Si vos non vultis mihi respondere ad quæstionem meam; pari ratione nec ego respondebo ad quæstionem vestrã: cùm duo ista in pari iure versentur. Ioan.8.v.3.&feqq. Scribæ & Pharisæi sperant, sc[?] Domino certò periculum creaturos, tali dilemmate: Aut absoluet hanc adulteram, aut condemnabit. Si absoluet eam, accusabimus eum, vt aduersarium legis. Si condemnabit, accusabimus eum, vt sibi non constantem; quippe qui meretrices & publicanos alias in gratiam recipit. Sed CHRISTVS ipso gestu euertit ratiocinationis istius fundamentum, hoc est, hypothesin, quâ illa nititur, nempe disiunctum ipsum; quia neutrum facit. Vnde constat dilemma non fuisse legitimum: vtpote cuius propositio nõ fuit ex immediatè oppositis. Porrò Christus interdum explicitè respondit, vt Matth. 22. verf. 20. 21. 32. interdum implicitè, vt Matth. 22. verf. 29. 30. Cæterum breuiter hic colligamus fallaciarum genera. Fallacia est formæ, vel materiæ. Fallacia formæ est, quando violatur canon aliquis syllogisticus. Fallacia materiæ est vocis, vel rei. Vocis, simplicis vel coniunctæ. Simplicis, Insolentia, vel Ambiguitas. Insolentia est fallacia vocis, obscuritate decipiens. Ambiguitas est sallacia vocis, multitudine significationum decipiens. Fallacia vocis coniunctæ est Amphibolia, vel Fallacia compositionis & diuisionis. Amphibolia est, cùm sententia decipit ambiguitate. Fallacia compositionis & diuisionis est, cùm disiunguntur coniungenda, & contrà. Fallacia rei est medii termini, vel propositionum. Fallacia medii termini est petitio principii, vel falsi argumenti pro vero sumtio. Petitio principii est, cùm, quod in quæstione est, adsertur pro argumento. Assumtio falsi medii est, cùm pro argumento adsertur, quod argumentum non est. Idque tot modis fieri potest, quot sunt argumentorum loci. Hinc est fallacia siue elenchus causæ, effecti, subiecti &c. Fallacia propositionum, est præmissarum, vel conclusionis. Præmissarum est, 1. fallacia consequentia, quando in maiore propositione partes non cohæret. 2. fallacia à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter, cùm ex limitato cócluditur absolutum. Fallacia conclusionis est 1. πολυζητήσεως, cùm quæstiones cumulantur. 2. ἰγνοζητήσεως, cùm argumentum aduersarii nostram sententiam non attingit: quæ dicitur ignoratio elenchi.
units.tr: X. The response is made either by concession or by solution. By concession, if the argument put forward by the adversary is validly concluded and clear, and does not weaken the thesis. By solution otherwise. A solution is either direct or indirect. A direct solution is one that answers straight to the form or the matter. To the form, by pointing out the syllogistic rule that has been broken. To the matter, by explaining obscure and unusual terms; by distinguishing ambiguous ones; by denying one of the premises, or both, if falsity lies in them; by rejecting the consequence; by limiting or distinguishing what is true according to [κατὰ τὰ] some respect; and, if the question has been twisted or changed, by recalling it. An indirect solution is one made by turning the argument back, by putting a difficult counter-question, by showing a contradiction in the objection, that is, a self-contradiction; or finally by rejecting the argument altogether. Let us look at some examples. In Isaiah 49 a Jewish objection is taken up: Jehovah has forsaken me. God, answering this antecedent as false, replies in this way: Can a woman forget her infant? And he adds: Even if she should forget her infant, yet I will not forget you. This mode of denial is plainly skilful. In Matthew 25 the objection of the unfaithful servant is met: I knew you to be a hard man. Therefore I did right when I buried the talent entrusted to me by you. The Saviour meets this objection by conceding the antecedent and turning the consequent back on the objector himself, as an unfaithful man, in this way: If you knew that I reap where I did not sow, and gather where I did not scatter, you ought therefore to have handed over my money to the bankers; and I, on my return, would have received what was mine with interest. Sometimes the consequence is answered by denial when it is not valid, as the apostle answers in Romans 9 that objection: If God loved Jacob and hated Esau before they were born, and when they had done neither good nor evil, then there is injustice with God. The apostle denies the consequence and adds the reason for the denial from the cause of that just judgment, which is the most free will of God, bound to no one. Sometimes the consequence is denied in such a way that the antecedent itself is also denied, as an excess: as in John 8, where the Jews object to Christ: We are the sons of Abraham. Therefore we are not slaves. Christ answers by denying the consequence, as if to say: It does not follow. Although you are the sons of Abraham according to the flesh, you are not therefore free, and you do not need to be set at liberty. He adds the reason for the denial: Whoever commits sin is a slave. Therefore you are slaves. Then, when the Jews made light of this answer and kept repeating their antecedent, Christ also denies the antecedent and establishes the denial in this way: If you were the sons of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham. Sometimes both the antecedent and the consequent are conceded, but something greater or equal is set against the consequent, and it is shown that the adversary's objection does not harm us, or even works for us.
