So in Matthew 15:2 and following, the Jews object to Christ: Your disciples transgress the tradition of the elders, since they do not wash their hands. Therefore they sin. Christ first answers by setting against it something greater: And you transgress the commandment of God through your tradition. Therefore you sin. He confirms the antecedent in verses 4 and 5. Then, in verse 10 and following, he also denies and refutes the consequence. In Luke 6:1, 2 and following, the Pharisees accuse Christ's disciples of breaking the sabbath by plucking ears of grain. Christ answers: Have you not even read what David did, etc.? This question has the force of a rebuke, and it is put [ἀλογιστικῶς] irrationally, as if the Lord said: If you have not read, you should be ashamed of your ignorance; if you have read, you should be ashamed of your sloth, because you have not understood, or of your malice, because you conceal what you have understood and pass a different judgment on similar deeds. In Luke 20:2 and following, Christ does not answer the question put to him directly or openly; and he does this not because he wished to evade answering that question, but so that he might draw from his adversaries some answer to his own question, and confirm his own answer by the admission of his adversaries. For if they had given a true answer to his question, namely that they held the baptism of John to be from heaven, the Lord would have drawn from it a reply to the question put to him, namely that he did what he had done and still does by a power divinely given to him, because John had indeed borne witness to him that he is the Christ. But when his adversaries fell silent, Christ argues from a parallel: If you will not answer my question, then by the same reasoning I will not answer yours, since these two stand on the same footing. In John 8:3 and following, the scribes and Pharisees hoped to bring Christ certainly into danger with this dilemma: Either he will acquit this adulteress or he will condemn her. If he acquits her, we will accuse him as an opponent of the law. If he condemns her, we will accuse him as inconsistent, since he otherwise receives harlots and publicans into favour. But Christ, by his very gesture, overturned the foundation of this reasoning, that is, the hypothesis on which it rests, namely the disjunction itself, since he does neither. Hence it is clear that the dilemma was not valid, since its proposition did not consist of immediately opposed alternatives. Moreover, Christ sometimes answered explicitly, as in Matthew 22:20, 21, 32, and sometimes implicitly, as in Matthew 22:29, 30. Furthermore, let us here briefly gather the kinds of fallacies. A fallacy is either of form or of matter. A fallacy of form occurs when some syllogistic rule is violated. A fallacy of matter is either of the word or of the thing. Of the word, either simple or compound. Simple, either obscurity or ambiguity. Obscurity is a fallacy of the word that deceives by being hard to understand. Ambiguity is a fallacy of the word that deceives by the multiplicity of its meanings. The fallacy of the compound word is amphibology, or the fallacy of composition and division. Amphibology occurs when a sentence deceives by its ambiguity. The fallacy of composition and division occurs when things that ought to be joined are separated, and conversely. The fallacy of the thing lies in the middle term or in the propositions. The fallacy of the middle term is begging the question, or taking a false argument for a true one. Begging the question occurs when what is in question is adduced as the argument. Assuming a false middle occurs when something is put forward as an argument which is not an argument. And this can happen in as many ways as there are topics of argument. Hence there arises the fallacy or elenchus of cause, effect, subject and so on. The fallacy of propositions lies in the premises or in the conclusion. In the premises there is: 1. the fallacy of consequence, when the parts do not cohere in the major proposition; 2. the fallacy of what is said with a qualification to what is said without qualification, when an unqualified conclusion is drawn from a qualified premise. The fallacy of the conclusion is 1. [πολυζητήσεως] of many questions, when several questions are piled together; 2. [ἀγνοζητήσεως] of ignorance of the question, when the adversary's argument does not touch our position; this is called ignoratio elenchi.

units.la: LXIV. JUDICIUM DE MAGIA EX SACRIS COLLECTUM.
units.tr: LXIV. JUDGEMENT ON MAGIC, COLLECTED FROM THE SACRED WRITINGS.

units.la: I. Magia ( quibusdam Pneumatica ) est pura, vel impura. Vox μαγ@ est Persica, vt ex Platone, Xenophonte, Strabone, Diogene Laërtio, & pluribus aliis constat. Affirmat idem Plinius initio lib.30. Hoc igitur primùm constare debet, Magos proprie dictos, Persarum sapientes fuisse, vel sacerdotes. Nam Herodotus, Strabo, atque alij, praecipuum illorum officium fuisse ostendunt, vt sacra Persarum curarent, & sapientiam profiterentur. Graeci, cùm de Persicis rebus hanc vocem usurpant, nunquam aliter accipiunt: at longè aliter, cùm de magis illis, qui inter ipsos Graecos occultarum scientiarum notitiam profitebantur. Tunc enim in malam partem, ut plurimum, id verbi accipitur, quia plerique religionis & arcanae scientiae obtentu, artes maleficas exercebant: unde querela illa Plinij & cum ipsius, tum aliorum multorum, detestatio magiae.
units.tr: I. Magic (by some called "pneumatic") is either pure or impure. The word μάγος is Persian, as is clear from Plato, Xenophon, Strabo, Diogenes Laertius and many others. Pliny says the same at the beginning of book 30. It must first be established, then, that the Magi, properly so called, were the wise men or priests of the Persians. For Herodotus, Strabo and others show that their chief duty was to tend the sacred rites of the Persians and to profess wisdom. When the Greeks use this word of Persian matters they never take it in any other sense, but they take it quite differently when they speak of those magi who among the Greeks themselves professed knowledge of hidden sciences. For in that case the word is generally taken in a bad sense, because most of these men, under the pretext of religion and secret learning, practised wicked arts. Hence Pliny's complaint, and the detestation of magic expressed by him and by many others.

units.la: Et Philo Iudaeus variis locis duplicem facit magicâ: legitimam unam, circa cognitionem naturae versantem, regibus maximis, praecipuè Persarum, coli solitam: alteram [illegible, ~2 words], adulterationem prioris. Aequiuoca igitur est vox μάγος, & μαγία. Bonam in partem accipitur Matth.2.v.1. vbi euangelista se explicat, cùm dicit, Magi ab oriente: nempe magos intelligit Persarum, ad quos proprie illa appellatio pertinuit.
units.tr: Philo the Jew, in various places, also divides magic in two: one legitimate, concerned with the knowledge of nature and customarily cultivated by the greatest kings, above all the Persians; the other a corruption of the first, [illegible, ~2 words]. The word μάγος and μαγία is therefore equivocal. It is used in a good sense at Matt. 2:1, where the evangelist explains himself when he says: Magi from the east, meaning by Magi the Persians, to whom that name properly belonged.

units.la: II. Magia pura est naturalis, vel mathematica. Haec partitio colligitur ex Basilio Magno, cuius verba sunt in natiuitate Christi de Magis: ἔθνος Περσικὸν τὸ μάγοι, [illegible, ~6 words], μαντείας, ἢ ἐπῳδαῖς, καὶ φυσικὰς [?] ... χρόντες, ἢ περὶ τὴν τήρησιν τῶν μεγάλων ἐχολακότες, Magi sunt populus Persicus, vaticiniis & incantationibus deditus, & obferuationi repugnantium proprietatum in rebus naturalibus: obferuationibus item rerum cœlestium vacant. Sane magos illos, de quibus in euangelio, fuisse deditos inter alia rebus cœlestibus, illarumq; contemplationi, vel hinc potest constare: quòd Deus ipsis obiecit stellam doctorem & ductorem. Nimirum solet Deus homines erudire per ea, quæ ipsis familiariter sunt nota. Cum quâ sententia non pugnat, quod plerique Patrum obseruant: extitisse inter Persas memoriam prophetiæ à Balaamo editæ Num. 23. v. 7. Deut. 23. v. 4. Vtrumque enim potuit fieri.
units.tr: II. Pure magic is either natural or mathematical. This division is drawn from Basil the Great, whose words in his sermon on the Nativity of Christ about the Magi are: "The Magi are a Persian people, given to prophecies and incantations, and [illegible] ... to natural [?] ... they are occupied with the observation of great things, and with the study of conflicting properties in natural things; they likewise devote themselves to the observation of heavenly things." That those Magi of the Gospel were devoted, among other things, to heavenly bodies and their contemplation, can be shown from this alone: that God set before them a star as teacher and guide. God is accustomed, of course, to instruct men through things that are familiar to them. Nor does it conflict with this view, which many of the Fathers observe, that there existed among the Persians a memory of the prophecy uttered by Balaam, Num. 23:7; Deut. 23:4. For both could have happened.

units.la: III. Magia naturalis est, quæ singulari pauci- sque cognito modo docet maritare naturas, hoc est, applicare actiua passiuis. Hæc definitio iuncta est ex Conclusionibus Iohannis Pici. Vnde patet, magum recte à Plotino vocari naturæ ministrum: & Ficinum in conuiuio Platonis nō sine causâ ita scribere: Magicæ opera, naturæ operæ sunt. Ars verò ministra. Ars enim, vbi naturali cognationi deest aliquid, per vapores, numeros, figuras, qualitates, opportunis supplet temporibus: quemadmodum in agriculturâ natura segetes parat, ars præparat. Quibus verbis vir doctissimus totam magiæ naturalis & mathematicæ artem ponit ob oculos. Magiæ naturalis exemplum est Gen. 30. v. 37. 38. 39. vbi Iacob, iussu Dei procul dubio, accepit baculos ex albâ populo virentes, coryloque, & platano: & decorticauit in eis spatia decorticationis alba, denudando alburnum quod erat in baculis istis. Postea baculos ita decorticatos collocauit in canalibus & aqualiculis: vt pecudes venientes ad bibendum incalescerent ad illas virgas, & incalescendo coirent, & inter coeundum intuerentur virgas diuersicolores, & per imaginationem vehementem, eiusdem coloris fœtus conciperent.
units.tr: III. Natural magic is that which teaches, by a single method known to few, how to join natures together, that is, how to apply active things to passive ones. This definition is put together from the Conclusions of John Pico. Hence it is plain that the magus was rightly called by Plotinus a minister of nature, and that Ficino was not without reason writing in his commentary on Plato's Symposium: The works of magic are the works of nature; art is only its minister. For art, where something is lacking in natural affinity, supplies it through vapours, numbers, figures and qualities at fitting times, just as in agriculture nature produces the crops and art prepares them. In these words that most learned man sets before our eyes the whole art of natural and mathematical magic. An example of natural magic is Gen. 30:37-39, where Jacob, undoubtedly at God's command, took rods of fresh poplar, hazel and plane, and peeled white strips in them, laying bare the white wood that was under the bark of those rods. Afterwards he set the rods, so peeled, in the gutters and troughs, so that the flocks coming to drink would become heated at the rods, and in heating would couple, and while coupling would look at the rods of varied colours, and through a strong imagination would conceive young of the same colour.

units.la: IV. Magia mathematica est, quæ vim numerorum, figurarum, motuum cœlestium, & temporum explicat & obseruat. Vim numerorum: quatenus scilicet numerus, non nudus, sed in certâ materiâ consideratur. Videmus enim res omnes certo constare numero, absque quo nihil in mundo potest agere. Videmus duo, tria, quatuor, quinque &c. rite coniuncta, alium atque alium edere effectum. Vim figurarum: quatenus triangula, quadrata, circuli, coni, pyramides, & aliæ figuræ diuersis actionibus inseruiunt. Videmus enim v. g. circularem figuram ad motum, quadratam ad quietem esse aptissimam. Vim motuum cœlestium: quia diuersi stellarum motus, positus, aspectus, & influxus, diuersa causantur in mundo sublunari. Denique vim temporum: quatenus diuersa tempora diuersis rebus conueniunt: vt ver, æstas, autumnus, hyems, dies, nox, solstitium, æquinoctium, &c.
units.tr: IV. Mathematical magic is that which explains and observes the power of numbers, figures, heavenly motions and times. The power of numbers: insofar as number is considered not bare, but in a definite matter. For we see that all things consist in a certain number, without which nothing in the world can act. We see that two, three, four, five and so on, rightly combined, produce one effect after another. The power of figures: insofar as triangles, squares, circles, cones, pyramids and other figures serve various actions. For we see, for example, that a circular figure is most suited to motion, and a square to rest. The power of heavenly motions: because the different motions, positions, aspects and influences of the stars cause different effects in the sublunary world. Lastly, the power of times: insofar as different times suit different things, such as spring, summer, autumn, winter, day, night, solstice, equinox, and so on.

units.la: V. Magia impura & infamis est, quæ præstigiis, incantationibus, coniurationibus, & similibus modis vtitur, & pacto cum dæmone nititur. Huius artis vetitæ professores fuerunt sapientes & præstigiatores Pharaonis. Exod.7.v.14.15.25. cap.8.v. 7. Tales etiam fuerunt magi, astrologi, præstigiatores & Chaldæi, regis Nebucadnezaris Dan.1.v.2. Etsi enim magi Ægyptij & Chaldæi procul dubio fuerunt etiam periti magiæ naturalis & mathematicæ: tamen illam cospurcarunt magiâ impurâ, & eam tantùm non obscurarunt atque suffocarunt: quemadmodum in his rebus vsuuenire solet. Inter magos Ægyptios, qui restiterunt Mosi, videntur præcipui, & velut coryphæi, fuisse, duo illi, quos apostolus nominat 2.Tim.3.v.8. videl. Ioannes & Iambres, quorum etiam Hebræi meminerunt in Talmud, de oblatio- nibus cap.9. In nouo testamento infames magi sunt Simon magus Act.8. & Bariehu siue Elimas Act.13. Porrò hæc infamis magia est diuinatrix, vel operatrix. Illa perficitur verbis, hæc constat variis actionibus: vtraque nititur pacto cum diabolo, eoque vel expresso vel tacito. Vide inter alios Martinum Delrio in disquisitionibus magicis, Peucerum de diuinatione, & Wierum de præstigiis. De nouem speciebus artium Magicarum à Mose prohibitarum videsupra Iurisprudentiam sacram.
units.tr: V. Impure and infamous magic is that which uses sleight of hand, incantations, conjurations and similar means, and relies on a pact with a demon. The professors of this forbidden art were the wise men and sorcerers of Pharaoh. Exod. 7:14, 15, 25; ch. 8: 7. Such also were the magi, astrologers, sorcerers and Chaldeans of King Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. 1:2. For although the Egyptian and Chaldean magi were undoubtedly also skilled in natural and mathematical magic, yet they defiled it with impure magic, and almost obscured and smothered it, as usually happens in such matters. Among the Egyptian magi who withstood Moses, the chief and as it were leaders were those two whom the apostle names, 2 Tim. 3:8, namely Jannes and Jambres, whom the Hebrews also mention in the Talmud, in the treatise on offerings, ch. 9. In the New Testament the notorious magi are Simon Magus, Acts 8, and Bar-Jesus or Elymas, Acts 13. Moreover, this infamous magic is either divinatory or operative. The former is accomplished by words, the latter consists of various actions; both rely on a pact with the devil, either express or tacit. See among others Martin Del Rio in his Magical Disquisitions, Peucer on divination, and Weyer on sleight of hand. Concerning the nine kinds of magical arts forbidden by Moses, see above, under Sacred Jurisprudence.

units.la: LXV.
units.tr: LXV.

units.la: STRATAGEMATOGRAPHIA SACRA.
units.tr: Sacred Stratagematography.

units.la: I. STratagematographia sacra est pars ethicæ, œconomicæ & politicæ de ratione stratagematum in Scriptură occurrentium.
units.tr: I. Sacred stratagematography is the part of ethics, economics and politics that concerns the method of the stratagems occurring in Scripture.

units.la: II. Stratagema est callidum & tempestiuū factum. Hæc est generalis notio huius vocis. Speciasiter est factum callidum, quo dux exercitus circumuenit hostem. Est autem stratagema simplex, vel mixtum. Stratagema simplex est bonum, vel malum: mixtum est, vbi bono coniunctum est malum. Quod attinet ad stratagema bonum simpliciter, istud est species illius doli, qui appellatur bonus, & definitur solertia prudenter & ingeniosè decipiens. Dolo bono opponitur dolus malus, qui est machinatio ad alium cum iniquitate decipiendum. Hinc patet deceptionem esse licitam, vel illicitam. Ita videmus parentes sæpenumero decipere liberos, ipsorū bono. Huc pertinet, quod vulgo dicitur de piâ fraude.
units.tr: II. A stratagem is a cunning and well-timed deed. This is the general meaning of the word. More specifically, it is a cunning deed by which the commander of an army outwits the enemy. A stratagem is either simple or mixed. A simple stratagem is either good or bad; it is mixed when evil is joined to good. A stratagem that is simply good is a species of that deceit which is called good, and is defined as deceiving prudently and ingeniously by skill. Opposed to good deceit is bad deceit, which is a scheme to deceive another with wickedness. Hence it is clear that deception may be either lawful or unlawful. Thus we often see parents deceive their children for the children's own good. To this belongs what is commonly said about pious fraud.

units.la: III. Stratagema est ethicum, œconomicum, vel politicum. Aliàs dicitur sophisma ethicum, œconomicū & politicum: cui opponitur sophisma logicum. Stratagema ethicum est mixtum & non-liquidum: œconomicum & politicum est simplex, planum, & liquidum.
units.tr: III. A stratagem is ethical, economic or political. Otherwise it is called an ethical, economic or political sophism, to which a logical sophism is opposed. An ethical stratagem is mixed and not clear; an economic or political stratagem is simple, plain and clear.

units.la: IV. Stratagema ethicum est, quo res ita geritur, vt cum virtute ethicâ vel etiam verâ fide concurrat vitium. Nobile huius stratagematis exemplum est Gen. 27. v. 11. & seqq. Nam ibi Rebecca ex fide agit, quòd posthabito cõsilio mariti operam dedit, vt dominatus Iacobo diuinitus promissus in illum conferretur. tur. Sed in eo peccauit, quòd huc adhibuit mendacium. Similiter Iacob ex fide egit, quòd posthabitâ offensione patris ac fratris, operam dedit, vt benedictionem primogenito debitam consequeretur, atque ita dominus fratris ex Dei promisso constitueretur. Sed peccauit in eo, quòd & ipse mentitus est, & nomine Dei abusus, v.22. Rebecca debuisset Isaaco in memoriam revocare promissionem Dei, eumque hortari, ne quid contra illam ageret: simulq; Deum orare, vt animum illius flecteret ad locum dandū admonitionisuæ. Cur verò, inquiat aliquis, Deus consilium suū voluit exequi per huiusmodi stratagema, quod non caret peccato? Resp. Deus, qui finem constituerat, idem quoque modum multiplicem iustitiâ coniunctum habebat ad manum, vt finem consilij sui reuelationisque assequeretur. Sed placuit ipsi, peccatum Isaaci castigare peccato Rebeccæ & Iacobi. Nam Isaacus in eo peccauit, quòd posthabitâ voluntate Dei, ex affectu humano aliquid diuinæ voluntati contrarium molitus est. Sciebat enim, diuino oraculo Rebeccæ dato minorem suū filium maiori prælatum esse: & nihilominus tamen dominatum attribuere volebat maiori. Hanc infirmitate Isaaci Deus sine peccato castigauit peccato, id est, dolo & mendacio tum Rebeccæ, tum Iacobi. Huius quoque stratagematis exemplū est Gen.29. v.23. vbi Laban Iacobo tradit Leam pro Rahele, quam tamen ipsi promiserat: item Ios.9. vbi Gibeonitæ falsâ narratione verficul. 9. 10.12.13. obtinent à Iosuâ, vt in fœdus recipiantur. Frausista moderatis pœnis à Iosuâ est castigata, verfic. 21. & sequen. Etsi autem Gibeonitæ non recte fecerunt, quòd mentiti sunt: Iosua tamen recte fecit, quòd iusiurandum, religiose factum, religiose seruauit. v.18.19.20. Eiusdem naturæ est stratagema labefitarum 1.Sam.11.v.10. Mentiti enim sunt, cùm affirmarunt, quòd vellent se Ammonitis dedere, quod tamen in animo non habuerunt. Idem iudicium est de stratagemate Iudith, quod ipsum quoque fuit coniunctum mendacio. Iudith 10. verf.12. & seqq. item Ptolemæi Maccab. 16. verf. 15. Sed concludamus hoc de stratagemate ethico, eleganti allatâ regulâ: Dolus, qui vacat expresso mendacio, bonus est: cuiusmodi est dolus ille, qui constat simulatione facti, cuius exempla iam sequuntur.
units.tr: IV. A stratagem is ethical when the deed is done in such a way that a moral vice runs alongside an ethical virtue or even true faith. A noble example of this kind of stratagem is Gen. 27. v. 11. & seqq. For there Rebecca acts out of faith, in that, setting aside her husband's counsel, she takes pains that the dominion divinely promised to Jacob should be conferred upon him. But she sinned in this, that she used a lie. Likewise Jacob acted out of faith, in that, disregarding the offence to his father and brother, he took pains to obtain the blessing owed to the firstborn, and so that the lordship of his brother should be established by God's promise. But he sinned in this, that he too lied and abused the name of God, v. 22. Rebecca ought to have brought to Isaac's memory God's promise, and urged him not to act against it, and at the same time to pray God to bend his mind to give place to her admonition. But why, someone may ask, did God wish to carry out his counsel through a stratagem of this kind, which is not free of sin? Answer: God, who had set the end, also had at hand, joined with justice, many means by which to attain the end of his counsel and revelation. But it pleased him to punish Isaac's sin with the sin of Rebecca and Jacob. For Isaac sinned in that, setting aside the will of God, he devised, from human affection, something contrary to the divine will. For he knew, from the divine oracle given to Rebecca, that the younger son was to be preferred to the elder; and yet nevertheless he wished to grant the dominion to the elder. This weakness of Isaac God punished, without sin on his own part, by the sin, that is, by the deceit and lie, of both Rebecca and Jacob. An example of this stratagem is also Gen. 29. v. 23., where Laban gives Leah to Jacob in place of Rachel, whom he had promised him; likewise Josh. 9., where the Gibeonites, by a false story (vers. 9, 10, 12, 13), obtain from Joshua that they be received into covenant. The deceit was punished by Joshua with moderate penalties (vers. 21 and following). Although the Gibeonites did not act rightly in lying, Joshua nevertheless acted rightly in keeping religiously an oath made religiously (v. 18, 19, 20). Of the same nature is the stratagem of the men of Jabesh (1 Sam. 11. v. 10). For they lied when they affirmed that they would surrender to the Ammonites, which they did not intend in their hearts. The same judgment holds for the stratagem of Judith, which was also joined with a lie (Judith 10. vers. 12 and following), and likewise for that of Ptolemy (Maccab. 16. vers. 15). But let us conclude this about the ethical stratagem with a neat rule: A deceit that is free of an express lie is good. Such is that deceit which consists in feigning a deed, of which examples follow now.

units.la: V. Stratagema oeconomicum est, quod facit ad compendium rei familiaris, neq; coniunctum est cum aliquo vitio. Stratagema ethicū appellauimus mixtum, quia habet admixtū mendacium: item non-liquidum, quia primā fronte non liquet fraus & dolus malus. Aliter se habent stratagemata oeconomica & politica. Illa siquidem sunt simplicia & liquida, siue plana. Potest etiam dici stratagema ethicum esse mixtum, quia facto miscetur dictum falsum. Sed videamus exemplum stratagematis oeconomici. Longè pulcherrimum est artificium illud Iacobi Gen. 30. vbi legitur virgas versicolores subiecisse in aqualiculos, vbi cùm aquarentur pecudes, incalescebant, & incalescentes ad aspectum virgarum versicolorum, varios & versicolores edebant fœtus. Occurrit & aliud artificium, quòd fœtus versicolores ita seponebantur, ex contractu, à Iacobo, vt semper versarentur ante oculos gregis quem sibi seruabat: ac proinde ex vnicoloribus varii & versicolores fœtus itidem ederentur. Accessit & haec ars, quòd pecudes compactas & vegetas, cùm incalescerent, hoc modo Iacob informabat, cùm incalescerent, alias serotinas non item. Hic duplex incidit quaestio, vna facti, vtrum fieri hoc possit: altera iuris, vtrum iustè Iacob has artes occupauerit? Resp. ad 1. Fieri hoc posse, constat ex eo, quòd maxima vis est phantasiae in natura. Cùm verò ad naturā peculiaris Dei reuelatio accesserit, ideò amplius fieri potuit, ad Iacobi commodum dispesante prouidentiâ Dei. Resp. ad 2. Videtur Iacob secundum communem vsum à dolo malo excusari non posse, cùm arte eiusmodi interuerterit rei alienae commoda, eaqj in rem suam verterit. Verùm consilij huius author fuit Deus: & finis Iacobo non fuit propofitus, vt rem alienam interciperet, sed vt tantum perciperet, quantum suâ benedictione Deus esset largiturus: denique media adhibita non aduersantur naturæ, sed sunt ex naturâ: neque etiam aduersantur contractui bonæ fi-deiinter Labanem & Iacobum, quia Iacob bonâ fide Labani dixit, se ab ipso non petere quidquam, sed à Domino expectare, qui suâ dispensatione fit effecturus, vt ipsius iustitia attestetur ipsi: quâ vnicâ exceptione probatur bona fides Iacobi, quia totam actione subiecit voluntati Dei.
units.tr: V. An economic stratagem is one that serves the advantage of household affairs and is not joined with any vice. We called the ethical stratagem mixed, because a lie is mixed into it; and not clear, because at first sight it is not plain whether there is fraud or bad deceit. Economic and political stratagems are otherwise: they are simple and clear, or plain. One could also say that the ethical stratagem is mixed because a false statement is mingled with the deed. But let us look at an example of an economic stratagem. Far the most beautiful is that artifice of Jacob in Gen. 30., where we read that he set variegated rods into the watering troughs, and when the flocks were watered there, they grew hot, and growing hot at the sight of the variegated rods, they brought forth varied and variegated offspring. Another artifice also occurs: by agreement with Jacob, the variegated offspring were set apart so that they were always placed before the eyes of the flock he kept for himself; and accordingly, varied and variegated young would likewise be produced from single-coloured parents. To this was added the art by which Jacob managed the sturdy and vigorous animals, when they grew hot, in this way, and the late-bearing ones not likewise. Here a twofold question arises: one of fact, whether this can be done; the other of right, whether Jacob justly made use of these arts. Answer to the first: that it can be done is clear from the fact that the power of imagination in nature is very great. But since a particular revelation of God was added to nature, it could happen all the more, by the providential arrangement of God for Jacob's benefit. Answer to the second: Jacob, according to common usage, seems unable to be excused from bad deceit, since by an art of this kind he turned the advantages of another's property to his own use. But the author of this counsel was God; and the end proposed to Jacob was not to seize another's property, but only to receive as much as God would bestow by his blessing. Finally, the means used do not oppose nature but arise from nature; nor do they oppose the agreement of good faith between Laban and Jacob, since Jacob said in good faith to Laban that he asked nothing of him but awaited it from the Lord, who by his dispensation would bring it about that his justice should bear witness to him. By this single proviso Jacob's good faith is proved, because he subjected the whole action to the will of God.

units.la: Deus autem voluntate suâ ad iustè dispensandam mercedem Iacobo media imperauit, quæ Iacob bonâ fide secundum Deum est executus. Teneatur hic regula: Opus non est malum, quod ex consilio, fine, & mediis constat bonis.
units.tr: God, moreover, by his will commanded Jacob the means by which the reward was to be justly dispensed, and Jacob, in good faith, carried them out according to God. Let this rule hold here: A work is not evil if it consists of good counsel, end and means.

units.la: VI. Stratagema politicum est, quo hostis decipitur & vincitur ex insidiis.. Dehuiusmodi stratagematis eleganter scribit Augustinus quaest.10.super Iosuam: Cum iustum bellum suscipitur, vtrum aperte quis pugnet, an ex insidiis, nihil ad iustitiam interest. Tale fuit stratagema quod Deus mandauit populo Exod. 14. v. 2. & Iosuæ in expugnatione Aii. Iof. 8. Gibeonis Iudic. 7. v. 17. & seqq. item Israelitarum in expugnandâ Gibeâ. Iud. 20. itè Ehudi in obtruncando rege Eglon. Iud. 3. v. 16. & seqq. itè Iudæ Maccabæi 2. Maccab. 8. v. 7. & c. 14. v. 29, vbi stratagema Nicanoris fuit elusum stratagemate Iudæ Maccabæi: item sacerdotum Nanæ aduersus Antiochum. 2. Maccab. 1. v. 13. Sed concludamus hanc Stratagematographiam duabus hisce regulis. 1. A Deo petendum est vtrumq;[?] & veritas iuris, & commoditas facti. 2. Militia Christiana non infima pars est, stratagematis piis vincere diabolum, carnem, & mundum.
units.tr: VI. A political stratagem is one by which an enemy is deceived and overcome by ambushes. Augustine writes elegantly on this kind of stratagem, Quaest. 10 on Joshua: when a just war is undertaken, it makes no difference to justice whether one fights openly or from an ambush. Such was the stratagem that God commanded the people (Exod. 14. v. 2), and that Joshua used in the capture of Ai (Josh. 8); that of Gideon (Judg. 7. v. 17 and following); likewise that of the Israelites in the taking of Gibeah (Judg. 20); likewise that of Ehud in slaying King Eglon (Judg. 3. v. 16 and following); likewise that of Judas Maccabeus (2 Maccab. 8. v. 7, and c. 14. v. 29, where the stratagem of Nicanor was foiled by a stratagem of Judas Maccabeus); likewise that of the priests of Nanaea against Antiochus (2 Maccab. 1. v. 13). But let us conclude this sacred stratagematography with two rules: 1. From God must be sought both the truth of right and the convenience of fact. 2. The Christian warfare is no small part of this: by pious stratagems to conquer the devil, the flesh and the world.

units.la: PERORATIO TRIVM- PHI BIBLICI
units.tr: PERORATION OF THE THREE BIBLICAL TRIUMPHS

units.la: EAnt nunc delicati philosophiæ gentilis amatores an pertinaces admiratores, iidemque sacrorum Bibliorum profani contemptores, & dicant, nihil philosophiæ profundioris[?] in sacro isto codice occurrere. Profecto hæc nostra delineatio abunde satis erit ad illos convincendum, inque viam rectam reducendum. Quòd si lineamenta ista, quæ ego primus ita duxi, amplificentur, magis magisque patebit verum esse illud nobis familiare: NON EST LIBER NISI SCRIPTVRA SACRA. Quidem sententia hunc triumphum obsigno, Deum precatus, ut verbi sui lucem clementer in his turbis conservet, ad nominis sui gloriam, & animæ salutem, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, Amen.
units.tr: Let the fastidious lovers of gentile philosophy, or its stubborn admirers, and at the same time the profane despisers of the holy Bible, now go and say that nothing of deeper philosophy is to be found in this sacred book. Certainly this outline of mine will be more than enough to convince them and to lead them back onto the right path. But if these sketches, which I have been the first to draw in this way, are enlarged, it will become ever more plain that this truth, familiar to us, is so: THERE IS NO BOOK EXCEPT SACRED SCRIPTURE. With this statement I seal this triumph, praying God that He would mercifully preserve the light of His Word amid these disturbances, to the glory of His name and the salvation of souls, through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
